Title: Diagnosis of MRSA with neural networks and logistic regression approach
Population_Description: 504 patients culture-positive for S. aureus within the first 24 hours of admission to five Pittsburgh-area medical facilities (March 1996-March 1997); UPMC 17.6%, VAMC 17.8%, community teaching hospital 27.7%, two suburban non-teaching hospitals 36.9%
Data_Source_Other: Compiled patient information (demographics, clinical and bacteriologic data) from five Pittsburgh-area medical facilities - not an EHR or registry extraction
Top_Predictive_Features: Logistic regression marked eight variables significant at alpha = 0.10: age, decubiti (Decub), diabetes mellitus (Dm), hospital worker (Employ type #1), extended-care worker (Employ type #2), peritoneal dialysis, skin wound/lesion, vancomycin use (Vanco). No ranked importance for the NN (weights not interpretable)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Neural network (feed-forward backpropagation, 38 input / 15 hidden / 1 output neurons, BrainMaker): AUC 0.928 (SD 0.016), overall classification accuracy 89.83% in subsample 1; logistic regression (8 significant variables): AUC 0.869 (SD 0.019), MSSA cases correctly classified 75 (86.21%) to 80 (91.95%), MRSA cases 67.74% to 77.42%
Best_Performing_Model: Neural network (NN)
Accuracy_Population_Set: NN model, four-fold cross-validation subsample 1 (test set of 118 patients)
AUROC_Population_Set: NN model applied to the complete data set of 472 patients (six models built from two-of-four partitions, best chosen)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and evaluated only by four-fold cross-validation with stratified sampling on 472 patients from one metropolitan area; no external or prospective validation reported
Reported_Limitations: All data came from health-care facilities within Pittsburgh, PA and surrounding suburbs; the study may not have general applicability because the population under investigation is unique
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Authors warn that a flexible NN with many hidden-layer parameters carries substantial overfitting risk, and that the NN's inability to explain its output makes justification of results difficult; the motivation cites vancomycin overuse harms (toxicity, resistance, cost)
Reviewer_Notes: PDF text layer carries no table bodies for tables 4 and 5 (the robustness and AUC computation tables), so all per-model figures quoted here come from the narrative text
Unresolved_Items: Full per-subgroup accuracy ranges and the table 5 AUC computation are not readable from the text layer; whether table 3's hit/false-alarm rates belong to the NN is left for the team
Sample_Size: 472 cases analysed (504 patients enrolled; two-of-four partitions = 354 training / 118 test per fold)
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients culture-positive for S. aureus within the first 24 hours of admission to one of five Pittsburgh-area facilities, March 1996 to March 1997
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients transferred from an acute facility or nursing home excluded (community-acquired MRSA focus); records with conflicting inputs/opposing outputs eliminated; incomplete records handled with an 'unknown' column
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 472 cases (504 patients enrolled)
Missing_Data_Method: Missing categorical/symbolic data coded with an added 'unknown' column (1 = missing, 0 otherwise); records with unknown facts excluded when few; the one continuous variable (age) had no missing values
Geographic_Representativeness: One metropolitan area only: five facilities in and around Pittsburgh, PA - university hospital 17.6%, VA medical centre 17.8%, community teaching hospital 27.7%, two suburban non-teaching hospitals 36.9%; authors note limited general applicability
Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture sites recorded as inputs: urine, respiratory tract, blood, post-op wound, skin wound/lesion, feces, plus 'unknown' site
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus: binary outcome of MRSA (output 1) versus MSSA (output 0) among patients culture-positive for S. aureus on admission
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (penicillin, cephalosporins); glycopeptides (vancomycin); aminoglycosides; quinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Penicillin, vancomycin, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, quinolones (use within 2 weeks before admission)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary classification of patients: output value 1 = positive diagnosis (MRSA), 0 = negative diagnosis (MSSA), from laboratory-confirmed culture results
AI_Purpose: Compare a neural network with logistic regression for diagnosing community-acquired MRSA at admission, to support the decision to give vancomycin
Feature_Engineering: 38 input neurons from table 1: normalised age, sex, employment type (hospital / extended-care worker), admission route, seven culture sites plus 'unknown', diabetes, peritoneal and haemodialysis, IV drug use, seven immunosuppression causes plus 'unknown', wound types, indwelling devices, and five antibiotic classes used in the prior 2 weeks plus 'unknown'
Feature_Selection_Method: All 38 risk factors entered the NN; logistic regression retained 8 variables considered significant at alpha = 0.10
Num_Features_Selected: 8 (logistic regression); no reduction for the NN
Class_Imbalance_Method: Stratified random sampling within the four-fold cross-validation, so the proportion of MRSA in each subset is approximately the same
Hyperparameter_Method: Trial and error over 1-30 hidden neurons (15 chosen: lowest root mean square error); learning rate 0.9 found empirically optimal; training stopped when 95% of training facts were accurately predicted
Software_Libraries: BrainMaker (commercial neural-network package, California Scientific Software); SAS used for the AUC fitting method cited
Other_Metrics: AUC with standard deviations (0.016 NN, 0.019 LR); z-statistic 3.0013 with p = 0.001; overall classification accuracy and its variation range across subsamples; hit and false-alarm rates by cutoff point
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression, fitted on the same cross-validation partitions
Baseline_Performance: AUC 0.869 (SD 0.019); MSSA cases correctly classified 75 (86.21%) to 80 (91.95%), MRSA cases 67.74% to 77.42%
Internal_Validation: Four-fold cross-validation with stratified random sampling (k = 4)
Train_Test_Split: Three of four partitions (354 patients) for model building, the fourth (118 patients) for testing; every partition served as test data in turn
Overfitting_Method: Warning that a flexible NN with many parameters in the hidden layer risks substantial overfitting; hidden neurons limited to 15 selected by lowest root mean square error
Clinical_Insights: Eight variables were significant for community-acquired MRSA - age, decubiti, diabetes mellitus, hospital worker, extended-care worker, peritoneal dialysis, skin wound/lesion and vancomycin use - and LR coefficients can be read as odds ratios
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the study may not have general applicability because the population under investigation is unique to Pittsburgh; the model is argued to suit urban facilities with scarce resources
Maturity_Evidence: Four-fold cross-validation with stratified random sampling on 472 patients; no external or prospective validation reported
Integration_Point: Clinician completes a survey and runs the model before culture results are available, so no laboratory work is needed prior to prediction
End_User_Described: Physicians admitting patients to health care facilities (clinicians)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction before culture results return, so appropriate antibiotics can be prescribed sooner; earlier suspicion enables prompt isolation (cohorting or barrier precautions), cutting lag time and nosocomial spread; an MSSA result lets vancomycin and isolation be avoided
Stewardship_Details: No stewardship impact measured for the model; the paper quantifies overtreatment under a risk-factor-based vancomycin policy (61%, 190/313) and undertreatment of 6% (29/472) to motivate the prediction tool
Barriers_List: NN lacks explanation power and accountability, so results are hard to justify; NN is short of uniqueness and reproducibility; danger of substantial overfitting; requires a large number of training cases and performs well only on data resembling the training set
Facilitators_List: No laboratory work needed before prediction; the clinician simply fills out a survey and runs the model; most beneficial where medical resources are scarce; NN handles many variables and interactions
Future_Directions: Show how prediction models can be developed and used for clinical problems such as MRSA in a specific community; the same approach is proposed for intensive care and nursing-home admissions
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Logistic regression significance testing at alpha = 0.10 (no importance ranking reported for the neural network)
Feature_Interactions_Method: No formal interaction testing; the NN is described as possessing flexible nonlinear modelling capabilities and as able to handle complicated factor interactions
Limitation_Categories: Single geographic area (Pittsburgh, PA and suburbs) limiting general applicability; missing data (~10%) and conflicting records removed; NN overfitting risk; neither model exceeded 0.95 accuracy
Data_Quality_Concerns: About 10% of patient records were incomplete (symbolically or numerically); records with very similar inputs but opposing outputs were eliminated because NN and LR cannot handle conflicting facts; data shuffled to avoid order effects
Reporting_Clarity: Model architecture, training, cutoffs and validation are described in narrative detail; the numeric robustness and AUC computation tables (4 and 5) are not readable in the text layer
Page_References: pp. 1-11 (journal pp. 287-297); performance results pp. 6-8

Title: DeepAMR for predicting co-occurrent resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Country_Countries: United Kingdom (lead author institution); study isolates come from 16 countries across six continents
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
WHO_Region: AFR; AMR; EMR; EUR; SEAR; WPR
Funder_Names: Royal Academy of Engineering; EPSRC; Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; Wellcome Trust; NIHR; Royal Society
Population_Description: 8388 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with phenotypic DST for all four first-line anti-TB drugs (INH, EMB, RIF, PZA) - a subset of >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs; isolates from TB patients in 16 countries across six continents. Lineages: 3000 unknown, 2200 European, 1300 CentralAsian, 1200 EastAsian, fewer WestAfrica1, WestAfrica2 and Animal
Data_Source_Other: Multi-country research cohort of MTB isolates with whole-genome sequences and phenotypic DST (CRyPTIC consortium; sequencing described in Walker et al. 2015)
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by permutation feature importance (Figure 3). INH: katG S315T, fabG1 C-15T, fabG1 G-17T (top three); also lineage-related or uncharacterised hits inhA S94A, katG S315N, embC V981L, rpoB C-61T, fabG1 T-8A. EMB: rpoB S450L, embB M306I, embB M306V, embB Q497R. RIF: nine of the top 11 SNPs are known RIF determinants (incl. rpoB S450L, rpoB H445Y, rpoB H445C, rpoB D435Y). PZA: manB D152N, rpoB C-61T, embC R738Q
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
Best_Performing_Model: DeepAMR (end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder) - decided on AUROC, the best AUROC for all six outcomes (e.g. 98.7% for MDR-TB)
Sensitivity_Value: 96.3% (DeepAMR, MDR-TB - highest sensitivity value for DeepAMR)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
Specificity_Value: 96.7% (DeepAMR, PANS-TB - highest specificity value for DeepAMR in Table 1)
Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; PANS-TB outcome
F1_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
AUROC_Value: 98.7% (DeepAMR, MDR-TB - highest AUROC reported for DeepAMR)
AUROC_Population_Set: Hold-out test set: 30% of the 8388 MTB isolates, mean across 100 bootstrap experiments; MDR-TB outcome
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validation is internal only: a single cohort of 8388 isolates split into training, validation and testing sets, with multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation performed 100 times and average performance reported on the hold-out test data. No external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment is reported
Reported_Limitations: Uneven resistance co-occurrence between drugs and equal objective weighting per drug; second-line cross-resistance ignored (inaccurate phenotyping, over-fitting risk with few resistant isolates); dataset too small for optimal multi-class classification; class weights computed on the training set may differ in testing (increased covariance); sensitivity/specificity/AUROC may not be the best evaluation for multi-label learning; t-SNE clusters are parameter-sensitive and may be false findings; permutation feature importance assumes feature independence and can over-rank rare SNPs
Sample_Size: 8388 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with DST for all four first-line drugs (primary analysis dataset; subset of >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs)
Conflicts_of_Interest: none declared
Inclusion_Criteria: MTB isolates with complete phenotype for the four first-line drugs (n = 8388); isolates were selected from the >13 000 tested with up to 11 drugs because there were few strains with resistance co-occurrence for second-line drugs
Exclusion_Criteria: MTB isolates without complete phenotype for the four first-line drugs (analysis restricted to n = 8388); resistance co-occurrence of second-line drugs excluded from modelling
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: CRyPTIC consortium multi-country TB isolate cohort (no named database; sequencing described in Walker et al. 2015)
Dataset_Size: 8388 isolates in the primary analysis set; >13 000 isolates tested with up to 11 drugs in the wider dataset; 13 403 MTB strains in the phenotype overview
Missing_Data_Method: Nucleotide bases that could not be called with confidence denoted 'null calls' and excluded from the analysis; same pre-processing as Yang et al. (2017)
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates drawn from 16 countries across six continents via the CRyPTIC consortium; lineage composition reported (3000 unknown, 2200 European, 1300 CentralAsian, 1200 EastAsian, fewer WestAfrica1, WestAfrica2, Animal), so the sample is globally distributed but lineage-imbalanced
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the four first-line anti-TB drugs isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB), rifampicin (RIF) and pyrazinamide (PZA), plus multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB, resistant to at least INH and RIF) and pan-susceptible TB (PANS-TB); predicted from WGS mutations and compared with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide); second-line drugs referenced in context (fluoroquinolones, injectable second-line drugs)
Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), ethambutol (EMB), pyrazinamide (PZA); MDR/XDR definitions also name fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) and amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Per-drug resistant/susceptible label predicted from WGS mutations; MDR-TB determined by the joint predicted resistance for INH and RIF, PANS-TB by predicted susceptibility to all four first-line drugs; reference standard is the phenotypic DST
AI_Purpose: To develop DeepAMR, an end-to-end multi-task deep denoising auto-encoder that predicts resistance to four first-line anti-TB drugs simultaneously (capturing resistance co-occurrence and the latent lineage structure), and to benchmark it against a direct-association SNP baseline, random forest, SVM, MLKNN and ensemble classification chains
Feature_Engineering: Binary input vector per isolate: presence of a SNP variable coded 1, absence 0; every isolate represented by a 5919-dimension binary vector
Feature_Selection_Method: None for the primary analysis (whole feature set F1); a secondary feature set F2 removed all previously identified resistance SNPs; SNP ranking by permutation feature importance
Num_Features_Total: 5919 SNPs
Num_Features_Selected: 5919 (feature set F1, all SNPs); feature subset F2 removes the previously identified SNPs - F2 dimension not reported
Class_Imbalance_Method: Class weight for individual labels set to the ratio of resistant to susceptible isolates in the training set (SVM and RF)
Hyperparameter_Method: Internal cross-validation on the training set of every experiment for SVM, RF and MLKNN; ECC and DeepAMR hyperparameters chosen by minimising hamming loss and then fixed across all bootstrap experiments
Software_Libraries: Keras (augmented cluster layer referred to the GitHub project 'Keras_Deep_Clustering')
Other_Metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, F1 score and AUROC (mean and SD across 100 bootstrap samples); hamming loss used for hyperparameter selection; adjusted rand index used to choose the number of clusters; Wilcoxon signed-rank test P-values versus the DA baseline
Baseline_Method: Direct association (DA): any resistance determinant for a drug present in the Walker et al. (2015) catalogue labels the isolate resistant ('OR' rule); at least one determinant for both INH and RIF labels MDR-TB; no resistance determinants for the four first-line drugs labels PANS-TB
Baseline_Performance: DA: best sensitivity 94.9% (RIF) and 94.1% (PANS-TB), best F1 95.1% (RIF) and 94.8% (PANS-TB); much worse for PZA (sensitivity 47.9%, AUROC 73.0%)
Internal_Validation: Single cohort split into training, validation and testing sets; 30% hold-out test data; multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation repeated 100 times (100 bootstrap experiments) with average test performance reported
Train_Test_Split: 30% of data held out for testing in every experiment (70/30 split), average results over 100 bootstrap samples
CV_Folds: Number of folds not stated; multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation performed 100 times
Overfitting_Method: Unsupervised pre-training of the denoising auto-encoders then fine-tuning; batch normalisation and dropout layers used only in training to avoid over-fitting; training stopped when validation loss stopped improving after 5 epochs
Clinical_Insights: INH and RIF resistance determinants dominate sensitivity variation for INH and RIF classification; both RIF and EMB determinants matter for EMB classification; lineage-associated SNPs contribute most to PZA classification, with RIF, EMB and SM determinants also affecting it - consistent with PZA resistance depending on co-occurrence with RIF, EMB and SM
Generalisability_Details: Authors note the dataset is too small for optimal multi-class classification and that t-SNE visual clusters are strongly influenced by parameter choice and may be false findings; kernel t-SNE and UMAP are suggested as alternatives
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence setting the level: internal hold-out validation only - a single cohort (8388 isolates) split into training, validation and testing sets with 30% held out, multi-label iterative stratified cross-validation repeated 100 times and average test performance reported; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment evidence
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing anti-TB treatment: the stated motivation is to speed up prescribing the best drug to individual patients
Barriers_List: Second-line drug phenotyping too inaccurate and too few resistant isolates (over-fitting risk), so cross-resistance beyond first-line drugs was ignored; dataset too small for optimal multi-class classification; class weight computed on the training set may not hold in testing; sensitivity/specificity/AUROC may not be best for multi-label evaluation; t-SNE parameter sensitivity and no out-of-sample extension; permutation importance assumes feature independence
Facilitators_List: End-to-end integration of non-linear dimensionality reduction and multi-label learning, so high-level data abstraction and classification are learned jointly; large multi-country cohort (8388 isolates, 16 countries); source code shared; unsupervised pre-training with fine-tuning
Future_Directions: Kernel t-SNE as a parametric extension giving explicit out-of-sample extension, and UMAP as a faster alternative that preserves more global structure; better SNP ranking by learning variable importance within the model rather than permutation importance
Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (genomic mutation features and WGS/DST laboratory measurements; no clinical, demographic, pharmacological, behavioural, environmental or temporal predictors)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation feature importance: the unscaled sensitivity reduction after randomly permuting one feature column at a time
Novel_Predictors_Details: inhA S94A and fabG1 T-8A are stated to be previously uncharacterized; other top-ranked SNPs are lineage-related (embC V981L, rpoB C-61T associated with the Central Asian sub-lineage, embC T270I) or belong to other drugs' resistance (rpoB S450L for RIF, rpsL K43R for streptomycin, embB G406S for EMB)
Limitation_Categories: Data: uneven resistance co-occurrence, small dataset, second-line drugs excluded. Modelling: equal objective weighting per drug, class-weight shift between training and testing, sensitivity/specificity/AUROC suboptimal for multi-label evaluation, permutation importance assumes independence and over-ranks rare SNPs, t-SNE parameter sensitivity and limitations, possible phenotype/DST errors
Data_Quality_Concerns: Phenotype errors on the four first-line drugs may mislead classification; class weight computed on the training set may differ in the testing set (increased covariance); inaccurate second-line drug phenotyping; rare SNPs ranked highly by permutation importance despite negligible sensitivity effect
Reporting_Clarity: Model development is well described (architecture, objectives, pre-training, thresholds, hyperparameter strategy), with detail deferred to Supplements C and G; however several items are absent (hardware, programming language, dataset identifiers, external validation, data availability) and Table 1's numbers are severely mangled in the pypdf text layer, making metric extraction error-prone
Page_References: Article pp. 3240-3249 (text layer pp. 1-10); abstract p. 1; methods pp. 2-4; Table 1 and its note p. 3; results pp. 5-7; discussion and limitations pp. 7-8; references pp. 8-10

Title: Using Natural Language Processing to Improve Accuracy of Automated Notifiable Disease Reporting
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: HL7 laboratory result messages containing the keywords 'MRSA', 'methicillin' or 'Aureus' from the Indiana Network for Patient Care (INPC): test set 232,776 messages from 131 data sources covering 53,338 unique patients; 64,554 messages (categories 1 and 2) interpreted, from 41 sources and 19,034 unique patients; training set 3,957 messages from 25 sources
All_Models_Evaluated: REX (Regenstrief EXtraction tool, rule-based NLP) - sensitivity 99.96%, specificity 99.71%, PPV 99.81%, F-measure 0.9989 on 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages; existing operational automated ELR notifiable condition processor with limited NLP - interpreted only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages as positive
Best_Performing_Model: REX (Regenstrief EXtraction tool) - highest sensitivity/specificity/PPV/F-measure versus the existing ELR processor
Sensitivity_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
Specificity_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 64,554 category 1 and 2 messages from the test set (January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008), reviewed against the gold standard
F1_Population_Set: test data (64,554 category 1 and 2 messages)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: REX's rules and knowledge base were adapted on a December 2007 training set and then applied to a separate one-year test set (232,776 messages) with physician manual review as the gold standard; the paper reports no prospective or external multicentre validation of this MRSA module
Reported_Limitations: Developer of the software also acted as the gold standard and evaluator of the data extraction process; negation detection more difficult in these messages; many free-text results disregarded grammatical rules (incomplete sentences, spelling errors, poor punctuation); substantial variation in laboratories' use of the HL7 standard; ambiguous reports
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: 74 false positives (73 caused by improper sentence detection, e.g. 'MRSA DNA....NEGATIVE') and 17 false negatives (a spelling error and 'rule out MRSA' phrasing); false positives add to public health's burden to cull spurious results
Sample_Size: 64,554 HL7 messages interpreted (categories 1 and 2) from 19,034 unique patients; test set 232,776 messages from 53,338 unique patients; training set 3,957 messages
Inclusion_Criteria: All INPC laboratory HL7 messages containing the keywords 'methicillin', 'MRSA' or 'Aureus': training set December 2007 (3,957 messages from 25 unique message sources); test set January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008 inclusive (232,776 messages from 131 data sources, 53,338 unique patients)
Exclusion_Criteria: Category 4 messages excluded using business rules: not originating from a known source of laboratory results messages; containing no result (HL7 OBX or NTE) segment; result pending according to the OBX-11 component. Non-laboratory reports (e.g. discharge summaries) and pending results were also excluded; only final results processed
Data_Types_Used: Free text / clinical notes
Data_Source_Name: Indiana Network of Patient Care (INPC)
Dataset_Size: 232,776 HL7 messages containing MRSA keywords over 12 months (test set); 64,554 interpreted; training set 3,957 messages
Geographic_Representativeness: Single regional health information exchange in Indiana, USA (INPC); 41 laboratory sources within that HIE; 232,776 messages from 131 data sources overall
Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture results (approximately 97% of the tests); blood culture result messages used for the comparison with the existing ELR system
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) positive laboratory reports for notifiable disease reporting
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); similar phrasing from Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus Epidermidis and Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Hominis caused potential false positives
Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin (the 'methicillin' keyword defines MRSA); clindamycin named only inside an example report phrase
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary message-level classification: category 1 = MRSA positive, category 2 = MRSA keyword present but negated; the final positive or negative determination was made by the physician reviewer and became the gold standard
AI_Purpose: To test whether a rule-based NLP system (REX) improves the accuracy and completeness of automated electronic laboratory reporting of notifiable conditions, using MRSA in unstructured free-text culture reports as the test case
Feature_Engineering: Keyword concepts ('methicillin', 'MRSA', 'Aureus') detected with regular expressions, plus a window of words before and after the keyword to determine context (negated, ambiguous, historical); false-negation pattern database; patterns added to handle variation in HL7 OBX-3, OBX-5 and NTE reporting formats
Feature_Selection_Method: Literature search plus training-set frequency analysis to identify frequently occurring words and phrases that express MRSA infection
Hyperparameter_Method: Iterative testing-analysis-modification cycle: after initially modifying the software and knowledge base, reports were processed to find false positive and false negative errors and subsequent adjustments were made to REX
Other_Metrics: F-measure 0.9989 for the test data; false positives 74 and false negatives 17 (Table 1: REX/manual review positives 39,491 vs 74, negatives 17 vs 24,972); reporting-rate comparison: existing ELR processor identified only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages
Baseline_Method: Existing operational automated ELR notifiable condition processor with limited NLP capability (longest common string comparator and basic negation detection)
Baseline_Performance: Identified only 166 (36.56%) of 454 true-positive blood culture messages as positive
Internal_Validation: Rules adapted on the December 2007 training set, then applied to a separate one-year test set; REX output compared with physician manual review as the gold standard
Train_Test_Split: Training set December 2007 (3,957 messages from 25 sources); test set January 25, 2007 to January 25, 2008 (232,776 messages from 131 data sources, 53,338 unique patients)
Clinical_Insights: Errors traced to sentence delimitation and negation context: a full stop before 'NEGATIVE' caused 73 false positives, and 'rule out MRSA' placed close to a positive MRSA phrase caused 16 false negatives
Maturity_Evidence: REX was adapted on a December 2007 training set and evaluated on a separate one-year test set against physician manual review (internal validation); the paper states REX is currently used to augment notifiable disease reporting to the ISDH but reports no prospective or external validation of this MRSA module
Integration_Point: HL7 message flow of the Indiana Network for Patient Care / automated ELR pipeline feeding the notifiable condition processor that transmits category 1 (positive) messages to public health
End_User_Described: Public health agencies (Indiana State Department of Health) receiving automated notifiable disease reports
Clinical_Workflow_Details: ELR system identifies potentially reportable candidate tests by LOINC codes and transmits positive results to public health; microbiology culture results arrive as unstructured free text; REX classifies HL7 messages into four categories and only category 1 (positive) messages are transmitted for public health reporting
Barriers_List: Free-text results with poor punctuation, spelling errors and incomplete sentences; substantial variation in how laboratories use the HL7 standard; look-alike organism names (S. epidermidis, S. hominis); ambiguous reports; sentence-level processing limits
Facilitators_List: Conforming HL7 laboratory messages to the HITSP standard (results in OBX-5, one result per segment, abnormal flags in OBX-8), including LOINC codes for test names and SNOMED-CT codes for results, which would reduce variation and improve detection accuracy
Future_Directions: Add other conditions (e.g. Shigella, Salmonella) to REX's database; move healthcare towards national HIT standardisation of HL7 message content
Limitation_Categories: Developer/evaluator overlap (software developer acted as gold standard and evaluator); negation and sentence detection errors in free text; HL7 format variation across laboratories; poor punctuation, spelling errors and incomplete sentences; ambiguous reports
Data_Quality_Concerns: Incomplete sentences, spelling errors and lack of proper punctuation in free-text results; substantial variation in laboratories' use of the HL7 standard; look-alike organism names; ambiguous reports
Reporting_Clarity: Clear reporting of the NLP design, dataset sizes, metrics and error analysis (Table 1 gives the full confusion matrix); no DOI, PMID, funding or conflict-of-interest statement is printed in the text layer

Title: Prediction of aminoglycoside response against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection in burn patients by artificial neural network modeling
Population_Description: 25 burn patients with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection hospitalized in the intensive care unit who received arbekacin (ABK)
Top_Predictive_Features: Peak plasma ABK level; serum creatinine level; duration of ABK administration; blood sugar level; burn area except area of skin graft (burn severity). Method: forward stepwise multiple regression for linear parameters + ANN best fit (lowest SS/AIC) for burn-severity covariate.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: ANN (rate of correct prediction RCP 100% modeling, 88% leave-one-out) vs logistic regression (RCP 72% modeling, 60% LOO); ANN hidden-layer neuron count 2-7 evaluated by SS/AIC
Best_Performing_Model: Artificial neural network (ANN) modeling
Accuracy_Population_Set: ANN modeling, discrimination analysis of 25 burn patients
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evidence supports internal validation only: leave-one-out cross-validation on the same 25-patient dataset; no external or prospective validation
Reported_Limitations: Small sample size (25 patients), limited PK/PD parameters; model not yet validated for practical clinical use
Inclusion_Criteria: Burn patients who received ABK against MRSA infection
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Missing_Data_Method: MIC value set to 1 mg/mL when not obtained from medical records (approximate MIC 1 mg/mL)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single Japanese tertiary hospital (Nippon Medical University Hospital)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Response of arbekacin (ABK) against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection in burn patients
Pathogens: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycoside
Specific_Antibiotics: arbekacin (ABK)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Response evaluated by changes in three clinical criteria: number of bacteria, white blood cell count, and C-reactive protein level (excellent/very good/good/poor)
AI_Purpose: To predict the ABK response against MRSA infection in burn patients considering burn severity, comparing ANN with logistic regression
Feature_Selection_Method: Forward stepwise multiple regression analysis (basic linear parameters); addition of one burn-severity covariate optimised in ANN by best fit (SS/AIC)
Hyperparameter_Method: Number of neurons in hidden layer varied (2-7) and selected by best fit (lowest SS/AIC)

Title: Identification of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus within the Nation’s Veterans Affairs Medical Centers using natural language processing

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: VA Informatics and Computing Infrastructure (VINCI) (VA HSR HIR 08-204); Consortium for Healthcare Informatics Research (CHIR) (VA HSR HIR 08-374); Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Prevention Epicenters Program (5U01CI000334, 07FED706504)
Population_Description: Nationwide patient-level, free-text microbiology reports from all VA VistA systems, 1990-2009: 33,024,796 unique records from 128 VistA sites representing 152 currently active acute care hospitals (170 total over the period); reference comparisons used data from eleven VA sites, VISN 4 (ten hospitals) and VA Salt Lake City
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Surveillance analyst / public health; Researcher

Training set: S. aureus sensitivity 99.6%, specificity 99.9%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 99.6%; methicillin resistance sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 99.9%, PPV 99.7%, NPV 99.9%. Validation set vs 5,927 electronic records: S. aureus 100%/99.9%/99.9%/100%; methicillin resistance 100%/99.9%/99.9%/100%. Validation set vs 3,092 expert-reviewed records: S. aureus 98.3%/99.7%/99.6%/98.6%; methicillin resistance 99.2%/99.4%/97.9%/99.8%. Separate MRSA-surveillance-screen string-searching algorithm: sensitivity 99.4%, specificity 97.9%.
Best_Performing_Model: Rule-based NLP information extraction system (Apache UIMA pipeline) - the only system developed and evaluated; no model comparison was performed, so there is no higher-scoring alternative
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 98.3% (S. aureus) and 99.2% (methicillin resistance)
Specificity_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 99.7% (S. aureus) and 99.4% (methicillin resistance)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Validation set - S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference compared with electronic (data warehouse) records; expert-reviewed comparison gave 99.6% (S. aureus) and 97.9% (methicillin resistance)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Training and test sets were created by randomly splitting the expert-annotated sample rather than separating sites or time periods; independently derived electronic data and expert annotation served as comparison standards rather than as separate external validation cohorts, and no prospective or site-level accuracy validation is reported.
Reported_Limitations: No valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; a random sample from more facilities would have improved the completeness analysis but was logistically infeasible; per-site samples were small so no VA site-specific accuracy estimates could be reported; completeness cannot be confirmed for unsampled VA sites.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Systematic biases can be introduced when data are derived from or processed electronically; microbiology data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA, and report-format variation across sites and years could affect extraction.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; accuracy could not be reported by VA site, so variation in performance across facilities or patient groups is unaddressed.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No governance risk raised; the study used existing VA microbiology records with approval from the VA Salt Lake City Health Care System Research Review Committee and the University of Utah Institutional Review Board.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-country (USA) national VA retrospective data-validation study of one rule-based NLP information extraction system. No model comparison: the NLP pipeline is the only system evaluated, so it is the unit of analysis for the metric fields. Absence-required Yes/No fields answered 'No'/'NR' where the text layer reports no such item; quotes given are the metrics/assessment sentences that demonstrate the absence. Not a predictive model, so predictor/feature-importance fields follow the system's rule inputs (text, organism, susceptibility, metadata terms).
Unresolved_Items: The paper reports accuracy against two reference sets (independently derived electronic data and expert-reviewed annotation) and at two levels (S. aureus identification and methicillin-resistance inference); it does not state which is primary, and the values differ. Whether the multi-site, multi-year VA comparison constitutes external validation is also a judgement call.

Drug_Classes: Antimicrobials recorded in susceptibility testing: penicillinase-resistant penicillins (oxacillin, nafcillin, methicillin) and cephalosporins (cefoxitin, cefazolin, cephalothin), plus mecA / penicillin binding protein 2A testing
Specific_Antibiotics: oxacillin; cefoxitin; cefazolin; cephalothin; nafcillin; methicillin (resistance); penicillin binding protein 2A / mecA
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA

AI_Purpose: Apply NLP information extraction to nationwide VA free-text microbiology reports to extract organisms and antibiotic susceptibilities and infer MRSA, then validate the extraction against independently derived electronic data and expert annotation

Facilitators_List: Reuse of existing, reliable VA data processes (RPCs and VistaWeb) that require no independent maintenance and can run as a background process; semi-structured report templates that support rule-based extraction; expert annotation and clinical expert involvement; availability of independent reference data sets
Future_Directions: Contribute the dataset and methods to a comprehensive infectious disease surveillance system; validate routine data warehouse pulls for completeness and concordance; extend the NLP methods to other organisms; combine data across non-VA health systems
Limitation_Categories: Reference standard and data access: no valid reference standard exists; limited accessible electronic data for comparison; only a sample of facilities could be studied; no VA site-specific accuracy estimates; small per-site samples; report-format variation across sites and over time
Data_Quality_Concerns: MUMPS has only one data type so there are no data type checks; data may be systematically or sporadically entered in the wrong place in VistA; microbiology report formats changed over the years and varied between centres; sequence gaps in accession numbers at about half the sites examined
Page_References: Journal pages 1-8 (PDF pages 1-8)

Title: Epidemiology and prediction of multidrug-resistant bacteria based on hospital level
Funder_Names: China Postdoctoral Science Foundation (No. 2021M693593); GuangDong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (No. 2021A1515111146)
Population_Description: Patients with bacterial infection detected at a large teaching hospital (the Eighth Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Shenzhen, China) between October 2010 and October 2020; only the first result of multiple tests in the same patient was included
Data_Source_Other: Monthly hospital reports (39 hospital-level indicators: hospital operation volume, nosocomial infection, antibacterial drug use, outdoor temperature, incidence of nosocomial infections)
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by random forest IncNodePurity: (1) number of hospital operations; (2) number of type I incision operations; (3) number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues; (4) number of discharged patients; (5) average hospital stay (days); (6) average rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions; (7) rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Programme manager / policymaker
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) model for variable-importance ranking (IncNodePurity) - no performance metric reported; regression tree (rpart/CART) prediction model with thresholds (hospitalised emergency rescues 314; hospital operations 1333; clinical pathway rate 9.3) and estimated case counts (about 14 vs as high as 77) - no accuracy, AUC or error metric reported
Best_Performing_Model: Regression tree (rpart/CART) - the model the paper uses to establish the prediction (early-warning) model for the number of patients with MDRB infection; no comparative performance metric is reported for it against the random forest
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The regression tree was fitted to the whole 10-year single-hospital dataset to derive thresholds; no internal validation (cross-validation or train/test split), external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment is reported
Reported_Limitations: Data came from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so the machine learning model could only produce monthly rather than weekly or daily estimates for real-time prediction; the ecological research design cannot demonstrate causality; the model was built on one hospital, so indicator thresholds may not be generalisable to other hospitals owing to differences in hospital volume
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Not discussed; the paper reports only age and sex distributions of infected patients (Supplementary Fig. S1) and performs no equity or fairness analysis
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Ethics approval is stated as not applicable; no other ethical or governance issues are discussed
Sample_Size: Monthly hospital-level data for October 2010 to October 2020 (39 indicators per month); the number of patients or isolates is not reported in the text
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients detected with bacterial infection by the hospital laboratory information system between October 2010 and October 2020; only the first result of multiple tests in the same patient was included
Exclusion_Criteria: Not otherwise specified; only the first results of multiple tests in the same patient were included
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: The Eighth Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University laboratory information system (LIS); monthly hospital reports
Dataset_Size: Monthly database of 39 hospital-level variables from October 2010 to October 2020
Geographic_Representativeness: One large teaching hospital in the central urban area of Shenzhen, a megacity in southern China with a permanent resident population of 13.43 million
Primary_AMR_Outcome: The number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) infection per month (variable c4) at hospital level, modelled from 39 hospital-level indicator variables; five MDRB categories analysed: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli), Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), Klebsiella Pneumonia (K. pneumoniae), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Haemophilus influenzae; the five MDRB analysed are ESBL-producing E. coli, MRSA, ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa
Num_Pathogens: 7 named species (E. coli, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, N. gonorrhoeae, A. baumannii, H. influenzae); five MDRB categories analysed in detail
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa); beta-lactams (ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae); methicillin (MRSA)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRB infection is counted as the number of patients with multidrug-resistant bacteria infection (dependent variable c4), predicted from 39 hospital-level predictor variables using real-world monthly data
AI_Purpose: Use a random forest model and cross-correlation analysis to explore hospital-level factors affecting MDRB infections and their predictive power, and build a regression tree model to predict the number of hospitalised patients with MDRB infection in order to build an early-warning platform for drug resistance
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (random forest for variable importance; regression tree/CART for prediction); no head-to-head performance metric is reported
Feature_Engineering: 39 factors collected in five groups (hospital operation volume x1-x15, nosocomial infection g1-g8, antibacterial drug use y1-y10, outdoor temperature, incidence of nosocomial infections c1-c3); all variables organised on a monthly basis to build a database; average daily, daily maximum and daily minimum temperature used to adjust for seasonal influence
Feature_Selection_Method: Random forest multivariate importance using increases in node purity (IncNodePurity), with the loss function selected through the best segmentation; the highest-ranked variables were carried into cross-correlation and regression tree analysis
Num_Features_Total: 39 independent variables
Num_Features_Selected: Not stated numerically; the highest-importance variables were selected for cross-correlation and regression tree analysis (number of hospital operations, number of type I incision operations, number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, number of discharged patients, average hospital stay, rate of unreasonable outpatient and emergency prescriptions, rate of antibiotics use in discharged patients)
Software_Libraries: pheatmap, randomForest, rpart, rpart.plot, ggplot2 (R version 4.0.3); IBM SPSS version 25.0 for cross-correlation
Other_Metrics: Regression tree thresholds and predicted case counts: emergency rescues <314, hospital operations <1333 and clinical pathway rate >9.3 give an estimated 14 MDRB patients in the hospital in the current month; emergency rescues >314 gives an estimate as high as 77
Overfitting_Method: Random forest selected partly because it prevents overfitting; no cross-validation or train/test split is reported
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Surgical, emergency and hospitalised rescue patients showed the highest risk of MDRB infection; more rational perioperative antibiotic use and a higher clinical pathway rate are linked to fewer patients with MDRB infection, while excessive surgical volume and inappropriate antibiotic use in emergency patients may increase MDRB numbers
Generalisability_Details: The model was built on data from one hospital, so the threshold values of the indicators may not be generalisable to other hospitals because of differences in hospital volume
Maturity_Evidence: Model developed on 10 years of monthly hospital-level data from a single hospital; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
Integration_Point: Hospital-level monthly drug-resistance early-warning platform; not integrated into clinical or laboratory systems
End_User_Described: Not explicitly described; the model is intended for hospital-level monitoring and early warning of MDRB infection
Barriers_List: Monthly (not weekly or daily) resolution of the data limits real-time prediction; the ecological design cannot demonstrate causality; the single-hospital model means indicator thresholds may not transfer to hospitals of a different volume
Future_Directions: Improving the accuracy of the data without changing the methods, and wider validation of indicator thresholds across hospitals with different volumes
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 groups of variables / 39 variables in total
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest IncNodePurity (increases in node purity) plus multivariate importance by removing predictor variables from each single tree in the forest
Novel_Predictors_Details: Hospital-management indicators highlighted as influential, including the number of hospitalised patients who received emergency rescues, the rate of rational perioperative antimicrobial drug use in type I and II incision operations, and the rate of clinical pathways

Data_Quality_Concerns: Data collected from monthly hospital reports over 10 years, so only monthly estimates could be produced

Title: Moving from predicting hospital deaths by antibiotic-resistant bloodstream bacteremia toward actionable risk reduction using machine learning on electronic health records

Expert-chosen input set - LASSO 0.778, decision tree 0.684, decision tree depth=6 0.686, random forest 0.761, boosted logistic regression 0.801 (best; sensitivity 0.750, specificity 0.740; ICU 0.726/0.689/0.684), support vector machine 0.623. Specificity_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)
AUROC_Population_Set: All patients (N=1,389); 30-day mortality=15.8% (189/1,389)

Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: UF Health adult patients (18+ years) admitted at inpatient or outpatient clinics with BSI diagnosis (ICD-9 790.7, 995.91, 995.92, 038.xx); at least two years of medical history; antibiogram result within 7 days of BSI-KP diagnosis
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: University of Florida (UF) Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
Dataset_Size: 1,398 patients in the study population (1,271 inpatient / 118 outpatient); model analysis set n=1,389; 266 distinct diagnostic codes above the set frequency

Geographic_Representativeness: Single health system in Florida; no data outside Florida; external validation emulated on clinics in one zip code area (322, Duval County, Jacksonville)
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood; urine

Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP); other members of the Enterobacteriaceae family
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides; Betalactams; Carbapenems; Fluoroquinolones; Sulfonamides
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin; Carbapenem; Cefazolin; Ceftriaxone; Piperacillin; Amikacin; Tobramycin; Trimethoprim; Ceftazidime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Antibiotic resistance and multi-drug resistance (MDR) prevalence estimated from the antibiogram test performed before or upon BSI-KP diagnosis, stratified by Klebsiella species and other organisms
AI_Purpose: Develop a machine learning prediction model of BSI-KP 30-day mortality from EHR data for general wards and the ICU, to improve on the qPitt score and support clinical decision-making
Num_Models_Compared: 7 (qPitt score baseline plus 6 machine learning models: LASSO, decision tree, decision tree depth=6, random forest, boosted logistic regression, support vector machine)

Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.631 in the whole study population, 0.589 in the ICU stays
Internal_Validation: Out-of-bag bootstrapping (25 samples)
Train_Test_Split: Emulated external validation: 19.4% of data points (269/1,389) held out by clinic zip code area (322)
CV_Folds: 25 out-of-bag bootstrap samples (no k-fold cross-validation reported)

Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Decision rules / surrogate tree; Intrinsically interpretable model

Title: PhageLeads: Rapid Assessment of Phage Therapeutic Suitability Using an Ensemble Machine Learning Approach
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Ministry of Higher Education of Malaysia (Program Konsortium Kecemerlangan Penyelidikan)
Population_Description: Phage protein sequences from NCBI RefSeq: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes for training (from 8368 phage GenBank files, 772,938 CDS); 45,231 protein sequences from 63 phage genomes (dated after March 2018) for validation; 423 phages (240 temperate, 183 lytic) in the lifestyle dataset. No human/patient subjects.
Data_Source_Other: NCBI RefSeq public database (phage complete genomes in GenBank format)
Top_Predictive_Features: Reduced tripeptide frequencies (50.32% of total features), dipeptide frequencies (33.54%), reduced dipeptide frequencies (9.58%), generic protein features (6.56%). Ranking by feature importance calculated from the XGBoost module.
All_Models_Evaluated: Five temperate-marker XGBoost predictors within the PhageLeads ensemble — validation MCC (accuracy, F1): integrase 0.92 (0.99, 0.92), Cro/CI 0.71 (0.99, 0.71), immunity repressor 0.87 (0.99, 0.86), ParA 0.76 (0.99, 0.75), antirepressor 0.92 (0.99, 0.92). Integrated lifestyle classification on the 423-phage lifestyle dataset: MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1-score 0.95 (16 mispredictions: 7 FP, 9 FN). Baseline BACPHLIP: 7 erroneous predictions on the same dataset. Random 10-fold CV MCCs: integrase 0.97, Cro/CI 0.91, immunity 0.96, ParA 0.90, antirepressor 0.94; clustered CV: 0.81, 0.16, 0.58, 0.44, 0.64 respectively.
Best_Performing_Model: PhageLeads ensemble lifestyle classification (XGBoost temperate-marker predictors) — highest on the review's primary metric (MCC): 0.92 on the phage lifestyle dataset (accuracy 0.96, F1-score 0.95)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Phage lifestyle dataset (423 phages: 240 temperate, 183 lytic), compiled by Mavrich and Hatfull
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation via 10-fold cross-validation plus validation on an independent external dataset (423-phage lifestyle dataset compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull, not used in training): MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. This independent external validation supports level 3.
Reported_Limitations: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases (some Cro/CI annotated as 'transcriptional regulators' or 'repressor', integrases as 'DNA-binding protein'/'recombinase', ParA as 'Chromosome partitioning protein'), some protein classes removed due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable and may bias models (hence no lifestyle info used in training); clustered 10-fold CV revealed low conservation for ParA (0.44) and Cro/CI (0.16) markers.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Lytic phages found to carry AMR or virulence genes are unsuitable for therapeutic use: five of 183 lytic phages encoded virulence proteins (increased serum survival proteins ISS, Type III secretion system effectors, Cytolethal distending toxins, Shiga toxins, NleG effectors), one encoded both chloramphenicol resistance (CatA1) and ISS, posing risk of adverse effects / gene transduction into host genomes.
Reviewer_Notes: Phage genomics/bioinformatics study developing the PhageLeads ensemble XGBoost tool to predict phage temperate markers and screen for AMR/virulence genes (via ABRicate) for therapeutic phage selection. Best model = PhageLeads lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) validated on the external 423-phage lifestyle dataset. No patient/clinical data; AMR aspect is detection of AMR/virulence genes in phage genomes. Data from NCBI RefSeq (training 188,080 proteins/7686 genomes; validation 45,231 proteins/63 genomes). Web-deployed (www.phageleads.dk).
Unresolved_Items: Best_Performing_Model unit: the paper's best model on its primary (training) dataset would be the individual temperate-marker predictors (integrase/antirepressor MCC 0.92), but the paper's headline application and its reported lifestyle accuracy are for the integrated ensemble lifestyle classifier; I coded the ensemble lifestyle classification (MCC 0.92, acc 0.96, F1 0.95) as the best-performing model. Clinical_Maturity_Level 3 rests on the independent external lifestyle dataset.
Sample_Size: Training dataset: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes (genomes, not patients)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared — 'The authors declare that there are no conﬂicts of interest.'
Exclusion_Criteria: Data-level exclusions: proteins <30 amino acids removed; hypothetical proteins and proteins with unclear annotations removed; ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) removed from respective datasets.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: NCBI RefSeq (phage complete genomes)
Dataset_Size: Training: 188,080 protein sequences from 7686 phage genomes; Validation: 45,231 protein sequences from 63 phage genomes; Lifestyle dataset: 423 phages
Geographic_Representativeness: Global public repository data: 8368 phage genomes from 17 families used to train PhageLeads; no geographic framing reported.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes and virulence genes in therapeutic phage genomes, detected via the ABRicate tool; and classification of phage lifestyle (temperate vs lytic) based on predicted presence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor).
Pathogens: None as study target — the subjects are bacteriophages (therapeutic phage candidates); no specific bacterial pathogen is the outcome organism
Drug_Classes: Phenicols (chloramphenicol resistance gene detected)
Specific_Antibiotics: Chloramphenicol (resistance gene CatA1, chloramphenicol O-acetyltransferase, detected in Stx2 converting phage vB_EcoP_24B)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Presence/absence of AMR genes (detected by ABRicate comparing predicted ORFs against NCBI, CARD, ARG-ANNOT, Resfinder, MEGARES, EcOH, PlasmidFinder, Ecoli_VF and VFDB databases) and presence/absence of temperate markers (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) — gene-presence labels, not clinical MIC/phenotype thresholds.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To develop an online single-step tool (PhageLeads) using an ensemble of extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) predictors to determine the presence of temperate markers in phage candidates and, with ABRicate, screen for AMR and virulence genes, in order to rapidly select safe therapeutic phages.
Num_Models_Compared: 5 temperate-marker predictors within the PhageLeads ensemble (integrase, Cro/CI, immunity repressor, ParA, antirepressor) plus the integrated lifestyle classification, compared against baseline BACPHLIP
Feature_Engineering: 1576 protein features extracted from protein sequences using custom scripts (per [26]): 400 dipeptide frequency, 100 reduced amino acid dipeptide frequency, 1000 reduced amino acid tripeptide frequency, 34 PROSITE domain features, and 42 generic protein features from the BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis module.
Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative feature reduction: for each round the 50 least-contributing features were removed until the minimal number was reached; final features selected based on Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) scores from testing each model on the test dataset. Overall selection driven by feature importance computed by the XGBoost module.
Num_Features_Selected: 626 unique features used for the final predictors (171 integrase, 90 Cro/CI, 59 immunity repressor, 18 ParA, 71 antirepressor; 1576 reduced per predictor to 350, 251, 142, 74, 201 respectively)
Class_Imbalance_Method: XGBoost 'scale positive weight' parameter (set = number of negative data / number of positive data) to compensate for unbalanced classes
Hyperparameter_Method: Prediction threshold tuning: iterating through incremental threshold values and selecting the threshold with the highest MCC on the training dataset (e.g. 0.252 integrase, 0.363 Cro/CI, 0.472 immunity, 0.03 ParA, 0.389 antirepressor)
Software_Libraries: XGBoost, scikit-learn (StratifiedKFold), python networkx, BioPython SeqUtils ProteinAnalysis, DIAMOND, cd-hit, ABRicate
Other_Metrics: Confusion matrix on lifestyle dataset (Lytic 177/7, Temperate 9/231); random 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.97, Cro/CI 0.91, immunity 0.96, ParA 0.90, antirepressor 0.94); clustered 10-fold CV MCCs (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16); prediction speed 1.6 s/phage for PhageLeads, 8.1 s for gene detection, 2.3 s for BACPHLIP.
Baseline_Method: BACPHLIP (random forest-based phage lifestyle predictor using presence of 206 lysogeny markers via HMM sequence similarity)
Baseline_Performance: BACPHLIP made 7 erroneous predictions on the lifestyle dataset (vs PhageLeads' 16 mispredictions, 7 FP + 9 FN); authors attribute BACPHLIP's higher accuracy to its smaller training data (634 genomes, 5 families)
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation (two variants: generic random via scikit-learn StratifiedKFold, and clustered using cd-hit at 60% identity where proteins from the same clusters stay in the same bins)
Train_Test_Split: 0.7 to 0.3 (training to testing)
External_Validation_Description: Independent external dataset: the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (240 temperate, 183 lytic) originally compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull [50], on which PhageLeads achieved MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95. Also a temporal hold-out validation set of 63 phage genomes dated after March 2018 (45,231 proteins).
Overfitting_Method: Feature reduction — iteratively removing the 50 least-contributing features per round to minimize overfitting probability and prediction time
Generalisability_Details: Clustered 10-fold cross-validation (cd-hit at 60% similarity, proteins from same clusters kept in same bins) assessed prediction of unseen protein clusters; clustered CV MCCs were lower (integrase 0.81, antirepressor 0.64, immunity 0.58, ParA 0.44, Cro/CI 0.16), indicating lower conservation for ParA and Cro/CI and the value of large training datasets.
Maturity_Evidence: Independent external validation on the 423-phage lifestyle dataset (compiled by Mavrich & Hatfull) achieving MCC 0.92, accuracy 0.96, F1 0.95 — evidence of external validation, hence level 3.
End_User_Described: Researchers / laboratory scientists assessing the therapeutic suitability of phages
Barriers_List: Ambiguously annotated proteins in databases; removal of some protein classes due to consistent misannotation; lifestyle information from literature reviews not completely dependable; low sequence conservation for ParA and Cro/CI markers limiting clustered-CV performance.
Future_Directions: Exploration of three-dimensional protein structures to resolve misannotations, in order to further improve PhageLeads performance; also applicable to predicting lysogenic markers for metagenomic contigs.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance scores calculated from the XGBoost module (used to select final features per predictor)
Limitation_Categories: Ambiguous protein annotations/misannotation; unreliable lifestyle labels from literature; low sequence conservation of specific markers (ParA, Cro/CI); false-positive temperate predictions in lytic phages.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Authors removed proteins <30 amino acids, hypothetical proteins, proteins with unclear annotations, and ambiguously annotated proteins (e.g. DNA binding protein, transcription regulator, repressors, DNA partitioning proteins without subunits) to reduce misclassification.

Title: Rapid, label-free pathogen identification system for multidrug-resistant bacterial wound infection detection on military members in the battlefield
Country_Countries: United States of America (Optowares, Inc., Woburn, Massachusetts; US military members)
AI_Application_Type: AI Signal Processing; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: DHA SBIR Program; U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command (USAMRDC); U.S. Air Force Material Command
Population_Description: 12 bacterial strains - six multidrug-resistant (MDR) and six antimicrobial-susceptible strains representing six species of the ESKAPEE group (Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli); all obtained from ATCC and cultured in a BSL-2 facility; bacteria spiked into wound-like samples; no human subjects / patient data
Data_Source_Other: In-house ATR-FTIR spectral data generated from cultured ATCC bacterial strains (six MDR and six susceptible) spiked into wound-like samples under laboratory conditions
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: SVMDA (sum vector machine discriminant analysis) classification model: >95% averaged analytical sensitivity and specificity for the six bacterial species (Fig 6A); 100% accuracy in classifying species identity in four unknown samples (Fig 6B). A PLSDA (partial least square discriminant analysis) pre-model was built first to check class boundaries, but SVMDA is the reported classification model
Best_Performing_Model: SVMDA (sum vector machine discriminant analysis) - the only classification model reported; >95% averaged analytical sensitivity and specificity; 100% accuracy on four unknown samples (metric used: analytical sensitivity/specificity and species classification accuracy)
Accuracy_Value: 100% (species identity classification in four unknown samples)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Four unknown samples (spectra from samples including those shown in Fig 3)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Six bacterial species (ESKAPEE group strains)
Specificity_Population_Set: Six bacterial species (ESKAPEE group strains)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Proof-of-concept laboratory study: system tested on spiked laboratory samples at the bench (under laboratory environment); no clinical deployment, external validation or prospective evaluation reported
Reported_Limitations: Weak bacterial peak intensities at low concentration (in the order of 10-3 range); 50 mL sample volume needed because of the filtration assembly size; only a small fraction of the PTFE membrane covered by bacteria at 104 cfu/mL
Sample_Size: 12 bacterial strains (six MDR and six antimicrobial-susceptible); SVMDA model trained on ATR spectra from Fig 1 (five spectra from the MDR and susceptible strains after antimicrobial incubation in each species)
Conflicts_of_Interest: none declared
Data_Types_Used: Other
Dataset_Size: 12 strains (six MDR, six antimicrobial-susceptible); ATR spectra of dried cell pellets at 109-1012 cfu/mL before and after antimicrobial incubation
Specimen_Type_Detail: Wound samples (wound sample / spiked wound samples); bacteria spiked into solutions including 5% dextrose/saline, fetal bovine serum/water, 0.85 wt% NaCl
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Distinguish multidrug-resistant (MDR) from antimicrobial-susceptible bacteria strains using antimicrobial-induced ATR-FTIR spectral changes, and identify bacterial species - for detection of MDR bacteria in infected combat-related wounds
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin); beta-lactams - penicillins (oxacillin sodium), cephalosporins (ceftriaxone disodium), carbapenems (ertapenem sodium)
Specific_Antibiotics: levofloxacin, oxacillin sodium, ceftriaxone disodium, ertapenem sodium (one antimicrobial per species; levofloxacin 8 ug/mL for E. cloacae, oxacillin sodium 20 ug/mL for S. aureus, ceftriaxone disodium for K. pneumoniae, ertapenem sodium 10 ug/mL for E. coli)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR vs antimicrobial-susceptible classification based on antimicrobial-induced changes to ATR-FTIR bacterial spectral features (peak shifts and peak intensity changes); each strain's susceptibility profile is against a single antimicrobial per species
AI_Purpose: To automate, objectify and quantify ATR-FTIR spectral analysis and unknown-sample classification so that MDR bacteria can be detected and bacterial species identified directly from wound samples in the field
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (SVMDA; a PLSDA pre-model was built to check class boundaries but was not compared as a separate classifier)
Feature_Engineering: ATR spectra baselined with an 'Automatic Baseline Correct' algorithm (one spectrum at a time) in OMNIC; min-max normalization of spectra; quantitative features via area-under-the-curve (AUC) of two spectral regions (3000-2750 and 1750-1500 cm-1)
Hyperparameter_Method: SVMDA model parameters were fine-tuned (method details not specified)
Software_Libraries: PLS_Toolbox (Eigenvector Research) on MATLAB platform; OMNIC software (ThermoFisher) for ATR spectra acquisition
Hardware_Details: Nicolet iS10 FTIR spectrometer (ThermoFisher) with custom-built ATR accessory (horizontal ATR/HATR, PIKE Technologies); multi-bounce silicon 45-degree trapezoidal ATR element; 47 mm glass vacuum filtration assembly
Other_Metrics: >95% averaged analytical sensitivity and specificity for the six bacterial species; 100% accuracy classifying species identity in four unknown samples; detection limit of 104 cfu/mL; % AUC reduction to quantify spectral changes
Internal_Validation: Tested on four different unknown samples not used to build the model; >95% sensitivity/specificity and 100% species classification accuracy reported
Maturity_Evidence: Laboratory proof-of-concept only: spiked samples tested under laboratory environment; model evaluated on four unknown samples; no clinical deployment, external dataset or prospective trial
Integration_Point: Battlefield / field - point-of-care detection of MDR bacteria in infected combat-related wounds (proposed, not deployed)
End_User_Described: Front line users (military personnel) in the battlefield environment

Data_Quality_Concerns: Low bacterial signal at 104 cfu/mL (peak intensities in the order of 10-3 range); only a small fraction of PTFE membrane covered by bacteria at low concentration
