Num_Features_Total: 1483 radiomics features extracted separately for the TIB sign and for nodules
Num_Features_Selected: 16 features from the TIB sign and 15 from nodules (31 in the combined model)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) applied to the training cohort to handle imbalance between DS-TB and MDR-TB patients
Software_Libraries: Python Scikit-learn package (Scikit-learn Version 0.21); SPSS version 26 for statistical analysis
Other_Metrics: DeLong test p-values comparing AUCs between the three models; decision curve analysis (DCA) net benefit across threshold probabilities; feature ICC for reproducibility.
Baseline_Method: DeLong test comparing the AUCs of the TIB, nodule and combined models; decision curve analysis against the treat-all and treat-none strategies.
Baseline_Performance: All three models offered net benefits over the treat-all or treat-none schemes within a certain range of thresholds in the combined training cohort, with similar results in the testing cohort; the DeLong test showed no significant AUC difference between the combined and nodules models (training p = 0.538).
Internal_Validation: Each training cohort randomly divided into parts at a ratio of 7:3 using tenfold cross-validation; feature reproducibility checked by ICC on a 30-patient resegmentation subset.
Train_Test_Split: Random 7:3 split of each training cohort (with tenfold cross-validation); the three external testing cohorts from hospital 2 served as independent test sets.
External_Validation_Description: Testing cohorts from hospital 2: 102 patients with the TIB sign, 97 with nodules and 81 with both signs (enrolled August 2017 to March 2022), separate from the hospital 1 training cohorts (December 2015 to January 2022).
Overfitting_Method: Tenfold cross-validation used to avoid overfitting; DeLong test used to evaluate whether overfitting occurred.
Clinical_Insights: The paper argues the TIB sign reflects endobronchial spread, caseous necrosis and granulomatous inflammation, but that imaging signs alone cannot separate MDR-TB from DS-TB, so quantitative radiomics is needed; the models (especially the combined and nodule models) are presented as supporting early, non-invasive identification of MDR before TB progression.
Generalisability_Details: The models were applied in the combined cohorts to guarantee stability and generalizability in clinical practice, and the limitations note that future prospective studies are needed to increase generalizability given the small testing cohort.
Maturity_Evidence: Best model of all models selected and tested on the corresponding cohort of three external testing cohorts (hospital 2); internal 7:3 split with tenfold cross-validation. No prospective evaluation, no integration into clinical systems and no routine use reported.
Integration_Point: Chest CT interpretation / radiology workflow, proposed as a non-invasive auxiliary diagnostic tool in routine clinical practice.
End_User_Described: Not explicitly named; the paper proposes use as a diagnostic tool in routine clinical practice, i.e. the clinician interpreting chest CT (radiologist / chest physician) is the implied end user.
Barriers_List: Retrospective design and small sample size with potential selection bias; models apply only to patients showing the TIB sign or nodules; limited clinical information and no clinical variables included; small testing cohort limiting generalizability.
Facilitators_List: Non-invasive imaging-based prediction of MDR-TB; user-friendly, before culture/DST results become available (4-8 weeks); net benefit over treat-all/treat-none strategies; complementary information from the TIB sign and nodules.
Future_Directions: Prospective studies with larger testing cohorts to increase generalizability, and investigation of radiomics in TB patients without the TIB sign or nodules.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Normalised importance, presented in Fig. 3 (no named importance or permutation method in the text)
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective single-period design; small sample size; selection bias; restricted to patients with the TIB sign or nodules; limited clinical information / no clinical predictors in the models; small testing cohort and need for prospective studies.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Cases with image artifacts or incomplete clinical information were excluded; feature reproducibility assessed by ICC (> 0.80 retained) on a 30-patient resegmentation subset; ROIs drawn manually layer by layer and confirmed by a second radiologist blinded to DST results.
Reporting_Clarity: Design, cohorts, feature selection (ICC, MIC, RFE), classifier, validation strategy and the three models' metrics are reported clearly, with AUC 95% CIs and Table 2 covering all three models; the individual radiomics features are shown only in figures, and the DST method and breakpoints used for the MDR/DS label are not specified.

Title: Direct prediction of carbapenem-resistant, carbapenemase-producing, and colistin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from routine MALDI-TOF mass spectra using machine learning and outcome evaluation
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Ministry of Science and Technology of Taiwan; China Medical University Hospital
Population_Description: 830 CRKP and 1462 carbapenem-susceptible K. pneumoniae (CSKP) isolates, plus 54 ColRKP and 1592 colistin-intermediate K. pneumoniae (ColIKP) isolates; a retrospective clinical evaluation included 34 hospitalised patients whose routine MALDI-TOF MS results were reported with the ML prediction.
Data_Source: Other national / population survey; Hospital / clinic registry
Data_Source_Other: Routine MALDI-TOF mass spectra generated in the clinical microbiology laboratory (plus AST and PCR gene detection used as labels)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: LightGBM classifier (multilabel model) only. CRKP/CSKP differentiation: accuracy 0.8869, AUC 0.9551, F1 0.8703; ColRKP/ColIKP: accuracy 0.8361, AUC 0.8447, F1 0.8925. No other ML algorithm was trained or compared in this study.
Best_Performing_Model: LightGBM (the only model applied, in the multilabel model; performance judged on accuracy, AUC and F1)
Accuracy_Population_Set: CRKP vs CSKP isolates, model performance across the three Ambler classes, CRKP and CSKP, under a five-fold train-test split
F1_Population_Set: CRKP vs CSKP isolates under a five-fold train-test split
AUROC_Population_Set: CRKP vs CSKP isolates under a five-fold train-test split
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The ML CRKP prediction was run on routine clinical isolates and the result and probability were conveyed to treating clinicians before the final culture report between February 25 and May 15, 2022, i.e. prospective use in the routine workflow; the outcome analysis itself was retrospective.
Reported_Limitations: Two author-stated limitations: (1) discoveries based on isolates collected in a local part of Taiwan, needing larger external validation; (2) MALDI-TOF MS results from one isolate were not sufficiently representative of the input data for drug-resistant phenotype prediction, and further biomarkers or functional experiments are needed to identify each important feature's role.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: None reported; the authors caution that the rapid screening assay cannot replace conventional molecular methods for detecting CRKP, CPKP and colistin resistance.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No ethical or governance risks are discussed; the study reports IRB approval (CMUH109-REC3-098 and CMUH112-REC2-027) and waiver of informed consent.
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis = LightGBM on the primary CRKP/CSKP task (accuracy 0.8869, AUC 0.9551, F1 0.8703); the colistin model's figures (0.8361/0.8447/0.8925) are recorded in All_Models_Evaluated. Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, confidence intervals, calibration and any baseline comparison are not reported. The same LightGBM model produces all outputs, so there is a single model and no model-vs-model comparison.
Unresolved_Items: Age, sex, and ethnicity of the 34 evaluated patients are not reported; specimen types used for the clinical evaluation are listed but not the per-specimen case counts beyond the aggregate.
Sample_Size: 830 CRKP isolates (plus 1462 CSKP and 227 CRKP from NTUH used for modelling and 419 CRKP from CMUH for validation); 54 ColRKP and 1592 ColIKP isolates; 34 patients in the clinical evaluation. Unit = isolates (and patients for the clinical evaluation).
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: Clinical specimens included patients with blood specimens, endotracheal aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage, body fluid from sterile sites, and catheter tip cultures; the isolate collections comprised K. pneumoniae isolates from the SMART programme, NTUH and CMUH.
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates with multiple carbapenemases were ruled out of the ML modelling because the MALDI-TOF target analyte is protein; the NG-Test CARBA 5 result was used first for follow-up ML.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: SMART (Surveillance of Multicenter Antimicrobial Resistance in Taiwan) programme of the Taiwan Centers for Disease Control; National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH); China Medical University Hospital (CMUH)
Dataset_Size: SMART/NTUH modelling set: 1462 CSKP and 227 CRKP isolates from NTUH plus 184 blood CRKP isolates from SMART; validation set: 419 CRKP isolates from CMUH; colistin set: 54 ColRKP and 1592 ColIKP isolates.
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates came from a single country (Taiwan) and the authors state the discoveries were based on isolates collected in a local part of Taiwan, requiring larger external validation.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood specimens, endotracheal aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage, body fluid from sterile sites, and catheter tip cultures
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem resistance (CRKP vs CSKP), carbapenemase Ambler class (A/KPC, B/NDM-VIM-IMP, D/OXA-48), and colistin resistance (ColRKP vs ColIKP) predicted directly from routine MALDI-TOF MS spectra
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (carbapenem-resistant CRKP, carbapenem-susceptible CSKP, carbapenemase-producing CPKP, colistin-resistant ColRKP and colistin-intermediate ColIKP isolates)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (ertapenem, imipenem, meropenem); polymyxins (colistin)
Specific_Antibiotics: ertapenem, imipenem, meropenem (carbapenem non-susceptibility definition); colistin (resistance criterion >=4 mg/L)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: CRKP = non-susceptible (intermediate and resistant) to at least one carbapenem antibiotic with an MIC value of >=1, >=2, and >=2 mg/L for ertapenem, imipenem, and meropenem respectively, according to CLSI guidelines; colistin resistance criterion >=4 mg/L by broth microdilution.
AI_Purpose: To build an ML model that predicts CRKP, carbapenemase-producing K. pneumoniae and colistin resistance directly from routine MALDI-TOF MS spectra, and to analyse retrospectively the clinical implications of reporting the predictions to physicians before the final report.
Feature_Engineering: Spectra resampled to a fixed sampling rate (1 Da); TopHat baseline correction, square root transformation and Savitzky-Golay filter for baseline correction, normalization and smoothing; min-max scaling to 0-1; spectra extracted from m/z 2000-20000 Da and grouped into 10 Dalton bins, taking the maximum peak intensity per bin.
Feature_Selection_Method: SHAP (SHapely Additive exPlanation) values used to rank features; the top 10 most important features were identified.
Num_Features_Total: Not stated as a count; spectra extracted over m/z 2000 to 20000 Da and grouped into 10 Dalton bins (one bin = one attribute)
Num_Features_Selected: 10 (top 10 most important features identified by SHAP)
Class_Imbalance_Method: The five carbapenemase genes (KPC, OXA, NDM, VIM, IMP) were regrouped into three Ambler classes - A (KPC), B (NDM, VIM, IMP) and D (OXA) - because the extreme imbalance across categories reduced the robustness and generality of the model.
Other_Metrics: None beyond accuracy, area under the curve (AUC) and F1 score for the models; the clinical evaluation reported the time saved, proportion of CRKP in the final culture, proportion of antibiotic regimen adjustments and hospital mortality rate.
Internal_Validation: five-fold train-test split for training and validation
Train_Test_Split: Five-fold train-test split (split proportions not stated)
External_Validation_Description: 419 CRKP isolates collected randomly from the China Medical University Hospital (CMUH) between 2019 and 2022 formed the validation set, separate from the SMART/NTUH isolates used for modelling.
Overfitting_Method: Regrouping the imbalanced carbapenemase classes into three Ambler classes and using a five-fold train-test split for training and validation.
Clinical_Insights: The top-ranking protein marker m/z 4520-4529 distinguishes KPC from OXA, NDM, IMP and VIM among CRKP isolates; SHAP-ranked m/z 4170-4179 separates ColRKP from ColIKP.
Generalisability_Details: The authors note the isolates came from a local part of Taiwan and that other isolates with different sequence types (the main sequence type was ST11) should be included for validation in further research.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence of external validation: the remaining 419 CRKP isolates for validation were collected randomly from CMUH between 2019 and 2022, separate from the SMART/NTUH modelling isolates; the model was also run prospectively on routine isolates for preliminary reporting between February 25 and May 15, 2022.
Integration_Point: Preliminary reporting of the MALDI-TOF MS-based ML CRKP prediction (result and probability) to the clinicians responsible for patient care before the final culture report, conveyed by texting.
End_User_Described: Clinicians responsible for patient care (physicians) receiving preliminary CRKP prediction results
Clinical_Workflow_Details: After modelling and validation the model operates within the routine clinical workflow: the MALDI-TOF MS results are used directly for prediction without any additional experimental procedures.
Stewardship_Details: Of patients with CRKP infection, 79.2% (19/24) received inappropriate empirical antibiotics and the antibiotic regimen was changed in 73.7% (14/19) of cases after the preliminary ML prediction results.
Barriers_List: Isolates from a local part of Taiwan requiring larger external validation; MALDI-TOF MS results from a single isolate not sufficiently representative for phenotype prediction; identity and resistance role of the important features not established.
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is a more suitable data source than genomic or genetic data for ML-based AMR prediction because it is obtained from routine clinical diagnostic workflows and the predictions can be applied clinically.
Future_Directions: Other isolates with different sequence types should be included for validation in further research; larger external validation is needed; further biomarkers or functional segment experiments are needed to reveal the identity of each important feature and its role in drug resistance mechanisms.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapely Additive exPlanation) values
Novel_Predictors_Details: The top-ranking protein marker m/z 4520-4529 could differentiate KPC from OXA, NDM, IMP and VIM carbapenemases among CRKP isolates, providing additional information beyond previous reports that compared mainly KPC2-positive and KPC2-negative isolates.
Feature_Interactions_Method: SHAP values, which consider the interactions between features and their effect on the model's predictions
Limitation_Categories: Geography/generalisability (single local region of Taiwan, need for larger external validation); data representativeness (single-isolate MALDI-TOF spectra); unexplained features (identity and resistance role of important features unknown); the assay cannot replace conventional molecular methods.
Data_Quality_Concerns: MALDI-TOF MS results from one isolate were not sufficiently representative of the input data for drug-resistant phenotype prediction given variation among samples; further biomarkers or functional experiments are needed to reveal the identity of each important feature.
Reporting_Clarity: The model, metrics and clinical evaluation are reported explicitly and the MALDI-TOF MS data were deposited in Zenodo; however no reporting guideline is named and no code is shared.

Title: Interpretable machine learning-based decision support for prediction of antibiotic resistance for complicated urinary tract infections
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Wellcome Trust; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre; NIHR Health Protection Research Unit; EU Horizon 2020; Royal Academy of Engineering; InnoHK
Population_Description: Patients diagnosed with potentially complicated UTIs (n=101,096 samples) with urine specimens tested for antibiotic susceptibility at MGH and BWH
Top_Predictive_Features: Prior antibiotic resistance and prior antibiotic exposure (across time frames); previous UTI history; comorbidities (paralysis, renal); long-term care facility stays; surgical procedures
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: LR, XGBoost, TabNet, TabNet-self; metrics AUROC/AUPRC/sensitivity/specificity/PPV/F1 per antibiotic (e.g. LVX XGBoost AUROC 0.814, AUPRC 0.624)
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost
Sensitivity_Population_Set: complicated UTI test set, LVX XGBoost model
Specificity_Population_Set: complicated UTI test set, LVX XGBoost model
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: complicated UTI test set, LVX XGBoost model
F1_Population_Set: complicated UTI test set, LVX XGBoost model
AUROC_Population_Set: complicated UTI test set, LVX XGBoost model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Temporal internal validation (train 2007-2013, test 2014-2016) plus external validation on an independent uncomplicated UTI cohort
Reported_Limitations: Single health system (MGH/BWH); binary ethnicity/race label; AMR-UTI dataset lacks EHR segments (symptoms, treatment dosage/duration, purchase history); class imbalance; decision-threshold transferability across datasets
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Binary ethnicity/race label may perpetuate bias in models; ethnicity can play a role in predicting diagnoses/treatment
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Dataset approved by Institutional Review Board of MGH with waived informed consent requirement
Conflicts_of_Interest: D.A.C. reports personal fees from Oxford University Innovation, BioBeats, Sensyne Health (outside submitted work); D.W.E. declares lecture fees from Gilead (outside submitted work); no other authors report conflicts
Sex_Distribution: Not available (sex not recorded for complicated UTI cohort)
Inclusion_Criteria: All specimens tested for any one or combination of NIT, SXT, CIP, or LVX, from patients with potentially complicated UTIs
Exclusion_Criteria: Specimens fulfilling Kanjilal et al. uncomplicated UTI criteria (the complicated cohort did not fulfil these)
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: AMR-UTI dataset (PhysioNet)
Dataset_Size: 101,096 complicated UTI samples; 15,806 uncomplicated UTI specimens
Missing_Data_Method: Binary encoding: 1=presence of observed element, 0=element not observed including missing cases
Ethnicity_Details: Binary white/non-white; 72.9% white (training), 73.6% (validation), 72.7% (test); 3% with race unrecorded default to non-white
Geographic_Representativeness: Two US hospitals (MGH, BWH) in Boston, Massachusetts, 2007-2016
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine specimens
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic resistance/non-susceptibility (binary S vs R) to nitrofurantoin, co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Drug_Classes: Nitrofurans (nitrofurantoin); sulfonamide/co-trimoxazole (SXT); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Nitrofurantoin (NIT); co-trimoxazole (SXT); ciprofloxacin (CIP); levofloxacin (LVX)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptibility: susceptible (S), intermediate (I), resistant (R); I and R both treated as resistant, based on 2017 CLSI breakpoints
AI_Purpose: To predict antimicrobial resistance for potentially complicated UTIs to support clinicians in selecting appropriate antibiotics and provide interpretable predictions
Feature_Engineering: All categorical variables one-hot encoded; features recorded across 14/30/90/180-day time frames; colonization pressure computed
Feature_Selection_Method: TabNet sequential attention for dynamic feature selection; feature importance/coefficients
Class_Imbalance_Method: Threshold adjustment (grid search to optimise balanced sensitivity/specificity); hyperparameter selection by best AUPRC to account for imbalance
Hyperparameter_Method: Five-fold cross-validation and grid search; chosen on best AUPRC
Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression (LR)
Baseline_Performance: LR AUROC range 0.662-0.791 across the four antibiotics (lowest of all models)
Internal_Validation: Temporal validation: trained 2007-2013, tested 2014-2016; 90/10 training/validation split; five-fold CV for hyperparameters
Train_Test_Split: 90% model development / 10% continuous validation; temporal split 2007-2013 train, 2014-2016 test
External_Validation_Description: Independent cohort of patients with uncomplicated UTI specimens (n=15,608 all; subset n=3,941 matching Kanjilal test set)
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Prior antibiotic resistance and prior antibiotic exposure are most predictive; comorbidities (paralysis, renal) and long-term care/surgical history important; supports empirical treatment decisions
Generalisability_Details: Validated on an independent uncomplicated UTI cohort with comparable AUROC to prior study; results may differ for other cohorts/hospitals
Maturity_Evidence: Temporal internal validation (train 2007-2013, test 2014-2016) plus external validation on an independent uncomplicated UTI cohort; proof of concept, not deployed
End_User_Described: Clinicians (prescribing decision support)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction of antibiotic resistance to support empirical prescribing at treatment initiation, before culture results are available; clinician/pipeline evaluates therapy suitability independently
Barriers_List: Need for further validation before widespread adoption; class imbalance and decision-threshold transferability; potential redundancy of ML predictions when susceptibility results available in ~24h; single health system; missing EHR data segments
Facilitators_List: Model interpretability supports clinical utility and integration into regular care; transfer learning enables model updating over time
Future_Directions: Training one multilabel classifier; focusing on CAUTIs or distinguishing community- vs hospital-acquired UTIs; excluding ASB patients; higher time-granularity and time-series models (CNN, LSTM); integrating additional EHR features; collaboration with domain experts/clinicians
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Coefficients (LR), importance scores (TabNet, XGBoost); leave-one-feature-set-out AUROC/AUPRC analysis
Feature_Interactions_Method: Comparison of XGBoost/TabNet (capturing non-linear interactions) vs logistic regression
Limitation_Categories: Single health system; binary ethnicity/race label; incomplete EHR data (symptoms, dosing, duration, purchase history); class imbalance; decision-threshold transferability; potential inclusion of ASB patients
Data_Quality_Concerns: Binary ethnicity with 3% unrecorded defaulted to non-white; missing dose/duration/purchase history; potential inadvertent inclusion of ASB patients; missing values handled by binary encoding

Title: Development and validation of a prediction model for unsuccessful treatment outcomes in patients with multi-drug resistance tuberculosis
Funder_Names: Social Development Project, Science and Technology Department of Shaanxi Province (2016SF-032); Medical Research Project of Science and Technology in Xi'an (21YXYJ0001, 21YXYJ0075)
Population_Description: 446 patients diagnosed with multi-drug resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (MDR-PTB) at a single special hospital in Xi'an, China, treated Jan 2017 - Dec 2019 and followed to treatment outcome
Age_Mean_Median: 38.1 ± 15.0 years (reported as median age, mean ± SD)
Top_Predictive_Features: 1) No health education; 2) advanced age; 3) male sex; 4) larger extent of lung involvement (lung lesion fields). Selected by LASSO regression (optimal lambda 0.062) then multivariable logistic regression; adjusted ORs 0.44 for health education, 2.43 for male sex, 1.04 per year of age, 1.25 per extra lung lesion field
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Only one model was developed and evaluated: the multivariable logistic-regression nomogram - AUC 0.757 (95%CI 0.711 to 0.804), C-index 0.75, bootstrap-corrected C-index 0.747, leave-one-out cross-validation C-index 0.765, sensitivity 0.640, specificity 0.773, calibration slope 0.968. Models from other studies are cited but not re-evaluated: Brazil 802-patient model (AUC 0.76) and a Hunan model with moderate AUC
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Training cohort (446 patients)
Specificity_Population_Set: Training cohort (446 patients)
AUROC_Population_Set: Training cohort (446 patients)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only - bootstrap sampling (1000 resamples, corrected C-index 0.747) and leave-one-out cross-validation (C-index 0.765); the model was not externally validated
Reported_Limitations: Observational study so confounding cannot be completely excluded and causality is not proven; conducted in one hospital with no external validation, a regional limitation; newer drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid) were not used so the model does not apply to newer regimens; HIV co-infection not analysed (only two HIV-positive cases) so the model cannot be used in HIV-positive patients; Mpb64 monoclonal antibody is not a recommended method of Mtb identification; systematic health education not yet widely conducted
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients diagnosed with MDR-PTB at Xi'an Chest Hospital between Jan 2017 and Dec 2019, treated with the 2016 drug-resistant TB treatment guidelines regimen for 18 to 24 months
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients who died before the start of MDR-TB treatment, received an incorrect regimen (lack enough core medication), were co-infected with non-tuberculosis mycobacterium, or received a short-term regimen
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results; Imaging
Data_Source_Name: Xi'an Chest Hospital electronic medical record system (no named dataset; managed in EpiData)
Dataset_Size: 543 patients diagnosed; 446 included in the analysis (299 successful, 147 unsuccessful)
Missing_Data_Method: 24 cases missing fluoroquinolone and injectable-agent drug sensitivity tests were inserted ('imputed') according to the resistance rate; older cases with longer use of these drugs were inserted as resistant
Geographic_Representativeness: Single hospital in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province, China; the authors compare their patient characteristics with a national survey in China, Japan and the 2020 Global TB Report and argue the model may apply to other regions
Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum/BALF smear
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Unsuccessful MDR-PTB treatment outcome (treatment failure, loss to follow-up, or death) versus treatment success (cure or treatment completion), reclassified from the six WHO treatment outcome categories
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis drugs: fluoroquinolones, injectable agents, linezolid, cycloserine, clofazimine, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, prothionamide, P-aminosalicylate
Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid, rifampin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, amikacin, capreomycin (DST panel); bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, clofazimine, cycloserine, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, prothionamide, P-aminosalicylate (drugs in regimens)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR-TB defined as M. tuberculosis resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin; drug sensitivity coded sensitive/resistant for fluoroquinolones and injectable agents by BACTEC MGIT 960 and absolute concentration methods; outcome label = unsuccessful treatment outcome
AI_Purpose: To develop and validate a simple clinical prediction model (nomogram) to predict unsuccessful treatment outcomes in patients with multi-drug resistant pulmonary tuberculosis
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single multivariable logistic-regression nomogram; no head-to-head model comparison)
Feature_Engineering: Lung lesion distribution derived from post-anterior chest radiographs divided into six fields (lines at the lower edge of the second and fourth ribs), counting lesion-bearing fields rather than lesion area; age and health-education status used as recorded
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression for selection, then multivariable logistic regression
Hyperparameter_Method: Optimal lambda (0.062) selected in LASSO regression via the partial likelihood deviance profile
Software_Libraries: Free Statistics software version 1.5 used alongside R version 3.3.2; no R packages named
Other_Metrics: AUC 0.757 (95%CI 0.711 to 0.804); C-index 0.75; bootstrap-corrected C-index 0.747; leave-one-out cross-validation C-index 0.765 and calibration slope 1.0; calibration slope 0.968 with bootstrap sampling; Youden index 0.382; decision curve analysis net benefit at threshold probabilities 0.086-0.713
Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap sampling for corrected ROC, C-index and calibration curve; leave-one-out cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: No separate train/test split reported; the full 446-patient cohort was used with internal validation (bootstrap sampling and leave-one-out cross-validation)
CV_Folds: Leave-one-out cross-validation (one held-out patient per fold); no k-fold scheme reported
Overfitting_Method: LASSO shrinkage used for variable selection and bootstrap-corrected C-index (0.747) reported; overfitting not discussed explicitly
Clinical_Insights: Each prognostc factor carries fixed nomogram points (age 60 years = 65 points, male = 25, 4 lung lesion fields = 18, no health education = 24), so a 60-year-old man with 4 lung lesion fields and no health education totals 132 points, about a 70% risk of unsuccessful outcome; a one-year increase in age raises incidence by 4% and each extra lung lesion field by 25%
Generalisability_Details: Authors argue their prognostic model may apply to patients in other regions of China on the basis of comparable patient characteristics, but state it was not externally validated, does not apply to newer regimens and is most useful in settings such as west China where newer drugs are unavailable
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation evidence only: 1000-sample bootstrap correction (C-index 0.747) and leave-one-out cross-validation (C-index 0.765); the paper states the model was not externally validated
Integration_Point: At the start of MDR-TB treatment, from baseline characteristics collected on admission, to identify patients at risk of an unsuccessful outcome
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating patients with MDR-PTB
Barriers_List: Newer drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid) were not used in this cohort and are not always available, especially in west China, so the model does not apply to newer regimens; systematic health education is not yet widely conducted; the model cannot be used in HIV-positive patients
Facilitators_List: All four factors are baseline characteristics that can be acquired easily; model showed good discrimination and calibration and was validated by bootstrap and leave-one-out cross-validation; systematic health education programme supported by FHI 360
Future_Directions: Wider implementation of systematic health education and further use of the nomogram to improve MDR-TB treatment outcomes
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Multivariable logistic regression adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs, LASSO regression selection and nomogram point scores
Limitation_Categories: Confounding / no causality (observational); single hospital and no external validation (regional limitation); treatment era / newer regimens (bedaquiline, delamanid not used); exclusion of HIV-positive patients; diagnostic method (Mpb64 monoclonal antibody not recommended); limited implementation of systematic health education
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data managed in EpiData and entered by individuals, with entered data and outcomes checked by attending doctors; 24 missing DST values inserted by imputation based on resistance rate
Reporting_Clarity: Clear reporting of design, participants, prognostic factors and model performance (AUC, C-index, calibration); no statement of adherence to any reporting guideline

Title: Derivation and validation of a risk assessment model for drug-resistant pathogens in hospitalized patients with community-acquired pneumonia
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (grant no. R01HS024277)
Population_Description: Adults aged 18 years or older hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia (principal diagnosis of pneumonia, or secondary pneumonia with respiratory failure/ARDS/respiratory arrest/sepsis) who had blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission; 138,762 patients analysed
Age_Mean_Median: mean 69.5 y (SD 16.2) in the derivation set, N=111,013
Data_Source_Other: Premier Healthcare Database, a multihospital administrative claims/discharge database; Cleveland Clinic Health System (CCHS) hospitals with data elements derived by electronic chart review
Top_Predictive_Features: Odds ratios in the final CARM (derivation set, N=111,013): resistant organism in previous year 2.66 (2.3-3.08); invasive mechanical ventilation 2.10 (1.91-2.3); pressure ulcer 1.86 (1.68-2.05); vasopressor administration 1.63 (1.47-1.80); paralysis 1.58 (1.41-1.78); ICU admission 1.55 (1.43-1.67); low functional status/weight loss 1.44 (1.34-1.54); hospital admission in previous year 1.43 (1.31-1.56); admitted from SNF/ICF 1.34 (1.21-1.49); chronic pulmonary disease 1.30 (1.22-1.39); male sex 1.28 (1.21-1.37); current tobacco smoker 0.77 (0.71-0.85)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: CARM (logistic regression): C-statistic 0.71 in the Premier holdout sample and 0.65 in CCHS; DRIP score: C-statistic 0.63 (Premier holdout) and 0.58 (CCHS); 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule and physician prescribing compared by cumulative gain curves
Best_Performing_Model: CARM (Cleveland Clinic Antibiotic Resistance Model), a multiple logistic regression model - highest C-statistic, 0.71 versus 0.63 for the DRIP score in the Premier holdout sample
AUROC_Population_Set: Premier 20% random holdout validation sample (CARM linear predictor)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal repeated 10-fold cross-validation and a random 20% Premier holdout sample, plus a fully independent external validation in the CCHS data (0.71 to 0.65 C-statistic); no prospective evaluation or CDS integration reported

Unintended_Consequences_Harms: An inescapable tradeoff: a threshold low enough to cover resistant infections requires treating more patients unnecessarily with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a DRIP cutoff of 4 would leave >80% of resistant infections uncovered
Reviewer_Notes: The performance measure reported for the study's own model is the C-statistic (AUROC); 0.71 is the CARM in the Premier 20% holdout validation sample (the derivation-set C-statistic is 0.70, Table 2). No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, AUPRC, kappa, MCC, RMSE or MAE figures are reported for the CARM; the paper reports C-statistics, calibration by deciles and cumulative gain curves. The DRIP score's original sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV are mentioned only as the published values of that external score, not as measures computed here.

No other authors have potential conflicts to disclose
Sex_Distribution: Female 56,640 (51.0), Male 54,373 (49.0) in the derivation set (N=111,013); male sex is a CARM predictor (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.21-1.37)
Inclusion_Criteria: Admissions between July 2010 and June 2015 to any of 177 Premier hospitals with microbiology data: patients aged 18 years or older with a principal diagnosis of pneumonia, or a secondary diagnosis of pneumonia paired with a principal diagnosis of respiratory failure, ARDS, respiratory arrest or sepsis, who had blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission
Exclusion_Criteria: Hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia; interhospital transfers; admissions with a diagnosis code for an alternate site of infection (eg, cholecystitis); for patients with multiple hospitalizations only 1 randomly selected admission was included
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: Premier Healthcare Database; Cleveland Clinic Health System (CCHS) hospitals (northeastern Ohio and Florida)
Dataset_Size: Premier: 151,715 pneumonia admissions screened, 138,762 analysed (80% derivation N=111,013; 20% validation N=27,749); CCHS external validation sample: all adults discharged 2017-2019
Ethnicity_Details: Race reported as White 85,654 (77.2%), Black 13,882 (12.5%), Other 11,477 (10.3%) in the derivation set (N=111,013); race (White, Black, or other) was a candidate predictor
Geographic_Representativeness: Premier hospitals throughout the United States representing approximately 25% of US admissions, varying in size and including nonprofit, nongovernmental, urban, rural, community and academic medical centres; CCHS validation from 10 northeastern Ohio hospitals and 1 Florida hospital
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood or respiratory cultures collected on admission (blood, bronchial or sputum); nares excluded from the outcome definition
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of a cultured organism to first-line CAP therapy: any organism grown from blood or respiratory source (other than the nares) resistant to either a quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin and a macrolide
Pathogens: Any organism grown from blood or respiratory cultures; probable contaminants (eg, coagulase negative Staphylococcus) and organisms not known to cause pneumonia (eg, Enterococcus spp) excluded; methicillin-resistant S. aureus and Pseudomonas named in the guideline/2-factor rule context
Drug_Classes: Quinolones (fluoroquinolones); third-generation cephalosporins; macrolides; beta-lactams
Specific_Antibiotics: quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide (resistance definition); ampicillin and ertapenem named in the resistant-organism footnote; prior-exposure variables cover fluoroquinolone, macrolide, beta-lactam, anti-MRSA agents and aminoglycoside
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary: positive culture with growth of a resistant organism from any blood or respiratory source other than the nares; organisms resistant to either a quinolone or the combination of a third-generation cephalosporin and a macrolide were counted as resistant to CAP therapy; patients who grew no organisms (or had no sample by a route) were considered negative
AI_Purpose: To validate the DRIP score in a large sample, derive and validate an improved risk prediction model (CARM) for resistance to first-line CAP therapy, and compare the model and the DRIP score with physician prescribing behaviour and the 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (CARM versus DRIP score), also benchmarked against the 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule and physician prescribing
Feature_Engineering: 43 candidate predictors assembled from ICD-9-CM diagnosis and procedure codes and diagnosis-related groups; comorbidities via HCUP Comorbidity Software version 3.1 (Elixhauser); lifestyle factors from ICD codes or billing for nicotine replacement therapy; previous hospitalisations and antibiotic exposures in the past year; severity indicators on the first hospital day; no laboratory values or vital signs available
Feature_Selection_Method: Multiple logistic regression with successive backward elimination of variables maximally reducing the Akaike information criterion (AIC), then removal of variables contributing little to discrimination (C-statistic) based on prevalence, odds ratio, and clinical and statistical judgment
Num_Features_Total: 43 candidate predictors
Num_Features_Selected: 12 (the 12-factor CARM)
Software_Libraries: SAS version 9.4 (data management), SAS/STAT version 15.1, R version 3.5 and version 4.0.0; HCUP Comorbidity Software version 3.1
Other_Metrics: C-statistic (AUROC), receiver operating characteristic curves, cumulative gain curves, calibration by risk deciles, slopes and intercepts of logistic regressions of resistance on the CARM linear predictor, outcome prevalence
Baseline_Method: DRIP score; 2-factor ATS/IDSA rule; physician prescribing (actual care provided)
Baseline_Performance: DRIP score C-statistic 0.63 in the Premier holdout and 0.58 in CCHS; a DRIP cutoff of 2 or more covered 53.5% of resistant organisms while treating 34.1% of all patients with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Internal_Validation: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation (20 repeats) in the derivation set and a random 20% Premier holdout sample
Train_Test_Split: Random 80% derivation / 20% validation split of the Premier data (N=111,013 derivation; N=27,749 validation)
External_Validation_Description: CCHS: 10 northeastern Ohio hospitals and 1 Florida Cleveland Clinic Health System hospital; all adult patients discharged between 2017 and 2019 meeting the same inclusion criteria, with data elements derived by electronic chart review; CCHS does not contribute to Premier
Overfitting_Method: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation (20 repeats) in the derivation set, evaluation in a random 20% holdout and an independent external sample
Clinical_Insights: Infection with a resistant organism in the previous year was the strongest predictor; markers of acute illness (need for mechanical ventilation, vasopressors) and chronic illness (pressure ulcer, paralysis) predicted resistant infections; smoking was inversely associated with resistance
Generalisability_Details: External validation confirmed degradation of discrimination in a different health system (C-statistic 0.71 to 0.65) and miscalibration of both models in the highest deciles; the authors argue this is why external validation matters
Maturity_Evidence: Internal: 20 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation and a random 20% Premier holdout sample. External: fully independent CCHS validation (C-statistic 0.71 to 0.65; miscalibration in high deciles). Model published as a 12-factor web calculator; no prospective evaluation, implementation or CDS integration reported
Integration_Point: Electronic health record as clinical decision support - proposed only: the 12-factor CARM could be incorporated into the EHR as clinical decision support for empiric therapy choice
End_User_Described: Clinicians (prescribers choosing empiric therapy for hospitalized CAP patients without culture results); hospitals unable to derive their own local risk models
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The model is applied before culture results are known, to all CAP admissions; each hospital picks a predicted-probability threshold for starting broad-spectrum antibiotics and the cumulative gain curves show the tradeoff between coverage of resistant organisms and broad-spectrum use
Stewardship_Details: Projected only, not measured: a 4% CARM threshold would cover the same 53.5% of resistant organisms while treating only 25% of patients versus 34.1% under a DRIP cutoff of 2 or more; a predicted probability above 11.5% would achieve the same coverage while treating fewer patients
Barriers_List: Most hospitals cannot derive their own local risk factors; the derivation database lacked laboratory values and vital signs; selective culture ordering and missed resistant organisms; ICD coding differences and drift; each hospital must choose its own treatment threshold; no decision-analytic model exists to optimise the threshold
Facilitators_List: All CARM variables are readily available to clinicians at admission; large nationally representative derivation sample; external validation; the 12-factor CARM is published as an online risk calculator that could be built into the EHR
Future_Directions: Determine whether locally derived models outperform the CARM and whether implementing such models improves patient outcomes; decision-analytic optimisation of treatment thresholds
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (sociodemographic, behavioural, healthcare utilisation, pharmacological, microbiological, clinical)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Multivariable logistic regression odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, ranked by odds ratio after backward elimination by AIC
Novel_Predictors_Details: Chronic-illness markers such as pressure ulcer and paralysis and the inverse association of current smoking were new relative to the DRIP score, which the authors discuss alongside markers of acute illness
Limitation_Categories: Data-source limitations (administrative database without laboratory values or vital signs); selective culture use and possible missed resistant organisms; ICD-coded diagnoses and comorbidities with differential coding and coding drift; outpatient antibiotics lowering culture yield; temporal and geographical differences between the 2010-2015 Premier derivation data and 2017-2019 CCHS data; organisms without CLSI break points excluded
Data_Quality_Concerns: No laboratory values or vital signs in the administrative database; cultures obtained in routine care with unknown reasons for missing cultures; diagnoses and comorbidities coded from ICD-9-CM with differential coding across hospitals and drift over time; some patients may have received outpatient antibiotics that lowered culture yields
Reporting_Clarity: Clear and complete: derivation and validation sets, model predictors with odds ratios and 95% CIs, C-statistics against comparators, calibration by deciles, cumulative gain curves and a limitations section are all reported
Page_References: pp. 1143-1150; Table 1 and Table 2 on pp. 1146-1147; Figure 1 p. 1145; Figures 2-4 pp. 1148-1149

Title: Deep learning and single-cell phenotyping for rapid antimicrobial susceptibility detection in Escherichia coli
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Oxford Martin School (Programme on Antimicrobial Resistance Testing); Wellcome Trust (110164/Z/15/Z); UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BB/N018656/1, BB/S008896/1); UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (Oxford-Nottingham Biomedical Imaging CDT, EP/L016052/1); National Institute for Health Research (NIHR200915; NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre)
Population_Description: Single cells of the laboratory reference E. coli strain MG1655 (untreated and antibiotic-treated) and single cells of six clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6) from human bloodstream infections with differing ciprofloxacin MICs; no patient-level data were accessed
Data_Source_Other: Wide-field fluorescence microscopy images of single bacterial cells (DAPI nucleoid stain, Nile Red membrane stain) acquired in-house; no clinical data source
Top_Predictive_Features: Nucleoid structure and organisation (classifier focuses primarily on this), with some attention given to the cell membrane — ranked by post-hoc saliency mapping of single-cell inputs; the co-amoxiclav phenotype was the least visually discriminable
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Segmentation: Mask R-CNN on a ResNet50 backbone (mAP 70 % at IoU 0.5; 92 % maximum total recall), Cellpose, YOLO v8; classification: DenseNet121 (>84 % single-cell accuracy on the holdout experiment) screened against models from the DenseNet, ResNet and EfficientNet families; selected pipeline Mask R-CNN + DenseNet121
Best_Performing_Model: Mask R-CNN (segmentation) + DenseNet121 (classification) — best combination of models; decided on classification accuracy on the holdout test set
Accuracy_Value: >84 % single-cell classification accuracy in the holdout experiments across all antibiotic conditions (the abstract's headline figure for the same models is 80 % single-cell accuracy)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Single cells from the MG1655 lab-reference strain, evaluated on an independent 7th 'holdout' experiment not used for training or hyperparameter optimisation; class-balanced, randomly sampled 1000 cells (800 for co-amoxiclav)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models trained on the MG1655 laboratory strain were validated on an independent holdout experiment and then deployed without retraining on six clinical E. coli blood-culture isolates (EC1-6) with different ciprofloxacin MICs; no prospective clinical evaluation or CDS integration is reported
Reported_Limitations: Explicit phenotype classes must be homogeneous across cells and isolates; further work required to validate across more species and antibiotics and to robustly demonstrate correlation with MIC-based susceptibility metrics; specific models must be trained for each antibiotic-species combination, which may not scale well; the assay still requires culture of isolates (not for direct patient specimens)
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: None reported. Risks discussed are assay-performance risks rather than patient harms: reliance on homogeneous phenotype classes (misclassification of cells not showing the full phenotype), possible over-smoothing of population heterogeneity, and the need for per-antibiotic/per-species models
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Analysed bacterial isolates were routinely stored diagnostic cultures; no sampling was undertaken for the study and no patient-related information was accessed, and under the UK Human Tissue Act such isolates required no ethical approval — the paper identifies no ethical or governance risk
Reviewer_Notes: Images-only input: the model sees DAPI/Nile Red micrograph channels, so all predictor-category fields except imaging are No. Per-class performance numbers (sensitivity/specificity/precision/recall) are shown only inside Fig. 3 panels and Supplementary Tables S2/S3, which are not in the PDF text layer, hence the 'No' answers for those metrics.
Unresolved_Items: Per-antibiotic and per-class classifier performance figures and all Supplementary Tables (S2, S3, S5, S6) are image-only or absent from the text layer, so no sensitivity/specificity/precision/F1 values could be quoted for the classification models
Sample_Size: 29,297 manually curated cells in 459 fields of view (segmentation training/cross-validation set); 9,044 cells in 115 fields of view (validation set); 13,247 ground-truth cells in 155 micrographs (segmentation holdout); classification holdout test set of 1,000 cells per antibiotic (800 for co-amoxiclav)
Conflicts_of_Interest: A.N.K. is a co-founder and shareholder of Oxford Nanoimaging, the company whose wide-field microscope was used for the work; the other authors declare no competing interests
Inclusion_Criteria: Laboratory reference E. coli strain MG1655 plus six clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6) recovered from human blood cultures and chosen to span a range of ciprofloxacin MICs
Data_Types_Used: Microscopy images; AST phenotypic results; Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: No named public dataset — in-house micrographs of E. coli MG1655 and Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust clinical isolates
Dataset_Size: 29,297 cells in 459 fields of view (training); 9,044 cells in 115 fields of view (validation); 13,247 ground-truth cells in 155 micrographs (holdout); ~50-200 cells per micrograph
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: clinical isolates from the Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust microbiology laboratory plus the MG1655 laboratory strain; no multi-site or multi-country sampling
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood culture isolates of E. coli
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Single-cell binary classification of E. coli cells as susceptible or resistant from fluorescence micrographs (80 % single-cell accuracy reported in the abstract), plus MIC-related information for ciprofloxacin from the dose-response of susceptible:resistant classification ratios
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (laboratory reference strain MG1655 and six clinical isolates EC1-6 from bloodstream infections)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin); aminoglycoside (gentamicin); beta-lactam / beta-lactamase-inhibitor combination (co-amoxiclav); rifamycin (rifampicin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin; gentamicin; co-amoxiclav; rifampicin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptible class = treated cells showing antibiotic-specific cellular phenotypic change; resistant class = untreated cells (phenotype unchanged by treatment); labels are cellular phenotypes, with clinical susceptibility separately defined by MIC/EUCAST breakpoints
AI_Purpose: A deep-learning pipeline (Mask R-CNN segmentation + DenseNet121 classifier, 'DASP') that reads widefield fluorescence micrographs of single bacterial cells and classifies them as susceptible or resistant phenotypes, to provide rapid (30 min) phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility information for E. coli
Num_Models_Compared: A range of segmentation models (Mask R-CNN, Cellpose, YOLO v8) and a range of classification models (DenseNet, ResNet and EfficientNet families) were screened; exact count not stated — per-model accuracies in Supplementary Table S6; the selected pipeline was Mask R-CNN + DenseNet121
Feature_Engineering: None manual — CNNs learn their own convolutional features from the images; preprocessing only: 30-frame averaging, RGB construction from Nile Red/DAPI channels, cross-correlation channel registration, 64x64 resizing, histogram equalisation within the segmentation mask, and on-the-fly augmentation (flips, translations, rotations, cutout, Gaussian blur, brightness, noise)
Feature_Selection_Method: None — learnt CNN features with no manual feature selection; saliency mapping used post hoc to show which image regions drive classifications
Num_Features_Total: No explicit feature count — pixel-level inputs from two fluorescence channels (Nile Red in red, DAPI in green) of 64x64-resized single cells
Class_Imbalance_Method: Class-balanced datasets: equal numbers of cells drawn randomly from each of the 6 experiments for training, and class-balanced holdout evaluation sets
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over batch size and learning rate for each model, with the best pipeline chosen by classification accuracy on the holdout test set
Software_Libraries: Keras 2.2.4 (classifier); Mask R-CNN implementation adapted from the standard matterport/Mask_RCNN TensorFlow/Keras implementation; Adam optimiser; initial weights from the MS COCO dataset
Other_Metrics: Segmentation quality: precision-recall curves across IoU thresholds, mean Average Precision (mAP) 70 % at IoU 0.5, 92 % maximum total recall (12,147 of 13,247 cells detected); classification: per-class confusion matrices, accuracy and percentage/absolute class counts in Fig. 3; clinical isolates: percentage of susceptible/resistant single-cell classifications per isolate and per ciprofloxacin concentration; dose-response inflection points 0.011 ± 0.001 mg/L (EC1) and 0.49 ± 0.18 mg/L (EC2) versus E-test MICs; Tukey range test p-values
Baseline_Method: Gold-standard growth-based AST: 24 h growth curves in the presence of ciprofloxacin (numerical integration of OD600, normalised to untreated cells) and E-test MIC determination
Baseline_Performance: Dose-response inflection points of the phenotype-based assay were close to the E-test MICs (EC1 E-test MIC 0.008 mg/L vs inflection 0.011 ± 0.001 mg/L; EC2 E-test MIC 0.5 mg/L vs inflection 0.49 ± 0.18 mg/L), and growth ratios followed a relationship reciprocal to the susceptible:resistant phenotype ratio
Internal_Validation: Experimental K-fold cross-validation (one of 6 imaging experiments withheld and rotated, result summed over 6 models) plus an independent 7th 'holdout' experiment used for neither training nor hyperparameter optimisation; class-balanced sampling
Train_Test_Split: Cross-validation dataset: cells pooled from 6 experiments and split randomly into training, validation and test sets without replacement; experimental K-fold: 6 experiments, one withheld for testing; holdout: a separate 7th experiment used only for final evaluation
External_Validation_Description: Models trained on the MG1655 laboratory strain were deployed without retraining on six clinical E. coli blood-culture isolates (EC1-6) with different ciprofloxacin MICs, untreated and treated with 10 mg/L ciprofloxacin for 30 min, to test whether single-cell classifications reflect MIC-defined susceptibility
Overfitting_Method: Independent holdout experiment excluded from training and hyperparameter optimisation; K-fold across separate imaging experiments; class-balanced sampling; augmentation to increase robustness against experimental variation
Clinical_Insights: Correct classifications are driven mainly by nucleoid structure and organisation (with membrane attention); misclassified cells did not display the full expected phenotype because of cell-to-cell heterogeneity, and the method may capture heteroresistance and mixed populations that colony-level ASTs miss
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the method should be applicable to a wide variety of antimicrobials and bacterial species because nucleoid and membrane phenotypes are established across organisms, but note this remains to be evaluated and that specific models must be trained per antibiotic-species combination
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation on MG1655 (K-fold across 6 experiments and an independent 7th holdout experiment) followed by deployment without retraining on six independent clinical E. coli isolates (EC1-6); no prospective clinical evaluation, workflow integration or routine use
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory AST workflow — replacing or shortening the culture-based AST step for E. coli by imaging single cells after 30 min of antibiotic exposure
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratories and clinicians using resistance classification around standard clinical breakpoints such as EUCAST
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinical isolates were prepared untreated or treated with ciprofloxacin at 10 mg/L for 30 min, processed identically to training samples (fixation, DAPI/Nile Red staining, agarose pads, widefield imaging), segmented and then classified cell-by-cell to give sample-wide statistics
Barriers_List: Reliance on homogeneous phenotype classes across cells and isolates; need for validation across more species and antibiotics and robust correlation with MIC-based metrics; a specific model required for each antibiotic-species combination (poor scaling with problem size); the assay still needs cultured isolates and does not yet bypass isolation/growth; predictions below a confidence threshold need more data to calibrate
Facilitators_List: Faster than other single-cell AST candidates because many single cells are interrogated simultaneously per field of view; no continuous tracking of live cells required; results within one bacterial life cycle (30 min); learnt features detect subtle phenotypic changes (e.g. co-amoxiclav) and reduce human bias; automated processing scales with data volume
Future_Directions: Microfluidics to bypass pathogen isolation and culture by concentrating bacteria directly from patient specimens; extension to additional antibiotics and bacterial species; coupling with rapid species identification (e.g. targeted FISH staining); reformulation to scale the modelling task; more data to set prediction-confidence thresholds and confirm dose-response correlation with clinical AST
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Saliency mapping (gradient-based attention heatmaps over single-cell inputs)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Post-hoc saliency mapping identified nucleoid structure and organisation as the dominant single-cell predictor, with membrane features secondary; the authors note cell-to-cell heterogeneity means some susceptible cells do not show the full phenotype and are misclassified as resistant
Limitation_Categories: Model/class-homogeneity assumptions; need for further validation in more species and antibiotics; scalability of per-antibiotic/per-species model training; residual culture requirement and CFU counts far above those in infected body fluids; limited antibiotic range demonstrated (E. coli only); phenotype plasticity; prediction-threshold calibration requires more data
Data_Quality_Concerns: Ground-truth segmentation masks required manual data annotation and curation; staining and illumination variation were compensated by histogram equalisation and augmentation; phenotype classes must remain homogeneous for the approach to work
Reporting_Clarity: Clear — defined metrics, full methods, code and data availability statements, and a limitations section are present
Page_References: pp. 1-12 (Results pp. 2-7; Discussion pp. 7-9; Methods pp. 9-10; data/code availability p. 10; acknowledgements and competing interests p. 12)

Title: Simple and Rapid Discrimination of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Based on Gram Staining and Machine Vision
Journal_Source: Microbiology Spectrum (American Society for Microbiology); July/August 2023, Volume 11, Issue 4; article 10.1128/spectrum.05282-22
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design_Other: Laboratory experimental / method-comparison study (bench evaluation of a new Gram-staining plus machine-vision assay on stored clinical isolates)
Funder_Names: Project of Ningbo Leading Medical&Health Discipline (no. 2022-B04); Ningbo 2025 Science and Technology Major Project (no. 2021Z018 and 2022Z148)
Population_Description: 150 Gram-staining images from 50 clinical S. aureus strains (33 MSSA and 17 MRSA collected at the Clinical Microbiology Laboratory, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China); one image per strain with 3 parallel experiments
Data_Source_Other: In-house bright-field microscope images of Gram-stained clinical S. aureus isolates (Leica inverted microscope DMi8); MRSA/MSSA reference labels from agar dilution AST

Best_Performing_Model: ANN (nonlinear artificial neural network) - highest accuracy (0.9733 vs 0.9667) and highest mean AUC (0.9936 vs 0.9930) of the two models; LDA retains the higher specificity (0.9804 vs 0.9608). Metric used: accuracy / mean AUC as stated in the results.

Sample_Size: 150 staining images (50 clinical S. aureus strains: 33 MSSA and 17 MRSA; one image per strain, 3 experiments repeated)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared: 'The authors declare no conﬂict of interest.' (p. 1) and 'We declare no conﬂict of interest.' (p. 8)
