Num_Pathogens: 1 (Staphylococcus aureus; both MRSA and MSSA isolates)
Drug_Classes: Cell wall synthesis inhibitors / beta-lactams (oxacillin sodium salt; methicillin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin sodium salt (used experimentally); methicillin (background); penicillin and vancomycin named in the background only
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotype label defined by oxacillin susceptibility: after oxacillin sodium salt treatment the cell wall of methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) is destroyed immediately and the cells appear Gram negative, whereas MRSA is relatively stable and appears Gram positive; the reference classification of the strains was made by agar dilution AST according to CLSI.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To use machine vision (machine-learning analysis of microscope images) to detect the oxacillin-induced colour change in Gram-stained S. aureus and thereby distinguish MRSA from MSSA rapidly, without overnight culture.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (linear discriminant analysis [LDA] and nonlinear artificial neural network [ANN])
Feature_Engineering: Gray statistics-based preprocessing: every staining image was grayscale-stretched to 0-255; the bacterial region of interest was segmented with an automatic global binary threshold from the image histogram; the reduced ROI image was split into red, green and blue channels and the average gray value of each channel (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean) formed the three feature values.
Feature_Selection_Method: No formal feature selection: all three extracted features (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean) were fed to both classifiers; PCA and t-SNE were used only for unsupervised visualisation of the feature space.
Num_Features_Total: 3 (R_mean, G_mean, B_mean)
Num_Features_Selected: 3 - all extracted colour features were used; no feature selection step is reported
Hyperparameter_Method: Repeated refitting while adjusting parameters until the best model performance was reached (search grid not specified); the ANN was fixed at three layers - one input layer, one hidden layer with 10 nodes and one output layer - with stochastic gradient descent (sgd) for weight optimisation and rectified linear unit (relu) activation in the hidden layer.
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn and seaborn packages in Python (version 3.8); image analyses performed on HALCON (v.12.0; MVTec Software GmbH, Germany)
Other_Metrics: Mean area under the ROC curve (AUC): 0.9930 (LDA) and 0.9936 (ANN); permutation test used to check for overfitting; Student's t test for P values; PCA and t-SNE for unsupervised visualisation of the feature data.
Baseline_Method: LDA (linear discriminant analysis) - named in the paper as the simple and reliable linear model, compared against the more complicated learning-based ANN
Baseline_Performance: LDA: accuracy 0.9667, sensitivity 0.9596, specificity 0.9804, precision 0.9899, F1 0.9744; mean AUC 0.9930
Internal_Validation: 3-fold cross-validation: two folds used for training and the remaining fold for validation, cycled three times until all data had been involved in training and testing
Train_Test_Split: No fixed hold-out split; the 150 images were randomly divided into three folds with 3-fold cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: Permutation test used to check whether the LDA and ANN classifiers modelled from the extracted gray-value features were overfitted (Fig. S52)
Clinical_Insights: The discriminative red-channel gray value reflects the purple (Gram-positive) versus pink (Gram-negative) appearance of the stained cells: when oxacillin destroys the MSSA cell wall the stain is no longer retained and the cells look Gram negative, while MRSA keeps the purple colour - the machine-vision feature therefore tracks a microbiologically meaningful stain change.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state that the new strategy could be used for other bacteria and represents a new rapid method for clinically identifying antibiotic resistance, with emergency applications; no formal assessment of transportability across sites, populations or instruments is reported.
Maturity_Evidence: 3-fold cross-validation of the LDA and ANN classifiers on 150 staining images from 50 clinical strains; no external data set, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment or CDS integration is reported.
Integration_Point: Not described - the method is a bench microscopy workflow (oxacillin treatment, Gram staining, imaging, MV analysis) and no clinical system or laboratory information system integration is reported.
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory (implicit): the method is proposed to fill the stated need for rapid, low-cost clinical identification of MRSA.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Oxacillin sodium salt (256 micrograms/mL) is added to the bacterial suspension, incubated for 30 min at 37 degrees C, washed and Gram stained, the slide is imaged by microscope and the image is analysed by MV to discriminate MRSA from MSSA; the whole process can be completed within 1 h, avoiding overnight incubation.
Future_Directions: The authors propose extending the strategy to other bacteria and developing it as a new rapid method for detecting clinical antibiotic resistance; they also note that because of the high concentration of antibiotics the proportion of pink spheres within MRSA increased, which they attribute to the antibiotic concentration.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: PCA loading coefficients of the first principal component, supported by 3D feature scatter plots and violin plots; no supervised importance metric such as permutation importance or SHAP is reported.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Staining images were normalised by grayscale stretching to eliminate variation from ambient brightness and camera parameters, and the oxacillin concentration and incubation time were optimised to avoid observation errors.
Reporting_Clarity: Model performance is fully tabulated - Table 1 gives accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 for both LDA and ANN - and the 3-fold cross-validation is described, but the paper has no limitations section, no code or data availability statement, and the ROC curves are cited as Fig. 5e/f in the text while the figure itself is numbered Fig. 6e/f.
Page_References: pp. 1-9 (all nine pages read; references run to p. 9)

Title: Machine learning to predict risk for community-onset Staphylococcus aureus infections in children living in southeastern United States
Funder_Names: National Library of Medicine (1G08LM013190-01); AHRQ K-08 Mentored Clinical Scientist Career Research Development Award (HS024338-01); National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences / NIH (UL1TR002378); NIH / NICHHD, NIDA, NIAID, NIEHS, NCI, NIMHD grants (R01HD092580, T32DA050552, R01AI149527, U01AI148069, UG3AI176853, R01ES033530, P30ES019776, R01CA266572, R21MD017943); CDC (6R49CE003072, 23IPA2312301)
Population_Description: Children <19 years of age treated for community-onset S. aureus infection (CO-MRSA or CO-MSSA) within a single pediatric healthcare system (Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta), 2002–2016; restricted to children with a georeferenced residential address in the 20-county Atlanta Metropolitan Statistical Area (block-group level area data from US Census/ACS).
Age_Range: Children <19 years of age (analysis age groups: 0–3, 4–12, >12 years)
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Other national / population survey
Top_Predictive_Features: Percent contribution (permutation importance in brackets) by model: population density 80.2% (84.1) MRSA 02–05, 84.8% (72.4) MSSA 02–05, 79.9% (89.3) MRSA 06–16, 92.2% (92) MSSA 06–16; proportion black race 4.7% MRSA 02–05; average distance to area hospital 3.7% MRSA 02–05 and 3.6% MSSA 02–05; average distance to day care 3.5% MRSA 02–05 and 3.8% MRSA 06–16; proportion white race 8.6% MRSA 06–16 and 2.1% MSSA 06–16; proportion with a Bachelor’s degree 4.7% MSSA 02–05.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
System_Level_Applications: AMR surveillance / trend prediction; Resource allocation / supply chain
All_Models_Evaluated: Four MaxEnt ecological-niche model runs (CO-MRSA 2002–2005 and 2006–2016; CO-MSSA 2002–2005 and 2006–2016); metric = AUC (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation/test 0.769–0.804) plus omission-rate binomial tests; jack-knife AUC for variable importance.
AUROC_Population_Set: Evaluation (test) points — highest of the four MaxEnt runs; evaluation AUC range 0.769–0.804 across runs; occurrence points from the 20-county Atlanta MSA dataset
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models developed and evaluated only by random subsampling within the same dataset (75% train / 25% evaluation); no external dataset, no prospective use, no clinical integration.
Reported_Limitations: (1) Only 14 variables selected; other built-environment variables (transportation access, housing quality/type) were incomplete and omitted. (2) Race categories beyond black, white and Asian could not be differentiated, and no Latinx sub-category could be assigned. (3) Cultural/community boundaries differ from census tract or block group boundaries, so community-level cultural influences are not captured. (4) Generalizability may be limited to urban settings in the southeastern U.S.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race and ethnic disparities in CO-S. aureus infection risk are noted and race is a leading model contributor; the authors caution that neighbourhood race variables need further elucidation because cultural communities are not captured by census block groups.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Study approved by the institutional review boards with waiver of parental/patient consent; no ethical or governance risks of the machine learning application itself are discussed.
Reviewer_Notes: POINTS OF JUDGEMENT. (1) Unit of analysis: the paper reports four MaxEnt runs (CO-MRSA/CO-MSSA x early/late) on one dataset and names no best run, so Best_Performing_Model is blank with Best_Performing_Model_NA = TRUE; AUROC_Value is the top of the reported evaluation range (0.804). (2) The abstract's AUC ranges (training 0.771–0.824; testing 0.769–0.839) disagree with the Results (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation 0.769–0.804). (3) Data_Types_Used 'Other' = census/ACS block-group socio-economic variables and geospatial distance variables. (4) Study_Setting coded Community because the model is a neighbourhood-level ecological niche model, although the patient data come from a hospital EHR. (5) Interpretability coded Post-hoc: MaxEnt percent contribution, permutation importance and jack-knife are global diagnostics of a fitted model. (6) Reporting_Guideline 'None reported' — no reporting checklist is named; the quote shows the Supporting information list.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the four MaxEnt runs should be treated as four separate models or one model applied to four strata, and whether a per-run AUC (only in Fig 2) should override the reported range. Whether MaxEnt percent contribution/jack-knife should count as intrinsic or post-hoc interpretability. No code, model or repository is shared.
Sample_Size: 16,124 unique patients / occurrence points with community-onset S. aureus (7,867 CO-MRSA; 8,257 CO-MSSA); 15,094 unique occurrence points analysed in the machine learning models
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
Inclusion_Criteria: Children treated for community-onset S. aureus infections from January 2002 through December 2016; first S. aureus culture per unique patient per 12-month calendar year; georeferenced residential address within the 20 counties of Atlanta’s MSA.
Exclusion_Criteria: Repeated culture results per unique patient excluded (only the first culture per patient per 12-month year counted); patients without a georeferenced address or living outside the 20 counties of Atlanta’s MSA excluded.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Other
Data_Source_Name: Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta electronic medical records (EMR); U.S. Census / American Community Survey (ACS) 2010 and 2013 block-group data; Atlanta Regional Commission (ARC) geospatial data
Dataset_Size: 22,366 S. aureus infections (2002–2016) yielding 16,124 unique CO-S. aureus occurrence points (7,867 CO-MRSA; 8,257 CO-MSSA); 15,094 occurrence points entered the MaxEnt models; 2,609 block groups (78% of 3,335)
Ethnicity_Details: Hispanic vs non-Hispanic; among 1,558 Hispanic children with S. aureus infections, 12% had CO-MRSA vs 16% CO-MSSA (p<0.0001); Hispanic ethnicity data not available for 2002–2005.
Geographic_Representativeness: 20-county Atlanta MSA, Georgia, USA; analyses included 78% (2,609) of the 3,335 block groups in the MSA; data from a single pediatric healthcare system (Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta) covering >90% of pediatric hospitalisations for this condition.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Microbiology culture from source of infection which resulted in positive S. aureus; majority of community-onset disease was skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI).
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance status of community-onset S. aureus infection: CO-MRSA vs CO-MSSA, classified by oxacillin susceptibility, modelled as the spatial probability of occurrence of each type across the 20-county Atlanta MSA.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA, and methicillin-sensitive, MSSA)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin susceptibility used as the marker of methicillin resistance)
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (defines MRSA vs MSSA)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Community-onset defined as a positive S. aureus culture within 48 hours between healthcare visit date and specimen collection date; resistance to oxacillin categorised as MRSA and susceptibility to oxacillin as MSSA.
Num_Models_Compared: 4 MaxEnt model runs (CO-MRSA early and late; CO-MSSA early and late)
Feature_Engineering: All area variables aggregated to census block group level; Euclidean distances to daycares, K-12 schools and children’s hospitals rasterised and averaged per block group using zonal statistics; rasters aligned at ~328 feet (100 m) resolution (QGIS v3.22, GDAL); duplicate infections within the same raster removed.
Feature_Selection_Method: A priori selection of 14 area-level variables previously reported as CO-MRSA/CO-MSSA risk factors; MaxEnt feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) chosen by lowest AIC using ENMeval
Num_Features_Selected: 14 (all area variables retained in the four MaxEnt runs; model feature classes reduced to linear, quadratic and hinge)
Hyperparameter_Method: Feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) selected on lowest AIC using R package ENMeval v2.0.3; all other MaxEnt settings kept at default
Software_Libraries: MaxEnt software v3.4.4; R package ENMeval v2.0.3; QGIS v3.22; ArcGIS Pro 2.9; GDAL/OGR; SAS 9.4 (PROC GLIMMIX)
Other_Metrics: Training AUC 0.771–0.837 and evaluation AUC 0.769–0.804 for the four MaxEnt runs (abstract reports testing AUC 0.769–0.839); predicted omission rate binomial tests; AUC jack-knife for variable importance; odds ratios with 95% CI for the multilevel models.
Baseline_Method: MaxEnt ROC plots against a random-prediction (AUC = 0.5) reference line; comparison of the machine learning results with previously reported spatial and multilevel regression analyses
Baseline_Performance: Random prediction reference line only; no baseline score quantified
Internal_Validation: Random subsampling: 75% of occurrence points for training, 25% held out for model evaluation; predicted-omission binomial test; jack-knife test of variable importance
Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% evaluation (per run, randomly subsampled occurrence points)
Overfitting_Method: Total number of variables limited to 14 to avoid collinearity and model overload; duplicate occurrence points within a raster removed; only three MaxEnt feature classes (linear, quadratic, hinge) retained after AIC-based selection
Clinical_Insights: Densely populated areas were the single largest predictor of CO-MRSA and CO-MSSA occurrence; population density alone performs nearly as well as all variables; distance to day care and hospitals contributes; race contributed more in CO-MRSA models than CO-MSSA; poverty and education contributed little despite high-density areas having higher poverty and lower education.
Data_Repository: Supporting information files (S1 Table XLSX, S2 Table CSV); no external repository named
Generalisability_Details: Findings are limited to geographic areas similar to the study area — an urban setting in the southeastern U.S.; the authors suggest comparing with settings that have multiple healthcare systems for children.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence = random-subsampling evaluation of the four MaxEnt runs on held-out occurrence points from the same 20-county dataset (no external validation).
Integration_Point: Population / area-level risk mapping at census block-group scale within the Atlanta MSA; not a point-of-care tool
End_User_Described: Local public health agencies and communities; hospitals (for surveillance and prevention planning)
Barriers_List: Built-environment variables (transportation access, housing quality/type) not available or incomplete; race/ethnicity categories collapsed (cannot identify beyond black, white, Asian; no Latinx sub-categories); cultural/community boundaries differ from census units; generalizability limited to similar urban southeastern U.S. settings; household crowding contribution may be underestimated after removal of duplicate raster locations.
Facilitators_List: Large georeferenced dataset spanning more than 10 years; hospital system captures >90% of paediatric admissions for this condition; block-group scale keeps all variables at the same spatial scale (MAUP eliminated).
Future_Directions: Re-run the MaxEnt models replacing non-contributing variables with ‘access’ variables; further elucidate neighbourhood-level race factors and compare with settings that have multiple paediatric healthcare systems.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 8 (clinical, microbiological, laboratory, healthcare utilisation, sociodemographic, environmental, temporal, geographic)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: MaxEnt percent contribution and permutation importance (Table 6); jack-knife test of AUC with each variable in isolation and excluded
Novel_Predictors_Details: Population density was by far the single most important predictor (80–92% contribution); proximity to paediatric congregate care (day care centres) and hospitals also predicted risk; household crowding contributed <1%, contrary to prior expectations.
Feature_Interactions_Method: MaxEnt feature classes — linear, quadratic and hinge features selected on lowest AIC via R package ENMeval v2.0.3 (quadratic and hinge features capture non-linear relationships and interactions)
Limitation_Categories: Variable selection / data completeness; race and ethnicity classification; generalizability and single health system; neighbourhood and cultural boundary mismatch.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data for candidate built-environment variables were not as complete as the variables selected and were therefore excluded; race/ethnicity recorded only as black, white, Asian or Hispanic.
Reporting_Clarity: AUC ranges are inconsistent between the abstract (training 0.771–0.824; testing 0.769–0.839) and the Results (training 0.771–0.837; evaluation 0.769–0.804), and per-run AUC values appear only in Fig 2; the four MaxEnt runs are described collectively.

Title: The use of infrared spectroscopy and artificial neural networks for detection of uropathogenic Escherichia coli strains’ susceptibility to cephalothin
Journal_Source: Acta Biochimica Polonica (Vol. 60, No 4/2013, pp. 713-718; actabp.pl)
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: National Science Center (Poland), decision DEC-2012/07/N/NZ7/01187
Population_Description: 109 uropathogenic E. coli strains isolated from urine samples of hospitalised patients with urinary tract infection (wards of hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008), stored at -80 degrees C; 10 colonies per strain harvested, giving 1090 IR spectra.
Data_Source_Other: Clinical E. coli isolates from urine cultures of hospitalised patients (hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008); ATR/FTIR spectra measured in-house.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Experiment 1 (3 groups): 10 MLP networks - validating-set correct classifications 83.43% (MLP 30-8-3) descending to 76.69%; 10 RBF networks - validating 58.90% down to 55.21%. Experiment 2 (2 groups): 10 MLP networks - validating 92.64% (MLP 30-9-2) down to 90.80%; 10 RBF networks - validating 65.03% down to 63.80%. Metric reported throughout is the percentage of correctly classified strains in the training / testing / validating subsets (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5).
Best_Performing_Model: MLP 30-9-2 (multilayer perceptron, 30 input - 9 hidden - 2 output neurons) for the two-group sensitive / 'non-sensitive' task: 92.64% correctly classified strains in the validating set (Table 4, ID 1) - the highest accuracy reported for any network in the paper.
Accuracy_Value: 92.64% correctly classified strains (validating set, MLP 30-9-2, two-group task)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Validating subset (15% of the 1090 IR spectra); two-group sensitive / 'non-sensitive' classification
Sensitivity_Value: 93.23% of cephalothin-sensitive strains correctly classified (validating set, best two-group network MLP 30-9-2)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validating set; true cephalothin-sensitive strains (two-group task)
Specificity_Value: 91.9% of 'non-sensitive' strains correctly classified (validating set, best two-group network)
Specificity_Population_Set: Validating set; 'non-sensitive' strains (intermediate + resistant combined, two-group task)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Performance is assessed on a randomly held-out validating subset (15%) of the same 1090 spectra; no external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no decision-support integration.
Reported_Limitations: The main limitation of the technique is the need for a large number of learning data, which grows with network complexity; the best three-group network's 83.43% is 'decidedly unsatisfactory'; performance for resistant (67.5%) and intermediate (77%) strains is much worse than for sensitive strains (95%).
Sample_Size: 109 uropathogenic E. coli strains (10 colonies per strain; 1090 IR spectra in total)
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Other
Dataset_Size: 1090 bacterial IR spectra
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: 109 E. coli strains isolated from urine of patients in the wards of hospital No. 2, Medical University of Lodz, Poland, 2006-2008; no other site, region or country.
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine samples (of hospitalised patients with urinary tract infection)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Susceptibility/resistance of uropathogenic E. coli to cephalothin, coded first as three groups (sensitive / intermediate / resistant) and then as two groups (sensitive vs 'non-sensitive').
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (uropathogenic E. coli)
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (first-generation cephalosporin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Cephalothin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptibility to cephalothin determined by an ATB UR5 (bioMerieux) susceptibility test: 51% of strains sensitive, 27% resistant and 22% intermediate; in the second experiment intermediate and resistant strains were merged into one 'non-sensitive' group.
AI_Purpose: Classification of uropathogenic E. coli strains as cephalothin susceptible/resistant from their ATR/FTIR infrared spectra by designed artificial neural networks (MLP, RBF).
Num_Models_Compared: 20 networks per experiment (10 MLP + 10 RBF; Tables 1-2 and 4-5) = 40 in total
Feature_Engineering: ATR/FTIR spectra pre-treatment: baseline fixed, calculation of the first derivative, scaling to the range 0-1; each colony spectrum averaged from 25 scans
Feature_Selection_Method: Wavenumbers related to cephalothin resistance identified by statistical methods; 30 input neurons used in the final topologies
Num_Features_Selected: 30 input neurons (selected wavenumbers)
Hyperparameter_Method: Manual comparison of network architectures: number of hidden neurons and the activation function varied across ten networks per experiment
Other_Metrics: Percentage of correctly classified strains per class and per subset (training / testing / validating). Validation subset of the best three-group network (Table 3, MLP 30-8-3): sensitive 95%, intermediate 77%, resistant 67.5% correctly classified. Best two-group network: sensitive 93.23%, 'non-sensitive' 91.9%.
Baseline_Method: Principal component analysis (PCA) and cluster analysis (CA)
Baseline_Performance: PCA and CA did not differentiate the E. coli strains (data not shown)
Internal_Validation: Random split of the 1090 IR spectra into independent learning (70%), testing (15%) and validating (15%) subsets
Train_Test_Split: 70% learning / 15% testing / 15% validation
Overfitting_Method: Network complexity used as a secondary selection criterion after the number of correct classifications in the validation subset
Clinical_Insights: Resistance information in the spectrum is dispersed rather than localised: specific enzymes (e.g. beta-lactamase) and transmembrane proteins may be reflected in the spectrum, but the features are spread over its whole length rather than concentrated in one peak.
Generalisability_Details: The authors conclude that ATR/FTIR plus ANNs 'may allow' rapid differentiation of strains by resistance/sensitivity, but no transportability analysis across sites, instruments or populations is reported.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only - random learning (70%) / testing (15%) / validating (15%) split of the 1090 IR spectra from the same 109 strains.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The assay is positioned inside the diagnostic pathway: a life-threatening infection needs correct antibiotic treatment within hours of symptom onset, and chemometric methods would allow susceptibility to be determined within several hours.
Barriers_List: ANNs need a large number of learning data, and larger learning sets are required as network complexity grows; conventional resistance testing is labour- and time-consuming; the best three-group result was 'decidedly unsatisfactory'; complex E. coli phenotypes distort the spectra.
Facilitators_List: ATR/FTIR is fast, cheap, non-invasive and needs no special sample preparation; neural networks resist certain data distortions and recognise patterns better than PCA/CA; susceptibility results could be obtained within hours.
Future_Directions: Use of modern chemometric methods (FTIR, MALDI-TOF) to determine bacterial drug susceptibility within several hours.
Limitation_Categories: Data requirements (need for large learning sets that grow with network complexity); model performance (unsatisfactory overall accuracy in the three-group task, poor recognition of resistant and intermediate strains); biological variability distorting the spectra.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Differences remaining after first-derivative conversion are slight and unstable, so resistant/sensitive strains cannot be separated on them; phenotype differences distort the IR spectrum and can be mistaken for random noise.
Reporting_Clarity: Model comparison tables are complete (topology, error and activation functions, training/testing/validating percentages), but the selected wavenumbers are never listed and the PCA/CA comparison is reported only as 'data not shown'.
Page_References: pp. 1-6 of the text layer (journal pp. 713-718)

Title: Predicting future hospital antimicrobial resistance prevalence using machine learning
Funder_Names: NIHR Health Protection Research Unit in Healthcare Associated Infections and Antimicrobial Resistance (University of Oxford / UKHSA); NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre; Pandemic Sciences Institute; Royal Academy of Engineering; InnoHK Hong Kong Centre for Cerebro-cardiovascular Engineering (COCHE)
Population_Description: Hospital groups (Trusts) in England providing bloodstream-infection susceptibility surveillance; aggregate AMR prevalence and antibiotic usage by Trust and financial year for 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations; 119 Trusts retained after exclusions
Data_Source_Other: IQVIA monthly antibiotic (pharmacy dispensing) usage data
Top_Predictive_Features: Top-10 features per pathogen-antibiotic model ranked by mean absolute SHAP (Tables 1-4). Generally: previous resistance to the same pathogen-antibiotic combination, resistance in a different pathogen to the same antibiotic, and usage of the same / same-class antibiotic. e.g. for E. coli amoxicillin/clavulanic acid the top feature was 'E. coli amoxicillin/clavulanic acid-res, prev1' (SHAP 2.87)
Target_End_User: Surveillance analyst / public health; Programme manager / policymaker

XGBoost best overall; previous-value forwards similar/slightly higher MAE; difference-forwards worst, then LTF.
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (lowest mean absolute error on the test set)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation on a temporal held-out test set: models trained on resistance up to FY2020-2021 (with 3-fold CV hyperparameter tuning) and evaluated on FY2021-2022 as the test outcome. No external dataset and no prospective deployment.
Reported_Limitations: Representativeness of tested isolates for the population served; imperfect antibiotic-usage denominator (bed-days); aggregation to financial years loses within-year seasonality; short time series (main statistical limitation); only one-year-ahead prediction; number of training examples too small for better-than-default hyperparameters.
Sample_Size: 119 hospital Trusts (hospital groups), each a training/test example; 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations, up to 6 financial years
Conflicts_of_Interest: D.W.E. declares lecture fees from Gilead, outside the submitted work; all other authors declare no competing interests.
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded Trusts testing <100 isolates per year; excluded Trust-pathogen-antibiotic-FYs with <=10 susceptibility results; 19 Trusts with <100 tested isolates/FY excluded (16 specialised Trusts).
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: UKHSA Second Generation Surveillance System (SGSS); IQVIA
Dataset_Size: 119 Trusts across up to 6 financial years, 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations
Missing_Data_Method: XGBoost learns, at each decision-tree split, the classification of the missing-value group that minimises MAE; small-number (<=10 results) cells excluded; usage missing for only a few Trusts in the highest-usage antibiotics.
Geographic_Representativeness: 138 hospital groups (Trusts) across England for FY2016-2022; 119 retained (data from ~98% of hospital microbiology laboratories); bloodstream infections representative via widespread testing in a high-income setting.
Specimen_Type_Detail: bloodstream infections (bacteraemia)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Future antimicrobial resistance prevalence (percentage of isolates resistant) in bloodstream infections, per hospital Trust per financial year, for 22 pathogen-antibiotic combinations (outcome in test set FY2021-2022).
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella species; methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus (MSSA/coagulase-positive staphylococci); Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug_Classes: Tetracyclines (doxycycline); macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin); lincosamides (clindamycin); glycopeptides (vancomycin); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin); third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime, ceftazidime, cefpodoxime, ceftriaxone); aminoglycosides (gentamicin); carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem); penicillin/beta-lactam combinations (co-amoxiclav, piperacillin/tazobactam)

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Percentage of isolates resistant to each antibiotic per Trust per financial year; intermediate susceptibility treated as susceptible (EUCAST increased-exposure recommendation).
AI_Purpose: Predict future antimicrobial-resistance prevalence at hospital-Trust level from historical aggregate resistance and antimicrobial usage, to target interventions and allocate resources.
Feature_Engineering: Time-series feature engineering: each Trust contributes one row of lagged historical features (resistance prevalence prev1-prev3/4, usage prev1-prev6); usage standardised to DDDs per 100 bed-days; optional feature selection by SHAP-importance threshold above white-noise.
Feature_Selection_Method: Refitting models using only features with feature importance (mean absolute SHAP) above white-noise level
Hyperparameter_Method: 3-fold cross-validation on the training dataset to tune number of estimators, maximum depth, and minimum child weight
Other_Metrics: Mean absolute error (MAE) as the primary performance metric; mean absolute SHAP values for feature importance / model interpretability.
Baseline_Method: Previous value (last resistance prevalence) taken forwards; difference between the previous two years taken forwards; linear trend forecasting (LTF)
Baseline_Performance: Previous value forwards similar to, or slightly higher MAE than XGBoost; difference-forwards worst (highest MAE), then LTF
Internal_Validation: 3-fold cross-validation on the training dataset for hyperparameter tuning
Train_Test_Split: Calendar-time split: training outcome FY2020-2021 (with up to 6 prior FYs of features), test outcome FY2021-2022
Overfitting_Method: Hyperparameter tuning (CV), feature selection, and feature engineering to improve generalisability; authors note over-fitting was reduced though performance barely improved.
Clinical_Insights: SHAP ranked features showed previous resistance to the same pathogen-antibiotic combination, resistance in a different pathogen to the same antibiotic, and usage of same / same-class antibiotics among the top features, indicating the model exploits cross-pathogen and cross-antibiotic resistance/usage relationships.
Generalisability_Details: Domain knowledge used to standardise usage across Trusts (DDDs and occupied beds); authors relate their results to European/national studies and note assumptions are reasonable in a high-income setting.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: temporal train/test split (test outcome FY2021-2022) with 3-fold CV hyperparameter tuning on the training set; no external dataset, no prospective or deployed use.
Future_Directions: As time series lengthen, deep learning (LSTM and transformer) models become viable; predicting >1 year ahead (autoregressive or encoder-decoder architectures); incorporating community antibiotic-usage features; potential quarterly granularity when numbers permit.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: mean absolute SHAP values (computed on the test set, averaged across Trusts)
Feature_Interactions_Method: Mean absolute SHAP feature-importance analysis; XGBoost inherently learns non-linear interactions between features
Limitation_Categories: Bias/representativeness (tested isolates vs population served); measurement (imperfect usage denominator); aggregation/seasonality (financial-year aggregation); time series length (too short for deep learning & multi-step); training sample size (too small to gain from hyperparameter tuning).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Uncommon outliers possibly reflecting data-quality issues; likely some large outliers remain despite data cleaning; Trust assignation in laboratory-only data historically poor (hence mandatory-surveillance linkage); possible supply interruptions and COVID-19 impacts.

Title: Extending outbreak investigation with machine learning and graph theory: Benefits of new tools with application to a nosocomial outbreak of a multidrug-resistant organism
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Swiss National Science Foundation
Population_Description: Patients of a 900-bed tertiary-care university hospital in Bern, Switzerland, whose medical records were generated during the first 2 years of the VRE outbreak: 560 VRE-positive patients (cases) compared with 86,684 controls tested or untested (N = 87,244); all patients including children were labelled
Age_Mean_Median: VRE positive: median 73 years [IQR 63 –82]; VRE negative or not tested: median 58 years [IQR 33 –75]
Data_Source_Other: Hospital IT systems (time and resource management system and device-tracking systems) supplying employee-contact, room and medical-device records
Top_Predictive_Features: Decision-tree importance: No. of different antibiotics 0.214; Charlson score, mean 0.191; No. of rooms 0.145; Age 0.107; Charlson score (last) 0.104; No. of hospitalizations 0.067; No. of surgeries, all stays 0.066; Length of stay (per 5 days) 0.064; ICU stay (at any time) 0.020; Sex 0.011; Patient had surgery at any time 0.010
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Task_Type_Other: Network graph / eigenvector centrality analysis of transmission pathways
All_Models_Evaluated: 1) Multivariable logistic regression (risk factors: age aOR 1.4 per 10 years; ICU stay aOR 1.5; Charlson score aOR 1.1; no. of different antibiotics aOR 1.6; no. of rooms aOR 1.1, all P < .001; no discrimination metric reported). 2) Decision tree, maximum depth 6 (feature importance: antibiotics 0.214, Charlson mean 0.191, rooms 0.145; confirmed the logistic-regression findings). 3) Network graph / eigenvector centrality (screening efficiency 40.0% fewer screenings, 95% CI 17.3 – 54.6; screening benefit 102 additional VRE-positive patients detected, 95% CI 66 – 138, versus proximity-based screening).
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validation was performed within the same hospital: the oncology ward screened all patients every week, giving a ground truth against which the model's weekly predicted VRE-positive cases were compared with the observed cases; no external (other-hospital) validation was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Monocentric study, not validated against data from another hospital; incomplete data -- physician interactions not documented so employee contacts limited to nursing staff, and only IT-tracked (larger, non-portable) medical devices included; no fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse, which slowed implementation; interpretations require consideration of data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Data-governance constraints rather than ethical harms: interactions documented by healthcare workers were limited to nursing employees because physician interactions are not recorded at that granularity, and only IT-tracked medical devices were included. The study was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Committee (Bern, Project ID no. 2020-00173).
Sample_Size: 560 VRE patients (cases) and 86,684 controls (patients), N = 87,244 patients
Conflicts_of_Interest: All authors report no conflicts of interest relevant to this article.
Sex_Distribution: VRE positive: male 346 (61.8%); VRE negative or not tested: male 44,019 (50.8%)
Inclusion_Criteria: All patients (including children) with VRE acquisition during the outbreak period January 1, 2018-December 31, 2019 were labelled VRE-positive (cases); all other patients, whether tested or not, were assumed VRE negative (controls). Data were electronic medical records from the first 2 years of the outbreak.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Project-specific data warehouse at Bern University Hospital (Inselspital), integrating electronic medical records from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2019
Dataset_Size: 87,244 patients: 560 VRE positive and 86,684 VRE negative or not tested
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary-care university hospital in Bern, Switzerland (900-bed, 60,000 admissions and 380,000 patient days per year), covering the whole hospital; the authors note that validation against data from another hospital would have improved the study.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: VRE colonization (VRE-positive, that is colonized or infected with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium), modelled as a binary outcome (0 = no, 1 = yes)
Pathogens: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VRE), sequence type 796 (ST796) predominant; all subtypes analysed
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptide (vancomycin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary VRE positivity from electronic medical records: the dependent variable of the logistic regression was colonization (0 = no, 1 = yes); patients were labelled VRE-positive (cases) if they had VRE acquisition during the outbreak period and all other patients, whether tested or not, were assumed VRE negative (controls).
AI_Purpose: To improve existing nosocomial outbreak investigation by applying machine learning (decision tree) and graph-theoretical network analysis to identify risk factors for VRE colonization, determine which patients should be screened, and locate transmission hot spots (devices, rooms, employees), and to compare the resulting prioritised screening with traditional proximity-based contact screening.
Feature_Engineering: No bespoke feature construction: the classification tree was built with the same independent and dependent variables as the logistic regression (the variables in Table 1); a minority-class oversampling step produced equal numbers of positive and negative samples.
Feature_Selection_Method: Logistic regression: most parsimonious model by forward selection then backward deletion, P > .10 inclusion criterion; decision tree: covariate importance ranking used to reveal the most predictive variables
Class_Imbalance_Method: Minority class oversampling, resulting in equal numbers of positive and negative samples
Software_Libraries: Python 3.7: pyodbc, numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, networkx, pytorch, seaborn, bokeh, Holoviz, Holoviews; R version 3.5 or newer: data.table, ggplot2, tableone, survey
Other_Metrics: Decision-tree feature importance (Table 3); screening efficiency: 40.0% fewer screenings compared with the current gold standard (95% CI, 17.3 – 54.6); screening benefit: 102 (95% CI, 66 – 138) VRE-positive patients detected who were missed by proximity-based screening
Baseline_Method: Proximity-based contact screening, described as the current gold standard (patients screened if hospitalized in the same room and ward as a newly detected VRE-positive patient in the prior 7 days)
Internal_Validation: Model validation on the oncology ward, which screened all patients every week, so that for each week the predicted VRE-positive cases from the model could be compared with the observed cases (ground truth); performance summarised as screening efficiency and screening benefit relative to proximity-based screening.
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: The decision tree provided thresholds that split the data appropriately and allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization. The network analysis identified 3 pathways linking the 560 VRE cases (healthcare personnel, medical devices, patient rooms) and produced a daily hotspot list of rooms, devices and employees ordered by likelihood of being colonized.
Generalisability_Details: The method provides the basis for a smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially for data-driven outbreak monitoring; the authors add that data-science interpretations should consider data-source maturity, the scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: predictions compared with the oncology ward's weekly screening ground truth within the same hospital; the authors state the study was monocentric and could have been improved by validating against data from another hospital.
Integration_Point: Outbreak management: the daily hotspot list is sent to the organisational unit that disinfects rooms and medical devices, and the network-graph method produces a prioritised screening list for patients in place of proximity-based contact screening.
End_User_Described: The organisational unit involved in disinfecting rooms and medical devices, plus those deciding how to isolate patients and clean devices and rooms.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The new prioritised screening list derived from the network graph is compared with the current gold-standard proximity-based screening; the hotspot list orders devices, healthcare personnel and patient rooms by likelihood of being colonized so that isolation, disinfection and potential screening of personnel can be targeted.
Barriers_List: Lack of a fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse, which slowed implementation; information on physicians and other key personnel absent from the time and resource management system, so employee contacts were limited to nursing staff; only IT-tracked (larger, non-portable) medical devices captured; data-source integration and operationalisation were the most time-consuming and resource-intensive steps; the popularity of machine-learning methods can lead to an analysis-driven approach ("85% of data science projects fail").
Facilitators_List: Availability of a hospital-wide, fully integrated data warehouse as a prerequisite for fast implementation and actionable results; a clear project mandate with metrics for success defined before the project started; data maturity, scope of included sources and consideration of confounding factors.
Future_Directions: A smart contact-tracing system for the next outbreak, independent of pathogen, and potentially data-driven outbreak monitoring; defining appropriate metrics at project initiation; validation against data from another hospital; consideration of data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Decision-tree feature importance (the rank of the covariate in splitting the data set: the higher the importance, the earlier the covariate is used in the branching process)
Novel_Predictors_Details: The decision-tree analysis allowed insights not apparent from the logistic regression: patients receiving antibiotics and those aged >55 years were at higher risk for colonization; number of rooms stayed in and patient-device interactions highlighted environmental contamination as an important factor.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Decision tree with a maximum depth of 6 levels, motivated by the complex interactions and multiple collinearities seen in the fitted statistical models; collinear variables were not estimated in the multivariable logistic model (Table 2 note).
Limitation_Categories: Monocentric / single-institution design and lack of external validation; incomplete data on physician and other personnel contacts; only IT-tracked medical devices; no fully integrated hospital-wide data warehouse; data-source maturity, scope of included sources and potential confounding factors.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Interactions documented by healthcare workers were limited to nursing employees because physician interactions are not documented at that granularity for in-patient care; for medical devices only interactions tracked in the IT systems were included, limiting the study to larger, often non-portable devices.
Reporting_Clarity: The article reports models, variables, software and the validation ward clearly, but the computation of the screening-efficiency and screening-benefit metrics is deferred to the Supplementary Material, and no discrimination metric (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC) is reported for any model.
