(The related-work section also notes the small number of instances typical of deep learning for medical imaging.)
Reviewer_Notes: Presented as the first model able to determine TB and the type of drug resistance from a single CXR image and to display an appropriate treatment regimen; delivered as the TB-DRC-DSS web application (https://itbru.com/TDRC01/) with source code at https://github.com/aiosmartlab/AMIS-Ensemble-DL.
Sample_Size: 5,606 training and 1,408 test CXR images (7,008 in the aggregate dataset)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: Portal dataset (TB Portals, NIAID); Montgomery County CXR dataset; Shenzhen CXR dataset; Dataset B (compiled by institutes under the Ministry of Health, Republic of Belarus); Kaggle public chest X-ray (COVID-19 and pneumonia) dataset
Dataset_Size: 7,008 CXR images in the aggregate dataset (5,606 train / 1,408 test); portal dataset 5,019 TB CXR images; Dataset A 800 images; Dataset B 306 images; Dataset C 6,432 images
Geographic_Representativeness: Data are pooled from several countries and sources - Montgomery County (USA) and Shenzhen (China) in Dataset A, institutes under the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Belarus in Dataset B, the multi-country TB Portals and the Kaggle repository - but geographic representativeness is not analysed or discussed.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of chest X-ray images into five classes - TB-negative (non-TB), drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB), drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) - with a recommended treatment regimen returned by the TB-DRC-DSS.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Anti-tuberculosis (anti-TB) drugs; no specific agent or drug class is named - the paper refers to the recommended TB treatment regimen that the pharmacist updates.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; XDR; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: The label of each CXR image is the patient's drug-susceptibility category obtained from drug susceptibility testing (not read off the image): binary DS-TB vs DR-TB pairs and the MDR-TB and XDR-TB resistance categories.
AI_Purpose: Detect TB and classify the drug-resistance category from a chest X-ray image, and provide treatment recommendations, through the TB-DRC-DSS decision support system.
Num_Models_Compared: 12 proposed models (N-1 to N-12) compared with one another, plus performance compared against 13 published methods from the literature
Feature_Engineering: Lung-field image segmentation with a modified U-Net (EfficientNetB7 encoder), image augmentation, cropping, normalisation and enhancement of the CXR images before the three heterogeneous CNNs, followed by UWA / AMIS-WCE / AMIS-WLCE decision fusion of the CNN outputs.
Hyperparameter_Method: AMIS metaheuristic used to find the optimal decision-fusion weights (Wi and Sij); fixed training settings of batch sizes 16 (MobileNetV2), 2 (EfficientNetB7) and 8 (DenseNet121), 200 epochs and the Adam algorithm
Software_Libraries: TensorFlow; HTML and JavaScript for the web application; CNN architectures MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB7, DenseNet121 and a modified U-Net with EfficientNetB7 encoder
Other_Metrics: Confusion matrices (Figure 1); per-class accuracy (non-TB 98.99%, DS-TB 92.2%, DR-TB 97.1%, MDR-TB 88.7%, XDR-TB 91.1%); average percentage difference versus prior methods (Table 4); TB-DRC-DSS per-class % correct classification (Table 8); six-item user agreement questionnaire scored out of 10 (Table 9).
Baseline_Method: Published single-architecture and feature-based comparators (VGG16, ResNet50, EfficientNet, MobileNetv2, FuseNet, MAG-SD, CoroNet, TBXNet) and prior drug-resistance models (Karki et al. ResNet18, Tulo et al. mediastinal shape, Jaeger et al. texture/shape/edge, Kovalev et al., Ureta and Shrestha CNN)
Baseline_Performance: Portal dataset, DS vs DR: best prior AUC 93.6 (Tulo et al.) and 79.0 (Karki et al.) vs proposed 97.2 AUC / 95.2 accuracy. Dataset A: best comparator TBXNet 98.9 vs proposed 99.4; Dataset B: TBXNet 99.2 vs proposed 99.3; Dataset C: TBXNet 95.1 vs proposed 97.4.
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation on the 5,606-image training set, with a separate 1,408-image (20%) held-out test set for final evaluation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test (5,606 training images, 1,408 test images)
Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers in the modified U-Net decoder to improve generalisation and prevent over-fitting; residual blocks to avoid vanishing gradients; data augmentation
Clinical_Insights: The Grad-CAM heatmaps show which lung sectors drive each class: non-TB uses all six lung areas, DS-TB the lung interior from top to bottom, DR-TB the upper left and right sectors, and MDR-TB and XDR-TB the lower and upper left/right sectors, with MDR-TB using the inner and XDR-TB the outer portion of the lung.
Generalisability_Details: Performance is compared across datasets from different sources and countries (Dataset A: Montgomery County and Shenzhen; Dataset B: Belarus; Dataset C: Kaggle), but there is no discussion of applicability to other patient populations or settings.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: five-fold cross-validation of the 5,606-image training set and a held-out 1,408-image test set; the model was then embedded in the TB-DRC-DSS web application, tested on 428 images drawn at random from the test dataset and rated by 31 medical staff. No external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported.
Integration_Point: TB-DRC-DSS web application: the user uploads a CXR image, the deep learning model predicts the disease type, and the system returns medication recommendations for that disease
End_User_Described: Physicians who are TB specialists (pulmonologists and internal medicine); the pharmacist administers the TB-DRC-DSS and updates the treatment regimen prescribed to the physician
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Medical staff upload CXR image files from their personal computers; the image is forwarded to a server that diagnoses the disease and suggests appropriate drugs and medications; the pharmacist updates the treatment regimen; the recommendation is sent back to the user.
Future_Directions: Three research gaps: (1) develop a more accurate model for multiclass drug-resistant classification and TB detection (better image segmentation, augmentation and normalisation, and denoising); (2) extend the web application to support therapy follow-up and further decisions based on the recommended protocol; (3) let the pharmacist follow WHO treatment regimens, record the patient's drug reaction and use data mining to adapt the regimen as resistance emerges.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Grad-CAM (GradCAM heatmap visualisations on the X-ray images)
Limitation_Categories: Accuracy ceiling (classification is not 100% accurate) and scope for better image preprocessing (segmentation, augmentation, normalisation, denoising); web application lacks therapy follow-up and downstream decision support; regimens must be updated as treatment resistance emerges, requiring WHO-conformant pharmacist input and data mining of patient drug reactions.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Drug-susceptibility labels associated with each image are not produced from the image itself but obtained through drug susceptibility testing, and the analysis pools heterogeneous public datasets from different countries and institutions.
Reporting_Clarity: Generally clear, with minor internal inconsistencies: Table 9 is headed '30 doctors' while the text and abstract report 31 medical staff, and the 'Total' row of Table 8 sums the percentage columns to 463.8% and 36.2%.
Page_References: pp. 1-27 (main text pp. 1-23; references pp. 24-27)

Title: Development of Predictive Models to Inform a Novel Risk Categorization Framework for Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli–Caused Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection
Journal_Source: Clinical Infectious Diseases (CID), Infectious Diseases Society of America; volume 79, issue 2, pp. 295–304
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: GSK
Population_Description: Female patients aged ≥12 years with a UTI diagnosis (no evidence of complicated UTI) and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of diagnosis; enrollees also needed documented pyuria and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result for at least 1 agent in the 4 antibiotic classes of interest.
Age_Mean_Median: Mean age ranged from 49.7 to 50.4 years across the training and test cohorts for each antibiotic class
Top_Predictive_Features: Top predictors by absolute standardized log odds ratio: race; number of previous UTI episodes (recurrence); US Census Bureau region (particularly residence in the South); prior nonsusceptibility to β-lactams; prior treatment with fluoroquinolones.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: LASSO models (per antibiotic class; the paper's optimal algorithm, test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72); random forest algorithms (compared against LASSO via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation, not selected as optimal); 4 final logistic regression models built on the union of the top 10 LASSO predictors — mean (SE) test-cohort AUROC 0.67 (0.010) for NTF, 0.66 (0.004) for SXT, 0.66 (0.005) for β-lactams, 0.72 (0.005) for fluoroquinolones.
Best_Performing_Model: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) predictive models — named the optimal predictive algorithm across all 4 antibiotic classes on mean AUROC and clinical interpretability; test-cohort AUROC 0.66–0.72
AUROC_Population_Set: Test cohorts (temporal validation); LASSO predictive models for nonsusceptibility to each of the 4 antibiotic classes
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were internally bootstrapped and temporally validated in the test cohorts of the same EHR dataset (training 1 October 2016–31 December 2018; test 1 January 2019–29 February 2020). No external validation was performed; the authors call for validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations, so the highest level supported is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: 1) Models and framework are not a decision algorithm recommending optimal antibiotic treatment; 2) population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates could not be included because the data were unavailable (Census Bureau region used as a proxy); 3) models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, limiting generalisability to diverse US populations; 4) models were anchored on the date of the susceptibility test result rather than the uUTI diagnosis date.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race was identified as a predictor of nonsusceptibility and the authors note it should not be given a causal interpretation or used alone to inform treatment decisions, because it correlates with socioeconomic indicators that were not available in the data.
Sample_Size: 87 487 patients with confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test results (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
Conflicts_of_Interest: R. K. S. is a paid consultant to GSK. W. Y. C., K. K.-S., D. I., F. K., C. G., M. M., L. P., and J. R. are employees of Analysis Group, Inc., a consultancy that received funding from GSK to conduct this study. A. V. J., F. S. M.-G., P. S., D. F., M. T. P., and J. H. are employees of and shareholders in GSK. R. C. has served as a paid consultant to GSK.
Sex_Distribution: All female (study population restricted to female patients ≥12 years)
Inclusion_Criteria: Female patients ≥12 years of age with a diagnosis of UTI, without evidence of complicated UTI, and a positive urine culture for E. coli within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis; documentation of pyuria within ±7 days of diagnosis; and a confirmed antibiotic susceptibility test result of the urinary E. coli isolate for at least 1 agent within the 4 antibiotic classes of interest within ±7 days of the UTI diagnosis.
Exclusion_Criteria: Evidence of complicated UTI
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Optum's de-identified Electronic Health Record (EHR) dataset
Dataset_Size: 87 487 patients (NTF n = 82 225; SXT n = 82 921; β-lactams n = 83 935; fluoroquinolones n = 81 223)
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), assuming data were missing at random; results were largely consistent using MICE versus a complete case analysis.
Ethnicity_Details: Race distribution reported as 85.1%–85.5% White across training and test cohorts (model predictor categories: White [ref.], Black, Asian, Other/unknown); ethnicity (e.g. Hispanic/Latino) is not separately reported.
Geographic_Representativeness: Patients were mostly from the Midwest (63.8%–66.3%) and mostly White, across US Census Bureau regions; US-only data, so generalisability to other populations is limited.
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine culture; urinary E. coli isolate
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Nonsusceptibility (intermediate or resistant) of the patient's urinary E. coli isolate to each of 4 antibiotic classes: NTF, SXT, β-lactams, and fluoroquinolones (4 separate endpoints/models).
Pathogens: Escherichia coli
Drug_Classes: Nitrofurantoin (nitrofuran); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (folate-pathway inhibitor); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Nitrofurantoin (NTF); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT); β-lactams; fluoroquinolones; fosfomycin is mentioned only as another first-line guideline option.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Nonsusceptibility at the class level was defined by a urinary E. coli isolate categorized as “intermediate” or “resistant” to at least 1 of the respective antibiotic agent(s) within each class based on susceptibility test results.
AI_Purpose: To develop and validate predictive models estimating the probability that a female patient's urinary E. coli isolate is nonsusceptible to each of 4 antibiotic classes for uUTI, to identify key predictors of nonsusceptibility, and to build a novel risk categorization framework (low/moderate/high risk) to inform empiric prescribing.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithm types compared (LASSO and random forest) via (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation; 8 fitted models in total (4 LASSO models and 4 final logistic regression models, one per antibiotic class)
Feature_Engineering: Candidate features (demographics, clinical characteristics, microbiology-related characteristics) were evaluated over a 12-month lookback period prior to the susceptibility test result date; Table 3 footnotes show window-based derivations (e.g. previous UTI episodes excluding the uUTI diagnosis date; antibiotic treatment from 6 months prior to 3 days preceding diagnosis; counts of oral antibiotic prescriptions and ED visits).
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO, with the top 10 predictors per class ranked by absolute standardized log odds ratio; the union of the top 10 predictors across the 4 LASSO models (22 features) was used in the final logistic regression models.
Num_Features_Selected: 22 features for each final logistic regression model (union of the top 10 predictors from the 4 LASSO models)
Hyperparameter_Method: (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation used to select the optimal algorithm (LASSO vs random forest); LASSO models fitted in the training cohort with internal bootstrap validation.
Software_Libraries: SAS (version 9.4, SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina) and Python (version 3.9); no specific libraries named
Other_Metrics: AUROC with standard error; predicted probability distributions (mean/SD, median/IQR, min–max) versus observed nonsusceptibility rates; calibration (mean calibration and calibration plots); odds ratios with 95% CIs and P values; proportions of patients in each risk category.
Baseline_Method: Previously published predictive models for antibiotic nonsusceptibility in uUTI (reference 17); US prevalence of nonsusceptibility to each antibiotic class is used as the comparator for the risk categories.
Internal_Validation: Internal bootstrap validation of the LASSO models in the training cohort (mean AUROC and SE); temporal validation in the test cohorts with the SE of the AUROC derived using 200 bootstrapping samples; model selection by (10,5) stratified nested cross-validation.
Train_Test_Split: Temporal split: susceptibility test result date 1 October 2016–31 December 2018 = training cohort; 1 January 2019–29 February 2020 = test cohort.
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
Clinical_Insights: The risk categorization framework separates risk better than US prevalence alone: a patient's probability of a truly nonsusceptible SXT isolate rises to 53.9% if their isolate is categorized high risk and falls to 15.3% if low risk, versus a 25.4% baseline prevalence; the proportion of patients with high-risk isolates was 3- to 12-fold higher among those with truly nonsusceptible isolates.
Generalisability_Details: Models were developed among patients who were mostly White and from the Midwest, with E. coli–caused uUTI, which may limit applicability to diverse US populations and to uUTI caused by other uropathogens; race and Census Bureau region were retained as predictors to improve external validity; future validation in different clinical settings and ex-US populations is proposed.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal bootstrap validation in the training cohort and temporal validation in the test cohorts (same Optum EHR dataset, different time periods); no external or prospective validation is reported.
Integration_Point: Not integrated; proposed future integration into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool that would present patients' predicted probabilities and risk profiles to clinicians.
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating uUTI (to inform empiric prescribing)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians would derive an isolate's predicted probabilities of nonsusceptibility to the 4 antibiotic classes, generate risk profiles, and integrate the framework into clinical workflows via a data visualization tool to assist empiric treatment decisions; the models are not a decision algorithm.
Barriers_List: Models are not a decision algorithm; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were unavailable; models developed among mostly White patients from the Midwest (limited generalisability); predictions anchored on the susceptibility test result date rather than the uUTI diagnosis date; race cannot be interpreted causally or used alone for treatment decisions.
Facilitators_List: First evaluation of nonsusceptibility to 4 commonly prescribed antibiotic classes for uUTI in the US using a large rich EHR database; features identified from a comprehensive literature search plus clinical expert input; two complementary approaches (predictive models with temporal validity and a risk categorization framework).
Future_Directions: Validate the models in different clinical settings and in ex-US populations, and recalibrate them to include population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates; use the models and framework to develop a data visualization tool integrated into clinical workflows.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Absolute standardized log odds ratio from the LASSO models (top 10 predictors per model, combined across models).
Limitation_Categories: Framing/scope (not a decision algorithm); missing data on population-level features (local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates); population representativeness / generalisability (mostly White, Midwest, E. coli only); timing of the prediction anchor (susceptibility test result date vs uUTI diagnosis date); race cannot be interpreted causally and socioeconomic indicators were unavailable.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing information on candidate features was limited and results were largely consistent using MICE versus complete case analysis; population-level features such as local antibiotic nonsusceptibility rates were not available in the data source.
Page_References: Article pp. 295–304 (CID 2024;79(2)); abstract p. 295; methods pp. 296–297 (data source, population, endpoints, model development); results pp. 297–301 (final model performance Table 2 p. 299; predictor log ORs Table 3 pp. 300–301); limitations pp. 302–303; conclusions pp. 303–304. AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a risk-prediction nomogram for multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas during the perioperative period, so that clinicians can assess infection risk before surgery and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.

Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit P = 0.970 (training cohort) and 0.674 (validation cohort); variance inflation factors 1.203-2.079 for the seven covariates; optimal cut-off 0.624; NPV 0.911 (training) and 0.810 (validation).
Internal_Validation: The 266 included cases were randomly divided 2:1 into a training cohort (n=177) for model development and a validation cohort (n=89) for assessing predictive performance; discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test) and decision curve analysis were reported for both cohorts.
Train_Test_Split: Random 2:1 split; training cohort n=177, validation cohort n=89
Clinical_Insights: The authors read the nomogram weights clinically: secondary surgery (reoperation) is a considerable setback that heralds adverse clinical outcomes and is itself an independent risk factor; prolonged hospital and ICU stays create a favourable environment for multidrug-resistant organisms; preoperative WBC/neutrophil and postoperative WBC levels reflect systemic inflammatory status; and postoperative CRP is an independent risk factor, so the model informs targeted infection prevention and rational antibiotic use.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state that although the study was divided into training and validation cohorts, further prospective studies are necessary to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; the small single-centre sample also limits generalisability.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence for the level: 2:1 random split of the 266 single-centre patients into training (n=177) and validation (n=89) cohorts, with AUC 0.905 (training) and 0.793 (validation), Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.970 and 0.674, and DCA in both cohorts. No external validation, no prospective evaluation, no CDS integration - internal validation only.
Integration_Point: Perioperative risk assessment of patients with gastrointestinal fistulas requiring surgery, to identify those at high risk of multidrug-resistant bacterial and fungal infection and target infection prevention and antibiotic selection.
End_User_Described: healthcare providers / clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Limited: the nomogram is proposed for use during the perioperative period to assess the risk of multidrug-resistant infection in patients with gastrointestinal fistulas requiring surgery and to support targeted infection prevention strategies and selection of antibiotics based on drug-sensitivity results; no workflow, pathway or integration detail is given.
Future_Directions: Prospective randomised controlled studies are planned for further exploration; prospective studies are needed to validate the nomogram's accuracy before widespread clinical application; antibiotic use should be incorporated in future analyses.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Nomogram points assigned from the multivariable logistic regression model (each independent risk factor given a specific weight in points, preoperative neutrophil level highest at 100 points)
Limitation_Categories: Study design / setting (retrospective, single centre, selection bias, small sample); absence of prospective validation before clinical application; missing predictor data (antibiotic use not analysed because of complexity, preoperative PCT/CRP excluded for missingness).
Data_Quality_Concerns: A certain proportion of preoperative PCT and CRP values were missing, so these indicators were excluded from the multivariable analysis; antibiotic-use data were incomplete/too complex to analyse because many patients had already received antibiotics before transfer; indicators with more than 20% missing values were discarded.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear and internally consistent for design, cohort flow, predictors and model performance, with AUC, calibration and DCA all reported; values differ between the abstract/Table 7 (AUC 0.905/0.793) and the results text (AUC 0.92/0.78), and the text layer carries kerning artefacts (e.g. 'preoperat i v eW B Cl e v e l'), but no ambiguity in the reported figures.

Generalisability_Details: Small image number may limit generalisability; high bacterial density in images (more magnified images might improve performance); simple microscopy gives limited spatial, temporal and contextual information.
Maturity_Evidence: Only internal validation: 20 % hold-out test set and 5-fold cross-validation on the same 150-isolate image dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment described.
Integration_Point: None described; the model is proposed as a rapid laboratory classification of microscopic images of Gram-stained isolates rather than an integrated clinical system.
End_User_Described: Clinicians, for predicting antibiotic resistance and personalising treatment
Barriers_List: Small number of images limiting generalisability; high bacterial density in the images; limited spatial, temporal and contextual information from simple microscopy; variability and artifacts from sample preparation and image acquisition.
Facilitators_List: Light microscopy: minimal sample preparation, reduced experimental time and cost, broader accessibility; non-destructive repeated imaging; imaging under near-physiological conditions.
Future_Directions: Use more magnified microscopic images; uncover the biological mechanisms driving the wavelet-feature/resistance correlation; extend to enhance applicability and precision of ML-based resistance classification.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) coefficients
Novel_Predictors_Details: Wavelet-transformed radiomics features (mainly GLSZM, GLDM and first-order features) were the most informative for resistance classification — a novel finding for microscopy-image-based resistance prediction.
Limitation_Categories: Sample size / image count; image characteristics (bacterial density, magnification); inherent limits of simple microscopy; sample preparation and acquisition variability/artifacts.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Variability and artifacts from sample preparation and image acquisition could affect reliability and reproducibility, mitigated by using a bacteriologist to discern staining artifacts and standardised protocols.
Reporting_Clarity: Methods reported in detail; all seven algorithms compared with a full metric table (Table 1); the extracted feature list is deferred to Supplementary 1.

Title: Predictive phage therapy for Escherichia coli urinary tract infections: Cocktail selection for therapy based on machine learning models
Journal_Source: PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), 2024, Vol. 121, No. 12, e2313574121
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Canine Welfare Grant from The Dog's Trust; National Council of Science and Technology of Mexico (CONACYT); University of Edinburgh; University of Glasgow; Roslin Institute PhD studentship supported by the BBSRC
Population_Description: 314 uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) strains from urinary tract infections in canine (n = 203) and human (n = 111) patients in the Edinburgh area (human urine n = 81 and human blood n = 30 isolates), whole genome sequenced; a further 10 newly isolated clinical strains were held back for validation
Data_Source_Other: Study-generated interaction dataset: 314 sequenced E. coli isolates challenged with 31 phage in artificial urine growth assays (plus Illumina whole genome sequences)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: 31 Random Forest regression models (one per phage, MUVR package, recursive feature reduction); average RMSE 8-23 across models (interaction score range 0-100); classifier metrics at a threshold of 60 with F1 highest for the generalist phage CHAP1 (0.83)
Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest ML model for the generalist phage CHAP1 (highest F1 = 0.83; F1 chosen as the performance metric)
F1_Population_Set: 301 of the 314 isolates, used for model training and testing; one 75-25 split with 10-fold cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest evidence level is external validation: models trained on 301 of the 314 isolates were applied to 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains not in the training set, and predicted bespoke cocktails were compared with observed bespoke cocktails and a general cocktail in artificial urine and canine urine
Reported_Limitations: Proof-of-principle study with a single species (E. coli) and 31 phage; artificial urine cannot reproduce the variability of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host factors); most genomic features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so receptor and resistance mechanisms cannot be dissected; a high rate of False Negatives can leave too few phage predicted active for cocktail design; feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples untested; wider adoption requires changes in licensing and management of expectations
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False Negatives are preferred to False Positives from a cocktail perspective, but a high False Negative rate can leave a paucity of phage predicted as active; antagonism was seen where a general cocktail scored higher (worse) than its best constituent phage, and bacterial resistance evolved against the general cocktail for some strains
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: ML models replicate biases in their training datasets (illustrated by phage A01, whose imbalanced dataset produced a model prone to False Negatives), and accuracy falls when models are applied to strains from a different population structure
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Safety and registration issues for predictive phage therapy, and licensing plus management of expectations of clinicians and the public
Reviewer_Notes: Extra review notes: (a) the study's unit of analysis is one Random Forest model per phage, so the best model is taken as CHAP1 (F1 = 0.83, the highest and the one the paper highlights); (b) the paper reports no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, AUROC, NPV, AUPRC, kappa, MCC, MAE or calibration figures in the article text - recall and precision values live in SI Appendix Fig. S2, which is not in the PDF; (c) no antimicrobial susceptibility testing, no patient-level clinical data and no environmental/SES variables are used; (d) no compute hardware is described
Unresolved_Items: Numeric recall and precision for the CHAP1 model are in SI Appendix Fig. S2 and per-model RMSE in SI Appendix Table S2 - not available in the article PDF, so Sensitivity_Reported/Precision_PPV_Reported are answered No per the spec note; the number of protein-variant features in the initial model is never stated; whether the Supplementary-Materials field means 'the study has SI' or 'the extractor used SI' is ambiguous
Sample_Size: 314 E. coli isolates (203 canine, 81 human urine and 30 human blood); 301 of the 314 used for ML model training and testing after filtering fragmented assemblies
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: E. coli isolates from canine and human urinary tract infections (plus human bacteraemia blood isolates) that were whole genome sequenced; for the ML analysis, isolates whose assemblies were not fragmented (<600 contigs), giving 301 of the 314 isolates
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates with fragmented assemblies (>=600 contigs) were excluded from ML model training and testing, leaving 301 of the 314 isolates
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
Data_Source_Name: Enterobase (workspace:97040, ecoli_train); Illumina sequencing by MicrobesNG
Dataset_Size: 31 phage x 314 isolates (>9,000 interactions, each in triplicate against a no-phage control); >27,000 growth curves in total
Geographic_Representativeness: Strains were collected from canine and human patients presenting at local clinics in the Edinburgh area only; the authors describe the collection as representative subpopulations rather than a geographically comprehensive sample of UPEC
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine (E. coli isolated from canine and human urinary tract infections) and blood (human bacteraemia isolates)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phage activity (phage susceptibility) of each E. coli isolate, quantified as an interaction score: the ratio of the area under the growth curve with phage to that of the no-phage control x 100
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (uropathogenic E. coli, UPEC)
Drug_Classes: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins (named as first-line UTI antibiotics in humans and pets; background, not modelled)
Specific_Antibiotics: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; fluoroquinolones; cephalosporins (background only; no antimicrobial susceptibility testing performed)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary Infection/No Infection label from the measured and predicted interaction scores at a threshold of 60: score <60 = infection (active interaction), score >60 = no infection
AI_Purpose: To train ML models on bacterial whole genome sequence features to predict phage activity against individual E. coli isolates, so that effective phage cocktails can be selected without manual screening
Num_Models_Compared: 31 (one Random Forest model per phage)
Feature_Engineering: Pangenome analysis (panaroo v1.2.9) of the 301 bacterial sequences to define predicted genes as protein variants (PVs), encoded as binary presence/absence vectors for each isolate
Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive feature reduction using the MUVR package: an initial model with all PVs, then top-ranking features retained to build a smaller model, repeating while RMSE stayed similar
Num_Features_Selected: 6 PVs (CHAP1 model, Fig. 3C)
Class_Imbalance_Method: F1 chosen as the performance metric to account for class imbalance; imbalanced interaction datasets (up to 85:15) were investigated for model bias via confusion matrices; a predefined F1 cutoff of 0.6 used for practical selection
Software_Libraries: MUVR (random forest regression and feature reduction); panaroo (v1.2.9); prokka (v1.14.5); gplots (v3.1.3); Enterobase Tool Kit (EToKi); SkanIt Software (Thermo); PRISM (GraphPad)
Other_Metrics: RMSE (score prediction); F1, recall and precision (classification at threshold 60); False Positive and False Negative counts for the CHAP1 model (7% FN, 10.8% FP); paired t tests with P values for cocktail comparisons
Internal_Validation: One 75-25 training/testing split with 10-fold cross-validation (MUVR)
Train_Test_Split: 75-25 (one split of training/testing data)
External_Validation_Description: 10 newly isolated clinical UPEC strains (3 canine and 7 human) not used in model training were genome sequenced and run through the models; predicted and observed bespoke cocktails were then tested in artificial urine and canine urine
Generalisability_Details: Models should hold within a similar population structure to the training set but accuracy falls on strains from different population structures; the strain collection covers local canine and human UPEC isolates only, and more generalist phage are needed to make cocktail selection broadly applicable
Maturity_Evidence: External validation on 10 independent sequenced clinical isolates: predicted bespoke cocktails were more effective than a generic cocktail and comparable to bespoke cocktails built from measured activity
Integration_Point: Clinical laboratory diagnostic sequencing: isolate genome sequence is fed to the models to select phage cocktails for the patient
End_User_Described: Clinicians (human and veterinary) and the general public as recipients of phage therapy; expectations of both must be managed
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Direct sequencing of nucleic acids from clinical samples (e.g. urine) gives the bacterial genome, which is run through the phage ML models to predict active phage and build a bespoke cocktail, with the interaction dataset continually reinforced by new observations
Barriers_List: Artificial urine cannot capture the complexity of real urine (pH, osmolarity, host response); most genomic features are unannotated grouped genes; class imbalance limits model reliability for narrow-host-range phage; feature extraction from long-read/mixed samples untested; licensing and expectation management needed for clinical adoption
Facilitators_List: High-throughput interaction platforms (e.g. 50 x 96-well plates) can generate the required training datasets quickly; direct sequencing of clinical samples already works for E. coli in canine urine; generalist phage with higher activity increase model reliability and cocktail options
Future_Directions: Include more generalist phage in interaction datasets and prefer phage targeting at least 30% of the population (class imbalance below 85:15); combine associative and function-based features in future phage selection pipelines; test feature extraction from long-read data of complex samples; continually reinforce the learning dataset with clinical sequencing; move into clinical practice with licensing and expectation management
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Recursive feature reduction / top-ranking feature selection with the MUVR package; no named features or importance values are reported
Limitation_Categories: Methodological: unannotated genomic features, no functional dissection, class imbalance, proof-of-principle scope, untested long-read/mixed-sample feature extraction. Applicability: artificial urine does not represent real urine; local strain population only. Translation: licensing, registration, safety, expectation management
Data_Quality_Concerns: High-quality training sets with phenotypic interaction data are critical; interaction datasets for some phage were highly imbalanced (up to 85:15); most features are grouped genes with no clear annotation, so functional meaning is uncertain
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: the interaction-score definition, the threshold of 60, and the formulas for precision, recall and F1 are all given in Materials and Methods, with per-model RMSE and F1 reported
Page_References: pp. 1-9 (main article); model results pp. 3-6; Materials and Methods pp. 7-8

Title: Risk factors and predictive model for nosocomial infections by extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
Funder_Names: Science Technology Department of Zhejiang province, China (LGC22H200018); Jinhua Science and Technology Bureau, Zhejiang province, China (2021-3-026)
Population_Description: Hospitalized patients at Jinhua Central Hospital infected with Acinetobacter baumannii: 212 XDRAB-infected and 347 non-XDRAB (NXDRAB) AB-infected, 559 in total; randomly split 7:3 into a training set (391) and a test set (168).
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: Paper ranks 10 LASSO-selected features (lambda.1se) and 8 independent risk factors from multivariable logistic regression and the nomogram (importance = LASSO coefficients / logistic ORs): ICU stay 1-7 days (OR=3.970), ICU stay >7 days (OR=12.316), hypoproteinemia (OR=3.249/3.261), glucocorticoid use (OR=2.371), urinary catheterization (OR=2.148), mechanical ventilation (OR=2.737), diabetes mellitus (OR=2.435), carbapenem use (OR=6.649), b-lactamase inhibitor use (OR=4.146); smoking history and CRP were in the LASSO 10 but not retained.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: One model only - a multivariable logistic regression nomogram (no model comparison): training-set C-index 0.932, AUC 0.9322; test-set AUC 0.9291 (0.929); Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47.
AUROC_Population_Set: Training set, n=391 (internal validation); test set, n=168 (validation set)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples from the training set (C-index 0.932) and a held-out test set that the authors label 'external' but which is a 7:3 random split of the same single-centre cohort; the authors themselves state that external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is still necessary.
Reported_Limitations: Single-centre study (coefficients may vary; geographic bias; limited generalizability; external validation with other institutions, regions and countries necessary); retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems may be incomplete and some intended factors could not be included; selection bias unavoidable; future prospective studies needed.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-model nomogram study (LASSO + multivariable logistic regression); no models are compared, so model-level metric fields were answered for the one nomogram on its primary dataset (training set n=391) and the fields for metrics the paper never computes are 'No'.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the 7:3 random-split test set that the authors call 'external validation' should be coded as external validation (level 3) or internal validation (level 2) for Clinical_Maturity_Level.
Sample_Size: 559 patients (212 XDRAB-infected, 347 non-XDRAB AB-infected); training set 391 cases, test set 168 cases
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: 1. Patients hospitalized at Jinhua Central Hospital from January 2021 to December 2023. 2. Patients meeting the CDC criteria for A. baumannii infection. 3. Clinically infected AB specimens include sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions and puncture fluid. 4. Only the first AB infection in each patient. 5. XDRAB defined as a strain susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline).
Exclusion_Criteria: 2. Patients infected with pathogens other than AB or colonized with AB without clinical infection. 3. Patients with AB infection detected within 48 hours of admission, transferred out within 48 hours of admission, who died, or who abandoned treatment. 4. Patients with significant missing clinical data. (Also: contaminated samples or duplicate strains from the same patient.)
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Jinhua Central Hospital (single-centre electronic medical records and laboratory systems)
Dataset_Size: 559 patients; 35 candidate variables screened by LASSO
Missing_Data_Method: VIM package used to visualize missing-value distribution; factors with more than 10% missing values excluded; MICE package multiple imputation for factors with less than 10% missing values.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre in Jinhua, Zhejiang, China (Jinhua Central Hospital), January 2021 - December 2023; the authors acknowledge geographic bias and limited generalizability.
Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, urine, pleural fluid, ascites, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, wound secretions, and puncture fluid
Primary_AMR_Outcome: XDRAB infection (nosocomial) among hospitalized A. baumannii-infected patients, modelled against non-XDRAB AB (NXDRAB) infection.
Pathogens: Acinetobacter baumannii (extensively drug-resistant, XDRAB; and non-XDRAB AB)
Drug_Classes: aminoglycosides; carbapenems; quinolones; beta-lactamase inhibitors; broad-spectrum cephalosporins
Specific_Antibiotics: tobramycin; amikacin; gentamicin; imipenem; meropenem; levofloxacin; ciprofloxacin; piperacillin-tazobactam; cefoperazone-sulbactam; ceftazidime; ceftriaxone; cefepime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: XDRAB is defined as a strain of A. baumannii susceptible to only one or two drugs with potential antifusobacterial activity (mainly polymyxins and tigecycline); the outcome is XDRAB infection versus non-XDRAB AB infection.
AI_Purpose: To establish a practical infection prediction model (LASSO regression variable selection plus multivariable logistic regression, visualized as a nomogram) that lets clinicians assess the risk of XDRAB infection and guide early isolation and treatment.
Feature_Engineering: ICU admission time recoded into three intervals (no ICU admission / 1-7 days / >7 days) calculated from admission to first AB detection; hypoproteinemia defined as serum albumin below 30 g/L; NLR and other blood parameters collected.
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation (lambda.1se = 0.03450), keeping 10 non-zero-coefficient features for the multivariable logistic regression.
Num_Features_Selected: 10 (non-zero coefficients at lambda.1se); 8 retained as independent risk factors in the nomogram
Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross-validation to determine the lambda value; lambda.min = 0.0065 (24 variables) versus lambda.1se = 0.03450 (10 variables), lambda.1se selected.
Other_Metrics: C-index 0.932 (training) / 0.929 (testing); AUC 0.9322 (training) and 0.9291 (test); Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; OR with 95% CI for each risk factor; decision curve analysis and clinical impact curve.
Baseline_Method: Univariate comparison of XDRAB versus NXDRAB groups (independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test for continuous variables, chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables).
Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples from the training set; C-index 0.932; Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.47; calibration curve close to the 45-degree line.
Train_Test_Split: 7:3 randomization by R software - training set 391 cases, test set 168 cases
External_Validation_Description: Test set of 168 cases from the same 7:3 random split of the single-centre cohort (AUC 0.9291); not an independent external cohort - the authors state external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
Overfitting_Method: LASSO penalisation to reduce dimensionality and multicollinearity-induced overfitting; internal validation by 1000 bootstrap samples.
Clinical_Insights: Clinicians can quickly assess the risk of XDRAB infection from existing clinical data and implement timely isolation and treatment; early transfer from ICU to general wards for eligible patients could reduce risk; rational use of carbapenems and b-lactamase inhibitors remains crucial.
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre, single-country cohort; coefficients may vary under different circumstances; external validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries is necessary.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples (C-index 0.932) and a held-out test set (AUC 0.9291) drawn from the same single-centre cohort; the authors state external validation with other institutions, regions and countries is still necessary - no prospective or deployed use.
Integration_Point: Early risk assessment of hospitalized patients (nomogram scoring from existing clinical data) to trigger timely isolation and treatment.
End_User_Described: Clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians score the nomogram from existing clinical data to assess XDRAB risk and implement timely isolation and treatment; the paper notes early transfer out of the ICU for eligible patients.
Future_Directions: External validation with datasets from other healthcare institutions, regions and countries; prospective studies to validate the findings further; more prospective studies on glycaemic control and XDRAB infection.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (sociodemographic, behavioural, clinical, laboratory, pharmacological, healthcare utilisation)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO regression coefficients at lambda.1se and multivariable logistic regression odds ratios; nomogram points scaled from the regression coefficients.
Limitation_Categories: Single-centre design / geographic bias / limited generalizability; retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems (incomplete data, intended factors not included); selection bias; need for external validation and prospective studies.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Retrospective data from electronic medical records and laboratory systems may be incomplete and some intended factors could not be analysed; individual missing values in continuous variables handled by exclusion (>10% missing) or MICE multiple imputation.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear, TRIPOD-guided reporting of variable selection, model development, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical utility.

Title: Pioneering Klebsiella Pneumoniae Antibiotic Resistance Prediction With Artificial Intelligence-Clinical Decision Support System-Enhanced Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry: Retrospective Study
Journal_Source: Journal of Medical Internet Research (J Med Internet Res)
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Tri-Service General Hospital (grant numbers TSGH-D-113105 and TSGH-D-113106)
Population_Description: Routine clinical bacterial specimens (165,299) submitted to the microbiology laboratories of Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospitals, Taiwan, January 2021-December 2023; 11,996 identified as Klebsiella pneumoniae, of which 11,127 (LEV) and 11,623 (CIP) had non-intermediate AST results. No patient-level demographic data reported.
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 15 m/z spectral features (m/z segment ranges of 2035-2040, 2067-2072, 2166-2171, 2180-2185, 2688-2695, 2759-2764, 3143-3152, 4363-4368, 4567-4572, 5278-5283, 5379-5384, 7238-7253, 7703-7708, 9136-9145 and 9532-9544); ranked by feature importance values (m/z segments with importance <0.01 filtered as background noise) and correlation with resistance in heat maps
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest classifier (RF) - highest area under the curve of 0.95 for both levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin resistance
Accuracy_Value: 0.87 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.86 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Sensitivity_Value: 0.88 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.89 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Specificity_Value: 0.86 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.82 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
Specificity_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Precision_PPV_Value: 0.81 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.86 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
F1_Value: 0.85 (random forest, ciprofloxacin, validation set); 0.87 (random forest, levofloxacin, validation set)
F1_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
AUROC_Value: 0.95 (random forest, testing AUC, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin validation sets; training AUC 0.99)
AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal validation set (specimens collected October-December), tested against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were developed on January-September specimens and validated on October-December specimens from the same hospital network; validation was against culture-based AST. No external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no routine clinical use is reported, so the highest level the paper's own evidence supports is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: Dataset balancing and feature selection intricacies; intermediate AST results introduce uncertainty and their exclusion (869 LEV, 373 CIP) may have omitted significant data, affecting generalizability to intermediate cases; resistance mechanisms not mediated at the protein-peptide level or outside m/z 2000-20,000 are not captured; further validation required
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: No formal equity analysis; the authors argue the approach is relevant to low- and middle-income countries where antibiotic use is escalating and access and stewardship are challenged
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No specific ethical or governance risks discussed; IRB approval obtained (TSGHIRB No. C202305073), informed consent waived for the retrospective design, data anonymized
Reviewer_Notes: Judgements recorded: (1) the study builds two parallel models (levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin) rather than one; the random forest is the best-performing model for both, so the performance Value fields report the random forest figure for each drug, labelled by drug; (2) Clinical_Maturity_Level coded 2 (internal validation) because the validation set is a later time window of the same hospital-network dataset, not an external dataset; (3) Data_Source coded 'Laboratory information system' - the data are routine hospital microbiology MALDI-TOF MS spectra and VITEK 2 AST results, no registry or EHR is named; (4) Funding_Source coded 'Public' - grants from the study hospital (TSGH), a public National Defense Medical Center hospital, conflicts declared 'None declared'.
Unresolved_Items: Which of the two parallel models (levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) is the review's single unit of analysis is not settled by the paper; both are reported. Also unresolved: whether a model validated on a later time window of the same 5-hospital dataset counts as internal validation (coded 2) or partial external validation.
Sample_Size: 11,996 KP specimens identified from 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,127 specimens analysed for LEV resistance and 11,623 for CIP resistance
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: Klebsiella pneumoniae specimens identified by MALDI-TOF MS that underwent AST for levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin with the VITEK 2 system
Exclusion_Criteria: Specimens with intermediate AST results: 869 excluded from the LEV analysis (leaving 11,127) and 373 from the CIP analysis (leaving 11,623)
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: No public dataset named - local Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospital MALDI-TOF MS/AST data (January 2021-December 2023)
Dataset_Size: 165,299 bacterial specimens; 11,996 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (11,127 LEV analysis, 11,623 CIP analysis)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single country (Taiwan); specimens from Tri-Service General Hospital and 4 district hospitals, no wider geographic sampling reported
Specimen_Type_Detail: bacterial specimens / Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) specimens (routine clinical samples; specimen site not stated)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae to levofloxacin (LEV) and ciprofloxacin (CIP), classified from MALDI-TOF MS spectra using machine learning
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (quinolones)
Specific_Antibiotics: Levofloxacin (LEV); ciprofloxacin (CIP)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype from VITEK 2 AST interpreted with CLSI clinical breakpoints; specimens with intermediate results excluded
AI_Purpose: Develop a web-based artificial intelligence-clinical decision support system (AI-CDSS) that combines machine learning with MALDI-TOF MS spectra to predict Klebsiella pneumoniae resistance to levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin and speed up diagnosis to guide antibiotic choice
Feature_Engineering: m/z ranges segmented into 1-unit intervals with a +/- 2-unit tolerance for grouping; peak intensity values for resistant and susceptible strains extracted and logarithmically transformed; segments with feature importance below 0.01 filtered out as background noise
Feature_Selection_Method: Feature importance thresholding (segments with a feature importance value below 0.01 removed as background noise)
Num_Features_Selected: 15 (top 15 spectral features / m/z segments)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Resampling with sklearn.utils: downsampling of over-represented classes and upsampling of underrepresented classes
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search for each model; best parameters in Multimedia Appendix 1
Software_Libraries: sklearn.utils (used for resampling); models include XGBoost and light gradient boosting machine (LGBM)
Other_Metrics: No metrics beyond training/testing AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and F1-score were reported (Tables 1 and 2); ROC curves presented graphically
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis as comparator algorithms; traditional culture-based AST as the clinical reference standard
Baseline_Performance: Ciprofloxacin: logistic regression testing AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.78; LDA testing AUC 0.80, accuracy 0.77 (versus random forest AUC 0.95, accuracy 0.87)
Internal_Validation: Temporal hold-out: October-December specimens used as the validation set, validated against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases)
Train_Test_Split: Temporal split - January to September specimens for training, October to December specimens for validation
Clinical_Insights: The same top 15 m/z spectral features are associated with resistance to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, suggesting a universal resistance mechanism despite the different modes of action; these spectral markers could support rapid resistance detection
Generalisability_Details: Exclusion of intermediate AST results may have omitted significant data and affected model generalizability to intermediate cases; future work should add intermediate cases and diverse data modalities to broaden applicability; further validation required
Maturity_Evidence: Temporal validation of the models on October-December specimens at Tri-Service General Hospital against culture-based AST (3339 LEV and 3487 CIP cases); no external cohort, no prospective evaluation, no documented routine clinical use
Integration_Point: Web-based AI-CDSS embedded in the microbiology/AST workflow: a culture sample is collected, MALDI-TOF MS spectra are analysed and the system predicts LEV/CIP resistance to inform antibiotic choice
End_User_Described: health care professionals (clinicians)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Sample collection, MALDI-TOF MS analysis and AI-CDSS resistance prediction integrated into the antibiotic resistance-testing workflow; predicted resistance determination in approximately 3 days versus the conventional 4-day timeline for standard AST
Stewardship_Details: Antimicrobial stewardship benefit is claimed (faster resistance determination is said to enhance stewardship and ensure appropriate and effective treatment) but no stewardship outcome was measured
Barriers_List: Resistance mechanisms not mediated at the protein-peptide level or outside m/z 2000-20,000 are not captured; intermediate AST results excluded and remain unpredictable; dataset balancing and feature selection are intricate; limited data and antibiotic access challenges in low- and middle-income countries
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is already indispensable for rapid and accurate microorganism identification in routine laboratories; ML plus MALDI-TOF is a faster route than NGS/PCR; a web-based AI-CDSS is easily distributed to health care professionals
Future_Directions: Incorporate intermediate AST cases and diverse data modalities to broaden applicability to a wider array of antibiotic-resistant organisms; further validate the results
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance values (m/z segments with importance below 0.01 filtered as background noise) plus correlation heat maps of the top 15 m/z segments
Novel_Predictors_Details: A shared set of top 15 m/z spectral features predicts resistance to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, suggesting a universal mechanism of resistance despite the different modes of action; the authors state no prior study had applied ML with MALDI-TOF to quinolone resistance in KP
Limitation_Categories: Dataset balancing and feature selection complexity; uncertainty and data loss from excluding intermediate AST results; incomplete coverage of resistance mechanisms (non-protein-mediated, m/z outside 2000-20,000); need for further validation
Data_Quality_Concerns: Intermediate AST results create label uncertainty and were excluded; genotypic data may not align with phenotype, but spectra are used instead of genotypes
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model algorithms, grid-search tuning (Multimedia Appendix 1), preprocessing, temporal split and per-model metrics for both drugs (Tables 1 and 2) are reported; the language, libraries and hardware are not fully specified
Page_References: pp. 1-12 (abstract and title p. 1; methods pp. 2-3; results and tables 1-2 pp. 5-6; discussion pp. 8-9; data availability and conflicts p. 9; appendices and PMID p. 10-12)

Title: Leveraging large-scale Mycobacterium tuberculosis whole genome sequence data to characterise drug-resistant mutations using machine learning and statistical approaches
Country_Countries: 66 countries across all WHO regions (Europe 37.4%, Africa 24.5%, South East Asia 15.4%, Western Pacific 11.1%, Americas 8.9%, Other 2.8%); study institutions in the United Kingdom
Funder_Names: UKRI (BBSRC BB/X018156/1; MRC MR/X005895/1; EPSRC EP/Y018842/1)
Population_Description: 35,777 M. tuberculosis isolates with WGS (> 20-fold coverage) and corresponding phenotypic drug-susceptibility test (pDST) data, sourced from 66 countries across all WHO regions
Data_Source_Other: Public repositories/archives of Illumina whole genome sequences with linked phenotypic drug-susceptibility test data for M. tuberculosis isolates
Top_Predictive_Features: Aggregated counts of rare variants per gene (highest total information gain for aggregated pncA mutations, PZA); loss-of-function variants (ethA 15/32 prioritised, pncA Glu173fs OR 182.28, Rv0678, Rv2752c); RIF- and INH-resistance mutations rank highly (permutation feature importance/information gain)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) and gradient boosted trees (GBT) on feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; best AUC per drug (Table 2): INH RF + F2 96.50; RIF RF + F2 96.60; EMB GBT + F1 91.70; PZA GBT + F2 88.30; STM RF + F2 89.60; AMK RF + F1 90.70; CAP RF + F2 84.10; KAN GBT + F2 91.00; CIP GBT + F2 95.40; OFL GBT + F2 88.10; MOX GBT + F2 89.10; ETH GBT + F2 86.30; LEV GBT + F1 93.50; RFB GBT + F2 94.90. External comparisons: DE19 (GBT-CRM, AUC 95.5-97.9), KO19 (AUC 84.4-97.8), GR22 (CNN, AUC 82.3-98.1), TB-Profiler (sensitivity 87-97% first-line, 79.2-92.2% second-line)
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest with the F2 feature set (RF + F2) - highest AUC in the study (RIF, AUC 96.6)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
AUROC_Population_Set: Hold-out test dataset; RIF, n = 33,087 isolates (RF + F2)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only: stratified five-fold cross-validation with randomised grid search on the training set and a 20% hold-out test set; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment reported
Reported_Limitations: Limited predictive performance for some drugs (e.g. CAP) that could benefit from larger sample size or broader genomic coverage; confounding from population structure; feature representation (one-hot encoding leading to sparse matrices and reference bias); difficulty comparing models across datasets due to varying software requirements, input formats and reproducibility issues in prior publications; variant interactions not yet explored
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the paper's Table 2 names a different best model per drug and no single overall best model. Coded RF + F2 (random forest, F2 feature set) as "best performing" because it attains the highest AUC in the study (RIF 96.6); the Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/PPV/NPV/AUROC values are that model's RIF row. Other models' figures are in All_Models_Evaluated.
Sample_Size: 35,777 M. tuberculosis isolates (primary dataset); 33,087 isolates in the RIF hold-out test set (RF + F2)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: M. tuberculosis isolates with publicly available Illumina WGS (> 20-fold coverage) plus corresponding pDST data; 35,777 isolates retained of 50,723 sourced from public repositories/archives
Exclusion_Criteria: Monomorphic SNPs, variants in non-unique regions of the genome (e.g. pe/ppe genes) and variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded; only loci with a non-major allele frequency > 0.1% (F1/F2) or > 0.5% (F3) were retained
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: "35k" dataset: publicly available M. tuberculosis WGS and pDST data (sample accession numbers in the GitHub repository SSID08/TB-ML)
Dataset_Size: 35,777 isolates (from 50,723 sourced); F1 56-143 variants, F2 895-1428 variants, F3 5603-10,487 variants
Missing_Data_Method: Variants with > 10% missing calls were excluded
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates sourced from 66 countries covering all WHO regions: Europe 13,381 (37.4%), Africa 8756 (24.5%), South East Asia 5518 (15.4%), Western Pacific 3964 (11.1%), Americas 3176 (8.9%), Other 982 (2.8%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary phenotypic drug resistance (pDST) to each of 14 anti-TB drugs, plus MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, Low resistance, High resistance, Resistant/Extreme) based on ECOFF thresholds
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb); Mycobacterium tuberculosis Complex (MTBC)
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (INH, RIF, EMB, PZA); second-line injectables (STM, AMK, CAP, KAN); fluoroquinolones (CIP, OFL, MOX, LEV); rifabutin (RFB); ethionamide (ETH); bedaquiline (BDQ) and clofazimine (CLF) in the loss-of-function and MIC analyses
Specific_Antibiotics: INH, RIF, EMB, PZA, streptomycin (STM), OFL, MOX, levofloxacin (LEV), amikacin (AMI), capreomycin (CAP), kanamycin (KAN), CIP, ethionamide (ETH) and RFB; BDQ and CLF also analysed
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistance/susceptibility from pDST for each drug; MIC phenotypes categorised into four incremental levels (Susceptible, 'Low' resistance, 'High' resistance, and Resistant ['Extreme']) based on recommended ECOFF thresholds; genotypic MDR/pre-XDR/XDR categories from TB-Profiler
AI_Purpose: To apply and evaluate ensemble tree-based machine learning (RF, GBT) on a large-scale WGS and pDST dataset to predict binary drug resistance for 14 drugs and MIC phenotypes, and to characterise drug-resistance mutations
Num_Models_Compared: 2 algorithms (RF, GBT) across feature sets F1, F2, F3 and F1 + ; 4 external comparators (DE19, KO19, GR22, TB-Profiler)
Feature_Engineering: Presence/absence (one-hot) encoding of SNPs and indels as 1/0 in a numpy matrix; F1 supplemented with aggregated counts of rare variants (MAF < 0.1%) predicted by SnpEff to have moderate-to-high functional impact (F1 + ); lineage predicted by TB-Profiler appended to the feature matrices
Feature_Selection_Method: bedtools intersect to retain drug-resistance-associated genes from the TB-Profiler list; MAF filtering (> 0.1% for F1/F2, > 0.5% for F3); permutation feature importance to rank variants
Num_Features_Selected: F1 56-143 variants; F2 895-1428 mutations; F3 5603-10,487 variants
Hyperparameter_Method: Randomised Grid Search with stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set (specified parameters and ranges, Table S7)
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (v1.4.1), XGBoost Python API (1.7.6), numpy; TB-Profiler; SnpEff (v5.1); BWA-mem (v0.7.17); Trimmomatic (v0.39); samtools; GATK GenotypeGVCFs (v4.1.3.0); bedtools (v2.31); MASS and nnet packages in R
Other_Metrics: Conditional odds ratios for LOF variant associations; relative-risk ratios from multinomial ordinal regression across MIC categories; information gain from permutation feature importance
Baseline_Method: Deelder et al. 2019 (DE19, GBT-CRM); Kouchaki et al. 2019 (KO19, best ensemble tree model with dimensionality reduction); Green et al. 2022 (GR22, CNN); TB-Profiler (in-silico rule-in classification)
Baseline_Performance: DE19 (n = 16,507) GBT models AUC 95.5-97.9, sensitivity 69.7-91.1%, specificity 94.2-98.9%; KO19 (n = 13,167) AUC 84.4-97.8; GR22 (n = 22,615) AUC 82.3-98.1 with higher sensitivity across all drugs; TB-Profiler sensitivity 87-97% first-line and 79.2-92.2% second-line
Internal_Validation: 20% hold-out test dataset plus stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set with randomised grid search for hyperparameter and classification-threshold optimisation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing
Overfitting_Method: MAF filtering to control the number of input features; 80/20 train-test split with hold-out evaluation; stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set
Clinical_Insights: Loss-of-function mutations in pro-drug activation genes (pncA for PZA, ethA for ETH, mshA) as resistance mechanisms; Rv0678 LOF mutations linked to BDQ/CLF cross-resistance via MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux; putative novel markers Rv3861 Ile27fs (STM) and Rv1907c Asp48fs (INH) absent from the WHO catalogue; inhA promoter variants associated with extreme INH resistance
Data_Repository: GitHub repository: https://github.com/SSID08/TB-ML (contains sample accession numbers, feature importance values and analysis code)
Generalisability_Details: Authors note that comparing models across datasets is challenging because of varying software requirements, input formats and reproducibility issues in prior publications, suggest standardised Docker-container environments (ML-TB), and call for direct same-dataset comparisons to separate sample-size from architecture effects
Maturity_Evidence: Highest level of evidence is internal validation: hyperparameter tuning and threshold optimisation by stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set plus a 20% hold-out test dataset; no external validation dataset, prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine use is reported
Barriers_List: Difficulty comparing models across datasets (varying software requirements, input formats, reproducibility issues in prior work); limited predictive performance for some drugs such as CAP requiring more samples/genomic coverage; confounding from population structure; sparse matrices and reference bias from one-hot encoding
Facilitators_List: Standardised containerised environments (Docker containers within ML-TB) for model comparison and reproducibility; interpretable targeted feature sets (drug-specific regions); aggregation of rare variants to capture under-sampled resistance mutations
Future_Directions: Optimising models for practical deployment; direct comparisons on the same dataset to separate sample-size from architecture effects; exploring variant interactions on MIC phenotypes; quantitative MIC resistance prediction with ML; functional validation of novel variants for genetic DST libraries
Predictor_Categories_Count: 1 - genomic/microbiological features (presence/absence of WGS variants and lineage) only
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation feature importance (information gain)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Two potential novel frameshift mutations observed across independent lineages and absent from the WHO mutation catalogue: Rv3861 Ile27fs (STM, OR = 7.0) and Rv1907c Asp48fs (INH, OR = 4.0)
Limitation_Categories: Model performance limited for some drugs (CAP) - needs larger sample size or broader genomic coverage; confounding by population structure; filtering of lineage-specific and synonymous mutations debated; feature representation (one-hot encoding) causing sparse matrices and reference bias; type of ML representation affects interpretability and deployment; variant interactions not examined; challenges comparing models across datasets
Data_Quality_Concerns: Potential pDST errors/phenotype misclassification; variants with > 10% missing calls excluded; monomorphic variants and non-unique genomic regions (pe/ppe) excluded; reference bias and sparse matrices from one-hot encoding on multi-lineage data
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: Table 2 reports, per drug, the best model with N, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and accuracy, with feature-set and model definitions in the caption; hyperparameter ranges and supplementary results in Tables S1-S11
Page_References: pp. 1-10 (Table 2 p. 3; Table 1 p. 3; Table 3 p. 6; Table 4 p. 7; Methods pp. 8-9; key results pp. 2-7)

Title: A novel hematological score (HS) and its related nomogram model to predict nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease in patients with suspected multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Scientific Research Fund of Wuhan, Hubei Province (grant WX16C33)
Population_Description: 935 patients with suspected multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis: 705 with MDR-PTB and 230 with NTM-PD, from Wuhan Jinyintan Hospital
Top_Predictive_Features: Independent predictors of NTM-PD: age >=54 (OR 4.222), male (inverse, OR 0.466), DM (OR 0.355), HIV infection (OR 18.816), ILD (OR 4.526), HS (OR 2.781)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification
All_Models_Evaluated: HS: AUROC 0.900 (training), 0.867 (validation); HS-based nomogram: AUROC 0.930 (training), 0.948 (validation); also DCA and calibration curves
Best_Performing_Model: HS-based nomogram model
AUROC_Population_Set: Training set and validation set (nomogram)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation on a randomised 7:3 training/validation split; no external validation or prospective evaluation
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design (unavoidable bias); single-centre (not multi-centre); model not externally verified (limits extrapolation); cannot distinguish MDR-PTB and NTM-PD co-infection or specific NTM strains
Conflicts_of_Interest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) results of NTM and MTB culture or molecular biology test (PCR), drug-sensitivity test (DST) or GeneXpert MTB/RIF; (2) NTM-PD: NTM sputum culture positive twice (same pathogen) or lavage-fluid culture/molecular positive, plus at least one anti-TB drug resistance by DST or GeneXpert; (3) MDR-PTB: positive MTB culture/NAAT and MDR-PTB confirmed by DST or GeneXpert; (4) ineffective after first-line ATT
Exclusion_Criteria: Age <18 years; only extrapulmonary infection; no information available; mixed infection of NTM-PD and MDR-PTB
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Wuhan Jinyintan Hospital electronic medical record (EMR)
Dataset_Size: 935 patients
Missing_Data_Method: missForest algorithm and single imputation
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: Wuhan Jinyintan Hospital, Wuhan, China; not externally verified
Specimen_Type_Detail: Sputum; bronchial lavage fluid/bronchoalveolar lavage fluid
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Prediction/differentiation of NTM-PD (vs MDR-PTB) among patients with suspected MDR-PTB
Pathogens: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MDR-PTB)
Drug_Classes: Second-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (MDR-PTB); macrolides/azalides, aminoglycosides, oxazolidinones (NTM-PD)
Specific_Antibiotics: isoniazid, rifampicin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, amikacin, linezolid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR-PTB confirmed by DST or GeneXpert MTB/RIF; NTM-PD by positive culture/molecular test
AI_Purpose: To develop a novel hematological score (HS) and nomogram model to identify NTM-PD in patients with suspected MDR-PTB, enabling prompt and appropriate therapy
Feature_Engineering: Computed ratio inflammatory indicators (PLR, SII, dNLR, NHR, CAR, UHR, PNI); continuous variables transformed to binary using ROC cut-offs
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression; ROC analysis; multivariate logistic regression
Num_Features_Selected: 10 variables selected by LASSO
Other_Metrics: Calibration curves (CC) and decision curve analysis (DCA)
Internal_Validation: Randomised 7:3 training/validation split
Overfitting_Method: LASSO regression
Clinical_Insights: Identifies older females, HIV infection and ILD as higher-risk groups for NTM-PD
Data_Repository: Available from corresponding author upon request
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre model not externally verified; extrapolation to other regions limited; external validation necessary
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation on a randomised 7:3 training/validation split only; no external validation, prospective evaluation or deployment
End_User_Described: Clinicians at any level of medical institution (especially resource-limited areas)
Future_Directions: Improve model through prospective cohort studies with larger samples and multi-centre data, with external validation
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Odds ratios from multivariate logistic regression
Novel_Predictors_Details: First-time report of a strong correlation between low UHR levels and NTM-PD; HS as a novel biomarker for NTM-PD
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design; single-centre; no external validation; cannot distinguish co-infection or specific NTM strains

Title: Evaluation of PhenoMATRIX and PhenoMATRIX PLUS for the screening of MRSA from nasal and inguinal/perineal swabs using chromogenic media
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation; AI Clinical Imaging Analysis
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Prospective cohort
Population_Description: Non-duplicate MRSA screening specimens (nasal and inguinal/perineal ESwabs) from patients at a Swiss tertiary care centre: 6,771 specimens used to train PhenoMATRIX, 17,223 sequential specimens for validation (09 February 2022 - 08 May 2023) and 1,409 sequential specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS (23 May 2023 - 03 July 2023).
