Data_Source_Other: Digital chromogenic culture plate images (CHROMID MRSA) captured on the Copan WASPLab; ground truth from technologists' manual reading of the same images
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Infection prevention and control team
Delivery_Platform: Laboratory information system (LIS) integrated; Instrument / device embedded

Best_Performing_Model: PhenoMATRIX PLUS
Sensitivity_Population_Set: 1,409 non-duplicate specimens analysed by PhenoMATRIX PLUS (23 May 2023 - 03 July 2023)
Specificity_Population_Set: 1,409 non-duplicate specimens analysed by PhenoMATRIX PLUS (23 May 2023 - 03 July 2023)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: PhenoMATRIX PLUS, MRSA detection from nasal and inguinal/perineal swabs on chromogenic media
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The validated settings were applied prospectively to sequential routine specimens and, in the PhenoMATRIX PLUS phase, negative results were automatically released to the LIS and negative plates automatically discarded in the routine workflow (checked manually for all 1,297 MRSA-negative specimens). No randomised or external-site evaluation and no clinical decision-support integration is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Impact on personnel load and productivity not measured; downstream effects in the clinical wards (e.g. unnecessary infection control measures) require further study; patient outcomes, antimicrobial prescribing and cost-savings not assessed.
Reviewer_Notes: Automated screening of chromogenic culture plate images (PhenoMATRIX / PhenoMATRIX PLUS) at a single Swiss tertiary centre; no patient-level demographic or clinical data. Abstract reports PhenoMATRIX sensitivity 99.8% while the results text and Table 1 give 99.9% (866/868 = 99.77%) and the abstract positivity rate 5% (866/17,223) differs from the results text 5% (868/17,223). The '100% accuracy' statement refers to the automatic release of negative results to the LIS and the automatic discharge of negative plates, not to classification accuracy.
Unresolved_Items: Whether PhenoMATRIX or PhenoMATRIX PLUS is this review's unit of analysis: the two software versions were assessed on different, non-overlapping specimen sets (17,223 validation specimens vs 1,409 specimens), so no head-to-head comparison exists and the paper names neither as best.
Sample_Size: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens (validation phase); 6,771 non-duplicate specimens (machine learning phase); 1,409 non-duplicate specimens (PhenoMATRIX PLUS)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Non-duplicate nasal and inguinal/perineal MRSA screening ESwabs (Copan 490CE.A) referred to the bacteriology laboratory and streaked on CHROMID MRSA plates, analysed sequentially during each study period.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; Other
Data_Source_Name: CHROMID MRSA chromogenic plates (bioMerieux) imaged on the Copan WASPLab; Copan 490CE.A ESwabs
Dataset_Size: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens (validation set); 6,771 non-duplicate specimens used for machine learning; 1,409 specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: Geneva University Hospitals, Switzerland. No multi-country or multi-region sampling; representativeness not discussed.
Specimen_Type_Detail: nasal and inguinal/perineal ESwabs streaked on CHROMID MRSA chromogenic media
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) from nasal and inguinal/perineal screening ESwabs on chromogenic media: agreement of PhenoMATRIX/PhenoMATRIX PLUS image classification with the manual reading (sensitivity, specificity).
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Other organisms named only as mixed-growth false positives: Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Bacillus sp.
Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is detection of methicillin resistance (cefoxitin/mecA), not an antimicrobial class outcome.
Specific_Antibiotics: cefoxitin (disk diffusion AST confirming methicillin resistance)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA; Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA positive/negative on CHROMID MRSA chromogenic plates (presumptively positive = green colonies on manual reading); positives confirmed by qPCR targeting femA and mecA and by disk diffusion AST on all femA-positive isolates.
AI_Purpose: Automated reading of chromogenic culture plate images: sorting plates as MRSA positive/negative, automatic release of negative results to the LIS and automatic discharge of negative plates from the incubators.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (PhenoMATRIX and PhenoMATRIX PLUS; assessed on different specimen sets)
Feature_Engineering: No hand-crafted features: several high-resolution digital images per plate taken under different light and exposure conditions at two incubation time points (0 h and 18 h) fed to the CNN.
Other_Metrics: Positive predictive value 40% and negative predictive value 100% (PhenoMATRIX PLUS); false positive rate 4.8% (67/1,409) for PhenoMATRIX PLUS and 0.85% (146/17,223) for PhenoMATRIX; MRSA positivity rate 5% (868/17,223) and 3.2% (45/1,409); TAT and time-of-day distributions of image availability; 100% accuracy of automatic release and plate discard for the 1,297 negatives.
Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the digital culture images by technologists (reference standard); qPCR targeting femA and mecA plus disk diffusion AST for confirmation of presumptive positives.
Baseline_Performance: Manual reading was the reference standard: PhenoMATRIX PLUS showed 100% sensitivity (no false negative among 1,409 specimens) and 95.2% specificity; for PhenoMATRIX, 99.9% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity against manual work-up.
Internal_Validation: Temporal validation: settings trained on 6,771 specimens and validated on 17,223 non-duplicate specimens prospectively analysed between 09 February 2022 and 08 May 2023; discrepancies reviewed by clinical microbiologists.
Train_Test_Split: Training: 6,771 non-duplicate specimens (machine learning phase); validation: 17,223 non-duplicate specimens; separate evaluation: 1,409 specimens for PhenoMATRIX PLUS.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the software could be implemented, after thorough validation, on a broad panel of culture-based analyses such as urines, GBS screening and other infection-control screening specimens.
Maturity_Evidence: Performance of both versions established against manual reading on consecutive routine specimens, with PhenoMATRIX PLUS prospectively releasing negative results to the LIS and discarding negative plates in the routine workflow; no external or randomised evaluation.
Integration_Point: Bacteriology laboratory WASPLab line (imaging after 18 h of incubation) with automatic notification of negative MRSA results to the Laboratory Information System, further validated by the Valab expert system before updating the electronic patient record.
End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists (who read culture images and release results) and the infection control team.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Negative MRSA results are automatically sent to the LIS by PhenoMATRIX PLUS, validated by the Valab expert system and used to update the electronic patient record without delay; presumptively positive plates are sent to the reading folder for technologist review and confirmatory tests.
Barriers_List: Time-consuming manual reading of negative plates and extended time to results; laboratory operating hours limiting the day shift; laboratory workload bottlenecks requiring priority criteria by specimen type; shortage of qualified personnel; availability of the WASPLab for plate discharge.
Facilitators_List: Total laboratory automation (WASPLab) giving 24/7 image availability; automatic release of negative results to the LIS set as a high priority so results are sent around the clock; automatic discharge of negative plates when the WASPLab is available (low priority).
Future_Directions: Broader application of the software to other culture-based analyses (urines, GBS screening, other infection-control screening) after thorough validation; studies of the precise impact on personnel load and productivity, patient outcomes, antimicrobial prescriptions and cost-savings.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (chromogenic culture-plate images / microbiological colony features; incubation time point)
Limitation_Categories: Unmeasured workflow/personnel impact; unexplored downstream clinical effects; absence of patient-outcome, prescribing and cost analyses; single-centre routine setting.
Data_Quality_Concerns: False positives driven by mixed growth of Enterobacterales, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Bacillus sp. (about 85% of false positives) and by non-specific colours on chromogenic plates; two false negatives from small, pale colonies with poorly specific features.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear methods and full 2x2 tables (Tables 1-2) with 95% CIs; minor internal inconsistencies (abstract sensitivity 99.8% vs 99.9% in the results text; abstract positivity 866/17,223 vs 868/17,223 in the results text).
Page_References: pp. 1-4 (objectives, methods, performance results and Tables 1-2); p. 5 and p. 8 (automatic release, PPV/NPV, workflow); pp. 9-10 (limitations, conclusions, funding, ethics).

Title: Proof of concept study on early forecasting of antimicrobial resistance in hospitalized patients using machine learning and simple bacterial ecology data
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Hôpital Européen Marseille; SESSTIM (Aix Marseille Univ, Inserm, IRD); PhD grant from ISSPAM, Aix Marseille Université
Population_Description: Hospitalised patients: 30,975 antibiograms isolated from 13,166 patients in 6 ward types (emergency room 25%, critical care 24%, surgery 20%, medicine 19%) at the Hôpital Européen Marseille, 2014-2020; specimens mainly urine 41%, lower respiratory tract 23%, blood 14%, abscesses 12%
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP ranking for the NN models, by stage: (1) history of MDR bacterial carriage in the last 3 months, a strong predictor at all stages with high absolute SHAP values (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); (2) aspect on direct examination, significant at stage 2; (3) cultural feature, largest contribution at stage 3 'culture'; (4) at stage 4 'species', species then cultural features are the strongest contributors; specimen origin, ward type and date had a less significant effect at all stages
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Frequentist (FRQ), Bayesian (BAY), logistic regression (LR), AdaBoost (ADA), Gradient Boosting (GBS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Bagging (BAG), Random Forest (RF) and neural networks (NN), compared on mean AUROC at each stage of the bacteriological process on the 2020 validation dataset. Overall mean AUROC of all models rose from 0.594 (stage 1 'sampling') to 0.708 (stage 2 'direct'), 0.773 (stage 3 'culture') and 0.847 (stage 4 'species'). BAY, NN, FRQ and XGB performed much better than GBS, ADA, BAG, RF and LR. NN had the highest mean AUROC (0.823) and the highest AUROC at each stage except stage 4, where BAY reached 0.918. For the least frequent situations BAY held mean AUROCs of 0.824 (stage 3) and 0.917 (stage 4); NN dropped from 0.693 to 0.512 at stage 1 and from 0.811 to 0.658 at stage 2; FRQ fell from 0.893 to 0.662 at stage 4; LR was worst at all stages (mean AUROC 0.554)
Best_Performing_Model: BAY (Bayesian inference) models and NN (neural network) models — named best on mean AUROC
AUROC_Value: 0.918 (BAY model, stage 4 'species', all isolates); highest NN mean AUROC 0.823 across stages
AUROC_Population_Set: 2020 validation dataset (all isolates); stage 4 'species' for the BAY model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Monocentric retrospective proof-concept study: models developed on the 2014-2019 dataset (80% training / 20% testing) and evaluated on the separate 2020 validation dataset (4,354 antibiograms) from the same hospital; the authors describe the work as a proof of concept and no external or prospective validation has been performed
Reported_Limitations: Low performance at the early stage 1 'sampling' (mean AUROC 0.693) because only a few features were included; no demographics, comorbidities or history of antibiotic treatment; AUROCs vary widely between antibiotics; concept drift complicates use of the date; predictions and performance are specific to the Hôpital Européen Marseille ecology; rare situations are poorly predicted; intervention studies and implementation science are still needed
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Data-protection governance only: use of anonymised bacterial ecology data under the GDPR; the wider project received authorisation DR-2020-047 from the French national commission for data protection (CNIL); the authors note that patient-related sensitive data are strictly controlled in Europe
Reviewer_Notes: Unit of analysis: the BAY and NN models named as best; AUROC taken from the 2020 validation dataset (all isolates) which the authors state is the dataset used for the reported results. Judgments: Breakpoint_Guideline = Other (French CA-SFM and European EUCAST guidelines); Infection_Type = Other (models cover a wide range of infected body sites, not one syndrome); Regulatory_Approval_Mentioned = No (the only regulatory mention is a CNIL data-protection authorisation, not a device/software clearance); Lifecycle_P5 left blank (deployment is aspirational, only a prototype is being tested at HEM); Study_Design ticked as development + retrospective cohort (the authors do not label the 2020 evaluation an external validation study)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All antibiograms performed by the bacteriology laboratory of the Hôpital Européen Marseille between January 2014 and December 2020, extracted from the laboratory information system
Exclusion_Criteria: Likely contaminants of bacterial culture, duplicates, and screening specimens (rectal and nasal swabs) sampled for MDR carriage; isolates with intermediate susceptibility were considered resistant
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: Hôpital Européen Marseille bacteriology laboratory information system (bacterial ecology data: positive cultures and antibiograms)
Dataset_Size: 44,026 antibiograms performed 2014-2020; cleaned dataset 30,975 antibiograms from 13,166 patients; 26,621 antibiograms (80% training + 20% testing, 2014-2019) and 4,354 validation antibiograms (2020)
Missing_Data_Method: Recommended expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance were used when susceptibility to a specific antibiotic was not available; when no similar situation existed in the training dataset a susceptibility probability of 0.5 was attributed so isolates were not excluded from AUROC estimation
Geographic_Representativeness: Single French general hospital (Hôpital Européen Marseille), in the popular central districts of a city of nearly 900,000 people in south-eastern France; the authors state the predictions reflect the specific bacterial ecology of that hospital; multi-centre evaluation planned in six French hospitals
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine (41%), lower respiratory tract (23%), blood (14%), abscesses (12%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Probability of antimicrobial susceptibility (binary susceptible / resistant) to 22 single antibiotics and 25 antibiotic combinations, predicted for each bacterial isolate at each of the four pre-antibiogram stages
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (29%), Staphylococcus aureus (12%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (10%), Enterococcus faecalis (9%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (8%); also Enterobacteriaceae-like and non-fermentative Gram-negative rods, Staphylococcus-like and Enterococcus-like Gram-positive cocci; the species variable had 384 possible values
Num_Pathogens: 384 (number of possible values of the species variable)
Drug_Classes: Penicillins/aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate), cephalosporins (cefazolin/oxacillin, cefotaxime/ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime), monobactam (aztreonam), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem), aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), folate pathway inhibitors (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), glycopeptide (vancomycin), rifamycin (rifampicin), lincosamide (clindamycin), macrolides, oxazolidinone (linezolid), nitroimidazole (metronidazole)
Specific_Antibiotics: 22 single antibiotics: Amoxicillin; Amox-Clav; Oxacillin/cefazolin; Pip-Tazo; Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone; Ceftazidime; Cefepime; Aztreonam; Imipenem; Meropenem; Ertapenem; Amikacin; Gentamicin; Ciprofloxacin; Levofloxacin; TMP-SMX; Vancomycin; Rifampicin; Clindamycin; Macrolides; Linezolid; Metronidazole — plus 25 antibiotic combinations
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptibility (susceptible or resistant) of each bacterial isolate to 22 single antibiotics and 25 antibiotic combinations; isolates with 'intermediate' susceptibility were considered resistant; missing susceptibility was filled using expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance
AI_Purpose: Predict the probability of antimicrobial susceptibility (and explain the contribution of cofactors) in hospitalised patients at four stages before the antibiogram is available, using only historical bacterial ecology data, to assist clinicians choosing empirical antimicrobial therapy; a prototype ML-CDSS was developed
Num_Models_Compared: 9 model families compared (FRQ, BAY, LR, ADA, GBS, XGB, BAG, RF, NN); SVM models were excluded after exploratory analysis; one dense multilayer NN classifier per antibiotic per stage
Feature_Engineering: Features built from antibiogram metadata: type of ward, body-site origin of the specimen, previous MDR bacterial carriage in the last 3 months, aspect at direct Gram stain, cultural feature, bacterial species, plus clinical-relevance (contaminant) and duplicate flags; the sampling date was normalised between 0 and 1, and categorical variables were label-encoded after comparing one-hot and label encoding
Num_Features_Total: 3-4 per stage
Hyperparameter_Method: Exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation over the training dataset
Software_Libraries: Scikit-Learn (ensemble-based machine learning models); Keras and KerasClassifier (neural networks); SHAP Python package (interpretability); Gradio (prototype web application)
Other_Metrics: Mean AUROC per model, stage and antibiotic, with AUROC distributions and between-antibiotic standard deviations (0.03-0.17); prediction omission rate for FRQ (0.7% stage 1 to 10.2% stage 4); root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of susceptibility between isolate categories; Spearman's rank correlation between NN SHAP values and BAY likelihood ratios (0.57; p = 0.0033)
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (LR), used as the baseline model
Baseline_Performance: LR was the worst model at all stages, mean AUROC 0.554
Internal_Validation: 80% training / 20% testing split of the 2014-2019 dataset with 10-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning, then evaluation on all 2020 antibiograms held out from training
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing of the 2014-2019 data (26,621 antibiograms, of which 4,915 in 2019 alone); validation on all 2020 data (4,354 antibiograms)
External_Validation_Description: None performed; external evaluation is planned in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals including HEM
Overfitting_Method: Dropout layers after each hidden dense layer and batch normalisation in the neural networks; XGB's higher regularisation mitigates overfitting; hyperparameters chosen by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation
Explainability_Methods: SHAP; Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model; Other
Clinical_Insights: History of MDR carriage in the last 3 months is a strong predictor at all stages (prior positive carriage lowers, prior negative carriage raises predicted susceptibility); the cultural feature dominates at the culture stage and species then culture type at the species stage; in a worked scenario predicted susceptibility to CTX/CRO was 0.87 at the culture stage (good probability) and 0.40 at the species stage (bad probability, for Citrobacter koseri in critical care); NN SHAP values and BAY likelihood ratios were moderately consistent (Spearman 0.57, p = 0.0033)
Data_Repository: No repository; anonymised data available from author S. Rebaudet upon reasonable request with a material transfer agreement
Generalisability_Details: The authors hypothesise that the overall architecture of the algorithms is generalisable and that similar models could be adapted to other hospitals trained with local bacteriological data; to be evaluated in an ongoing multi-centre study in six French hospitals and through an interoperable health data warehouse in eight hospitals, comparing federated learning with centralised and local approaches
Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective monocentric design; hyperparameters tuned by exhaustive grid search with 10-fold cross-validation on the training data; performance reported on the 2020 validation dataset (4,354 antibiograms) held out from the 2014-2019 training+testing data; no external, prospective or clinical-impact evaluation
Integration_Point: Prototype web application (Gradio, private HuggingFace space) being tested at HEM; planned embedding in the laboratory information management system (LIMS) to provide preliminary probabilistic antibiograms, in EMR systems or health data warehouses, or as a stewardship dashboard
End_User_Described: Hospital doctors/prescribers selecting empirical antimicrobial therapy; on-call infectiologists giving antimicrobial stewardship advice; antimicrobial stewardship teams (dashboard flagging prescriptions of low susceptibility probability)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Predictions at four stages matched to laboratory turnaround: stage 1 'sampling' (Day 0, specimen origin), stage 2 'direct' (Day 0-1, direct Gram stain aspect), stage 3 'culture' (Day 1-2, cultural feature) and stage 4 'species' (Day 2-3, species identification), used to refine empirical therapy until the antibiogram is available
Stewardship_Details: Studies underway in six hospitals will retrospectively describe the susceptibility probability and spectrum width of prescribed empirical therapies to assess potential efficacy gains and safe de-escalations; a stewardship dashboard flagging prescriptions with low susceptibility probability is proposed
Barriers_List: GDPR restrictions on patient-related sensitive data; EMR data stored in heterogeneous formats and not readily accessible in all hospital facilities; no demographics, comorbidities or antibiotic history, limiting stage 1 performance; concept drift makes the date difficult to model; BAY models are burdensome to program; rare situations are unmet in the training data; the system must not replace practice guidelines or prescriber decisions
Facilitators_List: Only simple bacterial ecology data are needed, easily extracted from any laboratory information system without GDPR restrictions after on-site anonymisation; NN models can be implemented and tuned with open-source packages and scale to new input variables; FRQ/BAY models are intrinsically interpretable and SHAP explains the NN; the probability output is designed to enrich the prescriber's reasoning rather than replace it
Future_Directions: Include demographic features (age, sex, residence), comorbidities and history of antibiotic consumption; impute subsequent-stage data; model month and year separately with temporal sliding windows, concept-drift detectors and continuous learning; assess model uncertainty; multi-centre and federated evaluations; intervention studies followed by implementation science
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for the NN models at population and individual level; feature-specific likelihood ratios for the BAY models
Limitation_Categories: Model performance: low AUROC at stage 1 with a limited feature set; metric variability between antibiotics. Data: absence of demographics, comorbidities and antibiotic history (GDPR); concept drift. Setting: single-centre data specific to one hospital's ecology; rare situations unmet in training. Methods: label encoding choice; BAY models burdensome to program. Evidence base: no prospective or clinical-impact evaluation yet
Data_Quality_Concerns: Removal of likely contaminants, duplicates and screening specimens before training; intermediate susceptibility recoded as resistant; missing susceptibility values filled by expert rules on intrinsic and cross-resistance; rare feature combinations absent from the training data cause prediction omissions; concept drift over time
Page_References: pp. 1-16 (full PDF text layer); title, abstract and DOI p. 1; dataset description and model comparison pp. 2-3; AUROC results pp. 3-5; best models p. 6; SHAP interpretability pp. 6-7; discussion, limitations and barriers pp. 8-10; methods pp. 10-14; data availability p. 14; acknowledgements p. 15; competing interests, ethics and supplementary note p. 16

Title: Amikacin Concentrations Predictive of Ototoxicity in Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Patients
Journal_Source: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy (Antimicrob Agents Chemother 59:6337-6343)
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health (grants R01AI097045 and R56AI111985-01)
Population_Description: 28 multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (MDR-TB) patients in Botswana, aged 15 years or older, started on MDR-TB treatment and with serum amikacin concentration measurements
Age_Range: 15 years of age or older (eligibility criterion); age ranges by group 28-70 years (Table 3)
Top_Predictive_Features: CART variable ranking on the drug-dose/PK model: primary node cumulative days of therapy; cumulative AUC ranked second (improved on the primary node by another 87%); AUC0-24 score 34%; initial weight score 29%. Cumulative AUC thresholds from the concentration-only tree: 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
All_Models_Evaluated: CART (classification and regression tree) models built in three steps with the Salford Predictive Miner System: (1) all potential predictors (AUROC 0.97 on the test sets); (2) pharmacokinetic/treatment factors only, primary node cumulative days of therapy, cumulative AUC second, AUC0-24 34%, initial weight 29% (AUROC 0.97); (3) drug concentrations only, identifying cumulative AUC thresholds of 54,519 and 91,914 days*mg*h/liter; plus a CART model forced to pick peak and trough, AUROC 0.46 on the test set. Also a 2-compartment population PK model (ADAPT 5), probit models (TC50 87,323 days*mg*h/liter, TC80 120,238) and frequentist group comparisons in STATA 13.
Best_Performing_Model: CART tree using cumulative days of therapy as the primary node with cumulative AUC second, test-set AUROC 0.97 - superior to the model forced to pick peak and trough (AUROC 0.46)
AUROC_Population_Set: Test set (internal cross-validation; random repeated training/test splits) for the CART model using drug-dose and pharmacokinetic factors
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model built and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation of each tree and random repeated training/test splits only; no external validation, no prospective evaluation of the model and no deployment, so the highest evidence-supported level is internal validation.
Reported_Limitations: Amikacin has a long half-life in cochlear tissue so hearing loss may occur long after therapy stops; only amikacin concentrations were measured although MDR-TB patients receive other ototoxic drugs; insufficient data on prior streptomycin exposure to examine that relationship; defining ototoxicity remains imprecise because conventional audiometers test only up to 8 kHz while amikacin affects hearing up to 20 kHz.
Sample_Size: 28 MDR-TB patients (patients, not isolates) with amikacin concentration measurements and audiometry assessments
Conflicts_of_Interest: T.G. has worked as a consultant for Astellas Pharma US, Inc., and LuminaCare Solutions and founded Jacaranda Biomed, Inc. All other authors have no conflicts to declare.
Inclusion_Criteria: All MDR-TB patients 15 years of age or older started on MDR-TB treatment between 1 January 2011 and 30 December 2012 with serum amikacin concentration measurements reported; at least one creatinine measurement within 1 month prior to or after the start of amikacin and one follow-up creatinine measurement (within the last 6 months prior to censoring).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Botswana national MDR-TB treatment programme (no named dataset)
Dataset_Size: 28 patients; 2 amikacin concentration samples per patient (1 h and 23.5 h after dose)
Geographic_Representativeness: All 28 patients were treated within one national MDR-TB programme in Botswana (one country, one programme), so the sample does not represent other settings.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Serum (plasma) amikacin concentrations; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Ototoxicity (audiometry-confirmed hearing loss) attributable to amikacin treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis - not a drug-resistance outcome
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, MDR-TB; pulmonary)
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycoside (amikacin); fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin); thioamide (ethionamide); cycloserine; pyrazinamide
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin; levofloxacin; ethionamide; cycloserine; pyrazinamide (prior streptomycin exposure in 10 patients)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Audiometry-determined neurosensory hearing loss defined as a shift or loss of 15 to 25 dB relative to baseline averaged at two or more contiguous frequencies in at least one ear, or loss of response at 3 consecutive frequencies where responses had previously been obtained; audiometry-confirmed hearing loss is synonymous with ototoxicity.
AI_Purpose: To identify clinical factors, including amikacin concentration thresholds, that predict ototoxicity in MDR-TB patients using an agnostic machine learning method (classification and regression tree analysis), and to derive threshold decision-making values for clinicians.
Num_Models_Compared: 3 CART models (all predictors; pharmacokinetic and treatment factors only, Figure 3; peak and trough forced) plus probit models for comparison
Feature_Engineering: Pharmacokinetic features derived from the population model (AUC0-24, cumulative AUC), cumulative dose and cumulative dose divided by weight, amikacin dose in mg/kg as daily and cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, peak and trough concentrations, plus clinical variables (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy). CART is used to break the collinearity of these highly correlated measures.
Feature_Selection_Method: CART classification and ranking subroutines (Gini splitting; predictors ranked in order of importance, with surrogate variables), tree pruning by AUROC and parsimony
Num_Features_Total: 14 candidate predictors listed (age, gender, initial weight, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy, amikacin dose, cumulative dose, time on amikacin therapy, daily dose mg/kg, cumulative dose mg/kg, AUC0-24, cumulative AUC, peak, trough)
Num_Features_Selected: not reported as a count; the final tree used cumulative days of therapy as the primary node and cumulative AUC second
Class_Imbalance_Method: Priors set to equal (equal probability assignment for all categories), with no penalty sets for misclassification
Software_Libraries: Salford Predictive Miner System; ADAPT 5 (including its SAMPLE subroutine); STATA version 13; COBAS INTEGRA assays
Other_Metrics: AUROC (0.97 test set for the best model; 0.46 for the peak/trough-forced model); CART relative improvement scores (87% for cumulative AUC, 34% AUC0-24, 29% initial weight); probit r2 for cumulative AUC 0.97, weight 0.95 and duration 0.98; cumulative AUC TC50 87,323 (CI 81,248-93,216) and TC80 120,238 days*mg*h/liter; correlations r2 between exposure measures
Baseline_Method: CART model forced to pick peak and trough concentrations as predictors - the parameters currently used for clinical dosing decisions
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.46 on the test set, inferior to the 0.97 of the duration-of-therapy and cumulative AUC model
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation of each tree, plus repeated random splitting of the data set into training and test data sets (predictive power assessed on the test set)
Train_Test_Split: Random repeated splits of the data set into training and test data sets; reported performance is that of the training-set-derived tree on the test set (test-set AUROC 0.97)
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Feature importance / permutation importance
Clinical_Insights: Threshold cumulative AUC of ~87,232 days*mg*h/liter for a 10% probability of ototoxicity and ~120,000 for 20%; ototoxicity risk rises after ~6 months of therapy and approaches certainty at 9 months; peak and trough concentrations are not useful monitoring parameters; optimal blood-draw times for therapeutic drug monitoring were 0, 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h.
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue the concentration-ototoxicity relationship is likely to hold as sample size increases because it was also identified by parametric probit models and is concordant with guinea pig animal experiments that give a biological basis for the findings.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: CART trees built with Gini splitting and 5-fold cross-validation, with repeated random training/test splits; no external validation data set, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment.
Integration_Point: Therapeutic drug monitoring and amikacin dosing decisions for MDR-TB treatment, using cumulative AUC and duration of therapy thresholds in place of peak and trough concentrations.
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating pulmonary tuberculosis / MDR-TB programmes
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Blood draws for amikacin therapeutic drug monitoring should be taken just before the dose and at 15 min, 2.5 h and 18.7 h after the dose rather than at peak and trough; cumulative AUC and duration thresholds are then used to judge the risk of ototoxicity during treatment.
Future_Directions: Measuring amikacin concentrations lets the optimal (safe) duration of therapy be calculated in the first week of therapy, and the identified sampling times (0, 15 min, 2.5 h, 18.7 h) should be used for therapeutic drug monitoring in tuberculosis programmes.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: CART importance ranking (relative improvement scores on the primary node)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Cumulative amikacin AUC and duration of therapy - and not the peak and trough concentrations currently used for dosing - are the predictors of ototoxicity; the AUC relationship was sigmoidal and gave explicit decision thresholds.

End_User_Described: Not reported - the paper names no specific end user for the models

Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance attribute for the tree-based models (XGBoost, GBC); absolute values of the logistic regression coefficients for LR

Title: Automated detection of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with the MRSA CHROM imaging application on BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System
Funder_Names: Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD Life Sciences — Integrated Diagnostic Solutions)
Population_Description: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one per patient) collected at three sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) between January and August 2019; a single 30 µl aliquot was inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II and imaged on the BD Kiestra TLA System. 1,775 specimens enrolled, 1,593 evaluable; deidentified patient age and gender recorded but no clinical characteristics reported.
Age_Range: 3% of specimens from patients less than 20 years of age; 27% aged 20–59 years; 69% aged 60 years and over; no demographic information for 1%
Data_Source_Other: Digital agar plate images of BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II captured by the BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation System and managed in the Colony Information System (CIS)/Clindex; ground truth from laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Infection prevention and control team
Delivery_Platform: Instrument / device embedded; Laboratory information system (LIS) integrated
All_Models_Evaluated: MRSA App (BD Kiestra methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus Application) — the only model evaluated: sensitivity 98.15% (95% CI, 96.03, 99.32), specificity 96.69% (95% CI, 95.55, 97.60), concordance 96.98%, PPV 88.11%, NPV 99.52%. Internally it comprises four machine-learning models (zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification, plate positivity) for which no per-model metrics are reported.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
Specificity_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites (Total row, Table 1)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: All 1,593 evaluable anterior nares specimens across the three sites
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level the paper's own evidence supports is external validation: this is the first evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, a locked commercial algorithm, applied without retraining to independent anterior nares specimens collected at three sites in two countries (two US, one Canada) and read against a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard, with sensitivity (98.15%) and specificity (96.69%) reported. No model development or training on the study data is described, and there is no prospective clinical impact evaluation, CDS integration or routine-use assessment of this cohort.
Reported_Limitations: Discrepant specimens were not available for repeat testing to confirm that discrepancies were not imaging artefacts, nor for confirmation of MRSA positivity by a different testing method; the study design allowed technologists at each site to choose one of two streaking patterns, so the higher false-positive count at Site 3 may reflect the pattern chosen, and de-identification prevented further analysis.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: False-positive App results carry the potential for unwarranted patient management: about one in ten MRSA-App-positive results could trigger isolation, topical or systemic antibiotics or other clinical attention although the patient is negative; in this study technologists were blinded to App results, and in real-world use all suspected positives would be reviewed by a technologist.
Reviewer_Notes: Laboratory-automation diagnostic accuracy study of an AI imaging application (BD Kiestra MRSA App) on chromogenic MRSA screening plates; no patient-level clinical or sociodemographic data beyond age band and gender. Two conventions had to be judged. (1) Validation/maturity: the paper reports no development or training data, so the multi-site evaluation of the pre-existing commercial algorithm is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only', Clinical_Maturity_Level 3) rather than internal validation of the study's own dataset — flagged for team discussion. (2) Best_Performing_Model: a single index test is evaluated and no models are compared, so the NA checkbox is ticked. Reported artefact: the negative predictive value CI is printed in reverse order ('98.96, 98.78') in the results text. Sex was collected (gender stored in Clindex/CIS) but no sex distribution is reported.
Unresolved_Items: Whether a locked, sponsor-developed commercial application evaluated for the first time on independent multi-site specimens is coded as external validation (Validation_Strategy 'External only' / Clinical_Maturity_Level 3, as recorded here) or as internal validation of the study's own dataset (level 2); the MRSA App's training/development data are not reported anywhere in the paper.
Sample_Size: 1,593 evaluable specimens (1,775 enrolled, 166 excluded, 16 without a standard-of-care result removed)
Conflicts_of_Interest: S.M., J.L., D.M., C.O., J.-M.V. and K.B. are employees of the study sponsor (Becton, Dickinson and Company) and own BD shares; D.R. has received research support for this investigation and performed sponsored research with Abbott, Altona, BD, bioMerieux, Cepheid, Luminex, Hardy Diagnostics, HelixBind, Hologic, Qiagen, Q-Linea, Roche, Specific Diagnostics, Cleveland Diagnostics, Thermo Fisher and Vela Diagnostics, served as an advisor for Roche, Thermo Fisher, Luminex/DiaSorin and Seegene, received travel funds from Cepheid and owns equity in Next Gen Diagnostics; M.D. has received research support for this investigation; P.P. and C.E.G. have no conflicts; E.M. has received research support for this investigation and is a sponsored speaker for BD.
Inclusion_Criteria: Remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens collected at the three participating sites (standard of care at each facility); only one Eswab per patient was eligible for inclusion.
Exclusion_Criteria: Plates removed from the incubator at any point before completion of the imaging process, or specimens meeting routine laboratory rejection criteria; after enrolment, 166 specimens were excluded (inoculation outside QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or failed image quality check, no truth collected) and 16 further cultures with no standard-of-care result were removed.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; Other
Data_Source_Name: BD Kiestra Total Lab Automation (TLA) System with the BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II (CHROMagar); Colony Information System (CIS) and Clindex (BD Clinical Information system)
Dataset_Size: 1,593 specimens evaluated (from 1,775 enrolled; 166 excluded; 16 without SOC result)
Geographic_Representativeness: Three clinical laboratory sites: two in the United States (Illinois, Ohio) and one in Canada (Ontario) — a North American, high-income multi-site sample; representativeness of the wider population is not discussed.
Specimen_Type_Detail: remnant MRSA anterior nares surveillance Eswab specimens (one 30 µl aliquot inoculated onto BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection of MRSA from anterior nares surveillance specimens: agreement between the MRSA App's automated colorimetric interpretation of CHROMagar MRSA II plate images (mauve colony growth) and the reference standard of laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images, reported as sensitivity, specificity, concordance, PPV and NPV.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant, MRSA). Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212 is named only as the negative quality-control organism.
Drug_Classes: Not modelled: the endpoint is presence/absence of MRSA (mauve colony growth) on chromogenic agar; no antimicrobial class outcome is modelled and no susceptibility testing was performed.
Specific_Antibiotics: Not tested: methicillin resistance is inferred from the chromogenic MRSA phenotype (mauve colonies); no susceptibility testing was performed.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Mauve-pigmented (chromogenic) colony growth on BD BBL CHROMagar MRSA II read from digital plate images = MRSA positive; plates are first assigned growth/no growth, and growing plates are assessed for chromogenic colony appearance signalling MRSA. The label is the laboratory technologist manual reading of the same images (standard of care / reference standard).
AI_Purpose: To automate the reading of chromogenic MRSA screening plates: the MRSA App uses digital plate images and conventional image processing plus a four-stage machine-learning pipeline to interpret colorimetric information (mauve colonies), detect MRSA growth and sort cultures into categories for batch reading, replacing manual reading of agar plate images.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (the MRSA App as a single index test, compared with the technologist reference standard; the App itself combines four machine-learning models — zone CFU/non-CFU classification, plate growth status, mauve/non-mauve CFU classification and plate positivity — with no per-model comparison)
Feature_Engineering: Areas of interest (pixel-value changes after incubation, i.e. CFUs or artefacts) are detected by conventional image processing; color, morphology, metrics and opacity are extracted from each zone and fed to an initial machine-learning model (CFU vs other), then plate-level metrics and descriptors of the detected CFU population feed a second model for growth status, with mauve/non-mauve classification and plate positivity in two further models.
Software_Libraries: R (R Core Team, 2020) version 4.0.2; MedCalc Software (v.22.021)
Other_Metrics: Concordance 96.98% (1,545/1,593); PPV 88.11% (95% CI, 84.62, 90.89); NPV 99.52% (95% CI, 98.96, 98.78 — as printed); 48 discrepant results (3.01%) with per-site discrepancy rates 0.8% (5/634), 2.7% (17/634) and 8% (26/325); 42 false positives and 6 false negatives; site-level sensitivities 99.56%, 91.30%, 98.00% and specificities 99.01%, 97.79%, 90.91%; chi-square tests across sites with P-values 0.0036, 0.0015, 0.0002, 0.0416, 0.9301NS and <0.0001.
Baseline_Method: Manual reading of the same digital agar plate images by two trained, blinded laboratory technologists at each site (with a third arbiter reader if consensus was not reached), used as the reference standard / standard of care.
Baseline_Performance: The technologist reading is the reference standard and is not scored separately; agreement with the MRSA App was 96.98% (1,545/1,593) with 42 App-only detections (false positives) and 6 technologist-only detections (false negatives).
External_Validation_Description: First evaluation of the pre-existing, sponsor-developed MRSA App, applied without retraining to anterior nares specimens collected independently at three clinical sites (two in the United States, one in Canada) and compared with a blinded laboratory technologist reference standard; no training or development dataset is reported in the paper.
Generalisability_Details: Authors argue that in real-world use, where technologists are not blinded to the App results, all suspected MRSA-positive plates would be reviewed by a technologist and the App's PPV would therefore likely be higher than the 88.11% measured here.
Maturity_Evidence: Multi-site diagnostic accuracy evaluation of the locked MRSA App against a blinded technologist reference standard on independent specimens (sensitivity 98.15%, specificity 96.69%); no model training on the study data, no prospective clinical impact evaluation, no CDS integration and no routine-use evidence reported for this cohort.
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory BD Kiestra TLA workflow: CHROMagar MRSA II plates imaged after 22-24 h of incubation, sorted by the MRSA App into batch-reading categories for technologist review and confirmation, with results then entered into the laboratory information system for viewing by physicians and clinical staff in the electronic medical record.
End_User_Described: Laboratory technologists / medical laboratory technologists who read and interpret the plate images (with clinicians receiving the results); no other end user is specified.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The App sorts MRSA screening cultures into growth/no growth categories so technologists can rapidly review and confirm pigmented colonies; cultures without growth can be batch-reviewed in up to 20 plates before final results, reducing data entry; in European laboratories mauve colonies are technologist-reviewed before reporting, no-growth cultures are automatically released and non-mauve growth is batch reported.
Stewardship_Details: Not measured: the paper states only that faster reporting may support antimicrobial stewardship efforts, without assessing any stewardship outcome.
Barriers_List: False-positive App results (42/1,593; PPV 88.11%) would need technologist review and confirmation to avoid unwarranted isolation and antibiotics; discrepant specimens were unavailable for repeat testing to exclude imaging artefacts; site-to-site variation in performance (lower sensitivity at Site 2, lower specificity at Site 3) and the two-option streaking pattern that could not be analysed further after de-identification; no visual explanation for 28 App-only detections.
Facilitators_List: Laboratory staffing shortages and an ageing workforce; existing laboratory automation (Kiestra TLA, Copan WASPLab) already integrated in clinical microbiology laboratories; batch reading of no-growth cultures (up to 20 plates) and European auto-release of no-growth cultures reduce hands-on time, data entry and reporting delays.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 2 (digital agar plate images / microbiological colony features; laboratory plate-level metrics and CFU descriptors)
Limitation_Categories: Discrepant specimens not available for repeat testing or confirmation by another method; study design allowed two streaking patterns, a possible explanation for the higher FP rate at Site 3 that could not be investigated further because specimens were de-identified; unexplained App-only detections (28 cultures); higher FP than FN balance driven by sensitivity-prioritising algorithm tuning.
Data_Quality_Concerns: 166 enrolled specimens were excluded (inoculation outside the QC-plate time span, missing incubation images, algorithm-detected issues such as a bead in the plate or a failed image quality check, plates with no truth collected) and 16 further cultures lacked a standard-of-care result; discrepant specimens were not retained for repeat testing; diffuse mauve pigment in the agar at the inoculation site and colony mixtures may explain some App-only detections.
Reporting_Clarity: Methods, index test, reference standard and per-site 2x2 data (Table 1) are reported with 95% CIs, but the NPV confidence interval is printed in reverse order as 98.96, 98.78 and the NPV/PPV are given only for the total, not per site.
Page_References: pp. 1-2 (abstract, background, AI program overview); p. 3 (specimen collection, MRSA App algorithm, processing, plate reading); p. 4 (QC, statistics, results incl. PPV/NPV); pp. 5-6 (discussion, Table 1, workflow); p. 7 (limitations, conclusions, funding, contributions); p. 8 (affiliations, data availability, supplemental material, references).

Title:
Emulation of a Target Trial to Estimate the Effect of Selective Serotonin 
Reuptake Inhibitors on the Development of Antimicrobial-Resistant 
Infections using Electronic Health Record Data and Causal Machine Learning
Study_Design_Other: Target trial emulation of a hypothetical randomised trial
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health (National Institute on Aging, R33AG062884; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, R01AI141810)
Population_Description: Adult UF Health patients with a bacterial infection diagnosis and antimicrobial susceptibility test results, restricted to those with a diagnosis of mood, anxiety or stress-related disorder; 1,715 SSRI-treated and 6,618 control patients before matching, 1,696 per group after 1:1 propensity score matching
Age_Mean_Median: Mean 54.5 years (SD 17.5) in the SSRI group and 54.5 years (SD 17.1) in the non-SSRI group after matching; overall mean about 54.5 years
Age_Range: Adults only (≥18 years at the index date); exact age range not reported
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
Task_Type_Other: Causal survival analysis — conditional average treatment effect estimation for a right-censored time-to-event outcome
All_Models_Evaluated: Kaplan-Meier survival curves (log-rank p<0.001); Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index and grouped zip code (adjusted HR for SSRI use 1.44, 95% CI 1.26-1.64); causal random survival forest (grf causal_survival_forest): average treatment effect -0.0499, standard error 0.0188
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were estimated and statistically evaluated only on the single-system UF Health matched cohort (Kaplan-Meier, adjusted Cox HR with 95% CI, causal survival forest ATE with SE); no external validation dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical integration is reported
Reported_Limitations: Cohort restricted to patients who had received antimicrobial susceptibility testing, mainly hospitalised patients; medication exposure captured only from the inpatient MAR so outpatient prescriptions may be missed (exposure misclassification); outcome misclassification when the relevant drug was not tested or testing occurred outside UF Health; residual confounding from unmeasured variables; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and about half the patients from one county, limiting generalisability
Reviewer_Notes: Target trial emulation on UF Health EHR data with causal machine learning; outcome is a binary antimicrobial susceptibility test result (resistant to at least one antibiotic) analysed as time-to-event. No discrimination or classification metrics (accuracy, AUROC, sensitivity, specificity) are reported, so all *_Reported metric fields are answered No for the best-performing-model unit of analysis; the three analytic approaches are reported as concordant rather than ranked, so Best_Performing_Model_NA is TRUE.
Sample_Size: 3,392 patients after matching (1,696 SSRI users and 1,696 non-SSRI patients); 8,333 patients before matching (1,715 treated and 6,618 control)
Sex_Distribution: After matching: female 1,201 (70.8%) in the SSRI group and 1,197 (70.6%) in the non-SSRI group; before matching: 1,211 (70.6%) and 4,783 (72.3%); 'Over 70% of the population was female'
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients at UF Health who (1) had a previous bacterial infection greater than 90 days before enrolment, (2) had at least two years of medication EHR data, (3) had not previously been given sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine or fluvoxamine, (4) had been diagnosed with mood, anxiety or stress-related disorder, and (5) did not have a bacterial infection at study initiation; each included patient also had a previous antimicrobial susceptibility test result or a diagnosis of bacterial infection more than 90 days before the index date
Exclusion_Criteria: No MAR Action containing the word 'GIVEN' for one of the SSRIs (patients may not have received the SSRI); fewer than two years of medication data before the index date; control-group patients whose last medication record or recorded death date preceded the index date; estimated age younger than 18 years at the index date; antimicrobial susceptibility test results or bacterial infection diagnostic codes within 30 days of the index date
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: University of Florida (UF) Health Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
Dataset_Size: 3,392 patients after matching (1,696 per group); 8,333 before matching (1,715 treated, 6,618 control)
Ethnicity_Details: After matching: Non-Hispanic White 1,137 (67.0%) SSRI vs 1,140 (67.2%) non-SSRI; Non-Hispanic Black 469 (27.7%) vs 470 (27.7%); Hispanic 51 (3.0%) vs 49 (2.9%); Other 39 (2.3%) vs 37 (2.2%)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single integrated academic health system (UF Health, North and Central Florida); about half of the patients came from the 326 grouped zip code (Alachua County area); the authors state the results may not be generalizable to other populations
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antimicrobial susceptibility test result of 'resistant' (including 'tentative interpretation: resistant' or 'non susceptible') to at least one antibiotic tested, from 30 to 1,825 days after the index date
Drug_Classes: SSRIs as the study exposure (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine, fluvoxamine); the outcome is resistance to at least one antibiotic tested, with no antimicrobial class specified
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary: an antimicrobial susceptibility test result of 'resistant', 'tentative interpretation: resistant' or 'non susceptible' for at least one antibiotic tested, from 30 to 1,825 days after the index date
AI_Purpose: To estimate the causal effect of SSRI exposure on the incidence of antibiotic-resistant infection, using a target trial emulation framework and causal machine learning (causal survival forest) alongside conventional survival regression
Num_Models_Compared: 3 analytical approaches (univariable/multivariable survival regression, Cox proportional hazards model, causal random survival forest)
Feature_Engineering: All diagnostic codes converted to the ICD-10-CM revision; ICD-10 code sets used to define bacterial infection and mood/anxiety/stress-related disorders; index date defined as the first MAR mention of an SSRI (treated) or a randomly sampled time before study initiation (control)
Num_Features_Total: 5 covariates (sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index, three-digit zip code)
Other_Metrics: Log-rank test p-value less than 0.001; adjusted hazard ratio 1.44 (95% CI 1.26-1.64); average treatment effect -0.0499 (standard error 0.0188); Kaplan-Meier probabilities of not developing an antibiotic-resistant infection with 95% confidence intervals
Baseline_Method: Multivariable Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for sex, age, race-ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index and grouped zip code (conventional regression comparator against the causal random survival forest)
Baseline_Performance: Adjusted hazard ratio 1.44 (95% CI 1.26-1.64) for SSRI users versus non-users
Clinical_Insights: The authors conclude that documented SSRI use is associated with a higher risk of antibiotic-resistant infection, framed as supporting prior in vitro findings and suggesting SSRI usage should be investigated as a possible driver of antimicrobial resistance
Generalisability_Details: Data come from one health system (UF Health) and about half of the patients came from one county (326 grouped zip code, Alachua County area); the authors state the results may not be generalizable to other populations
Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective single-system EHR cohort (2011-2023); all three analyses were fitted and evaluated on the same 1,696-per-group matched cohort, with no external validation cohort, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment reported
Barriers_List: Exposure measured only through the inpatient medication administration record, so outpatient SSRI use may be missed and patients misclassified into the control group; the outcome can be missed when the relevant drug was not tested or testing occurred outside UF Health; residual confounding from unmeasured variables; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and one county, limiting generalisability
Future_Directions: Further studies in human patients are needed to examine the effects of different SSRIs (for example sertraline versus escitalopram), dosages and lengths of treatment, and to explore differences in infection type, organism and type of AMR

Limitation_Categories: Restriction to patients who had antimicrobial susceptibility testing (mainly hospitalised); exposure measured from the inpatient MAR only; outcome and exposure misclassification; residual confounding; bias from converted ICD codes; EHR missingness and inaccuracies; single health system and one county limiting generalisability
Data_Quality_Concerns: EHR data are prone to missingness and inaccuracies; medication exposure captured only from the inpatient MAR; converted ICD codes may introduce bias; outcome may be missed when susceptibility testing was not performed for the relevant drug
