Title: Is it possible to predict multidrug-resistant organism colonization and/or infection at ICU admission?
Population_Description: 16,950 patients admitted consecutively (stay of at least >24 hours) to 147 Spanish ICUs participating in the ENVIN (National Surveillance Study of Nosocomial Infections in ICUs) registry
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Infection prevention and control team
All_Models_Evaluated: Admission-only multivariable logistic regression model: AUC-ROC 0.775 (95% CI 0.744-0.807) in the development sample, sensitivity 67.4%; AUC-ROC 0.712 (95% CI 0.665-0.759) on validation with the remaining 4,952 patients. Expanded model adding variables obtained after ICU admission (APACHE score, mechanical ventilation, catheters, immunodeficiency, parenteral nutrition, ventricular derivation, extrarenal depuration, non-invasive ventilation, tracheotomy, enteral nutrition, nasogastric tube): AUC-ROC 0.801 (95% CI 0.774-0.828), sensitivity 71.4% -- authors state prediction capability 'did not improve'.
Best_Performing_Model: Original admission-only multivariable logistic regression model (variables obtainable at ICU admission only): AUC-ROC = 0.775 (development) / 0.712 (internal validation). Judged the primary model because it is the one matching the study's stated aim (prediction at admission from easy-to-obtain factors) and the only one with an independently validated AUC-ROC; the expanded model's higher training AUC-ROC (0.801) is explicitly described by the authors as not an improvement in prediction capability.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was split-sample internally validated only (11,998 patients, 2/3, for development and 4,952 patients, 1/3, for validation) within the same registry and time window; no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or deployment is reported.
Reported_Limitations: MDRO prediction at ICU admission could not be based merely on clinical-demographic risk factors.
Unresolved_Items: Source PDF is the entire 201-page ISICEM 2015 / Critical Care Suppl 1 abstract book, not a standalone article; two closely related abstracts by the same author group appear back-to-back (P100, extracted here, on general MDRO prediction, and P101 on MRSA-specific prediction). Only P100 was extracted as the unit of analysis for this record.
Sample_Size: 16,950 patients (ICU admissions in the ENVIN registry, April-June 2010)
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients admitted consecutively (stay of at least >24 hours) to 147 Spanish ICUs participating in the ENVIN registry, April to June 2010.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: ENVIN (National Surveillance Study of Nosocomial Infections in ICUs) registry
Dataset_Size: 16,950 patients
Primary_AMR_Outcome: We tried to develop a predictive model for patients colonized/infected by any multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO-C/I) at ICU admission based on risk factors easy to obtain
Pathogens: Any multidrug-resistant organism (not limited to a single named pathogen)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: colonized/infected by any multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO-C/I) at ICU admission
AI_Purpose: being aware that foreseeing MDRO-C/I at ICU admission is key for appropriate empirical treatment and infection control
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariable screening followed by multivariable logistic regression
Num_Features_Selected: 7 (5 independent risk factors plus 2 protective factors in the admission-only model)
Internal_Validation: Split-sample: 11,998 patients (2/3) for model development, 4,952 (1/3) for subsequent validation
Train_Test_Split: 11,998 (2/3) development / 4,952 (1/3) validation
Maturity_Evidence: Validation with the remaining 4,952 patients (1/3) showed an AUC-ROC = 0.712 (95% CI, 0.665 to 0.759) and a P value on the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit test of 0.855 -- an internal, split-sample validation only.
Future_Directions: Taking into account local particularities and combining risk factors with a rapid laboratory test might be the most effective way forward.
Limitation_Categories: Model relies only on clinical-demographic risk factors, which the authors state is insufficient for adequate prediction of MDRO colonisation/infection at ICU admission.

Title: Performance of Risk Models for Antimicrobial Resistance in Adult Patients With Sepsis
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health / National Institute of General Medical Sciences (grant No. 1K08GM140310-01); Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital; Washington University Institute of Clinical and Translational Sciences grant No. UL1TR002345 from the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences of the National Institutes of Health
Population_Description: 39 893 adult patients with sepsis (85 238 sepsis episodes; 43 207 community-onset, 42 031 hospital-onset) admitted to 10 acute-care BJC hospitals in Missouri and Illinois, January 2016 to October 2021
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 10 features (SHAP values, gradient-boosting model), all episodes of community-onset sepsis: History of P aeruginosa; History of antibiotic administration; History of pneumonia due to P aeruginosa; Age; Albumin; History of resistance to multiple antibiotics; History of urinary tract infection; Pneumonia due to other GNB; BMI; ALT
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Deep learning model vs gradient-boosting model (XGBoost, dedicated to SHAP variable importance). Comorbidity/medical-history-only comparison: deep learning AUROC 0.81 (95% CI, 0.81-0.81) and AUPRC 0.30 (95% CI, 0.29-0.31); gradient boosting AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76) and AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23)
Best_Performing_Model: Deep learning model (deep neural network with fully connected, recurrent neural network and transformer subnetworks) - highest AUROC vs gradient boosting (0.81 vs 0.76) in the comorbidity-only comparison
AUROC_Value: Deep learning model, community-onset sepsis: AUROC 0.84 (95% CI, 0.83-0.84) for RS episodes and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79-0.83) for RR episodes
AUROC_Population_Set: Holdout testing dataset, community-onset sepsis episodes (RS and RR GNB isolates), 10 hospitals
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation: 80% of the data trained the models (70% training, 10% model selection) and 20% was held out for patient group-specific testing within the same 10 hospitals and period; no external or prospective validation, no CDS integration
Reported_Limitations: Limitations inherent to retrospective analyses based on EHR data; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); a large study capturing difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured data format is nearly impossible
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Widespread overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics (the unintended consequence of previous risk stratification tools derived at centres with high resistance prevalence), which may have detrimental effects at the population and patient levels; national study reporting only 0.9% of samples retrieved ARO GNB while 76% of those patients were flagged as candidates for double GNB coverage
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: The 3 example hospitals differ socioeconomically: an academic quaternary centre serving a socioeconomically diverse population, a suburban community hospital serving an affluent population, and a community-based hospital serving a socioeconomically disadvantaged population; model performance varied with local resistance prevalence rather than patient casemix, so the same patient subgroup falls into different risk categories depending on the institution
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Washington University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board approved the study and granted a waiver of consent due to the retrospective nature of the study; data sharing is via Supplement 2; no code or model sharing statement
Reviewer_Notes: Record built from the pypdf text layer. Main judgements: the paper evaluates 2 models (a deep learning model named as 'the main tool' and a gradient-boosting model dedicated to SHAP variable importance) and reports no single primary dataset - results are given separately for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, so Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/Precision/F1 are answered No and AUROC/AUPRC are reported for the deep learning model with both onset settings named
Unresolved_Items: No model-level AUROC is printed for the hospital-onset model (only AUPRC 0.25 for RS and 0.16 for RR); the AUROC 0.81 (0.81-0.81) figure appears only in the comorbidity-subset comparison and does not state which dataset; the paper names no single primary dataset for the review's unit of analysis
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr Vazquez Guillamet reported selling stocks in Carsima Therapeutics, Bionano Genomics, and Ocugen Inc in September 2023 outside the submitted work; Dr Fraser reported that their spouse is a former senior vice president/chief medical officer and now consulting for Cigna/Express Scripts; no other disclosures were reported
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients meeting the US CDC adult sepsis event criteria admitted to any of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals between January 2016 to October 2021; inclusion combined presumed infection (blood cultures and 4 qualifying days of antibiotics) with concomitant organ dysfunction (any of vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, increased creatinine or bilirubin levels, and thrombocytopenia)
Exclusion_Criteria: 148 patients excluded due to missing antimicrobial susceptibility results and 77 due to missing sex or race
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Electronic health record of the 10 acute-care BJC hospitals, greater St Louis region, Missouri and Illinois
Dataset_Size: 49 726 admissions and 85 238 sepsis episodes in the final dataset
Missing_Data_Method: Removed patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race); carried forward the last observation for missing laboratory results and vitals
Ethnicity_Details: Race and ethnicity: Black 9112 (22.8%), White 23 982 (60.1%), Other 6799 (17.0%) in the entire cohort
Geographic_Representativeness: Large and diverse dataset of patients across urban and rural areas of the greater St Louis region in Missouri and Illinois; 3 hospitals illustrated as examples of different patient casemixes, including a socioeconomically disadvantaged population
Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture specimen: Blood 1602 (13.7%), Urine 4575 (39.0%), Respiratory 2957 (25.2%), Other 2598 (22.1%)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: GNB antimicrobial resistance level in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis episodes, categorised as ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR)
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (36.2% of RR isolates, community-onset), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (56.6% of RS isolates in community-onset; 58.3% in hospital-onset), Klebsiella spp; non-GNB organisms (eg, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, viruses) were labelled SS
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefepime)
Specific_Antibiotics: ceftriaxone; cefepime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility results documented in the EHR; ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS; negative cultures and non-GNB cultures also labelled SS), ceftriaxone-resistant but cefepime-susceptible (RS), and ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR); the most resistant GNB microbe determined the category for polymicrobial cultures; intermediate isolates labelled susceptible; CLSI breakpoints based on minimal inhibitory concentration
AI_Purpose: To develop deep learning models based on artificial neural networks (separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis) that project levels of antimicrobial resistance in GNB, and to assess whether patient casemix and local prevalence rates of resistance explain the variable performance of a general risk stratification model across hospitals and patient subgroups
Feature_Engineering: All vitals and laboratory data points within 5 days of the culture timestamp were resampled and the mean value of every 4-hour window was used by the deep learning model; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; shock defined as vasopressor or inotrope use within 24 hours of the culture timestamp; age, time since admission, vital signs and laboratory results treated as continuous; hospital, sex and race categorical; procedures, antibiotic administration, comorbidities and previous susceptible or resistant culture results binary; all input variables screened at the culture timestamp
Feature_Selection_Method: Laboratory value and vital sign features selected considering redundancy, collinearity, and availability in the EHR; gradient-boosting model with SHAP dedicated to variable importance for the first 10 features contributing to the model
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to oversample the RR and RS minority groups and focal loss to reweight the loss of the minority group
Hyperparameter_Method: Gradient boosting implemented with tuned tree depth and feature subsampling; deep learning implemented with tuned network width and depth and learning rate; a 10% random validation split of the training set used to monitor validation performance and terminate training before overfitting
Software_Libraries: PyTorch version 2.1; XGBoost version 2.0.0; scikit-learn version 1.3.0
Other_Metrics: AUPRC for RS and RR isolates in community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis; SHAP values for feature importance; correlation (R) between AUPRC and RS/RR prevalence rates
Baseline_Method: Gradient-boosting model (XGBoost) compared with the deep learning model on the comorbidity and medical-history feature subset
Baseline_Performance: Gradient boosting: AUROC 0.76 (95% CI, 0.76-0.76); AUPRC 0.23 (95% CI, 0.23-0.23) (deep learning comparator: AUROC 0.81 [95% CI, 0.81-0.81]; AUPRC 0.30 [95% CI, 0.29-0.31])
Internal_Validation: 80/20 split: 70% training, 10% model selection, 20% holdout for patient group-specific testing (infections from the same patient exist only in either the training or the testing set); 10% random validation split of the training set to terminate training before overfitting; models tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis
Train_Test_Split: 80% train (70% for training and 10% for model selection); 20% holdout set for patient group-specific testing
External_Validation_Description: None - the general model was tested on holdout data from the same hospitals and period
Overfitting_Method: 10% random validation split of the training set used for both models to monitor validation performance during training and terminate training before overfitting; model brittleness (failure to generalise) addressed by developing a general model tested on same-hospital holdout data
Clinical_Insights: In community-onset sepsis, history of P aeruginosa infections and history of antibiotic administration were the strongest factors discriminating RS and RR from SS; history of antibiotic-resistant organisms and previous episodes of severe sepsis or septic shock were associated with RR. In hospital-onset sepsis, age and history of P aeruginosa infections were the most impactful factors; time since admission was associated with lower risk of SS and higher risk of RR. Vasopressor use and longitudinal data added minimal contributions.
Generalisability_Details: The results do not support widespread use of generalized models; model performance was associated with prevalence rates of resistant GNB and varied across hospitals and patient subgroups; future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates to accompany patient-level variables
Maturity_Evidence: Internal holdout testing only: 80/20 patient group-specific split, models trained on the whole training set and tested separately for community-onset and hospital-onset sepsis, results reported without oversampling; performance varied widely across hospitals and subgroups and the authors conclude against widespread use of generalized models
Integration_Point: Not described for this model (research model evaluated on holdout data); the Epic Sepsis Model is described as integrated into the clinical EHR system as prior work
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing between narrow- or broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics for patients with sepsis; risk stratification models that guide clinicians' empirical choices
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Prediction of antimicrobial resistance must occur at suspicion of infection to initiate empirical antibiotics, so all input variables were screened at the culture timestamp
Stewardship_Details: No stewardship outcome was measured; the authors state that future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates, and that the results argue against the use of generalized models for predicting resistant GNB etiologies in sepsis
Barriers_List: Difficult-to-extract variables such as nursing home residence are not usually stored in a structured data format, making a large study that captures them nearly impossible; study limitations inherent to retrospective EHR-based analyses; potential confounders not included (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices)
Facilitators_List: Model robustness against subgroup distribution heterogeneity may be improved using domain generalization approaches or group-fairness classification approaches, which the authors are considering for future work
Future_Directions: Future efforts to benchmark antimicrobial use may need to include community and hospital resistance rates (warranting availability of microbiology data) to accompany patient-level variables; institutions are encouraged to develop their own risk stratification models to identify patients at risk for resistant GNB, similar to maintaining local antibiograms; domain generalization and group-fairness approaches are being considered
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values from the gradient-boosting model, reported as mean impact on model output magnitude for the top 10 features
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective EHR-based analysis; unmeasured confounders (nursing home residence, outpatient prescriptions, duration of central lines and devices); difficult-to-extract variables not stored in structured format; no external or prospective validation; model performance not transferable across hospitals
Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients with any missing categorical feature (eg, sex and race) were removed; the last observation was carried forward for missing laboratory results and vitals; plausible ranges defined and implausible values excluded; missing antimicrobial susceptibility results handled by general logic rules for intrinsic resistance
Reporting_Clarity: Clear - STROBE reporting guideline and published recommendations for machine learning models followed; full feature list and preprocessing details in Supplement 1 (eTable, eFigures 1-2); all results reported with 95% CIs

Title: Enhancing Antibiotic Stewardship: A Machine Learning Approach to Predicting Antibiotic Resistance in Inpatient Care
Population_Description: Adult patients aged 18 and above admitted from the emergency department to Stanford University Hospital or ValleyCare Hospital between 2009 and 2023 who had positive blood, urine, or respiratory culture collected within 24 hours of hospitalization
Top_Predictive_Features: Demographics, prior antibiotic prescriptions, prior culture results, and the local antibiogram (SHAP feature importance)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: LightGBM (primary; AUROC 0.74-0.78 range across five antibiotic models, best cefazolin 0.78); logistic regression baseline (cefazolin AUROC 0.76)
Best_Performing_Model: Cefazolin susceptibility model (LightGBM)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation on a held-out temporal test set (2022-2023); no external validation or deployment.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center cohort; limited to positive cultures; did not account for false-negative clinical infections; correlation between data points from the same patient; COVID-19 pandemic testing period; EHR interoperability limits.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Implications of false negatives and positives acknowledged; model intended to augment, not replace, clinical judgment.

Exclusion_Criteria: Pediatric patients, outpatients, direct admissions or transfers, and patients with incomplete medical records

Data_Source_Name: STARR (Stanford Research Repository)
Dataset_Size: 49,872 patient-encounters
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation using chained equations (logistic regression only); no imputation for LightGBM
Geographic_Representativeness: Two hospitals in California: Stanford University Hospital (Palo Alto) and Tri-Valley ValleyCare Hospital (Pleasanton); single-center cohort.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood, urine, or respiratory
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary sensitive/resistant classification for each of five intravenous antibiotics
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Enterococcus (VRE), ESBL-producing organisms
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins (cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime); penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor (piperacillin/tazobactam); fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin)
Specific_Antibiotics: cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin/tazobactam, ciprofloxacin (also vancomycin, meropenem mentioned)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label (resistant vs susceptible) per antibiotic; resistant if any individual culture resistant
AI_Purpose: Predict antibiotic resistance and improve empirical antibiotic prescribing / antimicrobial stewardship
Feature_Engineering: Features derived from structured EHR data in domains: demographics, vital signs/lab extremes, medical-comorbidities, prior antibiotic use/hospitalizations, prior microbiological results, and yearly antibiogram
Feature_Selection_Method: SHAP feature importance ranking
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search with 5-fold cross-validation
Other_Metrics: Coverage rate (negative predictive value) plotted against percentage of excess broad-spectrum antibiotics averted
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression
Baseline_Performance: Cefazolin model AUROC 0.76 (0.75-0.77)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation during development; held-out temporal test set (2022-2023)
Clinical_Insights: Most important predictors related to demographics, prior antibiotic prescriptions, prior culture results, and local antibiogram; vital signs and laboratory values from the same encounter did not feature prominently
Generalisability_Details: Single-center cohort; external validation an essential next step; EHR interoperability limits inclusion of data from other health systems
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation on a held-out temporal test set (2022-2023); no external validation or deployment
Integration_Point: At the time of culture order to guide empirical antibiotic prescribing (bedside)
End_User_Described: Clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Model generates narrower antibiotic recommendations at culture order; clinician prescribes narrower suggestion, later confirmed by culture results
Stewardship_Details: Could avert 20% or more excess common antibiotic orders while maintaining a coverage rate of 80%
Barriers_List: Substantial data processing infrastructure needed for real-time predictions; EHR interoperability limits data from other systems; single-center
Facilitators_List: Local antibiogram data enable tailoring to institutional resistance patterns, facilitating scalability and adoption
Future_Directions: Validation across multiple centers; incorporation of unstructured information (e.g., symptoms, residence, functional status, zip code); real-time deployment
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley Additive ExPlanations)
Limitation_Categories: Single-center; positive cultures only; false negatives; correlated data points; COVID-19 testing period; EHR interoperability
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data (imputed for logistic regression only); dataset limited to positive cultures; EHR interoperability excluded data from other health systems
Page_References: pp. 1-8 (journal pp. 857-864)

Title: Machine Learning-Led Optimization of Combination Therapy: Confronting the Public Health Threat of Extensively Drug Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria
Country_Countries: United States of America (Buffalo and Troy, New York; Nutley, New Jersey; San Diego, California)
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments providing the pharmacodynamic data for a mechanism-based mathematical model
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (R01AI165997; R01AI148560; L30AI164450)
Population_Description: Four clinical, extensively drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada) studied in 7-day in vitro hollow fiber infection model experiments; regimens simulated in a critically ill patient population using published human population PK models (no human participants)
Data_Source_Other: In vitro hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) data from previously performed studies (35 experiments, 1,056 samples) and previously published human population pharmacokinetic models for each agent
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance; Dose optimisation
Task_Type_Other: Genetic algorithm (GA)-led optimisation of multi-drug dosing regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) against PK/PD/toxicodynamic end points; mechanism-based pharmacodynamic model fitting and Monte Carlo simulation
All_Models_Evaluated: Four GA fitness functions (F1-F4) tested across 13 optimisation end points: PD-only end points (F1, 10 2 CFU/mL at the 90th/80th/70th/60th prediction interval), polymyxin B TD-only end points (F2), and joint polymyxin B + aztreonam TD end points with two weighting schemes (F3 0.990/0.005/0.005; F4 0.90/0.05/0.05). Reported output is target attainment and regimen parameters (Table 1) - no accuracy, AUROC or error metric is reported for any optimisation scheme.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Highest level supported: the mechanism-based PD model was internally qualified with visual predictive checks and the GA regimens were evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation only; no external validation, prospective evaluation, CDS integration or routine clinical use is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Only four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates / 35 HFIM experiments, so a larger, more representative panel of isolates is needed to match current XDR epidemiology; regimens were optimised on literature PK reports from monotherapy studies in critically ill patients, whereas co-administration augments exposure and optimal doses could therefore be lower.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The GA 1:1 PD:TD weighting scheme had to be abandoned: it terminated early after 200 iterations with no change in the fitness function and produced a regimen that attained the polymyxin B AUC24,ss target of 100 mg·h/L but failed to produce bacterial killing. Toxicity targets (polymyxin B nephrotoxicity, aztreonam hepatotoxicity) also constrained the optimised regimens.
Reviewer_Notes: Prospective regimen-optimisation study, not a diagnostic model: no classification/discrimination metrics exist, so every *_Reported accuracy field is answered No rather than left blank. AI_Application_Type and Task_Type have no vocabulary entry for GA-based regimen optimisation, so 'Other' was used (with AI Predictive and Prognostic Models / AI Clinical Decision Support Systems ticked for the modelling and regimen-guidance aspects) and Needs_Team_Discussion is Yes.
Sample_Size: 4 clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); HFIM dataset of 35 experiments and 1,056 samples
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared no competing interests for this work.
Inclusion_Criteria: Four clinical K. pneumoniae isolates from previously performed hollow fiber infection model studies (ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada); no patient-level eligibility criteria are reported
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Other
Data_Source_Name: Not a named repository: hollow fiber infection model (HFIM) experiments from previously performed studies plus published human population PK models for aztreonam, ceftazidime/avibactam and polymyxin B
Dataset_Size: 35 7-day HFIM experiments (1,056 samples) across 4 isolates; 13 GA optimisation end points each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
Geographic_Representativeness: Four clinical XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so the authors state that a larger panel of isolates should be explored to properly generalise the results to current XDR epidemiology
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Bacterial killing of XDR K. pneumoniae by GA-optimised combination regimens: attainment of a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection) in the HFIM, while keeping polymyxin B and aztreonam exposures within their toxicity limits
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (four clinical extensively drug-resistant isolates: ARLG779, AR-0049, S200, KP-Nevada)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (aztreonam, ceftazidime); beta-lactamase inhibitor (avibactam); polymyxins (polymyxin B)
Specific_Antibiotics: Aztreonam; ceftazidime; avibactam; polymyxin B
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: XDR; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; ESBL; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Threshold definition, not a metric: the bacterial PD end point was a bacterial concentration of 10 2 CFU/mL at 168 hours (assay limit of detection, lower end of reported bacteraemia concentrations); the PK/TD end points were polymyxin B AUC24,ss = 100 mg/h/L and aztreonam AUCss = 1,336 mg/h/L, each evaluated at a prediction interval of simulated subjects
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: Use a genetic algorithm, driven by a mechanism-based PD model with human population PK, to optimise aztreonam + ceftazidime/avibactam +/- polymyxin B combination regimens de novo against joint efficacy and toxicity end points for XDR K. pneumoniae
Num_Models_Compared: No head-to-head comparison of predictive models: 4 GA fitness functions (F1-F4) across 13 optimisation end points, each with a final population of 75 candidate regimens
Feature_Engineering: Mechanism-based PD model translated to RxODE with HFIM PKs replaced by published human PopPK models; regimen inputs (dose, infusion time, doses per day, loading dose) rounded to the nearest milligram, 0.5 hours and integer value before GA evaluation
Software_Libraries: GA package in R (genetic algorithm); RxODE solved with the Livermore Solver for Ordinary Differential Equations
Other_Metrics: Regimen target attainment (10 2 CFU/mL at 168 h), median infusion duration 2 h (range 1.5-3 h), median dosing interval 9 h (range 6-12 h), mean aztreonam 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day, mean ceftazidime/avibactam 8.55 g/day (SD 1.45), mean polymyxin B 3.18 mg/kg/day (SD 1.05) producing AUC24,ss,avg 115 mg/h/L
Baseline_Method: Comparator regimens derived empirically over years of clinical use, and current FDA package labelling for each agent
Baseline_Performance: Optimised aztreonam daily dose 6.18 vs 7.16 g/day (with vs without an aztreonam TD end point) against FDA-labelled 6-8 g/day; optimised ceftazidime/avibactam dose exceeded the package label (mean 8.55 g/day); polymyxin B optimisation produced AUC24,ss,avg 93.5-115 mg/h/L against the 100 mg/h/L consensus target
Internal_Validation: Visual predictive checks used to internally qualify the mechanism-based PD model
Clinical_Insights: PD/TD weighting must be deferential to patient safety and clinical feasibility because missing an individual target carries consequences such as microbiological failure or drug toxicity; optimised regimens mirror empirically derived clinical dosing (prolonged beta-lactam infusion, higher avibactam exposure) and are proposed as a testing framework for new or special-population regimens
Generalisability_Details: Four XDR K. pneumoniae isolates only, so a larger and more representative panel of isolates is needed for the results to match current XDR epidemiology (strain types, virulence factors, resistance mechanisms); regimens rest on monotherapy PK data from critically ill patients
Maturity_Evidence: Internal qualification of the mechanism-based PD model by visual predictive checks and Monte Carlo evaluation of GA-optimised regimens; no external validation cohort, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported
Integration_Point: Output of the optimised regimens (dose, infusion duration, dosing interval, loading dose) is proposed for clinical trial simulation and preclinical regimen design; not integrated into any clinical, EHR or LIS system
End_User_Described: Not named explicitly: the framework is aimed at preclinical drug development and at regimen design for special patient populations, i.e. researchers and prescribers in critically ill patients
Barriers_List: Multiple PK end points must be met simultaneously for combination therapy and target attainment multiplies geometrically with each added drug, making optimisation experimentally intractable; choice of PD/TD weighting affects the search; PK variability between drugs; the 1:1 weighting scheme failed to explore the parameter space
Facilitators_List: GA-led regimen design can be integrated into preclinical drug development to produce testable regimens, avoid pre-existing notions of a 'best' schedule, reduce the number of animal experiments, and hypothesise alternative regimens for special patient populations with altered PK
Future_Directions: Expand the isolate panel to a representative sample of the most resistant isolates (by national prevalence of strain types, virulence factors and resistance mechanisms) so the results generalise to current XDR K. pneumoniae epidemiology; apply GA-led regimen design to new drugs and to special patient populations
Feature_Interactions_Method: Mechanism-based model interaction terms: avibactam reduces the aztreonam KC50 by up to 99.3%, and polymyxin B kills aztreonam-induced persister cells
Limitation_Categories: Limited isolate panel and generalisability; reliance on historical monotherapy PK data; modelling assumptions (persister cell subpopulation, two-subpopulation structure)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Regimens were optimised on prior literature PK reports in critically ill patients all studied in monotherapy; co-administration of aztreonam and ceftazidime/avibactam augments exposure, so optimised doses could be lower than reported
Reporting_Clarity: Model, GA implementation (13 end points, population size 75, weightings) and optimised regimen parameters are reported in detail, but only PK/PD target attainment is reported - no accuracy-type performance statistics, no confidence intervals, no calibration

Title: Development and validation of machine learning models to predict MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission by using electronic health record data
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: ICU patients (adults, ICU stay ≥24 h) from PLAGH-ICU (n=3,536) and MIMIC-IV (n=34,923) who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; outcome is MDRO colonization or infection.
Top_Predictive_Features: PLAGH-ICU (via SHAP values): C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), serum urea, duration of pre-ICU hospital stay, interleukin-6 (IL-6), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: LR, KNN, SVC, RF, XGBoost, MLP, and a stacking ensemble. In temporal validation the ensemble models performed best: PLAGH-ICU AUROC 0.786 [0.748, 0.825]; MIMIC-IV AUROC 0.744 [0.723, 0.766]. By AUROC, Random Forest, XGBoost and Ensemble outperformed the other algorithms.
Best_Performing_Model: Ensemble model
AUROC_Population_Set: Best-performing ensemble model on PLAGH-ICU temporal validation set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation performed: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615); therefore maturity level 3 (external validation).
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design requiring prospective validation; low precision (positive predictive value) at thresholds ensuring higher recall, entailing potential high costs if applied clinically; models built from specific institutions may not be directly applicable elsewhere; feature importance indicates correlation, not causality.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Low positive predictive value at high-recall thresholds could entail high costs if applied clinically at this stage.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Implementation challenges include data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, and regulatory compliance.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Sex_Distribution: PLAGH-ICU Table 1: male n (%) — non-MDRO 1,980 (63.6), MDRO 301 (71.2)
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients who underwent microbial culture within 24 h of ICU admission; aged ≥18 years; ICU stay ≥24 h.
Exclusion_Criteria: Age <18 years; ICU stay <24 h; MDRO detected within 14 days prior to ICU admission; positive MDRO within 1 day of ICU admission.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: PLAGH-ICU; MIMIC-IV version 2.2
Dataset_Size: 3,536 patients (PLAGH-ICU); 34,923 patients (MIMIC-IV)
Missing_Data_Method: Variables with >30% missing excluded; cases with >20% missing lab values excluded; Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) for the remaining missing data.
Geographic_Representativeness: Two centres: an ICU of the (Chinese) PLA General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (USA), the latter via the MIMIC-IV database.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Body fluid samples (not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission (binary outcome).
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (incl. MRSA), Enterococcus spp., Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp.
Drug_Classes: three or more classes of antimicrobial agents (not enumerated)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDRO = bacteria resistant to three or more classes of antimicrobial agents; MRSA directly categorized as MDRO; outcome is a binary MDRO colonization/infection label.
AI_Purpose: Early detection of patients at risk of MDRO colonization or infection on ICU admission, to curb MDRO proliferation and support empirical pharmacotherapy.
Num_Models_Compared: 7 (6 base algorithms + stacking ensemble)
Feature_Engineering: Min-max normalization before training LR, KNN, SVC and MLP models; Spearman correlation-based clustering to remove collinear features; MICE imputation; top-25 feature distillation.
Feature_Selection_Method: Spearman's rank correlation for stratified clustering (collinearity removal), then Random Forest permutation feature importance ranking; top 25 features retained.
Num_Features_Total: 25 (retained for the final prediction model)
Hyperparameter_Method: Bayesian optimization with 5-fold cross-validation
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, shap (Python); dplyr, ggplot2, pROC (R)
Other_Metrics: Brier score, calibration curve intercept and slope, decision curve analysis (standardized net benefit).
Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression (LR)
Internal_Validation: Temporal validation within each dataset (data 2017-2019, after training on 2008-2016); 5-fold cross-validation used for hyperparameter tuning.
Train_Test_Split: Training 2008-2016; temporal validation 2017-2019
External_Validation_Description: PLAGH-ICU model assessed on MIMIC-IV (peak AUROC 0.638 [0.628, 0.648]); MIMIC-IV model assessed on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615 [0.585, 0.646]).
Clinical_Insights: Interpretability allows clinicians to identify high-risk patients, understand individual risk profiles, and tailor treatment plans.
Data_Repository: MIMIC-IV via PhysioNet (physionet.org/content/mimiciv/2.2/); other data from the corresponding author on request
Generalisability_Details: Models show significant variance in feature selection and performance across institutions; collecting data from various hospitals/regions could enhance generalizability; unit-specific MDRO early-warning models may be preferable.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed in both directions: PLAGH-ICU model on MIMIC-IV (AUROC 0.638) and MIMIC-IV model on PLAGH-ICU (AUROC 0.615) — sets maturity at level 3.
Integration_Point: ICU-admission screening / risk stratification; future CDSS integration
End_User_Described: Clinicians (ICU)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Deployment with real-time data integration via EHR-compatible interfaces; models incorporated into a CDSS delivering alerts and recommendations.
Barriers_List: Data access, privacy concerns, hardware and software integration, physician adoption, regulatory compliance; limited feature-target correlations in early ICU EHR data; poor cross-institution transferability.
Facilitators_List: Models are easily adaptable to hospital EHR systems and use routinely available EHR data.
Future_Directions: Deployment in clinical settings with real-time data integration; integration into a CDSS; establishing a monitoring framework to continuously assess and enhance model performance.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP values
Novel_Predictors_Details: Shorter pre-ICU hospital stays in PLAGH-ICU surprisingly correlated with increased MDRO risk (possibly reflecting resistant-bacteria carriage among patients transferred from other hospitals or community-acquired MDRO).
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design; need for prospective validation; low precision (PPV) / potential clinical cost; limited cross-institution generalizability; feature importance reflects correlation not causality.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data handled by excluding variables with >30% missing and cases with >20% missing lab values, then MICE imputation.

Title: Machine learning algorithms to predict colistin-induced nephrotoxicity from electronic health records in patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infection
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Ministry of Education
Population_Description: 1392 patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDRGN) infection receiving their first intravenous colistin at three Taipei Medical University hospitals (TMUH, SHH, WFH), Taiwan, 2011-2020; adults (>=18 y) with >=2 d of colistin, no chronic dialysis and available serum creatinine records
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP feature importance (CAT-SVM-SMOTE): days of colistin use, cumulative dose, daily dose, latest C-reactive protein, and baseline haemoglobin
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: 15 models (CatBoost, LGB, RF x SVM-SMOTE, SMOTE, SMOTETL, Tomek and original data) compared by sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC on the temporal validation set (heatmap, Supplementary Table S11). Best RFE-estimated F1: CatBoost 0.603 (48 features), LGB 0.610 (46 features), RF 0.585 (16 features). Best model CAT-SVM-SMOTE: AUROC 0.823, AUPRC 0.737, sensitivity 0.860, F1 0.740, MCC 0.533
Best_Performing_Model: CAT-SVM-SMOTE (CatBoost with SVM-SMOTE resampling) - decided by the highest AUROC (0.823) and AUPRC (0.737), together with the highest sensitivity (0.860), F1 (0.740) and MCC (0.533) on the temporal validation set
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
F1_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal validation cohort (2018-2020; 402 patients)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The reported performance of the best model comes from a temporally separate validation cohort (2018-2020, n=402) distinct from the derivation cohort (2011-2017), i.e. TRIPOD type 3 temporal/external validation; no prospective or independent multi-centre external test is reported
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design limits applicability; multiple healthcare datasets needed to generalise; newer AKI biomarkers (cystatin C, NGAL, IL-18) not assessed; features with >25% missing data discarded may have introduced bias; covariate shift between the two cohorts
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: High-sensitivity predictions may elevate false positives, but the authors argue the benefits outweigh misidentifying false negatives
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Vulnerable patients developing AKI despite low colistin doses are identified (14 of 17 patients with very low daily doses were AKI-positive), but no equity analysis by demographic group is reported
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Only ethics approval is described: Joint IRB approval with a waiver of patient consent for de-identified registry data; no data-sharing or model-governance plan, and no regulatory clearance
Sample_Size: 1392 patients (989 in the derivation cohort and 402 in the temporal validation cohort)

Inclusion_Criteria: Admission to TMU Hospital (TMUH), Shuang Ho Hospital (SHH) or Wan Fang Hospital (WFH) with a first intravenous colistin course between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020; a patient needing more than two courses after a cured episode with an interval >90 d was treated as a new subject for the second course

Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validation (test) set, October-December, 10,227 S. aureus isolate spectra; CA-MRSA/HA-MRSA classification step, Random Forest (Table 2)

Dataset_Size: 345,748 bacterial specimens; 10,227 S. aureus isolates (5,872 MRSA, 4,355 MSSA); 2,848 SCCmec type IV isolates used for PVL prediction
Geographic_Representativeness: Five nationwide institutions: three northern urban centres specialising in chronic disease management and a fourth on an island serving a distinct population, selected to leverage geographic and demographic variation.

Primary_AMR_Outcome: MRSA status (methicillin/oxacillin resistance) vs MSSA, SCCmec subtype (Types I-V, grouped HA-MRSA Types I-III and CA-MRSA Types IV-V) and PVL gene presence in SCCmec type IV MRSA isolates, all predicted from MALDI-TOF MS spectra.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA and MSSA)

Feature_Engineering: Raw spectra 2000-20,000 Da segmented into consecutive 5-Da intervals with the peak intensity of each interval as the representative value; log transformation of bin intensities; StandardScaler standardisation of every m/z bin.

Hyperparameter_Method: GridSearchCV (scikit-learn) with 5-fold cross-validation, optimising AUC

Train_Test_Split: Chronological split - January through September for training, October through December for validation
Overfitting_Method: Ensemble algorithms (random forest, LGBM, XGBoost) selected for their capacity to mitigate overfitting on high-dimensional data; random forest feature selection; 5-fold cross-validated hyperparameter tuning.

Clinical_Insights: The 4445-4450 segment, previously proposed as the PVL marker peak (4448 m/z), correlates only modestly with PVL presence (r = 0.28), whereas m/z 6405-6410 and 5865-5870 correlate most strongly; supports a multifeature rather than single-peak approach.
Generalisability_Details: Generalisability depends on consistent spectral data acquisition and preprocessing across institutions and instruments; the five-institution sampling was intended to widen applicability, and further clinical validation is called for.
Maturity_Evidence: Temporal hold-out validation on the same five-institution dataset (train Jan-Sep, validate Oct-Dec); the paper reports validation (testing) AUC/accuracy rather than only training performance.
Integration_Point: Microbiology laboratory workflow, immediately after MALDI-TOF MS species identification; results surfaced to clinicians through a web interface.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (and the microbiology laboratory) using the web AI-CDSS interface
Clinical_Workflow_Details: MALDI-TOF MS species identification feeds a three-step hierarchical model (MRSA status, SCCmec genotype, then PVL presence in SCCmec type IV isolates); results and per-step confidence scores are displayed in the web interface for clinician interpretation.
Barriers_List: PCR-based genotyping: complex primer design, non-specific amplification, variable reaction conditions, long processing times, specialised instruments and trained personnel; AI-CDSS: dependence on consistent MALDI-TOF spectra quality across institutions.
Facilitators_List: Analysis of MALDI-TOF MS spectra already generated for species identification (no extra test); automated hierarchical workflow replacing PCR; web interface with per-step confidence; webinars, training and feedback collection for adoption.
Future_Directions: Proteomic experiments to link discriminative m/z features to proteins and to integrate additional biomarkers; further clinical validation of the impact on mortality.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest feature importance (importance score threshold > 0.01) plus correlation coefficients of each m/z segment with PVL+ status (Figure 2 heatmap); Table 1 counts how often each m/z segment appears in the top 10 per classification stage.
Novel_Predictors_Details: The 4445-4450 segment (the widely cited 4448 m/z peak) correlates only modestly with PVL (r = 0.28); m/z 6405-6410 and 5865-5870 are the strongest correlates, favouring a multifeature model over single-peak analysis.
Limitation_Categories: Data quality / spectral variation across institutions; generalisability and reproducibility; scope of modelled outcome (only PVL, not other virulence factors or resistance mechanisms); lack of biological explanation of m/z features; unquantified clinical impact and need for further validation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Consistency in spectral data acquisition and preprocessing is crucial for reproducibility and generalisability across diverse clinical environments.
Reporting_Clarity: Clear on dataset, hierarchical design, split and metrics, and the code stack is named; however Table 2 and the Results text report different PVL-stage metrics, no patient-level data are described, and feature counts after selection are not given.

Title: Discovering multiple antibiotic resistance phenotypes using diverse top-k subgroup list discovery

Population_Description: Hospitalised ICU patients from MIMIC-III whose culture grew an Enterococcus bacterium resistant to vancomycin (ERV); each instance is a strain of a microorganism obtained from a patient's culture during one admission
Top_Predictive_Features: Highest-ranked subgroups of the best phenotype P11 (ranked by MDL compression gain, Eq. 1, within the selected subgroup list): s1 culture_specimen_type_description = 'SWAB' + icu_when_culture = 'SICU' (416 positive instances); s2 culture_specimen_type_description = 'URINE' + treated_with_vancomycin_in_the_current_admission_before_culture = 'yes' (304 positive); s3 organ_transplant_in_previous_admissions = 'yes' + previous_colonization_with_erv = 'yes' + previous_colonization_with_stenotrophomonas_maltophilia = 'no' (89 positive; 68 contributed)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Task_Type_Other: Subgroup discovery / descriptive pattern mining (diverse top-k subgroup lists, i.e. phenotypes)
All_Models_Evaluated: EDSLM (proposed): best diverse top-3 phenotypes by quality (quality = 0.16, coverage = 0.94; P11 quality 0.14 / coverage 0.86, P12 0.17 / 0.61, P13 0.17 / 0.53) and by coverage (quality = 0.15, coverage = 0.97); SSD++ (baseline phenotyping): quality = 0.061, coverage 55% (1030/1872 positive, 1019/1872 negative); Random Forest validation models: accuracy 0.73 (model 1) vs 0.75 (model 2), p = 0.04 / 0.006; Logistic Regression: accuracy 0.66 vs 0.67 (p = 0.55) and 0.66 vs 0.68 (p = 0.02)
Best_Performing_Model: The best diverse top-3 phenotypes (P11, P12 and P13) — selected as the best model by the quality measure (Eq. 4): quality = 0.16, coverage = 0.94
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The only evaluation is an internal 70/30 train-test split with McNemar's test on the same mining view; no external validation, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment are reported
Reported_Limitations: Performance cost (the algorithm repeatedly explores the collection of candidate subgroups) and the fact that it only accepts nominal attributes
Ethical_Governance_Risks: None reported — the research uses a public database, so the ethics statement is not applicable
Unresolved_Items: Accuracy / AUROC / other classifier metrics are reported only for the Random Forest and Logistic Regression models used to test the predictive capacity of the phenotypes (model 1 vs model 2), not for the review's unit of analysis (the best diverse top-k phenotypes, reported by quality and coverage); recorded here rather than in the *_Value fields
Sample_Size: 3744 instances (strains) in the balanced mining view used in the experiments — 1872 positive (vancomycin-resistant) and 1872 negative; the mining view before subsampling contains 10,790 strains
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work
Inclusion_Criteria: All MIMIC-III patients who underwent culture tests using Vancomycin (strain-level instances from their cultures); only the first microorganism of a particular species per patient is kept
Exclusion_Criteria: Per CLSI M39-A4, only the first microorganism of a particular species from an individual patient is considered to avoid duplicate data that could introduce bias; preprocessing also deletes duplicated instances and attributes and removes empty or single-valued attributes
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: MIMIC-III (MIMIC-III database stored in a PostgreSQL database)
Dataset_Size: Query dataset: 12,796 instances (strains) x 44 attributes; final mining view: 10,790 instances x 32 attributes; balanced experimental mining view: 3744 instances (1872 positive / 1872 negative)
Missing_Data_Method: Missing values are treated as step (3) of the preprocessing pipeline ('treatment of missing values'); the imputation method itself is not specified in the paper
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-database study (MIMIC-III ICU patients, admissions 2001–2012); geographic representativeness is not discussed, but the authors acknowledge the data are 'solely focused on ICUs', 'temporally displaced' and not all relevant data are available in tabular format
Specimen_Type_Detail: Culture specimen description (culture_specimen_type_description): blood, sputum, urine, etc.; values appearing in the experiments include 'SWAB', 'URINE', 'SPUTUM', 'BRONCHOALVEOLAR_LAVAGE', 'CATHETER_TIP - IV' and 'BLOOD_CULTURE'
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Vancomycin resistance in Enterococcus (ERV): characterising groups of hospitalised patients whose culture grew an Enterococcus bacterium showing resistance to vancomycin; target of the phenotype mining is the susceptibility (sensitive/resistant) of the strain
Pathogens: Enterococcus (ERV) is the target pathogen; Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia appear as prior-colonisation covariate organisms
Num_Pathogens: 1 target pathogen (Enterococcus, ERV); 5 further organisms appear only as prior-colonisation covariates (Enterobacterales CRE, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, SARM, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia)
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptides (Vancomycin, the target drug); prior-exposure variables for third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, B lactams and antifungal agents
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin (VANCOMYCIN, target drug of the MICROBIOLOGYEVENTS table); previous exposure to third generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluorquinolones, aminoglycosides, b_lactam and antifungal agents
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary susceptibility label: 'Susceptibility: sensitive or resistant' (attribute culture_susceptibility) for the VANCOMYCIN antibiotic, with the target phenomenon being an Enterococcus strain resistant to vancomycin (ERV)
AI_Purpose: Mine diverse top-k antibiotic-resistance phenotypes (subgroup lists) from a real MIMIC-III use case, to give clinical experts multiple and diverse explanations of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus patterns and support decision-making
Num_Models_Compared: 2 phenotyping algorithms compared (EDSLM vs SSD++); Random Forest and Logistic Regression were additionally fitted (with and without phenotype attributes) for the statistical validation
Feature_Engineering: Two-stage pipeline: SQL query on MIMIC-III (PostgreSQL) creating previous-admission binary features, then preprocessing with (1) deletion of duplicated instances and attributes, (2) removal of empty or single-valued attributes, (3) treatment of missing values, (4) attribute discretization and (5) correlation analysis (Pearson coefficient, threshold 0.8)
Feature_Selection_Method: No explicit feature-selection step: all 32 mining-view attributes are used; a Pearson correlation analysis with a threshold of 0.8 is applied during preprocessing, and the overlap strategy places correlated attributes in different subgroup lists
Num_Features_Total: 44 attributes in the initial query dataset; 32 attributes in the final mining view
Num_Features_Selected: 32 attributes (all mining-view attributes); subgroups are limited to a maximum depth of 4 selectors
Class_Imbalance_Method: Subsampling of negative instances: from 8918 negatives to 1872 negatives to match the 1872 positive instances, giving a balanced mining view of 3744 instances
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid over 9 values of beta (0.0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0) and 8 values of max_positive_overlap / max_negative_overlap (0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.6), with k = 3 and sl_max_size = 10 fixed, giving 576 executions; model selection by quality (Eq. 4) and coverage (Eq. 5)
Software_Libraries: pandas 2.0.3, scikit-learn 1.3.0, matplotlib 3.7.2, numpy 1.24.3 (pipeline); pingouin 0.5.5 (McNemar's test); subgroups Python library (EDSLM implementation); RuleList library (SSD++)
Other_Metrics: Quality of the phenotypes (Eq. 3 and Eq. 4, based on the WRAcc quality measure of the subgroups) and coverage (Eq. 5) are the measures computed for every execution; overlap between phenotypes (Table 8) and McNemar's test p-values (Table 7) are additionally reported
Baseline_Method: SSD++ algorithm (RuleList library) applied to the same dataset as an alternative phenotyping approach; Random Forest and Logistic Regression fitted without the phenotype attributes (model 1) as the baseline against which model 2 (with phenotype attributes) is compared
Baseline_Performance: SSD++ phenotype: quality 0.061, covering 1030 of 1872 positive (55%), 1019 of 1872 negative (54%) and 2049 of the total instances (55%); Random Forest model 1 accuracy 0.73; Logistic Regression model 1 accuracy 0.66
Internal_Validation: 70% of the mining-view instances for training and 30% for testing, with McNemar's test (pingouin 0.5.5) comparing classification models with and without phenotype attributes (Table 7)
Train_Test_Split: 70% training / 30% testing
Clinical_Insights: The ERV phenotypes are dominated by general subgroups: patients with ERV in 'SWAB' cultures from surgical ICUs and in urine cultures with previous vancomycin exposure; a more specific subgroup has previous ERV colonisation and organ transplantation; further subgroups describe patients who are adults, largely women, and who do not die
Data_Repository: GitHub (query of stage 1 and source code of stage 2): https://github.com/antoniolopezmc/Discovering-multiple-antibiotic-resistance-phenotypes-using-diverse-top-k-subgroup-list-discovery; source data: MIMIC-III database
Generalisability_Details: The authors note that MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, temporally displaced (admissions 2001–2012) and not all relevant data are available in tabular format, while the extracted phenotypes remain interpretable
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: 70/30 train-test split of the balanced mining view with McNemar's test on predictive capacity; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment
Integration_Point: Not reported — the algorithm is delivered as the open-source subgroups Python library; no clinical system integration point is described
End_User_Described: Clinical experts / clinicians interpreting the phenotypes (and researchers using the subgroups library)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Phenotypes could be mined in different scenarios for decision-making, e.g. using patient data at hospital admission to carry out colonisation studies, or using microbiological diagnostic data to predict the growth of multiresistant bacteria
Barriers_List: Performance (the algorithm must repeatedly explore the collection of candidate subgroups) and the fact that it only accepts nominal attributes; also limited availability of MIMIC-III data (ICU-focused, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
Facilitators_List: Multiple and diverse explanations of the same dataset; an overlapping strategy improving diversity in terms of coverage; a deletion refinement strategy improving diversity in terms of descriptions; only subgroups covering at least one positive instance are added; the candidate subgroup collection can be filtered a-priori, improving legibility of results
Future_Directions: Apply the proposal to other clinical problems and datasets (e.g. drug repurposing); design algorithms that mine diverse top-k subgroup lists without previously generating candidate subgroups; explore other measures to assess diverse top-k phenotypes; adapt the approach to other subgroup models (subgroup sets, truly unordered rule sets); add support for numerical attributes; extend to a multiclass setting
Predictor_Categories_Count: 7 (clinical; microbiological; pharmacological; healthcare utilisation; laboratory; sociodemographic; temporal)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Minimum Description Length compression gain (Eq. 1) combined with the positive/negative overlap factor (Eq. 2) decides which subgroup is added to a phenotype; the WRAcc quality measure is used by VLSD when mining the candidate subgroups
Feature_Interactions_Method: Subgroups are conjunctive patterns: a pattern is a set of selectors forming a conjunction of conditions (up to a maximum depth of 4 selectors); phenotypes chain subgroups as else-if rules
Limitation_Categories: Performance / scalability (repeated exploration of the candidate subgroup collection); attribute type (only nominal attributes accepted); data limitations of MIMIC-III (ICU-only, temporally displaced, not all relevant data in tabular format)
Data_Quality_Concerns: MIMIC-III data for clinical problems are solely focused on ICUs, are temporally displaced and not all relevant data are available in tabular format; duplicates handled per CLSI M39-A4 and missing values treated during preprocessing
Reporting_Clarity: Clear reporting of dataset sizes, preprocessing steps, hyperparameter grid, quality/coverage values and statistical tests; the imputation method behind 'treatment of missing values' is not specified
Page_References: pp. 1-16 (full PDF text layer)

Title: Clinical scoring model for predicting cefotaxime-resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia: development and validation based on portal of entry
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with K. pneumoniae bacteraemia: 358 patients enrolled, 256 in the derivation cohort (March 2018-December 2019) and 102 in the temporal validation cohort (January-August 2020).

Age_Range: Adults aged ≥18 years (lower limit only; no upper limit reported)
Top_Predictive_Features: Age ≥65 years; hospital-acquired infection; previous antimicrobial use within 90d; updated CCI ≥3 points (1 point each, ranked by multivariable adjusted odds ratio)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Single model evaluated: four-component clinical scoring model from forward stepwise binary logistic regression. Derivation cohort AUC 0.761 (95% CI 0.690-0.832), sensitivity 73.6%, specificity 67.5%, PPV 37.1%, NPV 90.7% at cut-off ≥2; temporal validation cohort AUC 0.781 (95% CI 0.690-0.902), sensitivity 75.0%, specificity 69.5%, PPV 37.5%, NPV 91.9% at cut-off ≥2. No comparator model evaluated.
Best_Performing_Model: Four-component clinical scoring model (points-based score derived from the logistic regression model) - the only model under study
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
Specificity_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset), cut-off score ≥2
AUROC_Population_Set: Derivation cohort (primary dataset)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Temporal validation only, performed in the same single centre as the derivation cohort; the authors state that more extensive external validation is still needed.
Reported_Limitations: Single-centre derivation with same-centre validation (generalisability and regional cut-off differences; external validation needed); model can only be applied after bacterial identification, so the time to adjust antimicrobials may be little shortened; the study shows diagnostic value only and does not demonstrate reduced mortality.
Sample_Size: 256 patients in the derivation cohort (primary dataset); 102 patients in the temporal validation cohort
Conflicts_of_Interest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
Sex_Distribution: Male 161 (62.9%) of 256 in the derivation cohort (Table 1)
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with K. pneumoniae bacteraemia (derivation and validation cohorts)
Exclusion_Criteria: Polymicrobial bacteraemia; carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae bacteraemia (derivation cohort)
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 358 patients in total (256 derivation cohort, 102 validation cohort)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary-care hospital in Changwon, Republic of Korea (760 beds); the authors note that prevalence of resistance varies by centre and region, so the optimal cut-off may differ elsewhere.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood cultures: two sets (aerobic and anaerobic) drawn via a peripheral vein or central venous catheter
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Cefotaxime resistance (binary susceptible/resistant) in patients with Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteraemia
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime); extended-spectrum beta-lactamase / AmpC-mediated resistance; carbapenems discussed as the broad-spectrum alternative
Specific_Antibiotics: Cefotaxime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Antimicrobial susceptibility (including cefotaxime) determined by the Vitek II automated system and defined by the CLSI M100S16:2018 guidelines
AI_Purpose: To evaluate clinical factors associated with cefotaxime resistance in K. pneumoniae bacteraemia, to model a simple clinical scoring system predicting cefotaxime resistance, and to analyse resistance rates by portal of entry and validate the score.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single scoring model; no comparator model evaluated)
Feature_Engineering: Continuous clinical variables converted to binary variables using the Youden index (age at 65 years, updated CCI at 3 points) before multivariable analysis; each retained factor given one point to build a zero-to-four-point score.
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariable screening at p<.15 plus clinically meaningful variables, then forward stepwise binary logistic regression (variables with zero frequency excluded)
Software_Libraries: SPSS version 25.0 for Windows; R software version 4.2.1
Other_Metrics: Positive likelihood ratio 2.26 (95% CI 1.75-2.92) and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (95% CI 0.25-0.62) at cut-off ≥2; weighted accuracy analysis comparing cut-off scores 2 and 1 across resistance prevalences.
Internal_Validation: Temporal split: separate validation cohort collected January-August 2020 at the same centre (n=102)
Train_Test_Split: Derivation cohort March 2018-December 2019 (n=256) versus temporal validation cohort January-August 2020 (n=102)
Clinical_Insights: In this centre 45 of 138 (32.6%) derivation-cohort patients with cefotaxime-susceptible K. pneumoniae bacteraemia and a model score ≤1 had nevertheless received anti-pseudomonas penicillin, a fourth-generation cephalosporin or a carbapenem - suggesting the score could reduce unnecessarily broad empirical therapy.
Generalisability_Details: Single centre in the Republic of Korea; resistance prevalence differs by centre and region so the optimal cut-off may change, and more extensive external validation in larger multicentre studies is needed.
Maturity_Evidence: Temporal validation in a separate later cohort at the same centre gave AUC 0.781 (95% CI 0.690-0.902); no external validation and no prospective evaluation were performed.
Integration_Point: After bacterial identification (e.g. by MALDI-TOF MS) and before antimicrobial susceptibility results are available, to inform empirical antimicrobial choice
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing empirical antimicrobial therapy; antimicrobial stewardship programmes
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The score applies only after the species has been identified (e.g. by MALDI-TOF MS), so any reduction in the time to adjust antimicrobials may be limited; it is intended to support empirical prescribing before susceptibility results return.
Stewardship_Details: 45 of 138 (32.6%) patients predicted susceptible (score ≤1) received anti-pseudomonas penicillin, fourth-generation cephalosporin or carbapenem, suggesting about one-third could receive narrower empirical therapy.
Barriers_List: The score can only be applied after bacterial identification, limiting the time saving; single-centre derivation and same-centre validation limit generalisability; prevalence-dependent cut-off values.
Facilitators_List: Simplicity: four routinely available clinical variables, one point each, easy to apply at the bedside.
Future_Directions: More extensive external validation and larger multicentre studies; prospective evaluation of whether applying the model reduces mortality; adapting cut-off values to local resistance prevalence.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 (clinical, sociodemographic, pharmacological/antimicrobial exposure, healthcare utilisation, behavioural)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Adjusted odds ratios from forward stepwise binary logistic regression; the four retained factors had similar adjusted ORs (2.67 to 3.62) and were therefore weighted equally at one point each.
Limitation_Categories: Single-centre derivation and same-centre validation; limited generalisability / need for external validation and multicentre studies; only applicable after species identification, limiting time savings; diagnostic value only, no demonstrated mortality reduction.
Page_References: Article pp. 112-120 (Journal of Chemotherapy 37:2); model development and diagnostic performance pp. 113-114; Table 1 p. 115; Table 3 p. 117; limitations p. 118

Title: Artificial intelligence for screening drug resistance in tuberculosis

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: LPA strips from sputum/culture of TB patients screened for drug resistance to first-line (INH, RIF) and second-line (FQ, AMG) drugs across ICMR-NIRT and multiple Indian intermediate reference laboratories
Data_Source_Other: Line probe assay (LPA) sheets/strips from ICMR-NIRT and intermediate reference laboratories

Specificity_Population_Set: All FL- and SL-LPA strips across validation

AUROC_Population_Set: tubband and considered genes (merged ROC)

Exclusion_Criteria: Sheets with incomplete results or reporting blank/missing interpretations on LPA test results were excluded

Dataset_Size: >18,000 LPA strips (development/training); 2810 FL + 241 SL (validation)

Specimen_Type_Detail: sputum samples (culture used for smear-negative patients)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Tuberculosis drug resistance screening: AI interpretation of LPA strips into binary drug-resistance calls for first-line (isoniazid, rifampicin) and second-line (fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside) drugs

Drug_Classes: First-line (isoniazid, rifampicin); second-line (fluoroquinolone, aminoglycosides)

Title: Prediction model for severe mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia and analysis of macrolide-resistance in children: a case-control study
Funder_Names: Science and Technology Bureau of Sichuan Province; Key Research and Development Program of Sichuan Province; National Key Research and Development Program of China
Population_Description: 562 children with M. pneumoniae pneumonia (MPP) hospitalized at West China Second Hospital, Sichuan University (September 2022-February 2024): 519 with severe MPP (SMPP) and 43 with non-severe MPP; aged over 28 days and under 18 years; median age 6.5 years in both groups
Top_Predictive_Features: Eight key predictors (selected by LASSO regression): fever duration, peak body temperature, wheezing, extrapulmonary complications, hemoglobin levels, pulmonary consolidation, mosaic sign, and bronchial occlusion
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Nomogram including age (logistic regression): C-indices 0.973 (training) and 0.977 (validation); nomogram excluding age with 8 variables (final model): C-indices 0.972 (training) and 0.971 (validation), AUC 0.9722 (training) and 0.975 (validation)
Best_Performing_Model: Nomogram (logistic regression with 8 variables excluding age); decided by validation AUC 0.975
AUROC_Population_Set: Validation cohort of the nomogram (best-performing model, 8 variables excluding age)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Nomogram developed and validated by an internal training/validation split (7:3) of a single-centre cohort, with AUC, calibration curves and decision curve analysis; no external or prospective validation reported
Reported_Limitations: High proportion (92%) of severe MPP cases among hospitalized patients because mild cases treated outpatient or resolve spontaneously, making results more reflective of severe cases; single-centre retrospective design may introduce selection bias
Reviewer_Notes: Article is a nomogram (logistic regression) prediction model for SMPP in children with a secondary macrolide-resistance (MRMPP) analysis. Best-performing model under the review's unit of analysis is the final 8-variable nomogram (excluding age); AUROC reported as AUC. Accuracy/sensitivity/specificity/precision/F1 not reported (only AUC, C-index, calibration, DCA). Income_Classification and WHO_Region derived from China (Chengdu). Pathogen_Classification=Other because M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall (not gram-classifiable).
Unresolved_Items: Numerical sensitivity/specificity at a chosen cut-off are not reported in the text layer (only ROC AUC); the model-with-age variant had higher validation C-index (0.977) than the selected 8-variable model (0.971), yet the paper selected the 8-variable model — flagged for team awareness.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized patients aged over 28 days and under 18 years diagnosed with MPP, defined by typical clinical manifestations (fever, cough, tachypnea, abnormal breath sounds), characteristic chest imaging findings (interstitial infiltrates, segmental or lobar consolidation, hilar lymphadenopathy), and a positive M. pneumoniae RNA result by nucleic acid amplification testing from throat swab specimens
Exclusion_Criteria: Presence of severe underlying conditions (cardiac, hepatic, renal or other critical illnesses), immunodeficiency (congenital or acquired), or discharge against medical advice during hospitalization
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Imaging
Dataset_Size: 562 patients
Missing_Data_Method: Missing values in D-dimer, Fg, AST and ALT imputed using the median filling method
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre: West China Second Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, China; retrospective sample of hospitalized children reflecting severe case characteristics
Specimen_Type_Detail: Throat swabs (M. pneumoniae RNA and macrolide resistance gene mutation testing, A2063G/A2064G resistance mutation sites); venous blood samples; sputum culture; pharyngeal swabs (MP nucleic acid and resistance mutation testing)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Macrolide resistance in M. pneumoniae (MRMPP): whether children are macrolide-resistant versus non-resistant, determined by M. pneumoniae macrolide resistance gene mutation testing (A2063G/A2064G resistance mutation site testing)
Pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Macrolides
Specific_Antibiotics: Macrolides
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Macrolide resistance (MRMPP vs non-resistant) assessed by M. pneumoniae macrolide resistance gene mutation testing including A2063G/A2064G resistance mutation site testing
AI_Purpose: Develop and validate a nomogram (logistic regression) predicting the risk of SMPP in hospitalized children, integrating patient demographics, clinical characteristics, laboratory markers, imaging features and macrolide resistance
