Num_Features_Total: 9 (screened: age, fever duration, peak fever temperature, wheezing, extrapulmonary complications, hemoglobin, pulmonary solidity, mosaic sign, bronchial occlusion)
Other_Metrics: AUC (training 0.9722, validation 0.975); C-index; calibration curves (low mean absolute error); decision curve analysis (high net benefit)
Internal_Validation: Train/test split (7:3); 20-fold cross-validation for LASSO
Train_Test_Split: 7:3 (training : validation)
Overfitting_Method: Validation AUC (0.975) slightly higher than training AUC (0.9722) taken as evidence the model is not overfitted
Clinical_Insights: Nomogram provides quantitative risk assessment of SMPP by summing variable scores, supporting early identification of severe cases and treatment optimisation
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre retrospective sample more reflective of severe case characteristics; authors call for multicentre prospective cohort studies to validate clinical applicability across diverse populations
Maturity_Evidence: Internal train/validation split (7:3) of a single-centre cohort assessed by AUC, calibration curves and decision curve analysis; no external or prospective validation — supports internal validation (level 2)
Integration_Point: Early quantitative risk assessment of SMPP at admission to guide early identification and treatment of severe cases
End_User_Described: Clinicians managing hospitalized children with MPP
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians use the nomogram for quantitative risk assessment of SMPP, enabling early identification of severe cases and optimization of treatment strategies
Future_Directions: Multicentre prospective cohort studies to validate clinical applicability of the predictive model across diverse patient populations and disease severities; explore other biomarkers (cytokine profiles, microbiome, host genetic factors)

Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO regression (lambda 0.01163327, 20-fold cross-validation)

Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing values in D-dimer, Fg, AST and ALT were imputed using the median filling method because of non-normal distribution of these data

Title: Predicting resistance as indicator for need to switch from first-line antiretroviral therapy among patients with elevated viral loads: development of a risk score algorithm
Country_Countries: Multi-country: nine countries enrolled in the PEARLS trial (A5175); author affiliations include the United States of America (North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts), Malawi, South Africa, India and Brazil
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Randomised controlled trial
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (UM1 AI068634, UM1 AI068636, UM1 AI106701); Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals Inc., Bristol-Myers Squibb, Gilead Sciences and Viiv Healthcare/GlaxoSmithKline (study drug; Gilead also funded purchase of study drug); SER supported by F30 MH098731 and T32 GM008719
Population_Description: 290 participants of the PEARLS (ACTG A5175) Phase IV open-label randomised trial who had at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml after week 16 while on an NNRTI-based first-line regimen (from 1045 analysed participants, 305 with an elevated VL and 15 excluded for unavailable resistance results); 53 % male, age 19-65 years
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by weighted predictor score (2 x beta coefficient, rounded) in the best model, Model 1: VL at time of first VL >=1000 copies/ml of 10,001-100,000 (score 4) > time on therapy <7 months (3) > BMI >25.0 kg/m2, treatment initiation VL >100,000 copies/ml and VL >100,000 copies/ml (2 each) > age <=30 (1). Model 2 additionally retains screening CD4 <100 cells/mm3 (score 2) and Model 3 retains ever missed medications (score 1)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Three multiple logistic regression risk-score models (full and reduced): Model 1 (treatment initiation VL and CD4 eligible) reduced AUROC 0.8165, full 0.842; Model 2 (initiation VL excluded) reduced AUROC 0.7981, full 0.819; Model 3 (initiation VL and CD4 excluded, n = 260) reduced AUROC 0.7937, full 0.801. Risk-score (weighted) versions: Model 1 AUROC 0.813 (p = 0.69), Model 2 0.797 (p = 0.91), Model 3 0.802 (p = 0.57). Sensitivity analyses in resource-limited-settings-only population: AUROC 0.823 (Model 1), 0.812 (Model 2), 0.804 (Model 3); Models 4-9 re-categorised therapy duration, compared by AIC
Best_Performing_Model: Reduced Model 1 (multiple logistic regression including treatment initiation VL and CD4; AUROC 0.8165)
Sensitivity_Value: 28.0 % (weighted risk score cutoff >=9, Model 1, unrestricted population)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Weighted risk score cutoff >=9, unrestricted population (resource-limited settings and non-resource-limited settings), Model 1, n = 290
Specificity_Value: 96.7 % (weighted risk score cutoff >=9, Model 1, unrestricted population)
Specificity_Population_Set: Weighted risk score cutoff >=9, unrestricted population (resource-limited settings and non-resource-limited settings), Model 1, n = 290
AUROC_Population_Set: Primary analysis, all study sites, n = 290 (reduced Model 1 on treatment initiation VL and CD4)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and internally validated only (1000 bootstrap samples with replacement) on the trial dataset; performance assessed for Models 1-3 at risk-score cutoffs, with a sensitivity analysis restricted to resource-limited settings; no external or prospective validation performed - the authors state that these benefits must still be externally validated prospectively
Reported_Limitations: Controlled-trial population may not be representative of larger ART populations; frequent virological monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; >12 months used as the referent therapy-duration category; all participants on efavirenz-based first-line regimens, so resistance patterns and predictors may not apply to other regimens; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other sub-Saharan African cohorts; possible misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Premature switching to second-line therapy (false positives) occurs even at specificities >98 % and has significant person- and system-wide consequences: for patients, lost potential life years from remaining on first-line therapy; for the health system, drug costs 6-10 times those of first-line therapy. Conversely, missing resistant patients risks accumulation and transmission of resistant viral strains
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Trade-offs may vary by population: providers may be more willing to risk false positives in HIV-infected pregnant women because viral suppression at delivery prevents vertical transmission; acceptable true positive:false positive ratios may also differ with anticipated time-to-referral
Reviewer_Notes: Antiretroviral (HIV) drug resistance rather than bacterial AMR; the record codes it with the closest available vocabulary and flags the mapping choices in _notes. Model performance figures were read from the narrative text and Tables 2-3, which the text layer reproduces; the Additional file 1 supplementary tables (S1-S3) are not in the text layer
Unresolved_Items: Whether Provider_Facing_Applications should include 'Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)' when the model predicts resistance from clinical and demographic variables rather than from genotype or spectra; whether a modelled switching estimate in a hypothetical 10,000-patient cohort counts as stewardship impact; whether the paper's population estimates are healthcare costs 'reported'
Sample_Size: 290 participants with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml (final sample of the primary analysis); Model 3 used n = 260
Conflicts_of_Interest: The author(s) declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Post-hoc analysis of de-identified PEARLS (A5175) data restricted to participants initiated on NNRTI-based regimens (lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz) with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml at any point after week 16 of enrolment
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded from PEARLS: CD4 count >300 cells/mm3, previous ART exposure (except women given ART for prevention of mother-to-child transmission), pregnancy, acute illness or clinical instability. In this analysis, participants with two sequential visits with VL >=1000 copies/ml but no resistance test, and those without available resistance results at the time of confirmed elevated VL (n = 15), were excluded
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: PEARLS trial (Prospective Evaluation of Antiretrovirals in Resource-Limited Settings), Adult AIDS Clinical Trials Group A5175, NCT00084136
Dataset_Size: 1045 participants analysed; 305 with at least one VL >=1000 copies/ml after week 16; 15 excluded for unavailable resistance results; final sample 290

Geographic_Representativeness: Participants from all PEARLS study sites with a sensitivity analysis restricted to those enrolled from resource-limited settings; the authors caution that trial participants may not be representative of larger ART populations

Pathogens: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1)
Drug_Classes: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI); protease inhibitors excluded (PI class reserved for second-line therapy)
Specific_Antibiotics: Lamivudine/zidovudine/efavirenz or emtricitabine/tenofovir/efavirenz (first-line NNRTI-based regimens; also abbreviated 3TC/ZDV BID + EFV QHS and FTC/TDF/EFV QHS)

AMR_Outcome_Definition: Participants with NRTI or NNRTI resistance mutations, defined by 2014 International AIDS Society guidelines (excluding mutation 101P), were classified as resistant; resistance to protease inhibitors was not included; baseline and acquired resistance were not distinguished
AI_Purpose: Develop a risk score algorithm that predicts the need for ART change (resistance) among people with a single elevated viral load, so that providers in resource-limited settings can switch patients to second-line therapy without confirmatory VL testing
Feature_Engineering: Predictors collapsed into discrete categorical variables for point-of-care use; four categorisations of time on treatment tested and the one with the lowest AIC selected as the reference model; full models included all variables with bivariate p-value <0.5; variables with low frequency, extreme collinearity or insufficient detail for clinical implementation excluded
Feature_Selection_Method: Backward elimination in multiple logistic regression: starting with the largest p-value, variables removed one at a time until <=5 remained regardless of p-value; full models contained all variables with bivariate p <0.5
Num_Features_Total: 10 (full Model 1); 9 (full Model 2); 8 (full Model 3)
Num_Features_Selected: 5 in each final model
Software_Libraries: Stata statistical software, Version 13.0 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX); no machine-learning libraries named
Other_Metrics: AUROC for the models and for the derived weighted risk scores; sensitivity and specificity at each cutoff; Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration p-values; AIC for therapy-duration categorisation; likelihood-ratio tests between successive models; unadjusted prevalence odds ratios with 95 % CI; number of true and false positives in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients at varying resistance prevalence
Baseline_Method: Reduced logistic-regression Models 1-3 compared against each other (Models 2 and 3 exclude treatment-initiation VL and/or CD4 as eligible predictors); AUROC equality tested by chi-squared test; AIC used to choose the therapy-duration categorisation
Baseline_Performance: Reduced Model 2 AUROC 0.7981 and reduced Model 3 AUROC 0.7937 versus reduced Model 1 AUROC 0.8165; differences not statistically significant (p = 0.23 and p = 0.22)
Internal_Validation: 1000 bootstrap samples with replacement, assessed over 1000 replications
Clinical_Insights: In the best model, need for ART change was directly associated with higher treatment-initiation VL and higher VL at the first elevated measure, and inversely with treatment duration; age <30 and BMI >25.0 kg/m2 also predicted need for change; screening CD4 <100 cells/mm3 (Model 2) and ever missed medications (Model 3) were additionally retained
Generalisability_Details: The authors argue PEARLS' broad inclusion criteria improve generalizability, that participants were recruited largely from resource-limited settings and the risk score performed well in that subgroup, but caution that trial participants may not represent larger ART populations and that findings may not apply to non-efavirenz-based regimens
Maturity_Evidence: Development and internal validation with 1000 bootstrap samples on 290 trial participants; performance at risk-score cutoffs >=9 with a high-specificity threshold; sensitivity analysis restricted to resource-limited settings; no external or prospective validation reported
Integration_Point: Point-of-care use in ART clinics in resource-limited settings, based only on predictors available at the clinic, applied at the time of the first VL >=1000 copies/ml to decide immediate switch to second-line therapy instead of confirmatory testing
End_User_Described: Providers (clinicians) in ART clinics in resource-limited settings
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The risk score sits inside the WHO viral-load monitoring strategy: instead of the confirmatory test 3-6 months after an initial VL >1000 copies/ml, patients exceeding the algorithm threshold are switched immediately to second-line therapy; those below the threshold have confirmatory VL testing before any switch decision
Stewardship_Details: No stewardship impact was measured: the paper only models, in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 ART patients, how many would be switched immediately (Model 1 correctly identifying 700 and misclassifying 248 at ~25 % resistance prevalence; 1540 true positives and 149 false positives at 55 % prevalence)
Barriers_List: False positives cause premature second-line switching with significant person- and system-wide consequences (lost potential life years; drug costs 6-10 times first-line therapy); low sensitivity (~15-30 %) is accepted but means misses rely on confirmatory testing; resistance may be misclassified at low-level viraemia (<1000 copies/ml); frequent 8-weekly monitoring in the trial is unlikely in the intended settings; changing WHO CD4 eligibility could dampen efficiency gains
Facilitators_List: Only readily available, point-of-care predictors used; a limited number of categorical variables (five) to keep the score manageable; high specificity minimises false positives; may avoid confirmatory VL tests and so save laboratory costs and reduce transmission of resistant virus
Future_Directions: Prospective external validation and evaluation of the effect of the risk score on health outcomes and resource utilisation; modelling the consequences of delayed second-line initiation versus premature switching to understand threshold trade-offs; alternative cost-saving monitoring strategies such as pooled specimens and targeted VL testing
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 categories of potential predictors in the paper's own list (demographics; clinical diagnoses; immunological markers/CD4; self-reported and provider-assessed ART adherence; therapy duration); 7 coded predictor categories ticked above (clinical, microbiological, pharmacological, laboratory, behavioural, sociodemographic, temporal)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Weighted risk score: predictor score = two times the beta coefficient rounded to the nearest integer
Limitation_Categories: Trial population representativeness; frequent monitoring in the trial versus intended settings; referent category of therapy duration; efavirenz-based regimens only; changing WHO CD4 eligibility guidelines; lower resistance prevalence than other cohorts; misclassification of resistance at low-level viraemia
Data_Quality_Concerns: Resistance results unavailable for 15 participants with two sequential elevated VLs (excluded); resistance testing not performed for participants who resuppressed; frequent study-driven monitoring (every 8 weeks) unlikely in the intended settings; adherence self-reported and provider-assessed; resistance may be present at low-level viraemia below the 1000 copies/ml threshold
Reporting_Clarity: Clear: model development, candidate predictors, full and reduced model AUROCs, risk-score weights, sensitivity/specificity at defined cutoffs and calibration tests are all reported; no code or model repository link

Title: Utilization of machine learning to predict antibiotic resistant event outcomes in acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing induction chemotherapy
Journal_Source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
Country_Countries: United States of America (College Station, TX and Houston, TX)
Funder_Names: K01AI143881 (NIAID)
Population_Description: 95 adult patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) undergoing remission induction chemotherapy (IC) at MD Anderson Cancer Center, drawn from two longitudinal cohorts (PA13-0339, n=98; PA15-0780, n=56) with baseline stool metagenomics, baseline gut resistome data and complete antibiotic administration and clinical metadata.
Top_Predictive_Features: Mean variable importance score (mean decrease in Gini impurity, averaged over 100 iterations): Methanobrevibacter smithii 0.717, Blautia producta 0.630, macrolide resistance genes 0.573, lincosamide/macrolide/streptogramin resistance genes 0.542, remaining 11 bacterial taxa 0.522-0.622. Top three by mean SHAP value: M. smithii, Clostridium leptum, Bacteroides dorei
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Four Random Forest model variations (100 iterations, 500 trees each): Model 1 - ARG class presence/absence + antibiotics >=72 h + species abundance (AUC=0.667, Youden's=0.879); Model 2 - unique ARG counts by class + antibiotics >=72 h (AUC=0.689, Youden's=0.835); Model 3 - ARG presence/absence + any antibiotic administration (AUC=0.666, Youden's=0.871); Model 4 - unique ARG counts + any administration (AUC=0.687, Youden's=0.855); optimized Model 2 with top 15 variables (aggregate AUC=0.730, Youden's=0.863, sensitivity 0.630, specificity 0.643)
Best_Performing_Model: Model 2 - Random Forest using unique ARG counts by class, presence/absence of antibiotics administered >=72 hours and baseline species abundance, reduced to the top 15 variables; chosen on highest AUC, best sensitivity/specificity balance and balanced Youden's index
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables), aggregate of 100 iterations (80/20 stratified splits) in the 95-patient cohort with 14 AR events
Specificity_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables), aggregate of 100 iterations (80/20 stratified splits) in the 95-patient cohort with 14 AR events
AUROC_Population_Set: Optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables): aggregate AUC across 100 iterations (mean 0.742, median 0.745, range 0.505-0.969) in the 95-patient cohort
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was developed and internally validated only: 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits within the same 95-patient MDACC cohort, with no external or prospective validation
Reported_Limitations: Genus-level 16S rRNA abundance threshold for selecting stools for culture may have led to missed ARC events; pooling colonization and infection events may obscure biologically distinct processes; SHAP ambiguity from extensive feature interactions and zero-inflated microbial data; small cohort size, few events and single-institution analyses; no external validation
Ethical_Governance_Risks: IRB approval and written informed consent reported; no AI-specific ethical or governance risks discussed
Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre US retrospective analysis of two MDACC AML cohorts; the AI component is a Random Forest classifier of AR event outcomes (ARC or ARI combined), with SHAP and importance-based interpretation, plus sCCA and network analysis as secondary analyses. Sex, chemotherapy type and intensity were only compared between AR-event groups as baseline characteristics (not a subgroup performance analysis), so subgroup fields are answered No. Amikacin administration was the only variable differing between groups (p=0.041).
Unresolved_Items: Judgement calls: (1) Infection_Type left 'Not specified' because infection sites are never given, only the causative organisms; (2) Clinical_Outcomes coded No - AR infection/colonization is the prediction target, and no mortality, LOS, ICU or treatment-failure outcomes are reported; (3) Class_Imbalance_Addressed coded No although 80/20 splits were stratified - no resampling or class weighting is described; (4) Explanation_Level coded 'Both' because the SHAP beeswarm gives per-sample values aggregated to global mean absolute SHAP rankings; (5) Reporting_Guideline 'None reported' - no guideline is named anywhere in the text layer.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Sex_Distribution: AR-event group: female 8 (57.1%), male 6 (42.9%); no-event group: female 40 (49.4%), male 41 (50.6)
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult AML patients from the two MDACC cohorts with complete metadata and sequencing data: baseline stool metagenomics, baseline gut resistome data, complete antibiotic administration data for the study period, and gender, chemotherapy type and chemotherapy intensity available.
Exclusion_Criteria: Lack of baseline stool sample, lack of antibiotic administration data, lack of complete clinical metadata, and lack of resistome data.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: MD Anderson Cancer Center AML cohorts PA13-0339 and PA15-0780; NCBI Sequence Read Archive BioProjects PRJNA352060, PRJNA526551, PRJNA1124986, PRJNA1129514, PRJNA1128111
Dataset_Size: 782 stool samples from 154 patients (566 samples/98 patients in PA13-0339; 216 samples/56 patients in PA15-0780); 95 patients analysed
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case analysis: patients lacking a baseline stool sample, antibiotic administration data, complete clinical metadata or resistome data were excluded
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre US cohort of adult AML patients at MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, TX), collected September 2013-February 2020; the authors state validation in larger, multicentre cohorts and different high-risk populations is required
Specimen_Type_Detail: Baseline stool (fecal) samples; bacterial isolates from stool cultures on selective media and infectious isolates from the clinical microbiology laboratory
Primary_AMR_Outcome: AR event — a single combined outcome of confirmed AR colonization (ARC) or confirmed AR infection (ARI) with a CDC serious/urgent-threat pathogen (VRE, CRE, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA)
Pathogens: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE), carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (ESBL; Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae), multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (MDRP; carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa), methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones; nitroimidazoles; oxazolidinones; carbapenems; cephalosporins; aminoglycosides; folate pathway inhibitors; lipopeptides; beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations; glycylcyclines; tetracyclines
Specific_Antibiotics: levofloxacin, metronidazole, linezolid, meropenem, cefepime, amikacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, daptomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, cefpodoxime, ciprofloxacin, tigecycline, minocycline, ertapenem
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Confirmed AR colonization (ARC) if any bacterial isolate from a stool sample was confirmed CRE, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, VRE, MDRP or MRSA; confirmed AR infection (ARI) if the clinical microbiology lab diagnosed a microbially defined infection with those organisms; both combined as an "AR event"
AI_Purpose: To develop a Random Forest machine learning model that predicts antibiotic-resistant (AR) infection and colonization event outcomes in adult AML patients during induction chemotherapy by integrating baseline gut microbiome and resistome data with antibiotic administration and clinical data; secondary analyses were sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) and a correlation network of ARG classes and microbial taxa
Feature_Engineering: ARG classes encoded as presence/absence or as counts of unique genes per class; antibiotic administration encoded as presence/absence or as exposure >=72 hours; variables retained only if received by >=10% of patients; baseline microbiome filtered to abundance 0.001 and 10% prevalence; CLR transformation with a pseudocount (min relative abundance/2) for sCCA
Feature_Selection_Method: Averaged variable importance scores (mean decrease in Gini impurity) over 100 iterations; top 20, 15 and 10 variables tested; top 15 retained per model
Hyperparameter_Method: Final model optimized by increasing the value of mtry (number of variables randomly sampled at each split) and increasing the node size to increase tree depth; sCCA hyperparameters optimized with CCA.permute (nperms = 100, niter = 5)
Software_Libraries: PMA package (v. 1.2-2) in R; BugSeq (v4.0); minimap2; MetaPhlAn2 (v2.8.1); MEGAHIT (v1.2.8); metaSPAdes (v3.14.1); SPAdes (v3.14.1); VSEARCH; UNOISE3; Mothur; SILVA (version 138); QIIME 2; Seqtk (v1.3); Gephi
Hardware_Details: Grace computing cluster at Texas A&M University; Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S4 flow cell (North Texas Genome Center)
Other_Metrics: Youden's index (optimized Model 2: 0.863; models 1-4: 0.835-0.879); ROC curves with confidence intervals; variable importance (mean decrease in Gini impurity)
Baseline_Method: Four Random Forest configurations compared against each other (ARG presence/absence vs unique ARG counts; antibiotics >=72 h vs any administration), plus comparison with previously published ARI prediction models
Baseline_Performance: Model 1 AUC=0.667 (Youden's 0.879), Model 2 AUC=0.689 (0.835), Model 3 AUC=0.666 (0.871), Model 4 AUC=0.687 (0.855); published ARI models AUC 0.57-0.75
Internal_Validation: 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits per model, 500 trees each, variable importance averaged over the 100 iterations; the optimized Model 2 (top 15 variables) re-run 100 times to produce the final AUC-ROC curve; no k-fold cross-validation used
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing, stratified
External_Validation_Description: None performed; the authors state they could not find a similar independent clinical cohort with the same sequencing and clinical metadata
Overfitting_Method: Four model variants run across 100 independent 80/20 stratified splits, each with 500 trees; variables reduced to the top 15 most influential; final model optimized by increasing mtry and node size to limit overfitting
Clinical_Insights: Methanobrevibacter smithii, Clostridium leptum and Bacteroides dorei were consistently associated with reduced AR event risk (protective commensals supporting gut microbial resilience); ARG classes for lincosamides, macrolides and streptogramins were negatively associated with AR events
Data_Repository: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (BioProject IDs PRJNA352060, PRJNA526551, PRJNA1124986, PRJNA1129514, PRJNA1128111)
Generalisability_Details: Model is developmental and single-institution; validation and refinement in larger multicentre cohorts and different high-risk populations is needed before clinical implementation
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only - 100 independent 80/20 stratified training-testing splits with 500 trees per model; the authors state they were unable to validate the model on an independent cohort
Integration_Point: Not described; the model is developmental and is proposed for future implementation in infection risk stratification of AML patients on induction chemotherapy, with no system integration reported
End_User_Described: Clinicians - the authors state the findings offer valuable predictors for clinical decision-making and potential infection risk stratification
Barriers_List: Small cohort size and few AR events; single-institution data; no independent validation cohort with comparable sequencing and clinical metadata; model still in development
Facilitators_List: Model performance comparable to or exceeding other recent ARI prediction models (AUC 0.730 vs 0.57-0.75); integration of microbiome, resistome and clinical data; simultaneous assessment of AR infection and colonization risk
Future_Directions: Validation and refinement in larger, multicentre cohorts and extension to different high-risk populations; functional validation via metatranscriptomics, metabolomics or gnotobiotic models to determine the role of the predicted protective taxa, their metabolic products and contributory ARGs
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Raw sum of decreases in Gini impurity across all trees in the Random Forest (mean variable importance score, not normalised); SHAP (Shapely Additive exPlanations) values for ranking by mean absolute SHAP value
Novel_Predictors_Details: ARG classes conferring resistance to lincosamides, macrolides and streptogramins were unexpectedly associated with REDUCED AR event risk (top predictors in the Random Forest, covariation with taxa in sCCA, and negative correlation with AR events in the network analysis), despite such genes usually being linked to broad-spectrum antibiotic use and worse outcomes
Limitation_Categories: Ascertainment/label: 16S genus-level threshold may have missed ARC events; pooling of colonization and infection outcomes. Modelling: SHAP ambiguity from feature interactions and zero-inflated data. Sample: small cohort, few events, single institution, no external validation cohort.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Microbial taxa data are inherently zero-inflated (most taxa absent/low), contributing to ambiguity in SHAP interpretation; no spike-in standards used; batch effects addressed only by consistent protocols, library preparation and sequencing conditions
Reporting_Clarity: Model configurations, variable counts (89-92), validation scheme, AUC, Youden's index and sensitivity/specificity are reported in narrative form; further clinical metrics and confusion matrices are deferred to Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 (not in the provided text layer); dataset accession numbers and data availability statement are given

Title: Prediction of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae from Raman spectra by Artificial Intelligent Raman Detection and Identification System (AIRDIS) with machine learning
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation; AI Signal Processing
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: National Science and Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC 113-2320-B-039-010); China Medical University, Taichung, Taiwan (CMU113-MF-67)
Population_Description: 2041 clinical bacterial isolates: 988 S. aureus (including 475 MSSA and 513 MRSA) and 1053 K. pneumoniae (including 536 CSKP and 517 CRKP), collected from the SMART surveillance program (16 regional hospitals across Taiwan, 2017-2020) and China Medical University Hospital bacteraemia patients (2023-2024).
Data_Source: Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: SA model: Raman shift regions 1688-1702, 1200-1227, 457-476, 1547-1606 and 1128 cm-1 and the 1004 cm-1 peak. KP model: 1654-1690, 1124-1133, 1438-1449, 1573-1577 cm-1 and the 1205, 1267 and 810-811 cm-1 peaks. Ranked by mean absolute SHAP value (top 20 features).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: RamanNet (deep learning): S. aureus/MRSA - accuracy 0.88, AUROC 0.92, AUPRC 0.91, recall 0.88, precision 0.89, F1 0.88, MCC 0.76; K. pneumoniae/CRKP - accuracy 0.87, AUROC 0.96, AUPRC 0.92, recall 0.84, precision 0.89, F1 0.86, MCC 0.73. RF: S. aureus - accuracy 0.75, AUROC 0.84; K. pneumoniae - accuracy 0.70, AUROC 0.76. SVM: S. aureus - accuracy 0.75, AUROC 0.83; K. pneumoniae - accuracy 0.67, AUROC 0.74.
Best_Performing_Model: RamanNet (deep learning model); decided on AUROC (also outperformed RF/SVM on accuracy, AUPRC, F1, MCC)
Accuracy_Population_Set: S. aureus test dataset (722 isolates, 14,440 Raman spectra)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: S. aureus test dataset (722 isolates, 14,440 Raman spectra)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: S. aureus test dataset (722 isolates, 14,440 Raman spectra)
F1_Population_Set: S. aureus test dataset (722 isolates, 14,440 Raman spectra)
AUROC_Population_Set: S. aureus test dataset (722 isolates, 14,440 Raman spectra)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model trained on a subset of isolates and evaluated on held-out isolates from the same overall data pool (SMART + CMUH); no independent external validation cohort, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment reported.
Reported_Limitations: Prediction limited to MRSA/CRKP only, no AMR genotype detection so cannot replace AST; discriminating Raman shifts not confirmed as biomarkers; cannot link results to known resistance genes/mechanisms or distinguish CRKP mechanisms (KPC/NDM/OXA-48); needs larger, more diverse isolate sets and further validation before clinical implementation.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Misclassifying a resistant isolate as susceptible (false negative) was identified as more clinically consequential than the reverse, prompting the authors to shift the decision threshold toward higher sensitivity.
Sample_Size: 2041 clinical isolates (988 S. aureus; 1053 K. pneumoniae)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: Clinical S. aureus and K. pneumoniae isolates identified by MALDI-TOF/16S rRNA sequencing, from the SMART surveillance program (16 regional Taiwan hospitals, 2017-2020) or randomly obtained from bacteraemia patients at China Medical University Hospital (2023-2024).
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Other
Data_Source_Name: SMART (Surveillance of Multicentre Antimicrobial Resistance in Taiwan) program
Dataset_Size: 2041 isolates; 40,820 AIRDIS Raman spectrum files total (19,760 from S. aureus isolates + 21,060 from K. pneumoniae isolates)
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates limited to Taiwan: 16 regional SMART hospitals (2017-2020) plus one tertiary medical center, CMUH (2023-2024); no international representation.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Bacterial isolates cultured from clinical specimens; CMUH subset specifically from bacteraemia (bloodstream infection) patients
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary prediction of methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA vs MSSA) and carbapenem resistance in K. pneumoniae (CRKP vs CSKP) directly from Raman spectra.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus; Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin/oxacillin resistance in S. aureus; carbapenem resistance in K. pneumoniae)
Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin (for MRSA definition); carbapenems (for CRKP definition)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible label per isolate, assigned from automated Phoenix antimicrobial susceptibility testing results (e.g., MRSA/CRKP = resistant; MSSA/CSKP = susceptible), used as ground truth for the corresponding Raman spectra.
AI_Purpose: To develop AIRDIS, combining Raman spectroscopy with deep learning, to rapidly predict methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP) directly from bacterial isolates, bypassing slower conventional AST-based workflows.
Num_Models_Compared: 3 (RamanNet deep-learning model plus SVM and RF baselines)
Feature_Engineering: Raman spectra underwent baseline correction (polynomial fitting) and smoothing (Savitzky-Golay filter), then normalization; RamanNet further divided each spectrum into overlapping fragments (length 100, overlap 50) for automatic feature extraction.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Weighted F1-score used for model selection on the validation data
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search on the training dataset
Hardware_Details: Intel Core i7-14700K CPU, 128 GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU
Other_Metrics: Very major error rate, major error rate, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), reported per model in Table 3
Baseline_Method: Support vector machine (SVM) and random forest (RF)
Baseline_Performance: S. aureus: RF accuracy 0.75/AUROC 0.84; SVM accuracy 0.75/AUROC 0.83
Internal_Validation: Random 8:2 split of the training isolates into training/validation for hyperparameter tuning and model selection (by weighted F1-score); a separate held-out set of remaining isolates used as the test dataset.
Train_Test_Split: S. aureus: 266 isolates (5320 spectra) training vs 722 isolates (14,440 spectra) testing
Overfitting_Method: Dropout regularization (rate = 0.5) after concatenation of fragment features
Clinical_Insights: SHAP-identified discriminating Raman shifts near known carotenoid (staphyloxanthin) peaks for MRSA/MSSA, suggesting possible biochemical differences relevant to classification; discriminating KP-model shifts linked to lipopolysaccharide-related bands, potentially reflecting membrane changes affecting antibiotic binding.
Generalisability_Details: Authors call for further studies with a larger and more diverse set of isolates to expand the model's capability to a broader range of resistance phenotypes before wider use.
Maturity_Evidence: Model evaluated on a held-out set of clinical isolates (722 S. aureus / 768 K. pneumoniae) drawn from the same two source cohorts as training; no independent external cohort, prospective clinical trial, or deployed CDS integration reported.
Integration_Point: After species identification (MALDI-TOF) in the routine clinical microbiology workflow, replacing/augmenting the subsequent AST step
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory personnel, within existing hospital laboratory workflow
Clinical_Workflow_Details: AIRDIS is designed to be compatible with the existing clinical workflow (species ID via MALDI-TOF followed by AST via automated Phoenix system), allowing simultaneous bacterial identification and resistance prediction without additional equipment (Fig. 1).
Barriers_List: Cannot fully replace conventional AST (no genotype detection); cannot distinguish different resistance mechanisms (e.g., KPC, NDM, OXA-48) which limits guidance on newer antibiotic selection; requires further large-scale clinical validation before implementation.
Facilitators_List: Compact, built-in AI processing, lower cost than MALDI-TOF; simplified sample prep supporting batch operation (up to 96 samples/run); fully automated measurement, 1-3 minutes per sample; compatible with existing clinical workflow without added equipment.
Future_Directions: Expand the model to a broader range of pathogens and resistance phenotypes and distinguish specific resistance mechanisms; conduct further validation with larger, more diverse clinical isolate sets prior to clinical implementation.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), ranked by mean absolute SHAP value
Novel_Predictors_Details: Discriminating Raman shifts tentatively linked to lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-related bands in the KP model; structural LPS changes may reduce antibiotic-binding affinity, a candidate but unconfirmed biochemical correlate of carbapenem resistance.
Limitation_Categories: Restricted resistance scope (MRSA/CRKP only, no genotype detection); unconfirmed biomarker identity of discriminating features; cannot resolve specific resistance mechanisms; need for larger/more diverse validation cohorts.
Data_Quality_Concerns: The AIRDIS system enforces a minimum spectral-intensity acceptance threshold and dynamically adjusts laser power to maintain recognizable, consistent Raman spectra during sampling.

Title:
Predicting carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacteriaceae infections 
in pediatric liver transplant recipients
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: K. C. Wong Education Foundation
Population_Description: Pediatric patients (<12 years) who underwent liver transplantation at FAHZU (center 1, Jan 2020-Jun 2023) and at Tianjin First Central Hospital (center 2, Aug 2017-Aug 2018), reviewed retrospectively.

Title: Rapid Identification and Typing of Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae Using MALDI-TOF MS and Machine Learning
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Health Commission of Zhejiang Province
Population_Description: 267 Klebsiella pneumoniae clinical isolates from Quzhou People's Hospital: 137 CRKP from blood specimens (Jan 2014-Dec 2023, 58 used as validation strains), 60 intestinal-colonised CRKP from ICU patient screening (Jun 2022-Sep 2023, 20 for validation) and 70 non-replicated CSKP from blood (Jan 2022-Dec 2023, 20 for validation). Top_Predictive_Features: CRKP vs CSKP model (ClinProTools peak weights): m/z 2523.43 and 4520.11 (weights > 0.1). Different-sources model (QC weights): m/z 8876 (4.85), 8993 (1.48) and 9139 (1.45) Da.

All_Models_Evaluated: GA, SNN and QC (ClinProTools 3.0). CRKP-vs-CSKP typing model: SNN best (CV accuracy 90.08%, RC 95.80%); GA and QC figures not reported. Different-sources model: QC (CV accuracy 86.85%, RC 88.46%); SNN (CV 83.57%, RC 94.82%). Validation of SNN: 90% (18/20) CSKP, 89.66% (52/58) CRKP, PPV 96.30%, NPV 75%. Validation of QC: 81.82% (18/22) bloodstream, 95.00% (19/20) intestinal, PPV 94.74%, NPV 82.61%; direct mass spectrometry 66.67% (6/9).
Best_Performing_Model: SNN (Supervised Neural Network) for the primary CRKP vs CSKP typing model - superior performance by cross-validation accuracy (90.08%) and recognition capacity (95.80%); QC was best for the different-sources model (CV accuracy 86.85%, RC 88.46%)
Accuracy_Value: 89.66% (52/58) CRKP and 90% (18/20) CSKP on validation strains; cross-validation accuracy 90.08% for the SNN model; overall validation accuracy 89.74% (discussion)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Validation strains: 58 CRKP and 20 CSKP non-duplicate isolates (SNN resistance analysis model)
Sensitivity_Value: 90.08% (abstract reports this figure as the SNN model's sensitivity; the results section reports the same figure as cross-validation accuracy)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: SNN CRKP vs CSKP classification model (abstract-level report)
Specificity_Value: 95.80% (abstract reports this figure as the SNN model's specificity; the results section reports the same figure as recognition capacity (RC))
Specificity_Population_Set: SNN CRKP vs CSKP classification model (abstract-level report)
Precision_PPV_Value: 96.30% (positive predictive value of the SNN resistance analysis model)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Validation strains of the SNN model: 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP isolates
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model trained on 79 CRKP + 50 CSKP blood isolates and validated on held-out non-duplicate strains (20 CSKP, 58 CRKP) from the same hospital, with an additional 9-isolate clinical check; no external dataset and no prospective or routine-use evaluation.
Reported_Limitations: Small sample size; need for broader validation with additional strains; results reflect local (Quzhou) strain characteristics; inability to classify certain strains highlights limited accuracy of the software algorithm; discrepancies in protein peaks vs prior studies may follow from sample preparation and regional/temporal strain differences.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre MALDI-TOF MS + machine learning (ClinProTools GA/SNN/QC) study on 267 K. pneumoniae isolates, developing (1) a CRKP vs CSKP typing model and (2) a model separating bloodstream-infection from intestinal-screening CRKP. Unit of analysis = SNN on the primary CRKP vs CSKP dataset. Peak-level AUCs (0.84-0.88) are reported for individual mass peaks, not for the model as a discriminator, so AUROC_Reported is No. Abstract labels the SNN cross-validation accuracy (90.08%) and recognition capacity (95.80%) as sensitivity and specificity, while the results call them CV accuracy and RC - both readings noted in the *_Value fields.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the SNN's 90.08%/95.80% should be coded as sensitivity/specificity (abstract wording) or as cross-validation accuracy/recognition capacity (results wording); number of cross-validation folds is not stated; GA model performance figures are not reported; identities of the m/z 10,079 Da peak are unresolved by the authors.
Sample_Size: 267 K. pneumoniae isolates (137 bloodstream CRKP, 60 intestinal-screening CRKP, 70 CSKP); isolates
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 267 K. pneumoniae isolates in total; the mass-spectrometry modelling dataset comprised 79 CRKP and 50 CSKP blood isolates, with validation on 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP strains
Geographic_Representativeness: Single centre - Quzhou People's Hospital, Quzhou, China; authors state the results reflect local strain characteristics and predominantly represent Quzhou's resident population.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood specimens (bloodstream-infection isolates) and intestinal colonisation screening specimens from ICU patients (fecal-derived isolates in the clinical validation)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem resistance in K. pneumoniae: screening of specific mass peaks of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) versus carbapenem-sensitive K. pneumoniae (CSKP) from MALDI-TOF MS spectra, and differentiation of CRKP from intestinal screening versus bloodstream infection
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (carbapenem-resistant CRKP and carbapenem-sensitive CSKP isolates)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
Specific_Antibiotics: Ertapenem, imipenem, meropenem (susceptibility panel also includes meropenem, imipenem, aztreonam, cefazolin, cefuroxime, cefoxitin and others)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: CRKP defined as isolates with MIC of ertapenem >= 2 ug/mL or imipenem/meropenem >= 4 ug/mL per CLSI criteria; CSKP = carbapenem-sensitive K. pneumoniae. Second outcome: specimen source of CRKP (bloodstream infection vs intestinal screening), separated on spectral peak differences.
AI_Purpose: Apply MALDI-TOF MS with machine learning (ClinProTools GA, SNN and QC models) to identify CRKP from carbapenem-sensitive K. pneumoniae and to distinguish bloodstream-infection CRKP from intestinal-screening CRKP
Num_Models_Compared: 3 (GA, SNN and QC)
Feature_Engineering: No additional feature engineering beyond ClinProTools spectral processing: protein fingerprints analysed in Biotyper 3.0 and FlexAnalysis, peaks selected by ROC curve (p < 0.05, AUC > 0.8) and compared with gel plots
Feature_Selection_Method: ClinProTools 3.0 statistical peak screening: ROC curve of each characteristic peak (p < 0.05) with AUC > 0.8; algorithms then perform their own automatic feature selection (GA, SNN) or statistical ranking (QC)
Num_Features_Total: 25 characteristic peaks distinguished CRKP from CSKP (p < 0.000001); 6 peaks (m/z 4497.59, 4547.15, 5040.46, 8876.78, 8993.44, 9139.06 Da) distinguished the two CRKP sources
Num_Features_Selected: 4 peaks for the CRKP vs CSKP model (m/z 2523.43, 3041.62, 4520.11 and 10,079.18 Da); 6 peaks for the different-sources model (m/z 4497.59, 4547.15, 5040.46, 8876.78, 8993.44, 9139.06 Da)
Hyperparameter_Method: Automatic parameter tuning routines built into the ClinProTools algorithms; GA parameters (mutation rate, crossover rate, number of peaks in the model) described as adjustable to optimise performance
Software_Libraries: ClinProTools 3.0, FlexAnalysis and Biotyper 3.0 (Bruker) with the MBT2969 reference database; SPAdes for whole-genome assembly
Hardware_Details: Bruker Microflex LT/SH MALDI-TOF mass spectrometer; Siemens MicroScan WalkAway 96 PLUS automatic identification/susceptibility instrument; Illumina sequencing platform
Other_Metrics: Cross-validation accuracy and recognition capacity (RC) for every model; positive and negative predictive values for SNN (96.30%/75%) and QC (94.74%/82.61%); peak-level AUCs (> 0.84 for m/z 2523.43, 3041.62, 4520.11, 10079.18; > 0.85 for m/z 8993 and 9139; > 0.88 for m/z 2523 and 4520); peak weights; classification accuracies for CSKP/CRKP and for bloodstream/intestinal CRKP
Baseline_Method: Head-to-head comparison of the three ClinProTools algorithms (GA, SNN, QC) on the same spectral datasets
Baseline_Performance: CRKP vs CSKP model: SNN CV accuracy 90.08% / RC 95.80% (superior to GA and QC); different-sources model: QC CV accuracy 86.85% / RC 88.46% versus SNN CV 83.57% / RC 94.82%
Internal_Validation: Validation on held-out non-duplicate strains (20 CSKP, 58 CRKP for the SNN model; 22 bloodstream and 20 intestinal CRKP for the QC model) plus a 9-isolate clinical validation
Train_Test_Split: Training: 79 CRKP and 50 CSKP blood isolates (typing model); validation: 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP non-duplicate strains - no percentage split stated
CV_Folds: Cross-validation reported by ClinProTools but the number of folds is not stated
Clinical_Insights: Peak-level biological interpretation: the m/z 4520-4529 range is linked to different Ambler classes of carbapenemases (A/KPC, B/NDM-VIM-IMP, D/OXA-48); the m/z 8876, 8993 and 9139 peaks enriched in bloodstream CRKP are proposed to reflect siderophore systems and capsule regulators associated with systemic virulence.
Generalisability_Details: Single-hospital strain collection that predominantly represents Quzhou's resident population; authors call for broader validation with additional strains and note that protein-peak discrepancies between studies may reflect sample preparation and regional/temporal strain differences.
Maturity_Evidence: Validation of the SNN model on 20 CSKP and 58 CRKP non-duplicate strains from the same hospital (identification accuracy 90% and 89.66%) and a 9-isolate clinical validation (66.67%); no external dataset, no prospective evaluation and no clinical deployment.
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory MALDI-TOF MS workflow for rapid identification and typing of CRKP at the point of species identification, supporting early clinical diagnosis
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory staff and clinicians using MALDI-TOF MS identification results for early diagnosis of CRKP
Clinical_Workflow_Details: ClinProTools models are built from routine MALDI-TOF protein fingerprints; the best model is saved and used to identify and validate incoming strains, with results expressed as statistics for rapid CRKP/CSKP and source typing in the laboratory workflow.
Barriers_List: Software algorithm accuracy limits (ungrouped strains); poor mass-spectrometry scores of slime-type colonies; sample quality and preparation effects; small, single-centre, locally representative sample
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is rapid, cost-effective and easy to use and is already established in clinical laboratories; it is applied directly to routine protein fingerprints without additional assays
Future_Directions: Larger sample sizes and more advanced machine learning techniques to improve algorithm sensitivity and specificity; broader validation with additional strains; further mass spectrometry and algorithm optimisation
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Characteristic peak weight calculated by ClinProTools 3.0 for each model (GA, SNN, QC)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Peaks at m/z 8876, 8993 and 9139 Da are proposed as markers of source-specific virulence (siderophore/capsule factors) in bloodstream CRKP; the identity of the m/z 10,079 Da resistance-associated peak is explicitly unresolved and suggested to be fragments or expression products of resistance-associated proteins.
Limitation_Categories: Sample size; single centre / local population representativeness; algorithm accuracy and ungrouped strains; sample quality (slime-type colonies); no external validation; peak differences versus prior studies
Data_Quality_Concerns: Slime-type colonies gave poor mass spectrometry scores and were associated with misidentification/classification failure; sample preparation method and protein purity/concentration affect direct mass spectrometry accuracy
Reporting_Clarity: Methods and results reported in detail with peak statistics tables (Tables 1-3) and figures; however the abstract's naming of the SNN cross-validation accuracy and recognition capacity as sensitivity and specificity is inconsistent with the results section

Baseline_Performance: Not reported in the main text; performance metrics for the non-XGBoost models are in Supplementary Table 3.
Internal_Validation: 5-fold stratified cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing, alongside 5-fold stratified cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: 5-fold cross-validation combined with extensive hyperparameter tuning

Generalisability_Details: Authors expect the model trained on local data to be usable in other centres and argue the single-centre data can support adaptation elsewhere; generalisability is stated as improved by cross-validation and tuning.

End_User_Described: Clinicians / healthcare professionals
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Manual data entry into a web interface that returns real-time resistance predictions; the model operates independently of hospital systems and is deployed on a secure server.

Title: Development and validation of a predictive model for profiling antibiotic resistance phenotypes of Acinetobacter baumannii strains via clinical MALDI-TOF mass spectra: A multicenter study
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: National Natural Science Foundation of China; Research Foundation for Advanced Talents of Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital
Population_Description: 3644 Acinetobacter baumannii clinical strains isolated from blood, urine, respiratory tract and wound specimens (2019-2024) at Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital, Southern Medical University, China; plus an external multicenter validation set of 1629 isolates (n=648, 450, 531) from three independent hospitals (2023-2024).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Eight ML models trained/compared per antibiotic (class-level, Table 1; individual-drug level, Table 2): AdaBoost, Bagging, CatBoost, Decision Tree, GBDT, Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost. Best model varied by antibiotic; e.g. XGBoost best for aminoglycosides (accuracy 81.77%), CatBoost for carbapenems (83.85%), cephalosporins (81.21%), penicillins (83.55%) and glycylcyclines (95.31%), GBDT for quinolones (83.07%), XGBoost for sulfonamides (66.63%) and tetracyclines (94.79%).
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (imipenem resistance prediction) — the individual-antibiotic result the authors highlight as their headline finding (accuracy 84.90%); CatBoost/XGBoost/GBDT were each ‘best’ for different antibiotic classes so no single model is best overall.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Imipenem (individual antibiotic), internal 20% held-out test set, A. baumannii isolates
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Imipenem, internal 20% held-out test set
Specificity_Population_Set: Imipenem, internal 20% held-out test set
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Imipenem, internal 20% held-out test set
F1_Population_Set: Imipenem, internal 20% held-out test set
AUROC_Population_Set: Imipenem, internal test set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model was internally trained/tested (80/20 split, 5-fold CV) and then evaluated on MALDI-TOF spectra from three external, independent hospitals not used in training — external validation, but no prospective real-time clinical deployment or CDS integration was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Absence of external validation data for piperacillin (and gentamicin/ceftriaxone, not tested in validation cohorts) restricted evaluation of model performance for those agents.
Unresolved_Items: Abstract states resistance was analysed for 'nine antibiotic classes', but Tables 1-4 report only eight classes (aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cephalosporins, glycylcyclines, penicillins, quinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines); polymyxins/colistin were AST-tested (2.3) but not among the eight ML-modelled classes — discrepancy not explained in the text.
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: A. baumannii strains from blood, urine, respiratory tract and wound specimens (2019-2024); isolates unambiguously identified as A. baumannii by the automated MALDI-TOF reporting system after passing quality control.
Exclusion_Criteria: Spectra not identified as A. baumannii by MALDI-TOF MS were excluded from the dataset.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: VITEK MS IVD clinical database (bioMérieux)
Dataset_Size: 3644 isolates (internal, 80/20 train/test split); 1629 isolates across 3 external validation cohorts (n=648, 450, 531)
Geographic_Representativeness: All isolates drawn from hospitals in Guangdong Province, China (plus external validation from Guangzhou-area hospitals); no isolates from other provinces/countries.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood, urine, respiratory tract, and wound specimens
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant/non-resistant phenotype (per CLSI MIC breakpoint) predicted from MALDI-TOF mass spectra, for each of 21 antimicrobial agents / 8 antibiotic classes.
Pathogens: Acinetobacter baumannii
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cephalosporins, glycylcyclines, penicillins, quinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines (Tables 1/2); abstract states resistance to 'nine antibiotic classes' overall.
Specific_Antibiotics: amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin, imipenem, meropenem, cefepime, cefoperazone/sulbactam, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, tigecycline, ampicillin/sulbactam, piperacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, ticarcillin, colistin, polymyxin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, doxycycline, and minocycline
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label from CLSI MIC breakpoints determined by broth microdilution: resistant (1) if MIC exceeded the CLSI breakpoint, non-resistant (0) if MIC was at or below it.
AI_Purpose: To create a predictive model for antibiotic resistance phenotypes of A. baumannii from clinical MALDI-TOF mass spectra combined with machine learning, as a faster alternative to culture-based AST.
Feature_Engineering: Mass spectra binned by 10 Da to reduce feature space; each bin represented by its maximum intensity value.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search (GridSearchCV) evaluating all hyperparameter combinations with 5-fold cross-validation.
Other_Metrics: 5-fold cross-validation accuracy (5Fold-CV) reported for every model/drug (Tables 1-2); AUPRC reported alongside AUROC per antibiotic class/drug (e.g. imipenem AUPRC=0.9042).
Internal_Validation: 80%/20% train-test split; 5-fold cross-validation via GridSearchCV
Train_Test_Split: 80% train / 20% test
External_Validation_Description: MALDI-TOF spectra + AST results (8 antibiotics) from three independent hospitals (2023-2024): Guangzhou Medical University First Affiliated Hospital (N=648), Sun Yat-sen University Affiliated First Hospital (N=450), Sun Yat-sen University Affiliated Cancer Center (n=531).
Overfitting_Method: Overfitting inferred from the performance gap between internal test accuracy and external multicenter validation accuracy for imbalanced classes (e.g. tigecycline, doxycycline, minocycline).
Generalisability_Details: Confirmed via validation on three independent external hospital cohorts, particularly stable (~80% accuracy) for carbapenems.
Maturity_Evidence: Multicenter external validation on independent mass-spectra datasets from three hospitals not used in training.
Future_Directions: Refine resistance labeling (explicit susceptible/intermediate/resistant modeling, continuous MIC values); expand dataset diversity; integrate genomic data; improve model sensitivity and reduce overfitting.
Limitation_Categories: Class imbalance/overfitting for rare resistant phenotypes (glycylcyclines, tetracyclines); incomplete validation-cohort coverage (gentamicin, ceftriaxone and piperacillin not tested in the three external validation cohorts).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Significant class imbalance (few resistant isolates) for glycylcyclines/tetracyclines produced high nominal accuracy but poor sensitivity/specificity, indicating overfitting to the majority (non-resistant) class.
Reporting_Clarity: Results reported in structured tables by antibiotic class (Table 1) and individual antibiotic (Table 2), each row giving accuracy/precision/sensitivity/specificity/F1/5-fold-CV; note precision duplicates the accuracy value and specificity duplicates the sensitivity value in every row (Tables 1-2), likely a reporting artefact.
Page_References: Table 1 p.4; Table 2 p.4; Fig. 2 (AUROC/AUPRC) p.5; Table 3-4 p.7

Title: Early clinical predictors of macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in hospitalized children during the 2024 outbreak in South Korea
Journal_Source: European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
Funder_Names: Yonsei University College of Medicine (6-2024-0099); National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF)/Ministry of Science and ICT (RS-2026-25540008); Seokchun Caritas Foundation (SCY2501P)
Population_Description: 458 hospitalized children and adolescents aged 1 month to 18 years with PCR-confirmed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia admitted to Yongin Severance Hospital (South Korea) during the 2024 outbreak
Top_Predictive_Features: ESR (aOR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01-1.06) and MP PCR Ct value (aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.73-0.83) - the two variables that remained independently associated with macrolide resistance after multivariable logistic regression adjustment
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Clinical model (age, sex, neutrophil %, ESR, CRP): AUC 0.659; clinical model + CXR findings: AUC 0.673; clinical model + MP PCR Ct value: AUC 0.806; clinical model + CXR findings + Ct value: AUC 0.808
Best_Performing_Model: Clinical model plus CXR findings and MP PCR Ct value (AUC 0.808, the highest of the four models compared by ROC/AUC)
AUROC_Population_Set: Complete-case dataset of the full cohort (458 hospitalized children with PCR-confirmed MP pneumonia)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model discrimination (AUC) was evaluated on the same retrospective complete-case cohort used to fit it; no internal validation technique (e.g. cross-validation, bootstrap) or external validation was performed, and the authors explicitly state the model was not externally validated.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective single-center study during a specific outbreak (limits generalizability); fever duration, total symptom duration, and outpatient antibiotic-exposure timing were inconsistently documented and excluded; no external validation or clinically actionable thresholds for ESR/Ct were defined; PCR Ct values are assay-dependent and not direct quantitative measures of bacterial burden.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Authors caution that Ct value/ESR thresholds are not externally validated and should not be used as stand-alone criteria for treatment escalation, to avoid inappropriate antibiotic-escalation decisions.
Unresolved_Items: This study uses conventional multivariable logistic regression and ROC/AUC analysis rather than a machine-learning algorithm; its coding as an 'AI application' and the Task_Type/Interpretability fields for this AI/ML scoping review required judgment.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized children and adolescents aged 1 month to 18 years with PCR-confirmed MP pneumonia admitted to Yongin Severance Hospital between January and December 2024
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Imaging
Data_Source_Name: Electronic medical records (single institution)
Dataset_Size: 458 patients (74 MSMP; 384 MRMP)
Missing_Data_Method: Variables with inconsistent/incomplete documentation (fever duration, symptom duration, outpatient antibiotic timing) were excluded from analysis rather than imputed
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-center study conducted at one hospital in Yongin-si, South Korea, during a specific outbreak period; authors note this may limit generalizability
Specimen_Type_Detail: Nasopharyngeal specimen
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MRMP), defined by detection of point mutations at position 2063 or 2064 in domain V of the 23S rRNA gene
Pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (primary pathogen studied for macrolide resistance); co-tested respiratory panel: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis, Bordetella parapertussis, Legionella pneumophila
Drug_Classes: Macrolides
Specific_Antibiotics: Azithromycin, Clarithromycin (first-line macrolides); Doxycycline, Levofloxacin (second-line)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Macrolide resistance defined by detection of point mutations at position 2063 or 2064 in domain V of the 23S rRNA gene of M. pneumoniae
AI_Purpose: To describe the epidemiological burden of macrolide resistance and identify admission-stage clinical, laboratory, and radiographic factors that predict macrolide-resistant M. pneumoniae in order to support early risk stratification
Feature_Engineering: Chest radiographic findings were categorized into ordinal groups (normal, unifocal pneumonia, multifocal/bilateral pneumonia, pneumonia with pleural effusion) for use as a covariate
Feature_Selection_Method: Candidate predictors were screened via univariable logistic regression; those associated with resistance were then entered into the multivariable logistic regression model
Software_Libraries: IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA)
Other_Metrics: Odds ratios (OR/adjusted OR) with 95% CI from univariable/multivariable logistic regression; area under the ROC curve (AUC) for model discrimination
Baseline_Method: Clinical model including age, sex, neutrophil proportion, ESR, and CRP (without PCR Ct value or CXR findings)
Baseline_Performance: AUC 0.659 (clinical model alone)
Clinical_Insights: Molecular pathogen load (Ct value) and inflammatory index (ESR) provide superior predictive performance for macrolide resistance than clinical/radiographic findings alone; incorporating them at admission could guide timely escalation to second-line therapy
Generalisability_Details: Retrospective, single-center study during a specific outbreak period, which may limit generalizability to other populations and settings
Maturity_Evidence: Discrimination (AUC) computed on the same retrospective complete-case cohort used to fit the model; authors explicitly state no external validation or clinically actionable thresholds were established
End_User_Described: Physicians/clinicians managing hospitalized children with MP pneumonia at admission
Future_Directions: External validation and definition of clinically actionable thresholds for ESR and PCR Ct values are needed before clinical use
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Multivariable logistic regression odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CI and p-values used to rank independent predictors
Novel_Predictors_Details: Lower MP PCR Ct value (higher pathogen load) identified as a robust, independent predictor of macrolide resistance
Limitation_Categories: Study design (retrospective, single-center); data completeness (excluded variables due to inconsistent documentation); validation (no external validation or defined thresholds); measurement (Ct value assay-dependence)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Fever duration, total symptom duration, and timing of outpatient antibiotic exposure were inconsistently documented in retrospective records and excluded from analysis
Page_References: Table 1 (p.3); Table 2 (p.3-4); Table 3 (p.4); Table 4 (p.4); Figure 1 (p.5)

Title: Predicting VRE Infection After Liver Transplantation With a Time-Updated Colonization Score
Funder_Names: Sao Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP); Fundacao de Apoio a Universidade de Sao Paulo (FUSP)
Population_Description: Single-center retrospective cohort of all adult patients who underwent liver transplantation (LT) between January 2010 and December 2022, followed from 90 days before to 180 days after LT.
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: Fine-Gray model hazard ratios ranked post-transplant VRE colonization as the strongest predictor (HR 7.59), followed by intraoperative bleeding (HR 4.06), early re-transplantation (HR 3.85), pre-transplant VRE colonization (HR 3.20), renal replacement therapy/dialysis (HR 2.01), and ICU length of stay (HR 1.01-1.02/day).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Pooled Fine-Gray competing-risks regression (landmarking approach; AUC-ROC 75.67%-81.67% on test set across landmarks) vs. random forest for competing risks (randomForestSRC, logrankCR splitting rule, node-depth none/2/5/10; lower AUC-ROC than Fine-Gray at all landmarks, exact values in Table S4).
Best_Performing_Model: Pooled Fine-Gray competing-risks regression (landmarking model)
Accuracy_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
Sensitivity_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
Specificity_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
F1_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
AUROC_Population_Set: External (held-out) test set, landmark times 0-28 days post-transplant
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model was evaluated on a held-out test fold described by the authors as an external test set, but prospective validation across diverse LT populations is stated as still required.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center design with substantial class imbalance; decreased test-set sensitivity after threshold optimisation; need for prospective validation across diverse LT populations; restriction to first VRE episode only, limiting applicability to recurrent infection.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Reliance on the score to guide empiric therapy could increase broad-spectrum antibiotic use, with potential unintended consequences for antimicrobial resistance and microbiota disruption.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Decisions on empiric VRE-directed therapy should not rely solely on this score and must consider local epidemiology and burden of other MDROs.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the 'external test set' (a held-out fold from the same single-center cohort) should be treated as true external validation or as internal validation only; the numeric discrepancy between the abstract's most-common-infection figure (intra-abdominal, 58.4%) and the Results text (surgical site infection, 56.6%).
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: All adult patients who underwent liver transplantation from January 2010 through December 2022.
Exclusion_Criteria: Absence of VRE surveillance cultures; age under 18 years; death within 48 hours post-transplant.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Dataset_Size: 1348 LT patients screened; 139 excluded; 1209 in final cohort
Missing_Data_Method: Single missing covariate (antibiotic prophylaxis for SBP, 5 patients) resolved via manual chart review and coded as negative.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-center study at a tertiary academic hospital in Sao Paulo, Brazil (~120 LTs/year); no multi-region or multi-country representation.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Surveillance cultures (chromogenic VRE-selective agar) and clinical/blood cultures for infection sites (e.g., blood cultures for bloodstream infection).
Primary_AMR_Outcome: VRE (vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus) infection after liver transplantation
Pathogens: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp.: Enterococcus faecium, Enterococcus faecalis, other Enterococcus species
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin; teicoplanin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: VRE; Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: VRE infection defined as isolation of VRE (vancomycin resistance determined via CLSI MIC breakpoints) from a normally sterile body site with compatible clinical signs and symptoms.
AI_Purpose: Machine-learning (random forest) comparator benchmarked against a Fine-Gray survival-regression model to predict post-liver-transplant VRE infection risk and compare discrimination.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 model classes compared (Fine-Gray regression vs. random forest); random forest additionally tested at 4 node-depth settings
Feature_Engineering: Post-transplant VRE colonization modelled as a binary time-dependent covariate via a stacked landmarking approach (landmark times 0,7,14,21,28 days) rather than a fixed baseline covariate.
Feature_Selection_Method: Stepwise (forward and backward) variable selection guided by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)
Num_Features_Selected: 11 covariates in the final pooled model
Hyperparameter_Method: Manual exploration of random-forest node-depth parameter (none, 2, 5, 10)
Other_Metrics: Youden's index and maximum F1 score used for threshold selection; cumulative incidence function (CIF) reported for baseline risk.
Baseline_Method: Random forest for competing risks (randomForestSRC, logrankCR splitting rule) as machine-learning comparator
Baseline_Performance: Yielded lower AUC-ROC values than the Fine-Gray model across all landmarks (exact values in Table S4)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation (training on four folds, validating on the fifth)
Train_Test_Split: Data partitioned into 6 non-overlapping folds; 5 folds used for training/cross-validation, 1 fold held out as test set (~83%/17%)
External_Validation_Description: One of six non-overlapping folds (stratified by outcome) held out as the authors' 'external test set' for final evaluation; this is a held-out fold from the same single-center cohort, not an independent external cohort.
Overfitting_Method: BIC-penalised stepwise feature selection to reduce overfitting risk; 5-fold cross-validation with a held-out test fold
Clinical_Insights: Autoimmune and viral hepatitis emerged as unexpected protective factors for VRE infection, likely reflecting confounding by underlying cirrhosis aetiology and MELD score rather than a causal biological effect.
Generalisability_Details: The drop in sensitivity observed in the test set suggests a trade-off in generalisability, potentially due to threshold optimisation based on internal validation.
Maturity_Evidence: Model evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation plus a held-out fold the authors call an external test set; prospective validation across diverse LT populations is stated as not yet done.
Integration_Point: Proposed point-of-care use to guide empirical anti-VRE therapy decisions at post-transplant landmark timepoints (days 0,7,14,21,28)
Future_Directions: This methodological approach (competing-risks landmarking with time-dependent colonization) has potential clinical applicability and can be replicated for other multidrug-resistant organisms.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (clinical, microbiological, laboratory, healthcare utilisation, sociodemographic, temporal)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Hazard-ratio magnitude from the pooled Fine-Gray competing-risks regression (stepwise BIC-selected covariates)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Autoimmune and viral hepatitis were unexpected protective factors for VRE infection; the Charlson Comorbidity Index was also an unexpected protective factor, attributed to a competing-risk effect (death before infection).
Limitation_Categories: Single-center design; class imbalance; reduced test-set sensitivity after threshold optimisation; pending prospective/external validation; restriction to first VRE episode only.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Only one variable (antibiotic prophylaxis for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) had missing data, in 5 of 1209 patients, resolved via manual chart review.
Reporting_Clarity: Minor inconsistencies: duplicated phrase 'due to due to' in the Data Availability Statement; the abstract's most-common-infection-type figure (intra-abdominal, 58.4%) does not match the Results text figure (surgical site infection, 56.6%).
