Title: Interpretable large language models for early prediction of antimicrobial multidrug resistance
Funder_Names: Spanish federal grants TED2021-130347B-I00, PID2019-105032GB-I00, PID2019-107768RA-I00, PID2022-136887NB-I00, PID2023-149457OB-I00 (funded by AEI/10.13039/501,100,011,033); Autonomous Community of Madrid (Madrid ELLIS Unit)
Population_Description: Dataset of EHRs of ICU patients at the University Hospital of Fuenlabrada (UHF), Madrid, Spain; 3,502 unique patients, ICU admissions from January 2004 to February 2020.
Top_Predictive_Features: Per SHAP analysis: Blocks-LLM prioritizes procedural/therapeutic variables (number of catheters, antibiotic exposure — AMG, ATF, ATI — and, at longer horizons, mechanical ventilation duration); InstructTime-LLM prioritizes microbiological variables (prior cultures positive for Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus). Importance method: SHAP (mean |SHAP value| over top 20 features, averaged across 3 test-set repetitions).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Baselines: LSTM, GRU, Transformer, Mamba, GCNN. Proposed LLM-based: Blocks-LLM, InstructTime-LLM, LLMFew-GPT2, LLMFew-OPT, LLMFew-Neo (10 models total x 3 temporal windows x 3 repetitions = 90 configurations). All evaluated on ROC-AUC, sensitivity, specificity and F1 (see Table 7): best overall figure InstructTime-LLM T=7 ROC-AUC 0.792+/-0.009; best baseline GRU T=7 ROC-AUC 0.738+/-0.008.
Best_Performing_Model: InstructTime-LLM (7-day prediction window) — paper states it 'achieved the highest ROC-AUC across all settings'
Sensitivity_Population_Set: InstructTime-LLM, 7-day prediction window, held-out test set (mean ± SD over 3 repetitions)
Specificity_Population_Set: InstructTime-LLM, 7-day prediction window, held-out test set (mean ± SD over 3 repetitions)
F1_Population_Set: InstructTime-LLM, 7-day prediction window, held-out test set (mean ± SD over 3 repetitions)
AUROC_Population_Set: InstructTime-LLM, 7-day prediction window, held-out test set (mean ± SD over 3 repetitions)

Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)

Maturity_Evidence: External validation on an independent cohort from a second hospital (n=819) achieved AUC=0.816; no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment beyond a research web calculator was reported.

Future_Directions: Explore alternative feature-selection algorithms (e.g., Boruta); pursue prospective, multicenter studies incorporating dynamic trajectory analysis and genomic (genotypic resistance) data to evaluate real-world clinical utility.

Other_Metrics: PRAUC (AUPR): training 0.597 (0.522-0.669), test 0.522 (0.376-0.701), temporal validation 0.240 (0.153-0.373); Brier score: training 0.093 (0.082-0.105), test 0.096 (0.073-0.123), temporal validation 0.083 (0.065-0.102)

Internal_Validation: Derivation cohort randomly split into training (n=1117) and test (n=280) sets at 8:2 ratio by stratified sampling
Train_Test_Split: 8:2 ratio (training n=1117, test n=280), stratified sampling

External_Validation_Description: Independent temporal validation cohort of 431 children (Jan 2025-Mar 2026), consecutively including all children meeting identical criteria as the derivation cohort

End_User_Described: Clinicians (empiric antibiotic selection) and antimicrobial stewardship teams
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Patient sample collection and data input -> system preprocesses data -> trained models generate susceptibility predictions -> predictions guide empiric antibiotic selection and stewardship interventions.
Barriers_List: Class imbalance; model calibration drift over time; dependence on data quality; need for prospective validation; periodic model updating; integration/linkage with laboratory information systems.
Future_Directions: Prospective validation, periodic model updating, and seamless linkage with laboratory information systems to support real-world, resource-limited clinical implementation.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design / causal inference; single-institution & geographic generalizability; selection bias from colonization isolates; absence of clinical outcome data (mortality, treatment response, length of stay).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data required exclusion of antibiotics with >80% missingness; reliance on phenotypic susceptibility data; inclusion of colonization isolates (e.g. nasal swabs) whose resistance profiles may differ from invasive-disease isolates.
Reporting_Clarity: Methods section contains several apparent transcription/typographical errors in the reported hyperparameter search grids (e.g. malformed values), otherwise the paper follows a clear TRIPOD-informed IMRAD structure.
Page_References: Table 1 (per-antibiotic model performance) and Table 2 (prediction comparison) are the key data tables.

Title: Machine learning-based analysis of drug resistance mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Population_Description: 3,065 drug-resistant TB patient details, including WGS analysis results and drug-resistant mutations associated with 21 drugs in the first- and second-line categories, used to create the model.
Data_Source_Other: NIAID-NIH TB Portal - globally accessible multi-country TB data repository (clinical, laboratory, genomic, radiological data)
Top_Predictive_Features: For RR-TB, top SHAP-ranked features: duplication at position 1299 (sequence TTC) and missense mutations D435A, N437S, Q432L, each with SHAP value 0.16 (importance method: SHAP feature attribution).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: 8 supervised ML algorithms compared (all trained on the binary mutation-presence feature matrix): Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, SVM, KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes; only Random Forest's aggregate metric is given individually - 99% accuracy on both training and test sets (chosen as the best-performing/base classifier).
Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest (decided on accuracy: 99% on training and test sets)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Training and test sets (80/20 split), Random Forest classifier
Sensitivity_Value: Recall (reported per class, Random Forest): HR-TB 0.99; MDR-TB 1.00; Pre-XDR-TB 1.00; RR-TB 0.96; XDR-TB 0.89; Others 0.98
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Per drug-resistance-type class (multi-class), test set, Random Forest classifier (Table 1)
Precision_PPV_Value: Precision (reported per class, Random Forest): HR-TB 1.00; MDR-TB 1.00; Pre-XDR-TB 0.99; RR-TB 0.93; XDR-TB 0.87; Others 1.00
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Per drug-resistance-type class (multi-class), test set, Random Forest classifier (Table 1)
F1_Value: F1-score (reported per class, Random Forest): HR-TB 0.99; MDR-TB 1.00; Pre-XDR-TB 1.00; RR-TB 0.95; XDR-TB 0.89; Others 0.98
F1_Population_Set: Per drug-resistance-type class (multi-class), test set, Random Forest classifier (Table 1)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal train/test evaluation only (80/20 split, stratified 10-fold cross-validation for tuning); external validation explicitly not performed due to lack of independent comparable datasets.
Reported_Limitations: Missing data for several drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, para-aminosalicylic acid, clofazimine); insufficient XDR-TB cases (excluded as a classifier class, Pre-XDR-TB used instead); no external validation performed due to lack of comparable independent datasets.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
Inclusion_Criteria: Drug-resistant TB cases (RR-DR, Hr-DR, poly-DR, pre-XDR, MDR, non-XDR, and others) from the NIAID-NIH TB portal.
Exclusion_Criteria: 1,373 drug-sensitive mutations were excluded because the primary objective was multi-class classification among drug-resistant types rather than binary resistant-vs-sensitive classification.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: NIAID-NIH TB Portal
Dataset_Size: 4,438 entries total (1,373 drug-sensitive; 3,065 drug-resistant); 3,065 drug-resistant cases used
Missing_Data_Method: Removed 'NULL' and '–' markers from the data to ensure consistency
Geographic_Representativeness: Multi-country dataset spanning 12 countries (not individually named); no country-level breakdown of results reported.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multi-class prediction of TB drug-resistance category (target variable: RR-TB, HR-TB, MDR-TB, Pre-XDR-TB) from a binary mutation-presence feature matrix.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First- and second-line anti-TB drugs: rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, streptomycin, amikacin, capreomycin, cycloserine, fluoroquinolones, kanamycin, bedaquiline, clofazimine, delamanid, ethionamide, levofloxacin, linezolid, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin, para-aminosalicylic acid, and aminoglycosides.
Specific_Antibiotics: rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, streptomycin, amikacin, capreomycin, cycloserine, fluoroquinolones, kanamycin, bedaquiline, clofazimine, delamanid, ethionamide, levofloxacin, linezolid, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin, para-aminosalicylic acid, and aminoglycosides.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; XDR; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance category label = drug-resistance classification assigned in the TB portal dataset (RR-TB, HR-TB, MDR-TB, Pre-XDR-TB), predicted as a multi-class target from a binary mutation-presence feature matrix.
AI_Purpose: To identify and evaluate genomic variants associated with drug-resistant TB by analysing mutation profiles across 3,065 isolates using machine learning.
Feature_Engineering: Mutations extracted from comma-separated strings and each mutation encoded as a separate binary feature (presence=1/absence=0) after removing NULL/missing markers.
Feature_Selection_Method: Post-hoc filtering of features with non-zero SHAP values (SHAP-based feature relevance filtering)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Restructured target classes in response to imbalance: excluded XDR-TB as a separate classifier class (insufficient samples) and used Pre-XDR-TB instead.
Hyperparameter_Method: GridSearchCV with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; Random Forest hyperparameters optimised over n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_split, and max_features.
Hardware_Details: Windows 11 system with 16 GB RAM
Internal_Validation: 80/20 train-test split with stratified 10-fold cross-validation (GridSearchCV) for hyperparameter tuning
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test
Overfitting_Method: Independent held-out test set never used during training or hyperparameter optimisation; stratified 10-fold cross-validation during tuning.
Clinical_Insights: Improved interpretability of ML algorithms may support more informed clinical decision-making (aspirational, not demonstrated prospectively).
Data_Repository: Supporting Information files (within manuscript); source dataset from NIAID-NIH TB Portal (tbportals.niaid.nih.gov)
Maturity_Evidence: Internal train/test evaluation (80/20 split, 10-fold CV) with strong held-out performance; no external or prospective evaluation performed.
Future_Directions: Furthermore, an improved ML framework, supported by experimental validation, can advance the understanding of drug resistance patterns and inform future clinical decision-making.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature importance
Novel_Predictors_Details: rpoB-I480T, rpoC-G332R, L527V, gyrA-D94V, KatG-G99E, A106V, W191R, W328C, T380I, and M420T — mutations not reported in the WHO catalogues, identified via post-prediction comparative analysis.
Limitation_Categories: Data completeness (missing data for several drugs); sample-size limitation (insufficient XDR-TB cases, necessitating exclusion of the XDR-TB class); lack of external validation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Dataset lacked information on certain drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, para-aminosalicylic acid, clofazimine) and had insufficient XDR-TB case numbers.

Title: Predicting macrolide resistance in pediatric Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia: A machine learning modeling study
Journal_Source: European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: National Natural Science Foundation of China (82575140)
Population_Description: 968 pediatric patients with MPP, including 664 with MRMPP and 304 with MSMPP
Top_Predictive_Features: Overall, IL-17A, IFN-gamma, CRP, A/G Ratio, pre-hospital medication, and Pre-hospital Course were identified as significant predictors, ranked via SHAP values computed for the XGBoost and RF models.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Table 1 gives, for each of the nine models, AUC/Cutoff/Accuracy/Sensitivity/Specificity/PPV/NPV/F1-Score/Kappa: XGBoost AUC 0.779; LR AUC 0.669; LightGBM AUC 0.619; RF AUC 0.805; AdaBoost AUC 0.764; DT AUC 0.612; GBDT AUC 0.724; KNN AUC 0.654; SVM AUC 0.597.
Best_Performing_Model: Stacking ensemble model (second-layer Logistic Regression meta-learner over XGBoost, AdaBoost, and Random Forest) - AUC 0.857
Accuracy_Population_Set: Internal validation set
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Internal validation
Specificity_Population_Set: Internal validation
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Internal validation set
F1_Population_Set: Internal validation set
AUROC_Population_Set: Internal validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model underwent external validation on an independent, retrospective temporal cohort from a second site (AUC 0.812); no prospective evaluation or clinical workflow/CDS integration was reported, so the highest supported level is external validation.
Reported_Limitations: The lack of sample representativeness, combined with a single-center design, may introduce selection bias.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: A co-infection could elevate non-specific inflammatory markers independent of true resistance status, potentially misclassifying a co-infected, macrolide-sensitive case as high-risk MRMP.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: A key limitation pertains to the model's clinical applicability despite robust statistical performance, since it relies on multiple non-routine, costly laboratory markers (a full cytokine panel) often unavailable in primary care settings, raising concerns about premature/inequitable real-world deployment.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients must meet the diagnostic criteria for MPP; conducted resistance gene locus testing; duration of illness not exceeding 14 days; aged 14 years or younger.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with a confirmed bacterial or viral infection, a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, chronic pulmonary diseases, airway mucus clearance disorders, immunodeficiency disorders, or connective tissue diseases were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Mendeley Data (dataset rg64vk8tsz)
Dataset_Size: 968 pediatric patients (664 MRMPP, 304 MSMPP)
Missing_Data_Method: Random forest-based imputation model (multiple imputation), variables with >30% missingness excluded
Specimen_Type_Detail: Serum (MP antibody titer); MP-DNA/MP-RNA testing (specimen type for PCR not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Macrolide-resistant vs macrolide-sensitive Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MRMPP vs MSMPP), defined genotypically by 23S rRNA domain V mutations (2063 A:G, 2064 A:G) detected by PCR.
Pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Macrolides
Specific_Antibiotics: Azithromycin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Genotypic definition: mutations at the 2063 (A:G) and 2064 (A:G) sites of the 23S rRNA gene, detected by PCR
AI_Purpose: To develop a machine learning-based clinical prediction model for macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MRMPP) in children, facilitating early identification of resistant cases and guiding targeted therapeutic interventions.
Feature_Engineering: Composite indicators constructed: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII = platelet count x neutrophil count/lymphocyte count).
Feature_Selection_Method: Two-step selection: univariate significance test followed by LASSO regression, with stability selection requiring a non-zero coefficient across all 5 CV folds
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search
Other_Metrics: Kappa (concordance), Brier score / calibration error, DeLong test p-values for AUC comparisons
Baseline_Method: Best individual (single) model, Random Forest (RF)
Baseline_Performance: RF (best individual base model): AUC 0.805 (95%CI 0.719-0.891), Accuracy 0.71, Sensitivity 0.662, Specificity 0.79, PPV 0.848, NPV 0.591, F1 0.737
Internal_Validation: Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test per CV fold
External_Validation_Description: 98 children diagnosed with MPP, hospitalized between March 1, 2025 and May 31, 2025, used as a temporal external validation cohort.
Clinical_Insights: IL-17A is associated with Th17 cell-mediated inflammatory responses, with elevated levels indicating immune hyperactivation; LDH, CRP, D-dimer, and SII may serve as indicators of more severe conditions.
Generalisability_Details: Future prospective, multicentre validation across healthcare institutions from diverse regions is anticipated to evaluate generalizability in areas with varying resistance rates.
Maturity_Evidence: External (temporal, retrospective, second-site) validation achieved AUC 0.812, described as reasonable generalization to real-world data; no prospective evaluation or clinical workflow integration was reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians in medical facilities unable to diagnose drug resistance
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Envisioned future integration: embedding predictive results into electronic medical records to trigger automated alerts as part of clinical pathways.
Stewardship_Details: Early identification of high-risk patients for resistance allows for targeted and restricted empirical use of alternative antibiotics, establishing a data-driven paradigm for antimicrobial stewardship.
Barriers_List: Reliance on multiple non-routine, costly laboratory markers (a full cytokine panel) that are often not immediately available, particularly in primary care settings.
Facilitators_List: Web-based tool requiring no genetic sequencing or susceptibility testing, easing use in resource-limited settings.
Future_Directions: Multidisciplinary collaboration is anticipated to validate and adapt this host-response-based framework to other domains of resistant infections.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)
Limitation_Categories: Insufficient dynamic monitoring: the model relies on static data collected at admission and fails to capture the dynamic evolution of resistance phenotypes throughout treatment.
Data_Quality_Concerns: The study did not systematically use multiplex molecular assays to screen for other common respiratory pathogens (e.g., influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2 variants), so undetected co-infections could confound the non-specific inflammatory-marker predictors.

Title: Predicting probability of perirectal colonization with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) and other carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs) at hospital unit admission
Funder_Names: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Epicenters Program; CDC MIND-Healthcare Program; Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ); The Sherrilyn and Ken Fisher Center for Environmental Infectious Diseases
Population_Description: Patients aged >=16 years admitted to the Johns Hopkins Hospital (JHH) medical intensive care unit (MICU) or solid organ transplant (SOT) unit between July 1, 2016 and July 1, 2017.
Top_Predictive_Features: CRO decision-tree root node (most discriminatory variable, chosen via Gini-impurity splitting): recent CRO-positive culture in the previous 6 months; second split: >=26 days of PPI use in the prior 3 months; third split: >=51 days of hospitalization in the prior 6 months.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Infection prevention and control team
All_Models_Evaluated: CRO decision tree (CART): C statistic 0.57 (unchanged after cross-validation), sensitivity 9.8%, specificity 99.9%, PPV 87.5%, NPV 93.1%. CPO decision tree (CART): C statistic 0.58 (unchanged after cross-validation), sensitivity 16.7%, specificity 99.8%, PPV 54.5%, NPV 99.0%. CRE decision tree (CART) reported only in Supplemental Material (not detailed in main text). Sensitivity analyses (not separately quantified in main text): random forests and cost-weighted CART improved performance by ~15%-20%; CART restricted to first unique patient encounters (n=2,165) and CART/random forests restricted to molecularly-confirmed CPO outcome performed similarly to the primary analyses.
Best_Performing_Model: CRO decision tree (CART) -- the paper's primary/final decision tree, built for the review's primary outcome (CRO colonization); discrimination reported as C statistic (AUROC-equivalent) = 0.57.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Full swabbed cohort -- 2,878 admission swabs from 2,165 patients
Specificity_Population_Set: Full swabbed cohort -- 2,878 admission swabs from 2,165 patients
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Full swabbed cohort -- 2,878 admission swabs from 2,165 patients
AUROC_Population_Set: Full dataset (n=2,878 swabs), internally validated via leave-one-out cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and evaluated only via internal leave-one-out cross-validation on a single-center retrospective cohort; no external or prospective validation performed.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center study (results may not generalize to other, lower-risk populations or higher-endemicity areas); phenotypic-molecular carbapenemase concordance lower than expected (particularly for E. cloacae); likely missing exposure data (e.g., outpatient antibiotic use not captured across hospitals).
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr Milstone reports personal fees from Becton Dickinson Diagnostics. Dr Rock and Dr Maragakis report grant support from the Clorox Company. Dr Cosgrove reports personal fees from Novartis and Theravance. Dr Tamma reports grants from Merck (all outside scope of submitted work). Dr Simner reports grants/personal fees from multiple diagnostics companies, also outside scope. All other authors report no potential conflicts of interest.
Sex_Distribution: 46% female (1,325/2,878) in total swabbed cohort; 46% (99/217) among CRO-colonized; 44% (14/36) among CPO-colonized
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients aged >=16 years admitted to the JHH MICU or SOT unit, July 1, 2016 - July 1, 2017, with a stored admission perirectal screening swab.
Exclusion_Criteria: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia isolates excluded due to intrinsic carbapenem resistance (no explicit patient-level exclusion criteria stated).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 2,878 admission swabbed encounters from 2,165 unique patients; 134 collected variables used in prediction modeling
Missing_Data_Method: No formal imputation described; authors note likely missing exposure data (e.g., outpatient antibiotic use not captured across hospitals) as a limitation.
Ethnicity_Details: Race (not Hispanic/Latino ethnicity) reported for total swabbed cohort (n=2,878): White 1,317 (46%); Black 1,272 (44%); Asian 61 (2%); American Indian/Alaska Native/Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 13 (0.5%); Other 215 (8%).
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-center (Johns Hopkins Hospital, Baltimore, Maryland) MICU/SOT population; authors note results may not generalize to lower-risk hospitals or higher-endemicity areas such as New York City.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Perirectal Eswabs (COPAN Diagnostics)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Prevalence of, and probability of, perirectal colonization with carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs; including CRE) and carbapenemase-producing organisms (CPOs) at hospital unit admission, predicted via machine-learning decision trees.
Pathogens: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE, e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae); glucose non-fermenting gram-negative organisms including Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Aeromonas categorized with non-fermenters); Stenotrophomonas maltophilia excluded due to intrinsic carbapenem resistance.
Num_Pathogens: 7 (bacterial species in which carbapenemases were molecularly identified)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem, imipenem) -- colonization/resistance outcome; antibiotic-exposure predictor classes: extended-spectrum penicillins, third/fourth-generation cephalosporins, aztreonam, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides.
Specific_Antibiotics: Ertapenem, meropenem, imipenem (carbapenem susceptibility testing); extended-spectrum penicillins; third/fourth-generation cephalosporins; aztreonam; fluoroquinolones; aminoglycosides; proton-pump inhibitors / H2-blockers (risk-factor exposures, not antimicrobials).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MDR; ESBL; MRSA; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Enterobacteriaceae resistant to ertapenem, meropenem, or imipenem categorized as CRE; glucose non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli resistant to meropenem and/or imipenem categorized as NFCROs; carbapenemase production confirmed by modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) defines CP-CRE/CP-NFCRO (collectively CPOs).
AI_Purpose: To predict individual patients' probability of CRO/CPO perirectal colonization at hospital unit admission, to inform targeted infection-control screening.
Feature_Engineering: Variable permutations tested, including varied retrospective look-back periods and composite vs. individual variable-category coding.
Feature_Selection_Method: Implicit selection via CART recursive-partitioning / Gini-impurity splitting (rpart package) -- only variables entering a tree split are retained.
Num_Features_Selected: 3 (CRO decision tree, the review's primary/best-performing model)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Cost-sensitive CART refitting -- imposing a greater misclassification cost for false negatives (colonized patients classified as negative), as a sensitivity analysis.
Software_Libraries: rpart (recursive partitioning and regression trees) package, version 4.1-13
Baseline_Method: Current CDC-recommended targeted screening criteria (e.g., recent foreign hospitalization)
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: In-sample (original) vs. out-of-sample (leave-one-out cross-validated) discrimination compared; found unchanged, indicating no substantial overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: Recent CRO-positive culture combined with >=26 days of PPI use (93% probability) or >=51 days of hospitalization (80% probability) identifies patients at high risk of CRO colonization.
Generalisability_Details: Results may not generalize to lower-risk hospitalized populations or higher-endemicity areas (e.g., New York City); single-center study; authors state results should be validated in other cohorts.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal leave-one-out cross-validation only (no external or prospective validation performed).
Integration_Point: Manual bedside application by clinical / infection-control staff (branching-logic decision tree, not software-integrated).
End_User_Described: Infection control programs / bedside clinical staff
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Targeted surveillance using recent CRO-positive culture plus PPI use (>=26 days) or prior hospitalization (>=51 days) as triggers would capture 21 of 217 colonized patients while producing only 3 false-positive screening referrals.
Stewardship_Details: Screening intended to enable individualized/targeted empiric antibiotic therapy for colonized patients; actual stewardship impact not measured.
Barriers_List: Risk factors reflect relative, not absolute, risk and are poor predictors when the affected group is small; high bacterial/genomic diversity increases outcome heterogeneity; EMR data may be incomplete (e.g., colonization predating retrospective look-back windows); non-traditional community exposures (e.g., farms, retail seafood) are not systematically captured in the EMR.
Facilitators_List: Recent CRO/CRE-positive culture is consistently the strongest predictor and is already captured/flagged by many infection control programs; VRE co-colonization (24%/33% of CRO/CPO cases) already triggers contact precautions independent of dedicated CRO surveillance.
Future_Directions: Further whole genome sequencing is planned to clarify the phenotypic-molecular carbapenemase concordance discrepancy.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 5 (demographic; pre-existing medical condition; procedure; medication; other clinical data)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: CART decision-tree root-node selection via Gini-impurity splitting criterion
Feature_Interactions_Method: Decision-tree (CART) splitting inherently accommodates variable collinearities and interaction effects by default.
Limitation_Categories: Single-center / generalizability; phenotypic-molecular diagnostic concordance discrepancy; missing / incomplete EMR exposure data; host and organism heterogeneity.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Likely missing exposure data (e.g., outpatient antibiotic use, data that does not interface across hospitals); lower-than-expected concordance between phenotypic and molecular carbapenemase assays, particularly for E. cloacae.
Reporting_Clarity: Well-structured: structured abstract (Background/Objective/Methods/Results/Conclusions) and stepwise decision-tree presentation.

Title: proteomics-based plasma biomarkers for predicting CRKP infection in ICU sepsis patients
Funder_Names: Self-funded (no named external funder)
Population_Description: ICU sepsis patients (aged over 18) caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, classified as CRKP-infected or CSKP-infected (control), at two tertiary hospitals in China
Age_Range: >18 years (inclusion threshold; no cohort age range reported)
Data_Source_Other: Plasma proteomic (mass spectrometry) data generated for this study (not an existing named data source)
Top_Predictive_Features: XGBoost feature-importance ranking of 28 DEPs (11 retained) followed by LASSO regression (5-fold CV) selecting 10 key proteins: CFHR4, PLXNB1, MINPP1, S100A1, SEZ6L2, IGHV3-30, PCK2, SEPTIN14, CRHBP, RAC2
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Multiple logistic regression models built from combinations of the 10 LASSO-selected proteins; optimal model chosen by highest AUC (discrimination) and lowest Brier score (calibration) via three-fold cross-validation; final model = PLXNB1+S100A1 (AUC 0.918 training / 0.917 testing).
Best_Performing_Model: PLXNB1 and S100A1 (two-protein diagnostic model), selected via XGBoost and LASSO from 10 candidate protein biomarkers
Accuracy_Population_Set: Training and testing sets
AUROC_Population_Set: Training and testing sets
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only an internal stratified train/test split (75/25%) and cross-validation were used; no external cohort or prospective evaluation was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Small sample size limited to ICU sepsis patients (restricting generalizability); candidates not validated by orthogonal methods (e.g., ELISA); absence of comparison cohorts with other multidrug-resistant organisms (e.g., A. baumannii).
Sample_Size: 28 patients (14 CRKP vs. 14 CSKP matched pairs)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared this work was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Aged over 18 years; sepsis caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolation of more than one pathogen during the ICU stay; pregnancy or lactation
Data_Types_Used: Other
Dataset_Size: 1,432 proteins and 13,482 peptides quantified across 28 plasma samples (n=28 participants)
Missing_Data_Method: Left-censored imputation simulating a normal distribution near the MS detection limit (downshift 1.8 SD, width 0.25 SD); proteins with >50% missing values in both groups excluded before imputation.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Plasma
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Early differentiation of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) infection from carbapenem-sensitive K. pneumoniae (CSKP) infection using plasma protein biomarkers
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP and CSKP strains)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem, imipenem)
Specific_Antibiotics: Ertapenem, meropenem, imipenem
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary phenotypic classification: CRKP = K. pneumoniae resistant to at least one carbapenem (ertapenem, meropenem, or imipenem); CSKP = carbapenem-susceptible control
AI_Purpose: To identify plasma protein biomarkers via ML-based feature selection (XGBoost, LASSO) and construct a logistic-regression diagnostic model differentiating CRKP from CSKP infection in ICU sepsis patients
Feature_Engineering: Contaminant protein removal; log-transformation of the protein intensity matrix; MaxLFQ normalization for label-free quantification
Feature_Selection_Method: Differential expression (fold change, two-sided P<0.05), then XGBoost refinement, then LASSO regression with cross-validation
Num_Features_Total: 28 (differentially expressed proteins)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Propensity score matching (age, gender; caliper 0.2) to obtain 1:1 matched pairs from an initially unbalanced 18 vs 14 group split
Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold cross-validation for LASSO regularisation parameter selection
Other_Metrics: Brier score (calibration): 0.082 training, 0.085 testing; Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test: p=0.825 training, p=0.295 testing
Internal_Validation: Stratified train/test split; model selection via AUC (discrimination) and Brier score (calibration) using three-fold cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% testing (stratified by group)
Clinical_Insights: DEPs were linked to neural/cardiovascular pathways consistent with known sepsis complications (neurological dysfunction, septic cardiomyopathy); PLXNB1 and S100A1 proposed as mechanistically plausible biomarkers of CRKP-associated systemic inflammatory injury
Generalisability_Details: Small sample size and restriction to ICU sepsis patients across two centres may limit generalisability; absence of cohorts with other MDR organisms limits determining whether the signature is CRKP-specific
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supports only internal validation: a stratified random 75/25 train/test split of the pooled retrospective cohort with cross-validated model selection; no external cohort or prospective test was performed
Integration_Point: Proposed point-of-care / ICU diagnostic workflow for early non-culture-based differentiation of CRKP vs CSKP to guide targeted antimicrobial therapy (not yet implemented)
End_User_Described: Implied clinical workflow use for diagnosis/therapy guidance (specific end-user role, e.g. clinician, not explicitly named)
Future_Directions: Future studies involving diverse pathogen cohorts and targeted immunoassay validation are warranted to fully delineate the diagnostic specificity and clinical utility of PLXNB1 and S100A1

Title: Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Hotspots in Oliver Reginald Tambo District Municipality, Eastern Cape, South Africa

Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
All_Models_Evaluated: Linear Regression: R2=0.865, MSE=507.175, MAE=18.65; Random Forest: R2=0.882, MSE=443.226, MAE=19.03 (both forecasting future annual DR-TB case counts from 2018-2021 historical data).
Best_Performing_Model: Random Forest
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were fit to historical DR-TB case-count data (2018-2021) and assessed with in-sample R2/MSE/MAE; no train/test split, cross-validation, external dataset, or prospective evaluation is described, so forecasts for 2022-2026 are unvalidated projections.
Reported_Limitations: The Linear Regression model assumed a linear trend and may have overestimated progress (projecting elimination/negative case counts); the Random Forest model's stabilization forecast is more conservative; COVID-19-related healthcare disruption may have caused underreporting in later years.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Poverty, lack of education and low income are linked to higher DR-TB burden relative to the general population, and females are underrepresented among DR-TB patients relative to their share of the general population; the paper calls for gender-sensitive and education-focused interventions.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients with DR-TB between 2018 and 2020 treated at five decentralized DR-TB facilities in the O.R. Tambo District Municipality.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Dataset_Size: Annual DR-TB case counts 2018-2021 (186 cases in 2018 down to 15 in 2021) used for model training/forecasting; overall cohort n=456 patients.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) type classification (RR-TB, MDR-TB, Pre-XDR-TB, XDR-TB, INHR-TB) and predicted future annual DR-TB case counts.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Rifampicin, isoniazid (first-line); fluoroquinolones, second-line injectables, bedaquiline, linezolid (second-line)
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin, isoniazid, fluoroquinolone, second-line injectable, bedaquiline, linezolid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: DR-TB subtypes defined by drug-resistance profile: RR-TB (rifampicin-resistant, isoniazid-susceptible), INH-R TB (isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible), MDR-TB (resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin), Pre-XDR-TB (MDR plus resistance to a fluoroquinolone or a second-line injectable), XDR-TB (MDR plus fluoroquinolone and second-line injectable or additional drugs).
AI_Purpose: To identify geographic clusters/hotspots of DR-TB transmission (DBSCAN clustering and Getis-Ord Gi hotspot analysis of patient GPS coordinates) and to forecast future annual DR-TB case counts (Linear Regression and Random Forest) to inform public health strategy.
Other_Metrics: R² (coefficient of determination): Linear Regression 0.865, Random Forest 0.882; MSE: Linear Regression 507.175, Random Forest 443.226.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supports only proof-of-concept: models were fit to and evaluated on the same 2018-2021 historical series (in-sample R2/MSE/MAE) with no held-out split, external dataset, or prospective test of the 2022-2026 forecasts.
Future_Directions: Focused interventions (improved healthcare access, educational campaigns, nutritional support) and strategies to improve treatment adherence and address gender-specific risks, plus continued monitoring/adaptive public health strategies to sustain DR-TB reduction progress and avoid plateauing.

Title: Convolutional neural networks quantify antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis with diagnostic grade accuracy and predict treatment response
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: National Institutes of Health (NIH); National Science Foundation (NSF)
Population_Description: 14,834 MTBC isolates with measured MICs, obtained from CRyPTIC, NCBI, PATRIC, Harvard TB CETR, the WHO Resistance Mutation Catalog, and unpublished MIC-ML consortium sources.
Data_Source_Other: CRyPTIC data compendium, NCBI database, PATRIC, Harvard TB CETR, WHO Resistance Mutation Catalog, unpublished MIC-ML consortium data
Top_Predictive_Features: Saliency (DeepLIFT) analysis concentrates elevated-MIC associations in ethR and katG (74% of 247 novel salient nucleotides), with additional sites in mmpL5 and Rv0678.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: CNN vs. linear (Ridge) regression: CNNs achieve significantly lower MAE than regression across all 8 drugs (MAE range 0.18-0.67 log2-MIC on hold-out test sets, p<2x10-4).
Best_Performing_Model: CNN (multimodal nucleotide + amino-acid + lineage convolutional neural network) -- outperforms linear regression on mean absolute error (MAE) across all 8 drugs.
Sensitivity_Value: +2.2 percentage points higher sensitivity than the WHO catalog classification method on average across the 8 drugs (CNN, dichotomized MIC predictions)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Hold-out test sets, binary resistance classification (MIC dichotomized at critical concentration) across 8 anti-TB drugs, vs. WHO catalog
Specificity_Value: +1.6 percentage points higher specificity than the WHO catalog classification method on average across the 8 drugs (CNN, dichotomized MIC predictions)
Specificity_Population_Set: Hold-out test sets, binary resistance classification (MIC dichotomized at critical concentration) across 8 anti-TB drugs, vs. WHO catalog
AUROC_Value: AUC 2.5 percentage points higher than logistic regression (one-sided Welch's t-test p=2.4x10-4), for the binary pyrazinamide CNN
AUROC_Population_Set: Binary pyrazinamide resistance classification, 5-fold cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models trained/tested on consortium isolate data were subsequently applied, without retraining, to an independent South African patient cohort (TRUST) whose MIC distributions differ from the training data -- i.e. external validation, not prospective clinical deployment.
Reported_Limitations: The CNN models are not without limitations. The models are still limited by the adequacy of training data. For example, due to low rates of bedaquiline resistance, the CNN sensitivity for binary resistance prediction is still low.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: CNNs may assume mutations of different types occurring on the same codon have similar effects, potentially mispredicting resistance/susceptibility for co-located mutations.
Sample_Size: 14,834 isolates (primary genomic/MIC dataset; per-drug totals in Table 1)
Conflicts_of_Interest: All authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Participants had rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary TB diagnosed by GeneXpert-TB/RIF or -Ultra, treated with a 6-month RIPE regimen, followed for 12 months, with WGS of bacterial cultures performed within the first two weeks of enrollment.
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded: participants who changed treatment regimens due to developing rifampicin resistance or needing a liver-friendly regimen; participants without WGS within the first two weeks of enrollment; participants with incomplete data.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Imaging
Data_Source_Name: CRyPTIC; PATRIC; NCBI; WHO Resistance Mutation Catalog; MIC-ML Consortium; TRUST study
Dataset_Size: 14,834 MTBC isolates (per-drug n ranges 1,021-12,069; with augmentation 7,800-14,107)
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation (mice package, v3.16.0, R v4.4.2) across 30 imputed datasets, pooled using Rubin's rules
Specimen_Type_Detail: Sputum (culture) and bacterial WGS from cultured isolates
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for eight anti-tubercular drugs, predicted from MTBC genomic sequence, dichotomized at the drug critical concentration for binary resistance
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC)
Drug_Classes: Rifamycins, isoniazid/prodrugs, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, ethionamide/prothionamide, fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline (diarylquinoline)
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ethionamide, bedaquiline
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Drug resistance diagnosed as present/absent at an expert-determined drug critical concentration (CC); MIC is the underlying continuous/semi-continuous phenotype predicted by the CNN
AI_Purpose: To rapidly and accurately predict minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) directly from MTBC genomic sequence, enabling quantitative, interpretable resistance prediction and identification of clinically relevant sub-critical-concentration resistance.
Feature_Engineering: One-hot encoded nucleotide sequence (5 x L per locus); amino-acid biochemical properties (molecular weight, isoelectric point, Eisenberg hydrophobicity) as a 3 x K matrix; 62 Coll lineage-defining SNPs as a binary vector.
Feature_Selection_Method: Relevant core genes/loci selected per drug based on known or hypothesized resistance mechanisms (not data-driven selection)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Phenotypic augmentation with additional resistant isolates from the WHO mutation catalog (bedaquiline, pyrazinamide); stratification of train/validation/test splits by binary resistance phenotype
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over Ridge regularization strength (powers of 10 from 10^-5 to 10^5) minimizing validation loss (regression); early stopping (200-epoch patience on validation/test loss) for CNNs
Hardware_Details: Orchestra High Performance Compute Cluster, Harvard Medical School (NIH NCRR-funded); no specific CPU/GPU model given
Other_Metrics: Essential agreement (EA, proportion of predictions within 1 doubling dilution): 79-93% (avg 89%) across the 8 drugs
Baseline_Method: Linear (Ridge) regression on one-hot encoded sequence features
Baseline_Performance: Regression MAE significantly higher than CNN MAE across all 8 drugs (one-sided Welch's t-test p<2x10-4)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation on the training/validation data; final model then trained on the full dataset
Train_Test_Split: 80% training, 10% validation, 10% testing, stratified by binary resistance phenotype and primary lineage
External_Validation_Description: Independent TRUST cohort of 373 South African patients with rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary TB; pretrained CNNs applied without retraining; MIC distributions differ from the training data.
Overfitting_Method: Early stopping (patience of 200 epochs on validation/test loss plateau); L2-regularized Ridge regression for the baseline; reduced input loci to limit overfitting to hard-to-interpret variants
Clinical_Insights: Higher CNN-predicted rifampicin MIC below the critical concentration is associated with unfavorable TB treatment outcomes, supporting the clinical relevance of sub-critical-concentration resistance.
Data_Repository: SRA (sequencing data); GitHub (code, https://github.com/sanju99/MtbQuantCNN); Zenodo (code archive, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19269138)
Generalisability_Details: The rifampicin MIC range in the TRUST cohort was very narrow (0.03-0.07 ug/mL), so the estimated hazard ratio for CNN-predicted MIC may not generalize to other cohorts with wider MIC distributions.
Maturity_Evidence: Pretrained models validated on hold-out test sets (internal) and then applied unmodified to an independent South African patient cohort with a different MIC distribution (external validation); no prospective or CDS-integrated deployment reported.
Barriers_List: High labor and material cost; biohazardous testing conditions; low reproducibility of phenotypic MIC testing
Facilitators_List: Increasing adoption of targeted next-generation sequencing for mutation detection; commercial assays already cover most of the CNN's input loci
Future_Directions: Explore CNNs in clinical trials (prospectively or via retrospective reanalysis) on larger datasets; extend MIC prediction to new/repurposed drugs (linezolid, delamanid, pretomanid), which may need different architectures given the current rarity of resistant isolates.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: DeepLIFT attribution algorithm (saliency scores per nucleotide/lineage SNP), with permutation-test significance; Getis-Ord Gi* spatial clustering statistic on predicted MIC in 3D protein structure
Novel_Predictors_Details: 20 novel ethionamide resistance associations identified in mshA, Rv0565c, Rv3083, and ndh (mostly nonsense/LoF mutations), all previously graded 'uncertain' in the WHO catalog; also 247 nucleotides genome-wide with significant elevated-MIC association not currently in the WHO catalog.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Combinatorial analysis of co-occurring loss-of-function mutations across the ethionamide-activating genes (ethA, mshA, Rv3083, Rv0565c, ndh); CNN convolutional architecture itself models higher-order interactions among genetic variants.
Limitation_Categories: Training data adequacy/size (especially bedaquiline resistance); assumption that co-located mutations on the same codon have similar effects; limited generalisation to unseen/very rare mutations without additional structural priors.

Reported_Limitations: Geographic/data representativeness limitation: resistance estimates may be skewed by unequal geographic representation, with some regions underrepresented or lacking longitudinal data (additional limitations noted elsewhere: lack of clinical/diagnostic detail in ATLAS data, cross-country lab-standard variability, and the need for genotype data).
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: LSTM forecasts mathematically exceeded 100% resistance for some antibiotics and had to be manually capped at the biological ceiling.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: These results highlight the criticality of context-specific interventions, better funding for surveillance in LMICs particularly, and targeted implementation of AMR policies.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Only countries with ≥3 years of data were included in this analysis.
Exclusion_Criteria: Antibiotics with incomplete or insufficient resistance data (e.g., few or no reported results) were excluded during preprocessing to ensure data quality and consistency.

Data_Source_Name: Vivli AMR Pfizer ATLAS Antibiotics repository
Dataset_Size: >1.2 million isolates from 65 countries
Missing_Data_Method: Missing entries were removed (complete-case deletion) for continuity in the resistance trends.
Geographic_Representativeness: Resistance estimates may be skewed by the dataset's unequal geographic representation, with some regions underrepresented or lacking comprehensive longitudinal data.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Annual country-level mean antibiotic-resistance score, calculated from isolate-level susceptibility interpretations (resistant/intermediate/susceptible) converted to numeric scores.

Baseline_Performance: SARIMA RMSE by antibiotic: amikacin 26.146, cefepime 14.645, ceftazidime 21.068, levofloxacin 16.984, piperacillin-tazobactam 19.100 (vs. LSTM's much lower RMSE for each).

Reported_Limitations: (1) Binary susceptible/non-susceptible framing (intermediate+resistant grouped) does not capture MIC distributions, heteroresistance or full genotype-phenotype relationship; (2) AST method differed by specimen source (microdilution vs disk diffusion) and CLSI criteria changed over time, introducing possible label variation; (3) repeated spectra/isolates/cultures from the same patient could introduce correlation or leakage; (4) clinical deployment analysis limited to MRSA prediction in SAB with historical controls, limiting causal inference and generalisability to other syndromes; (5) cross-country analysis limited to Taiwan and Switzerland, not establishing portability across all instruments/labs/regions/populations.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Authors note the clinical consequences of false-susceptible or false-resistant predictions should be assessed before implementation at each site.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Federated learning was used specifically so that patient-level raw data would not need to be exchanged between institutions/countries, addressing governance, privacy and cross-jurisdictional collaboration concerns.
Sample_Size: 90,064 MALDI-TOF MS spectra (retained after quality control, from more than 300,000 raw spectra)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Sex_Distribution: XBugHunter group: Male 98 (63%), Female 57 (37%); historical controls: Male 301 (66%), Female 154 (34%) (table 2)
Inclusion_Criteria: Spectra were eligible for analysis if species-level identification was confirmed by MALDI Biotyper score greater than 2.0 and an AST result was available for the target pathogen–antibiotic phenotype.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients who died before XBugHunter prediction became available were excluded from the evaluable clinical-impact cohort.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: DRIAMS-A, DRIAMS-B, DRIAMS-C (Swiss MALDI-TOF repository)
Dataset_Size: 90,064 MALDI-TOF MS spectra retained after QC (from >300,000 raw spectra)
Geographic_Representativeness: The cross-country analysis included Taiwan and Switzerland but does not establish portability across all instruments, laboratories, regions or bacterial populations.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood, respiratory tract specimens, sterile cavity fluids, urine, wound exudates and pus
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic non-susceptibility (binary, intermediate+resistant grouped as non-susceptible) for five predefined pathogen–antibiotic targets: vancomycin non-susceptibility in E. faecium, oxacillin non-susceptibility in S. aureus (surrogate for MRSA), ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility in K. pneumoniae, multidrug resistance in A. baumannii, and ceftriaxone non-susceptibility in E. cloacae/E. aerogenes.
Pathogens: Enterococcus faecium; Staphylococcus aureus; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter baumannii; Enterobacter cloacae; Enterobacter aerogenes
Drug_Classes: Glycopeptides; Third-generation cephalosporins
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin; Oxacillin; Ciprofloxacin; Ceftriaxone
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: AST results were binarized as susceptible versus non-susceptible; intermediate and resistant isolates were grouped as non-susceptible.
AI_Purpose: This study evaluates whether AI models trained on routine MALDI-TOF MS spectra can rapidly predict antibiotic non-susceptibility at the time of microbial species identification.
Feature_Engineering: Raw MALDI-TOF MS data converted using readBrukerFlexData and preprocessed using MALDIquant (R): baseline subtraction (top-hat method), denoising (median absolute deviation, half-window 10), spectral alignment, peak detection (signal-to-noise threshold 5) and intensity normalization; species-specific type templates generated via kernel density estimation to create standardized binned feature vectors.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Reported AUPRC in addition to AUROC for cross-country MRSA analyses because MRSA prevalence differed across datasets.
Other_Metrics: AUPRC: DRIAMS 0.47 before transfer learning (AUROC 0.73); after transfer-learning adaptation DRIAMS AUPRC 0.70 (AUROC 0.85), LCGH AUPRC 0.85 (AUROC 0.85), KCGH AUPRC 0.81 (AUROC 0.82).
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation performed during model development within the training data.
Train_Test_Split: Geographic validation: trained on LCGH, tested on KCGH. Time-dependent validation: trained on isolates before 30 June 2018, tested on isolates from 1 July 2018 onward.
External_Validation_Description: Geographic validation using an independent hospital site (KCGH) not used for training (trained on LCGH); further cross-country external evaluation using the Swiss DRIAMS-A/B/C repositories.
Clinical_Insights: The m/z 3006.311 feature corresponded to a phenol-soluble modulin of the delta-lysin family, providing biological context for one susceptibility-associated peak; other model-prioritized peaks were compared with literature-reported MRSA lineage, SCCmec and protein annotations (table 3).
Generalisability_Details: Transfer-learning-based adaptation improved DRIAMS performance while maintaining clinically relevant discrimination in the Taiwanese datasets; findings support domain-adapted generalisation, not universal plug-and-play portability.
Maturity_Evidence: Predictions were generated and used in real time during routine care, with clinicians changing antimicrobial therapy in 45% of patients on the basis of predictive AST results, and process/outcome measures (turnaround time, DDD reduction, 28-day mortality) collected during deployment.
Integration_Point: At the time of MALDI-TOF MS-based species identification, while conventional AST proceeded in parallel.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (physicians) managing S. aureus bacteraemia, supported by the microbiology laboratory workflow.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: T0 = positive blood-culture alert time; Tsp = time XBugHunter prediction released; Tfinal = time final conventional AST reported; time to actionable susceptibility information and XBugHunter's time advantage were calculated from these timestamps.
Stewardship_Details: XBugHunter-guided care was associated with a reduction of 114.77 defined daily doses, particularly for glycopeptides and third-generation cephalosporins, consistent with earlier escalation/de-escalation according to predicted methicillin susceptibility.
Barriers_List: Generalization across laboratories is a major barrier for clinical AI in microbiology; MALDI-TOF MS spectra may shift across institutions because of differences in instrument calibration, sample preparation, culture conditions, preprocessing pipelines, local epidemiology and circulating bacterial lineages.
Facilitators_List: The approach leverages data already generated in routine care, requiring no additional assays, instrumentation or cost.
Future_Directions: Prospective multicenter trials are now needed to determine whether this framework improves antimicrobial stewardship and patient outcomes under controlled clinical implementation.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest-based Gini importance and SHAP (TreeSHAP/KernelSHAP)
Limitation_Categories: Reference-standard/label definition (binary framing); measurement heterogeneity (AST method by specimen source, evolving CLSI criteria); potential data leakage from repeated isolates/spectra; observational design with historical controls limiting causal inference; limited cross-country generalisability (Taiwan/Switzerland only).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Binary susceptible/non-susceptible framing does not capture MIC distributions or heteroresistance; AST reference method differed by specimen source and CLSI interpretive criteria changed over time, which may introduce label variation; repeated spectra/isolates/cultures from the same patient could introduce correlation or leakage if not handled at the patient/isolate level.
Reporting_Clarity: Explicit statement of adherence to STARD 2015 and TRIPOD reporting guidelines, with extensive Supplementary Methods/Tables/Figures referenced throughout.

Population_Description: Adult patients meeting CDC Adult Sepsis Event criteria, admitted to any of 10 acute-care BJC hospitals in Missouri and Illinois between January 2018 and December 2023 (retrospective cohort); sepsis episodes classified as community-onset or hospital-onset and stratified by resistance of the causative Gram-negative bacilli to ceftriaxone/cefepime.
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 10 SHAP-ranked features for COS (panel A): History of Gram-negative infection, History of antimicrobial resistance, History of sepsis, Creatinine, Age, Calcium, Albumin, Platelets, Lactate, History of bacterial pneumonia (SHAP/XGBoost feature importance).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: DeepAMR (deep learning model, structured EHR data): AUROC 0·85/AUPRC 0·40 for COS and AUROC 0·81/AUPRC 0·50 for HOS episodes. Best-performing LLM alone was Medical-LLaMa3-8B on full notes: AUROC 0·74/AUPRC 0·21 for COS and AUROC 0·67/AUPRC 0·30 for HOS. Five LLMs tested (BioGPT, BioClinicalBERT, ClinicalBERT, Clinical-Longformer, Medical-LLaMa3-8B), alone and combined with DeepAMR; combining deep learning and LLMs did not significantly improve prediction of resistant GNB compared to deep learning alone.

AUROC_Population_Set: COS episodes; DeepAMR combined with BioGPT (Assessment section); holdout test set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were developed and evaluated only via internal cross-validation on a retrospective single-health-system cohort; no external validation, prospective evaluation, or deployment/EHR integration was performed.
Reported_Limitations: This study had several limitations. This was retrospective analyses based on EHR data from a single healthcare system and our results may not be representative of the use of these models in other systems. Notes used in analysis were not assessed for accuracy or bias and we included only H&P documents in our analyses as these offer the most comprehensive summary of a patient's history and presentation. Previous work emphasized the dominant effect of comorbidities in predicting AMR, even in hospital-onset sepsis. Our study was preliminary in nature and we did not conduct a prospective evaluation or attempt to deploy the DeepAMR along with LLMs in the EHR, as has been done in other studies. Additionally, there is often a delay between clinical reasoning and note filing in the EHR, potentially impeding prospective validation for real-time antibiotic selection.
Conflicts_of_Interest: MCVG owned personal stock in OCGN, BNGO, SESN with value less than $1,000 in September 2023 and received personal fees from Merck & Co, Inc of less than $5,000 for educational unbranded videos on hospital-acquired pneumonia unrelated to this project; all other authors report no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: All adult patients who met the CDC Adult Sepsis Event Criteria admitted to 10 BJC hospitals between 1/2018-12/2023.
Exclusion_Criteria: 216 episodes excluded due to missing antimicrobial susceptibility data.

Dataset_Size: 29,517 patients; 32,806 admissions; 23,949 COS episodes; 25,101 HOS episodes
Missing_Data_Method: Last observation carried forward (LOCF) used to impute missing laboratory and vital sign values; implausible values removed based on predefined physiological ranges.
Ethnicity_Details: Race reported as White and Black with counts/percentages by resistance group (COS): White 15952 (66.6%), Black 7055 (29.5%) of 23949 episodes
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood cultures (sepsis episodes defined by blood culture orders)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Sepsis episodes caused by Gram-negative bacilli stratified as ceftriaxone-susceptible (SS), ceftriaxone-resistant/cefepime-susceptible (RS), or ceftriaxone- and cefepime-resistant (RR) based on antimicrobial susceptibility testing results.
Pathogens: Gram-negative bacilli generally, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli (most common resistant GNB in COS) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Serratia marcescens, Enterobacter cloacae (most common resistant GNB in HOS).
Num_Pathogens: 5 (named as the most common resistant GNB species; broader Gram-negative bacilli category also studied)
Specific_Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone, cefepime
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Ceftriaxone/cefepime susceptibility-based categories (SS/RS/RR) assigned from antimicrobial susceptibility testing results, per CLSI guidelines; culture-negative/non-GNB sepsis labeled SS; intermediate isolates labeled susceptible.
AI_Purpose: Predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Gram-negative bacilli causing sepsis, to test whether combining a deep learning model on structured EHR data with biomedical LLMs analyzing clinical notes improves prediction over structured data alone.
Num_Models_Compared: 11 (1 DeepAMR + 5 LLMs alone + 5 combined DeepAMR+LLM models)
Feature_Engineering: Vital sign and laboratory data within five days of the culture timestamp were resampled to 4-hour window means; implausible values removed based on predefined physiological ranges; last observation carried forward used for missing laboratory/vital-sign values.
Feature_Selection_Method: No dedicated feature-selection step reported for DeepAMR (all available structured data used); a separate XGBoost gradient-boosting model with SHAP was used to rank the first 10 important features.
Hyperparameter_Method: 10% of the training data used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection; XGBoost tuned for tree depth and feature subsampling; deep learning model tuned for network width, depth and learning rate.
Baseline_Method: DeepAMR (deep learning model on structured EHR data alone) used as the reference/baseline against which LLM and combined models are compared.
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0·85 (COS, DeepAMR alone; reference line in Fig. 3)
Internal_Validation: 10 independent 10-fold cross-validation runs; 80/20 patient-level train/test split with a 10% hyperparameter-tuning subset.
Train_Test_Split: 80% training (70% training / 10% hyperparameter tuning) / 20% testing (patient-level split)
Overfitting_Method: 10% random validation split of the training set used to monitor validation performance during training and stop training before overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: History of infections caused by GNB and other prior infections were significant predictors of resistant GNB in both COS and HOS; longer times since admission were also associated with a higher likelihood of resistant GNB in HOS.
Generalisability_Details: This was retrospective analyses based on EHR data from a single healthcare system and our results may not be representative of the use of these models in other systems.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence is limited to internal 10-fold cross-validation performance on a retrospective, single-health-system holdout test set; the authors explicitly state no prospective evaluation or EHR deployment was attempted.
Integration_Point: Not yet integrated; envisioned to be deployed directly in the EHR workflow at the time of suspected infection to support empiric antibiotic selection.
End_User_Described: Clinicians choosing empiric anti-GNB antibiotics
Barriers_List: Single-institution/retrospective data limiting generalisability; notes not assessed for accuracy or bias; only H&P notes used; clinical notes often contain redundant, inaccurate, or auto-populated administrative/billing content diluting signal; LLMs not fine-tuned for AMR prediction; delay between clinical reasoning and note filing in the EHR.
Facilitators_List: Pairing LLM analysis with note-generation AI software that records patient-provider interactions with higher fidelity, independent of administrative/billing requirements, to improve signal quality for LLM analysis.
Future_Directions: Future use of LLMs may require task-specific fine-tuning, better integration architectures, and careful curation of clinical text inputs; a multi-stage LLM framework (extraction of clinical factors followed by relevance verification/supervised fine-tuning) may enhance specificity and reduce noise.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 8 (clinical, microbiological, pharmacological, healthcare-utilisation, laboratory, sociodemographic, temporal, text/NLP)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) applied to a gradient-boosted XGBoost model, ranking the first 10 important features.
Limitation_Categories: Single-institution/retrospective design and limited generalisability; notes not assessed for accuracy/bias; restricted note type (H&P only); no prospective evaluation or EHR deployment; delay between clinical reasoning and note filing.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Clinical notes used by LLMs, such as H&P documents, are often created for administrative and billing purposes and may contain redundant, inaccurate, or auto-populated content, diluting the signal-to-noise ratio and potentially degrading model accuracy.

Title: Construction and internal-external validation of a machine learning-based risk prediction model for multidrug resistance in ICU patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: AECOPD patients admitted to the ICU, retrospectively extracted from MIMIC-IV: 1,018 patients split 7:3 into a training set (n=712) and internal validation set (n=306), with MDR occurrence as outcome; plus an external validation cohort of 324 AECOPD patients admitted to the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University (Jan 2024-Oct 2025).
Age_Range: ≥18 years (lower bound only; no upper bound stated)

Specificity_Population_Set: Internal validation set (MIMIC-IV, n=306)

AUROC_Population_Set: Internal validation set (MIMIC-IV, n=306)

Conflicts_of_Interest: The author(s) declared that this work was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

Hyperparameter_Method: Grid-search hyperparameter tuning with 10-fold cross-validation

Clinical_Insights: Hematocrit and SpO2 were the dominant SHAP drivers of predicted MDR risk; mechanistically linked to hypoxia-induced airway-epithelial injury, disrupted mucosal barrier integrity, and impaired host defense favoring resistant bacterial colonization.
Generalisability_Details: MIMIC-IV comprises only ICU admissions; transportability of the model to AECOPD patients in emergency departments or general medical wards (different severity, comorbidity burden, MDR epidemiology) remains uncertain and requires dedicated prospective validation.
Maturity_Evidence: Highest evidence level supported is external validation: an independent 324-patient cohort from a second hospital showed AUC 0.926, but no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment was performed.

End_User_Described: Clinicians
Stewardship_Details: Discussed conceptually only: the model is expected to promote rational antimicrobial use and curtail indiscriminate broad-spectrum prescribing, aligning with tiered antibiotic-stewardship policy; no stewardship outcome was empirically measured.
Future_Directions: Expand sample size; integrate additional clinical characteristics (genetic biomarkers, inflammatory mediators); exploit deep-learning architectures; conduct prospective interventional trials to test whether model-guided management reduces MDR infection rates and mortality; multicenter validation with higher event rates and non-ICU settings.

Population_Description: 188 pediatric patients diagnosed with M. pneumoniae infection, admitted to the Department of Pediatrics at Suzhou University Affiliated Fourth Hospital (Dushu Lake Hospital), Suzhou, China, from September 2023 to August 2024; ages 3-14 years; categorized into macrolide-resistant (MRMP, detection group, n=118) and non-macrolide-resistant (NMRMP, nondetection group, n=70) based on 23S rRNA mutation status at positions 2063/2064.
Age_Mean_Median: Detection/MRMP group: median age 8 years (IQR 5.00-9.00); Non-detection/NMRMP group: median age 7 years (IQR 5.25-9.00).
Top_Predictive_Features: Random Forest feature importance ranking (Figure 4): monocyte count, neutrophil count, D-dimer, and prealbumin (PA/ALB) concentration were the top contributors; patient age and PA were highlighted as critical baseline features distinguishing this ML approach from traditional regression. Full ranked variable list shown in Figure 4: Lobar_pneumonia, NEU, MONO, Weight, ALB, Lesion_location, Age, DD, Gender, Fever.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Standard Logistic Regression (AUC=0.771), Random Forest (AUC=0.784), and Gradient Boosting (AUC=0.817, best) compared under stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the 188-patient cohort (main-text Results figures). NOTE: Figure 3's ROC-curve legend gives different AUCs for the same three models (Logistic regression 0.735, Random forest 0.768, Gradient boosting 0.748), inconsistent with the Results-text values -- flagged, see _notes.
Best_Performing_Model: Gradient Boosting (AUC = 0.817 per Results text, the highest of the three models compared under 5-fold cross-validation; Figure 3's legend instead shows 0.748 for the same model -- see _notes).
AUROC_Value: 0.817 (Gradient Boosting, best-performing model, 5-fold cross-validation, per Results text; Figure 3's legend shows 0.748 for the same model -- see _notes).
AUROC_Population_Set: 188 children with M. pneumoniae infection (118 MRMP / 70 NMRMP), stratified 5-fold cross-validation.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal (within-cohort) stratified 5-fold cross-validation was performed; no external dataset, prospective cohort, or deployed CDS integration described.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective, single-center design carrying risk of selection bias and limiting generalizability to other regions; postadmission variables (hospital stay, anti-Mycoplasma therapy duration, systemic corticosteroid administration) deliberately excluded as predictors because they may proxy for disease severity rather than function as independent baseline predictors; future multicenter prospective validation with larger samples recommended.
Sample_Size: 188 children with M. pneumoniae infection (118 MRMP, 70 NMRMP)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Sex_Distribution: 101 female and 87 male of 188 patients (Results, Section 3.1); NOTE: Methods Section 2.1 separately states 107 female and 81 male for the same 188-patient cohort -- the two counts are inconsistent in the source, see _notes.
Inclusion_Criteria: Diagnosis/resistance testing per national MP pneumonia guideline (2023 Edition); not readmitted for similar illness within the past 6 months and had complete clinical records.
Exclusion_Criteria: Severe underlying disease under immunosuppressant/biologic treatment; poor compliance, discontinuous disease course, or incomplete clinical records.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Imaging
Dataset_Size: 188 children (118 MRMP, 70 NMRMP)
Missing_Data_Method: Median imputation (applied to missing baseline laboratory findings, e.g. D-dimer)
Specimen_Type_Detail: Nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal swabs tested by fluorescent PCR for MP and resistance mutation sites A2063G/A2064G; venous blood for laboratory testing.

Drug_Classes: Macrolides
Specific_Antibiotics: Azithromycin (first-line antibiotic therapy)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug

AI_Purpose: Early, noninvasive prediction of macrolide-resistant M. pneumoniae (MRMP) status from baseline clinical and laboratory data obtained at admission, to guide antimicrobial selection before molecular resistance testing results are available.
