Title: Prediction of KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae by MALDI-TOF MS, ensemble learning, and spectral peak annotation
Country_Countries: Spain, United States, Colombia, Chile, Lebanon, and Singapore
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation; AI Signal Processing
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Instituto de Investigacion Sanitaria Gregorio Maranon (IISGM); Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII); National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), National Institutes of Health (UM1AI104681)
Population_Description: 435 clinical isolates of K. pneumoniae, including KPC-producing (n = 237) and non-KPC-producing (n = 198) isolates
Data_Source_Other: Antibacterial Resistance Leadership Group (ARLG) Biorepository isolate collection
Top_Predictive_Features: Five most discriminative peaks ranked by AUC: 3,372 m/z (AUC=0.67); 5,251 m/z (AUC=0.87); 5,555 m/z (AUC=0.74); 6,017 m/z (AUC=0.56); 11,109 m/z (AUC=0.79)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Clinician / prescriber; Antimicrobial stewardship team
All_Models_Evaluated: 92 classifiers tested (4 ML algorithms: PLS-DA, SVM, LGBM, RF, each on 2 peak matrices [full-spectrum F and 5-peak 5P] as single models, plus all pairwise (n=28) and triplet (n=56) ensemble combinations); ensemble combinations increased specificity to over 95% and sensitivity to 72%, significantly higher than the MALDI Biotyper KPC module comparator
Best_Performing_Model: F-PLS-DA + F-RF + 5P-SVM (Training 2 triplet ensemble; external validation sensitivity = 72%, specificity = 96%, F1 = 0.82 - highest F1 among reported 'outstanding' triplet combinations)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Training 2 external validation set (remaining isolates after adding 20 representative Mayo Clinic/ARLG isolates to training), N = 334
Specificity_Population_Set: Training 2 external validation set, N = 334
F1_Population_Set: Training 2 external validation set, N = 334
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation was performed using Mayo Clinic and ARLG isolate collections, geographically and institutionally distinct from the HGM training set; no prospective clinical evaluation, CDS integration, or routine use is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Different isolate collections had different susceptibility profiles (ARLG=all carbapenem-resistant, Mayo=all carbapenem-susceptible); KPC presence was defined by different approaches (WGS for ARLG vs phenotypic detection for HGM); single-subculture protein extraction may have influenced results; repeat testing was not performed on all isolates.
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr. Patel reports grants from MicuRx Pharmaceuticals, ImmuCell, and bioMerieux; is a consultant to PhAST, Iterum Therapeutics, Deepull Diagnostics, Nostics, bioMerieux, and CARB-X; holds several patents; and receives honoraria from Up-to-Date and the Infectious Diseases Board Review Course.
Inclusion_Criteria: Clinical K. pneumoniae isolates from three collections (HGM Spain, Mayo Clinic USA, ARLG Biorepository), classified as KPC-producing or non-KPC-producing
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; MALDI-TOF mass spectra
Data_Source_Name: Antibacterial Resistance Leadership Group (ARLG) Biorepository
Dataset_Size: 435 clinical isolates (237 KPC-producing, 198 non-KPC-producing)
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates included from Spain, the United States, Latin America (Colombia and Chile) and Lebanon; authors note most prior studies were from Asian countries, limiting comparability due to geographic variation.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Detection/prediction of KPC (Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase) production in K. pneumoniae isolates from MALDI-TOF mass spectra using machine learning
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: KPC status defined by NG-Test Carba 5 (immunochromatographic assay) for HGM isolates, and by whole-genome sequencing (gene presence) for ARLG isolates
AI_Purpose: To integrate MALDI-TOF MS with ensemble machine learning to improve detection of KPC-producing K. pneumoniae isolates, and to develop an annotated MALDI-TOF MS spectrum for peak interpretation
Feature_Engineering: Spectral preprocessing: smoothing (Savitzky-Golay filter), baseline subtraction (top-hat filter), alignment, and normalization by total ion current, prior to constructing full-spectrum (F) and reduced 5-peak (5P) matrices
Feature_Selection_Method: AUC (area under the curve)-based ranking to select the five most discriminative peaks (5P matrix)
Software_Libraries: Clover MS Data Analysis Software (Clover MSDAS; Clover Biosoft, Granada, Spain)
Other_Metrics: Balanced accuracy and Youden's index were also computed as composite metrics for each model
Baseline_Method: MALDI Biotyper KPC detection module (commercial single-peak [11,109 m/z] detection module)
Baseline_Performance: Sensitivity = 32% (63/196 KPC isolates positive), specificity = 100% (no false-positive results)
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation
External_Validation_Description: External validation with Mayo Clinic and ARLG isolate data sets (Training 1: N = 354; Training 2, after adding 20 representative isolates to training: N = 334)
Clinical_Insights: An annotated MALDI-TOF MS spectrum for K. pneumoniae was developed via in silico prediction of protein masses to enable peak identification, including peaks potentially related to antimicrobial resistance
Data_Repository: GenBank (accession number PRJNA658369); raw mass spectra available from corresponding author on reasonable request
Generalisability_Details: Adding 20 representative Mayo Clinic/ARLG isolates to the HGM-only training set was intended to increase heterogeneity so models generalise better to external data sets; this increased most metrics for pairwise/triple ensembles, though sensitivity remained low (maximum 72%).
Maturity_Evidence: Models were developed on an HGM (Spain) training set and evaluated on geographically/institutionally distinct external isolates (Mayo Clinic, ARLG); no prospective clinical deployment or CDS integration reported.
Integration_Point: MALDI-TOF MS spectra acquisition software / workflow (post-acquisition classification of spectra)
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory staff / clinicians (implied via 'clinical microbiology workflows' and antimicrobial stewardship)
Stewardship_Details: Mentioned only as rationale/motivation ('...informing optimal therapeutic options and strengthening antimicrobial stewardship'), not as a measured outcome
Barriers_List: Technical variability in spectral acquisition; need for additional spectral quality control beyond that used for species identification; need to develop an informatics workflow to automate the process from spectral acquisition to result
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is already the standard, widely used method for bacterial identification and gives rapid results as soon as bacteria are recovered in culture
Future_Directions: Future approaches to reduce technical variability could include automated MALDI-TOF-spotting systems; future studies could evaluate optimisation using protein extraction or subcultures passaged twice
Top_Features_Importance_Method: AUC (area under the curve) values indicating relevance for KPC isolates
Novel_Predictors_Details: Three previously unreported/unidentified peaks (3,372, 5,251, and 6,017 m/z) were found to be mostly present in KPC-producing isolates and used in the models; authors note these may reflect clonal or geographic signatures rather than resistance determinants
Limitation_Categories: Heterogeneous isolate collections with different susceptibility profiles; inconsistent KPC-definition methods across collections; single-subculture protein extraction; incomplete repeat testing
Data_Quality_Concerns: Spectral acquisition performed via single-subculture on-plate extraction from frozen stocks, which may have influenced results compared to double subculture; repeat testing not performed on all isolates

Title: Identifying and forecasting importation and asymptomatic spreaders of multi-drug resistant organisms in hospital settings
Funder_Names: NSF; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Modeling Infectious Diseases In Healthcare program; National Institutes of Health; National Center for Advancing Translational Science; Facebook (faculty research award); Dolby (faculty research award); Georgia Tech
Population_Description: Patients admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) at the University of Virginia hospital, July 1, 2019 to December 31, 2019 (n=1117 patients, of whom 74 were MRSA importation cases).
Top_Predictive_Features: Contact with more MRSA patients in the past 7/14 days prior to ICU admission; device usage history; came from or was discharged to another healthcare facility last time (ranked by SHAP value from the trained neural network).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
All_Models_Evaluated: NeurABM (best on all tasks); machine learning baselines: feedforward neural network, decision tree, naive bayes, XGBoost, Autoencoder+KNN; mechanistic modeling baselines: SIS-ABM model, SILI-ABM model; clinical heuristic baseline: length of stay. Evaluated via AUPRC, AUC-ROC, recall/precision/F1 at fixed precision thresholds, and NPV (e.g., NeurABM AUPRC 0.60 vs best baseline lower, for identifying importation cases).
Best_Performing_Model: NeurABM — best on recall at fixed precision, AUPRC, NPV and AUC-ROC across all three tasks (identifying importation cases, identifying current nosocomial infection, forecasting future nosocomial infection).
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Identifying MRSA importation cases, UVA ICU dataset, at the precision=0.25 operating point
Precision_PPV_Value: 0.25 (chosen operating point at which recall=0.74 is achieved)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Identifying MRSA importation cases, UVA ICU dataset
AUROC_Population_Set: Identifying MRSA importation cases, UVA ICU dataset
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Single-site (UVA ICU) retrospective evaluation using an internal, weekly walk-forward temporal train/test split; no external-site validation, prospective deployment, or clinical-workflow integration is reported.
Reported_Limitations: The SIS-ABM model oversimplifies MRSA carriage with only two states (susceptible, carriage), lacking an explicit colonization state or differentiation of clinical infection types; contact networks are constructed only from co-location data with a well-mixed assumption; evaluation is limited to the UVA ICU due to data availability.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients admitted to UVA ICUs, July 1, 2019 to December 31, 2019, who received an MRSA test within (t-3, t+3) days of ICU admission (those testing positive within this window classified as importation cases).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Other
Dataset_Size: 1117 patients (6445 patient days), 2385 healthcare workers, 77 locations, July 1 - December 31, 2019
Specimen_Type_Detail: MRSA nares testing (mentioned as widely used in clinical practice; not explicitly confirmed as this study's own specimen source)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Identifying MRSA importation cases at ICU admission and forecasting future nosocomial MRSA infections (carriage/infection status determined from culture and PCR test results).
Pathogens: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Specific_Antibiotics: MRSA-active antibiotics (not further specified)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary carriage/infection status per patient-day, defined from lab test results: positive if the patient tested positive (culture or PCR) on that day or their most recent test was positive; negative otherwise.
AI_Purpose: To integrate a neural network and an agent-based model (NeurABM) to identify MRSA importation cases from EHR risk factors and forecast future nosocomial MRSA infections, combining mechanistic transmission modeling with patient-level EHR data.
Num_Models_Compared: 9 (NeurABM plus 8 baselines: feedforward neural network, decision tree, naive bayes, XGBoost, Autoencoder+KNN, SIS-ABM, SILI-ABM, length of stay)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Weighted binary cross-entropy loss, with weights for positive/negative observations set by the inverse ratio of negative to positive counts.
Other_Metrics: False positive rate (1-specificity), reported alongside recall/F1/AUPRC/NPV/AUC-ROC at fixed precision thresholds in the results tables.
Baseline_Method: Feedforward neural network, decision tree, naive bayes, XGBoost, Autoencoder+KNN (machine learning); SIS-ABM model, SILI-ABM model (mechanistic modeling); length of stay (clinical heuristic).
Baseline_Performance: Best baseline (feedforward neural network) recall = 0.40 at precision = 0.25 for identifying importation cases, versus NeurABM recall = 0.74 at the same precision.
Internal_Validation: Weekly walk-forward (rolling-origin) evaluation: for each week k, the model is trained on contact networks, risk factors and lab results up to week k-1 and used to identify/forecast cases in week k.
Train_Test_Split: Baselines trained on ground-truth importation labels from January-June 2019 and tested on July-December 2019 (same period as NeurABM); NeurABM itself uses a weekly walk-forward train/test scheme with no fixed single split.
Clinical_Insights: Patients with contact with more MRSA patients in the past 7/14 days prior to ICU admission, with a device usage history, or who came from/were discharged to another healthcare facility, were considered higher risk of being importation cases; consistent with real-world clinical observations.
Data_Repository: GitHub: https://github.com/AdityaLab/NeurABM (code, demo and a synthetic dataset; the real EHR data used to develop the models is not released because it is highly sensitive).
Generalisability_Details: Authors note NeurABM is currently evaluated only in the UVA ICU due to data availability, and that adding more risk factors or conducting experiments in other settings/healthcare facilities could give a more comprehensive assessment; the framework is also described as flexible/generalisable to other ABMs, datasets and HAIs (e.g., Clostridioides difficile).
Maturity_Evidence: Retrospective, single-site (UVA ICU), internally validated via weekly walk-forward evaluation on EHR data; no external-site validation or prospective/real-time clinical deployment reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians, who can use the model's risk-factor findings to better respond to potential MRSA importation cases.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Patients are ranked by NeurABM's forecasted infection/carriage probability from high to low and tested in that order (a risk-based screening/testing prioritisation strategy); e.g. testing the top 20% of ranked patients identifies 88% (86/98) of carriage patients.
Barriers_List: Data availability limits evaluation to a single site (UVA ICU); real EHR data cannot be shared publicly because it is highly sensitive.
Facilitators_List: NeurABM is flexible and not tied to a specific agent-based model, so the SIS-ABM component can be replaced with other ABM designs, allowing adaptation to other healthcare-associated infections; the datasets required are straightforward to extract from EHRs.
Future_Directions: Extending agent-based methods to predict MRSA testing outcomes for potential future clinical application; adding more patient risk factors (e.g., chronic disease history, Apache II scores) or experiments in other settings/facilities; forecasting future contact networks rather than assuming they equal the last observed network; enriching the ABM with intervention representations; extending patient-specific parameterisation beyond importation probability.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP
Limitation_Categories: Model simplification (SIS-ABM has only 2 states, no explicit colonization state, no differentiation of clinical infection types); contact-network construction assumption (co-location treated as interaction, well-mixed assumption); single-site data availability (UVA ICU only).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Machine-learning approaches to this problem face bias in the data because testing for MDROs is generally not done in a systematic manner.
Reporting_Clarity: Framework, results and STROBE-guided methods are clearly reported; some details (full risk-factor list, additional metrics tables, SIS-ABM parameter details) are deferred to Supplementary Information not included in this PDF.

Geographic_Representativeness: External validation cohort drawn from a single tertiary hospital in China; authors note this may limit generalizability to primary care, pediatric, or other regional populations with distinct pathogen epidemiology.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug resistance (MDR), defined as resistance to at least three classes of antimicrobial agents.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR was defined as resistance to at least three classes of antimicrobial agents.
AI_Purpose: To develop and validate an interpretable ML model to predict MDR risk in pneumonia patients and assess its utility for clinical decision support.
Feature_Engineering: Binary variables cast to Int64; continuous variables/label cast to float64/Int64; missing continuous values imputed iteratively (IterativeImputer); skewed distributions corrected via Yeo-Johnson transform (PowerTransformer); extreme values winsorized by IQR; low-variance continuous variables removed (VarianceThreshold); highly correlated variables (|r|>0.9) removed; remaining continuous features z-score standardized and filtered via L1-regularized logistic regression; binary variables' missing values filled with 0 and filtered via chi-square test (p<0.05).
Feature_Selection_Method: Chi-square test (p<0.05) for binary variables; LASSO (L1-regularized logistic regression, C=1.0) for continuous variables, retaining variables with non-zero coefficients.
Num_Features_Selected: 23 (2 binary + 21 continuous)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Dynamic class weights based on training-set event rate: class_weight parameter (LR, RF, LightGBM); scale_pos_weight parameter (XGBoost), optimized during hyperparameter tuning.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over hyperparameters (regularization strength, max tree depth, learning rate, number of estimators, min sample split, L1/L2 regularization), optimized via 5-fold stratified cross-validation using AUROC as the primary metric.
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn, xgboost, lightgbm, shap, pandas, numpy
Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration test (p>0.05); decision curve analysis (net benefit vs treat-all/treat-none strategies).
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (LR) used as the conventional statistical benchmark, compared against ensemble tree-based ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM).
Baseline_Performance: LR (the benchmark model) achieved AUROC 0.798, the highest among the four models compared.
Internal_Validation: 5-fold stratified cross-validation (hyperparameter tuning); internal train/test split of the MIMIC-IV cohort, stratified by MDR outcome.
External_Validation_Description: Independent cohort from Jilin Provincial People's Hospital, China (n=213; 44 MDRO, 169 non-MDRO), same inclusion/exclusion criteria, patients admitted January 2024-June 2025.
Overfitting_Method: L1-regularized logistic regression (LASSO, C=1.0) for feature selection/regularization.
Clinical_Insights: SII identified as top-ranked predictor by SHAP; elevated SII (reflecting excessive inflammatory activation/impaired immune competence) strongly positively correlated with MDR risk, consistent with prior literature on SII and drug-resistant pathogens.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the model showed limited overfitting and stable predictive ability across two geographically/ethnically distinct cohorts, but explicitly frame this as evidence of stability rather than confirmation of broad generalizability; further multi-center, multi-regional prospective validation called for.
Maturity_Evidence: Independent external validation on a Chinese tertiary-hospital cohort (n=213) achieving AUROC 0.845, beyond internal validation alone; no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
Future_Directions: Future studies should focus on further validation and integration of more diverse clinical data sources; large-scale, multi-center, multi-regional prospective validation across diverse healthcare settings, age groups and ethnic populations is needed before widespread clinical implementation.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (mean absolute SHAP value; SHAP beeswarm plot for global feature importance)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Authors describe SII, albumin, LYM abs, CAR, WBC and antibiotic-class count as consistent with prior literature on inflammation/immune markers and MDR risk, rather than as novel/unexpected predictors.
Feature_Interactions_Method: SHAP dependence plots for the top 4 most important continuous variables, to visualize marginal effects and potential feature interactions.
Limitation_Categories: Study design (cross-sectional, causality); external validity / generalizability (single-institution external validation cohort).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Multiple imputation for missing data assumes a multivariate Gaussian distribution, which may not fully represent highly skewed inflammatory markers; estimation bias cannot be completely excluded.

Conflicts_of_Interest: No reported conflicts of interest. All authors have submitted the ICMJE Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest.

Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data

Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine, blood, lower respiratory tract, fecal/rectal swab, other
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Susceptibility (binary susceptible vs nonsusceptible) to each of 8 antimicrobial groups for E. coli and Klebsiella spp. isolates, with particular emphasis on carbapenem resistance detection.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella spp. (excluding Klebsiella aerogenes)
Drug_Classes: Narrow-spectrum cephalosporins; expanded-spectrum cephalosporins; aminopenicillins; aminopenicillin/BLI combinations; antipseudomonal penicillins/BLI combinations; carbapenems; fluoroquinolones; trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug

Class_Imbalance_Method: Multitask joint modeling across antimicrobial classes, leveraging cross-resistance correlations to improve learning for infrequent outcomes (e.g., carbapenem resistance); also prevalence-aware metrics (AUPRC, PPV, NPV) and sensitivity/specificity-prioritized thresholds.
Hardware_Details: AWS VA Enterprise Cloud enclave ("Prospect")
Other_Metrics: Brier score / Brier skill score (relative to logistic-regression antibiogram baseline)
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression using conventional hospital antibiogram as the sole predictor variable, per published protocol
Baseline_Performance: Overall (combined) AUROC N/A (not reported for baseline); Brier skill score expressed as reference (0) for hospital antibiogram; multitask AUROC 0.862 (E. coli), 0.848 (Klebsiella spp.)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation (patient-clustered folds) during training; temporally-held-out internal test set (Oct 2023-Sep 2024) for simulated prospective testing
Train_Test_Split: Training: Jan 2017-Sep 2023 (536 252 E. coli / 246 898 Klebsiella spp. isolates); Test: Oct 2023-Sep 2024 (75 138 E. coli / 38 015 Klebsiella spp. isolates)
Clinical_Insights: Model predictions were primarily driven by prior susceptibility history and recent antimicrobial exposure within clinically meaningful time windows; antimicrobial-specific models were most influenced by the corresponding prior susceptibility result and recent exposure to the same/related drug classes, with additional contribution from comorbidities and demographics.
Generalisability_Details: Findings may not generalize to pathogens other than E. coli and Klebsiella spp.; future research should explore applicability to a broader range of organisms and antimicrobial agents. VHA population is older/more male than the general US population, though VHA's national, multi-state presence is argued to support adaptability to varying settings.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal temporally-held-out test-set evaluation only ("simulated prospective testing"); no external-site validation, no real prospective deployment, no CDS integration or routine clinical use reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (empiric antimicrobial prescribing)
Facilitators_List: VHA's status as the only US integrated healthcare system with a presence in all states, spanning varying AMR prevalence, environmental factors, and care complexity, is presented as an opportunity for developing broadly adaptable models.
Future_Directions: Continuous updating/validation of the model; extending applicability to a broader range of organisms and antimicrobial agents; prospective studies to evaluate impact on prescribing and outcomes.

Title: Discrimination of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus by MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry with Machine Learning Techniques in Patients with Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia

Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)

Sensitivity_Population_Set: Independent testing dataset (182 S/N samples)
Specificity_Population_Set: Independent testing dataset (182 S/N samples)
AUROC_Population_Set: Independent testing dataset (182 S/N samples)

Unresolved_Items: Whether the 110 archived SCCmec-typed isolates (Section 3.5), collected/stored separately and typed in a prior study, should count as an external-validation dataset or merely an internal bias-check is ambiguous; coded here as not constituting external validation since all data derive from the same institution.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Blood samples obtained Dec 2020-Jul 2021; positive blood culture; species identified as S. aureus.
Exclusion_Criteria: MALDI Biotyper species-identification matching scores of 1.7 or below (no organism identified / low confidence) were not enrolled.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: Chi Mei Medical Center hospital-constructed clinical/MS database (not a named public repository)
Dataset_Size: 548 total samples (366 training + 182 independent testing)
Geographic_Representativeness: All samples came from a single hospital (Chi Mei Medical Center, Tainan, Taiwan); no statement of national or multi-region representativeness.

Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin resistance (MRSA vs MSSA), defined by oxacillin resistance on antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin/methicillin resistance)
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin (surrogated by a 30 ug cefoxitin disk)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary MRSA/MSSA label based on oxacillin resistance in AST, coded -1/+1
AI_Purpose: To classify MRSA vs MSSA from MALDI-TOF mass spectra using machine learning, enabling earlier identification of methicillin resistance than conventional AST.
Feature_Engineering: Modified binning method: bin size automatically adjusted by peak width (0.5-fold FWHM) rather than a fixed bin size, to build reference-peak features from raw MS peaks.
Feature_Selection_Method: Decision-tree feature_importances_ (Gini impurity-based)
Hyperparameter_Method: Genetic algorithm (GA)
Other_Metrics: 10-fold cross-validation accuracy used during GA parameter optimization (e.g. best SVM CV accuracy 0.8187) and GA fitness values.
Baseline_Method: Default (non-GA-optimized) scikit-learn parameter settings for each ML model, using all 508 features
Baseline_Performance: SVM default parameters, independent testing: accuracy 0.5879, sensitivity 0.0972, specificity 0.9091, AUC 0.5910
Internal_Validation: 80/20 random train-test split repeated 100 times for feature-importance evaluation; 10-fold cross-validation during GA parameter optimization; temporal hold-out (Dec2020-May2021 training vs Jun-Jul2021 independent testing)
Train_Test_Split: 366 training samples (Dec 2020-May 2021) / 182 independent testing samples (Jun-Jul 2021)
Overfitting_Method: Comparing training vs. independent-testing performance to detect overfitting; using only important (DT-selected) features rather than all features to reduce overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: Manually elevating the importance of the feature at m/z 2410-2417, a previously reported characteristic marker (PSM-mec-related) of SCCmec type II, dramatically improved recognition of type II MRSA isolates.
Generalisability_Details: Authors note ML models should be built with regional/local samples to avoid train-test differences, and recalibrated over time as genotype prevalence shifts.
Maturity_Evidence: Trained on retrospectively collected samples from one hospital and validated only on a temporally later, same-hospital independent test set; no independent-site external validation reported.
Integration_Point: Post species-identification, pre-AST-result laboratory workflow step (MALDI-TOF MS run already performed for ID)
End_User_Described: Laboratory staff (to run the model) and physicians (to act on the resistance prediction)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Once established, running the model requires only a few minutes of laboratory staff time to analyze MS sample data; a positive (resistant) result would indicate anti-MRSA therapy, shortening time to appropriate treatment by 18-24h, while a negative result keeps current therapy pending AST.
Barriers_List: Thorough validation still required before clinical implementation.
Facilitators_List: Minimal additional cost and labor time; feasible integration into existing MALDI-TOF laboratory workflow.
Future_Directions: Post-implementation evaluation and recalibration of models as genotype prevalence changes over time; thorough (e.g. external/regional) validation before clinical implementation.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Decision-tree feature_importances_ (Gini impurity-based)
Limitation_Categories: Clonal/genotype (SCCmec-type) bias in training data composition affecting subgroup accuracy; need for local/regional recalibration.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Reproducibility of MALDI-TOF peak abundance is generally poor because of the crystallization nature of MALDI.

Title: A methodological comparison of risk scores versus decision trees for predicting drug-resistant infections: A case study using extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) bacteremia
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (R36HS025089); Sherrilyn and Ken Fisher Center for Environmental Infectious Diseases; National Institutes of Health (K23-AI127935)
Population_Description: Adults hospitalized at Johns Hopkins Hospital with Escherichia coli or Klebsiella spp bacteremia, 2008-2015; only the first bacteremia episode per patient included; 1,288 patients total, 194 (15%) ESBL-positive.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Infection prevention and control team
All_Models_Evaluated: Logistic regression-derived clinical risk score: 14 variables, naive C statistic 0.87, cross-validated C statistic 0.89, sensitivity 49.5%, specificity 99.5%, PPV 94.6%, NPV 91.8% (at cutoff >=7.25). Machine learning-derived decision tree (CART): 5 variables, C statistic 0.77 (unchanged cross-validated), sensitivity 51.0%, specificity 99.1%, PPV 90.8%, NPV 91.9%.
Best_Performing_Model: Logistic regression-derived clinical risk score (higher C statistic/AUROC than the decision tree)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Full cohort (1,288 patients with E. coli/Klebsiella spp bacteremia), risk score cutoff ≥7.25 points
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Full cohort (1,288 patients), risk score cutoff ≥7.25 points
Specificity_Population_Set: Full cohort (1,288 patients), risk score cutoff ≥7.25 points
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Full cohort (1,288 patients), risk score cutoff ≥7.25 points
AUROC_Population_Set: Full cohort (1,288 patients); cross-validated value from leave-one-out cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were internally validated (leave-one-out cross-validation) at a single center; no external validation cohort, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center study, no external validation cohort; possible missing data for patients treated outside the Epic Care Everywhere network leading to possible exposure misclassification; case study intended as a practical introduction rather than an exhaustive machine-learning comparison.
Reviewer_Notes: Extraction judgement calls: (1) AI_Application_Type/Provider_Facing_Applications coded from the paper's own framing of CART as machine learning and of both models as 'decision support tools'; the resistance-prediction checkbox option (phenotype from genotype/spectra) was not ticked because predictors are clinical/epidemiological, not genomic/spectral. (2) Delivery_Platform coded 'Not yet deployed' because the discussion explicitly says automating the tool into the EHR 'would have been challenging' and the tool is presented as a printable bedside form. (3) Baseline_Comparison coded Yes treating the previously-published decision tree (ref 8, Goodman 2016) as the comparator for the newly derived risk score. (4) Software_Language forced to a single value ('R') though Stata was also used for part of the analysis (noted in Software_Libraries/_notes). (5) Country/WHO Region/Income Classification derived from the Baltimore, Maryland institutional affiliation, since the paper never states 'United States' outright.
Unresolved_Items: Exact number of candidate predictor variables considered before stepwise elimination is not stated (only the final 14 are listed); exact AST platform (e.g., broth microdilution vs automated system) is not named, only the MIC-dilution interpretive criteria.
Sample_Size: 1,288 patients (bacteremic with E. coli or Klebsiella spp)
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: Adults hospitalized at Johns Hopkins Hospital with E. coli or Klebsiella spp bacteremia, 2008-2015; only first episode of bacteremia per patient.
Exclusion_Criteria: Subsequent bacteremia episodes in the same patient were excluded (only the first episode per patient was included).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: Epic Care Everywhere Network (Johns Hopkins Health System electronic medical records)
Dataset_Size: 1,288 patients
Ethnicity_Details: Self-identified Asian race (used as a risk-score predictor variable)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single academic tertiary-care hospital in Baltimore, Maryland; authors note the sample may not generalise to other settings.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood culture (bacteremia)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Likelihood that a bacteremic patient (E. coli or Klebsiella spp) was infected with an ESBL-producing organism
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella spp
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactam antibiotics (excluding carbapenems); third-generation cephalosporins
Specific_Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone (MIC screening); clavulanic acid (combination testing for ESBL confirmation)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotypic definition: ceftriaxone MIC >=2 microg/mL triggered ESBL testing; ESBL confirmed by a decrease of >=3 doubling dilutions in MIC for a third-generation cephalosporin plus clavulanic acid versus the drug tested alone.
AI_Purpose: To develop a logistic-regression risk score from the same ESBL dataset used for a prior decision tree, to compare the two modelling approaches and offer guiding principles for choosing between them.
Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables (e.g., age, antibiotic days) converted to ordinal categories; regression coefficients rescaled to integer point values for the risk score.
Feature_Selection_Method: Stepwise variable selection with backward elimination (alpha = 0.05)
Software_Libraries: RPART (Recursive Partitioning and Regression Trees) package in R; Stata 13.0
Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (calibration); overall classification accuracy at each cutoff; Gini impurity criterion used for tree splitting.
Baseline_Method: Previously published machine learning-derived decision tree (Goodman et al, 2016)
Baseline_Performance: Decision tree: sensitivity 51.0%, specificity 99.1%, PPV 90.8%, NPV 91.9%, naive and cross-validated C statistic 0.77
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: Pruning / branching-stop criteria; internal validation via cross-validation when external testing data are unavailable.
Clinical_Insights: Many risk-score predictors (e.g., antibiotic use, prior ESBL colonization) were also retained in the decision tree, consistent with other MDRGN risk-factor studies.
Generalisability_Details: Authors encourage external validation of the risk score in other patient populations, particularly settings that differ from their single academic tertiary-care hospital.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal (leave-one-out) cross-validation performed; no external validation cohort, so evidence supports internal-validation level only.
Integration_Point: At the time of organism genus and species identification, for bedside use prior to full susceptibility results
End_User_Described: Clinicians and hospital epidemiologists
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Printable bedside risk score applied at the time of organism genus/species identification, before full antimicrobial susceptibility results are available.
Barriers_List: Manual tabulation of 14 variables creates bedside utilisation burden; some variables require clinical judgment or are not hard-coded in the EHR (e.g., infection source, foreign travel entered as free text), making automation challenging.
Facilitators_List: Intuitive, calculation-free decision-tree branching logic; risk score cutoff points are user-adjustable to prioritise sensitivity or specificity.
Future_Directions: Authors encourage others to evaluate and validate the risk score in their own patient populations.
Limitation_Categories: Single-center design; lack of external validation cohort; possible missing/misclassified exposure data for patients treated outside the health system's EHR network.

Title: Rapid identification and discrimination of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus strains via matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: 452 clinical S. aureus isolates (194 MRSA and 258 MSSA), isolated from various clinical specimens at Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital, Chengdu, China, between 2012 and 2018
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: RBF-SVM: Accuracy 0.86, Specificity 0.88, Sensitivity 0.84, AUC 0.89; RF: Accuracy 0.82, Specificity 0.88, Sensitivity 0.74, AUC 0.87 (both on test data)
Best_Performing_Model: RBF-SVM (non-linear SVM with radial basis function kernel) — highest accuracy, sensitivity and AUC of the two models compared
Accuracy_Population_Set: test data
Sensitivity_Population_Set: test data
Specificity_Population_Set: test data
AUROC_Population_Set: test data
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evaluated only via an internal 90%/10% train-test split with repeated ten-fold cross-validation on isolates from one hospital; no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment is described.
Reported_Limitations: A caveat that occurred to us during this study is that the accuracy of the classification was capped around 86%, implying that the classification model needs to be further optimized. On the other hand, the detection range and performance of MALDI-TOF MS deserve further development. As suggested by Van Belkum et al, the validation set and training set should cover the isolates with the widest geographic, temporal, and clonal diversity possible.
Sample_Size: 452 clinical S. aureus isolates (194 MRSA, 258 MSSA)
Conflicts_of_Interest: Not reported
Inclusion_Criteria: clinical S. aureus isolates identified by colony morphology and Vitek MS, collected 2012-2018 at Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital
Exclusion_Criteria: spectra acquired from fewer than 100 laser shots were excluded and the sample re-coated and re-analyzed
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 452 isolates; 2601 unique spectral peaks identified; 134 m/z features retained after alignment and binning
Missing_Data_Method: m/z features with missing intensity values in no more than two-thirds of isolates were selected for the subsequent analysis (features with excessive missingness were excluded)
Geographic_Representativeness: As suggested by Van Belkum et al, the validation set and training set should cover the isolates with the widest geographic, temporal, and clonal diversity possible.
Specimen_Type_Detail: various clinical specimens
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary discrimination of methicillin resistance status (MRSA vs MSSA) in S. aureus isolates using MALDI-TOF MS m/z features and machine-learning classifiers
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA and MSSA strains)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (oxacillin, cefoxitin used to define the methicillin-resistance phenotype)
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin; Cefoxitin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA: Oxacillin Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) > = 4 μg/mL or Cefoxitin Screen (6 μg/mL) positive; MSSA: Oxacillin MIC < = 2 μg/mL and Cefoxitin Screen (6 μg/mL) negative.
AI_Purpose: Our study developed a workflow using a discriminative machine-learning algorithm for rapid MRSA/MSSA classification in minutes based on m/z features employing the MALDI-TOF MS instrumentation routinely available in clinical microbiology laboratories.
Feature_Engineering: similar m/z values (tolerance = 0.002 Da) were binned together across all the isolates to equalize their mass ... The average m/z value within each bin was chosen as a new m/z feature.
Feature_Selection_Method: Lasso regression
Hyperparameter_Method: grid search with (repeated) ten-fold cross-validation used to determine the kernel parameter (γ) and cost parameter (C)
Baseline_Method: Random forest (RF) model
Baseline_Performance: 0.82 accuracy, 0.88 specificity, 0.74 sensitivity, 0.87 AUC (RF, test data)
Internal_Validation: ten-fold cross-validation (repeated ten times) with grid search on the training data; best parameters applied to the held-out test data
Train_Test_Split: 90% training data / 10% test data
Clinical_Insights: some small molecule proteins indicating resistance may exist in this range and can be detected, such as PSM at m/z 2415 that may appear in some MRSA strains. Nevertheless, PSM does not appear in all MRSA strains, but only in a part.
Generalisability_Details: As suggested by Van Belkum et al, the validation set and training set should cover the isolates with the widest geographic, temporal, and clonal diversity possible. Our algorithm can continue to be used in our routine work for optimizing and improving robustness and portability.
Maturity_Evidence: internal 90%/10% train-test split with repeated ten-fold cross-validation; accuracy 0.86 on held-out test data; no external validation or prospective evaluation reported
Integration_Point: our approach can be readily integrated into the database currently used to facilitate subsequent studies into early diagnosis and control of MRSA and MSSA
End_User_Described: routine microbiology laboratories
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The routine data acquisition workflow of Vitek MS in In Vitro Diagnostic (IVD) mode is as follows: (1) Obtain the cultured strain; (2) Coat the strain directly on the target plate; (3) Add the CHCA matrix solution to the surface of the colony; (4) Naturally dry in air; (5) IVD system acquisition; (6) Results output.
Barriers_List: the detection range of MALDI-TOF MS (m/z 2000-20,000) misses high-molecular-weight resistance enzymes such as extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (>27 kDa) and penicillin-binding protein 2A (~76 kDa) — an inevitable defect in the detection of bacterial resistance by MALDI-TOF MS
Facilitators_List: a rapid and easy-to-use method ... easy to implement in routine microbiology laboratories, it suggests a cost-effective and time-efficient alternative to conventional resistance detection
Future_Directions: the classification model needs to be further optimized. On the other hand, the detection range and performance of MALDI-TOF MS deserve further development ... Our algorithm can continue to be used in our routine work for optimizing and improving robustness and portability.
Novel_Predictors_Details: We noticed that a considerable percentage of the m/z features screened out in this work were also mentioned in previous works, such as the peaks at m/z 2288.0 (2288), 2327.4 (2330), 2649.9 (2647), 2865.6 (2867.9), 6574.5 (6576) ... the contribution of these peaks involved in this study may not be completely consistent with previous studies
Limitation_Categories: model accuracy capped around 86% (needs further optimization); MALDI-TOF MS detection range/performance limitations; need for wider geographic, temporal and clonal diversity in validation and training sets
Data_Quality_Concerns: PSM at m/z 2415 does not appear in all MRSA strains, but only in a part, so the absence of characteristic peaks may not be diagnostically informative

Title:
AI-based mobile application to ﬁght antibiotic
resistance
AI_Application_Type: AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: the Medecins Sans Frontieres Foundation, the Laboratoire de Mathematiques et Modelisation d'Evry, the Genoscope, the bacteriology laoratory of the Universitary Hospital Henri Mondor, Creteil France; 2019 Google AI Impact Challenge (Google.org)
Population_Description: AST groups A1 and A2 consist of 571 and 74 antibiograms prepared during working routine in the microbiology laboratory of the University Hospital in Creteil, France (samples collected from hospital patients); AST set A3 consists of eight Petri dishes inoculated with ATCC reference strains, prepared at the MSF Hospital in Amman, Jordan.

ML models for resistance-mechanism detection (proof-of-concept, not incorporated into final App): accuracy higher than 99.7% for induction (MLSb-inducible resistance) and 98% for synergy indicative of ESBL production.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Antibiotic disk label classification, AST sets A1 and A2
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The App's automatic procedure was tested on an independent set (A3) acquired at a different institution/country (MSF Hospital, Amman, Jordan) with different hardware and operators than the development site; the App is not yet released or in routine clinical use, pending CE certification.
Reported_Limitations: Difficulty obtaining constant image quality with smartphone hardware/software (cannot standardize acquisition to the level of dedicated commercial hardware); small training sets for the resistance-mechanism CNN models raising overfitting risk.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Classification errors in automatic resistance-mechanism detection can have very serious consequences for AST interpretation and patient treatment, so the App requires user confirmation before acting on such automatic detections.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Release of the App as open-source software is being withheld pending CE-mark certification as a clinical device (IVDD Directive 98/79), because distributing an uncertified medical device could expose the legal manufacturer (Fondation MSF) to legal pursuit in France.
Sample_Size: 570 antibiograms (Petri dish plates) / 8168 antibiotic disks (AST set A1, primary/largest dataset)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Exclusion_Criteria: Antibiotics for which a breakpoint was not provided are excluded.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Imaging
Data_Source_Name: Custom AST image dataset (Pascucci et al.; available at http://stat.genopole.cnrs.fr/ast.zip); SIRscan (i2a) used as reference/control system
Dataset_Size: A1: 570 plates / 8168 antibiotic disks; A2: 75 plates / 649 antibiotic disks; A3: 8 plates / 98 antibiotic disks
Specimen_Type_Detail: Disk-diffusion antibiogram (Petri dish culture); AST plates prepared on Mueller-Hinton or blood-enriched Mueller-Hinton agar
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic susceptibility categorization (Susceptible/Intermediate/Resistant) of the tested antibiotics, from automatic reading of disk-diffusion inhibition zone diameters
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Klebsiella pneumoniae (carbapenemase producer; SHV-18-ESBL producer); Escherichia coli (fluoroquinolone susceptible); Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus; Enterococcus faecalis (vancomycin-sensitive; gentamicin-resistant) — named for AST set A3; species distribution for A1/A2 shown only in Fig. 5, not enumerated in running text.
Num_Pathogens: 6 (named species in AST set A3; full species distribution for A1/A2 is shown only in Fig. 5)
Specific_Antibiotics: Clindamycin (macrolide-inducible resistance / MLSb detection) and antibiotics associated with Extended-Spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production; the full antibiotic panel tested in AST sets A1-A3 is not individually enumerated in the text.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary S/I/R categorization determined by comparing the measured inhibition zone diameter to EUCAST clinical breakpoints
AI_Purpose: Automate image-based reading and interpretation of disk-diffusion antibiotic susceptibility tests on a smartphone, reducing inter-operator variability and enabling AST in resource-limited settings.

Hardware_Details: PC with a 2.3 GHz Intel Core i5 processor (<1 s per antibiogram); high-end smartphone Pixel 3 (1.5 s); low-end smartphone Samsung A10 (6.6 s), for a 12-megapixel picture with 16 antibiotic disks.
Other_Metrics: Agreement (%) and disagreement (very-major/major/minor, %) between the App's automatic susceptibility categorization and the control; unweighted Cohen's kappa as a further agreement measure
Baseline_Method: Commercial automated zone reader (SIRscan, i2a) for A1/A2; manual ruler measurement by eight lab technicians for A3
Baseline_Performance: Not a separate performance figure — SIRscan/manual measurements served as the reference standard against which the App's agreement (Table 2) was computed
External_Validation_Description: AST set A3: eight Petri dishes inoculated with ATCC/NCTC reference strains, prepared and imaged at the MSF Hospital, Amman, Jordan, by eight independent laboratory technicians using a different smartphone (Samsung A10) than sets A1/A2 (Honor 6x, Creteil, France).
Overfitting_Method: The two resistance-mechanism CNN models were excluded from the deployed App because of the small training sets and consequent overfitting risk
Generalisability_Details: The resistance-mechanism detection models were not incorporated into the App partly because the authors were not confident the models would generalize; they may reconsider inclusion in a future version if the models can be generalized to a larger and more diverse dataset.
Maturity_Evidence: The App's automatic reading procedure was benchmarked on an independent set (A3) collected at a different site/country by different operators/hardware than the development data, which supports external validation; no evidence of prospective clinical deployment or routine use is reported.
Integration_Point: Used by laboratory technicians at the bench, immediately after AST plate incubation, to replace/assist manual reading of the antibiogram
End_User_Described: Laboratory technicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Petri dish photographed with a smartphone in a simple cardboard acquisition setup; the plate image is cropped and the antibiotic disks are found; each disk image is fed to a ML model that identifies the antibiotic; the inhibition-zone diameter is measured with an original algorithm; the Expert System uses the diameters to output interpreted results.
Stewardship_Details: The App will support selective reporting of antibiotic sensitivity, described as a future antimicrobial-stewardship-strategy component (not yet evaluated for impact)
Barriers_List: Price, hardware and infrastructure requirements of commercial automatic AST readers unsuited to resource-limited settings
Facilitators_List: Smartphone applications are easy to adopt if they follow established design patterns and benefit from an ecosystem that facilitates setup and updates; the acquisition setup is inexpensive and easy to integrate into laboratory routine; the App works fully offline.
Future_Directions: Further clinical investigations using the App in MSF hospitals to estimate patient benefit; open-source release of the App pending CE-authority approval as a clinical device; contributing data to global AMR surveillance bodies (WHO GLASS and/or WHONET); maintaining a list of recommended smartphone devices; possible future reconsideration of resistance-mechanism detection models if they can be generalized to a larger, more diverse dataset.

Integration_Point: Point-of-care alert: baseline model runs at hospital admission; dynamic/real-time model continuously monitors high-risk patients during antibiotic therapy and triggers a clinician alert when predicted risk is high.
End_User_Described: Doctors / clinicians

Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search

Title: Prediction of Multidrug-Resistant TB from CT Pulmonary Images Based on Deep Learning Techniques
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Imaging Analysis
Population_Description: While there are 444 subject data sets in total with 230 for training and 214 for testing, only the training sets of 230 subjects (with 134 of DS and 96 of MDR) have known ground truth.

All_Models_Evaluated: CNN + orderless pooling + SVM + slice: 64.71% (subject); CNN + patch (Softmax): 79.30% patch / 84.44% subject; Alexnet with Softmax + patch: 79.65% patch / 91.11% subject; dense SIFT + SVM + patch: 83.56% patch / 88.88% subject; CNN + SVM + patch: 79.80% patch / 91.11% subject.

Reported_Limitations: Small test set (45 subjects, only 7 MDR); the official ImageCLEF test set's ground truth is unknown so results are not directly comparable; recommend embedding medical knowledge of MDR disease patterns and considering 3D segments (rather than 2D patches) to further improve accuracy.

Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing financial interest.

Data_Types_Used: Imaging
Data_Source_Name: ImageCLEF 2017 Tuberculosis Task (CLEF 2017)
Dataset_Size: 230 subjects (134 DS, 96 MDR) with known ground truth, 11,366 patches total (Table 2)
Specimen_Type_Detail: 3D CT lung (pulmonary) images
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of tuberculosis as multidrug-resistant (MDR) vs drug-sensitive (DS) based on CT pulmonary images.

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR

Feature_Selection_Method: Manual (and semi-automatic SIFT-assisted) selection of lesioned vs normal patches
Class_Imbalance_Method: Random subsampling of DS (majority class) patches to balance with MDR patches

Other_Metrics: Accuracy rate (%) is the only performance metric reported, at both patch level and subject level, per class (DS/MDR) and averaged, across all five compared methods (Tables 3-6).

Baseline_Performance: 88.88% (subject), 83.56% (patch)
Internal_Validation: Hold-out split into training / validation / testing subsets (150 / 35 / 45 subjects; Table 2)
Train_Test_Split: Training 150 subjects (8000 patches); validation 35 subjects (1346 patches); testing 45 subjects (2020 patches)

Best_Performing_Model: AMRQuest (logistic regression model) -- highest AUC (0.979), sensitivity (98.7%) and specificity (97.7%) among all models compared

Sensitivity_Population_Set: 537 S. aureus isolates (231 MRSA, 306 MSSA), testing set
Specificity_Population_Set: 537 S. aureus isolates (231 MRSA, 306 MSSA), testing set
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 537 S. aureus isolates, testing set
AUROC_Population_Set: 537 S. aureus isolates (231 MRSA, 306 MSSA), testing set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Independent training (927 isolates) and testing (537 isolates) sets; prospective, randomized, single-blind clinical evaluation across three tertiary-care hospitals following the Korean regulatory in-vitro-diagnostic clinical-performance evaluation guideline.

Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing financial interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: S. aureus isolates from clinical blood cultures at three tertiary-care hospitals, with methicillin susceptibility determined by MIC (oxacillin/cefoxitin), cefoxitin disk diffusion, or mecA gene detection.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: Training set: 927 isolates (430 MRSA, 497 MSSA); Testing set: 537 isolates (231 MRSA, 306 MSSA)
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates were collected from three tertiary-care hospitals in Seoul/Seongnam, Republic of Korea; authors note further evaluation is needed on isolates from various regions.
Specimen_Type_Detail: S. aureus isolates from clinical blood cultures
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary classification of S. aureus isolates as MRSA or MSSA via the AMRQuest score (cutoff >=0.5 = MRSA), benchmarked against the cefoxitin disk diffusion reference test.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus
Specific_Antibiotics: Oxacillin; Cefoxitin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA defined per CLSI: MIC >=4 ug/mL (oxacillin) or >=8 ug/mL (cefoxitin), cefoxitin disk diffusion inhibition zone <=21 mm, or mecA gene detection.
AI_Purpose: To rapidly screen S. aureus isolates for methicillin resistance directly from MALDI-TOF mass spectra via a machine-learning score, avoiding the multi-day turnaround of conventional culture-based AST.
Feature_Engineering: Mass spectra processed via quality control, smoothing, baseline correction, intensity calibration and peak detection; feature matrix built by binning spectra into m/z ranges of 5 across m/z 2,000-20,000.
Other_Metrics: Cohen's kappa coefficient = 0.96
Baseline_Method: Cefoxitin disk diffusion test (reference/standard method)
Baseline_Performance: Jeon et al. (2022) -- previous RF-based version of AMRQuest: sensitivity 91.8%, specificity 83.3%, AUC 0.876
Internal_Validation: 4:1 random train/test split of the training-set binned spectra used to train the logistic regression model
Train_Test_Split: 4:1 (training:testing) split of training-set spectra; independent 537-isolate testing set used for final clinical evaluation
External_Validation_Description: Independent testing set of 537 S. aureus isolates (231 MRSA, 306 MSSA) from three tertiary-care hospitals, separate from the 927-isolate training set.
Clinical_Insights: Top SHAP/ANOVA m/z features corresponded to known MRSA biomarkers (PSM-mec peptide, formylated delta-toxin, 50S ribosomal proteins L30/L32/L36, DNA-binding protein HU); several unidentified features suggest additional or modified biomarkers linked to methicillin resistance.
Generalisability_Details: Authors note further evaluation is needed on isolates from various regions, and that AMRQuest's applicability to methicillin resistance in species other than S. aureus has not been validated (it was trained only on S. aureus).
Maturity_Evidence: Independent training/testing sets; prospective, randomized, single-blind, multi-site clinical evaluation following a national IVD clinical-performance evaluation guideline; consistent PPV/NPV across all three sites.
Integration_Point: Embedded directly within the MicroIDSys LT MALDI-TOF MS bacterial identification system; MRSA screening runs on the same spectrum immediately after species identification.
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratories / laboratory personnel operating the MALDI-TOF MS identification system
Clinical_Workflow_Details: AMRQuest screening is completed within a few seconds immediately after MALDI-TOF MS bacterial identification, versus >1 day for conventional phenotypic AST (broth microdilution, disk diffusion, modified Hodge test, automated devices) or 2-4 h for SCCmec-based molecular testing.
Stewardship_Details: Faster MRSA detection is discussed as potentially enabling faster treatment and reducing unnecessary antimicrobial overuse, but this stewardship benefit was not directly measured.
Facilitators_List: AMRQuest is designed as a software module that reuses the MALDI-TOF spectra already acquired during routine bacterial identification, requiring no additional MALDI processing step.
Future_Directions: Expand AMRQuest to other bacterial species and other antimicrobial-resistance testing algorithms (with algorithm assignment based on bacterial identification); further studies on causes of cefoxitin/AMRQuest discrepancies and unidentified biomarker features.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) and ANOVA
Novel_Predictors_Details: 13 of the top 20 SHAP-ranked m/z feature ranges have not yet been identified as known biomarkers, suggesting additional or modified MRSA-associated biomarkers.
Limitation_Categories: Insufficient discrepant cases for root-cause analysis; limited regional/geographic coverage; not validated for non-S. aureus species; software trained only on S. aureus.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Only 8 discrepant cases (cefoxitin vs AMRQuest) were available for SCCmec-based root-cause analysis, which the authors say was insufficient to determine the cause of false positives/negatives.
Reporting_Clarity: Generally well-structured with a detailed comparative Table 1, but PPV/NPV values for the testing set differ slightly between the Results (97.4%/99.7%) and Discussion (97.4%/99.6%) without explanation.
Page_References: pp. 15667-15675 (PDF pp. 1-9 of the extracted text layer)

Unresolved_Items: Prediction of multidrug resistance is flagged by the authors as an unaddressed avenue for future work.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Exclusion_Criteria: Entries with missing MIC/AMR interpretation values were excluded during downstream processing, as their absence reflects susceptibility testing not performed rather than random omission.

Missing_Data_Method: 'NA' placeholder for missing MIC/AMR interpretation values; not imputed, excluded during downstream processing

Specimen_Type_Detail: Sources such as urine, blood, or respiratory (specimen source variable)

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Other
