Maturity_Evidence: No external validation performed; only internal cross-validation, per the study's own limitations statement.
Integration_Point: Electronic health record (EHR) system, at the point of culture collection/processing
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed (not implemented) workflow: as soon as a culture is collected and processed, EHR-integrated models would analyze the data in real time and provide insights such as identifying potential pathogens or antibiotic resistance patterns.
Future_Directions: Further dissemination of the findings is described as crucial to ensure broader implementation and adoption in healthcare systems (implicitly alongside the need for external validation flagged in the Limitations).
Novel_Predictors_Details: Discussion explicitly frames the identified risk factors as similar to those previously reported for non-surgical ICU patients, not as novel/unexpected predictors.
Feature_Interactions_Method: No explicit interaction-term analysis reported; the authors state ANN was chosen (over regression alone) specifically for its capacity to detect complex non-linear relationships and 'all possible interactions between predictor variables' — a methodological rationale rather than a reported set of identified interactions.
Limitation_Categories: External validation / generalisability (single-dataset limitation)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients with incomplete information were excluded prior to analysis; also, the Results section reports control patients as ‘63.10% (1190/4542)’, which is inconsistent with Table 1's control total of 2866 (1676 cases + 2866 controls = 4542) — an apparent reporting error in the source, noted but not corrected.

Title: Clinical predictors of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pyogenic liver abscess and nomogram construction: A retrospective analysis
Population_Description: 268 patients diagnosed with Gram-negative pyogenic liver abscess (PLA) at a single major healthcare facility (The Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University), January 2019 to February 2025.
Top_Predictive_Features: Nomogram point scoring (derived from multivariate stepwise regression coefficients): malignant tumor (53 pts) > age >=60 years (26 pts) > diabetes (19 pts) > CRP (11 pts per 50 mg/L decrease) > PT (7 pts per 5 seconds increase).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Multivariate stepwise logistic regression nomogram (single model): AUROC 0.769 (95%CI 0.675-0.857), sensitivity 82.1%, specificity 76.5% at the optimal (Youden-index) cutoff.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Full derivation cohort (n = 268), at the optimal cutoff (65.4% predicted probability)
Specificity_Population_Set: Full derivation cohort (n = 268), at the optimal cutoff (65.4% predicted probability)
AUROC_Population_Set: Full derivation cohort (n = 268)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal bootstrap-validated calibration and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit testing were performed on the single-center derivation cohort; the authors state explicitly that no external validation was done.
Reported_Limitations: Unmeasured host factors (chronic malnutrition, prior antibiotic exposure, cellular immune competence) may modulate MDR susceptibility beyond the identified predictors.
Conflicts_of_Interest: All the authors report no relevant conflicts of interest for this article.
Sex_Distribution: Male sex: 181/268 (67.54%) overall; 67/105 (63.81%) MDR group; 114/163 (69.94%) non-MDR group.
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) Clinical symptoms such as fever and abdominal pain; (2) imaging confirmation via ultrasound or CT; (3) microbiological verification through blood or pus cultures; (4) abscess confirmation via percutaneous biopsy or surgical intervention.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with amebic or tuberculous liver abscesses, other non-bacterial abscesses, or incomplete medical records were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 268 patients; 278 pathogenic isolates
Missing_Data_Method: Random forest imputation
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary-referral center in East China; authors note the K. pneumoniae-predominant cohort (72.7%) reflects regional epidemiology and may not generalise to regions where E. coli predominates.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood and drainage fluid (pus) cultures
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacterial infection status (MDR vs non-resistant), classified by antibiotic susceptibility profile.
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae; Escherichia coli; Serratia spp.; Enterobacter cloacae; Klebsiella aerogenes; Enterobacter asburiae; Morganella morganii; Klebsiella variicola; Klebsiella oxytoca; Acinetobacter baumannii; Pseudomonas spp.
Drug_Classes: Third-generation cephalosporins; aztreonam (monobactam); carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem)
Specific_Antibiotics: Carbapenems and beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations (broad-spectrum antibiotics recommended above the risk threshold)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR defined as resistance to at least three antimicrobial classes, classified from antibiotic susceptibility profiles into MDR vs non-resistant groups.
AI_Purpose: Develop a predictive nomogram for personalised MDR-GNB risk assessment to enhance the timeliness of empirical antibiotic selection.
Feature_Engineering: CRP was analysed as a continuous variable (not dichotomised) to preserve full statistical information and predictive power.
Feature_Selection_Method: Multivariate stepwise regression with backward elimination, from variables significant on univariate analysis.
Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit (P = 0.777); bootstrap-validated calibration mean absolute error = 0.017; variance inflation factors (collinearity), 1.08-1.48.
Internal_Validation: Bootstrap-validated calibration and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test
Clinical_Insights: The counterintuitive inverse association between lower CRP and MDR-GNB infection is interpreted as reflecting an immunocompromised state prevalent in the MDR cohort.
Generalisability_Details: Single-center study without external validation; K. pneumoniae-predominant cohort reflects East China regional epidemiology and may not generalise to E. coli-predominant regions.
Maturity_Evidence: Bootstrap-validated calibration (mean absolute error = 0.017) and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit testing (P = 0.777) on the single-center derivation cohort; no external or prospective evaluation performed.
Integration_Point: Proposed (not implemented) integration as a clinical decision support module within EHR systems, or as a bedside scorecard in resource-limited settings.
End_User_Described: Healthcare providers
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed risk-threshold tailoring by care setting (lower threshold in tertiary hospitals to maximise sensitivity; higher threshold in primary care to prioritise specificity), with future EHR-embedded CDS or a simplified bedside scorecard in resource-limited settings.
Future_Directions: Future multicentre, multi-ethnic, prospective studies are needed to externally validate and extend the nomogram; further investigation of resistance-gene transmission and host-pathogen interactions is recommended.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Nomogram point-scoring derived from multivariate stepwise logistic regression coefficients
Novel_Predictors_Details: Lower CRP levels were counterintuitively associated with MDR-GNB infection, attributed to an immunocompromised state in the MDR cohort.
Limitation_Categories: Unmeasured confounders; single-center/retrospective design and selection bias; lack of external validation; limited pathogen-distribution generalisability.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Unmeasured host factors (chronic malnutrition, prior antibiotic exposure, cellular immune competence) not captured in the dataset.

Title: Evaluating antimicrobial resistance and clinical outcomes in surgical ICU using a machine learning perspective: a retrospective observational study
Population_Description: 106 postoperative patients admitted to the surgical ICU, predominantly male (63.2%), median age 66 years (IQR 50.5-78.0); most common comorbidities hypertension (33.7%) and diabetes mellitus (26.9%), followed by gastrointestinal cancer (14.4%) and ischemic heart disease (13.2%).
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP-ranked predictors (mean absolute SHAP value): Gram-negative infection (1.76), Gram-positive infection (1.36), length of therapy/LOT (1.31), age (1.14), total hospitalization period (0.87), total number of antibiotics used (0.48); bowel perforation had negligible impact (0.00).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: XGBoost: test ROC-AUC 0.786, mean CV AUC 0.896 +/- 0.05, 70% accuracy, macro F1-score 0.70. LR baseline: test AUC 0.743, 77% accuracy, higher sensitivity but lower specificity.
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (chosen over the logistic-regression baseline on cross-validation/test ROC-AUC and 'superior discriminative ability', despite lower raw test-set accuracy: 70% vs LR's 77%)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Held-out test set (n = 22)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Held-out test set (n = 22), class 1 (resistant isolates)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Held-out test set (n = 22), class 1 (resistant isolates)
F1_Population_Set: Held-out test set (n = 22), macro-averaged across classes
AUROC_Population_Set: Held-out test set (n = 22)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: 80%/20% train/test split (stratified by outcome) plus five-fold cross-validation on the single 106-patient cohort; no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Single tertiary-centre design in southern Iran limiting generalisability (compounded by an unusually high 91.5% mortality rate); microbiological features intentionally excluded to avoid data leakage, potentially reducing predictive precision; retrospective design and EHR reliance may have introduced information bias or incomplete data capture; small sample size and limited test set (n=22) increase overfitting risk and reduce model stability; absence of external validation restricts applicability; larger multicentre datasets incorporating molecular data are needed.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The model's recall for MDR/XDR cases (0.71) emphasises identification of high-risk patients, but the precision for non-resistant cases (0.60) indicates a higher rate of false positives; this trade-off may lead to unnecessary interventions.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No governance risks beyond standard ethics oversight are discussed; IRB approval (IR.SUMS.MED.REC.1403.267) and adherence to the Declaration of Helsinki are reported.
Reviewer_Notes: Single-centre retrospective cohort (Namazi Hospital, Shiraz, Iran; Jan 2022-Dec 2023) of 106 postoperative surgical ICU patients predicting patient-level clinically-significant AMR (MDR/XDR) with XGBoost (Optuna-tuned) vs a logistic-regression baseline; SHAP used for global feature importance; no external validation, no fairness/equity assessment, no deployment.
Unresolved_Items: Whether XGBoost (higher AUC, lower raw accuracy) or LR (lower AUC, higher raw accuracy 77%) should be coded as the 'best-performing model' for this review's unit of analysis.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients (>= 18 years) admitted to the surgical ICU post-surgery were included.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with incomplete microbiological culture or antibiogram data were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 106 patients (primary modelling dataset)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre cohort from a tertiary hospital in southern Iran; authors state findings may not generalise to other institutions, particularly developed countries with different demographics/AMR patterns/healthcare practices.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Organisms identified from clinical specimens such as blood, sputum, wound swabs, and urine.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary outcome: clinically significant antimicrobial resistance (patient has at least one MDR/XDR isolate) vs not (including culture-negative patients).
Pathogens: E. coli, Acinetobacter (baumannii), Klebsiella (pneumoniae), Enterococcus spp., Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, folate pathway inhibitors, beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, carbapenems, fourth-generation cephalosporins, glycopeptides, polymyxins, oxazolidinones, nitrofurans, macrolides, tetracyclines, lincosamides.
Specific_Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, cefotaxime, gentamicin, amikacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, piperacillin/tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, imipenem, meropenem, cefepime, ceftazidime.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; XDR; PDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR: non-susceptibility to >=1 agent in >=3 antimicrobial categories; XDR: non-susceptibility to all agents except <=2 antimicrobial categories; PDR: non-susceptibility to all agents in all tested categories (Magiorakos et al. 2012 framework).
AI_Purpose: To develop a machine learning model to predict resistance based on patient-level data, thereby informing clinical decision-making.
Feature_Engineering: Antimicrobial-Free Days (AFD) engineered as total hospital length of stay (LOS) minus Length of Therapy (LOT), representing days without antibiotic administration.
Feature_Selection_Method: Features with zero SHAP values were removed for XGBoost, and variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis (threshold <=10) was employed for logistic regression to mitigate multicollinearity, ensuring robust model performance.
Hyperparameter_Method: Optuna (100 trials)
Software_Libraries: Python 3.8 with unnamed libraries; named tools: XGBoost, Optuna (hyperparameter tuning), SHAP (feature importance)
Other_Metrics: LR confusion matrix reported: 4 true negatives, 5 false positives, 0 false negatives, 13 true positives.
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (LR)
Baseline_Performance: Test AUC 0.743, test accuracy 77% (vs XGBoost test AUC 0.786, accuracy 70%)
Internal_Validation: 80% training / 20% test split (stratified by outcome) plus five-fold cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% test set, stratified by outcome
Clinical_Insights: Gram-negative (1.76) and Gram-positive (1.36) infections, followed by length of therapy (LOT) (1.31) and age (1.14), exhibited the highest mean absolute SHAP values.
Data_Repository: Not a named external repository; dataset provided as Additional file 3 (supplementary material) within the article
Generalisability_Details: Single-centre design in southern Iran, coupled with unusually high mortality (91.5%), limits generalisability to other ICUs; lack of external validation further restricts applicability.
Maturity_Evidence: 80/20 train-test split stratified by outcome, plus five-fold cross-validation, on the single 106-patient cohort; no external validation or prospective evaluation reported.
Future_Directions: Further research is needed to refine predictive performance, integrate molecular resistance data, and evaluate generalisability in larger, multicentre cohorts; future studies should clarify the AMR-outcome relationship in broader, less selective populations to inform clinical management and stewardship strategies.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mean absolute SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) value
Feature_Interactions_Method: SHAP interaction analysis (SHAP plots visualising global feature importance and interactions)
Limitation_Categories: Generalisability (single centre, high mortality); data-leakage/predictive-precision trade-off (microbiological features excluded); information bias (retrospective/EHR reliance); small sample size and overfitting risk; absence of external validation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: The retrospective design and reliance on electronic medical records may have introduced information bias or incomplete data capture, potentially affecting model performance.
Page_References: BMC Infect Dis 25:1434 (16 pp.): Abstract p.1; Introduction pp.1-2; Methods pp.3-4; Results pp.4-9; Discussion pp.9-14; Limitations/Conclusion p.14; Declarations pp.15-16.

Title: The Gut Resistome Atlas in Preterm Infants Enables Prediction of Necrotizing Enterocolitis Onset
Country_Countries: United States, United Kingdom, Finland, China, Russia, Estonia, Luxembourg
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: National Key Research and Development Program; National Natural Science Foundation of China; Department of Science and Technology of Sichuan Province; Fundamental Research Funds for the Central University; Sanming Project of Medicine in Shenzhen
Population_Description: 98 preterm infants who developed NEC (cases, n=1168 samples) and 285 preterm infants free of NEC (controls, n=3012 samples), matched for gestational age, delivery mode, feeding pattern, and antibiotic exposure history before sampling
Age_Mean_Median: median gestational age 28.0 weeks (IQR 25.9-31.0 weeks); median age at sampling 25 days (IQR 15-45 days)
Data_Source_Other: Public metagenomic sequencing repository (NCBI SRA)
Top_Predictive_Features: Three subtypes of multidrug__mdtK, multidrug__msbA, and MLS_macB were the most predictive; other top-10 subtypes included beta-lactam_ACT-17, beta_lactam__K. pneumoniae OmpK37, polymyxin__pmrF, and multidrug__acrF
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest trained on ARG subtypes (AU-ROC=0.823, 95% CI 0.819-0.834); bacterial species (AU-ROC=0.727, 95% CI 0.696-0.728); combined ARG subtypes+bacterial species (AU-ROC=0.798, 95% CI 0.797-0.815) - all evaluated in the external validation preterm birth cohort
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest model trained on gut resistome (ARG subtype) abundance features
AUROC_Population_Set: External validation preterm birth cohort
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model was trained on six public cohorts and evaluated on an independent, prospectively sampled external preterm-birth validation cohort (AU-ROC=0.823); no evidence of prospective clinical deployment or CDS integration is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Limited sample size of case infants in the meta-cohorts (n=98) and validation cohort (n=9); NEC-associated ARG features identified in silico and not validated with experimental techniques (e.g. quantitative PCR) due to inadequate DNA amounts
Sample_Size: 34 pre-NEC samples from 9 cases and 37 matched samples from 16 controls (external validation cohort)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Stool metagenomic sequencing data from preterm infants (<37 gestational weeks) from birth to three years old (up to March 2023)
Exclusion_Criteria: Samples that did not correctly match the metadata were removed
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Environmental / metagenomic
Data_Source_Name: Genome Sequence Archive, National Genomics Data Center, China (GSA-Human: HRA005473; GSA: CRA015134); public data from NCBI SRA; code on GitHub
Dataset_Size: 5684 stool metagenomic samples from 682 preterm infants
Geographic_Representativeness: 19 cohorts, geographically distributed in seven countries over three continents
Specimen_Type_Detail: stool samples (fecal metagenomes)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Gut resistome (ARG) composition and abundance used as an indicator to predict necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) onset
Pathogens: Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Streptococcus, Enterobacter, Escherichia (predominant ARG-harbouring genera); ESKAPEE species (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter spp., Escherichia coli)
Num_Pathogens: 6 predominant ARG-harbouring genera (plus additional ESKAPEE and other species named)
Drug_Classes: tetracycline, beta-lactam, erythromycin, streptogramin, streptogramin B, fosfomycin, clindamycin, lincosamide, quinolone, cephalosporin, phenicol, kanamycin, tylosin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistome defined as ARG type/subtype abundance, normalised as copies of ARGs per prokaryote's cell (capc)
AI_Purpose: To use the gut resistome as a machine-learning-based tool to prescreen/predict NEC onset before it occurs in preterm infants
Feature_Engineering: Model features were raw abundance profiles of ARG subtypes (n=1633), bacterial species (n=515), or their combination (n=2148); no additional engineered features described
Num_Features_Total: 1633 ARG subtypes; 515 bacterial species; 2148 combined
Hyperparameter_Method: mtry parameter tuned from 1 to the total number of features present in samples; 500 estimator trees
Baseline_Method: Random forest model trained on bacterial species abundance alone (instead of ARG subtypes)
Internal_Validation: Bootstrapping (100 iterations) on training features for significance testing
Train_Test_Split: Trained on six public studies (BrooksB_2017, LouYC_2024, MasiAC_2021, RahmanSF_2018, RavehSadkaT_2016, ThanertR_2024); tested on an independent external validation cohort
External_Validation_Description: Independent preterm birth cohort recruited at three NICUs in Guangdong province, China (2021-2022); 9 NEC cases (34 samples) and 16 controls (37 samples), sampled prospectively and longitudinally
Clinical_Insights: Monitoring the trend or specificity of ARGs in the gut of preterm infants holds potential as a reliable proxy to support clinical prediction of NEC and treatments (e.g. guiding antibiotic administration)
Data_Repository: Genome Sequence Archive, National Genomics Data Center, China (GSA-Human: HRA005473; GSA: CRA015134); GitHub: https://github.com/Biofarmer/ELGR
Generalisability_Details: Further investigations from multi-center studies with larger sample sizes are necessary to refine the predictive model
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed on an independent, prospectively-sampled preterm birth cohort (AU-ROC=0.823); model not integrated into a clinical workflow or CDS system
End_User_Described: Clinicians (guiding antibiotic administration decisions)
Stewardship_Details: Findings emphasize the need for local resistome profiling to guide targeted (rather than broad-spectrum) antimicrobial therapy and improve antibiotic stewardship in the NICU
Barriers_List: Limited case sample size (n=98 discovery; n=9 validation); NEC-associated ARGs identified in silico without experimental (e.g. qPCR) validation due to inadequate DNA amounts

Title: Exploring multidrug resistance patterns in community-acquired Escherichia coli urinary tract infections with machine learning
Funder_Names: Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR), project ANR-22-PAMR-0003 (COMBINE)
Population_Description: E. coli isolates from community-acquired urinary tract infection (UTI) cases collected by France's PRIMO national surveillance system of clinical laboratories, 2018-2022.
Data_Source: Laboratory information system; Other national / population survey
Task_Type_Other: Association-rule / frequent-pattern mining (Apriori algorithm) to detect co-resistance patterns, plus network analysis of the resulting resistance associations
All_Models_Evaluated: Association-set mining via the Apriori algorithm: for ESBL-EC, 52,824 patterns identified in 2018 rising to 123,116 patterns in 2022, subsequently pruned by eSup/cLift significance thresholds.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The method's robustness was checked only with internal sensitivity analyses (regional-proportion reweighting and a stricter antibiotic-selection criterion) on the same national data set; no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or clinical/CDS deployment was reported.
Reported_Limitations: Seven numbered limitations are reported, including that the PRIMO surveillance system covers only community clinical laboratories and its representativeness of the total community-acquired E. coli UTI population in France cannot be fully guaranteed.
Sample_Size: 360,287 E. coli community-acquired UTI isolates in 2018 rising to 628,993 in 2022 (PRIMO surveillance, France)
Conflicts_of_Interest: G.B. reports receiving grants from Santé Publique France during the conduct of the study. None of the other authors report any conflict of interest.
Sex_Distribution: 84.0%-84.5% of isolates came from women across the study years
Inclusion_Criteria: AST results from E. coli urine samples collected in community laboratories, 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2022, excluding nursing homes.
Exclusion_Criteria: Carbapenemase-producing isolates were excluded from the analysis as their low frequency of testing did not allow for a robust analysis of their specific multiresistance patterns.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: PRIMO (Surveillance and Prevention of Antibiotic Resistance in Primary Care and Nursing Homes), France
Missing_Data_Method: Simulated null-hypothesis datasets were matched to the observed data in size, resistance prevalence, and positions of missing AST results; eSup/cLift quality measures were used to account for missing data rather than imputation.
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates came from all regions of metropolitan France, with varying proportions across the years; a sensitivity analysis reweighted regions proportional to population to test robustness.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine samples (community-acquired E. coli UTI isolates)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug resistance (MDR) association patterns among antibiotic resistance traits in E. coli, expressed via expected support (eSup) and conditional lift (cLift) of resistance patterns used to build resistance-association networks.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli
Drug_Classes: Penicillins (± beta-lactamase inhibitors), cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and cotrimoxazole (sulfonamide-trimethoprim combination)
Specific_Antibiotics: Cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime (among 27 antibiotics tested overall)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Isolates categorised Susceptible / Susceptible-increased-exposure / Resistant per antibiotic according to EUCAST breakpoints (Susceptible-increased-exposure grouped with Resistant for analysis).
AI_Purpose: To detect and characterise non-random multidrug-resistance (co-resistance) patterns among antibiotic resistance traits in community-acquired E. coli UTI isolates using a machine-learning association-mining approach.
Feature_Engineering: MDR patterns decomposed into pairwise antibiotic-resistance associations (e.g., {A,B,C} to {A,B}, {B,C}, {A,C}) to construct network edges.
Feature_Selection_Method: Apriori pattern pruning using eSup (expected support) and cLift (conditional lift) thresholds set at the 95th percentile of values obtained from simulated mutual-independence null datasets.
Num_Features_Selected: 27 antibiotics
Other_Metrics: Network density; expected support (eSup); conditional lift (cLift); rule overlap ratio (ROR); cumulative rule stability (CRS); Kolmogorov-Smirnov test statistic; Pearson/Mann-Kendall trend-test P-values.
Baseline_Method: Simulated datasets generated under the null hypothesis that all antibiotic resistance traits are mutually independent (independent binomial random variables matching observed prevalence), used as the comparator for detecting non-random resistance associations.
Baseline_Performance: In 2022, the observed distribution of resistance counts per isolate differed significantly from the simulated independence baseline (P = 6.81x10-3, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test); 39% of isolates were pansusceptible in the observed data vs 9% in the simulated data.
Generalisability_Details: Results are valid for E. coli isolates only, and not for other Enterobacterales, potentially limiting their generalisability.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal robustness/sensitivity analyses only (regional reweighting, stricter antibiotic-selection criterion); no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment reported.
Future_Directions: Future research could use other machine learning approaches to further analyse the PRIMO data sets and get a deeper understanding of resistance associations; extending the approach to other pathogens and linking phenotypic associations to genotypic co-resistance mechanisms are also suggested.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Men-specific resistance-association networks showed additional associations involving cefuroxime, an unexpected finding the authors link to cefuroxime's use as surgical prophylaxis in prostate procedures in older men.
Feature_Interactions_Method: MDR patterns (multi-item frequent itemsets from Apriori) decomposed into pairwise antibiotic-resistance co-occurrence associations, from which resistance-association networks were built.
Limitation_Categories: Data-quality/temporal (COVID-19 dip in 2020); setting representativeness (community-only); diagnostic uncertainty (no confirmed UTI diagnosis); measurement/testing-frequency bias (rarely tested antibiotics); outcome-label definition (susceptible-increased-exposure grouped with resistant); pathogen-scope generalisability (E. coli only); algorithmic/methodological choice (Apriori thresholds and metrics).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Some antibiotics were tested on a very small number of isolates in the PRIMO database; only antibiotics tested on at least 10% of isolates were retained to minimise bias.

Title: Levofloxacin Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics, Dosing, Susceptibility Breakpoints, and Artificial Intelligence in the Treatment of Multidrug-resistant Tuberculosis
Funder_Names: Baylor Research Institute; Wellcome Trust, UK; National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (U01AI119954)
Population_Description: 41 Tanzanian patients with pulmonary MDR tuberculosis treated with 750 mg levofloxacin, in combination with kanamycin, cycloserine, ethionamide, and pyrazinamide

Reported_Limitations: Levofloxacin concentrations used as an external check on PK modeling were from a retrospective study and only levofloxacin (not companion-drug) concentrations were measured; the external-validation dataset for tuberculous meningitis modeling was relatively small.

Test set) abbreviations, implying a learn/test split and possible ROC-curve analysis for the random forest models, but no ROC curve, AUROC number, or split methodology is described anywhere in the body text. Conflicts_of_Interest: No reported conflicts of interest
Inclusion_Criteria: 41 Tanzanian patients with MDR tuberculosis treated with 750 mg levofloxacin who had levofloxacin concentrations measured 2 hours after dose 4 weeks after starting therapy
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables
Dataset_Size: 41 patients
Primary_AMR_Outcome: AUC0-24/MIC exposure threshold associated with maximal microbial kill (146) and with suppression of acquired drug resistance (360) for levofloxacin against Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (quinolones)
Specific_Antibiotics: Levofloxacin; kanamycin; cycloserine; ethionamide; pyrazinamide
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Susceptibility breakpoint defined by MIC threshold (proposed at 0.5 mg/L)
AI_Purpose: To identify, from PK/PD and clinical variables, the most important predictors of sputum conversion, acquired drug resistance, and death in MDR tuberculosis patients treated with levofloxacin

Other_Metrics: Variable-importance percentage (random forest); odds ratio with 95% CI derived from applying the CART threshold in standard statistics

Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Decision rules / surrogate tree
Clinical_Insights: The CART-derived AUC0-24/MIC threshold of 160 (based on ofloxacin MIC, used as a proxy since levofloxacin MICs were not measured) was interpreted as translating to a putative levofloxacin AUC0-24/MIC of 320, given that ofloxacin MIC is often 1 tube dilution higher than levofloxacin.

Title: Optimising personalised antibiotic treatment for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections in ICU patients using a deep learning–based causal inference approach

Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance

Limitation_Categories: Retrospective/selection bias; missing data (portal of entry, dosing); unmodelled drug interactions; small sample size; class imbalance; low-frequency subgroup (ceftaroline); single institution; lack of external/prospective validation.

Title: Confidence-based prediction of antibiotic resistance at the patient level
Country_Countries: 30 European countries (TESSy/ECDC surveillance; individual countries listed in Acknowledgments)
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Swedish Research Council (VR); Chalmers AI Research Centre (CHAIR); National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia (JPI AMR / SEARCHER)
Population_Description: Bacterial isolates (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa) from blood and cerebrospinal fluid of hospitalized patients across 30 European countries (TESSy/ECDC surveillance).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Proposed transformer model (patient data + AST data, best performing); ablation model using AST results only (no patient data); naive pairwise co-resistance-frequency classifier — VMEs significantly smaller for the proposed model vs. both comparators (P<0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
Best_Performing_Model: The proposed transformer-based model (patient data + AST data) — average accuracy 93% across bacterial species and antibiotics.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Average across all three bacterial species and antibiotics (exact data split not specified in the abstract)
F1_Value: 74–96% depending on antibiotic class and pathogen (e.g., cephalosporins 91% E. coli/96% K. pneumoniae; penicillins 74% E. coli/88% K. pneumoniae)
F1_Population_Set: Test data set, by antibiotic class and pathogen (E. coli, K. pneumoniae)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validated only through internal 5-fold cross-validation and a held-out test split (15%) from the same retrospective TESSy data set; no external data set or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: A very major error (false-negative resistance prediction) may lead to ineffective antibiotic treatment, considered especially serious for life-threatening infections.
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: AST tests with a resistant (R) or susceptible (S) result (intermediate (I) results excluded); antibiotics with resistance rate ≥8%; isolates tested for ≥5 antibiotics.
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates tested for fewer than five antibiotics were removed (also: AST tests with an intermediate (I) result and antibiotics with <8% resistance rate excluded).
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: TESSy (The European Surveillance System, ECDC)
Dataset_Size: 1,629,257 bacterial isolates; 12,433,856 AST results
Missing_Data_Method: Incomplete/untested AST results treated as masked model outputs to predict; input sequences padded to fixed length with PAD tokens where data are absent.
Geographic_Representativeness: Data drawn from 30 European countries via ECDC/TESSy surveillance; relative contribution per country not detailed in the main text.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood and cerebrospinal fluid
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Prediction of antibiotic susceptibility (resistant/susceptible) for untested antibiotics, from incomplete AST results plus patient data.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug_Classes: aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cephalosporins, penicillins, and quinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Ceftazidime; ciprofloxacin; piperacillin (PIP); moxifloxacin; nalidixic acid; amoxicillin (AMX); ampicillin (AMP) — named individually in the running text (the full panel of 20 antibiotics is listed in Table 1, p.5).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant (R) / susceptible (S) AST result per antibiotic; intermediate (I) results excluded.
AI_Purpose: To predict unmeasured/untested antibiotic susceptibility from available (incomplete) AST results and patient data, paired with conformal-prediction uncertainty estimates for patient-level decision support.
Num_Models_Compared: Proposed model plus a naive pairwise co-resistance baseline, an AST-only (no patient data) ablation, and multiple architecture variants (1–2 encoder heads/layers × embedding size 64/128 × feed-forward size 128/256 × with/without patient data).
Feature_Engineering: Categorical patient and AST variables encoded as discrete input 'words' (species, country, gender, age, sampling date, per-antibiotic AST result), converted to learned linear embeddings (d=128); sequences padded with PAD tokens to a fixed length.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Per-antibiotic class weights on the cross-entropy loss function (susceptible/resistant), Table 1.
Hyperparameter_Method: Comparison of architecture hyperparameters: 1 or 2 encoder heads/layers, word-embedding size 64 or 128, feed-forward layer size 128 or 256, with and without patient data (Fig. S13–S15).

Title: Generalizable machine learning models for rapid antimicrobial resistance prediction in unseen health care settings
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: ETH AI Center
Population_Description: 54,283 unique mass spectra associated with 631,167 antimicrobial resistance phenotypes, covering 65 antimicrobials; each entry is a pathogen mass spectrum from a patient sample with susceptibility/resistance annotations.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: 6 input configurations combining 3 antimicrobial representations (Morgan fingerprints, MoLFormer, SELFIES) with 2 spectra encodings (binned MALDI-TOF, masked autoencoder), plus the baseline (binned MS + Morgan fingerprints); reported metric AUPRC.
Best_Performing_Model: MAE (masked autoencoder) mass-spectra encoding combined with Molformer antimicrobial encoding, judged by AUPRC
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The model is only cross-validated within the single DRIAMS database (hospital/year zero-shot splits from the same source), with no external dataset from outside DRIAMS and no prospective clinical evaluation; the authors state prospective, real-world validation is still needed.
Reported_Limitations: Reduced interpretability of alternative encodings (MAE, Molformer, SELFIES); MALDI-TOF-based resistance detection is limited to mechanisms with a spectral signature; the 4 hospitals studied are geographically close (northern Switzerland), so results may reflect regional similarity.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The models' predictions can evoke high confidence despite being incorrect when applied to unseen-distribution data, potentially misleading users and resulting in poor decision-making; data shift can also introduce biases into model predictions, leading to unfair or inequitable outcomes for certain groups.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Data shift can introduce biases into model predictions, leading to unfair or inequitable outcomes for certain groups.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Not yet ready for direct clinical deployment; beyond legal and regulatory considerations, several key steps remain before it can be integrated into clinical practice.
Unresolved_Items: Whether External_Validation should be 'No' (all splits drawn from the single DRIAMS database) or should credit the hospital/year zero-shot design as a form of external validation; whether Study_Setting is best coded 'Laboratory / in silico only' given the data are patient-derived MALDI-TOF spectra but the study itself performs no clinical-setting work.
Sample_Size: 54,283 unique mass spectra associated with 631,167 antimicrobial resistance phenotypes; 65 antimicrobials
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared that they have no competing interests.
Exclusion_Criteria: Data from the HospitalHygene workstation within DRIAMS-A were excluded because samples were captured using a different medium and skewed heavily toward resistant samples.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: DRIAMS
Dataset_Size: 54,283 unique mass spectra; 631,167 antimicrobial resistance phenotypes; 65 antimicrobials
Geographic_Representativeness: Data come from 4 diagnostic laboratories, all geographically close in northern Switzerland; the authors note the models may still benefit from regional similarities and that hospitals in more distant/diverse locations could reveal additional generalizability challenges.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistance vs. susceptibility of a pathogen to an antimicrobial, predicted from the pathogen's MALDI-TOF mass spectrum and the antimicrobial's molecular representation.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: a binary label y is provided, where 0 indicates sensitivity and 1 indicates resistance, for each pathogen-antimicrobial combination with an available susceptibility test outcome
AI_Purpose: To develop a novel model architecture that improves generalizability, reducing the need to develop separate AMR-prediction models for each hospital or data collection year.
Feature_Engineering: Mass spectra were binned (bin size 3 m/z units) and, alternatively, re-encoded with a masked autoencoder (MAE); antimicrobials were re-encoded with Morgan fingerprints, the Molformer transformer, or SELFIES one-hot encodings.
Hyperparameter_Method: Parameter search over MAE hyperparameters (copies per sample, mask ratio, encoding dimension, epochs, batch size, learning rate), reported in Supplementary Table S4 / Fig. S7.
Software_Libraries: pytorch_lightning, scikit_learn, shap, tensorflow, torch, tqdm
Other_Metrics: Balanced accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), reported alongside AUPRC (with supplementary figures for MCC and balanced accuracy).
Baseline_Method: Baseline model: 6,000-dimensional binned MALDI-TOF mass spectra vector for pathogen representation with Morgan fingerprints for antimicrobial encoding.
Baseline_Performance: AUPRC scores ranging from 0.56 for 2015 data to 0.77 for samples from 2017 (same-year/same-hospital training and testing)
Internal_Validation: Hospital zero-shot split (train on hospital i, test on hospital j != i) and year zero-shot split (train on year i, test on year j != i), all within the DRIAMS dataset.
Train_Test_Split: Hospital zero-shot: train on 1 hospital's 2018 data, test on a different hospital's 2018 data. Year zero-shot: train on DRIAMS-A data from one year, test on a different year.
Data_Repository: GigaDB (GigaScience repository); code also on GitHub (ZeroShotAMR)
Generalisability_Details: The whole study is a quantification of AMR-model generalizability across unseen hospitals and years (zero-shot settings), showing baseline performance declines and testing encodings (MAE, Molformer, SELFIES) that improve zero-shot AUPRC.
Maturity_Evidence: Models are cross-validated across hospitals/years within one dataset (DRIAMS) with no separate external dataset and no prospective clinical evaluation; authors state prospective real-world validation is still needed before clinical use.
Integration_Point: At the time of species identification by MALDI-TOF (24-48 hours after sampling), alongside existing species ID, before the additional 24-48h AST step.
End_User_Described: Clinician (prescriber) and laboratory
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The clinician's workflow remains unchanged; alongside species identification, the laboratory would deliver an ML-based resistance prediction, shortening the diagnostic process by 24-48 hours and supporting earlier therapy optimization.
Barriers_List: Missing routinely-available patient-level features (prior antibiotic use, recent hospitalization, immunosuppression, travel history); unclear role within antimicrobial stewardship decisions; lack of prospective, real-world validation; legal/regulatory considerations.
Facilitators_List: Workflow compatibility: the clinician's existing workflow is unchanged, with the laboratory simply adding an ML-based resistance prediction alongside the species identification it already delivers.
Future_Directions: Long-term, such ML systems could provide ranked susceptibility predictions integrating clinical and epidemiological data, to (i) improve initial treatment success by identifying the most likely effective antibiotics and (ii) enable de-escalation to narrower-spectrum agents, supporting antimicrobial stewardship.
Limitation_Categories: Reduced interpretability of advanced encodings; resistance-detection limited to mechanisms visible in the mass-spectral profile; limited geographic diversity of the 4 study hospitals (all in northern Switzerland).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data bias existed within DRIAMS-A from one workstation (HospitalHygene) that used a different sample medium and was skewed heavily toward resistant samples; this workstation's data were excluded.
Page_References: Methods pp.2-4; Results pp.4-7; Discussion/Limitations pp.7-9

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; AmpC; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility results (susceptible, intermediate, or resistant) for each culture were mapped to resistance mechanisms, e.g. an Enterococcus resistant to vancomycin flagged as VRE.
AI_Purpose: Compare predictive performance of different antimicrobial-resistance look-back periods across five MDR mechanisms to identify an optimal look-back period for empiric antimicrobial clinical decision support.

Class_Imbalance_Method: Selection of imbalance-robust evaluation metrics (precision, recall, PR-AUC, F1) rather than resampling.

Generalisability_Details: Restriction of the study cohort to a single healthcare system in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex may limit generalizability of the results to other populations.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal evaluation of predictive performance (recall, precision, F1, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, odds ratios) on the study's own retrospective dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation, or deployed CDS integration described.
Integration_Point: Points during the antimicrobial decision process: empiric antibiotic selection, Gram stain result, and organism identification (illustrated using MRSA).
End_User_Described: Clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians have varying and incrementally increasing information available throughout the antimicrobial decision process (empiric antibiotics, Gram stain results, bacterial identification without susceptibility results, susceptibility report).

Title: Machine Learning Model for Predicting Multidrug Resistance in Clinical Escherichia coli Isolates: A Retrospective General Surgery Study
