Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic resistance status of E. coli isolates, modeled per antibiotic as a binary classification target (resistant vs not), for 12 antibiotics.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli)
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides; Carbapenems; Cephalosporins; Beta-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations; Fluoroquinolones; Sulfonamides/Trimethoprim
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin; Ertapenem; Meropenem; Cefoxitin; Cefuroxime; Ceftazidime; Ceftriaxone; Cefepime; Ciprofloxacin; Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole; Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid; Ampicillin; Piperacillin/tazobactam
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: each antibiotic was modeled separately as a binary classification problem, where the resistance status of a specific antibiotic served as the target variable
AI_Purpose: To utilize ML algorithms to classify E. coli isolates from general surgery wards based on their antibiotic susceptibility profiles, facilitating early detection of resistance and supporting personalized therapy choices.
Feature_Engineering: Given that the dataset comprised entirely categorical variables, One-Hot Encoding was applied to transform these variables into a numerical format suitable for subsequent machine learning analyses.
Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique)
Other_Metrics: Brier score (calibration); Balanced Accuracy
Baseline_Method: Logistic Regression
Baseline_Performance: mean accuracy of 0.86
Internal_Validation: 70:30 train-test split; 5-fold cross-validation; 10-fold cross-validation
Clinical_Insights: Feature importance analysis highlighted strong inter-antibiotic resistance links, especially among β-lactams, and some influence of demographic factors.
Generalisability_Details: Dataset limited to a single-city context, which may affect generalizability; external validation with data from other regions is stated as needed.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supports internal validation only (70:30 split plus 5-fold/10-fold CV); no external or prospective evaluation reported.
Integration_Point: Proposed integration into laboratory information systems (LIS) and electronic health records (EHR); not yet implemented.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (surgeons, infectious disease specialists) and hospital-level antimicrobial stewardship programs.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Example: for a patient presenting with an SSI, the model could provide an early prediction of likely antimicrobial resistance in the causative E. coli isolate before conventional AST results are available, guiding clinicians toward more appropriate empiric therapy.
Barriers_List: First, the integration with existing hospital information systems can be technically demanding, requiring substantial IT support. Second, the possible variability in microbiology laboratory practices, as well as differences in data quality and completeness, may impact model reliability. Third, successful implementation requires clinician training and user-friendly interfaces to build trust and ensure routine adoption of ML outputs in clinical workflows. Finally, financial and logistical constraints, including hardware requirements, software maintenance, and the need for dedicated IT support, may limit scalability in resource-constrained healthcare environments.
Facilitators_List: Deploying the system in synchrony with current methodologies and gradually transitioning it into an alternative to the active system is suggested as a more sustainable and effective implementation approach.
Future_Directions: Future research directions should focus on external validation with multicentric datasets, integration of interpretable ML frameworks to ensure transparent clinical decision-making, cooperative analyzing with WGS data, and incorporation into real-time hospital information systems to enable dynamic surveillance of antibiotic resistance surveillance and strengthen antimicrobial stewardship efforts.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: permutation importance
Limitation_Categories: Single-city/generalizability; need for external validation; low-prevalence-antibiotic reliability (e.g. Meropenem, treated as exploratory); lack of explainability (no SHAP); implementation/deployment barriers (IT integration, lab variability, clinician training, cost).
Data_Quality_Concerns: the possible variability in microbiology laboratory practices, as well as differences in data quality and completeness, may impact model reliability

Title: A machine learning and neural network approach for classifying multidrug-resistant bacterial infections
Population_Description: 624 patients with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacterial (MDR-GNB) carriage, EHR dataset from Thatphanom Crown Prince Hospital (a mid-sized 120-bed community hospital in northeastern Thailand), collected January 2016-December 2020; 41 input features plus one binary output feature.
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP-ranked most influential risk factors for the MLP model: recent steroid usage (past 90 days), urinary catheter usage (past 90 days), hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and inappropriate antibiotics usage (past 90 days).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: LR, RF, SVM, XGBoost, KNN, MLP, LightGBM; optimal (feature-selection + augmentation) performance per Table 3: LR ACC 0.64/AUC 0.67; RF ACC 0.65/AUC 0.67; SVM ACC 0.59/AUC 0.62; XGBoost ACC 0.73/AUC 0.64; KNN ACC 0.69/AUC 0.64; MLP ACC 0.76/AUC 0.70 (best); LightGBM ACC 0.66/AUC 0.66.
Best_Performing_Model: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) — highest accuracy (0.76), AUC (0.70), G-Mean (0.68) and specificity (0.85) among the seven classifiers (feature selection SFS + SMOTE-Tomek augmentation).
Accuracy_Population_Set: Test set (20% hold-out from stratified 80:20 split, evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Test set (20% hold-out from stratified 80:20 split, evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation)
Specificity_Population_Set: Test set (20% hold-out from stratified 80:20 split, evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation)
AUROC_Population_Set: Test set (20% hold-out from stratified 80:20 split, evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation was performed: stratified 80:20 train/test split with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on a single-institution retrospective EHR dataset. No external dataset, no prospective evaluation, and no clinical deployment/CDS integration were described.
Reported_Limitations: Despite challenges such as limited data availability and dataset imbalance, the models developed in this study demonstrated performance comparable to other studies.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The MLP model produced risk-direction predictions that conflicted with prior clinical evidence for several factors (e.g., predicted CKD as lower-risk, contrary to Chandrasekhar et al.), raising a risk of misleading clinical interpretation if the model's feature-attribution output were used uncritically for decision-making.
Unresolved_Items: Internal inconsistency in the source: the page-9 prose states the MLP 'sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and G-mean scores were found to be 0.55, 0.85, 0.76, and 0.68' (labelling 0.76 as AUC), whereas Table 3 reports AUC=0.70 and ACC=0.76 for the same model/configuration. Table 3 was treated as authoritative for Accuracy_Value/AUROC_Value because it is the structured results table explicitly captioned as the optimal performance table.
Conflicts_of_Interest: Corresponding author confirms no known conflicts of interest; certifies the research was conducted independently without commercial or financial support from external entities.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: HOSxP (hospital information system); MLAB database (version 5.58.22.02.28, laboratory information system)
Dataset_Size: Dataset imbalance ratio (IR) of 2.24
Missing_Data_Method: None required — the dataset was checked and no missing values were found.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary classification of MDR-GNB carriage: whether the patient has suffered from an MDR-GNB carriage or not.
Pathogens: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (MDR-GNB); not broken down by individual species in the text.
Drug_Classes: Quinolones, colistin, aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cephalosporins, macrolides, penicillin, sulfonamides
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR is defined as resistance to at least one agent in three or more classes of antibiotics, based on CLSI-compliant AST results (AST drugs: quinolones, colistin, aminoglycosides, carbapenems, cephalosporins, macrolides, penicillin, sulfonamides).
AI_Purpose: To develop machine-learning/neural-network predictive models for MDR-GNB colonization and infection among hospitalized patients using electronic health records, to support clinical decision-making.
Feature_Engineering: Label encoding (categorical to numerical, fit-transform) and Min-Max scaling of numerical features to a 0-1 range.
Feature_Selection_Method: Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV); Sequential Forward/Feature Selection (SFS); SelectKBest; Variance Threshold.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Data augmentation: ADASYN, Borderline-SMOTE, SMOTE-ENN, SMOTE-Tomek; Focal Loss (gamma, alpha tuning) also used for the MLP model.
Hyperparameter_Method: GridSearchCV (systematic search across models); MLP-specific tuning of activation function, optimizer, learning rate, and Focal Loss gamma/alpha.
Hardware_Details: Laptop computer: 13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900HX processor, 64.0 GB RAM, Windows 11.
Other_Metrics: G-Mean (geometric mean of sensitivity & specificity), MCC and Cohen's kappa (KS) also reported; for the best model (MLP, SFS+SMOTE-Tomek): MCC=0.47, KS=0.41 (Table 4).
Baseline_Method: Default-settings models (no feature selection or data augmentation) compared against models using optimal feature-selection + data-augmentation combinations.
Baseline_Performance: MLP at default settings: SP 0.87, SN 0.23, ACC 0.68, AUC 0.55, G-mean 0.46, execution time 0.815s.
Internal_Validation: Stratified 5-fold cross-validation combined with an 80:20 train/test split.
Train_Test_Split: 80:20 (80% training, 20% testing)
Overfitting_Method: Early stopping during MLP training (50 epochs, batch size 32); K-fold cross-validation also used to reduce overfitting/variance.
Clinical_Insights: SHAP identified recent steroid use, urinary catheter use, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and inappropriate antibiotic use as top MDR-GNB risk factors (consistent with prior literature), but the model's predictions diverged from prior evidence for CKD, heparin-lock use, nasogastric-tube use, and COPD.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state future work should further enhance model sensitivity and generalizability via additional feature-selection techniques, multicenter healthcare databases (for sufficient data), and advanced deep learning architectures — implying the present single-center dataset limits generalizability.
Maturity_Evidence: Highest maturity evidence is internal validation only (stratified 80:20 split + stratified 5-fold cross-validation) on a single-institution retrospective dataset; no external or prospective validation and no clinical deployment/integration described.
End_User_Described: Clinical decision-making support for healthcare professionals (implied via 'clinical decision-making'; no specific role formally named).
Future_Directions: Enhance model sensitivity and generalizability through additional feature-selection techniques, use of multicenter healthcare databases to obtain sufficient data for deep learning models, and application of advanced deep learning architectures.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) Beeswarm plot
Novel_Predictors_Details: The MLP model's predictions diverged from prior published risk-factor evidence for four factors — CKD, heparin-lock (HL) usage, nasogastric-tube usage, and COPD — all predicted as lower-risk for MDR-GNB by this model, contrary to cited prior studies.
Limitation_Categories: Limited data availability; dataset/class imbalance; single (community-hospital) data source (implied via the future-work call for multicenter data).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Dataset imbalance ratio (IR) of 2.24, addressed via data augmentation techniques; no missing values were found after data-quality checks.
Page_References: Table 3 (p.11) is the primary optimal-performance results table for the feature-selection + data-augmentation models.

Title: Prediction of ciprofloxacin resistance in hospitalized patients using machine learning
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Retrospective cohort; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Israel Science Foundation (ISF 1286/21)
Population_Description: Hospitalized patients with positive bacterial cultures tested for ciprofloxacin susceptibility at Meir Medical Center, Israel, during 2016-2019; final dataset of 10,053 susceptibility test results from 5,540 patients across six bacterial species.
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: Five most influential variables in the bacteria-agnostic model, ranked by mean absolute SHAP value: previous ciprofloxacin resistance in the past 60 days; whether the patient arrived from an institution; recent resistance to any antibiotic in similar hospital units; previous ciprofloxacin resistance in the previous 61-180 days; recent resistance to any antibiotic in the hospital.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Bacteria-agnostic dataset, ensemble (best): ROC-AUC 0.737 (95% CI 0.715-0.758). Bacteria-gnostic dataset: neural network 0.82, LASSO logistic regression 0.835, random forest 0.812, XGBoost 0.832, ensemble (best) 0.837 (95% CI 0.821-0.854). Ensemble models were well-calibrated.
Best_Performing_Model: Ensemble model (stacked super-learner combining LASSO logistic regression, random forest, gradient-boosted trees/XGBoost, and a neural network); it consistently outperformed all individual base learners on both the agnostic and gnostic datasets by ROC-AUC.
AUROC_Population_Set: Ensemble model, bacteria-agnostic dataset, independent test set
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The train/test split is temporal (calendar-time based, not random), and the authors explicitly describe this as a form of external validation simulating deployment on future, previously unseen data; no geographically external site or prospective clinical evaluation was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Our study has several limitations. First, our dataset lacks relevant community-related patient information, such as antibiotic consumption in the community and in patients' surroundings (neighborhoods and households).
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The authors note that continuous probability outputs from antibiotic-prescribing decision-support systems have been suggested to promote over-prescription of antibiotics, so decisions about output format should be made with caution.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized patients with positive bacterial cultures tested for ciprofloxacin susceptibility, retrieved from Meir Medical Center EMRs, between 2016 and 2019.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 10,053 susceptibility test results; 5,540 patients; 73 variables
Geographic_Representativeness: The authors state that ciprofloxacin resistance rates and patient covariates in their dataset are comparable to hospitalized patients in other developed countries, so they expect a reasonable degree of consistency if the model were developed on a comparable dataset elsewhere.
Specimen_Type_Detail: urine, wound, and blood cultures
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary prediction of ciprofloxacin resistance (resistant vs. susceptible; cultures with intermediate results were coded as resistant) in bacterial cultures from hospitalized patients.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Morganella morganii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus mirabilis, Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolone
Specific_Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible outcome per culture, determined by antimicrobial susceptibility testing; cultures with intermediate results were coded as resistant.
AI_Purpose: To predict the probability of ciprofloxacin resistance in hospitalized patients' bacterial cultures, to support empiric antibiotic treatment decisions.
Num_Models_Compared: 5 (four base learners: LASSO logistic regression, random forest, gradient-boosted trees/XGBoost, and a neural network; plus the stacked ensemble)
Feature_Engineering: Additional features related to previous infections with resistant bacteria, previous antibiotic usage, and previous hospitalizations were engineered from the patients' EMRs.
Hyperparameter_Method: 200 random searches with five-fold time-series cross-validation
Software_Libraries: NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, XGBoost, TensorFlow, Matplotlib, SHAP
Other_Metrics: Calibration (calibration plots) and decision-curve analysis (standardized net benefit) were also reported, alongside ROC-AUC.
Baseline_Method: Individual base learners (neural network, LASSO logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) compared against the stacked ensemble
Baseline_Performance: Bacteria-agnostic dataset base-learner ROC-AUCs: 0.716 (neural network), 0.736 (LASSO), 0.719 (random forest), 0.729 (XGBoost).
Internal_Validation: Five-fold time-series cross-validation, used for hyperparameter tuning of the base learners
Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% test, split by calendar date (not randomly)
External_Validation_Description: Temporal (calendar-time) train/test split: models trained on earlier data and evaluated on a later, chronologically held-out independent test set, which the authors describe as a form of external validation.
Clinical_Insights: Highly influential predictors (previous resistant infections, patient origin from another facility, local/hospital resistance frequencies) matched known clinical risk factors for ciprofloxacin resistance.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state their models are not necessarily immediately generalisable to other settings or to the same setting in different time periods, given variation in demographics, antibiotic consumption, and the dynamic nature of AMR; they note under-representation of younger patients and that site-specific retraining would likely be needed elsewhere.
Maturity_Evidence: The evidence supporting the coded maturity level is the temporally held-out (calendar-time split) independent test-set evaluation, which the authors explicitly describe as a form of external validation; no prospective or site-external evaluation was performed.
End_User_Described: Clinician (decision-maker) weighing the cost-benefit trade-off of treating with ciprofloxacin
Future_Directions: Improvement of such models depends on advances in algorithm development, specific feature engineering, and augmentation of the quantity and quality of EMR data; future studies could further leverage the presented models and available EMR data to improve AMR prediction and reduce antibiotic misuse.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mean absolute SHAP value (Kernel SHAP)
Limitation_Categories: Missing community-level antibiotic-consumption data; limited generalisability to other settings/time periods; under-representation of younger patients.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Under-representation of younger patients in the dataset.

Title: Leveraging Large Data, Statistics, and Machine Learning to Predict the Emergence of Resistant E. coli Infections
Population_Description: 4776 microbial E. coli cultures identified through Kaiser Permanente's EHR at KP Vacaville Medical Center (April 2013-December 2019), covering all sources of infection (abscess, blood, urine, wounds).
Top_Predictive_Features: Top three factors (random forest recursive feature elimination, ranked by %IncMSE): amoxicillin, cefazolin, and piperacillin/tazobactam.
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest model with cefazolin (no lag): best RMSE/MAE on test set but underfit on train set, so disqualified. ARIMA model with cefazolin (no lag), followed by ARIMA with cephalexin (no lag), performed best on RMSE and MAE across both train and test sets.
Best_Performing_Model: ARIMA model with cefazolin (no lag) as exogenous regressor
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models trained on 2013-2018 data, evaluated on a held-out 2019 test set from the same single facility only; no external-site or prospective validation performed.
Reported_Limitations: Single-facility, rural/low-migration sample limiting generalisability; no external-facility validation; the 2020 predictions have not been validated against actual 2020 data (prospective follow-up beyond current scope); observational design cannot establish causation.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: All E. coli cultures (urine, blood, abscess, wound, genital, GI abscess); admission to KP Vacaville 1 Apr 2013-31 Dec 2019; administration of the listed antibiotics (dosed as DOT/1000 patient days); for patients with multiple resistant-E.-coli episodes (resistance to ceftriaxone), only the first episode included.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients not meeting inclusion criteria.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 4776 microbial cultures of E. coli
Geographic_Representativeness: Data from a single facility (Kaiser Permanente Vacaville) in a rural region of California with relatively low population migration; authors flag limited generalisability and suggest multi-facility data for a more generalised model.
Specimen_Type_Detail: All E. coli cultures (urine, blood, abscess, wound, genital, and GI abscess).
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Identification of the antibiotic most strongly associated with increased antibiotic resistance in E. coli (indicated by resistance to ceftriaxone); secondary outcome was resistance-rate prediction for 2020.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli)
Drug_Classes: Cephalosporins, beta lactams, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides.
Specific_Antibiotics: cefazolin; cephalexin; cefadroxil; cefotetan; cefoxitin; ceftriaxone; cefpodoxime; cefepime; piperacillin/tazobactam; amoxicillin; amoxicillin/clavulanic acid; ampicillin; ampicillin/sulbactam; moxifloxacin; levofloxacin; ciprofloxacin; gentamicin; tobramycin; amikacin.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible outcome defined as resistance to ceftriaxone.
AI_Purpose: To use statistical and machine-learning models to explore the relationship between antibiotic usage and antibiotic resistance over time, and to predict the clinical and financial costs associated with resistant E. coli infections.
Feature_Engineering: Time-lags (monthly, up to 1 year in both directions) were constructed via cross-correlation analysis between each antibiotic's usage series and the resistance series, and the most significant lag used to build the exogenous regressor for the time-series models.
Feature_Selection_Method: Correlation analysis (p<0.05, R-squared>0.3), stepwise linear regression (stepAIC, lowest AIC), and recursive feature elimination with random forest (%IncMSE).
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over three 'mtry' values (total predictors, one-third of total, square root of total) using caret's 'train' function with a time-slice trainControl (fixed 12-month validation window).
Software_Libraries: 'caret' library (rfe() function for random-forest recursive feature selection; train()/trainControl() for time-slice hyperparameter tuning); RandomForest package.
Other_Metrics: Multiple R-squared and adjusted R-squared, F-statistic and p-value for the stepwise linear regression model; correlation coefficients and p-values (Table 2); variance inflation factor (VIF) for multicollinearity.
Internal_Validation: Temporal train/test split: trained on 2013-2018 data, tested on held-out 2019 data.
Train_Test_Split: Train: 1 Apr 2013-31 Dec 2018; Test: 1 Jan-31 Dec 2019.
Overfitting_Method: Compared the ratio of model performance (RMSE/MAE) on training data vs test data; the model with the least sign of overfitting/underfitting by this ratio was selected for prediction.
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Despite weaker model performance than cefazolin/cephalexin, piperacillin/tazobactam (broad-spectrum) was identified as a more practical ASP intervention target because narrow-spectrum agents like cefazolin/cephalexin are hard to target under stewardship programs that focus on restricting broad-spectrum drugs.
Generalisability_Details: A more generalised model could be developed using data from multiple facilities; the present study is framed as a region-specific framework for local ASP clinicians rather than a generalisable model.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal temporal train/test split only (train 2013-2018, test 2019 held-out); no external-site validation and no prospective validation of the 2020 forecasts were performed.
End_User_Described: ASP (antimicrobial stewardship program) clinicians
Stewardship_Details: Both time-series models (piperacillin/tazobactam, or amoxicillin+cephalexin) showed about a 0.5-percentage-point drop in resistance (from ~5.5% to ~5%) with a 25% reduction in the respective antibiotic's usage.
Barriers_List: The antibiotics most strongly linked to resistance (cefazolin, cephalexin) have relatively narrow spectrums of activity, making them difficult targets for ASP interventions, which typically focus on restricting broad-spectrum agents.
Facilitators_List: Piperacillin/tazobactam's broad spectrum of activity, combined with reasonably good time-series model performance, makes it a practical ASP intervention target for this facility.
Future_Directions: Develop models for other Gram-negative infections and include outpatient antibiotics-use data; conduct a follow-up study with data from multiple Kaiser Permanente facilities and from 2020.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest recursive feature elimination, ranked by percent increase in mean squared error (%IncMSE).
Novel_Predictors_Details: Amoxicillin and cephalexin, despite negligible recorded inpatient use (0.15% and 0.57% respectively), emerged as significant predictors of resistant E. coli, likely because these oral antibiotics are frequently prescribed just before/after discharge and their fuller use is not captured by inpatient records.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Built combined-predictor time-series models (e.g., cefazolin + piperacillin/tazobactam; amoxicillin + cephalexin) and compared them against single-predictor models; assessed multicollinearity between combined predictors using the variance inflation factor (VIF).
Limitation_Categories: Single-facility, rural/low-migration sample limiting generalisability; predictions for 2020 not yet validated against actual 2020 data (no prospective follow-up performed).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Recorded antibiotic usage for amoxicillin and cephalexin likely underestimates actual use, because these oral antibiotics are frequently prescribed at/around discharge and only briefly captured during the inpatient stay.

Title: Multi task learning based early prediction model for antibiotic resistance using multi institutional cohort data
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology (KIAT); IITP (Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation); National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF)
Population_Description: Patients aged 19 years or older, hospitalized for at least 3 days, with available culture test results, drawn from three Korean tertiary-care institutions.
Age_Range: 19 years or older (no upper bound stated in the main text)
Top_Predictive_Features: Previous antibiotic resistance / previous culture test results (top SHAP predictor), plus age, length of hospital stay, and vital signs, ranked by SHAP value.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: STL: LR, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, MLP; MTL: hard parameter sharing (HS), soft parameter sharing (SS). Internal/external average AUC and PRC given for each (e.g. HS external AUC 79.63/PRC 80.26; LGBM external AUC 78.19/PRC 79.07).
Best_Performing_Model: Hard parameter sharing (HS) multi-task learning model — highest AUC/PRC in external validation, averaged 79.63/80.26 across the nine antibiotic classes
AUROC_Value: 79.63 (HS model, external-validation average AUC across the nine antibiotic classes)
AUROC_Population_Set: External validation (test) data, average across nine antibiotic classes, hard parameter sharing model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation performed across three independent institutions; the model was explicitly not applied in a prospective cohort study.
Reported_Limitations: Not applied prospectively; missing-label loss handling may introduce learning bias; no sensitivity analysis on the proportion of missing labels; reduced accuracy when prior culture results are absent; single-modality data only (no text/genomics).
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Aged 19 years or older; hospitalized for at least 3 days; available culture test results
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 59,551 individuals
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) and missing indicators
Geographic_Representativeness: Cohort drawn from three regions of Korea; authors consider it representative of Koreans and Asians, while noting institutional heterogeneity in resistance rates/data volume as a robustness concern.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic resistance status (resistant vs. not) 3 days after admission, predicted separately for nine antibiotic classes (TGC, MAC, FGC, FLU, BLA, CAR, AMI, AG, GLY)
Pathogens: Not specified by species — bacterial strains only, categorized by resistance to nine antibiotic classes rather than by organism
Drug_Classes: TGC, MAC, FGC, FLU, BLA, CAR, AMI, AG, and GLY (nine antibiotic classes)
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin/Gentamicin (AG)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary antibiotic resistance status 3 days after admission, based on culture test result, coded separately for each of nine antibiotic classes
AI_Purpose: Develop and compare machine learning models to predict resistance to nine antibiotic classes in hospitalized patients, addressing the high-cost labeling challenge of medical data
Feature_Engineering: Standard Scaler feature scaling; MICE imputation with missing indicators for missing data
Software_Libraries: TensorFlow 2.10.0 (Python); R 4.3.3 used for statistical analysis/visualization
Other_Metrics: Calibration slope (CS), assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow method
Baseline_Method: Single-task learning models: Logistic Regression, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Multi-Layer Perceptron
Baseline_Performance: Internal test: LR AUC 74.16/PRC 77.69, XGB 74.15/77.80, LGBM 77.33/80.33, Cat 76.26/79.45, MLP 76.21/79.37 (vs. HS 78.64/81.32); external test values also reported for each.
Internal_Validation: Random 70:30 train/test split of the internal data, repeated 30 times, with paired t-tests for statistical comparison
Train_Test_Split: 7:3 (70% training / 30% test)
External_Validation_Description: Korea University Ansan Hospital cohort of 16,150 individuals, used as an independent external test set
Clinical_Insights: SHAP identified previous antibiotic resistance/culture results, age, length of stay, and vital signs as key risk factors; cross-resistance associations between antibiotic classes can inform empirical prescribing.
Generalisability_Details: Cohort drawn from three regions of Korea, considered representative of Koreans/Asians; between-institution heterogeneity in resistance rates and data volume noted as a robustness caveat.
Maturity_Evidence: Rigorous external validation performed across three independent Korean institutions; no prospective evaluation reported.
Integration_Point: Hospital EMR system, as a clinical decision support tool for empirical antibiotic selection
End_User_Described: Physician / clinician, at the point of empirical antibiotic prescribing
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Model sized/timed for EMR integration with sub-second response, as typically expected for clinical decision support applications
Barriers_List: Prospective validation, system integration complexity, clinical workflow compatibility, regulatory approval (e.g. FDA), and ongoing performance monitoring are all needed before clinical implementation
Facilitators_List: Small model size (2.58 MB) and fast inference (~39.76 ms/100 samples) compatible with standard hospital servers, without specialized hardware
Future_Directions: Further prospective studies, such as randomized controlled trials, to test whether the model-guided approach improves on standard care
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Vital signs did not significantly predict resistance (except for MAC, FGC, FLU, CAR, BLA), indicating resistance is difficult to infer from patient severity alone.
Limitation_Categories: No prospective validation; possible learning bias from missing-label loss calculation; no missing-label sensitivity analysis; reduced accuracy without prior culture data; single-modality data (excludes text/genomics)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Prediction accuracy is poor when previous culture test results are missing from the EMR

Title: Feature selection and prediction of treatment failure in tuberculosis
Population_Description: TB Portals patients from Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Moldova and Romania; complete-case analysis cohort of 587 patients (68% male), median (p25-p75) age 40 (30-51) years, with treatment failure in about one quarter.
Top_Predictive_Features: Patterns of drug sensitivity, imaging findings, microscopy (Ziehl-Nielsen stain) findings, education status, and employment status.

Feature_Selection_Method: Low-variance filtering removed four binary variables with near-zero variance: is_A_calcoaceticus, is_RC, is_ESBL, and is_A_lwoffi.

Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold grid search on training folds (max depth, learning rate, subsample ratio, number of estimators)

Baseline_Performance: mean AUROC ≈ 0.75 ± 0.11 (five-fold stratified cross-validation)
Internal_Validation: stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the 2020-2023 training set
Train_Test_Split: Training set (2020-2023): n = 210 episodes; Hold-out test set (2024): n = 60 episodes.

Generalisability_Details: Larger multi-center datasets are needed to ensure generalizability and model stability.
Maturity_Evidence: Discrimination under temporal drift. Five-fold cross-validation on 2020-2023 yielded an AUROC of 0.924 (95% CI: 0.868-0.968). On the unseen 2024 cohort, the same model achieved 0.586 (0.468-0.695), an absolute decline of 0.338 that remained highly significant
Integration_Point: at the point of infection detection (episode-level alert), before susceptibility results become available
End_User_Described: Clinicians (episode-level alerts); infection control teams and administrators (hospital-level forecasting)
Stewardship_Details: The proposed framework delivers explainable patient-level PDR risk scores and competitive 4-week and multi-year incidence forecasts despite temporal drift, supporting antimicrobial stewardship and ICU capacity planning.
Future_Directions: Enhancing this framework will require the following: Multi-center validation to ensure model robustness across diverse clinical contexts. Genomic feature integration such as resistance gene profiles or plasmid detection to boost phenotype prediction accuracy, especially in borderline or novel cases. Real-time clinical dashboards that present per-patient risk scores and dynamically update hospital-level forecasts for use by infectious disease teams and administrators.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (5 categorical feature groups + 1 continuous feature group, per the feature-matrix description)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: permutation-based SHAP (mean absolute SHAP values) on the 2024 test set
Novel_Predictors_Details: AB_4 stands out with a positive correlation with the pan_resistant label, raising concern about either mislabeling or a biologically atypical pattern. This feature will be specifically audited before modeling.
Feature_Interactions_Method: TabTransformer self-attention across embedded categorical features
Limitation_Categories: Despite encouraging findings, several limitations must be acknowledged: Single-center data: All 270 episodes were drawn from a single tertiary hospital, limiting external validity. Assumptions and imputation: We treated “not tested” resistance values as susceptible and excluded some episodes with missing timestamps, potentially introducing bias. TFT approximation: Due to software constraints, we implemented a simplified LSTM model with attention rather than the full TFT architecture. Though this model performed well, future work should test whether the full TFT improves both accuracy and interpretability. The low EPV (2.1) and corresponding shrinkage factor (0.70) highlight the risk of overfitting, particularly when using high-capacity models such as TabTransformer. Although bootstrap correction and regularization were applied, these adjustments cannot fully eliminate optimism bias. Larger multi-center datasets are needed to ensure generalizability and model stability.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Notably, 8 episodes (2.9%) had a Time to Infection = 0 days, potentially representing community-acquired infections or data entry errors. These were retained as their impact on distribution and modeling was minimal.

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Basic Research Cooperation Project of Beijing, Tianjin and Hebei Province, China (Grant/Award Number: 20JCZXJC00030)
Population_Description: 174 nonrepetitive K. pneumoniae clinical isolates from patients at Tianjin Haihe Hospital, collected January 2019-December 2020 (demographics in Table 1).
Data_Source: Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: LASSO: training AUC 0.9726 / test AUC 0.9100; LR: training AUC 1.0000 / test AUC 0.8581; SVM: training AUC 0.8462 / test AUC 0.6263; NN: training AUC 1.0000 / test AUC 0.7180. Test-set accuracy: LASSO 87%, LR 79%, SVM 62%, NN 68%.
Best_Performing_Model: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) — identified by the authors as having the highest test-set AUC among the four models compared.
Accuracy_Value: 87% (LASSO, test set; note: Discussion section on page 6 reports 82% for the same LASSO test-set accuracy — see _notes)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Test set (17 imipenem-sensitive + 17 imipenem-resistant isolates), LASSO model
AUROC_Population_Set: Test set, LASSO model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed and evaluated using only an internal train/test split of isolates from a single hospital; no external or multicentre validation was performed, and the authors state multicentre big-data studies are still needed to improve accuracy before clinical application.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center exploratory study; authors state multicenter big data studies are needed to improve overall accuracy and drive clinical application, and describe the AI/ML diagnostic approach as still at an early stage of exploration for clinical diagnosis.
Unresolved_Items: Internal inconsistency in the source paper: the Abstract states LASSO test-set accuracy as 87% (see Accuracy_Value quote, page 1), but the Discussion section (quoted here) reports LASSO test-set accuracy as 82% for what appears to be the same result.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 3457 mass spectrometry peaks extracted per bacterial isolate, used as model input parameters
Specimen_Type_Detail: Broncho-alveolar lavage, blood, pleural fluid, pus, secretion, sputum, urine (isolate counts by specimen type in Table 1)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Imipenem resistance status of K. pneumoniae isolates (sensitive vs resistant), defined by MIC via VITEK-2 and predicted from MALDI-TOF-MS spectral data using machine learning.

Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (imipenem)
Specific_Antibiotics: Imipenem
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug

Feature_Engineering: Mass spectral peak intensity/m/z data preprocessed via standardization, normalization, Gaussian filtering (smoothing), White Top Hat baseline correction, and equal-distance binning prior to peak extraction.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Balanced sampling: equal numbers of imipenem-sensitive and -resistant isolates selected for training (70:70) and test (17:17) sets.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search combined with 3-fold cross-validation

Internal_Validation: Random train/test split (140 isolates training: 70 sensitive + 70 resistant; 34 isolates test: 17 + 17), with model/hyperparameter selection by Grid search and 3-fold cross-validation.
Train_Test_Split: 140 isolates (70 sensitive + 70 resistant) training; 34 isolates (17 + 17) test
Generalisability_Details: Authors state that multicenter big data studies are needed to further improve overall accuracy and drive clinical application, implying the single-center model's generalisability is currently limited.

End_User_Described: Clinicians, for antimicrobial application decision-making
Barriers_List: Need to develop specialised ML models for each common bacterial species (a single model does not generalise across species with different characteristics); prediction accuracy still needs improvement before clinical application.

Title: A Novel Risk Predictive Scoring Model for Predicting Subsequent Infection After Carbapenem-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria Colonization in Hematological Malignancy Patients

Population_Description: Adult hematological malignancy (HM) inpatients at Wuhan Union Hospital screened for CR-GNB colonization on admission and weekly thereafter; those with a positive CR-GNB rectoanal swab were included and followed until hospital discharge.
Top_Predictive_Features: Mucositis and duration of agranulocytosis >=15 days identified as the strongest predictors (ranked via regression-coefficient-derived scoring: mucositis score 2, agranulocytosis >=15d score 2, agranulocytosis 1-14d score 1, remission induction chemotherapy score 1, hypoalbuminemia score 1).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Single model: multivariate-logistic-regression-derived integer risk score (4 predictors, score range 0-6); AUC=0.697, 95%CI 0.647-0.747.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: All colonized patients (n=392) classified at risk-score cutoff >=4
Specificity_Population_Set: All colonized patients (n=392) classified at risk-score cutoff >=4
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: All colonized patients (n=392) classified at risk-score cutoff >=4
AUROC_Population_Set: All colonized patients (n=392), integer risk-score model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model was derived and applied/validated only on the same 392-patient cohort used to build it; authors state an external validation cohort is still needed.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective, observational design; no identification of the specific carbapenemase enzyme type (KPC, OXA, etc.); no external validation cohort; small transplantation-subgroup sample size limiting subgroup comparison; reproducibility not yet tested in prospective studies.
Unresolved_Items: Abstract Method states patients 'were prospectively followed', while the Methods and Limitations sections describe the study as a 'retrospective, observational' review of inpatient data; coded Study_Design as Retrospective cohort per the latter, more explicit self-characterisation.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: All hospitalized HM patients were screened for CR-GNB colonization on admission and weekly thereafter; once positive CR-GNB screening was found, patients were included and followed until hospital discharge.
Exclusion_Criteria: Unidentified Group excluded: patients who developed fever/infection signs but had absence of CR-GNB and non-CR-GNB/fungal evidence with ineffective anti-infective treatment, or confirmed non-CR-GNB/fungal infection with ineffective targeted treatment.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 437 patients screened positive for CR-GNB colonization; 45 excluded (unidentified group); 392 analyzed
Specimen_Type_Detail: Rectoanal swab (colonization screening); blood, rectoanal swabs, vein catheter samples, tracheal secretions, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, intraperitoneal fluid, or pleural drainage fluid (infection diagnosis)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Subsequent clinical CR-GNB infection developing after CR-GNB colonization in hematological malignancy patients.
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae; Escherichia coli; Acinetobacter baumannii complex; Enterobacter cloacae; Klebsiella acidogenes; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Klebsiella ozaenae; Citrobacter freundi; Enterobacter aerogenes; Enterobacter polycluster; Proteus (plus an unspecified 'others' 3.6%)
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
Specific_Antibiotics: Cephalosporins; Aminoglycosides; Carbapenems; Quinolones (antimicrobial exposure variables assessed)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug

Feature_Engineering: Categorical risk factors converted to dummy (0/1) variables per category, with points assigned via a regression-coefficient-based scoring formula (Points = D/B).
Feature_Selection_Method: Forward stepwise selection with the likelihood ratio test (following univariate logistic regression screening).
Num_Features_Total: 16 candidate variables assessed in univariate analysis (Table 2)
Other_Metrics: Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals reported for each candidate/independent risk factor and for the high-risk vs low-risk score comparison.
Internal_Validation: Apparent/resubstitution validation: the score was applied back to the same 392-patient derivation cohort (no separate validation cohort).
Train_Test_Split: Not split; same cohort (n=392) used for both model derivation and validation.
Clinical_Insights: High-risk (score >=4) colonized patients are >3 times more likely to develop subsequent CR-GNB infection than low-risk patients (OR 3.347, 95% CI 2.218-5.094).
Generalisability_Details: Authors state an external validation cohort is needed to assess the model's discriminatory ability and goodness of fit.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only, on the same 392-patient derivation cohort; no external or prospective validation performed.
End_User_Described: Clinicians
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Patients screened for CR-GNB colonization on admission and weekly thereafter; once colonization identified and a subsequent infection risk score computed, high-risk patients (score >=4) are recommended early CR-GNB-targeted empirical therapy while low-risk patients receive anti-non-CR-GNB treatment and monitoring.
Stewardship_Details: Recommends early CR-GNB-targeted empirical therapy for the high-risk group, and anti-non-CR-GNB treatment with close monitoring (rather than empirical anti-CR-GNB therapy) for the low-risk group.
Future_Directions: An external validation cohort is needed to assess the model's discriminatory ability and goodness of fit, and it is needed to determine whether the scoring model is reproducible through relevant prospective studies.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Regression coefficients (bi) from the multivariate logistic model used to assign scoring points.
Limitation_Categories: Study design (retrospective, observational); missing mechanistic/genotypic data (no carbapenemase enzyme typing); lack of external validation; small transplantation-subgroup sample size; lack of prospective validation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: No information on the specific carbapenemases (KPC, OXA, etc.) identified in the studied population, due to species preservation and equipment limitations.

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study

Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Three stepwise-selection models (models 1-3: significant univariable predictors at p<0.1, p<0.05, and multivariable-retained p<0.1, respectively) plus 5 Bayesian-model-averaging models (lowest BIC); model 7 (4 predictors: tracheostomy/endotracheal tube, skin infection, pleural effusion, pneumatoceles) had the best ROC and sensitivity, AUC 0.70 (0.63-0.77) dataset / 0.71 (0.64-0.78) bootstrap.
Best_Performing_Model: Model 7 (four predictors: tracheostomy/endotracheal tube, skin infection, pleural effusion, pneumatoceles) — best ROC and sensitivity among models compared.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Primary dataset (n=207) and 1000 bootstrap samples, threshold 0.3
Specificity_Population_Set: Primary dataset and 1000 bootstrap samples, threshold 0.8
AUROC_Population_Set: Dataset and 1000 bootstrap samples

Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results; Imaging
Dataset_Size: 207 patients
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-center study at Cho Ray Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam; authors note this restricts generalizability.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood or a respiratory source (sputum, endotracheal aspirate, bronchoalveolar lavage, or pleura)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus spp. (MRSA and MRCoNS) infection in pneumonia patients, detected from blood or a respiratory source by culture and/or real-time PCR and deemed clinically significant.
Pathogens: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp. (MRCoNS)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (methicillin/oxacillin resistance)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA; Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRS defined as MRSA or MRCoNS detected from blood or a respiratory source (sputum, endotracheal aspirate, BAL, or pleura) via culture and/or real-time PCR, deemed clinically significant infection.
AI_Purpose: To develop a predictive model (nomogram) estimating individual risk of MRS infection in pneumonia patients, to guide empiric anti-MRSA antibiotic therapy decisions.
Num_Models_Compared: 8 (3 stepwise-selection models + 5 Bayesian-model-averaging models)
Feature_Engineering: Comorbidity burden derived as Charlson Comorbidity Index computed from ICD-10-CM codes.

Num_Features_Total: 9 candidate predictors significant at p<0.1 in univariable analysis

Other_Metrics: Calibration curve; decision curve analysis; clinical impact curve
Baseline_Method: Treat-all strategy compared via decision curve analysis net benefit

Internal_Validation: Bootstrap resampling, 1000 bootstrap samples with replacement
Train_Test_Split: No separate train/test split; bootstrap resampling of the full dataset (n=207) was used instead.

Future_Directions: Conduct additional validation studies in diverse settings; further investigate implementing the model for early administration of MRS antibiotics.

Data_Quality_Concerns: Sample size relatively small in relation to number of covariates, potentially leading to an overfitted model.
Page_References: Methods pp. 2-3; Results pp. 3-7; Discussion/Limitations/Declarations pp. 8-9.

AUROC_Population_Set: IPM, Lasso regression classifier, development dataset (n=1,054 ECC strains)

Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic resistance/susceptibility (R/S) of Enterobacter cloacae complex to imipenem (IPM), meropenem (MEM), ciprofloxacin (CIP), levofloxacin (LEV), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT), predicted from whole-genome and metagenomic sequencing data.
Pathogens: Enterobacter cloacae complex (ECC): E. cloacae, E. hormaechei, E. kobei, E. asburiae, E. cancerogenus
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem)
Specific_Antibiotics: Imipenem (IPM), meropenem (MEM), ciprofloxacin (CIP), levofloxacin (LEV), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant (R) / susceptible (S) call per antibiotic, based on detection (or absence) of AMR genomic features and, where absent, sufficiency of sequencing depth.
AI_Purpose: Rapid, accurate prediction of antibiotic resistance/susceptibility for Enterobacter cloacae complex from WGS/mNGS data, to shorten AST turnaround time versus conventional culture-based methods and guide earlier, targeted antibiotic therapy.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single Lasso regression classifier, fit separately per antibiotic — not a comparison of alternative algorithms)
Feature_Engineering: Candidate AMR features derived from (1) alignment of genome contigs to CARD-database resistance genes, and (2) predicted open reading frames from the genomes.
Feature_Selection_Method: Lasso regression
Num_Features_Selected: 6 to 20 resistance features (1 to 11 resistance genes), varying by antibiotic
Hyperparameter_Method: Number of markers/features selected via cross-validation (chosen when AUC is higher or cross-validation error is smaller).
Other_Metrics: Turnaround time: 17.95 ± 0.15 h (mNGS-AST) vs 87.59 ± 18.03 h (culture-based AST); effective/predictable report ratio (e.g. 80.76%, 84/104 overall in clinical validation).
Baseline_Method: Conventional culture-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST)
Baseline_Performance: Culture-based AST turnaround time 87.59 ± 18.03 h (vs 17.95 ± 0.15 h for mNGS-AST); culture-based species misidentification rate 74%
Internal_Validation: Cross-validation (used for feature/marker selection during Lasso model development)
External_Validation_Description: 104 independent clinical respiratory specimens (103 sputum, 1 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) from suspected respiratory tract infection patients with positive ECC culture, Shanghai Children's Hospital, October 2022-June 2024, tested by mNGS.
Clinical_Insights: Key resistance genes (blaKPC, blaNDM, blaVIM, NmcR for IPM/MEM; dfr family for SXT) and mutation sites (gyrA aa83, parC aa80 for CIP/LEV) identified as primary resistance determinants, consistent with known AMR biology.
Generalisability_Details: Isolates obtained solely from a single paediatric hospital limit sample size and diversity; broader validation using clinical samples from general hospitals is warranted to assess model robustness and extend clinical relevance.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed on 104 independent clinical respiratory specimens; clinical-impact/treatment-decision assessment was a retrospective simulation rather than real-time prospective deployment or CDS integration.
Integration_Point: Clinician treatment-adjustment decision point on Day 1 (D1), after mNGS/mNGS-AST results become available, ahead of D2-D7 culture-based results.
End_User_Described: Physicians/clinicians making antibacterial therapy recommendations (de-escalation, escalation, maintenance)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Specimens collected on D0 for bacterial culture and clinical mNGS; clinicians could adjust treatment on D1 using mNGS results, and further from D2-D7 using culture results and patient response.
Stewardship_Details: Evaluated whether earlier mNGS-based AST results would change clinician antibacterial therapy recommendations (de-escalation, escalation, or maintenance) for 48 patients with complete medication records.
Barriers_List: High proportion of human-derived sequence limiting pathogen genomic coverage (mNGS); undetected/novel resistance features causing false-susceptible calls for CIP/LEV; single-institution (paediatric hospital) sampling limiting diversity/generalisability.
Future_Directions: Further investigation of quinolone resistance mechanisms and collection of more resistant ECC strains to update/optimise the model; broader validation using clinical samples from general (non-paediatric) hospitals.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Lasso regression coefficient-based association/selection
Limitation_Categories: Data/coverage quality (human-DNA background reducing pathogen genomic coverage); residual undetected resistance features (false-susceptible calls); single-institution sampling limiting generalisability.
Data_Quality_Concerns: High proportion of human-derived sequence in clinical mNGS specimens reduces pathogen genomic coverage (often <100% at 20M-read depth), leaving 19.25% (84/104) of samples unable to be clearly predicted.

Title: Risk factors for multidrug resistance in pulmonary tuberculosis patients with diabetes mellitus

Title: Benchmark evaluation of deepseek AI models in antibacterial clinical decision-making for infectious diseases
Journal_Source: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making (2026) 26:62
AI_Application_Type: AI Chatbots and Digital Health Communication; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: Yuebei People's Hospital (clinical research project LCYJZX/2025/71)
Population_Description: 101 real-world infectious disease (ID) consultation cases with effective antibacterial therapy, selected from 1,069 ID specialists' consultation cases at Yuebei People's Hospital (Nov 2024-Mar 2025) via inclusion/exclusion criteria
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
Task_Type: Natural language processing; Generative (LLM / chatbot); Recommendation / personalisation
All_Models_Evaluated: DeepSeek-V3: overlap rate 71.29%, precision 44.91%, recall 85.84%, F1 58.97%; DeepSeek-R1: overlap rate 75.78%, precision 40.91%, recall 95.58%, F1 57.30%; DeepSeek-R1+WS: overlap rate 75.29%, precision 37.20%, recall 82.3%, F1 51.24%; ChatGPT o1: overlap rate 76.24%, precision 30.12%, recall 90.27%, F1 45.17%.
Best_Performing_Model: DeepSeek-V3 (best F1 score, 58.97%, among the four AI systems compared)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Single-antibacterial-regimen cases recommended by DeepSeek-V3 (86 of 101 cases)
Sensitivity_Value: 85.84% (reported as recall for DeepSeek-V3, the best-performing model by F1 score)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: 101 real-world ID consultation cases
Precision_PPV_Value: 44.91% (DeepSeek-V3, the best-performing model by F1 score)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: 101 real-world ID consultation cases
F1_Value: 58.97% (DeepSeek-V3, the highest F1 score among the four AI systems)
F1_Population_Set: 101 real-world ID consultation cases

Reported_Limitations: Monocentric design and modest sample size (85-101 cases) limiting generalisability given geographic variation in AMR patterns; some normal-range test results were not provided in full to the AI, with unclear impact on the overlap rate; the 101-case cohort, while sufficient for preliminary validation, limited statistical power to detect subtle performance differences.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: No ethical or governance risks beyond standard approvals are discussed; the paper reports IRB approval (Yue Bei People's Hospital, Approved No. YBSKY-2025-040-001) with a waiver of informed consent, and no competing interests.
Reviewer_Notes: Retrospective benchmarking of pre-existing LLMs (DeepSeek-V3/R1/R1+WS, ChatGPT o1) against ID specialists on 101 real consultation cases from one Chinese hospital; unit of analysis for *_Value fields taken as DeepSeek-V3, the model the paper itself names as achieving the best F1 score. 'Recall' in Table 3 is treated as equivalent to Sensitivity (no separate Recall field exists in the schema).
Unresolved_Items: Whether 'available from the corresponding author on reasonable request' should code Data_Shared as Yes or No is inconsistently handled elsewhere in this review's records; coded No here. Whether the regimen-count stratification (Table 4/5) should satisfy Subgroup_Analysis_Reported given it is not a demographic subgroup.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Infectious diseases consultation cases (drawn from the 1,069 ID specialists' consultation cases at Yuebei People's Hospital, Nov 2024-Mar 2025)
Exclusion_Criteria: Febrile patients without normalised/declining temperature within 72h of antibacterial therapy (n=284); patients whose PCT fell <50% within 72h (n=195); failure to recheck PCT within 72h (n=175); prescribed restricted antibiotics (n=101); ID specialists' recommendations not followed (n=34); discharged or died within 72h after consultation (n=78)
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Imaging
Dataset_Size: 101 cases (of 1,069 screened)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre dataset (Yuebei People's Hospital, Guangdong, China); geographical location information was explicitly excluded from case data provided to the AI, and the discussion flags geographic variation in AMR patterns as a generalisability limitation.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Concordance between AI-generated (DeepSeek-V3/R1/R1+WS, ChatGPT o1) and ID specialists' antibacterial regimens for real infectious-disease cases, and the proportion of AI regimens escalating therapy to higher-tier/broader-spectrum antibacterials under WHO's AWaRe classification.
Specific_Antibiotics: Illustrative agents named in the paper: piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, cefoperazone-sulbactam
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Concordance defined by regimen-level agreement with the ID specialist's regimen: full concordance = identical agents, dosage (mg/kg/day) and frequency; partial concordance = therapeutically equivalent substitution or same antibiotic with modified dose/frequency; discordance = clinically non-interchangeable regimens (escalation, unindicated combination therapy, or misidentified colonising/contaminating organisms as pathogenic).
AI_Purpose: To benchmark DeepSeek (V3, R1, R1+WS) and ChatGPT o1 as antibacterial clinical decision-making tools by comparing their AI-generated regimens against ID specialists' regimens and evaluating the AI models' performance and timeliness.
Num_Models_Compared: 4 (DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1+WS, ChatGPT o1)
Feature_Engineering: Raw HIS case data were de-identified and reorganised into nine fixed categories (demographic data, clinical diagnosis, vital signs, imaging studies, microbiological information, inflammatory markers, hepatic & renal function, drug regimen, treatment effect evaluation), then consolidated into a structured key-value text summary for prompting the LLMs.
Software_Libraries: SPSS statistical package, Version 29.0.2.0 (no machine-learning libraries named; DeepSeek/ChatGPT o1 used as-is via their web interfaces)
Other_Metrics: Concordance rate (full/partial/total) and discordance rate between AI and ID specialists' regimens; proportion of regimens escalated to higher-tier groups per WHO's AWaRe classification; overlap rate; ID specialists endorsement rate; search latency; search success rate (in addition to precision, recall and F1-score, which have dedicated fields).
Baseline_Method: ChatGPT o1 (general-purpose reasoning LLM) used as the comparator/benchmark model against DeepSeek
Baseline_Performance: ChatGPT o1: overlap rate 76.24%, precision 30.12%, recall 90.27%, F1 45.17% (also 54.46% total concordance with ID specialists, per Table 1)
Internal_Validation: Retrospective comparison against 101 real-world consultation cases from a single hospital, with outputs independently evaluated by five clinical pharmacists
Clinical_Insights: Discordance is attributed to differing decision-making paradigms: ID specialists prioritise clinical contextualisation and individual patient factors, whereas the AI systems rely predominantly on pattern recognition learned from training data, which the authors link to the AI's tendency toward broader-spectrum escalation.
Generalisability_Details: The monocentric design and modest sample size (85-101 cases) limit generalisability, particularly given geographic variation in antibacterial resistance patterns.
Maturity_Evidence: The paper's own evidence is a single retrospective benchmarking pass of pre-existing, publicly deployed LLMs against 101 real cases from one hospital, with no external dataset, prospective test, or clinical deployment reported; the authors themselves frame this as limited by monocentric design and modest sample size.
Integration_Point: Not integrated into the hospital's clinical workflow/HIS; models were queried via their own standalone public web interfaces, simulating a remote deployment rather than an embedded CDS tool.
End_User_Described: Five independent clinical pharmacists evaluated the AI outputs; ID specialists' own regimens served as the real-world reference standard.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Consultation cases were identified via the HIS consultation management module at the Clinical Pharmacy Work Station; de-identified case data were structured into fixed categories and consolidated into a text summary, then submitted with a fixed instruction template to DeepSeek/ChatGPT o1's web interfaces; outputs were independently evaluated by five clinical pharmacists.
Stewardship_Details: Proportion of regimens escalated to higher-tier/broader-spectrum antibacterials (WHO AWaRe classification): ID specialists 39.6% (40/101) vs DeepSeek-V3 52.5%, DeepSeek-R1 67.4%, DeepSeek-R1+WS 70.6%, ChatGPT o1 62.4% (chi-square P<0.005) — AI models showed significantly greater escalation than specialists.
Barriers_List: Copyright restrictions constraining ChatGPT o1's widespread adoption
Facilitators_List: Open-source accessibility; low operational costs; local deployment enhancing data privacy
Future_Directions: Further investigation into hybrid human-AI collaborative workflows for antibacterial decision-making
Predictor_Categories_Count: 9 (demographic, clinical diagnosis, vital sign, imaging, microbiological, inflammatory markers, hepatic & renal function, drug regimen, treatment effect evaluation)
Limitation_Categories: Generalisability (monocentric design, modest sample size, geographic variation in AMR); data completeness (incomplete provision of normal-range test results); statistical power (101-case cohort limits detection of subtle performance differences).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Some laboratory/test results within the normal value range were not provided in full to the AI systems; the authors note it is unclear what impact this incompleteness had on the AI's overlap rate with ID specialists.

Title: Modeling Pneumococcal Resistance to Penicillin in Southern Sweden Using Artificial Neural Networks
Funder_Names: European Commission 6th framework programme (PREVIS contract LSHM-CT-2003-503413); Swedish Institute for Infectious Disease Control

Inclusion_Criteria: All persons identified through the Swedish notification system since 1996 carrying or infected with the epidemic 9V PRP clone; retrospective study restricted to the Skane Region owing to limited case numbers elsewhere.
Data_Types_Used: Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: Swedish Institute for Infectious Disease Control (SMI) notification registry; Apoteket AB national prescription database; National Travel Survey (Statistics Sweden)
Dataset_Size: 156 PRP cases notified in 2003; weekly incidence counts across the 32/33 municipalities of Skane, 1997-2003
Geographic_Representativeness: Restricted to the Skane Region (33 municipalities, ~1.15 million inhabitants) in southern Sweden; the retrospective study was limited to Skane owing to limited PRP case numbers elsewhere in the country.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Isolates (one from each patient); serotyped, with selected isolates further genetically typed by PFGE and MLST
Primary_AMR_Outcome: The number of PRP cases (index + contact) notified this week, this municipality - i.e. weekly incidence of penicillin-resistant pneumococci (target/outcome variable of the ANN).
Pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the international epidemic penicillin- and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole-resistant serotype 9V clone)
Drug_Classes: Penicillin (penicillin G) for the resistance outcome; whole ATC J01 systemic-antibacterial class used for the antibiotic-consumption predictor variable
Specific_Antibiotics: Penicillin G (PcG); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Penicillin-resistant pneumococci (PRP) defined by penicillin G (PcG) MIC >= 0.5 mg/L
AI_Purpose: To develop an iterative ANN model to describe and predict the spread of penicillin-resistant pneumococci (PRP) in space and time as a function of antibiotic consumption and other confounders.
Feature_Engineering: Antibiotic-consumption (recipe) data were deseasonalized to separate the effect of consumption from seasonal effects.
Feature_Selection_Method: No automated feature-selection algorithm; five pre-specified alternative input-variable sets were each independently topology-optimized.
Hyperparameter_Method: Cross-validation used to select ANN topology (number of hidden nodes)
Software_Libraries: Web-based ANN computing tool (webnn, Medical University of South Carolina); mirror hosted by Microcortex Inc.
Other_Metrics: Correlation coefficient between predicted and observed values; mean square prediction error (MSPE)
Baseline_Method: Two reference models: median number of cases per week and per county; median number of cases per county
Baseline_Performance: Reference 'median per time per county': r=0.413 (1997-2000)/MSPE=0.126 (2001-2003); Reference 'median per county': r=0.298/MSPE=0.136
Internal_Validation: Cross-validation for topology selection; each of the 5 models retrained 5 times to check stability against random weight initialization; best network chosen by correlation.
Train_Test_Split: Training: 1997-2000; evaluation/test: 2001-2003 (temporal split)
Clinical_Insights: Sensitivity analysis found seasonality had the highest impact on predicted PRP incidence in all models; antibiotic sales, child population, and travel intensity also had effects, while past PRP case counts had low sensitivity despite the data being autocorrelated.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supports only internal (temporal holdout + cross-validation) evaluation: trained on 1997-2000 data, evaluated on 2001-2003 data from the same population, with no external dataset or deployment.
End_User_Described: Public health surveillance context (implied by the stated aim of efficient surveillance); no specific end-user role is named.
Future_Directions: Compare alternative output transfer functions (e.g. inverse sigmoid or linear instead of a bounded sigmoid) for modeling AMR emergence; use a truly (topologically) recurrent neural network to address autocorrelation in the data.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Sensitivity analysis: each input varied while the rest were held constant, and the resulting change in output relative to the input variation gave the sensitivity / relative importance.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Despite the autocorrelation function showing PRP cases autocorrelated up to 1 year back, sensitivity analysis found the past-case-count variables had low sensitivities (<=1%), indicating little dependency on the past - a contrast the authors highlight.
Limitation_Categories: Inability to identify a smaller subset of most predictive parameters (possibly diffuse causal mechanisms or missing indicators); model interpretability of the ANN; sigmoid output-layer bound; autocorrelation in the data; no error estimate for sensitivities.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Possible absence of critical experimental indicators/predictive parameters from the dataset.
