Title: Improved prediction of antimicrobial resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae using machine learning
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación; Generalitat Valenciana
Population_Description: K. pneumoniae genome collection (n=5,907): 4,487 genomes with MIC data from the public PATRIC database plus 1,605 genome assemblies from the SKPCV genomic surveillance project in 8 Spanish hospitals (Comunidad Valenciana, Jan 2017-Feb 2020); genomes mainly from Europe, Asia and America, corresponding mainly to clinical isolates from humans.
Data_Source_Other: Public genomic database (PATRIC)
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 10 k-mers (15-mers) ranked by XGBoost relative importance and SHAP value per antibiotic model (Table 2); notable annotated features include a 16S rRNA (guanine(1405)-N(7))-methyltransferase and the Msr(E) ribosomal-protection gene region (amikacin), an intergenic region/hypothetical protein WP_002887322.1 near fosA (fosfomycin), and a LysR-family transcriptional regulator within an integron plus the dmsB anaerobic DMSO reductase gene (piperacillin/tazobactam).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: ResFinder (rule-based): accuracy 0.39-0.96 across 12 antibiotics (Table 1). XGBoost k-mer ML models trained for the 3 antibiotics where ResFinder accuracy was below 75%: amikacin (AUC 0.95, accuracy 0.90, bAcc 0.92, F1 0.83), piperacillin/tazobactam (AUC 0.86, accuracy 0.80, bAcc 0.80, F1 0.83), fosfomycin (AUC 0.78, accuracy 0.74, bAcc 0.73, F1 0.67).
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (k-mer based) model for amikacin resistance prediction - highest AUC (0.95) among the three ML models trained
Accuracy_Population_Set: Amikacin resistance prediction test set (375 genomes; 1,125 used for training)
F1_Population_Set: Amikacin resistance prediction test set (375 genomes)
AUROC_Population_Set: Amikacin resistance prediction test set (375 genomes)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were trained and evaluated using an internal random 75%/25% train/test split of the pooled genome dataset (max 1,500 genomes/antibiotic) with 10-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter selection; no external validation cohort or prospective/clinical evaluation was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Computational cost restricted the analysis to data subsets and smaller k-mers, limiting possible biological insight; a categorical R/S outcome (rather than continuous MIC) had to be used because AST/MIC results were not directly comparable across clinical settings and years; dataset diversity/representativeness may limit generalisation because some clonal groups and geographic regions may be overrepresented.
Inclusion_Criteria: Genome assemblies with a strong Kleborate species match to K. pneumoniae, genome size 5-6 Mb, assembled in fewer than 800 contigs; SKPCV isolates were non-susceptible strains to 3rd-generation cephalosporins and/or carbapenems collected Jan 2017-Feb 2020 in 8 hospitals; PATRIC genomes required associated MIC data.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: PATRIC; SKPCV (Surveillance of Klebsiella pneumoniae in the Comunidad Valenciana)
Dataset_Size: 5,907 genomes (4,487 from PATRIC + 1,605 from SKPCV, after filtering)
Geographic_Representativeness: Genomes mainly from Europe (50%), Asia (7.7%) and America (33.7%); the Spanish surveillance subset (SKPCV) is concentrated in the Comunidad Valenciana region.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Machine-learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance phenotype (resistant/susceptible) in K. pneumoniae from genomic data, focused on antibiotics for which rule-based prediction fails (amikacin, fosfomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam).
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems; Aminoglycosides (explicitly named by the paper); the panel also included other beta-lactams (ampicillin, aztreonam, cefepime, ceftazidime, piperacillin/tazobactam), a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) and fosfomycin, not explicitly grouped into classes by the authors.
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin, ampicillin, aztreonam, cefepime, ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, fosfomycin, gentamicin, imipenem, meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, tobramycin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MIC values for each antibiotic classified as susceptible (S) or resistant (R) using the AMR v2.1.0 R library and EUCAST 2018 clinical breakpoints (intermediate MICs counted as susceptible).
AI_Purpose: To apply ML models to improve the accuracy of AMR phenotype prediction from genomic data for antibiotics where rule-based (ResFinder) prediction performs poorly, and to identify genomic determinants underlying resistance.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 prediction approaches (ResFinder rule-based vs XGBoost ML), each applied across the 3 antibiotics selected for ML training
Feature_Engineering: K-mer (k=15) counts extracted per genome, summarised into a binary genome x k-mer presence/absence matrix, then deduplicated to keep one k-mer per unique presence/absence profile.
Feature_Selection_Method: K-mers filtered to keep only those with a possible association with the AMR phenotype (p<0.1) via Fisher's exact test, Holm-corrected.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over learning rate (0.04-0.07) and subsampling percentage (0.3-1.0) using gentamicin data (10 random subsets), selecting parameters via Kruskal-Wallis/Levene's tests on the AUC distribution.
Software_Libraries: XGBoost, stats, caret, pROC, AMR (R libraries); GenomeTester4, Kleborate, ResFinder, Prokka, Panaroo, IQ-TREE 2, iTOL, mlplasmids (bioinformatics tools)
Other_Metrics: Balanced accuracy (bAcc)
Baseline_Method: ResFinder rule-based prediction (identification of AMR genes/point mutations; database v2.2.1, Pointfinder v4.0.1)
Baseline_Performance: ResFinder prediction accuracies ranged from 39% to 96% across the 12 antibiotics tested (Table 1)
Internal_Validation: Random 75%/25% train/test split per antibiotic (max 1,500 genomes sampled), with 10-fold cross-validation used to select the optimal number of XGBoost boosting iterations.
Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% testing
Overfitting_Method: Maximum tree depth limited to 4 in all XGBoost models to limit model complexity and prevent overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: K. pneumoniae commonly carries the fosA gene chromosomally, but its expression is insufficient to confer clinical fosfomycin resistance, explaining ResFinder's false-positive misclassifications; the ML model's top features were located in genes other than fosA.
Generalisability_Details: Dataset diversity/representativeness may limit generalisation of the findings because some clonal groups and geographic regions may be overrepresented in both the PATRIC and SKPCV datasets.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supports only internal validation: a random train/test split of the pooled retrospective genome dataset, with no external cohort or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Future_Directions: Continued exploration/evaluation and enhancement of ML techniques for genomic AMR surveillance and prediction, aiming toward integration into clinical practice and public health/surveillance strategies.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: XGBoost feature (relative) importance ranking plus SHAP values
Novel_Predictors_Details: The Msr(E) ribosomal-protection gene region (top amikacin k-mer) was not previously associated with amikacin resistance in the ResFinder database; several other top-ranked k-mers (intergenic regions, a putative tyrosine kinase, a LysR regulator/glnQ within an integron, dmsB) were likewise not established rule-based AMR determinants for the antibiotics studied.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Bimodal SHAP-value distribution for one feature's absence was interpreted as evidence of a possible interaction with other genetic elements (not formally/statistically tested).
Limitation_Categories: Computational-cost constraint on data/k-mer size; outcome-definition simplification (categorical R/S instead of continuous MIC) due to cross-setting/cross-year AST variability; dataset representativeness (clonal group and geographic overrepresentation).
Data_Quality_Concerns: AST/MIC results varied across different clinical settings and years and were not directly comparable, requiring a categorical (R/S) rather than continuous MIC-based outcome.

Title: Predicting Carbapenem Resistance in Hospitalized Patients Using Machine Learning: A Retrospective Analysis of the MIMIC-III Database
Population_Description: Adult patients with available microbiological cultures and positive carbapenem-susceptibility test results; 3,277 unique admissions included after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria (from a base MIMIC-III cohort of 94,000 hospitalized patients).
Top_Predictive_Features: Permutation feature importance (XGBoost) ranked highly specific diagnostic categories highest (e.g. DIAGNOSIS_SHORTNESS OF BREATH, DIAGNOSIS_ASTHMA/COPD EXACERBATION, DIAGNOSIS_HYPERGLYCEMIA); GLUCOSE was the only general biochemical marker in the top 15.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Decision trees, random forests, and XGBoost
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting) — best performance based on AUC of 0.955 (also highest precision, sensitivity, specificity)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Testing dataset
Specificity_Population_Set: Testing dataset
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Testing dataset
AUROC_Population_Set: Testing dataset
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation grid search on a single retrospective MIMIC-III cohort; no external validation performed (future work recommends multi-center external validation).
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design introduces potential biases and dependence on the quality of historical data; the model may be susceptible to unmeasured confounders not captured in the available dataset.
Sample_Size: 94,000 hospitalized patients (base cohort); 3,277 patients with carbapenem-resistant infections (analytic subset)
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult patients with available carbapenem-resistance antibiotic testing results (Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria) who had fluid or blood samples collected at admission or during hospitalization.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: MIMIC-III (v1.4)
Dataset_Size: 94,000 hospitalized patients (base MIMIC-III cohort); 3,277 patients/admissions in the analytic sample
Missing_Data_Method: Rows with missing values were discarded (complete-case handling).
Specimen_Type_Detail: Fluid or blood samples collected at admission or during hospitalization
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence of carbapenem resistance (binary 'RESISTANT' label derived from microbiology culture interpretation)
Pathogens: ESKAPE group named as focus: Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter species
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems
Specific_Antibiotics: Meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary 'RESISTANT' label from MICROBIOLOGYEVENTS: a patient is resistant if at least one microbiology event has INTERPRETATION='R' to meropenem, imipenem, or ertapenem.
AI_Purpose: Predict carbapenem resistance early (before culture results available) to optimize empirical antibiotic therapy and reduce unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic use.
Feature_Engineering: DIAGNOSIS high-cardinality field reduced by extracting its initial component; categorical features one-hot encoded with drop_first=True to avoid multicollinearity; binary HAD_ANTIBIOTIC flag engineered from MICROBIOLOGY EVENTS to capture prior antibiotic exposure.
Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold cross-validation grid search
Software_Libraries: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn (via Google Colab)
Hardware_Details: Multicore virtual machine; Google Colab collaborative development environment
Baseline_Method: Decision trees and random forests (compared against XGBoost)
Internal_Validation: 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation grid search for hyperparameter tuning
Overfitting_Method: 5-fold cross-validation grid search; 80/20 train-test split to prevent memorization of training data
Clinical_Insights: Top predictors aligned with known resistance risk factors (prior carbapenem exposure, ICU admission, elevated lactate/creatinine, abnormal WBC, recent severe infection, prior hospitalization within 90 days), enhancing model credibility for clinical decision-making.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state future multi-center external validation is needed to enhance the model's generalizability and predictive accuracy.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation on a single-center retrospective dataset; no external or prospective validation performed.
Integration_Point: Point of clinical suspicion, before culture and susceptibility results are available; usable within the first hours of ICU admission.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (to guide empiric antibiotic selection); medical staff (alerted automatically in the proposed EHR-integration concept).
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed integration into electronic health systems to automatically alert medical staff to high carbapenem-resistance risk, streamlining critical decision-making in the ICU (proposed, not yet implemented).
Stewardship_Details: Paper asserts the model could improve antibiotic stewardship and inform early clinical decision-making, but does not report a quantitative stewardship-impact assessment.
Facilitators_List: Cloud-based infrastructure/programming platforms proposed as an avenue for enhancing early detection; real-time hospital-system implementation suggested to improve clinical outcomes and reduce inappropriate antibiotic use.
Future_Directions: Multi-center external validation; integrating advanced genetic resistance markers; cloud-based infrastructure for real-time hospital implementation; updating the study using the newly released MIMIC-IV database.

Novel_Predictors_Details: Highly specific diagnostic categories (e.g. shortness of breath, asthma/COPD exacerbation, hyperglycemia) were top predictors, while clinically expected predictors (prior carbapenem exposure, ICU admission at culture time, lactate, creatinine) did not rank among the most important features.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design (bias, dependence on historical data quality); unmeasured confounders not captured in the dataset.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Dependence on the quality/completeness of historical retrospective EHR data; possible unmeasured confounders not captured in the dataset.

Title: Computational antimicrobial peptide design and evaluation against multidrug-resistant clinical isolates of bacteria
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Department of Biotechnology (DBT), India
Population_Description: 61 recent multidrug-resistant clinical bacterial isolates (ESBL-producing, methicillin-resistant, and carbapenem-resistant) obtained from MS Ramaiah Medical College, Bangalore, India, used to test the two lead designed peptides
Data_Source_Other: Microbial Type Culture Collection (MTCC), Chandigarh, India (reference culture collection used for the initial 30-culture screening panel)
All_Models_Evaluated: Bi-LSTM regression model ranked 6415 candidate peptide sequences by predicted antimicrobial activity (Bi-LSTM score); the 10 lowest-scoring (best-predicted) sequences were chosen for synthesis and experimental evaluation.
Best_Performing_Model: NN2_0050 and NN2_0018 (peptide scores of 15 and 10 respectively, on the paper's own peptide_score metric: number of test cultures for which the peptide had the lowest MIC)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The designed peptides were validated only within this same study (in vitro susceptibility testing and an in vivo mouse infection model); no independent external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, or clinical integration was performed.
Reported_Limitations: Structural elucidation and structure-function analyses of NN2_0018 are described as important future steps, and the mechanisms behind the differential Gram-positive/Gram-negative activity of NN2_0018 and NN2_0050 are flagged as needing further investigation.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: NN2_0050 possessed an IC50 of 64µg/ml against HeLa cells (unlike NN2_0018, whose IC50 exceeded 128µg/ml), leading the authors to conclude NN2_0050 lacks specificity for prokaryotic cells and may cross-react with eukaryotic tissue.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest with the contents of this article.
Inclusion_Criteria: Recent clinical isolates obtained from a hospital collection, most displaying multidrug resistance (ESBL production, methicillin resistance, or carbapenem resistance).
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: YADAMP (Yet Another Database of Antimicrobial Peptides)
Dataset_Size: Bi-LSTM regression model trained on 501 sequences from the YADAMP database with available MIC data against E. coli
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre convenience sample of clinical isolates from one hospital collection in Bangalore, India; no discussion of broader geographic representativeness.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Clinical bacterial isolates displaying multidrug resistance (ESBL, methicillin resistance, and carbapenem resistance)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug-resistance phenotype of clinical bacterial isolates (ESBL, methicillin resistance, carbapenem resistance), measured as minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) against the AI-designed peptides.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Acinetobacter baumannii; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Staphylococcus aureus; coagulase-negative staphylococci
Drug_Classes: Antimicrobial peptides (novel designed class); meropenem (carbapenem class, used as an in vivo comparator)
Specific_Antibiotics: Meropenem (in vivo efficacy comparator)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; ESBL; CRE / carbapenemase-producing; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance/susceptibility defined phenotypically via minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) assay (modified resazurin protocol) against each designed peptide; isolates were separately characterised as ESBL-producing, methicillin-resistant, or carbapenem-resistant.
AI_Purpose: To train an LSTM/Bi-LSTM language model to learn the sequence 'grammar' of known antimicrobial peptides and use it to generate and rank novel antimicrobial peptide candidates for synthesis and experimental testing against multidrug-resistant pathogens.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (a generative LSTM language model and a Bi-LSTM regression scoring model used sequentially; no alternative ML architectures were benchmarked against each other)
Feature_Engineering: Candidate sequences were filtered by net positive charge (≥4 positively charged lysine/arginine/histidine residues) and by an amphiphilicity index (H*) computed from a helical-wheel projection, before Bi-LSTM scoring.
Feature_Selection_Method: Charge (≥4 positively charged residues) and amphiphilicity index (H* ≥ 0.33) thresholding
Other_Metrics: Custom peptide_score (Equation 2): number of test cultures for which a peptide achieved the lowest MIC among all designed peptides; Bi-LSTM predicted-activity score used for candidate ranking.
Baseline_Method: Shuffled-sequence peptide controls (same composition, randomised order) and poor Bi-LSTM-scoring peptides
Baseline_Performance: MIC values for unshuffled (designed) peptides were lower than their shuffled counterparts in all cases tested
Internal_Validation: Comparison against shuffled-sequence and poor-scoring control peptides, and against a panel of clinical isolates
Train_Test_Split: 1011 sequences (≤30 residues) used as LSTM training input, filtered from 2525 manually annotated YADAMP sequences
Data_Repository: Supporting Datasets S1-S3 (journal supplementary information); code/pipeline at https://github.com/Tushar-N/amp-lm
Maturity_Evidence: Highest evidence is internal experimental validation: in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing against clinical isolates and an in vivo mouse toxicity/efficacy study; no external or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Future_Directions: Structural elucidation and structure-function analysis of NN2_0018, and further investigation of the mechanisms behind its differential Gram-positive/Gram-negative activity relative to NN2_0050, are identified as next steps.
Limitation_Categories: No dedicated 'Limitations' section; authors note structural characterisation of NN2_0018 is preliminary/ongoing and that the mechanistic basis for differential Gram-positive/Gram-negative activity needs further study.

Title: Scalable machine learning improves resistance prediction and identifies novel determinants in Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Data_Source_Name: CRyPTIC (EBI FTP repository, June 2022 release)
Dataset_Size: 12,185 MTB isolates; 13 antibiotics tested per isolate
Missing_Data_Method: Exclusion of isolates lacking phenotypic susceptibility data for that antibiotic
Geographic_Representativeness: Described only as 'globally diverse'; no country-level breakdown given.
Specimen_Type_Detail: MTB clinical isolates (whole-genome sequences, assembled contigs)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype prediction (from WGS-derived k-mer features) for 13 first-line, second-line, and repurposed anti-TB drugs, using CRyPTIC-provided susceptible/resistant labels.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides (amikacin, kanamycin) explicitly named as a drug class (rrs-encoded 16S rRNA binding site).
Specific_Antibiotics: ethambutol, rifampicin, isoniazid (first-line); amikacin, kanamycin, moxifloxacin, levofloxacin, ethionamide, rifabutin (second-line); linezolid, delamanid, clofazimine, bedaquiline (NRDs)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible label from CRyPTIC AST; intermediate phenotypes (reported only for ethionamide and ethambutol) grouped with the resistant class.
AI_Purpose: To develop a GPU-accelerated, pangenome-scale ML framework (AURA) for de novo prediction of antibiotic resistance in MTB from WGS data.
Num_Models_Compared: 6 (AURA plus 5 competing tools: TBProfiler, ResFinder, Mykrobe, KvarQ, MTB++)
Feature_Engineering: k-mer frequency feature matrix built from assembled genomes (GPU-accelerated k-mer counting via Gerbil), stored as compressed sparse row (CSR) matrices.
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate chi-square (χ2) test of independence
Num_Features_Total: Billions of unique k-mers (exact total figure not given as one number)
Num_Features_Selected: 524,288 (isoniazid, optimized final model)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid-style search over k-mer length, number of top-ranked k-mers (exponential series), and classifier family (LR, RF, SVM, XGB, NB), selected by validation-set performance (70%/10% train/validation split).
Software_Libraries: NVIDIA RAPIDS AI (GPU data-science library suite)
Hardware_Details: AURA ran on a single AMD EPYC 75F3 CPU core with an NVIDIA A100 GPU (80 GB VRAM).
Other_Metrics: F1-score, precision, recall, sensitivity, specificity (Tables 1, 5, 6); computational runtime, RAM and VRAM usage benchmarks (Table 3).
Baseline_Method: TBProfiler, ResFinder, Mykrobe, KvarQ, MTB++ (existing mutation-catalog / alignment-based resistance prediction tools)
Baseline_Performance: For isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol — where AURA did not have the absolute highest score — it remained within 1-2% of the top performing comparator tool.
Internal_Validation: 70% training / 10% validation / 20% held-out test per antibiotic; k-mer length, feature count and classifier family tuned on the 70/10 split, then evaluated once on the untouched 20% test set.
Train_Test_Split: 70% training / 10% validation / 20% held-out test (final protocol); an earlier 80%/20% description also appears in Methods.
Overfitting_Method: Random Forest's ensemble of decision trees (bagging) is noted as preventing overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: Identified loci validate known resistance genes (katG, pncA, rpoC) and highlight novel regions (PE/PGRS family) implicated in immune evasion and host-pathogen interactions.
Data_Repository: CRyPTIC dataset via EBI FTP repository; AURA code at https://github.com/M-Serajian/AURA
Generalisability_Details: AURA is constrained by the scope of CRyPTIC, which covers only lineages 1-4 of 10 recognized MTB lineages and 13 antibiotics; extending to other lineages/drugs needs further curated datasets.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal train/validation/held-out-test split only (70/10/20%); no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Barriers_List: Prior CPU-parallelized tools (e.g. MTB++) faced severe scalability barriers, unable to scale to tens of thousands of genomes due to prohibitive computational demands.
Facilitators_List: GPU acceleration (NVIDIA RAPIDS AI, A100 GPU) enabling a 6.2x speedup in feature matrix generation and a 215-fold acceleration in feature selection.
Future_Directions: Extending AURA to operate on read-derived k-mers without assembly, and evaluating allele-frequency-aware representations.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Model-specific importance: XGBoost feature weight, Random Forest mean decrease in Gini impurity, Logistic Regression/SVM coefficient magnitude.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Recovered 151 loci previously reported by CRyPTIC and identified 59 novel resistance-associated loci (e.g. PE_PGRS57/Rv3514 linked to 5 antibiotics).
Limitation_Categories: Data quality/labeling dependency (primary theme); see _notes for additional categories each with their own passage (lineage/drug coverage, class imbalance for NRDs, non-causal associations, assembly artifacts, univariate feature selection).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Predictive performance depends on input sequencing data quality, AST accuracy/consistency, and the clinical ECOFFs used to dichotomize MICs.

Title: Rapid prediction of WHO-priority multidrug-resistant pneumonia pathogens: A metaheuristic-optimized interpretable ensemble model with dual feature selection for antimicrobial stewardship

Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification
Delivery_Platform: Cloud API / service; Not yet deployed

Precision_PPV_Population_Set: independent test set
F1_Population_Set: independent test set
AUROC_Population_Set: independent test set

Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared that no competing interest exists.

Exclusion_Criteria: Samples with missing values (5-23 missing entries per feature) were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 1,334 CBC samples (P. aeruginosa n=190, E. coli n=670, S. aureus n=121, S. pneumoniae n=341)
Missing_Data_Method: Listwise exclusion of samples with missing values (5-23 missing entries per feature)
Specimen_Type_Detail: Complete blood count (CBC) samples / routine hematological blood parameters
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Which of four WHO-priority pathogens (P. aeruginosa, E. coli, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae) caused the bacterial pneumonia — a four-class pathogen-species classification from CBC data, not a resistance-phenotype (R/S) outcome
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Escherichia coli; Staphylococcus aureus; Streptococcus pneumoniae
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Four-class pathogen-species label (P. aeruginosa / E. coli / S. aureus / S. pneumoniae) assigned from confirmed bacterial pneumonia diagnosis, not a binary resistance phenotype
AI_Purpose: To rapidly and non-invasively classify four WHO-priority multidrug-resistant bacterial pneumonia pathogens from routine CBC data, using an interpretable ensemble to support antimicrobial stewardship

Feature_Selection_Method: Boruta all-relevant feature selection combined with LASSO regression (LASSOCV)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Stratified sampling during modeling; SMOTE oversampling also tested but found to degrade performance and was not used in the final model
Hyperparameter_Method: Dung Beetle Optimizer (DBO), a swarm-intelligence metaheuristic, combined with five-fold cross-validation
Other_Metrics: False-negative rate (FNR = 13.3%) reported for the best-performing model (DBO-Stacking/PreBP)
Baseline_Method: Five DBO-optimized baseline ML models (DBO-XGBoost, DBO-RF, DBO-ExtraTrees, DBO-MLPNN, DBO-AdaBoost) and conventional PCR/culture-based diagnostics
Baseline_Performance: Best baseline DBO-XGBoost: accuracy 0.850, AUC 0.894, sensitivity 0.850, precision 0.850, F1 0.849
Internal_Validation: Stratified train/independent-test split combined with five-fold cross-validation (k=5) during DBO hyperparameter optimization
Train_Test_Split: Stratified sampling into training and independent test sets (exact split ratio not stated)
Overfitting_Method: Five-fold cross-validation to reduce random-partition bias; SMOTE oversampling tested but rejected after it increased overfitting risk and degraded performance
Clinical_Insights: RDW-SD > 48.2 fL quantified as a specific SHAP-derived threshold (89%) for P. aeruginosa infection, offered as a visual basis for rapid clinical decision-making
Generalisability_Details: Five-fold cross-validation showed low inter-fold accuracy variance (2.1%, range 0.832-0.883), interpreted as evidence of the model's resilience and adaptability to changing data; no external-population validation was performed
Maturity_Evidence: Only internal stratified train/test partitioning plus five-fold cross-validation was performed on one institutional dataset; no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation is reported
Integration_Point: Proposed for rapid, low-cost cloud-based use ahead of/in place of 24-72-hour culture-based pathogen identification and AST, to guide precision antimicrobial therapy before antibiotic selection
End_User_Described: Clinicians (described in terms of clinician acceptance/confidence in the AI-assisted diagnosis)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Figure 1 contrasts the conventional sputum-culture/AST workflow (collection, digestion, culture, colony ID, AST) with the proposed CBC-based AI prediction workflow feeding into precision antimicrobial therapy decisions

Novel_Predictors_Details: A novel combination of platelet distribution width (PDW) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) was identified via LASSO-Boruta; RDW-SD > 48.2 fL was quantified as a specific threshold for P. aeruginosa infection
Data_Quality_Concerns: Right-skewed distributions with outliers noted for several hematologic parameters (e.g., HGB, MCV), interpreted as possible data anomalies requiring standardization/transformation; 5-23 missing entries per feature led to sample exclusion

Title: A Machine Learning–Guided Clinical Decision Support System for Early Antibiotic Selection in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Bloodstream Infections Among Onco-Hematology Patients: A Multicenter Study
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: National Natural Sciences Foundation of China (82470208); Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Innovation Fund for Medical Sciences; National Key R&D Program of China; Noncommunicable Chronic Diseases-National Science and Technology Major Project; Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities; Beijing Xisike Clinical Oncology Research Foundation
Population_Description: Patients with monomicrobial Pseudomonas aeruginosa bloodstream infection admitted to three hematology centers in China (IHCAMS, Wuhan Union Hospital, Third Xiangya Hospital); median age 41 years; 924 patients total.

Top_Predictive_Features: Feature importance (Fig. S3) revealed prior use of fluoroquinolones, piperacillin-tazobactam and carbapenems, BSI during antibiotic treatment, hematologic relapse, male sex, skin-origin BSI, diabetes, primary BSI and hypoalbuminemia as key predictors of MDRPA; CRO colonization was also an important predictor.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Decision Tree were compared; logistic regression demonstrated the best overall performance (Fig. S2).
Best_Performing_Model: Logistic regression
Sensitivity_Value: 0.688 (Recall, reported as the review's proxy for sensitivity)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: CRPA model, Test Set 1 (2nd of 5 columns: MDR, CRPA, TZPR, CER, FQR)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: CRPA model, Test Set 1
F1_Population_Set: CRPA model, Test Set 1
AUROC_Population_Set: CRPA model, Test Set 1
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation was performed on two independent test sets (an internal temporal set and an external multicentre set), but no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment was reported.
Reported_Limitations: This study is a retrospective analysis spanning nearly 10 years, with limited data on the use of novel antibiotics (which became more widely used after 2020), thus the dataset lacks sufficient information on antimicrobial susceptibility for these newer agents.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) monomicrobial PA BSI confirmed by blood culture; (2) inclusion of only the first BSI episode during a single hospitalization to avoid duplication; (3) availability of complete microbiological susceptibility profiles and clinical records.

Data_Source_Name: Institutional electronic medical records of three hematology centers: IHCAMS, Wuhan Union Hospital, and Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University (no named public dataset).
Dataset_Size: 924 patients total (550 training, 177 Test Set 1, 197/199 Test Set 2)
Missing_Data_Method: Features with >40% missing values in test sets were excluded from the model.
Geographic_Representativeness: Three hematology centers in China (Tianjin, Wuhan, Changsha); Test Set 2 drawn from two centers in southern China distinct from the training center.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood culture (bloodstream infection)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antimicrobial resistance profiles: MDR-PA, CRPA, TZP-resistant PA (TZPR), cephalosporin-resistant PA (CER), and fluoroquinolone-resistant PA (FQR).
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug_Classes: carbapenems, piperacillin-tazobactam (TZP), cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Carbapenems; piperacillin-tazobactam (TZP); cephalosporins; fluoroquinolones

AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR-PA: Non-susceptibility to ≥3 antimicrobial classes.

Feature_Selection_Method: Variables were prioritized based on clinical relevance, literature evidence, and model generalizability; features with >40% missing values in test sets were excluded.

Baseline_Method: Physician (clinician) empirical antibiotic decisions, compared against CDSS/model recommendations

Train_Test_Split: 7:3 split of training data
External_Validation_Description: Test Set 2: data from two other centers (January 2014 to December 2021, n=197/199) used to evaluate model generalizability across institutions.
Clinical_Insights: Feature importance analysis highlighted prior antibiotic use and prior resistance as significant risk factors.
Data_Repository: Available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (no named public repository).
Generalisability_Details: Despite the inherent limitations due to unequal data distributions across centers, further expansion of the sample size and threshold adjustments tailored to local positive rates will enhance the model's generalizability.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation was performed on an independent multicentre test set; the authors themselves recommend future prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials to validate clinical value, indicating prospective/deployment evidence does not yet exist.
Integration_Point: Point of blood-culture positivity, before AST results are available (within the 72-hour pre-AST window)
End_User_Described: Clinicians making early empirical antibiotic decisions
Clinical_Workflow_Details: The initial step determines whether CRPA is suspected. For patients with high suspicion and those predicted by the model to harbor MDR, first-line therapy consists of novel agents or combination regimens, avoiding carbapenems.

Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance ranking (Fig. S3), method not further specified

Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design spanning nearly 10 years; limited data on novel antibiotics used after 2020, resulting in insufficient antimicrobial susceptibility information for these newer agents.
Data_Quality_Concerns: >40% of colonization data were missing in external centers, and thus not used in the unified model for the Test Set 1 and Test Set 2.

Sensitivity_Population_Set: Test dataset (pooled nested cross-validation test folds)

AUROC_Population_Set: Test dataset (pooled nested cross-validation test folds)
