Title: Machine Unlearning for GDPR Right-to-Erasure in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction Models
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: Two datasets: the Antibiotic Resistance Microbiology Dataset (ARMD; n = 1,245,767 EHR records, Stanford Health Care, 1999-2024) and the BV-BRC/PATRIC genomic AMR surveillance dataset (n = 400,372 records).
Data_Source_Other: BV-BRC/PATRIC public genomic AMR surveillance database (GenBank-derived)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: On ARMD (Table 2): Original 84.89% Acc./0.808 AUC; Full Retrain 84.90%/0.807; SISA 84.91%/0.808 (proposed method); Label-Flip Retraining 84.89%/0.807; Influence Reweighting 84.89%/0.807; Selective Tree Pruning 84.24%/0.801.
Best_Performing_Model: SISA
Accuracy_Population_Set: ARMD held-out test set (20% stratified split)
AUROC_Population_Set: ARMD held-out test set (20% stratified split)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only an internal train/test split (80/20, stratified) on two retrospective secondary datasets is reported; no external validation, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment is described.
Reported_Limitations: Genomic phenotypes partly computationally predicted rather than experimentally validated (may lower baseline accuracy); MIA implementation uses a confidence-based heuristic; forget set assumed to lie within a single shard (best-case speedup); only Random Forest evaluated; single random seed used.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: GDPR Article 17 right-to-erasure requires patient data be removable from trained models, not just storage; equivalent obligations exist under the Australian Privacy Act 1988 and the CCPA.
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: ARMD: culture/susceptibility records filtered to binary Resistant/Susceptible phenotypes after merging cohort, demographics, and ward tables.
Exclusion_Criteria: PATRIC/BV-BRC records capped at up to 250,000 per class (Resistant/Susceptible) to keep class balance.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: ARMD (Antibiotic Resistance Microbiology Dataset); BV-BRC/PATRIC
Dataset_Size: ARMD n = 1,245,767 records; PATRIC/BV-BRC n = 400,372 records
Specimen_Type_Detail: Microbiological culture and susceptibility test records (ARMD); genomic/phenotypic AMR records (PATRIC/BV-BRC)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary Resistant/Susceptible phenotype classification with Random Forest classifiers, evaluated by accuracy and AUC-ROC before and after machine unlearning.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary Resistant/Susceptible label per organism-antibiotic record (ARMD); genomic AMR phenotype including log-transformed MIC (PATRIC/BV-BRC).
AI_Purpose: Efficient GDPR-compliant machine unlearning (data deletion) for clinical AMR resistance-prediction models, avoiding costly full retraining.
Feature_Engineering: Categorical features one-hot encoded (top 20-30 categories retained per feature); MIC values log-transformed.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Class-balanced sampling: Resistant and Susceptible phenotypes queried separately, capped at up to 250,000 records per class.
Other_Metrics: Membership inference attack (MIA) gap; wall-clock unlearning time; speedup; cumulative 12-month deletion cost.
Baseline_Method: Full Retraining (Gold Standard) — a new Random Forest trained from scratch on the retained set; all speedup values reported relative to this baseline.
Baseline_Performance: ARMD: 84.90% accuracy, AUC 0.807 (Full Retrain)
Internal_Validation: 80/20 stratified train/test split; no k-fold cross-validation described.
Train_Test_Split: 80% train (retain set) / 20% test, stratified sampling
Data_Repository: MIT ClinicalML (clinicalml.org/data/amr-dataset) — ARMD; NIH BV-BRC REST API (bv-brc.org/api/genome_amr) — PATRIC
Generalisability_Details: Notes the experimental setup assumes the forget set lies within a single shard (best case for SISA speedup); real-world deletions may span multiple shards and reduce efficiency gains; only Random Forest was tested, gradient boosting/deep learning AMR predictors warrant separate investigation.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence limited to an internal train/test split (80/20, stratified) on two retrospective secondary datasets; no external validation, prospective testing, or clinical deployment reported.
End_User_Described: Compliance officers / clinical informatics practitioners processing GDPR deletion requests.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Compliance officers can process individual GDPR deletion requests interactively (~7.5s per operation) rather than via overnight batch retraining with model validation/redeployment overhead.
Barriers_List: Real-world deletion requests may span multiple shards, increasing retraining costs beyond the best-case single-shard scenario tested.
Facilitators_List: SISA's sub-10-second per-deletion computation is manageable within existing clinical informatics infrastructure; readily implementable with standard ML tooling and no specialised hardware.
Future_Directions: Evaluate gradient boosting and deep learning AMR predictors; assess multi-shard forget-set scenarios; evaluate robustness across multiple random-seed initializations.
Limitation_Categories: Label/data quality (computationally predicted vs experimentally validated genomic phenotypes); MIA methodology (confidence-based heuristic); best-case single-shard forget-set assumption; single model class (Random Forest only); single random seed.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Genomic (PATRIC) phenotypes are partly computationally predicted rather than experimentally validated, which may contribute to lower baseline accuracy (67% vs 85% on ARMD).
Page_References: Abstract p.2; Methods pp.4-7; Results (Tables 2-3) pp.8-9; Discussion pp.11-13; Limitations p.12; Data availability p.15.

Title: A Hybrid AutoML Ensemble Integrating Conventional Learners and Gradient-Boosting Models for Multi-Outcome Prediction in ICU Patients with Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Zhejiang Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention Science and Technology Program (2025JK198); Clinical Medical Research Fund of Zhejiang Medical Association (2024ZYC-A257)
Population_Description: 847 adult ICU admissions with P. aeruginosa isolates at a tertiary hospital in Hangzhou, China (Jan 2018-Dec 2024); median age 79 years (77.1% aged >=65), 70.5% male.
Age_Mean_Median: median age of 79 years (77.1% aged >=65 years)
Top_Predictive_Features: SHAP-ranked top contributors to IHM prediction (LGB-C/RF-C models): age, TAMT (triple antimicrobial therapy duration), PMX (ATC/DDD per DOT), UC-days, CARB (ATC/DDD per DOT), CARB (ATC-DDD), CVC-days.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Regression models across 4 outcomes (CRR, CRR-PA-Last2, ICU-LOS, ICU-Death interval; mean[SD] MSE/RMSE/MAE/R2, Friedman avg rank), Table 4: XGB-R avg rank 1.95 (R2 0.77); VR 2.95 (0.74); GBRT 3.40 (0.72); CAT-R 4.60 (0.66); RF-R 5.15 (0.69); SR 5.25 (0.64); LGB-R 5.75 (0.66); BR 6.95 (0.65). Classification AUCs (Table 2, two binary outcomes) reported separately for each of 9 classifiers.
Best_Performing_Model: CatBoost Regressor (CAT-R) for CRR prediction (cRMSD=0.1663, r=0.8849, R2~0.78); LightGBM Classifier (LGB-C) for LastPaAST classification (AUC=0.981); note: XGB-R had the best overall average Friedman rank (1.95) across all 4 regression outcomes combined (Table 4).
Accuracy_Population_Set: LastPaAST outcome, best model LGB-C, fixed sensitivity threshold 0.800 (Table 2)
Sensitivity_Value: 0.800 (fixed threshold applied to all classifiers, LastPaAST target, LGB-C best model)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: LastPaAST outcome, best model LGB-C, fixed sensitivity 0.800 (Table 2)
Specificity_Population_Set: LastPaAST outcome, best model LGB-C, fixed sensitivity 0.800 (Table 2)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: LastPaAST outcome, best model LGB-C, fixed sensitivity 0.800 (Table 2)
AUROC_Population_Set: LastPaAST outcome, best model LGB-C (Table 2 / Fig. 3b)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal nested 5-fold cross-validation on a single retrospective cohort was performed; no external or prospective validation was reported, and authors state multicentre prospective validation is still needed.
Reported_Limitations: (1) retrospective single-center design limiting generalizability; (2) subjective/empirical threshold choices in the VTF-MI-L1 feature-selection pipeline; (3) computational complexity of AutoML/cross-validation challenging resource management and real-time deployment.
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) aged >=18 years; (2) ICU stay of at least 24 h; (3) at least one specimen (blood, urine, secretions, or excretions) positive for P. aeruginosa during admission.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with missing clinical data were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 3,293 ICU admissions screened; 847 met inclusion criteria (P. aeruginosa isolates).
Missing_Data_Method: Median imputation (numerical variables); mode imputation (categorical variables); Z-score normalization and one-hot encoding applied afterward.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single center in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China; no broader regional/national representativeness discussed.
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood, urine, secretions, or excretions
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem resistance rate (CRR): proportion of P. aeruginosa isolates resistant to >=1 carbapenem, per CLSI M100; also antimicrobial susceptibility (R/S) of the last isolate before discharge (LastPaAST).
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems; aminoglycosides; antifungals; beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors; fluoroquinolones; glycylcyclines; imidazoles; lincosamides; lipopeptides; macrolides; monobactams; nitrofuran derivatives; oxazolidinones; penicillin; phosphonics; polymyxins; rifamycins; 2nd/3rd-generation cephalosporins.
Specific_Antibiotics: Polymyxin B, meropenem (combination therapy discussed); also polymyxin E and colistin sulfate.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: CRR = proportion of isolates resistant to >=1 carbapenem (CLSI M100 breakpoints); LastPaAST = binary R/S AST classification of the last P. aeruginosa isolate before discharge.
AI_Purpose: Multi-outcome prediction (carbapenem resistance rate, last-isolate AST result, in-hospital mortality, ICU length of stay, ICU-to-death interval) via an interpretable hybrid AutoML ensemble, to support antimicrobial stewardship and infection control decision-making.
Num_Models_Compared: 9 classification models (Table 2); 8 regression models (Table 4)
Feature_Engineering: Three-stage VTF-MI-L1 pipeline: Variance Threshold Filter removes near-zero-variance features; Mutual Information (plus Pearson/ANOVA F) univariate filtering keeps top-quartile features; embedded L1 (LASSO / L1-logistic) regularization yields the final sparse feature set; reduced 93 candidate features to 48.
Feature_Selection_Method: VTF-MI-L1 (Variance Threshold Filter + Mutual Information + L1/LASSO embedded regularization)
Software_Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, TensorFlow
Hardware_Details: Intel 13th-Gen Core i5-13400F (10 cores/16 threads, base 2.5 GHz, turbo up to 4.6 GHz), 32 GB DDR4 RAM; Python 3.8, scikit-learn 1.1.2, XGBoost 1.5.0, LightGBM 3.3.2, CatBoost 1.0.5
Other_Metrics: sigma-ratio and centered root-mean-square difference (cRMSD) via Taylor diagrams; Friedman average rank across models
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (LR-C for classification)
Baseline_Performance: LR-C AUC 0.945 (LastPaAST, Table 2)
Internal_Validation: Nested 5-fold cross-validation (5-fold for regression; stratified 5-fold for classification)
Clinical_Insights: Global SHAP explanations were consistent with established clinical risk factors (age, prolonged mechanical ventilation, central venous catheterization), paralleling the APACHE II scoring system.
Data_Repository: Supplementary files with the medRxiv preprint (S1 File: patient-level features; S2 File: clinical outcome indicators)
Generalisability_Details: Authors state that multicentre prospective validation is warranted to confirm generalizability, given the single-center retrospective design.
Maturity_Evidence: Only internal (nested) cross-validation on one retrospective single-center cohort was reported; no external or prospective validation; authors call for multicentre prospective validation.
Integration_Point: Not integrated into a clinical system; evaluated offline on a standalone research workstation for inference-latency benchmarking only.
Future_Directions: Multicentre prospective validation to confirm generalizability; recalibration of VTF-MI-L1 thresholds for specific scenarios; balancing AutoML/cross-validation computational complexity against real-time deployment needs.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)
Feature_Interactions_Method: XGB-R-based analysis identified interactions between time-from-admission-to-event, dynamic support indicators (MV-days, CVC-days), and cumulative medication intensity
Limitation_Categories: Single-center/retrospective design limiting generalisability; methodological subjectivity in VTF-MI-L1 feature-selection thresholds; computational complexity of AutoML/cross-validation constraining resource management and real-time deployment.

Title: Hardware-Free Testing for Antimicrobial Resistance Using Artificial Intelligence
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: Laboratory (bench) study: whole blood from healthy donors, commercially obtained, spiked with known concentrations (0-10^5 CFU/ml) of a resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae strain and blind-tested (n = 17 spike concentrations) using the NEIDx system; no clinical patient population was studied.
Data_Source_Other: In-house generated bubble-signal images from a custom immunoassay (KPC-2/SHV-1 enzyme detection), not a named external dataset
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: YOLOv8n object-detection/ROI-cropping + MobileNetV2 CNN classification pipeline (NEIDx Bubble App): 93/100 test images correctly classified (93% accuracy), AUC 0.98 on spiked-PBS images; compared against a MobileNetV2-only model (no numeric value given), which performed worse.
Best_Performing_Model: YOLOv8n + MobileNetV2 pipeline (NEIDx Bubble App)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
Specificity_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
F1_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
AUROC_Population_Set: Klebsiella pneumoniae-spiked whole blood samples (n = 17)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Performance was evaluated internally on lab-spiked whole-blood samples from healthy donors (n = 17 concentrations) generated by the same research team; no external site, independent dataset, or prospective clinical evaluation was performed.
Sample_Size: 10,556 prelabeled bubble-signal images (training/validation set for the NEIDx app)
Inclusion_Criteria: Healthy blood donors (commercially obtained)
Data_Types_Used: Imaging
Dataset_Size: 10,556 images (8,625 training + 1,931 validation) from 26 videos
Specimen_Type_Detail: Whole blood (spiked with Klebsiella pneumoniae)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Qualitative (positive/negative) detection of AMR-associated beta-lactamase enzymes (KPC-2, SHV-1) via an AI-interpreted bubble-signal immunoassay, evaluated by sensitivity (82.61%) and specificity (92.31%) in blood samples.
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (KPC-2 carbapenemase confers carbapenem resistance; SHV-1 beta-lactamase)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Concentration-threshold-based binary label: samples with target enzyme concentration >=0.1 ng/ml labeled positive, <0.1 ng/ml labeled negative.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: AI (YOLOv8n object detection + MobileNetV2 CNN classification) is used to image and interpret bubble-signal formation from a catalytic-nanoparticle immunoassay, enabling hardware-free, cellphone-based qualitative detection of AMR-associated enzymes.
Feature_Engineering: YOLOv8n object detection used to identify and crop the bubble-solution region of interest (ROI) before CNN classification
Class_Imbalance_Method: Balanced 50%/50% negative/positive sampling around the concentration threshold used to build the test set
Hyperparameter_Method: Batch size 32, number of epochs 100, learning rate 0.001
Software_Libraries: TensorFlow (Google) deep learning framework; MobileNetV2 CNN architecture
Hardware_Details: App tested on Android (Motorola XT1575), iOS (Apple iPhone 14 Pro), and Windows (Lenovo IdeaPad S145-15IWL) devices
Other_Metrics: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) = 0.74
Baseline_Method: MobileNetV2-only model (without YOLOv8n object-detection/ROI-cropping preprocessing)
Internal_Validation: Held-out validation split (1,931 of 10,556 images) plus a separate spiked whole-blood evaluation (n = 17) from the same lab
Train_Test_Split: 8,625 training images / 1,931 validation images (of 10,556 total)
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only: performance metrics computed on lab-spiked whole-blood samples (n = 17 concentrations) produced by the same research group; no external dataset, independent site, or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Integration_Point: Point-of-care, hardware-free testing directly from blood samples via a cellphone app
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Three-step app workflow: user captures or loads a sample image, the PWA's YOLOv8n+MobileNetV2 algorithm processes/classifies it, and the result and processed image are displayed on screen.
Barriers_List: Need for healthcare-professional involvement and expensive instrumentation in existing AMR testing approaches; limited internet connectivity in resource-constrained settings
Facilitators_List: Offline app functionality; hardware-free operation; cross-platform compatibility (Android/iOS/Windows); simple 3-step user interface
Future_Directions: Positioned as a tool for future point-of-care AMR testing translation in diverse and resource-limited healthcare settings (no specific concrete next steps stated)

Title: Machine Learning–Driven Drug Optimization for Typhoid Fever Based on Patient Profiles
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Population_Description: 5,760 patient records (13 variables) of individuals diagnosed with typhoid fever; demographics (age, gender), laboratory parameters (hemoglobin, platelet count, calcium, potassium), blood/urine culture results, medication administered, treatment duration, and treatment outcome.
Data_Source_Other: Publicly released dataset described in the Limitations as containing synthetic data generated via nearest-neighbour sampling from a single-center cohort (not a named EHR/registry system).
Top_Predictive_Features: Treatment Outcome model (ranked by mean absolute SHAP value): platelet count, age, hemoglobin (g/dL), potassium (mmol/L), calcium (mg/dL); Severity_Score and Culture_Type also contributed.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Treatment Duration (regression, XGBoost): R² 0.8027±0.0054, MAE 0.7841±0.0324, MSE 1.6423, RMSE 1.2815; Resistance Proxy (regression, XGBoost): R² 0.9014±0.0036, MAE 0.7596±0.00334, MSE 1.5922, RMSE 1.2618; Treatment Outcome (classification, XGBoost): ROC AUC 0.9996±0.0000; Suspected Typhoid (classification, XGBoost): ROC AUC 0.9870±0.0000.
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost Treatment Outcome classifier (highest reported metric among the four task-specific models: AUROC 0.9998±0.0001)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, held-out test set, n=1,296
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, test set, n=1,296
Specificity_Value: 0.99 (recall of the negative/Failure class, read as specificity)
Specificity_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, negative (Failure) class, test set n=1,296
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, test set, n=1,296
F1_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, macro-averaged, test set n=1,296
AUROC_Population_Set: Treatment Outcome model, bootstrap-resampled test set (10 runs), n=1,296
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only (repeated nested cross-validation plus bootstrap resampling on a held-out split from the same single-center dataset); the paper explicitly states no external or temporal validation was done.
Reported_Limitations: Synthetic-data/joint-distribution fidelity; miscalibration (overestimation at high confidence); unmeasured confounding and associational (not causal) interpretation of ΔProbability; lack of external/temporal validation and single-center cohort; system remains exploratory, pending prospective validation.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Authors caution that unpredictable failure of the AI system in unusual or under-sampled cases could mislead clinicians absent professional infectious-disease oversight.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Safe implementation is said to require mechanisms to ensure equity and patient privacy, alongside ethical governance and stakeholder consultation.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Institutional readiness needs identified: ethical governance, stakeholder consultation, regulatory compliance, transparent reporting, and equity/privacy safeguards prior to clinical translation.
Sample_Size: 5,184 complete patient records (final analytical cohort, after listwise deletion of missing-outcome records)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The author declares no commercial or financial relationships construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Individuals diagnosed with typhoid fever (dataset of 5,760 patient records with clinical/microbiological data).
Exclusion_Criteria: Records with missing values in the target (outcome) variables were excluded from further analysis; duplicates de-duplicated to first record per patient.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: N = 5,760 records, 13 variables (raw); 5,184 complete records after cleaning
Missing_Data_Method: Median imputation (numeric) / 'Unknown' category (categorical) for predictor missingness; listwise deletion for records missing outcome/target values.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood Culture Bacteria and Urine Culture Bacteria (organism identification)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance Proxy Score — a composite regression target estimating likelihood of antimicrobial resistance/treatment failure, computed from culture discordance, symptom severity, and treatment duration (explicitly not a substitute for antimicrobial susceptibility testing).
Pathogens: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (primary); Staphylococcus spp.; Escherichia coli (also isolated in culture data)
Num_Pathogens: 3 (S. Typhi primary; Staphylococcus spp. and E. coli also identified in culture data)
Specific_Antibiotics: Amoxicillin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance Proxy Score = (1 – Culture Concordance) × Normalized Treatment Duration × Severity Score
AI_Purpose: Multi-task XGBoost framework to predict treatment outcome, treatment duration, a resistance-proxy score, and suspected typhoid, plus counterfactual drug-simulation to compare actual vs. model-recommended antibiotics for typhoid fever treatment optimization.
Num_Models_Compared: 4 (task-specific XGBoost models: treatment outcome, treatment duration, resistance proxy, suspected typhoid)
Feature_Engineering: Extensive engineered features: severity score, culture concordance/type, Salmonella presence, sex code, medication one-hot indicators, intensity score, normalized treatment duration, resistance proxy score, lab-value status categories (hemoglobin/platelet/calcium/potassium), suspected-typhoid composite label, and simulated metabolomic (SimMet_*) features plus PCA-derived latent components.
Feature_Selection_Method: Removal of features with possible leakage and high multicollinearity, based on Pearson correlation analysis (and VIF for the duration model)
Num_Features_Selected: 21 (Treatment Outcome model; 20–22 across the four task-specific models)
Class_Imbalance_Method: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), applied only to the training partition within each CV fold
Hyperparameter_Method: RandomizedSearchCV across 30 sampled configurations, performed within nested cross-validation to avoid optimistic bias
Software_Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, XGBoost, imbalanced-learn (SMOTE), UMAP, t-SNE, SHAP, Seaborn, matplotlib-venn, Matplotlib
Hardware_Details: Linux workstation, Intel Xeon processor, 64 GB RAM
Other_Metrics: Brier score (calibration): Outcome model 0.0110; Typhoid model 0.0432 (Section 3.5); MSE also reported alongside RMSE/MAE for the regression tasks (Table 1).
Internal_Validation: Repeated nested 5-fold (outer) x 5-fold (inner) cross-validation across 10 random seeds, plus bootstrap resampling (10 runs) on a held-out test set
Train_Test_Split: 75:25 (train:test)
Overfitting_Method: Nested cross-validation to separate hyperparameter tuning from performance assessment and avoid optimistic bias; XGBoost L2/gamma regularization
Clinical_Insights: SHAP-identified hematological (platelet count, hemoglobin) and biochemical (calcium, potassium) features reflect central roles in patient stratification and treatment-response estimation, consistent with prior clinical typhoid/sepsis literature.
Generalisability_Details: Single-center cohort with no external or temporal validation; models trained in one context may perform poorly elsewhere given the dynamic nature of resistance and changing clinical practice.
Maturity_Evidence: Nested cross-validation and bootstrap resampling performed on a single-center dataset only; authors explicitly state no external or temporal validation was conducted and the system 'remains exploratory'.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (decision-support tool intended to augment, not replace, clinical expertise)
Stewardship_Details: The Top-2 (near-miss) match group had the lowest predicted resistance-proxy scores, suggesting the model occasionally favored antimicrobial-stewardship-consistent options over strict prescribing agreement.
Barriers_List: Lack of external/prospective validation; single-center data; unmeasured confounding; need for institutional readiness (ethical governance, stakeholder consultation, regulatory compliance, transparent reporting, equity/privacy safeguards) before clinical translation.
Future_Directions: Mixed-methods prescriber feedback, causal inference frameworks (e.g. DAG-guided adjustment, propensity/inverse-probability weighting), and uncertainty quantification; external/prospective validation; integration with microbiological/genomic resistance data.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (TreeExplainer), ranked by mean absolute SHAP value
Novel_Predictors_Details: Engineered simulated-metabolomic features (SimMet_EnergyDisruption, SimMet_CatabolicBurst) showed pronounced SHAP importance for the suspected-typhoid model, reflecting specialized metabolic-stress markers.
Limitation_Categories: Synthetic-data/joint-distribution fidelity; model calibration and uncertainty; unmeasured confounding/associational (non-causal) interpretation; generalizability (single-center, no external or temporal validation).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing values in several fields of the raw N=5,760 dataset: Symptoms Severity (n=629), Blood Culture Bacteria (n=832), Treatment Duration (n=731), Treatment Outcome (n=576).

Title: An interpretable and interactive clinical AI agent for personalized anti-infective decision support in carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infection
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: China Postdoctoral Science Foundation (Grant No. 2025M782168); Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant 62476087); Shanghai Municipal Education Commission's Initiative on Artificial Intelligence-Driven Reform of Scientific Research Paradigms and Empowerment of Discipline Leapfrogging
Population_Description: Hospitalized patients with microbiologically confirmed CRAB infection who received systemic antibiotic therapy, from Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, China (development and temporal validation cohorts).
Top_Predictive_Features: In the XGBoost-SFM (survival prediction), older age, higher comorbidity burden, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and greater oxygen requirement were the top features associated with lower predicted survival probability, ranked by mean absolute SHAP value.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Seven model families (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, random forest, logistic regression, SVM, KNN) evaluated as Full-Feature Models (FFM) and Selected-Feature Models (SFM) across four tasks. Representative survival-prediction results (development cohort, Precision/AUROC-optimized subset): CatBoost-SFM AUROC 0.791, AUPRC 0.905; SVM-SFM F1-score 0.865, Recall 0.954; RF-SFM Recall 0.951.
Best_Performing_Model: CatBoost-SFM (survival prediction, development cohort, feature subset optimized for Precision and AUROC): AUROC 0.791 -- the highest AUROC explicitly reported for a single model on the primary dataset.
AUROC_Population_Set: Development cohort, survival prediction, CatBoost-SFM (Precision/AUROC-optimized feature subset)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation was performed in two independent MIMIC-IV cohorts (CRAB n=42, CRPA n=286); no prospective evaluation or routine clinical use was reported — the system is described as a deployable clinical prototype rather than one in active clinical use.
Reported_Limitations: First, the development cohort size was modest, reflecting the difficulty of recruiting large cohorts of critically ill patients with rare CRGNB infections in a single-center setting (mitigated by external MIMIC-IV validation). Second, models rely on static baseline variables rather than longitudinal trajectories. Finally, SHAP explanations reflect associations rather than causality.
Unresolved_Items: This paper covers four prediction tasks (clinical efficacy, survival, polymyxin resistance, treatment duration) with multiple model families and no single authors-named 'best' model overall. Best_Performing_Model and the *_Value metric fields were anchored to survival prediction (the paper's most emphasised task, and the one used for the antibiotic-recommendation simulation) using AUROC as the deciding metric (CatBoost-SFM, AUROC 0.791). Team should confirm this task-selection convention for multi-task papers.
Conflicts_of_Interest: All authors declare no financial or non-financial competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: (1) microbiological confirmation of CRAB infection; (2) receipt of polymyxin-based therapy; and (3) availability of complete baseline clinical data and key laboratory measurements.
Exclusion_Criteria: Only the first infection episode for each patient was retained; patients with missing key outcome data were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: MIMIC-IV (v3.1)
Dataset_Size: 441 patients (development cohort)
Missing_Data_Method: Median imputation for continuous variables; mode imputation for categorical variables
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Four multitask prediction outcomes in CRAB/CRGNB infection: clinical efficacy (treatment response), survival outcome (in-hospital mortality), polymyxin resistance (MIC-based binary classification), and antibiotic treatment duration.
Pathogens: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA, external validation)
Drug_Classes: Polymyxins
Specific_Antibiotics: Polymyxins (polymyxin B / colistin)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Polymyxin resistance defined by MIC threshold: isolates with polymyxin MIC ≥2 μg/mL classified as resistant/resistance-risk positive; MIC <2 μg/mL classified as susceptible/resistance-risk negative, with reference to CLSI M100.
AI_Purpose: Interactive clinical AI agent (Dr.BUG) for personalized anti-infective decision support in CRGNB (CRAB) infection, integrating multi-task prognostic prediction, SHAP-based interpretability and model-based antibiotic regimen recommendation.
Feature_Engineering: Missing continuous values imputed by median, missing categorical values by mode; tree-based models trained without standardization while linear/distance-based models were standardized; imputation and scaling performed within each training fold and applied to the corresponding validation fold to avoid leakage.
Feature_Selection_Method: Consensus-driven hierarchical feature-set selection integrating SHAP-based feature attribution, exhaustive subset enumeration and cross-model consensus evaluation.
Num_Features_Total: 22 continuous variables and 25 categorical variables, plus 10 antibiotic-related features
Num_Features_Selected: 1–10 features per subset (from a candidate pool of the top 10 SHAP-ranked features per model)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Built-in class-balancing strategies, used when supported by the model
Other_Metrics: Standard deviation (±) reported alongside AUROC for the external CRPA cohort (e.g. LightGBM AUROC 0.736 ± 0.060; logistic regression AUROC 0.744 ± 0.079)
Baseline_Method: Full-Feature Model (FFM) — model trained on the entire (unreduced) candidate feature set
Baseline_Performance: CatBoost-FFM and RF-FFM AUROC ≈ 0.76, AUPRC ≈ 0.89 (survival prediction, development cohort)
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation
External_Validation_Description: Two cohorts from the MIMIC-IV (v3.1) database: an external CRAB cohort (n=42) for direct transfer of the development cohort's survival feature subsets, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation; an external CRPA cohort (n=286) in which the feature-selection workflow itself was re-run to test transferability.
Clinical_Insights: SHAP-identified drivers of lower survival probability (older age, higher comorbidity burden, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, greater oxygen requirement) reflect a clinically coherent pattern of poorer baseline condition, greater acute illness severity and more advanced organ dysfunction.
Generalisability_Details: Survival-associated feature subsets from the development cohort transferred to an independent external CRAB cohort, and the feature-selection workflow itself recovered stable predictive subsets in a related CRPA population, supporting generalisability beyond a single center or dataset.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation in two independent MIMIC-IV cohorts (CRAB n=42, CRPA n=286); temporal validation cohort (n=111) with no retraining. No prospective clinical evaluation or routine-use evidence.
Integration_Point: Point-of-care / bedside decision support after early CRAB diagnosis
End_User_Described: Clinicians / healthcare staff
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Clinicians use local data to complete data quality review, task configuration, feature-set selection, model training, performance evaluation and versioned model release through Dr.BUG. After deployment, healthcare staff input a patient's clinical features and empirical antibiotic regimen; the system generates multidimensional predictions, SHAP-based explanations of key drivers, and a ranked list of alternative recommended antibiotic regimens.
Stewardship_Details: Discussed conceptually (not empirically measured): individualized regimen rankings framed as aligning with antimicrobial stewardship goals by helping minimise unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure and potentially reduce selective pressure for resistance.
Barriers_List: Operational barrier of requiring programming or modelling expertise for clinicians to use predictive-model tools.
Facilitators_List: Dialogue-driven natural-language interface removing the need to write code or switch between separate analytical modules, improving accessibility for routine clinical use.
Future_Directions: Extend Dr.BUG beyond CRGNB to diverse pathogens/infection types; extend expert evaluation of AI-prioritised regimens beyond non-survivors to survivors and de-escalation scenarios and real-world workflows; assess concordance with clinician judgement, prescribing behavior and patient outcomes; incorporate richer multimodal data, including pathogen genomics and resistance mechanisms.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mean absolute SHAP value (top 15 features ranked in the CatBoost-FFM; top 10 retained as the candidate pool)
Feature_Interactions_Method: SHAP interaction values / feature interaction networks (tree-based models)
Limitation_Categories: Sample size / single-center recruitment; static (non-longitudinal) baseline variables; associational (non-causal) interpretability from SHAP.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Variables with more than 30% missingness were excluded from candidate features.

Title: A digital twin for hospital antimicrobial resistance forecasting and constrained intervention optimisation
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Population_Description: Simulated (not real) hospital population: a digital-twin agent-based simulation of a medium-scale hospital (10 wards, 200 patients, 300 staff), generating daily patient/staff contact graphs; trajectories simulated over 60 days (360 days for the Step 8 distribution-shift benchmark, 12 replicates per family). No real patients or real hospital data were used.
Data_Source_Other: Simulated / synthetic data generated by a mechanistic agent-based hospital digital-twin simulator; no real-world dataset used.
Top_Predictive_Features: No per-feature importance ranking is reported; the closest analogue is a representation ablation showing node-level features (role, latent AMR state, antibiotic exposure, isolation status) matter more to performance than edge-weight information.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
All_Models_Evaluated: Only one model architecture was evaluated (an edge-aware GraphSAGE–Transformer temporal graph model / digital twin), tested across multiple experimental conditions (canonical baseline, representation ablations, surveillance perturbations, regime sweep, distribution-shift benchmark, zero-shot transfer). Canonical ground-truth baseline: test AUROC=0.997, accuracy=0.989, F1=0.989, sensitivity=1.000, specificity=0.978 (Table 4).
Accuracy_Population_Set: frozen external test set (canonical ground-truth track, Step 4 baseline)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: frozen external test set (canonical ground-truth track, Step 4 baseline)
Specificity_Population_Set: frozen external test set (canonical ground-truth track, Step 4 baseline)
F1_Population_Set: frozen external test set (canonical ground-truth track, Step 4 baseline)
AUROC_Population_Set: frozen external test set (canonical ground-truth track, Step 4 baseline)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Although the study performs internal and 'external' validation within the simulator (frozen external test set of independently generated synthetic trajectories), the authors state the platform does not yet establish clinical validity in a real hospital environment, capping maturity at proof-of-concept.
Reported_Limitations: The study is entirely synthetic and does not yet establish clinical validity in a real hospital environment; the intentionally controlled benchmark improves interpretability but cannot capture the full complexity of routine practice.
Sample_Size: 10 wards, 200 patients, and 300 staff (medium-scale synthetic digital-twin hospital); canonical trajectories simulated over 60 days (360 days for the Step 8 distribution-shift benchmark, 12 replicates per trajectory family).
Conflicts_of_Interest: Not stated in the manuscript (no conflicts-of-interest statement present).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Epidemiological surveillance data; Other
Dataset_Size: 10 wards, 200 patients, 300 staff; 60-day canonical trajectories (360-day trajectories with 12 replicates per family for the Step 8 distribution-shift benchmark).
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary classification of whether future hospital resistant emergence over a 7-day horizon is predominantly driven by endogenous transmission/within-host selection versus importation on admission.
Pathogens: No specific pathogen species is named; resistance is modelled abstractly as colonisation/infection states (uncolonised / colonised-sensitive / colonised-resistant / infected-sensitive / infected-resistant) without organism identity.
Drug_Classes: Antibiotic exposure abstracted as treatment under one of C generic antibiotic classes (not individually named).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label defined by whether contact-mediated resistant transmission plus within-host resistant selection dominates importation-driven resistant emergence over the forecast horizon (endogenous share ≥ 0.5).
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To forecast whether future hospital resistant emergence is driven by endogenous transmission/selection versus importation, using graph neural networks and transformers, and to provide decision support via mathematical programming optimisation.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (a single GraphSAGE–Transformer architecture evaluated across multiple experimental conditions/ablations, not multiple distinct model types).
Feature_Engineering: Each fully observed node is encoded by role, latent AMR state, antibiotic exposure, isolation status, same-day new resistant acquisition, and same-day new resistant infection.
Num_Features_Total: 6 (predictive-track node features: role, latent AMR state, antibiotic exposure, isolation status, same-day resistant acquisition indicator, same-day resistant infection indicator).
Class_Imbalance_Method: Paired endogenous-favouring/importation-favouring cohort generation before pooling to avoid mechanism-label imbalance; Step 8 additionally applies an explicit pre-training mechanism-label balance gate.
Other_Metrics: Causal (intervention-selection) task metrics reported separately from the primary predictive task: tie-aware and strict policy accuracy, top-2 accuracy, mean/median regret, baseline-improvement rate, oracle-best-row AUROC (0.676 both tracks), macro precision/recall/F1, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy (Table 6).
Baseline_Method: Baseline simulator policy / no-change comparator (action a0), used in the causal intervention-ranking experiment as the reference against which candidate screening-response interventions are compared.
Baseline_Performance: Chosen (predicted) actions strictly improved on the baseline policy in 64.3% of held-out states (ground-truth track), with a tie-aware non-worse rate relative to baseline of 1.000.
Internal_Validation: Causal-experiment samples were split into train/validation/test partitions by disjoint seed ranges (no k-fold CV).
Train_Test_Split: Four independently generated canonical trajectory cohorts: two pooled for training, two pooled into the frozen external test set (disjoint seed ranges).
External_Validation_Description: A frozen external test set pooled from two independently generated canonical trajectory cohorts (disjoint seed ranges from training), restored before each downstream comparison and used unchanged throughout the study.
Clinical_Insights: Post hoc translational summaries aggregate learned attribution signals into ward- and staff-level views intended to be clinically legible to IPC teams.
Generalisability_Details: The study is synthetic and does not yet establish clinical validity in a real hospital environment; the intentionally controlled benchmark cannot capture the full complexity of routine practice.
Maturity_Evidence: Validation performed is entirely within-simulator (a frozen external test set of independently generated synthetic trajectories); no real-world or clinical-setting validation is reported.
Integration_Point: Conceptual only: a downstream MILP decision layer intended to convert model predictions into feasible screening/isolation policy choices; described as a proof-of-concept module, not integrated into any real hospital system.
End_User_Described: IPC (infection prevention and control) teams
Barriers_List: Threshold calibration and zero-shot portability across regimes; need for repeated-seed robustness assessment; cleaner decoupling of observation from intervention; a real-world extension would require mapping hospital information systems onto the graph representation and addressing missingness explicitly.
Facilitators_List: Modular platform design allowing users to engineer new learning tasks and probe the platform under their own settings/hypotheses.
Future_Directions: Repeated-seed robustness, formal calibration, threshold tuning, sensitivity analysis around surveillance assumptions, cleaner decoupling of observation from intervention, richer action spaces coupling optimisation to ward/staff-level levers, and real-world extension mapping hospital information systems onto the graph representation.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Representation ablation (comparing performance with edge-weight variation removed vs. node features compressed to a core subset), not a formal per-feature importance ranking.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Graph, state-summary, and action-descriptor embeddings combined via concatenation, element-wise interactions, and absolute differences before an MLP scoring head.
Limitation_Categories: Threshold calibration and zero-shot transfer instability under distribution shift; limited/imbalanced action-space coverage in the retained causal test set; reliance on a synthetic, intentionally controlled benchmark rather than real-world data; need for repeated-seed robustness and formal calibration.
Data_Quality_Concerns: The core data-quality caveat is that all data are simulator-generated rather than real-world; the study does not yet establish clinical validity in a real hospital environment.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of Time Series Forecasting Approaches for Facility-Level Antibiotic Resistance Outcomes in the Veterans Health Administration
Population_Description: 30 high-volume VHA (Veterans Health Administration) facilities, Jan 2007-Mar 2022, representing ~half of all VHA admissions and patient-days nationally; hospital-onset infection isolates aggregated to facility-month level.
Top_Predictive_Features: Antibiotic use-rate predictors ranked by RMSE ratio in zero-out analysis; macrolide use rate had the highest RMSE ratio (most influential) for MRSA and fluoroquinolone-resistant S. aureus.
Target_End_User: Antimicrobial stewardship team; Infection prevention and control team
All_Models_Evaluated: ARIMA, VAR and LSTM, each in outcome-only and antibiotic-use-enhanced versions, evaluated by RMSE on standardized time series across 104 facility-level series; antibiotic-use-enhanced LSTM achieved the lowest RMSE in 97/104 (93.3%) series.
Best_Performing_Model: LSTM (antibiotic-use-enhanced)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models tuned via an expanding-window scheme and evaluated retrospectively against held-out later months (25-183) of the same VHA facilities; no external dataset, prospective evaluation, or deployment was performed.
Reported_Limitations: LSTM hyperparameters were tuned from prior literature/limited experimentation rather than a full grid search; RMSE was the sole performance metric and does not quantify forecast uncertainty.
Sample_Size: 104 facility-level monthly outcome time series (30 facilities x 4 resistance outcomes, after exclusion of high-missingness series)
Inclusion_Criteria: Incident isolates only: the first isolate per patient-pathogen pair within a 30-day period.
Exclusion_Criteria: Outcome time series with >70% of facility-month values equal to zero excluded; predictor series with >90% zero values excluded.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: VHA (Veterans Health Administration) national electronic health record system
Dataset_Size: 104 facility-level monthly time series (30 facilities, 4 outcome definitions), Jan 2007-Mar 2022 (183 months)
Missing_Data_Method: Missing/unreported months treated as zero counts; visually inspected via line charts for irregular patterns.
Geographic_Representativeness: 30 of 124 VHA facilities (the highest-volume), representing ~half of total national VHA admissions/patient-days; majority located in urban areas and classified as high-complexity.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Facility-level monthly antibiotic resistance rate (resistant isolates per 1,000 patient-days) among hospital-onset infections, for four outcomes: MRSA, fluoroquinolone-resistant S. aureus, 3rd/4th-generation cephalosporin-resistant E. coli, and fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli.
Pathogens: Acinetobacter sp., Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Enterococcus faecium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia marcescens, Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Anti-staphylococcal beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, 3rd/4th-generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistant defined as a resistant OR intermediate AST result; resistance rate = number of resistant isolates per 1,000 patient-days, aggregated monthly by pathogen and facility.
AI_Purpose: Forecast facility-level, drug-specific antibiotic resistance rates in hospital-onset infections using time series models (ARIMA, VAR, LSTM), comparing outcome-only vs antibiotic-use-enhanced predictors, to guide local antimicrobial stewardship and infection control.
Feature_Engineering: Predictors constructed as monthly facility-level rates in five clinically-defined groups, then lagged at orders 1 through 12 months; STL decomposition, standardization and (if needed) first-order differencing applied for stationarity.
Feature_Selection_Method: Predictors selected by clinical relevance to each outcome (Table 1), not by a data-driven/automated selection algorithm.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search (ARIMA p,d,q and VAR lag order) evaluated via expanding-window RMSE; LSTM hyperparameters set from prior work/initial experimentation rather than grid search.
Software_Libraries: R: DBI, odbc, tidyverse, forecast, vars, parallel; Python: darts
Other_Metrics: Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Baseline_Method: Outcome-only model (lagged values of the outcome time series only, no predictors)
Internal_Validation: Expanding window: training set began at 12 months and expanded by 1 month each iteration, with a fixed 3-month validation window immediately following the training set, used for ARIMA/VAR parameter tuning.
Train_Test_Split: Final models evaluated on months 25-183 (of 183 total months, Jan 2007-Mar 2022); expanding window used during tuning.
Overfitting_Method: Dropout (rate 0.2) between LSTM layers; early stopping if training loss failed to improve by more than 0.001 over 10 consecutive epochs.
Clinical_Insights: Antibiotic-class importance for resistance prediction was outcome-specific: macrolide use was most influential for MRSA and fluoroquinolone-resistant S. aureus prediction, while fluoroquinolone use had the largest impact for fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli.
Maturity_Evidence: Level set by internal (expanding-window) validation and retrospective hold-out evaluation on months 25-183; no external or prospective validation reported.
Future_Directions: Integrate additional facility-level covariates (infection control interventions, prescribing practices, regional epidemiology); incorporate patient-level data for personalised forecasting; move toward real-time implementation within stewardship programs.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Zero-out analysis (RMSE ratio when a predictor/group is zeroed out of the LSTM model)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Macrolide use rate (not the antibiotic class targeted by the MRSA/fluoroquinolone-resistant S. aureus outcomes themselves) emerged as the most influential predictor for those S. aureus resistance phenotypes.
Limitation_Categories: Limited/heuristic hyperparameter tuning for LSTM (not a full grid search); evaluation limited to RMSE without uncertainty quantification.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Many facility-month values were zero (treated as missing/zero rather than true absence); visual inspection via line charts used to flag discontinuities, implausible fluctuations, or prolonged flat segments not captured by summary statistics.
Page_References: Abstract p.1; Methods pp.2-6; Results pp.7-11; Discussion pp.11-12.

Title: Development and validation of a dynamic risk stratification tool for predicting multidrug-resistant bacterial infections in ICU patients: A clinical prediction model and web-based calculator
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Population_Description: All adult patients admitted to the ICU of the First Affiliated Hospital of Dali University during the study period, excluding those with <48h stay, known immunodeficiency, or confirmed bacterial colonization at admission.
Top_Predictive_Features: Duration of mechanical ventilation, antibiotic usage patterns, and urinary catheter days, identified as top contributors via SHAP analysis on the XGBoost model.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Logistic Regression AUC=0.772 (best); Neural Network AUC=0.768; XGBoost AUC=0.767; Naive Bayes AUC=0.740; Decision Tree AUC=0.724; Random Forest AUC=0.709; Support Vector Machine AUC=0.669 (all in validation group, Table 3).
Best_Performing_Model: Logistic Regression (AUC = 0.772, 95% CI 0.733-0.812 in the validation group, outperforming XGBoost and Random Forest)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
Specificity_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
F1_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
AUROC_Population_Set: Validation group (tuned Logistic Regression model, n=1088)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation was performed (70/30 split, 5-fold CV, bootstrap resampling); the authors' own limitations state the single-center design necessitates external validation, which was not conducted, despite the web calculator being technically deployed online.
Reported_Limitations: Single-center retrospective design requiring external validation; the MDR outcome definition did not differentiate bacterial species or resistance phenotypes; unmeasured confounders (hand hygiene adherence, environmental contamination) were not captured.
Inclusion_Criteria: All adult patients admitted to the ICU during the study period
Exclusion_Criteria: Length of hospital stay <48 hours; known immunodeficiency; confirmed bacterial colonization at admission.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables
Dataset_Size: 3,631 patients (training n=2,543; validation n=1,088)
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case exclusion (patients with missing data in key variables were excluded)
Specimen_Type_Detail: Clinical specimens (specific specimen type not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Occurrence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial infection during ICU stay, confirmed by isolation of pathogens resistant to >=3 antimicrobial classes from clinical specimens.
Pathogens: Not specified by species; the study addresses multidrug-resistant bacterial infection generally.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial categories (binary MDR yes/no outcome).
AI_Purpose: To develop an interpretable, dynamic risk-stratification model with a web calculator to improve clinical applicability for MDR infection prediction.
Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables (antibiotic type count, ventilator/catheter duration) were transformed into categorical variables for clinical interpretability.
Feature_Selection_Method: Boruta algorithm (random-forest-based, 100 RF runs, shadow attributes, P<0.01)
Num_Features_Total: 19 candidate variables
Num_Features_Selected: 5 (final predictors in the multivariable model)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search with 5-fold cross-validation (e.g., linear vs RBF kernel for SVM; m-try/n-tree for random forest; cp for decision tree; size/decay for neural network)
Other_Metrics: G-mean and Brier score also reported for each tuned model (Table 3).
Baseline_Method: Comparison against six machine learning algorithms (Neural Network, XGBoost, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine).
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation and bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations)
Train_Test_Split: 70% training (n=2543) / 30% validation (n=1088)
Overfitting_Method: Bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations) showed minimal optimism (0.005), indicating negligible overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: SHAP analysis identified duration of mechanical ventilation, antibiotic usage patterns, and urinary catheter days as the top contributors to model predictions.
Generalisability_Details: Single-center study; external validation across diverse healthcare settings is needed before broader generalisation.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only (train/test split, 5-fold CV, bootstrap); no external or prospective validation; deployed online as a calculator but not integrated into a clinical workflow or EHR.
Integration_Point: Bedside point of care, via a web-based R Shiny calculator used by clinicians during the ICU stay.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (who enter five key predictors into the calculator)
Clinical_Workflow_Details: For low-risk patients the tool helps avoid unnecessary escalation to broad-spectrum antibiotics or excessive isolation; for high-risk patients (>30%) it prompts early contact isolation, increased microbiological testing, or adjustment of empirical antibiotic therapy.
Barriers_List: Prior MDR prediction models lack visual interactive tools or online calculators, limiting translation and application in clinical practice.
Facilitators_List: Model parsimony and transparency (nomogram) plus SHAP-validated interpretability are highlighted as facilitators of clinical translation and end-user trust.
Future_Directions: External validation across diverse healthcare settings is needed.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Boruta algorithm (random-forest-based feature selection) and SHAP analysis.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Frequency of abnormal procalcitonin (PCT) tests, a repeated dynamic measure, rather than a single static PCT value, was used to capture evolving risk.
Limitation_Categories: Single-center/generalisability; outcome-definition granularity (no species/phenotype differentiation); unmeasured confounders (infection-control practices).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Patients with missing data in key variables were excluded; MDR outcome defined only as non-susceptibility to >=3 classes without species/phenotype differentiation; potential unmeasured confounders not captured.
Page_References: Abstract pp.1-2; Methods pp.3-5; Results pp.5-17; Discussion/Limitations pp.18-19.

Title: Deep learning on routine Gram-stain images to estimate ESBL risk in urinary Escherichia coli and distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci in blood cultures: temporal and leave-one-site-out external validation in a prospective multicentre diagnostic study
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Prospective cohort
Funder_Names: NHO Network Research Program
Population_Description: Adult inpatients and outpatients (>=18 years) across seven National Hospital Organization hospitals in Japan with urine or blood cultures submitted Feb 2024-Apr 2025, screened via routine Gram-stained smears.
Age_Range: Adults, aged >=18 years (inclusion criterion; no mean/median reported)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Diagnosis / species identification
All_Models_Evaluated: Single CNN-Vision Transformer deep-learning model (EfficientNet-B0 patch encoder + Transformer encoder, GAN-augmented): ROC-AUC 0.973 (95% CI 0.967-0.978) jointly classifying ESBL-positive vs ESBL-negative E. coli and S. aureus vs CoNS in the primary temporal external validation; ROC-AUC 0.973 (95% CI 0.967-0.978) in the primary leave-one-site-out (hospital B hold-out) validation.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
Specificity_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
F1_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
AUROC_Population_Set: Temporal external validation (latest 30% of episodes within each site), patient level
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The paper's own evidence is prespecified temporal holdout and leave-one-site-out external validation of a single model; no prospective clinical-impact trial, CDS integration, or routine-use evidence is reported (future work per Conclusion).
Reported_Limitations: Non-consecutive enrolment (spectrum-bias risk); moderate calibration overconfidence (slope 0.53); possible GAN-augmentation-related optimism in external test performance; single national health system limiting generalisability; only selected resistance phenotypes assessed (e.g. MRSA specifically not evaluable).
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Two authors (HM, KY) hold a pending patent related to the technology described, owned by the National Hospital Organization; a potential conflict of interest around commercialisation.
