Inclusion_Criteria: Adult inpatients/outpatients (>=18y) with urine cultures yielding a single E. coli isolate (ESBL-producing or non-ESBL) or positive blood cultures with Gram-positive cocci subsequently identified as S. aureus (MSSA/MRSA) or CoNS, Feb 2024-Apr 2025.
Exclusion_Criteria: Urine specimens with non-E. coli Gram-negative rods; images of inadequate quality or incomplete anonymisation; cases with missing/incomplete reference data or unusable images.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Microscopy images
Dataset_Size: 1,246 original Gram-stain images (urine 552; blood 694), expanded to 11,214 images after GAN-based augmentation
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case analysis: cases with missing/incomplete reference data or unusable images were excluded.
Geographic_Representativeness: All data from a single national health system (Japan); LOSO evidence of robustness across sites but generalisability to other countries, especially low-resource settings with more variable staining/imaging, requires further validation.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine sediment and positive blood culture smears (Gram-stained)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Deep-learning estimation of ESBL risk in urinary Escherichia coli, and discrimination of Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) in blood cultures, from routine Gram-stain images.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA and MRSA); coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS)
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase [ESBL] resistance in E. coli; methicillin resistance defining MRSA in S. aureus)
Specific_Antibiotics: Carbapenems vs narrower-spectrum agents (ESBL E. coli decision); methicillin (MSSA/MRSA distinction)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: ESBL; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Unified binary classification: non-ESBL vs ESBL-producing E. coli (urine); CoNS vs S. aureus, including both MSSA and MRSA (blood), reference-standard defined by culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
AI_Purpose: Estimate ESBL risk in urinary E. coli and distinguish S. aureus from CoNS in blood cultures, directly from routine Gram-stain images.
Feature_Engineering: None reported: features are learned end-to-end by an EfficientNet-B0 CNN backbone directly from image patches (no manual feature engineering described).
Hyperparameter_Method: Model selection/hyperparameter tuning restricted to the development data; early stopping used a small patient-level validation subset (not used for performance reporting); full hyperparameters deferred to eMethods 7-8.
Other_Metrics: PR-AUC (precision-recall AUC) 0.979 (95% CI 0.974-0.983); Brier score 0.070 (95% CI 0.063-0.079); calibration slope 0.527 (95% CI 0.492-0.567) - temporal external validation.
Internal_Validation: A small patient-level subset of the development data was reserved only for monitoring training/early stopping; it was not used for threshold optimisation or performance reporting (no k-fold cross-validation was used).
Train_Test_Split: Temporal: earliest 70% of specimens for development, latest 30% as temporal test set per hospital.
CV_Folds: Not used — k-fold cross-validation was explicitly not performed on the development data.
External_Validation_Description: Two prespecified external validation strategies: (1) temporal — earliest 70% of specimens per hospital for development, latest 30% as temporal test set; (2) site-wise leave-one-site-out — one hospital held out as external test set, remaining hospitals used for development (primary: hospital B hold-out).
Overfitting_Method: Restricted all model selection/hyperparameter tuning to the development data and treated external test sets as lockboxes used only for final evaluation.
Clinical_Insights: Authors speculate the model extracts subtle, human-imperceptible patterns — fine variation in staining intensity, micro-architectural clustering, and smear background features — that correlate with underlying resistance mechanisms (not confirmed via a formal interpretability method).
Generalisability_Details: All data from a single national health system (Japan); staining reagents/timing and microscopy setups varied across the 7 sites and LOSO supports robustness, but generalisability to other countries — especially low-resource settings with more variable staining/imaging — requires further validation.
Maturity_Evidence: Prespecified temporal-holdout and leave-one-site-out external validation of a single model were performed and reported; no prospective clinical-impact trial or deployed-system evidence is presented.
Integration_Point: Same decision point at which Gram-stain results are first reported (routine microbiology workflow), without additional assays or equipment.
End_User_Described: Not explicitly named as a role; described via the clinical decision it informs (choice between carbapenems and narrower-spectrum agents for ESBL E. coli).
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Risk estimates obtainable within ~10 minutes of Gram-stain reporting, without altering existing microbiology workflows or requiring additional equipment; framed as decision support at the point Gram-stain results are first reported.
Barriers_List: Non-consecutive enrolment/spectrum-bias risk; probability miscalibration (overconfidence); possible GAN-augmentation optimism; single-country/single-health-system data; limited coverage of other resistant organisms (e.g. MRSA specifically not separately evaluable).
Facilitators_List: Operates entirely on routine Gram staining already produced in standard workflows; no additional equipment or per-test costs; usable in low-resource laboratories with limited access to rapid molecular diagnostics.
Future_Directions: Extend to additional resistant pathogens; assess performance under low-cost imaging and greater Gram-stain variability internationally; evaluate Gram stain-based AI decision support in randomised implementation trials for impact on therapy, antibiotic consumption, length of stay, and outcomes.
Limitation_Categories: Spectrum/selection bias (non-consecutive enrolment); calibration (overconfidence); augmentation-related optimism (GAN domain shift); geographic/health-system generalisability; limited resistance-phenotype coverage.
Data_Quality_Concerns: GAN-based style-transfer augmentation may have attenuated inter-site appearance differences (domain shift), potentially leading to modestly optimistic performance estimates in the external test sets.
Page_References: Abstract pp.9-10; Methods pp.11-20; Results pp.20-24; Discussion pp.24-29; Tables 1-3 pp.33-35 (Table 2 = primary temporal external validation results).

Title: Hospital unit colonization pressure and nosocomial acquisition of drug susceptible and drug resistant pathogens
Funder_Names: NLM (2T15LM007092-31); Department of Population Medicine (institutional funding); AHRQ (K08-HS030118); AHRQ (K08 HS027841-01A1)
Population_Description: Adult inpatients (>=18 years) admitted to any of the 8 community or 2 tertiary Mass General Brigham hospitals in the New England area between May 25 2015 and July 7 2024.
Age_Mean_Median: Mean 63.6 years (SE ± 0.2) cases; 63.9 years (SE ± 0.1) controls (pooled cohort)
Top_Predictive_Features: For the XGBoost MSSA model, ranked mean SHAP values: MSSA colonization pressure (0.086), drug susceptible Enterobacterales CP (0.085), ESBL Enterobacterales CP (0.064), Elixhauser index (0.056), vancomycin-susceptible Enterococcus CP (0.047).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Infection prevention and control team; Researcher
All_Models_Evaluated: Conditional logistic regression (AUROC 0.56-0.66 across 11 organism-specific models, per Table S8); XGBoost (AUROC 0.56 for ESBL K. pneumoniae to 0.63 for C. difficile).
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost model for C. difficile (highest AUROC among XGBoost models, 0.63)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: C. difficile cohort, XGBoost model
AUROC_Population_Set: C. difficile cohort, XGBoost model
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal 5-fold cross-validation was performed on the single-institution dataset; no external validation dataset or prospective evaluation; authors describe the work as proof-of-principle.
Reported_Limitations: Modest sample sizes restricting feature inclusion; possible residual confounding despite matching; inability to detect silent/undetected carriage; data from a single healthcare system limiting generalizability.
Sample_Size: 592 cases and 881 controls (C. difficile cohort, patients)
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr Pak received AHRQ funding (K08HS030118) during the study; the authors state none of the funders had a role in study design, conduct, analysis, or publication decisions.
Inclusion_Criteria: Adults (>=18 years) admitted to an MGB hospital, staying in one room >48 hours during a 30-day observation period, with no antibiotic exposure day -7 to day +3, and no prior evidence of the target organism in the preceding 6-12 months.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients actively treated for infection (antibiotic exposure day -7 to day +3) and those with prior evidence of the target organism in the previous 12 months (S. aureus/Enterococcus) or 6 months (other organisms) were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: PhysioNet, project ‘Nosocomial pathogen acquisition due to hospital unit colonization pressure’
Dataset_Size: 18,626 patients total (14,923 cases matched to 28,480 controls), pooled across 11 organism cohorts
Geographic_Representativeness: Data come from a single healthcare system in the northeast US; authors caution against extrapolating to other geographic areas/healthcare systems.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Any body site (clinical or surveillance culture)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Nosocomial acquisition of 11 common drug-susceptible and drug-resistant pathogens (enteric, skin and environmental niches), detected via clinical or surveillance culture.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (drug susceptible and ESBL); Klebsiella pneumoniae (drug susceptible and ESBL); Enterococcus faecalis (vancomycin susceptible); Enterococcus faecium (vancomycin resistant); Clostridioides difficile; Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA and MRSA); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (drug susceptible and drug resistant)
Drug_Classes: Penicillins, anti-staphylococcal penicillins, extended-spectrum penicillins, cephalosporins, extended-spectrum cephalosporins, carbapenems, glycopeptides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, tetracyclines, anti-anaerobic antibiotics, oral vancomycin
Specific_Antibiotics: 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins, piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime (used to define drug susceptible/resistant phenotypes)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL; MRSA; VRE
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary phenotypic susceptible/resistant classification based on susceptibility to specific antibiotics (e.g. drug susceptible E. coli/K. pneumoniae = susceptible to 3rd/4th generation cephalosporins and piperacillin-tazobactam; ESBL = resistant to these).
AI_Purpose: To model/predict nosocomial acquisition of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant pathogens using colonization pressure and comorbidity burden as covariates, comparing conditional logistic regression and XGBoost.
Feature_Engineering: Colonization pressure engineered as a negative-log, time-weighted prevalence of the target organism among ward co-occupants over the prior 6 months.
Num_Features_Total: 10 (9 colonization-pressure organism/organism-set predictors plus Elixhauser comorbidity index)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search
Other_Metrics: Likelihood ratio positive (LR+) and likelihood ratio negative (LR-)
Baseline_Method: Conditional logistic regression
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.66 (95% CI 0.66-0.66), C. difficile, conditional logistic regression
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: 8:1:1 (train:validation:test) per fold, XGBoost
Generalisability_Details: Single healthcare system in the northeast US; caution warranted when extrapolating to other geographic areas/healthcare systems differing in patient demographics, antibiotic consumption and infection control practices. Authors suggest combining data across health systems via a common data model or federated learning.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal 5-fold cross-validation only, on the same single-institution dataset; authors explicitly describe results as proof-of-principle, not a validated deployable tool.
End_User_Described: Infection control informatics tool / research community
Barriers_List: Small sample sizes limiting model performance (low PPV/NPV); colonization pressure alone is only one of many factors needed for real-time clinical decision-making.
Facilitators_List: CP can be calculated using data already present in the EHR, without requiring additional surveillance infrastructure, and can be applied to any organism in any hospital area.
Future_Directions: Improve predictive performance by adding host-specific factors and integrating clinical pathogen whole genome sequencing; improve generalizability by incorporating data from other hospital systems.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Exponentiated coefficients (conditional logistic regression); Shapley (SHAP) values (XGBoost)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Novel relationships identified for drug-susceptible organisms, and unexpected inverse (protective) colonization-pressure associations between organisms inhabiting different niches.
Limitation_Categories: Sample size / statistical power; residual confounding; outcome/label misclassification (silent carriage); single-institution generalisability.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Inability to detect silent/undetected carriage of target organisms and lack of insight into microbiology specimens/antibiotic prescriptions occurring outside the MGB healthcare system.

Title: Screening swabs surpass traditional risk factors as predictors of MRSA bacteremia
Population_Description: 376 adult patients with a first positive blood culture for Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia at the McGill University Health Centre (April 2010-April 2015), of whom 100 (26.6%) had MRSA and 276 had MSSA.
Age_Mean_Median: Median age (IQR): 65.5 (51, 76.25) years in MSSA patients; 66 (54.75, 77) years in MRSA patients
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: MRSA screening swab / colonization status was by far the top-ranked predictor in both random forest analyses. The next best 5 variables, ranked by Mean Increase in Accuracy and separately by Mean Decrease in Gini index, were (30-Day criteria): Tumor without Metastasis, CCI, Congestive Heart Failure, Dementia (by accuracy) and Age, CCI, Admissions (12 Months), Myocardial Infarction (by Gini).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest: MRSA colonization/screening-swab status had by far the greatest accuracy and discriminatory power of all variables tested (see Table 2/3). LASSO logistic regression (10-fold CV, one-SE rule): MRSA colonization was the only variable with clinically relevant predictive power, with odds ratios of 10.3 (min 5.99, max 16.1, 30-Day criteria) and 8.14 (min 6.01, max 14.8, Ever-Positive criteria) per the abstract; the Results-section text gives slightly different average odds ratios for the same two criteria of 10.6 (min 5.08, max 19.2) and 8.26 (min 5.23, max 15.8) respectively.
Best_Performing_Model: MRSA screening swab / colonization status - identified via LASSO logistic regression (10-fold CV, one-SE rule) as the only variable with clinically relevant predictive power for MRSA bacteremia, and via random forest as the top-ranked variable by Mean Increase in Accuracy and Mean Decrease in Gini index.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal analysis of a single retrospective single-network cohort was performed (variable selection via 10-fold cross-validated LASSO and random forest); no external cohort, prospective evaluation, or CDS integration was reported, and the authors explicitly frame prospective evaluation as future work.
Reported_Limitations: Three limitations: (1) small numbers of patients within individual comorbidity categories in Table 1, partly mitigated by using the aggregate CCI score and healthcare-exposure counts as separate variables; (2) retrospective, hypothesis-generating design; (3) the institution's MRSA screening protocol regularly samples only the nares, not all body sites.
Sample_Size: 376 patients with S. aureus bacteremia (100 MRSA, 276 MSSA)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All consecutive adult patients with S. aureus bacteremia at the McGill University Health Center (2 hospitals, Montreal, Canada) between April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2015; only the first positive blood culture per patient was included.
Exclusion_Criteria: Subsequent positive blood cultures beyond a patient's first were excluded, to prevent patients with multiple positive blood cultures from biasing the results.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 376 patients (100 MRSA, 276 MSSA), consecutive S. aureus bacteremia episodes, April 2010-April 2015
Specimen_Type_Detail: MRSA screening swab of the nares (other sites accepted case-by-case); blood culture for S. aureus bacteremia diagnosis.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Whether a patient's Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia isolate was methicillin-resistant (MRSA) versus methicillin-susceptible (MSSA), modelled from patient-level factors and prior MRSA colonization/screening-swab status.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA and MSSA)
Specific_Antibiotics: Vancomycin (empiric anti-MRSA agent under study); beta-lactams (comparator empiric agents)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA; Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MRSA colonization status was defined two ways from screening-swab history: the “30-Day criteria” (positive swab within the 30 days preceding bacteremia) and the “Ever-Positive criteria” (any positive swab at any point in the patient's hospitalization history before bacteremia).
AI_Purpose: To develop, using LASSO regression and random forest variable selection, a clinical prediction score combining patient-level factors and MRSA colonization/screening-swab status to estimate an individual patient's risk of MRSA (vs MSSA) bacteremia, in order to inform the decision to add empiric vancomycin coverage and reduce vancomycin overuse.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (random forest; LASSO logistic regression)
Feature_Engineering: Comorbidities were converted into the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) via a validated ICD-10-based algorithm; number of prior emergency-room and inpatient visits in the preceding 6/12 months was computed as a proxy for acute healthcare exposure; MRSA colonization status was engineered as two binary exposure definitions (30-Day and Ever-Positive criteria) from screening-swab history.
Feature_Selection_Method: Random forest variable importance (Mean Increase in Accuracy; Mean Decrease in Gini index) and LASSO with 10-fold cross-validation and the one-standard-error rule
Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross-validation selecting the LASSO penalty via the one-standard-error (1SE) rule
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation (for LASSO penalty selection, one-SE rule)
Overfitting_Method: Chose LASSO (10-fold CV, one-SE rule) and random forest over methods (e.g. stepwise regression) judged more susceptible to multiple-hypothesis-testing-driven overestimation of effect size.
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Screening-swab-based MRSA colonization status is an independent predictor of MRSA bacteremia regardless of patient comorbidities; the burden of comorbid disease (CCI) and healthcare-exposure counts (ED visits, admissions) were poorly related to methicillin resistance, a departure from the assumption that colonization is mainly a proxy for comorbidity/healthcare exposure.
Maturity_Evidence: Variable selection performed with 10-fold cross-validated LASSO and random forest on a single retrospective cohort; no external validation cohort, no prospective evaluation, and no clinical/CDS integration reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians who want to estimate the risk of MRSA bloodstream infection
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed: depending on local prevalence of methicillin resistance and absence of a nosocomial MRSA outbreak, known MRSA colonization status could be factored into the decision to start IV vancomycin (in stable patients) versus an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam, to limit both under- and over-treatment.
Stewardship_Details: Proposed (not measured) application: use known MRSA colonization status and local susceptibility prevalence to guide empiric anti-MRSA therapy decisions, limiting both under- and over-treatment with vancomycin.
Future_Directions: Prospective studies to demonstrate that, in appropriately selected hemodynamically stable patients, using known MRSA colonization status reduces overuse of potentially toxic therapies, increases early targeted beta-lactam therapy, and improves patient outcomes.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Random forest: Mean Increase in Accuracy and Mean Decrease in Gini index; LASSO: variable retention under 10-fold cross-validated one-standard-error-rule regularisation, ranked by logistic-regression odds ratio.
Limitation_Categories: Small sample size within individual comorbidity categories; retrospective, hypothesis-generating design; incomplete specimen sampling (nares-only MRSA screening, not all body sites).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Small numbers of patients within individual comorbidity categories in Table 1; mitigated by using the aggregate CCI score and a separate healthcare-exposure count rather than the individual sparse comorbidity variables.

Title: Machine Learning Predicts Accurately Mycobacterium tuberculosis Drug Resistance From Whole Genome Sequencing Data
Country_Countries: Global / multiple countries (isolates described as 'sourced globally'; individual countries not named in the main text)
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Newton Institutional Links Grant (British Council); Medical Research Council UK; BBSRC
Population_Description: 16,688 M. tuberculosis isolates that have undergone WGS and laboratory drug-susceptibility testing (DST) across 14 antituberculosis drugs, with 22.5% being multidrug resistant and 2.1% being extensively drug resistant
Data_Source_Other: Aggregated whole-genome-sequenced M. tuberculosis isolate/DST dataset; raw sequence data deposited in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA), not a clinical registry or EHR
Top_Predictive_Features: Known drug-resistance loci overlapping across the CT-KDG, CT-ALL and GBT-ALL models for each drug were confirmed as the strongest predictors of resistance (specific loci listed in Table 1, e.g. rpoB, katG, pncA, embB, gyrA)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Five modelling approaches were fitted and compared: CT-KDG (classification tree, known drug-resistance-gene SNPs), CT-ALL (classification tree, genome-wide SNPs), GBT-ALL (gradient-boosted tree, genome-wide SNPs, excluding co-occurrent resistance markers), GBT-CRM (gradient-boosted tree, genome-wide SNPs including co-occurrent resistance markers), and LR-KDG (logistic regression, known drug-resistance-gene SNPs)
Best_Performing_Model: GBT-CRM
Accuracy_Population_Set: Test set (20% held-out split), MDR-TB, GBT-CRM model
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Test set (20% held-out split), MDR-TB, GBT-CRM model
Specificity_Population_Set: Test set (20% held-out split), MDR-TB, GBT-CRM model
AUROC_Population_Set: MDR-TB (and amikacin, kanamycin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — top-performing drugs overall
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation was performed (80/20 train-test split on a single aggregated dataset with 5-fold cross-validation); no external cohort or prospective clinical evaluation was reported
Reported_Limitations: The inclusion of co-occurrent resistance markers might lead to overoptimism in the estimated performance that may not translate optimally into clinical practice; this may be caused by DST measurement errors, sequential testing, data from settings with unregulated drug availability, dataset stratification, and resistance mechanisms not captured in the database
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: The inclusion of co-occurrent resistance markers might lead to overoptimism in the estimated performance that may not translate optimally into clinical practice
Conflicts_of_Interest: Author WD was employed by the company Dalberg Advisors in Switzerland. The remaining authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: SNPs and indels included those with low levels of missing genotypes (<2%)
Exclusion_Criteria: SNPs/indels in the hypervariable PE/PPE gene families were excluded
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 642,580 genome-wide SNPs (plus indels)
Missing_Data_Method: Missing values were imputed using a nearest neighbor imputation approach; SNPs with low levels of missing genotypes (<2%) were included
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates described only as 'sourced globally'; no individual countries or regions itemised in the main text
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary drug resistance phenotype (resistant vs susceptible), derived from laboratory DST as gold standard, predicted from WGS genomic data across 14 anti-TB drugs and the composite MDR-TB phenotype
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide); second-line fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin) and injectables (amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin)
Specific_Antibiotics: INH, RIF, ETH, PZA, EMB, STM, AMK, CAP, KAN, CIP, OFL, MOX, CYS, and PAS, as well as the composite MDR-TB phenotype
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: M. tuberculosis strains resistant to at least RIF and INH are termed multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB)
AI_Purpose: To predict M. tuberculosis drug resistance and uncover any associated novel putative mutations using non-parametric classification-tree and gradient-boosted-tree machine learning models
Feature_Engineering: Aggregated count of all nonsynonymous mutations per gene included as an additional covariate, to allow the models to use this as a potential starting point and cover known low-frequency resistance mutations
Feature_Selection_Method: Two SNP sets used: one restricted to known drug-resistance genes (N=1,421 SNPs; CT-KDG/LR-KDG) and one using all genome-wide SNPs (N=641,159; CT-ALL); CT algorithms otherwise produce a single interpretable tree
Num_Features_Selected: CT-KDG: 1-4 SNPs/loci; CT-ALL: 1-10 predictors; GBT-ALL: 30-134 predictors
Class_Imbalance_Method: Oversampling of resistant isolates during dataset assembly, yielding resistance prevalence higher than typically seen in clinical or surveillance settings
Hyperparameter_Method: Five-fold cross-validation on the training set to select the maximum tree depth (CT/GBT); the penalized logistic-regression model was cross-validated on the L1 regularization strength C
Software_Libraries: SHAP; scikit-learn (decision tree classifier, v0.19.1); Xgboost (v0.70)
Hardware_Details: Medical Research Council UK funded eMedLab (HDR UK) computing resource
Baseline_Method: TB-Profiler mutation panel/software (rule-in known-SNP panel) and a mixed-model regression GWAS approach
Baseline_Performance: As TB-Profiler includes mutations occurring at low frequencies, the predicted accuracy was superior than the machine learning approaches for most drugs
Internal_Validation: 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set
Train_Test_Split: 80% training/validation, 20% test
Overfitting_Method: One-standard-error rule for selecting the maximum tree depth via cross-validation, to induce parsimonious models and mitigate the risk of over-fitting
Clinical_Insights: Discordance between DST and genotypically inferred resistance may be explained by DST errors, novel rare mutations, hetero-resistance, and nongenomic drivers such as efflux-pump upregulation
Generalisability_Details: Due to oversampling, resistance rates in this dataset are higher than those typically seen in clinical or surveillance settings
Maturity_Evidence: Best evidence supports internal validation only: an 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation on a single aggregated isolate dataset; no external or prospective evaluation was reported
Facilitators_List: Rollout of WGS-based TB diagnosis across many countries motivating the development of global TB datasets/databases and 'big data' analytical (ML) approaches to assist clinical and control-programme decision making
Future_Directions: Future studies should aim to use quantitative minimum inhibitory concentration scores as phenotypes
Top_Features_Importance_Method: GBT weight/coverage/importance scores from a two-dimensional mutation-ranking graph (importance gain vs weight, coverage as bubble size)
Novel_Predictors_Details: A number of known candidates (e.g., Rv1463 for RIF resistance) presented with marginal evidence; no confirmed novel SNPs met the detection thresholds
Feature_Interactions_Method: Gradient-boosted-tree ensembles implicitly capture covariate (SNP) interactions; GBT-CRM's improved performance was attributed partly to this ability
Limitation_Categories: Overoptimism/optimism bias from co-occurrent resistance markers; DST measurement error; dataset stratification/heterogeneity; unregulated drug-availability settings affecting resistance mechanisms
Data_Quality_Concerns: Discordance between DST and genotypically inferred resistance may be explained by DST errors, novel rare mutations, hetero-resistance, and nongenomic drivers such as efflux-pump upregulation

Title: Genomic prediction of tuberculosis drug-resistance: benchmarking existing databases and prediction algorithms
Country_Countries: Not stated as a single country — isolates were compiled from public databases and literature studies spanning multiple countries worldwide
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Funder_Names: NUS Graduate School for Integrative Sciences and Engineering
Population_Description: 6756 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with whole genome sequences and drug-susceptibility phenotypes, compiled from the PATRIC and ReSeqTB public databases and a literature-review (LitRev) isolate set
Data_Source_Other: Public genomic/drug-susceptibility databases (PATRIC, ReSeqTB) plus an isolate set assembled from a literature review (LitRev)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: TBProfiler, MyKrobe, KVarQ and PhyResSE were each evaluated for sensitivity and specificity in predicting resistance to 14 anti-TB drugs; TBProfiler had consistently higher sensitivity than the other three across most drugs, at the cost of somewhat lower specificity (see Table 1)
Best_Performing_Model: TBProfiler — named as having the highest sensitivity across most of the 14 drugs (e.g. 90% sensitivity for amikacin vs 75-79% for the other three tools), though with correspondingly lower specificity
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Amikacin (AMK), 1649 isolates
Specificity_Population_Set: Amikacin (AMK), 1649 isolates
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The four tools are pre-existing software; this study benchmarks them against a large, largely independent set of isolates, explicitly excluding samples known to have been used to train the tools — i.e. external validation, not a prospective clinical evaluation or deployed decision-support use.
Reported_Limitations: Recalibrating performance against inferred DST errors risks overfitting, since each software's adjustment partly relies on overlapping sets of genetic markers.
Sample_Size: 6756 Mtb isolates (with WGS and drug-resistance phenotype data for at least one drug)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests
Inclusion_Criteria: Isolates from clinical samples; at least 10 samples per contributing study; DST performed on at least 4 of the 5 first-line drugs; the study must include at least one drug-resistant TB isolate
Exclusion_Criteria: Samples with poor-quality sequencing or genomes incorrectly classified as Mtb were excluded
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: PATRIC; ReSeqTB
Dataset_Size: 6756 isolates total (2302 present in all three source databases)
Missing_Data_Method: No-call or discordant predictions across sequencing-read sets for a sample/drug were treated as missing
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates were pooled from public databases and studies described only as spanning “different parts of the world”, with no further representativeness assessment
Specimen_Type_Detail: Isolates from clinical samples (specific specimen type, e.g. sputum, not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant/susceptible drug-susceptibility phenotype for each of 14 anti-TB drugs, genetically predicted from WGS and benchmarked against laboratory DST
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb)
Drug_Classes: First-line agents, second-line injectables, oral second-line drugs, and fluoroquinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), pyrazinamide (PZA), ethambutol (EMB), streptomycin (STM), amikacin (AMK), capreomycin (CAP), kanamycin (KAN), ethionamide (ETO), prothionamide (PTO), p-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), ciprofloxacin (CIP), moxifloxacin (MFX), ofloxacin (OFX)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label: Yj = 1 if the sample is predicted/observed resistant, 0 if susceptible, NA otherwise, per drug
AI_Purpose: To benchmark the sensitivity and specificity of four existing WGS-based bioinformatics tools for predicting TB drug resistance, and to evaluate the fidelity of reported DST phenotypes in public databases
Hardware_Details: High-performance computing clusters of the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, National University of Singapore
Other_Metrics: DST credibility score (posterior probability that a sample's reported phenotype is correct, given the four tools' predictions), and a database misclassification/error rate derived from it
External_Validation_Description: 6756 Mtb isolates compiled from PATRIC, ReSeqTB and a literature-review (LitRev) set, excluding samples known to have been used to train the four tools
Overfitting_Method: Discussed conceptually, not empirically tested: the authors note the recalibrated performance risks overfitting because each software's adjustment partly relies on overlapping sets of genetic markers
Generalisability_Details: Infrastructural limitations still constrain widespread WGS adoption for DR-TB identification in resource-poor settings, even though accurate bioinformatics predictors would be valuable for translating genetic sequences into clinically actionable information
Maturity_Evidence: Evaluated on a large, largely independent set of isolates (samples used to train the tools were excluded), i.e. external validation rather than prospective or deployed clinical evaluation
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiologists, who interpret the software's output
Barriers_List: Infrastructural limitations to widespread WGS adoption for identifying drug-resistant TB in resource-poor settings
Facilitators_List: Availability of accurate bioinformatics predictors, valuable for translating genetic sequences into clinically actionable information to guide efficacious drug prescription
Future_Directions: Need for a clearer understanding of the genetic biomarkers of drug resistance and their penetrance, and for more powerful algorithms capturing cross-drug resistance intricacies (as has been done for HIV and cancer), to improve prediction for low-sensitivity drugs (ETO, PAS, PTO, PZA)
Limitation_Categories: Possible overfitting of recalibrated performance estimates; limited genetic-biomarker knowledge and small sample sizes for some second-line drugs (ETO, PTO, PAS, PZA); infrastructural limitations to WGS adoption in resource-poor settings
Data_Quality_Concerns: Laboratory-based DST phenotypes in public databases carry non-trivial error rates, reaching as high as 31.1% for prothionamide, with ReSeqTB phenotypes more error-prone than the other databases

Title: Identifying and forecasting importation and asymptomatic spreaders of multi-drug resistant organisms in hospital settings
Funder_Names: NSF; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Institutes of Health (NIH); National Center for Advancing Translational Science (NCATS); Facebook (faculty research award); Dolby (faculty research award); Georgia Tech
Population_Description: Patients admitted to the intensive care units (ICUs) at the University of Virginia (UVA) hospital, July 1, 2019 to December 31, 2019 (1117 patients; 74 identified as MRSA importation cases).
Top_Predictive_Features: Contact with other MRSA patients in the 7-14 days before ICU admission; device usage history; prior transfer from or discharge to another healthcare facility (ranked via SHAP feature-importance values on the neural network).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: NeurABM (proposed) vs. baselines: feedforward neural network, decision tree, naive Bayes, XGBoost, Autoencoder+KNN (machine-learning); SIS-ABM, SILI-ABM (mechanistic modelling); length of stay (clinical heuristic) — compared via AUPRC, AUC-ROC, NPV, and recall/F1/false-positive-rate at fixed precision (0.25/0.5/0.75); NeurABM highest on every metric across all three tasks (identifying importation, identifying current nosocomial infection, forecasting future nosocomial infection).
Best_Performing_Model: NeurABM — highest AUC-ROC (0.86 for identifying importation cases) among all compared baselines.
Sensitivity_Value: 0.74 recall (sensitivity) at a precision operating point of 0.25, for identifying MRSA importation cases
Sensitivity_Population_Set: UVA ICU patients; identifying MRSA importation cases at precision=0.25
AUROC_Population_Set: UVA ICU patients; identifying MRSA importation cases
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evaluated with a rolling (weekly) internal temporal train/test split on a single site's retrospective data only; no external-site or prospective validation reported.
Reported_Limitations: SIS-ABM oversimplifies MRSA carriage (only susceptible/carriage states, no colonization state, no distinction between infection types); contact networks assume co-located individuals interact (a 'well-mixed' assumption that may be sub-optimal); evaluated only at a single site (UVA ICU) due to data availability.
Sample_Size: 1117 patients in UVA ICUs (July 1-December 31, 2019); 74 identified as MRSA importation cases
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All patients in the UVA ICUs; an MRSA importation case is any patient who received an MRSA test within (t-3, t+3) days of ICU admission and tested positive within that window.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Other
Dataset_Size: 1117 patients, 6445 patient-days, 2385 healthcare workers, and 77 locations (July 1-December 31, 2019)
Specimen_Type_Detail: MRSA culture tests and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests (specimen/site not further specified)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Identification of MRSA importation (colonization/infection present at or near ICU admission) and of current/future nosocomial MRSA infection during the ICU stay, based on positive MRSA culture or PCR test results.
Pathogens: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Drug_Classes: MRSA-active antibiotics (methicillin/beta-lactam resistance implied by the MRSA phenotype); no specific drug class further detailed
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary positive/negative MRSA status per patient per day, defined from a positive culture test or a positive/negative PCR test.
AI_Purpose: To identify patients already infected/colonized with MRSA at admission (importation) and to forecast future nosocomial MRSA infections, by coupling a neural network (patient-level risk prediction from EHR data) with an agent-based transmission model (ABM), trained end-to-end.
Feature_Engineering: 19 patient-level risk factors extracted from pre-ICU-admission EHR data (e.g., comorbidities, medical history) used as neural-network input; ward-level co-location contact networks built from EHR movement data used by the ABM.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Weighted binary cross-entropy loss, with the positive/negative class weights set from the ratio of negative to positive observations.
Other_Metrics: False positive rate; negative predictive value (NPV); area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC); recall and F1 score at fixed precision thresholds of 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.
Baseline_Method: Feedforward neural network, decision tree, naive Bayes, XGBoost, Autoencoder+KNN (machine-learning baselines); SIS-ABM and SILI-ABM (mechanistic modelling baselines); length of stay (clinical heuristic baseline).
Baseline_Performance: Best baseline (feedforward neural network) achieved 0.40 recall at a precision of 0.25 for identifying importation cases, versus 0.74 recall for NeurABM.
Internal_Validation: Weekly walk-forward (rolling-origin) temporal split: for each week k, the model is trained on all contact-network, risk-factor and lab-test data available up to week k-1 and evaluated on week k.
Train_Test_Split: Machine-learning baselines trained on January-June 2019 ground-truth labels and tested on July-December 2019 (same test period used for NeurABM).
Clinical_Insights: Patients with recent (7-14 day) contact with other MRSA patients, a device-usage history, or recent transfer from/discharge to another healthcare facility were flagged as higher risk, consistent with known clinical risk factors for MRSA importation.
Generalisability_Details: The authors note NeurABM is evaluated only in the UVA ICU due to data availability and that adding more risk factors or testing in other settings/healthcare facilities could give a more comprehensive assessment; they frame the framework as adaptable to other ABMs, EHR datasets and HAIs.
Maturity_Evidence: Evaluated only via retrospective, single-site (UVA ICU) rolling internal temporal validation against historical data; no external-site validation or prospective clinical deployment reported.
Integration_Point: Not integrated into a clinical workflow; discussed conceptually as informing testing/quarantine/infection-control prioritisation decisions.
End_User_Described: Clinicians (to better respond to potential MRSA importation cases)
Future_Directions: Extend agent-based methods to predict MRSA testing outcomes for clinical application; add more patient risk factors (e.g., chronic disease history, APACHE II scores) or evaluate in other settings/healthcare facilities; forecast future contact networks instead of assuming they equal the most recent day; enrich the ABM with intervention representations; extend to other patient-specific parameters (e.g., recovery rate); adapt NeurABM to other HAIs such as Clostridioides difficile.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values
Limitation_Categories: Model oversimplification (SIS-ABM's two-state carriage model, no colonization state, no infection-type distinction); contact-network construction assumption (well-mixed co-location assumption); single-site evaluation (UVA ICU only, due to data availability).
Data_Quality_Concerns: MRDO testing is generally not performed systematically across all patients, introducing bias in the underlying data.
Page_References: Abstract p.1; Results pp.3-6; Discussion pp.6-8; Methods pp.8-9; Ethics/Data/Code availability pp.9-10

Pathogens: Escherichia coli (uropathogenic E. coli, UPEC)
Drug_Classes: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams, cephamycins)
Specific_Antibiotics: ampicilin, cefuroxime, piperacillin, nitrofurantoin, ceftriaxone, gentamicin, ceftazidime, amoxicillin/clavul A, amikacin, cotrimoxazole, nalidixic acid, ofloxacin, piperacill/tazobact, ciprofloxacin, meropenem, and tobramycin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: ESBL

Title: Beyond multidrug resistance: Leveraging rare variants with machine and statistical learning models in Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistance prediction
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: NIH BD2K (K01 ES026835); Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (OPP1115887)
Population_Description: 3601 Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains (training set) enriched for resistance to first- and second-line drugs, with 1228 multidrug resistant strains; validated on an independent set of 792 MTB isolates.
Data_Source_Other: Curated multi-source WGS/targeted-sequencing and phenotype dataset assembled via the ReSeqTB knowledgebase (a public research data-sharing platform), plus targeted sequencing performed for this study and literature-curated isolate collections; not a clinical EHR, hospital registry or laboratory information system.
Top_Predictive_Features: embA N54D (top ethambutol predictor, ranked 3rd most important); embC variants (V104M, R567H, frameshift in codon 986 - associated with susceptibility); rpsA variants (top-30 predictor for pyrazinamide when pooled in the derived category).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: MD-WDNN (multidrug wide-and-deep NN), SD-WDNN (single-drug WDNN), deep MLP, L2 regularized logistic regression, random forest - compared on the full predictor set by repeated cross-validation AUROC; MD-WDNN highest average AUC 0.953, logistic regression 0.949, random forest inferior for 3 of 4 first-line drugs.
Best_Performing_Model: MD-WDNN (multidrug wide-and-deep neural network)
Sensitivity_Value: 87.9% (first-line drugs); 82.0% (second-line drugs) - MD-WDNN, independent validation set
Sensitivity_Population_Set: MD-WDNN, independent validation set, averaged across first-line vs second-line drugs
Specificity_Value: 92.7% (first-line drugs); 90.1% (second-line drugs) - MD-WDNN, independent validation set
Specificity_Population_Set: MD-WDNN, independent validation set, averaged across first-line vs second-line drugs
AUROC_Value: MD-WDNN: 0.937 (first-line, independent validation); 0.891 (second-line, independent validation); 0.979 (first-line, repeated cross-validation); 0.936 (second-line, repeated cross-validation)
AUROC_Population_Set: MD-WDNN; independent validation set and repeated 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats); first-line vs second-line drug averages
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were trained/tuned with repeated cross-validation and then evaluated on a separate, non-overlapping, geographically/lineage-distinct independent validation set of 792 isolates - external validation evidence, not yet prospective or CDS-integrated.
Reported_Limitations: We acknowledge some limitations of our study. First, one source of bias could be errors during phenotyping (low reproducibility/high variance of susceptibility testing for some drugs); MICs close to the testing breakpoint may lower Sn/Sp. Second, only mutations occurring in >=0.8% of isolates (individually or aggregated) were included, so some rare predictors may have been missed. Third, third-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (e.g. cycloserine, para-aminosalicylic acid) were not included owing to lack of phenotypic data.
Sample_Size: 3601 MTB isolates (training set), with 1228 multidrug resistant strains
Conflicts_of_Interest: Dr. Ezewudo and Dr. Schito report grants from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation during the conduct of the study; all other authors have nothing to disclose.
Inclusion_Criteria: All isolates included underwent culture based antibiotic susceptibility testing to two or more drugs at WHO approved critical concentrations and met other quality control criteria.
Exclusion_Criteria: Strains with a coverage of <95% at 10x or more in the regions of interest, or a mapping percentage of <90% to Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, were excluded; poorly covered genome regions and low-quality/low-purity/non-PASS variants were filtered out.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: ReSeqTB
Dataset_Size: 3601 MTB isolates total (training), with 3227 unique genetic-mutation/phenotype patterns
Missing_Data_Method: Missing genotype values were imputed with a status of 0.5
Geographic_Representativeness: Independent validation set was intentionally geographically/lineage-distinct from the training set (higher proportion of East Asian lineage; lower proportions of Euro-American, Central Asian and other lineages), supporting a genuinely external test of generalisability.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Clinical Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates (whole genome / targeted sequencing)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phenotypic drug resistance (resistant/susceptible) to 10 anti-tuberculosis drugs, predicted from genomic/genotypic variant data.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First-line drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol); streptomycin; second-line injectable drugs (capreomycin, amikacin, kanamycin); fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin).
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, capreomycin, amikacin, kanamycin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin (ciprofloxacin excluded from final independent-validation performance reporting owing to limited phenotypic data).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Phenotype classified per drug as resistant, susceptible, or not available, based on culture-based antibiotic susceptibility testing at WHO-approved critical concentrations.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To explore machine and statistical learning algorithms and expanded genetic predictor sets (including rare variants) to build a high-performing, fast model predicting anti-tuberculosis drug resistance directly from sequencing data, circumventing slow conventional phenotypic AST.
Feature_Engineering: Rarer mutations (present in <30 isolates) were aggregated into 'derived' categories by gene locus (coding, intergenic, promoter) and variant type (SNP, frameshift indel, non-frameshift indel for coding regions; indel or SNP for non-coding regions).
Feature_Selection_Method: Frequency threshold: individual and derived predictors required in at least 30 MTB isolates were retained as the final predictor set.
Num_Features_Total: 6342 variants identified across 30 regions; 222 used as final predictors (166 common mutations + 56 derived rare-variant categories)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Class-weighted (upweighted sparser class per drug's susceptible-resistant ratio) binary cross-entropy loss; single-drug models stratified by class label.
Hyperparameter_Method: Bayesian optimization (Spearmint)
Software_Libraries: Keras 1.2.0 (Python 2.7, TensorFlow 0.10.0 backend); scikit-learn 0.18.1 (random forest, logistic regression); R 3.4.0 / Rtsne 0.13 (t-SNE, lineage clustering).
Hardware_Details: NVIDIA GeForce GTX Titan X GPU
Other_Metrics: Average precision (AP) from the precision-recall curve, reported for capreomycin, amikacin and moxifloxacin (MD-WDNN APs 0.5, 0.74, 0.63 vs logistic regression 0.45, 0.64, 0.55); model prediction runtime (MD-WDNN 0.0352 s; logistic regression 0.00291 s).
Baseline_Method: Direct association (DA): splitting genetic variants into resistance-associated vs. not, via a rule list, to classify a sample as resistant or susceptible.
Baseline_Performance: DA Sn/Sp of 24% and 99% for pyrazinamide when prediction is attempted on all isolates including uncharacterized variants (vs. MD-WDNN Sn 75.2%/Sp 91.2%).
Internal_Validation: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats; 50 validation sets total)
Train_Test_Split: Independent validation set of 792 isolates, non-overlapping with the 3601-isolate training set
External_Validation_Description: 792 MTB isolates pooled from ReSeqTB (non-overlapping with training set) plus other whole genome sequences and manually curated phenotype data from external references; geographically/lineage-distinct from the training set.
Overfitting_Method: Dropout and L2 regularization at each layer of the network to mitigate overfitting; evaluated on an independent validation set to check for it.
Clinical_Insights: embC and embA are known ethambutol targets; embA mutations (esp. N54D) ranked as important resistance predictors while several embC variants were instead associated with susceptibility, consistent with/extending prior genome-wide association findings.
Generalisability_Details: External validation used a geographically/lineage-distinct isolate set; authors note performance may improve and the Sn/Sp gap for second-line injectables/fluoroquinolones should shrink as more diverse sequencing data are incorporated.
Maturity_Evidence: Independent, non-overlapping, geographically distinct validation set (n=792) used to confirm cross-validation performance was not simply overfitting.
End_User_Described: Researchers and clinicians using whole genome sequencing to predict MTB drug resistance
Facilitators_List: Declining whole-genome sequencing costs enabling more routine WGS; very fast prediction runtime (well under 1 second) so turnaround is limited mainly by sequencing time rather than by the model.
Future_Directions: Incorporate more genetic loci / more routinely generated sequencing data as it becomes available (models can be rapidly updated); model phenomena like linkage disequilibrium (e.g. via convolutional neural networks); use MIC data rather than binary phenotype; identify the impact of a wider range of genetic variants.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation test (MD-WDNN) and bootstrapped exponentiated beta coefficient / odds-ratio confidence intervals (L2 logistic regression)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Non-canonical and rare variants ranked among the top predictors, e.g. embA N54D for ethambutol (3rd most important); rare rpsA variants (aggregated) among the top 30 predictors for pyrazinamide.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Wide-and-deep neural network (MD-WDNN): the 'deep' MLP component models arbitrarily complex epistatic/gene-gene interactions, alongside a 'wide' logistic component for additive effects.
Limitation_Categories: Phenotyping/measurement error (label noise); rare-variant frequency threshold (possible missed predictors); missing third-line drugs (lack of phenotypic data).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Possible errors during phenotyping - susceptibility testing for some drugs has low reproducibility/high variance; some resistance mutations may yield MICs close to the testing breakpoint, lowering Sn/Sp when predicting a binary phenotype.

Title: Predictive model of unfavorable outcomes for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
Funder_Names: São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP)
Population_Description: All cases diagnosed with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) between 2006 and 2015 in the 645 municipalities of the state of São Paulo, Brazil, drawn from the state TB case notification system (TBWeb); 802 patients remained after removing duplicate reports.
Age_Range: ≤14 to ≥60 years (categorical age bands reported; no mean/median given)
Data_Source_Other: State-level tuberculosis case notification system (TBWeb)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Logistic regression / nomogram for abandonment (ROC-AUC 0.65, 95%CI 0.57-0.73); for death (ROC-AUC 0.70, 95%CI 0.61-0.79); for treatment failure (ROC-AUC 0.80, 95%CI 0.76-0.84).
Best_Performing_Model: Treatment-failure logistic regression / nomogram model (highest ROC-AUC of the three outcome-specific models, 0.80)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Full retrospective cohort (n=802), internal validation only
AUROC_Population_Set: Full retrospective cohort (n=802), internal validation only
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The nomogram's discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.65-0.80) was assessed only within the same retrospective cohort used to build it; the authors state the results are internally valid and that other populations would require separate validation.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design with no control over data collected via TBWeb; likely underreporting due to diagnostic difficulty and limited access to technology such as GeneXpert.
Unresolved_Items: The paper reports three separate outcome-specific models (abandonment/death/treatment failure) rather than a single head-to-head model comparison; this record treats the treatment-failure model (highest ROC-AUC, 0.80) as Best_Performing_Model per the review's unit-of-analysis convention, though Best_Performing_Model_NA could be argued instead. Separately, Table 3 lists 'Gender (n = 856)' for the regression models, which exceeds the 802-patient cohort reported elsewhere in the paper (apparent source typo).
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: All cases diagnosed with MDR-TB between 2006 and 2015 in the 645 municipalities of the state of São Paulo, notified in the TBWeb system.
Exclusion_Criteria: Duplicate case reports for the same individual (matched on full name, mother's name and date of birth) were removed, keeping only the most current outcome.
Data_Types_Used: Demographic variables; Clinical / EHR variables; Epidemiological surveillance data
Data_Source_Name: TBWeb
Dataset_Size: 1,168 MDR-TB case reports identified; 802 patients after removing duplicates
Ethnicity_Details: White 358 (44.6%); Black/brown 267 (33.3%); Others (yellow, indigenous) 6 (0.7%); No information 171 (21.3%)
Geographic_Representativeness: Authors note the São Paulo / Brazilian Southeast cohort had worse cure outcomes than other Brazilian studies and may be a distinct, non-representative subset of the rest of the country.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Unfavorable MDR-TB treatment outcome (death, treatment abandonment, or treatment failure) versus cure
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (multidrug-resistant strains)
Drug_Classes: Isoniazid and rifampicin (first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs)
Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid; Rifampicin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin (the two main first-line anti-TB drugs)
AI_Purpose: To identify factors related to unfavorable MDR-TB treatment outcomes and build a nomogram-based predictive model estimating individual probabilities of abandonment, death, and treatment failure.
Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables were dichotomised for use as regression predictors (e.g. age ≤40 vs >40 years in the regression models).
Feature_Selection_Method: Forward stepwise selection (likelihood ratio) of variables with a significant crude OR
Other_Metrics: McFadden pseudo R2 and Wald statistic reported per model (e.g. treatment-failure model).
Clinical_Insights: Illicit drug use, number of previous MDR-TB treatments, and place of diagnosis (emergency/hospital vs outpatient) were identified as the key clinically actionable risk factors for unfavorable outcomes.
Generalisability_Details: Authors suggest the São Paulo / Brazilian Southeast cohort may be a specific, distinct population (different from a Rio de Janeiro cohort in the literature), limiting generalisation to the rest of the country; they also state results require separate validation in other populations.
Maturity_Evidence: The nomogram's ROC-AUC (0.65-0.80) was computed on the same cohort used to fit the logistic models; authors explicitly describe this as internal validation requiring further validation elsewhere.
End_User_Described: TB control programme / health service teams providing follow-up and patient-centred care to MDR-TB patients
Barriers_List: Restricted primary-care hours/low PHC coverage; cultural preference for emergency-service entry; limited access to diagnostic technology (e.g. GeneXpert); stigma associated with illicit drug use.
Facilitators_List: Post-treatment educational actions about the disease and psychosocial support for patients and families, associated with better retreatment outcomes.
Future_Directions: Authors note the nomogram is internally valid only and that other populations/scenarios require a separate validation process.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Having one or more previous MDR-TB treatments was protective (reduced odds) for abandonment, death and treatment failure, an outcome the authors describe as unexpected.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective/secondary-data design; underreporting / case-ascertainment limitations; limited diagnostic technology access.
Data_Quality_Concerns: The notification form's 'entry-type' field was often incomplete, making it impossible to tell whether retreated patients' prior episode ended in abandonment, failure, or relapse.
Reporting_Clarity: Table 3 lists 'Gender (n = 856)' for the regression models, which exceeds the 802-patient cohort reported in Table 1 and the Results text (apparent inconsistency in the source).

Title: Application of machine learning techniques to tuberculosis drug resistance analysis
Country_Countries: Pakistan; China; Sweden; Singapore; Taiwan (consortium contributor sites named in the author/members list; the paper states the cohort spans 16 countries across 6 continents overall but does not individually name all of them in the main text)
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Oxford Biomedical Research Centre; CRyPTIC consortium (Wellcome Trust/Newton Fund-MRC Collaborative Award; Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation Trust); Wellcome Trust; Royal Society
Population_Description: 13,402 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected from across the world (16 countries, 6 continents), with whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing for up to 11 anti-TB drugs.
Top_Predictive_Features: Table 3 lists the top 10 mutations ranked by the top-performing classifier for each of the 11 drugs (e.g. INH: katG_S315T, fabG1_C-15T, fabG1_L203L, katG_S315N, rpoB_S450L…); ranking method is the feature-importance output of whichever classifier (LR-L1/LR-L2/GBT) performed best for that drug.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Six base classifiers compared by AUC(%) across 11 anti-TB drugs and the F1 feature space: LR (L1 and L2), SVM (linear and RBF kernels), RF, Adaboost, PM and GBT (Fig. 1); also evaluated with SPCA/SNMF dimension reduction (Fig. 2) and against the DA baseline per drug (Table 2, e.g. INH best F1+LR-L2 AUC 97.89% vs DA 94.95%).
Best_Performing_Model: Logistic regression (LR) and gradient tree boosting (GBT) were the overall best-performing classifiers (judged by AUC); per drug, F1+LR-L2 was best for INH, EMB, RIF, PZA, SM, KAN and CIP, while F1(+SPCA)+GBT/LR-L2 was best for AK, MOX, OFX and CAP (Table 2).
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Test set (20% held out per fold, averaged over 100 iterations of 5-fold cross-validation); PZA
Specificity_Population_Set: Test set (20% held out per fold, averaged over 100 iterations of 5-fold cross-validation); PZA
F1_Value: 64.36% — PZA, best model F1+LR-L2 (vs 55.55% for the DA baseline)
F1_Population_Set: Test set (20% held out per fold, averaged over 100 iterations of 5-fold cross-validation); PZA
AUROC_Population_Set: Test set (20% held out per fold, averaged over 100 iterations of 5-fold cross-validation); PZA
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Evaluated only via repeated internal cross-validation (100 iterations of 5-fold CV) on the pooled multi-site cohort; no independent external cohort, prospective evaluation, or clinical deployment reported.
Reported_Limitations: Authors list several limitations: error in phenotypes (imperfect ground-truth labels), the assumption that resistance is independent across drugs (labels learned independently), independence of the feature space for classification, treating all variants as equally important, ignoring missing labels, and coding null calls as 'no variant'.
Conflicts_of_Interest: None declared
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: CRyPTIC Consortium (and the 100,000 Genomes Project)
Dataset_Size: 5,919 variants across 23 candidate genes (13,402 isolates)
Missing_Data_Method: Low-confidence bases were coded as 'null calls' and treated as absence of the variant (0) rather than imputed — a conservative choice made because only 0.19% of gene-position calls were null.
Geographic_Representativeness: Framed as more geographically diverse than prior ML-for-TB studies (161, 1839 and 1397 isolates in single/limited settings); this cohort spans 16 countries and 6 continents.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture isolates (whole-genome sequenced)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype to each of up to 11 anti-TB drugs, predicted from the isolate's genomic mutation profile.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First-line: isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide. Second-line: streptomycin, fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin), kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin.
Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), ethambutol (EMB), pyrazinamide (PZA), streptomycin (SM), ofloxacin (OFX), moxifloxacin (MOX), ciprofloxacin (CIP), kanamycin (KAN), amikacin (AK), capreomycin (CAP).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible label per drug, derived from phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing.
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To predict per-drug resistance phenotype from WGS-derived mutation data and to identify resistance-associated mutations, using a larger and more geographically diverse cohort than prior ML-for-TB studies.
Num_Models_Compared: 8 (SVM-linear, SVM-RBF, LR-L1, LR-L2, PM, RF, Adaboost, GBT)
Feature_Engineering: Binary mutation presence/absence vector (5,919 variants across 23 candidate genes); three feature sets compared (F1 = all variants, F2 = known resistance-associated variants only, F3 = drug-specific resistance genes); optional linear dimension reduction (SPCA/SNMF, 100 components).
Feature_Selection_Method: Sparse PCA / sparse non-negative matrix factorisation (100 components retained)
Num_Features_Total: 5,919 variants (23 genes)
Num_Features_Selected: 100 components (SPCA/SNMF, F1+dimension reduction)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Random under-sampling of the majority (susceptible) class in the training partition to create a balanced training set.
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over a range of values, optimised via internal cross-validation on the training data.
Other_Metrics: Wilcoxon signed-rank test P-values comparing each ML method with the DA baseline (P < 0.01 for the improvements reported).
Baseline_Method: Direct association (DA): a rule-based classifier using an 'OR' rule over a predetermined library of known resistance-associated variants (Walker et al., 2015).
Baseline_Performance: PZA (DA method): Sensitivity 43.11% (±2.97), Specificity 98.46% (±0.27), AUC 70.78% (±1.46).
Internal_Validation: 100 iterations of 5-fold cross-validation, with the 80% training partition further split 80:20 into balanced training and validation sets for parameter and threshold selection.
Train_Test_Split: 20% held out as test set per fold (5-fold CV); within the remaining 80%, a further 80:20 split into training and validation sets.
Overfitting_Method: Cross-validation and regularisation terms, plus using a larger, more diverse cohort than prior small single-community studies (which the authors note can lead to over-fitted models).
Clinical_Insights: Top-ranked mutations recapitulated known resistance markers and also revealed lineage-associated and previously unreported (non-library) mutations; e.g. fabG1_L203L actually acts as a promoter mutation that increases expression of the inhA gene rather than being a fabG1 coding change.
Generalisability_Details: Authors note their larger, more diverse cohort should better generalise to future samples, but also flag a 'lack of generalizability of the resistance co-occurrence predictions' compared with prior work.
Maturity_Evidence: Best evidence is repeated internal cross-validation on a large pooled multi-site cohort (Table 2); no external cohort or prospective clinical evaluation is reported.
Future_Directions: Considering whole-genome positions outside the 23 candidate genes, deep networks for non-linear classification and dimension reduction, and optimising the number of SPCA/SNMF components.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature-importance ranking from the top-performing classifier per drug (method not further specified beyond 'considering the top performing models').
Novel_Predictors_Details: Several top-ranked mutations were not in the known resistance library and were not lineage-defining, for EMB, PZA, SM, AK, OFX, MOX and CAP (marked 'o' in Table 3).
Limitation_Categories: Phenotype measurement error; independence assumptions (across-drug label independence, feature independence); equal weighting of all variants; ignoring missing labels; null-call coding as absence of variant.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing phenotypic labels for many isolates/drugs (e.g. only ~4% tested for CIP); highly imbalanced resistant/susceptible counts per drug; 34% of isolates carry one or more null (low-confidence) genotype calls.
Page_References: Table 2 p.5 (performance vs baseline); Table 3 p.4/6 (mutation ranking); Fig. 1-2 p.4 (AUC by classifier).

Internal_Validation: Random split: 75% training set, 25% test set
