Title: Prediction of rifampicin resistance beyond the RRDR using structure‑based machine learning approaches
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Melbourne Research Scholarship; Newton Fund RCUK-CONFAP Grant (Medical Research Council, MRC, and FAPEMIG, MR/M026302/1); Jack Brockhoff Foundation (JBF 4186); C. J. Martin Research Fellowship, National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC, APP1072476); Victorian Government's OIS Program
Population_Description: Missense mutations in gene rpoB with a resistant/susceptible rifampicin phenotype: training set 203 resistant + 28 susceptible mutations (LSHTM in-house database); independent non-redundant blind test set 67 resistant + 21 susceptible mutations (TBDreamDB, tbvar, GMTV) — a mutation-level dataset, not a patient cohort.
Data_Source_Other: Curated genomic mutation databases and literature: LSHTM in-house database (training set); TBDreamDB, tbvar and GMTV (blind test set); literature-curated mutation sets for M. leprae, P. aeruginosa and S. aureus.
Top_Predictive_Features: Ranked by MCC contribution of feature-class subset models on the blind test: change in ligand binding affinity (MCC=0.56, top contributor); physicochemical properties (0.22); graph-based signature (0.19); protein flexibility (0.17); protein-nucleic acid interactions (0.15); protein–protein interactions (0.13); conservation (0.10); intramolecular interaction counts (0.03); presence in RRDR (lowest).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Algorithms compared for the Rif-resistance classifier: Gaussian, Multinomial and Complement Naive Bayes, Stochastic Gradient Descent, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, Extra Trees, AdaBoost and GradientBoosting; individual per-algorithm metric values (other than the selected KNN model) are not reported in the text — KNN was consistently the best classifier at all oversampling levels.
Best_Performing_Model: K-nearest neighbours (KNN), k=3, selected by consistency of Matthew's Correlation Coefficient (MCC) between training and blind test set
Accuracy_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations, non-redundant blind test set, n=88, whole gene
Sensitivity_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations, non-redundant blind test set, n=88, whole gene
Specificity_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations, non-redundant blind test set, n=88, whole gene
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations, non-redundant blind test set, n=88, whole gene
F1_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations, non-redundant blind test set, n=88, whole gene
AUROC_Population_Set: M. tuberculosis rpoB dataset, n=319 (full training + blind test)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation performed on independent M. tuberculosis clinical mutation datasets (Miotto et al. 2017; Schleusener et al. 2017) and cross-species translation datasets (M. leprae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus); tool is deployed as a public web server for direct clinician/researcher use, but no prospective clinical evaluation or EHR/CDS-workflow integration is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Bacterial lineage was not tested as a feature and lineage information was not always available in the curated data, which may explain lineage-specific misclassifications; Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) values were not consistently available; insufficient data across the whole mutation list to model epistatic effects (rpoC, gyrA).
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Discusses that high sensitivity in detecting resistance avoids giving Rif unnecessarily to patients with a resistant strain (avoiding toxicity, delaying effective treatment, and unnecessary healthcare costs) — implying that low sensitivity/missed resistance calls would risk inappropriate Rif treatment and its toxicities.
Sample_Size: 319 M. tuberculosis rpoB missense mutations (203 resistant + 28 susceptible training; 67 resistant + 21 susceptible independent blind test)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Missense mutations within rpoB (and homologous positions in M. leprae/S. aureus/P. aeruginosa) with a documented resistant or susceptible phenotype curated from LSHTM/literature databases; the independent test set was required to be non-redundant with the training set.
Exclusion_Criteria: Mutations already present in the training set were excluded from the non-redundant independent blind test set.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: LSHTM in-house database; TBDreamDB; tbvar; GMTV
Dataset_Size: 319 total M. tuberculosis rpoB mutations (231 training, 88 blind test); plus 42 M. leprae, 18 P. aeruginosa and 51 S. aureus translation-dataset mutations; 298 candidate features, 41 retained in the final model.
Missing_Data_Method: No imputation; authors instead segregated datasets by source (trained on lineage-representative LSHTM mutations, tested on non-redundant literature-identified datasets) to address inconsistent lineage information, and MIC was simply not used as a feature because it was not consistently available.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Not a physical clinical specimen — missense mutations in rpoB derived from clinical M. tuberculosis sequencing information
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant-vs-susceptible phenotype classification for missense mutations in rpoB conferring rifampicin resistance, predicted by the structure-based SUSPECT-RIF classifier.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Mycobacterium leprae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Rifamycins (rifampicin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin (Rif)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible mutation phenotype label (curated from source databases/literature), distinguished statistically as two phenotype classes (resistant n=270 vs susceptible n=49 in the Mtb feature-analysis set); not an MIC-threshold-based definition — the paper notes MIC values were not consistently available.
AI_Purpose: To build a structure-based machine learning classifier (SUSPECT-RIF) that predicts rifampicin resistance from missense mutations in rpoB, including mutations outside the RRDR missed by the current gold-standard molecular test (GeneXpert-MTB/RIF), and to translate this classifier to other clinically relevant organisms.
Feature_Engineering: 298 features calculated across five classes: graph-based signatures, local environment (stability, flexibility, dynamics, intramolecular interactions), interactions (ligand/nucleic-acid/protein-protein affinity via the mCSM suite), pharmacophore changes, and conservation scores; redundant features removed via correlation analysis; greedy feature selection reduced the set to 41 features in the final model.
Feature_Selection_Method: Bottom-up greedy feature selection based on Matthew's Correlation Coefficient (MCC), after manual removal of statistically redundant features via a correlation matrix.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Oversampling of the minority class, testing different oversampling levels (nOS = 0 to nOS = 6) at each stage of training and optimisation.
Hyperparameter_Method: Manual sweep of KNN k values (1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15) combined with oversampling level (nOS 0–6), selecting the combination with the best/most consistent MCC between training and blind test.
Hardware_Details: Web-server hosting infrastructure: Linux server running Apache (for the SUSPECT-RIF web tool); no ML-training compute hardware (CPU/GPU) specifications are given.
Other_Metrics: Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC): training 0.72, blind test 0.71; AUC (Area Under Precision-Recall Curve): training 0.99, blind test 0.89.
Baseline_Method: GeneXpert-MTB/RIF, the current WHO-endorsed molecular test, which solely targets variants within the RRDR.
Baseline_Performance: Based on the assumptions underlying GeneXpert-MTB/RIF, outside the RRDR it captured 0% of resistant mutations and 100% of susceptible mutations (vs SUSPECT-RIF's 89.1% sensitivity / 89.8% specificity outside the RRDR).
Internal_Validation: Non-redundant blind test set (n=88 mutations: 67 resistant + 21 susceptible, from TBDreamDB/tbvar/GMTV), held out from the LSHTM-derived training set.
Train_Test_Split: Training n=231 (203 resistant + 28 susceptible, LSHTM); independent non-redundant blind test n=88 (67 resistant + 21 susceptible, TBDreamDB/tbvar/GMTV).
External_Validation_Description: Cross-species translation datasets from the literature: M. leprae (n=42, including a Brazilian-Amazon reservoir study), S. aureus (n=51), and P. aeruginosa (n=18); plus independent M. tuberculosis clinical mutation sets (Miotto et al. 2017, n=32; Schleusener et al. 2017 curated set, n=539, and n=7 Sanger-sequenced).
Overfitting_Method: Models were selected/ranked by consistency of MCC between the training set and the blind test set, specifically to reduce the risk of overfitting and bias toward the majority (resistant) class.
Clinical_Insights: Identifies that Rif-resistance mechanisms differ by organism (e.g. ligand-affinity loss dominant in S. aureus vs protein-protein/nucleic-acid affinity disruption in Mtb/M. leprae/P. aeruginosa), informing understanding of species-specific resistance mechanisms and the classifier's cross-species translatability.
Generalisability_Details: The Mtb-trained classifier generalises/translates to M. leprae, P. aeruginosa and S. aureus despite low sequence identity (55–95% SI) with Mtb RpoB, per independent validation on each organism's mutation dataset.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation on independent Mtb clinical datasets (Miotto 2017; Schleusener 2017) and cross-species translation (M. leprae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus); no prospective clinical trial or EHR/CDS integration evidence is reported.
Integration_Point: Standalone interactive web server (not integrated into an EHR/LIS or clinical workflow); used directly by a clinician or researcher who inputs a mutation list.
End_User_Described: clinician or researcher
Stewardship_Details: Discussed only as the 'potential significance' of SUSPECT-RIF for Rif stewardship efforts (broad cross-organism applicability); not empirically assessed as a stewardship outcome.
Barriers_List: MIC values not consistently available for mutations used in model development; insufficient data across the whole mutation list to model epistatic interactions (rpoC, gyrA) — both noted as unaddressed factors that may explain misclassifications.
Facilitators_List: Resistance identification via SUSPECT-RIF depends only on the time, cost and availability of genome sequencing techniques and an internet connection; the tool is free, web-based, and usable directly by a clinician or researcher with just a mutation list.
Future_Directions: The robustness of SUSPECT-RIF across species is presented as a basis for developing a universal rifampicin resistance predictor.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Subset-model comparison: models trained on different feature-category subsets, ranked by Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) on the blind test.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Of the many possible graph-based signature features (different interatomic distance patterns), feature selection retained only one — Inter-HP:4.50 (hydrophobic/polar interactions within 4.50 Å of the mutation site) — meaning overall global structural effects are not well represented in the final model.
Limitation_Categories: Missing/incomplete lineage information (risk of lineage-specific misclassification); missing/inconsistent MIC data; insufficient data to model epistasis (rpoC, gyrA interactions).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Lineage information was not always present in curated mutation sources; MIC values were not consistently available across the mutations used in model development.

Sex_Distribution: MDR UTI group: Male 267, Female 500; non-MDR group: Male 149, Female 569
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients admitted March 2012–March 2019 (7 years); isolates from infections occurring 48h or more after admission, meeting the CDC nosocomial infection definition
Exclusion_Criteria: Duplicate isolates discarded (same patient, specimen, ward, species and similar antibiotic pattern within 20 days)
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 1486 clinical samples (767 with MDR UTI, 718 without)
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine samples
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Onset of a multidrug-resistant (MDR) urinary tract infection (patient resistant to one or more antibiotic classes), coded R=1 vs S=0
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary R/S label: R=1 for a patient with a microorganism resistant to one or more antibiotic classes (MDR, per CDC definition), S=0 otherwise
AI_Purpose: To build a Machine Learning model able to predict a hospitalized patient's risk of contracting a multidrug-resistant urinary tract infection, via the DSaaS cloud platform
Feature_Engineering: Categorical variables transformed into dichotomous (dummy, 0/1) variables; data type transformation, filtering and selection; under- and over-sampling for class balance
Feature_Selection_Method: Predictors selected a priori based on prior UTI literature, not by a data-driven feature-selection algorithm
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), under-sampling the majority class and over-sampling the minority class
Hyperparameter_Method: Caret package (v6.0-82) combined with Genetic Algorithm optimisation (GA package v3.2) to automatically tune model parameters
Hardware_Details: Necessary hardware to run the models was provided by Logical System Spa (Jesi, Italy); no CPU/GPU/RAM specification given
Other_Metrics: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and area under the Precision-Recall curve (AUC-PRC), reported alongside accuracy, AUC-ROC, sensitivity, specificity and F1 score
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation with three repeats; 70%/30% train/test split
Train_Test_Split: 70% training / 30% test
Overfitting_Method: 10-fold cross-validation (three repeats); CatBoost's random-forest structure noted as robust to training/test error
Generalisability_Details: Cases were extracted from a small-scale hospital, so the generalizability of the findings may be limited; the authors plan to gather cases from a wider variety of hospitals in future work.
Maturity_Evidence: 10-fold cross-validation with three repeats plus a 70%/30% train/test split on a single-hospital retrospective dataset; no external validation or prospective/clinical deployment evaluation reported
Integration_Point: Proposed future integration into the hospital's computerized physician order entry (CPOE) system to alert physicians of MDR UTI risk
End_User_Described: Physicians treating hospitalized patients
Future_Directions: Enrich DSaaS with unsupervised ML, streaming data analysis, distributed calculation, big data storage/management, a dataflow editor, R scripting, a Stewardship UI, and topological-data-analysis methods; gather cases from a wider variety of hospitals
Limitation_Categories: Unmeasured/unavailable risk factors (diabetes, catheter, sexual-related factors, antibiotic use, renal transplantation); single-institution generalizability
Data_Quality_Concerns: Potential risk factors unavailable from the review of medical records were not considered

Title: Predicting treatment failure risk in a Chinese Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis with surgical therapy: Development and assessment of a new predictive nomogram
Funder_Names: Thirteen-Fifth Mega-Scientific Project on “prevention and treatment of AIDS, viral hepatitis and other infectious diseases” (grant no. 2017ZX10201301-003-002); Natural Science Foundation of Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region (grant no. 2019D01A78)
Population_Description: 132 drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) patients (111 MDR-TB, 21 XDR-TB) recruited retrospectively from two Chinese infectious-disease hospitals; divided into treatment success and treatment failure groups (95 males, 37 females; mean age 40.12±12.79 years, range 18-75 years).
Top_Predictive_Features: Lesion (L, OR 14.211), Recurrent chest infection (RCI, OR 6.633), Treatment history (T, OR 2.947), and MDR or XDR (OR 1.549), ranked by odds ratio from the multivariable logistic regression model after LASSO feature selection.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Multivariable logistic regression nomogram (Lesion, Treatment history, RCI, MDR or XDR) — Harrell's C-index 0.905 (apparent, cohort) / 0.876 (bootstrap-corrected, 1000 resamples); no other model type compared.
Best_Performing_Model: Multivariable logistic regression nomogram incorporating Lesion, Treatment history, RCI, and MDR or XDR; C-index 0.905 (apparent) / 0.876 (bootstrap-corrected) — the only model developed.
AUROC_Value: C-index (Harrell's C, binary-outcome equivalent of AUROC) 0.905 apparent; 0.876 bootstrap-corrected
AUROC_Population_Set: Development cohort, 132 DR-TB surgical patients; bootstrap-corrected (1000 resamples)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal (bootstrap) validation has been performed; the authors state the nomogram still requires external validation before its appropriateness elsewhere is known.
Reported_Limitations: The nomogram has only been internally validated (bootstrapping) in a single retrospective cohort and requires external validation, with further research needed to determine whether it is suitable for predicting surgery risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients.
Unresolved_Items: Whether the nomogram is appropriate for predicting surgery risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients requires further research and external validation.
Sample_Size: 132 patients (111 MDR-TB, 21 XDR-TB), the primary/only analysed dataset
Conflicts_of_Interest: No authors have a conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Sputum continuous positive or repeated positive; presence of a tuberculosis cavity; destruction of lung tissue that can cause sputum-negative tuberculosis recurrence (the most common surgical indications).
Exclusion_Criteria: Anti-TB chemotherapy treatment lasting <2 months; X-ray/CT showing the lesion had changed; mental illness precluding compliance; cerebrovascular, hypertensive, diabetic or other surgical contraindications; or poor compliance.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 132 patients; 10 candidate features reduced to 4 selected features
Specimen_Type_Detail: Sputum (sputum culture / sputum smear status underlying diagnosis and surgical indication)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Treatment failure after surgery in drug-resistant (MDR/XDR) tuberculosis patients, predicted via a nomogram combining Lesion, Treatment history, RCI, and MDR/XDR status; C-index 0.905 (apparent) / 0.876 (bootstrap-corrected).
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (drug-resistant: MDR-TB and XDR-TB)
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-tuberculosis drugs (e.g. rifampicin, isoniazid) and second-line drugs defining MDR-TB/XDR-TB status
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin and/or isoniazid (used to define resistance); unspecified second-line drugs (defining XDR-TB)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR; XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDR-TB = resistant to at least two main first-line drugs; XDR-TB = additionally resistant to two or more second-line drugs; patients were diagnosed as rifampicin- and/or isoniazid-resistant by drug sensitivity testing.
AI_Purpose: To develop and internally validate a treatment-failure risk prediction nomogram (LASSO feature selection + multivariable logistic regression) to help clinicians estimate individualised surgery-related treatment-failure risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients and support surgical decision-making.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (single logistic regression nomogram; no alternative model types compared)
Feature_Engineering: Ten candidate demographic, disease, and treatment features (age, gender, Lesion class, Treatment-history class, Body-condition class, Surgery type, Cavitary status, Hemoptysis, RCI, MDR/XDR) defined from clinical/radiological assessment before LASSO selection.
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression, retaining features with nonzero coefficients
Hyperparameter_Method: Five-fold cross-validation to select the optimal LASSO regularisation parameter (lambda), using the minimum-criteria and 1-SE criteria
Other_Metrics: Harrell's C-index (discrimination), calibration plot, decision curve analysis / net benefit, and odds ratios with 95% CI and P-values for each predictor.
Baseline_Method: Decision curve analysis comparing the nomogram's net benefit against 'intervention-all-patients' and 'intervention-none' strategies.
Internal_Validation: Bootstrapping validation (1000 resamples) to calculate a bootstrap-corrected C-index
CV_Folds: 5 (five-fold cross-validation used to select the LASSO regularisation parameter, lambda)
Overfitting_Method: Bootstrapping validation (1000 resamples) to calculate a bootstrap/optimism-corrected C-index
Clinical_Insights: L1 (stable, localized lesion) scores lowest and L3 (diffuse/bilateral or extrapulmonary disease) scores highest; the L1 patient has better outcomes after surgery than the L3 patient.
Generalisability_Details: The authors state the nomogram requires external validation and that further research is needed to determine whether it is suitable for predicting surgery risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients, i.e. generalisability beyond this single retrospective, two-centre cohort is not yet established.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal bootstrap validation only (1000 resamples), C-index 0.905 apparent / 0.876 corrected; the authors state external validation is still required.
Integration_Point: Used at the point of surgical decision-making, after standardised anti-TB treatment of more than 4 months when sputum remains continuously/repeatedly positive, to predict postoperative treatment-failure risk before surgery.
End_User_Described: Clinicians and patients deciding on surgery for MDR/XDR-TB
Clinical_Workflow_Details: After standardised anti-tuberculosis treatment of more than 4 months, if sputum is continuously or repeatedly positive (with cavity/lung destruction), the nomogram is used to predict postoperative treatment-failure risk and inform the surgery decision.
Future_Directions: External validation of the nomogram and further research on its suitability for predicting surgery risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: LASSO regression (nonzero-coefficient shrinkage, five-fold CV lambda selection) for feature selection; final predictor weights given as multivariable logistic regression odds ratios (β, OR with 95% CI, P-value).
Novel_Predictors_Details: Recurrent chest infection (RCI) — the authors state no prior study had found RCI to affect the surgical outcome of tuberculosis.
Limitation_Categories: Lack of external validation (the nomogram requires external validation before its appropriateness for predicting surgery risk in MDR/XDR-TB patients elsewhere can be confirmed).

Title: A novel risk factor for predicting anti-tuberculosis drug resistance in patients with tuberculosis complicated with type 2 diabetes mellitus
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: National Science & Technology Pillar Program during the 13th Five-year Plan Period (Grant No. 2018ZX10715003); Youth Innovation in Medical Research Subject in Sichuan Province of China (No. Q17020)
Population_Description: 657 TB patients complicated with type 2 diabetes mellitus (TB-T2DM), from four hospitals across three Chinese provinces (Henan, Sichuan, Gansu), diagnosed March 2014-June 2019; 390 in the HbA1c<7% group and 267 in the HbA1c≥7% group.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Model A (HbA1c grading + age, ESR, hemoglobin, CRP): C-index 0.754/AUC 75.4% (training, n=509), C-index 0.739/AUC 73.9% (internal validation, n=148). Model B (same indicators without HbA1c grading): C-index 0.719/AUC 71.9% (training), C-index 0.699/AUC 69.9% (internal validation).
Best_Performing_Model: Model A (HbA1c grading (7%), age, ESR, hemoglobin, CRP) — best by AUC/C-index on the training set (Sichuan and Gansu).
AUROC_Population_Set: Model A, training set (Sichuan and Gansu), n=509
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Model developed on a training set (Sichuan and Gansu, n=509) and evaluated on an internal validation set from a third province (Henan, n=148) drawn from the same retrospective multicentre cohort; no external (independent institution/country) validation or prospective evaluation reported.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective design; inability to assess influence of different hypoglycemic treatments and socio-economic status due to limited records.
Sample_Size: 657 TB-T2DM patients (training set n=509, internal validation set n=148)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors report no conflicts of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Eligible cases must have met the following criteria: (i) diagnosed as both TB and T2DM based on Chinese Diagnostic Criteria for Tuberculosis (NHFPC, 2017) and Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (2018), respectively; (ii) having no other lung diseases, liver disorders or immunodeficiency diseases; (iii) having no history of anti-TB treatment before the research; and (iv) having complete clinical data.
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded if other lung diseases, liver disorders or immunodeficiency diseases; prior anti-TB treatment history; or incomplete clinical data (embedded within the eligibility criteria).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Gene presence / AMR genotype; Imaging
Dataset_Size: n=657 total (390 HbA1c<7%, 267 HbA1c≥7%)
Missing_Data_Method: Indicators with >30% missing excluded; missing data classified as MCAR/MAR/MNAR; multiple imputation used to supplement missing data.
Ethnicity_Details: Nationality/ethnicity Han/others: 321/69 (HbA1c<7% group), 241/26 (HbA1c≥7% group)
Geographic_Representativeness: Four hospitals across three provinces (Henan, Sichuan, Gansu) in central, southwestern and northwestern China selected to represent high TB-burden areas; training data from Sichuan/Gansu, internal validation from Henan.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Anti-tuberculosis drug resistance (rifampicin resistance, isoniazid resistance, and multidrug-resistance/MDR), determined by molecular detection.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Rifamycins (rifampicin); isonicotinic acid hydrazides (isoniazid) — both first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs.
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin; Isoniazid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Rifampicin resistance = any resistance to rifampicin; isoniazid resistance defined analogously; MDR = resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin.
AI_Purpose: A predictive model for MDR, incorporating objective and routine clinical/laboratory indicators, established to guide the clinician to take preventive measures for TB-T2DM patients and reduce the risk of developing MDR.
Feature_Engineering: HbA1c dichotomised into <7% vs ≥7% groups using the ADA-recommended cut-off; this 'HbA1c grading' variable added to the logistic-regression model.
Feature_Selection_Method: Variable selected by logistic regression (specific selection algorithm not detailed).
Num_Features_Selected: 5 (Model A)
Software_Libraries: R version 3.6.1 (nomogram); SPSS version 20.0 (logistic regression); Review Manager Version 5.3 (meta-analysis pooling, not ultimately used); G*Power 3.1.3 (sample-size calculation).
Other_Metrics: C-index, corrected C-index, net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
Baseline_Method: Model B: same indicators (age, ESR, hemoglobin, CRP) but without HbA1c grading.
Baseline_Performance: AUC 71.9% (training set), 69.9% (internal validation set)
Internal_Validation: Geographic split: model trained on pooled Sichuan+Gansu data, evaluated on an internal validation set from Henan.
Train_Test_Split: Training set (Sichuan and Gansu) n=509; internal validation set (Henan) n=148 (see Table 3).
Overfitting_Method: Bootstrapping was used for bias correction (of the nomogram/logistic-regression model).
Clinical_Insights: HbA1c grading (7%) identified as an independent risk factor for isoniazid resistance and MDR in TB-T2DM patients; incorporating it improved the model's predictive capacity and reclassification performance.
Generalisability_Details: Authors caution that direct application of the model to different populations/situations may not be appropriate given overfitting to the studied population, and recommend the model be adjusted to the local population before wider use.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation on a geographically distinct held-out province (Henan) within the same retrospective cohort; discrimination (AUC) and calibration assessed; no external or prospective evaluation.
Integration_Point: Standalone web application (Shinyapps.io risk calculator); not described as integrated into an EHR/LIS or clinical workflow.
End_User_Described: Clinician
Barriers_List: Model overfitting to the specific studied population; direct application to different situations/populations may not be appropriate without local adjustment.
Facilitators_List: A released web application (calculator) of the model, described as facilitating its clinical application.
Future_Directions: Recommend the predictive model be adjusted to the local population for optimal performance before wider application.
Novel_Predictors_Details: HbA1c grading, rarely studied previously as a risk factor for TB drug resistance, identified as an independent risk factor for isoniazid resistance and MDR.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design; incomplete records precluding assessment of hypoglycemic treatment regimens and socio-economic status.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Limited/incomplete records prevented assessment of the influence of different hypoglycemic treatments and socio-economic status.
Page_References: Print pages 69-77 (PDF pages 1-9)

Title: Interpreting k-mer–based signatures for antibiotic resistance prediction

Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study

Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: 7 different antibiotic classes (specific class names not enumerated in the main text; 10 antibiotics listed in Table 1)
Specific_Antibiotics: Amikacin, Aztreonam, Cefepime, Cefoxitin, Ceftazidime, Ciprofloxacin, Imipenem, Meropenem, Piperacillin/tazobactam, Tetracycline
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Reference MICs cast into resistant/susceptible/intermediate per CLSI breakpoints; intermediate and resistant merged into a single non-susceptible (NS) category vs susceptible (S)
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: Predicting the antibiotic resistance profile of a Klebsiella pneumoniae strain from its genome, with an emphasis on producing interpretable genomic signatures
Feature_Engineering: k-merization of training genome contigs via DBGWAS (k=31, minor allele frequency filter <1%) to build a compacted de Bruijn graph and a binary presence/absence pattern matrix
Feature_Selection_Method: Screening step: standard lasso-penalized logistic regression fit across a regularization path to identify an initial set of 'active' features, later extended to correlated feature clusters (cluster-lasso)
Num_Features_Total: 1,234,397 distinct presence/absence patterns (example given for the cefoxitin feature matrix; the number varies by antibiotic)
Num_Features_Selected: 25 (lasso) / 35 (cluster-lasso) selected features for ciprofloxacin (support size varies by antibiotic; see Table 2 for all 10 drugs)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Model selection optimised balanced accuracy (bACC, the average of sensitivity and specificity) rather than raw accuracy
Hyperparameter_Method: 10-fold cross-validation (repeated 3 times) to optimise the regularization parameter; screening/clustering thresholds set from preliminary experiments
Hardware_Details: Single Xeon E5-2690-V3 CPU
Other_Metrics: Balanced accuracy (bACC) and number of unitigs/support size (Table 2, Table 3)
Baseline_Method: Standard lasso-penalized logistic regression (vs the proposed cluster-lasso)
Baseline_Performance: Both strategies show similar performance in terms of both bACC and AUC, confirming that taking into account, or not, the correlation between features has a limited impact on predictive performance
Internal_Validation: 10-fold cross-validation, repeated 3 times, stratified by sequence type and phenotype
Train_Test_Split: Independent test dataset of 634 strains, separate from the training genome panel
External_Validation_Description: Independent test dataset of 634 K. pneumoniae strains (114 from the bioMérieux collection, NCBI BioProject PRJNA449293/PRJNA597427; 520 from the PATRIC database), mostly from the USA, UK, Serbia, Greece and other European countries
Overfitting_Method: Selected the sparsest model achieving balanced accuracy within 1 point of the maximum, to reduce overfitting risk
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Identification of known and potentially novel resistance determinants (e.g. the blaKPC gene, ompK36 mutations) from the k-mer/cluster signatures
Data_Repository: GigaDB (data/code archive); genomesinfo.csv in Supplementary Material
Generalisability_Details: A serious drop between cross-validated and test-set performance was observed (>5 points of bACC for 6/10 drugs; up to ~10-13 points for amikacin, cefoxitin, imipenem, meropenem), attributed to the training panel not capturing the full genomic diversity of K. pneumoniae
Maturity_Evidence: An independent, differently-sourced 634-strain test set was used to evaluate the models (external validation); no prospective clinical evaluation or deployment is reported
End_User_Described: Clinicians and microbiologists (routine diagnostics)
Future_Directions: The method is generic and can be transposed to other bacterial traits/species and other sparse ML algorithms (e.g. xgboost, set cover machines); re-sampling strategies for stable clusters and tree-guided lasso are suggested extensions
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Lasso / cluster-lasso model coefficient magnitude
Novel_Predictors_Details: Known and potentially novel resistance determinants identified from the k-mer/cluster signatures, e.g. the blaKPC gene and ompK36-region variants
Limitation_Categories: Sampling/representativeness limitation (training genome panel over-represented 2 sequence types, ST307 and ST258, at 60% of isolates); measurement/label limitation (AST method differed between training and test sets)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Reference resistance labels were generated with different AST methods in training (Phoenix) vs test (agar dilution, broth microdilution, VITEK 2) sets, a known source of technical variability/noise in AST results

Title: Prediction of Acquired Antimicrobial Resistance for Multiple Bacterial Species Using Neural Networks
Country_Countries: Denmark (institution location only; the underlying isolate collections are multi-national — see _notes)
Funder_Names: European Union's Horizon 2020 (grant agreement no. 643476, COMPARE); The Novo Nordisk Foundation (grant NNF16OC0021856, Global Surveillance of Antimicrobial Resistance)
Population_Description: Whole-genome sequence data and antimicrobial susceptibility profiles from 3,528 Mycobacterium tuberculosis, 1,694 Escherichia coli, 658 Salmonella enterica, and 1,236 Staphylococcus aureus isolates
Data_Source_Other: Public bacterial genomic sequence repositories: the Relational Sequencing TB Data Platform (platform.reseqtb.org) for M. tuberculosis, and the Pathosystems Resource Integration Center (PATRIC) database for E. coli, S. enterica and S. aureus
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest and artificial neural network models (metric: AUC), compared for single- vs multiple-output prediction on M. tuberculosis data (Table 2)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were assessed with held-out test-set and 5-fold cross-validation (internal), and additionally tested on a completely new species (900 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates) never used in training — a genuine external-validation attempt, though generalisation to this untrained species was poor
Reported_Limitations: Study lacked a sufficiently diverse dataset (more species) to reach accurate predictions for metagenomics-scale applications; the species-independent model could not predict the AMR profile of a completely unknown species (K. pneumoniae)
Sample_Size: 3,528 M. tuberculosis, 1,694 E. coli, 658 S. enterica, and 1,236 S. aureus isolates (whole-genome sequence data)
Conflicts_of_Interest: We have no conflicts of interest to declare.
Inclusion_Criteria: M. tuberculosis isolates required resistance profiles for rifampin, isoniazid, streptomycin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide (n=1,785), or complete profiles for those five plus ciprofloxacin (n=92)
Exclusion_Criteria: Streptomycin (S. enterica) and rifampin (S. aureus) profiles excluded due to unknown breakpoints and an insufficient (<5%) number of resistant isolates, respectively
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: PATRIC; Relational Sequencing TB Data Platform (ReSeqTB)
Dataset_Size: 3,528 M. tuberculosis; 1,694 E. coli; 658 S. enterica; 1,236 S. aureus isolates
Missing_Data_Method: Missing output (resistance-profile) values for the random forest model were imputed using predictions from a random forest trained only on isolates with complete profiles; the neural network handled missing outputs natively
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary (resistant/susceptible) antimicrobial resistance profile prediction, per antimicrobial, from whole-genome sequence-derived chromosomal mutations and mobilizable resistance genes
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Escherichia coli; Salmonella enterica; Staphylococcus aureus
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampin, isoniazid, streptomycin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, ciprofloxacin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: AMR profiles represented in binary format (resistance marked 1, susceptibility marked 0) based on the results of phenotypic susceptibility tests interpreted against clinical breakpoints
Infection_Type: Not applicable (in silico / no patient data)
AI_Purpose: To determine the feasibility of including information from multiple bacterial species to predict AMR for an individual species, potentially easing training/updating of resistance predictions across species and improving predictions
Feature_Engineering: A combined binary+scored representation was tested, where each mutation is represented by two features (a score and a binary presence/absence indicator); mobilizable genes represented by template coverage
Num_Features_Total: E. coli: 1,119 (binary), 2,167 (scored), 4,219 (scored+binary), 52,199 (amino acid), 14,483 (nucleotide) features; M. tuberculosis: 6,735 (binary), 11,120 (scored), 21,975 (scored+binary), 261,085 (amino acid), 87,205 (nucleotide) features
Class_Imbalance_Method: Up-sampling: each resistant S. enterica isolate was repeated five times in the (vastly imbalanced) dataset, with repeats kept in the same cross-validation partition
Hyperparameter_Method: Learning rate varied by input data type: 0.01 for binary-type data (binary, amino acid, nucleotide representations) and 0.001 for continuous data (scored and scored+binary representations); tuned on average validation-data performance
Other_Metrics: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), used to compare machine-learning and Point-/ResFinder predictions (Table 5)
Baseline_Method: Point-/ResFinder (literature/database-curated rule-based AMR detection tools)
Baseline_Performance: Point-/ResFinder MCC by species-drug combination (Table 5): e.g. E. coli-ciprofloxacin 0.71/0.70 (validation/test) vs machine learning 0.96/0.94; M. tuberculosis-ethambutol 0.60/0.60 vs 0.18/0.18; overall Point-/ResFinder outperformed the ML models in 6 of 8 species-drug combinations
Internal_Validation: One-sixth of genome clusters held out as an independent test set; remaining clusters used for 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning and model assessment
Train_Test_Split: One-sixth of clusters held out as test data; remaining five-sixths used for 5-fold cross-validation (training/validation)
External_Validation_Description: The multispecies (E. coli, M. tuberculosis, S. enterica, S. aureus) ciprofloxacin-resistance model was tested on a completely new dataset of 900 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates with ciprofloxacin resistance profiles from PATRIC
Overfitting_Method: Training/validation loss plots tracked across 5,000 training epochs; held-out test data (not used for hyperparameter tuning) used to assess overfitting
Clinical_Insights: Some features important to RF/NN predictions were not associated with any Point-/ResFinder resistance determinants, suggesting machine learning may allow discovery of novel chromosomal mutations and mobilizable genes mediating AMR (verifiable experimentally)
Data_Repository: Bitbucket (code); isolate accession numbers listed in supplementary Data Set S1 (linking to PATRIC / Relational Sequencing TB Data Platform records)
Generalisability_Details: The species-independent model was not able to predict the AMR profile of a completely unknown species (K. pneumoniae); authors recommend enriching training data with related (same-genus) species for future generalisation
Maturity_Evidence: Prediction of ciprofloxacin resistance for K. pneumoniae (a genuinely external test species) was close to random, capping the demonstrated maturity at an external-validation attempt rather than successful external validation
Future_Directions: Further studies needed to validate multispecies predictions, including additional antimicrobial agents, isolates and species, to capture global AMR variation, paving the way for applying multitask ML models to metagenomic studies
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Feature importance from the trained random forest and neural network models; top 20 and top 50 features per species reported in supplementary Tables S3 and S4
Novel_Predictors_Details: Some important RF/NN features were not associated with any resistance profile in the Point-/ResFinder databases, implying possible discovery of new chromosomal mutations/mobilizable genes mediating AMR
Limitation_Categories: Data diversity / generalisability limitation (insufficient species diversity for metagenomic-scale prediction; poor generalisation to an untrained species)
Data_Quality_Concerns: Phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) is described (citing prior studies) as unreliable for ethambutol and pyrazinamide in M. tuberculosis, which the authors suggest may have caused incorrectly profiled isolates and biased the Point-/ResFinder prior knowledge

Title: Machine learning reveals that Mycobacterium tuberculosis genotypes and anatomic disease site impacts drug resistance and disease transmission among patients with proven extra-pulmonary tuberculosis
Population_Description: Of 75 consecutive culture-positive extrapulmonary (non-pulmonary) Mtb isolates from unique patients submitted from 8 of 25 DOTS/TB facilities in Tshwane, South Africa, 5 were excluded (M. bovis); 70 isolates from unique EPTB patients (28 female, 40%) were analysed.
Age_Range: 1 to 85 years (text); Table 1 gives median range 1-82 years
Data_Source: Laboratory information system; Hospital / clinic registry
Top_Predictive_Features: Disease site (100% relative variable importance) and DOTS/TB facility (92%) were the top-ranked predictors of genotypic clustering, from stochastic-gradient-boosting/CART variable-importance analysis (Fig. 3c).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
Target_End_User: Laboratory scientist / microbiologist; Programme manager / policymaker; Surveillance analyst / public health
All_Models_Evaluated: CART for any drug resistance (Fig. 4c) and CART for MDR-TB/Rifampin monoresistance (Fig. 4d): sensitivity 0.72 (95% CI 0.56-0.84) for both; positive predictive value 0.44 (95% CI 0.32-0.57) for any resistance and 0.36 (95% CI 0.25-0.48) for MDR-TB/rifampin monoresistance. A separate CART for genotypic clustering (Fig. 3d) reached ROC 0.744 (train) / 0.688 (test), sensitivity 0.56, PPV 0.74, error rate <3%.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: CART trees for any drug resistance (Fig. 4c) and MDR-TB/Rifampin monoresistance (Fig. 4d), n=67 isolates
Specificity_Population_Set: MDR-TB/rifampin-monoresistant prediction using EPTB disease site plus Mtb genotype (Fig. 4d)
Precision_PPV_Value: 0.36 (95% CI: 0.25-0.48) for MDR-TB/Rifampin monoresistance (the latter); 0.44 (95% CI: 0.32-0.57) for any resistance (the former)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: CART trees for any drug resistance (Fig. 4c, 'former') and MDR-TB/Rifampin monoresistance (Fig. 4d, 'latter')
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal five-fold cross-validation is reported; no external dataset or prospective evaluation is described.
Reported_Limitations: Inadequate sample size, imprecise/missing information (e.g. HIV status), reliance on spoligotyping alone for clustering (biases resolution, may overestimate clustering), misclassification of EPTB disease sites, isolates not serialised and no data on drug-therapy timing, incomplete medical history.
Reviewer_Notes: Sensitivity/specificity/PPV for the drug-resistance CART are reported inconsistently across the Results text and the Fig. 4 legend (main text: sensitivity 1.00/specificity 0.64 improving to 0.84 with genotype added; Fig. 4 legend: sensitivity 0.72, PPV 0.44/0.36) — the main-text sentence spans a page break around a figure caption and could not be quoted as one continuous span, so the Fig. 4 legend values were used for Sensitivity/PPV and the main-text passage for Specificity.
Unresolved_Items: Study_Setting (clinic-collected specimens processed at a central reference laboratory) and Pathogen_Classification (Mycobacterium tuberculosis is acid-fast, not conventionally Gram-typed) required judgement calls; see _notes.
Conflicts_of_Interest: All authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: All 75 consecutive culture-positive isolates from unique EPTB patients identified across DOTS/TB facilities in Tshwane during the six-month study period (1 Jul 2014 - 31 Jan 2015) were eligible.
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates that grew nontuberculous mycobacteria or Mycobacterium bovis were excluded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Gene presence / AMR genotype
Dataset_Size: 67 isolates analysed in the MDR-TB/Rifampin-monoresistance CART (Figs. 4c/d), excluding 3 isoniazid-monoresistant isolates from the 70-isolate cohort.
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates were drawn from 8 of 25 DOTS/TB facilities across the Tshwane metropolitan area (Gauteng), a densely populated, multi-ethnic region including migrants from across sub-Saharan Africa.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Pleural, peritoneal, lymphatic, meningeal, genitourinary, cutaneous, disseminated, and unclassified 'other' EPTB anatomic sites
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Rifampin and/or isoniazid drug resistance (mono-resistance or MDR-TB) detected by the Genotype MTBDR plus mutation assay, modelled with machine learning against EPTB disease site and Mtb genotype.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb)
Drug_Classes: Rifampin (rifamycin); Isoniazid
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampin; Isoniazid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Isolates resistant to only rifampin or only isoniazid (by MTBDR plus mutation detection) were categorised mono-resistant; those resistant to both were categorised MDR-TB.
AI_Purpose: To use agnostic machine-learning algorithms (stochastic gradient boosting, CART, random forest, MARS) to find clinically meaningful patterns linking EPTB anatomic disease site and Mtb genotype to drug resistance and to genotypic-clustering-inferred transmission.
Feature_Engineering: Categorical variable levels were grouped by similarity using GINI-based criteria (CART/MARS).
Software_Libraries: TreeNet version 8.3; STATA; GraphPad; BioNumerics ver. 7.5
Other_Metrics: Attributable risk (AR) and number needed to screen (NNS), with 95% CIs (Newcombe/Wilson; Klopper-Pearson exact binomial).
Internal_Validation: Five-fold cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: Train/test (cross-validated) ROC comparison: 0.744 vs 0.688, with training error rate <3%.
Explainability_Methods: Feature importance / permutation importance; Decision rules / surrogate tree; Intrinsically interpretable model
Clinical_Insights: Disease site (sanctuary sites: lymphadenitis, meningitis, cutaneous TB, with poor rifampin penetration) and Mtb genotype were the dominant, clinically actionable predictors; conventional epidemiological factors such as age and sex were far less important (sex scored zero for clustering).
Generalisability_Details: Authors describe Tshwane's large, diverse, multi-ethnic population (including migrants from across sub-Saharan Africa) as an ideal setting to obtain generalisable findings on Mtb transmission dynamics with or without drug resistance.
Maturity_Evidence: Only internal five-fold cross-validation reported (no external validation, no prospective evaluation, no CDS integration) -> Level 2.
End_User_Described: Implied: clinicians/screening staff, since the screening information (disease site) 'can be ascertained by history and clinical examination'.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed workflow: identify high-risk EPTB patients via disease site (+/- genotype) at history/clinical exam, screen with drug susceptibility testing, then adjust treatment regimens to prevent therapy failure and reduce transmission.
Future_Directions: Investment in improved EPTB diagnostics and in ML algorithms trained on large clinical datasets to predict EPTB, to reduce unnecessary treatment and accelerate transmission reduction and WHO TB elimination targets.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Variable importance scores from Random Forest (and stochastic gradient boosting)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Disease site and DOTS/TB facility dominated variable importance for clustering, while conventional epidemiological factors (age, and especially sex, which scored zero) were far less important than expected.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Stochastic gradient boosting / MARS two-way interaction detection (TreeNet)
Limitation_Categories: Sample size / power; missing data (HIV status, treatment history); measurement method bias (spoligotyping only); outcome misclassification (EPTB disease site); lack of serial isolates/therapy-timing data.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Imprecise and missing information (e.g. HIV infection status); incomplete medical history on laboratory request forms limited ability to identify immunosuppressed patients.
Reporting_Clarity: Sensitivity/specificity/PPV figures for the drug-resistance model are given inconsistently in the main text vs. the Fig. 4 legend (see Reviewer_Notes); several sentences are also split by intervening tables/figures in the pypdf text layer.
Page_References: Methods pp.4-5; Results pp.5-8; Discussion pp.8-13

Title: A Decision Tree Using Patient Characteristics to Predict Resistance to Commonly Used Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics in Children With Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infections
Journal_Source: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, 2020;9(2):142-9
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health
Population_Description: All patients admitted to Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh from June 2009 through June 2015 with >=1 blood culture (peripheral or central catheter source) growing gram-negative bacteria; 689 episodes among 387 patients during 638 admissions.
Age_Mean_Median: Median age 2.4 years (IQR 0.9-8 years), overall cohort
Data_Source: Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: In order of discriminatory potential: prior carbapenem treatment for >=7 days, prior culture with CPT resistance within 6 months, intestinal transplantation, >=7 prior episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infections, and age >=3 years (ranked via the Gini splitting index).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Decision tree (recursive partitioning, rpart in R): sensitivity 46%, specificity 91%, AUC 0.70 (after leave-one-out cross-validation); AUC 0.68 before cross-validation.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Decision tree; entire cohort, leave-one-out cross-validation
Specificity_Population_Set: Decision tree; entire cohort, leave-one-out cross-validation
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Decision tree; prevalence-based (31% prevalence of BSA-resistant infection)
AUROC_Population_Set: Decision tree; entire cohort, leave-one-out cross-validation
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internally validated only, via leave-one-out cross-validation on the same single-center retrospective cohort used to develop the tree; no external or prospective validation performed.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective, single-center design without outpatient data (possible misclassification/missing data); possible unrecorded bloodstream infections from outside facilities; additional risk factors may be uncaptured; unable to separately model cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam resistance vs carbapenem resistance owing to small numbers; same dataset used for tree development and validation (only internal LOOCV).
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Decision tree may misclassify close to 50% of high-risk BSA-resistant episodes as low risk (potential undertreatment) and 9% as high risk (potential overtreatment).
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Authors note clinical judgment and deviation from the tree's prediction is necessary given its suboptimal sensitivity, particularly for critically ill or non-improving patients.
Sample_Size: 689 episodes of gram-negative bloodstream infections (387 patients; 638 hospital admissions)
Conflicts_of_Interest: P.D.T. received an investigator-initiated research grant from Merck (unrelated to this work); A.M.M. reports consulting for Becton Dickinson (unrelated); all other authors report no potential conflicts.
Sex_Distribution: 55% male (evenly distributed by sex) overall cohort
Inclusion_Criteria: All patients admitted to Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, June 2009-June 2015, with >=1 blood culture (peripheral or central catheter source) growing gram-negative bacteria.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients not admitted to the hospital, or with insufficient antibiotic susceptibility information; uniformly susceptible respiratory pathogens (e.g. Haemophilus influenzae); pathogens primarily associated with gastroenteritis (e.g. Salmonella, Shigella); organisms intrinsically resistant to cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam (e.g. Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: CHP microbiology database / institutional data warehouse (not a publicly named repository)
Dataset_Size: 689 episodes; 387 patients; 638 hospital admissions
Missing_Data_Method: Manual chart review used to collect missing data for specific variables (prior cultures with resistant organisms, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, country of birth).
Ethnicity_Details: Race reported (not ethnicity per se): predominantly white (77%) overall; Table 2 breaks down White/Black/Asian/Other by resistance status.
Geographic_Representativeness: Single tertiary pediatric hospital serving Western Pennsylvania; described as managing most complex cases in the region.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood culture (peripheral or central catheter source) growing gram-negative bacteria
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Bloodstream infection with a gram-negative organism resistant to broad-spectrum antibiotics (BSAs): nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, or imipenem-cilastatin, or meeting ESBL production criteria.
Pathogens: Klebsiella species, Escherichia species, Enterobacter species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia species, Acinetobacter species, Citrobacter species, Proteus mirabilis, Morganella morganii, Achromobacter species, and other gram-negative organisms (Chryseobacterium meningosepticum/Flavobacterium, Pantoea agglomerans, Aeromonas hydrophila).
Num_Pathogens: 11 organism categories in Table 1 (10 named genera/species plus an 'other' category comprising 3 additional species)
Drug_Classes: Broad-spectrum antibiotics: cefepime (cephalosporin), piperacillin-tazobactam (beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor), meropenem and imipenem-cilastatin (carbapenems).
Specific_Antibiotics: Cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: BSA resistance = culture (1) nonsusceptible to cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, or imipenem-cilastatin, or (2) meeting criteria for ESBL production.
AI_Purpose: To develop a user-friendly clinical decision aid predicting the risk of resistance to commonly prescribed broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics for children with gram-negative bloodstream infections, to inform empiric antibiotic selection.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (the decision tree; a multivariable logistic regression was also fit but only to estimate odds ratios, not evaluated with sensitivity/specificity/AUC)
Feature_Engineering: Most variables represented as continuous scales, with the tree permitted to generate its own cutoff values; number of prior admissions converted to ordinal categories; days of antibiotic exposure in prior 6 months dichotomized at >=7 days.
Feature_Selection_Method: Gini splitting index (recursive partitioning selected the variable that best minimized misclassification at each split)
Software_Libraries: rpart (Recursive Partitioning and Regression Trees) package in R
Other_Metrics: C statistic / area under the ROC curve; positive predictive value; negative predictive value
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation
Train_Test_Split: Not applicable; leave-one-out cross-validation used on the entire cohort instead of a held-out train/test split.
CV_Folds: Leave-one-out cross-validation (n folds = number of episodes)
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Decision rules / surrogate tree
Clinical_Insights: Prior carbapenem treatment, prior CPT-resistant culture, intestinal transplantation, age >=3 years, and >=7 prior gram-negative BSI episodes are associated with increased resistance risk; two hypothetical patient scenarios illustrate high-risk vs low-risk classification and resulting treatment choice.
Generalisability_Details: Findings may not generalize to other infection types or colonization status; the tree was developed at a single, high-transplant-volume center and needs validation in diverse populations before clinical use.
Maturity_Evidence: Evidence supporting maturity level is internal validation only (leave-one-out cross-validation) in a single-center retrospective cohort; authors explicitly state external/broader validation is still needed before clinical use.
Integration_Point: Proposed for use at the time a Gram stain from a positive blood culture reveals a gram-negative organism, before organism ID or susceptibility results are available, to guide empiric antibiotic selection.
End_User_Described: Clinicians deciding on empiric antibiotic therapy for children with gram-negative bloodstream infection
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Illustrated with two hypothetical scenarios: Patient A (recent cefepime-resistant E. coli UTI, treated with piperacillin-tazobactam) is classified high risk and may warrant broader therapy; Patient B (chemotherapy via central catheter, no carbapenem history, 2 prior sensitive GNB-BSI episodes) is classified lower risk and may be treated empirically with cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam.
Stewardship_Details: Paper frames the tool as supporting stewardship by identifying children who could avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, but no empirical stewardship outcome (e.g., days of broad-spectrum therapy) was measured.
Barriers_List: Suboptimal sensitivity (46%) of the tree; limited number of carbapenem-resistant cases preventing a staged CPT/carbapenem prediction approach; larger cohorts needed for more refined models.
Facilitators_List: Variables selected for practical utility so they are available to clinicians via patient interview or brief chart review; decision tree avoids need to compute a composite score at point of care; easy-to-use cutoff values for continuous variables.
Future_Directions: Future analyses should examine additional patient characteristics/variables to improve sensitivity; larger cohorts needed to develop a staged approach distinguishing CPT resistance from carbapenem resistance; studies on longitudinal within-patient evolution of susceptibility over time.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Gini splitting index used to rank/select the 5 clinical risk factors by discriminatory potential
Feature_Interactions_Method: Recursive partitioning (decision tree) inherently accommodates interactions between predictor variables via sequential Gini-based binary splits.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective design (misclassification/missing data risk); no outpatient data; single-center generalizability; possible uncaptured risk factors; inability to separately model CPT vs carbapenem resistance owing to small numbers; same dataset used for tree development and validation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Possible bloodstream infections not captured if patients initially presented and had cultures drawn at an outside facility; missing data required manual chart review.
Reporting_Clarity: Outcome definition (BSA resistance) stated explicitly and a priori, with clear methodological justification.

Specificity_Population_Set: Random Forest, 80 peaks selected, leave-one-out cross-validation, 46 CRKP and 49 CSKP mass spectra

Title: Development and validation of a diagnostic model of antimicrobial resistance by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases in community-acquired urinary tract infections. How to adjust the prediction in variable outcome prevalences? The usefulness of contracting predictors with LASSO regression
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Cross-sectional
Funder_Names: Recursos propios de los autores (authors' own resources)
Population_Description: Adult patients with community-acquired urinary tract infection confirmed by a positive urine culture, attending the emergency services of two medium-complexity hospital institutions in Medellín, Colombia (2012-2016).
Age_Mean_Median: 52 ± 21 years (total, n=303); 64 ± 19 in ESBL-positive; 50 ± 20.9 in ESBL-negative
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Cross-validated (unpenalized) logistic regression model and LASSO-penalized logistic regression model, re-estimated at 11% and 9% outcome prevalence (Table 2, Table 4).
Best_Performing_Model: LASSO-penalized multivariable logistic regression model (final predictors: age, catheter use, antimicrobial cycles, urological pathology); discrimination assessed by AUROC = 0.85.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Internal (cross-)validation, development sample (n=303)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Internal (cross-)validation, development sample (n=303)
Specificity_Population_Set: Internal (cross-)validation, development sample (n=303)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Internal (cross-)validation, development sample (n=303)
AUROC_Population_Set: Internal (cross-)validation, development sample (n=303)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: External validation was performed in two independent samples with lower ESBL prevalence than the development sample (11% and 9%), assessed by Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration and AUROC discrimination above 0.8; no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment was reported.
Reported_Limitations: The model shows serious limitations when used in populations where the proportion of ESBL-producing isolates in urine is below 9%.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: For institutions with an ESBL prevalence below 10% the predictors have a minimal effect and the authors do not recommend using the model there, implying a risk of poor performance if the rule is applied outside its intended prevalence range.
Unresolved_Items: The final model retains 'Patología urológica' (p=0.07, Table 2) even though the stated variable-elimination rule removed non-significant predictors at P>0.05; the paper does not explain the retention.
Conflicts_of_Interest: Los autores declaran ausencia de conflictos de interés.
Inclusion_Criteria: Adult individuals with community-acquired UTI confirmed by positive urine culture, attending emergency services of participating clinics between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2016.
Exclusion_Criteria: Prior carbapenem treatment in the last 15 days, asymptomatic bacteriuria, ED admission by referral from another institution, or more than one concurrent septic process at admission.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 303 patients (development); 220 patients (validation, two external samples combined)
Missing_Data_Method: Multiple imputation (R 3.2, MICE), assuming data missing completely at random, using the same method as the main analysis.
Geographic_Representativeness: Two medium-complexity hospital institutions in the city of Medellín, Colombia; findings are specific to this urban setting and its local ESBL prevalence.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urocultivo (urine culture)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence or absence of an ESBL (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase) producing microorganism in urine culture, determined by the VITEK 2 Compact automated system.
Pathogens: Enterobacteriaceae (not further speciated in this study's own results; background regional surveillance cites Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae as the predominant ESBL-producing species).
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams — third-generation cephalosporins (inactivated by the ESBL resistance mechanism).
Specific_Antibiotics: Carbapenems (mentioned as an exclusion criterion — recent carbapenem treatment); third-generation cephalosporins (via the ESBL mechanism).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary presence/absence of an ESBL-producing microorganism in urine culture, determined phenotypically by the VITEK 2 Compact automated system.
AI_Purpose: To develop and externally validate a diagnostic prediction model, adjustable via LASSO shrinkage, for identifying ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae in community-acquired UTI, to guide early empirical isolation and remain robust to varying outcome prevalence across populations.
Feature_Engineering: Predictor variables were measured over a fixed 3-month look-back window before emergency-department admission; final multivariable coefficients were rounded to derive a simplified clinical scoring rule.
Feature_Selection_Method: Best-subset selection using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), prioritising the most parsimonious model; multivariable logistic regression with elimination of non-significant variables at P>0.05.
Hyperparameter_Method: LASSO penalty (lambda) tuned/adjusted for varying outcome prevalence (Table 4).
Software_Libraries: MICE (Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations), R 3.2
Other_Metrics: NPV 0.88 (95% CI 0.84-0.92); LR+ 13 (95% CI 5.88-30); LR- 0.65 (95% CI 0.53-0.81); null deviance 268; residual deviance 189; AIC 199 (Table 2, internal cross-validation model).
Baseline_Method: Unpenalized (cross-validated) logistic regression model coefficients used as the comparator against LASSO-penalized coefficients (Table 2 / Table 4).
Baseline_Performance: AUROC 0.85, accuracy 0.86, sensitivity 0.36, specificity 0.97 (unpenalized cross-validation model, Table 2).
Internal_Validation: Leave-One-Out: the development sample was split into 10 sub-samples with iterative leave-one-fraction-out analysis, followed by LASSO shrinkage of coefficients.
Train_Test_Split: Development sample: 303 patients; validation samples: 220 patients total (two external sets of 118 and 112).
External_Validation_Description: Two external validation samples drawn from prior years with lower ESBL prevalence: n=118 (11% outcome prevalence) and n=112 (9% outcome prevalence), assessed by Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration and AUROC.
Overfitting_Method: LASSO penalization / shrinkage regression
Clinical_Insights: Absence of catheter use >24h, recent antimicrobial exposure, urological pathology and age under 65 gives a high negative predictive value for ESBL resistance; presence of >=3 of 4 predictors indicates need for empiric antimicrobial therapy plus preventive isolation and microbiological confirmation.
Generalisability_Details: Diagnostic performance decreases, and the model becomes inadequate, when applied to populations with lower (<9%) ESBL prevalence than the development population; prediction error increases substantially when the model is applied to a population different from the one it was built on.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation performed in two independent samples with different ESBL prevalence (11%, 9%); discrimination AUROC above 0.8 and calibration via Hosmer-Lemeshow p>0.05 in both external samples.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: If >=3 of 4 predictors (age >65, urological pathology, >=1 antimicrobial cycle in the past 3 months, or bladder catheter use >24h in the past 3 months) are present, or >=2 antimicrobial cycles plus any other predictor, apply preventive isolation and take a urine culture.
Future_Directions: Future diagnostic prediction models for infectious diseases should specify descriptive population characteristics (e.g. proportions of isolates with a given attribute) to assess similarity to the original population, and should include a penalization method to reduce overfitting and improve external validity.
Limitation_Categories: Overfitting / poor generalisability to populations with a different (lower) outcome prevalence than the development population.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Three outlier values were identified via diagnostic plots; the registration, data-entry and information-source process was reviewed with no errors found, so the outliers were retained in the model.

Title: Predicting the occurrence of multidrug-resistant organism colonization or infection in ICU patients: development and validation of a novel multivariate prediction model
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Xiamen Municipal Bureau of Science and Technology Project (No: 3502Z20199129 and 3502Z20154006) and Fujian Provincial key discipline Project (No: 2018. 145)
Population_Description: Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) admitted to the ICU who underwent at least one microbial culture during their ICU stay, excluding those with MDROs detected before ICU entry or within the first 48 hours in the ICU.
Top_Predictive_Features: Male sex, higher CRP level, and higher Pitt bacteremia score were the independent predictors selected for the final nomogram via multivariable logistic regression with backward stepwise (AIC-based) selection.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Multivariable logistic regression nomogram (sex, CRP, Pitt score): AUC 0.77 (95% CI 0.70-0.84) in the external validation cohort; no alternative model architectures were compared.
Best_Performing_Model: Multivariable logistic regression nomogram incorporating male sex, CRP and Pitt score (the only model developed); AUC 0.77 (95% CI 0.70-0.84) in the external validation cohort.
AUROC_Population_Set: external validation cohort (independent cohort from a second hospital, n=181)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The nomogram was developed on a primary cohort and externally validated in an independent cohort from a second hospital (AUC 0.77, 95% CI 0.70-0.84); no prospective evaluation, CDS integration, or routine clinical use was reported.
Reported_Limitations: Developed retrospectively at a single center using only patients who had a microbial culture, limiting extension to all ICU patients; other valuable predictors may have been omitted; the nomogram predicts occurrence only and does not establish a causal relationship between its predictors and MDRO colonization/infection.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Aged ≥18 years and underwent at least one microbial culture during ICU stay.
Exclusion_Criteria: MDROs detected before the patient entered the ICU or within the first 48 h in the ICU.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 331 patients (primary cohort); 181 patients (validation cohort)
Missing_Data_Method: Monte Carlo multiple imputation methods
Specimen_Type_Detail: cerebrospinal fluid, sputum, urine, faeces, secretions, serous cavity effusion, bile, blood, catheters, etc.
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Occurrence of multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) colonization or infection during the ICU stay.
Pathogens: Gram-negative: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Burkholderia cepacia, Meningitis Elizabeth [sic], Enterobacter cloacae, Citric acid bacteria [sic], Haemophilus influenzae, Proteus mirabilis, Sphingosporin oligosporium [sic]. Gram-positive: Enterococcus faecium, MRSA, Staphylococcus haemolyticus, Staphylococcus capitatus, MSSA, Coagulase negative-Staphylococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MDROs defined as organisms simultaneously resistant to three or more antimicrobial agents.
AI_Purpose: To construct an easy-to-use nomogram predicting the occurrence of MDRO colonization or infection in ICU patients, aiding empirical treatment decisions and screening of high-risk patients.
Feature_Engineering: Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) computed by dividing absolute neutrophil count by absolute lymphocyte count, as a candidate predictor (not retained in the final model).
Feature_Selection_Method: Univariate logistic regression screening (p≤0.2) followed by multivariate logistic regression with backward stepwise selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).
Other_Metrics: Decision curve analysis (net benefit vs. threshold probability); useful threshold-probability range approximately 30-95%.
External_Validation_Description: Independent cohort of 181 patients retrospectively enrolled from Xiamen Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, over a similar period, using the same inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Clinical_Insights: CRP (an established inflammatory marker) and Pitt score (a severity-of-illness score) are discussed as clinically plausible predictors of MDRO colonization/infection, consistent with prior literature on their prognostic use in critically ill patients.
Generalisability_Details: Authors note the nomogram was developed on a single-center retrospective sample restricted to patients with a microbial culture, and that further study is needed before extending it to all ICU patients; it is also stated to apply only to adult ICU patients.
Maturity_Evidence: External validation in an independent cohort from a second hospital, AUC 0.77 (95% CI 0.70-0.84); no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
Facilitators_List: Ease of use; predictor parameters are well defined, easily measured, and routinely available in the early ICU stay.
Future_Directions: Further studies are warranted to explore whether the nomogram can be extended to all ICU patients.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Backward stepwise regression based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), following univariate screening at p≤0.2.
Novel_Predictors_Details: The authors state this is the first study to determine that CRP level has predictive value for MDRO colonization/infection, and the first to assess Pitt score as an indicator of MDRO colonization or infection.
Limitation_Categories: Single-center retrospective design; sample restricted to patients with microbial culture; possible omission of other valuable predictors; no causal relationship established between predictors and outcome.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Data obtained retrospectively at a single center from patients who underwent microbial culture only, which may limit generalisability of the case-report-form-derived variables.

Title: Prediction of aminoglycoside response against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection in burn patients by artificial neural network modeling
