Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Response defined by change in 3 clinical criteria (bacteria count, WBC, CRP): all 3 improved = excellent, 2 = very good, 1 = good, 0 = poor; scored 3/2/1 for ANN training; ANN output x thresholded at 1.5 and 2.5 to classify predicted response.
AI_Purpose: To predict the response of aminoglycoside antibiotic (arbekacin, ABK) treatment against MRSA infection in burn patients, incorporating burn-injury severity, using an artificial neural network compared against logistic regression.
Num_Models_Compared: 2 (artificial neural network; logistic regression)
Feature_Engineering: Peak/trough plasma ABK concentration, elimination constant (ke), clearance (CL), and AUC derived from raw drug-level data via pharmacokinetic equations (Eqs. 1-3).
Feature_Selection_Method: Forward stepwise multiple regression (significance level p < 0.25) to select linear physiologic parameters, then addition of one burn-severity covariate compared via goodness of fit.
Num_Features_Selected: 5 (four linear parameters: peak plasma ABK level, serum creatinine, duration of ABK administration, blood sugar level; plus one burn-severity indicator: burn area after skin graft)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over the number of hidden-layer neurons (2-7 tested, Table 4); six neurons selected based on best fit.
Other_Metrics: Sum of squares (SS) between observed and predicted values, and Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC), used as goodness-of-fit measures; rate of correct prediction (RCP) used for discrimination analysis.
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression
Baseline_Performance: Logistic regression: RCP 72% (in-sample) / 60% (leave-one-out cross-validation).
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)
Overfitting_Method: Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC), an estimator of generalization error, used to guard against overfitting when selecting model complexity; robustness also assessed via leave-one-out cross-validation.
Clinical_Insights: The burn area (excluding skin-graft area) was identified as affecting not only the pharmacokinetic but also the pharmacodynamic response of ABK.
Generalisability_Details: Authors state the 25-patient sample size appears very small to establish an accurate and robust model for practical use in a clinical setting.
Maturity_Evidence: ANN trained and evaluated via leave-one-out cross-validation on a single retrospective cohort (n=25); no external cohort, prospective test, or clinical deployment reported.
Future_Directions: Using the ANN model to identify burn patients likely to have a poor ABK response, to facilitate selection of subsequent treatment choice and design of an appropriate antibiotic regimen.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Forward stepwise multiple regression analysis (parameters selected at significance level p < 0.25).
Novel_Predictors_Details: Blood sugar level selected as a predictor because burn-related catecholamine secretion depletes liver glycogen, raising blood sugar as part of the systemic response to the burn.
Limitation_Categories: Small/limited sample size; limited collection of PK/PD parameters
Data_Quality_Concerns: Limited collection of PK/PD parameters in severe burn patients; MIC values not always available from medical records and imputed with a representative value when missing.

Title: Development and validation of a diagnostic model of antimicrobial resistance by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases in community-acquired urinary tract infections. How to adjust the prediction in variable outcome prevalences? The usefulness of contracting predictors with LASSO regression
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Cross-sectional
Funder_Names: Recursos propios de los autores (authors' own resources — self-funded, no external funder)
Population_Description: Adult patients with community-acquired urinary tract infection (UTI), confirmed by positive urine culture, presenting to emergency services of two medium-complexity hospital institutions in Medellín, Colombia (Jan 2012-Dec 2016).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Infection prevention and control team
All_Models_Evaluated: Cross-validated (unpenalized) logistic regression model: AUROC 0.85, accuracy 0.86 (development sample, n=303); LASSO-penalized versions of the same model recalibrated at 11% and 9% outcome prevalence in external validation samples, AUROC >0.8 in both.
Best_Performing_Model: Cross-validated logistic regression model (4 predictors: age, urinary catheter use, number of antimicrobial cycles, urological pathology), selected by AUROC = 0.85.
Accuracy_Population_Set: Development sample, cross-validated model (n=303)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Development sample, cross-validated model (n=303)
Specificity_Population_Set: Development sample, cross-validated model (n=303)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Development sample, cross-validated model (n=303)
AUROC_Population_Set: Development / internal cross-validation sample (n=303)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The study performed internal (leave-one-out) validation and external validation on two independent historical samples with different ESBL prevalence, but did not conduct prospective evaluation or clinical deployment/CDS integration.
Reported_Limitations: The model shows serious limitations when used in populations where the proportion of ESBL-producing isolates in urine is lower than 9%.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Sex_Distribution: Female 72% (219/303) total development sample; 53% (26/49) among ESBL-positive cases; 75% (193/254) among ESBL-negative cases
Inclusion_Criteria: Adults with community-acquired UTI confirmed by positive urine culture, presenting to the participating clinics' emergency services between 1 Jan 2012 and 31 Dec 2016.
Exclusion_Criteria: Prior carbapenem treatment in the last 15 days; asymptomatic bacteriuria; ED admission by referral from another institution; more than one active septic process at admission.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 303 (development); 118 and 112 (two external validation samples)
Missing_Data_Method: Assumed missing completely at random; handled via multiple imputation (MICE, R version 3.2)
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine (urocultivo / urine culture)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Presence or absence of an ESBL (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase) resistance pattern in urine culture, determined by the VITEK 2 Compact automated susceptibility testing system.
Pathogens: Enterobacteriaceae, including Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (third-generation cephalosporins) — resistance mediated by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL)
Specific_Antibiotics: Carbapenems (prior treatment was an exclusion criterion)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary outcome: presence or absence of an ESBL resistance pattern in urine culture, determined by the VITEK 2 Compact automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing system.
AI_Purpose: To develop and validate a diagnostic prediction model for ESBL resistance in community-acquired UTI, and adjust its performance for populations with variable ESBL prevalence.
Num_Models_Compared: 4 (cross-validated model; LASSO model; LASSO model recalibrated at 11% prevalence; LASSO model recalibrated at 9% prevalence)
Feature_Engineering: Candidate predictors coded as presence/absence within the 3 months preceding emergency-department admission.
Feature_Selection_Method: Best-subset selection using the Bayesian Information Criterion, prioritising the most parsimonious model, followed by multivariable logistic regression with elimination of non-significant variables (p>0.05).
Num_Features_Total: 6 candidate predictors
Num_Features_Selected: 4 (number of antimicrobial cycles, age, urinary catheter use, urological pathology)
Class_Imbalance_Method: LASSO shrinkage regression used to adjust coefficients for lower/variable outcome prevalence across populations.
Hyperparameter_Method: LASSO penalization parameter (lambda) increased with lower outcome prevalence (0 in the cross-validated model, up to 0.074 in the 9%-prevalence LASSO model).
Other_Metrics: Positive/negative likelihood ratios (LR+ 13, LR- 0.65); Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit p-value; AIC; null/residual deviance.
Internal_Validation: Leave-one-out (LOO) resampling across 10 development subsamples, followed by LASSO-shrinkage re-estimation of coefficients.
Train_Test_Split: Not a fixed split — leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation used for internal validation.
External_Validation_Description: Two external validation samples drawn from earlier-year urine-culture data with lower ESBL prevalence: n=118 (11% prevalence) and n=112 (9% prevalence).
Overfitting_Method: LASSO shrinkage/penalized regression used to reduce overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: Presence of >=3 of 4 predictors (age >65, urological pathology, antimicrobial exposure, urinary catheter use) indicates need for preventive isolation and microbiological confirmation; their absence gives a high negative predictive value.
Generalisability_Details: Prediction error increases substantially when the model is applied to a population different from the one in which it was originally developed.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal leave-one-out validation and external validation performed on two independent samples with lower ESBL prevalence; no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians at emergency-department services deciding on empirical antimicrobial therapy and preventive isolation.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Preventive isolation and urine culture recommended for patients with >=3 of 4 predictors (age >65, urological pathology, >=1 antimicrobial cycle in the prior 3 months, or urinary catheter use).
Barriers_List: Model performance/utility degrades substantially, and the 'age' predictor loses relevance, in populations with ESBL prevalence below 9%.
Facilitators_List: Simplicity of the four predictors makes the model practical to apply clinically.
Future_Directions: Recommend specifying descriptive population characteristics (e.g. proportion of resistant isolates) when designing diagnostic models, and always including a penalization method to reduce overfitting and improve external validity.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Not performed — sample size restrictions precluded interaction testing.
Limitation_Categories: Statistical/generalisability limitation: model performance and predictor relevance degrade in populations with ESBL prevalence below 9%.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing data did not exceed 5% for any predictor; assumed missing completely at random and handled via multiple imputation (MICE).
Reporting_Clarity: Abstract states validation was carried out in 220 patients, while the Results section reports two external validation samples of 118 and 112 (total 230) — a minor internal inconsistency in reported sample counts.
Page_References: pp. 683-689 (Table 1 p.686; Table 2 p.687; Tables 3-4 pp.687-688)

Title: Feature selection based multivariate time series forecasting: An application to antibiotic resistance outbreaks prediction
Funder_Names: SITSUS project (Ref: RTI2018-094832-B-I00) funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities (MCIU), the Spanish Agency for Research (AEI) and the European Fund for Regional Development (FEDER); Fundación Séneca del Centro de Coordinación de la Investigación de la Región de Murcia (Project 20988/PI/18)
Population_Description: Hospital-level monthly time series (not individual patients): incidence of Staphylococcus aureus methicillin-sensible (SA) and methicillin-resistant (MRSA) infections, influenza incidence, and total days of therapy of Levofloxacin and Oseltamivir, at Hospital Universitario de Getafe, Spain, January 2009-January 2018.
Top_Predictive_Features: Top 11 attributes ranked by importance for the best model (MOES-GP-RMSE-LL6): Lag_Influenza-4, Levofloxacin, Lag_Levofloxacin-2, Influenza, Lag_SA.meticilin.resistant-5, Lag_SA.meticilin.resistant-4, Lag_SA.meticilin.resistant-6, Lag_SA.meticilin.sensible-1, Lag_Levofloxacin-5, Lag_SA.meticilin.sensible-3, Lag_Oseltamivir-1 (importance = univariate wrapper ranking score).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Infection prevention and control / outbreak detection
All_Models_Evaluated: Regression algorithms compared (RMSE and MAE metrics, Tables 3-4, 6-7): Deep Learning (Dl4jMlpClassifier), Gaussian Processes, k-Nearest Neighbours (IBk), Linear Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine regression (SMOreg); plus autoregressive MARIMA and VAR models. Best: GaussianProcesses on MOES-GP-RMSE-LL6 (RMSE=0.1349/0.1304/0.1325, MAE=0.1003/0.0960/0.0987 for 1/2/3 steps-ahead).
Best_Performing_Model: GaussianProcesses regression on the MOES-GP-RMSE-LL6 reduced database (chosen via the multi-criteria decision process combining RMSE and MAE across 1-3 steps-ahead, RMSE=0.1349/0.1304/0.1325, MAE=0.1003/0.0960/0.0987)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal validation only: 70/30 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation (10 repetitions) with repeated statistical testing, all on a single hospital's 2009-2018 historical dataset; no external dataset, no prospective evaluation, and integration into clinical practice is explicitly future work.
Reported_Limitations: Failure to consider the use of other antibiotics; failure to consider surveillance samples for MRSA; the objective was not clinical validation but demonstration of prediction-capacity improvement; the choice of ad hoc time series.
Sample_Size: 108 monthly time points (observations) per series, single hospital, Jan 2009-Jan 2018
Data_Types_Used: Epidemiological surveillance data; Prescription / dispensing data
Dataset_Size: 16 attributes (LL2), 26 attributes (LL4), 36 attributes (LL6) transformed databases; 34 databases total (3 transformed + 31 reduced)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Forecasting future monthly incidence (1-3, up to 6 steps-ahead) of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) using multivariate time series feature selection and regression.
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-sensible (SA); Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-resistant (MRSA)
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolones (quinolones / levofloxacin)
Specific_Antibiotics: Levofloxacin (antibacterial); Oseltamivir (antiviral - tracked as a covariate, not an antimicrobial-resistance-relevant drug)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MRSA
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Methicillin resistance operationalised as classification into methicillin-sensible (SA) vs methicillin-resistant (MRSA) Staphylococcus aureus; outcome tracked as monthly incidence, i.e. the proportion of inpatients newly affected out of total inpatients.
AI_Purpose: To forecast future MRSA outbreak incidence via feature-selection-based multivariate time series regression, supporting surveillance and prevention.
Num_Models_Compared: 204 forecasting models (6 regression algorithms x 34 databases), plus MARIMA and VAR autoregressive models = 206 total
Feature_Engineering: Database transformation into lagged variables via weka.classifiers.timeseries.core.TSLagMaker, at lag lengths 2, 4 and 6, producing 16/26/36-attribute transformed databases.
Feature_Selection_Method: Wrapper feature selection combining MultiObjectiveEvolutionarySearch (ENORA/NSGA-II) with 6 regression algorithms and 2 performance metrics via WrapperSubsetEval; also filter/wrapper methods CFS, mRMR and RFE.
Num_Features_Total: 16 (LL2), 26 (LL4) or 36 (LL6) attributes depending on lag length
Num_Features_Selected: 11 attributes (best model, MOES-GP-RMSE-LL6)
Software_Libraries: Weka (MultiObjectiveEvolutionarySearch/ENORA/NSGA-II, WrapperSubsetEval, Dl4jMlpClassifier, GaussianProcesses, IBk, LinearRegression, RandomForest, SMOreg); R packages caret (rfe) and marima; mRMRe (mRMR.classic)
Other_Metrics: MAPE (mean absolute percentage error), reported alongside RMSE/MAE for 1-6 steps-ahead predictions (Tables 9-10)
Baseline_Method: GaussianProcesses regression without feature selection, on the full LL6 (6-lag) transformed database
Baseline_Performance: RMSE = (0.1733, 0.1752, 0.1740), MAE = (0.1349, 0.1426, 0.1461) for 1, 2, 3 steps-ahead (no feature selection); feature selection reduced RMSE by 23.17% and MAE by 30.36%
Internal_Validation: 70/30 train-test split; 10-fold cross-validation with 10 repetitions for statistical comparison of databases/algorithms
Train_Test_Split: 70% train / 30% test
Clinical_Insights: Attribute ranking (Table 11) supports an epidemiological reading of the SA/MRSA-influenza-levofloxacin relationship; the paper concludes with a recommendation to reduce levofloxacin (and fluoroquinolone) use, particularly at seasonal peaks.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation via 70/30 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation on a single hospital's historical dataset; no external validation, prospective evaluation or clinical deployment evidence found.
End_User_Described: Epidemiologist experts (clinical epidemiology)
Future_Directions: Incorporate dose information; automate the methodology (automatic selection of relevant time series); develop a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to jointly optimise lag length, attribute selection and regression algorithm at prediction intervals; provide results as probability/confidence intervals to enable integration into clinical practice.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Univariate wrapper feature ranking (Weka ClassifierAttributeEval, leaveOneAttributeOut=false) using the GaussianProcesses regression algorithm and RMSE metric to evaluate each attribute separately.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Multivariate wrapper feature selection (the paper's chosen FS methods, e.g. MultiObjectiveEvolutionarySearch), which evaluates attribute subsets jointly rather than one attribute at a time.
Limitation_Categories: Scope of predictors (other antibiotics and MRSA surveillance samples excluded); non-clinical validation objective; choice of ad hoc time series.

Title: Nomogram to predict multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
Journal_Source: Ann Clin Microbiol Antimicrob (Annals of Clinical Microbiology and Antimicrobials)
Funder_Names: Medical and Health Science and Technology Plan Project of Zhejiang Province (2018KY861); Chinese Medicine Science and Technology project of Jinhua City (2017jzk05); Science and Technology Project of Jinhua City (2020XG-15, 2020-4-013)
Population_Description: 700 confirmed TB patients enrolled in Peru between September 2010 and September 2013 (a secondary analysis of a completed prospective cohort study).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Nomogram (multivariable logistic regression on 5 LASSO-selected predictors): AUC 0.759 (95% CI 0.719-0.799) on the development cohort; internal bootstrap validation (500 resamples) AUC 0.757 (95% CI 0.715-0.793). No alternative model type was compared.
AUROC_Population_Set: Development cohort - full study population (700 TB patients, Peru)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal validation was performed, via bootstrap resampling (500 resamples) on the same development cohort; no external or prospective validation was reported.
Reported_Limitations: Single-country (Peru) cohort limiting generalisability; cannot determine whether MDR-TB was acquired vs. primarily transmitted; some variables (treatment regimens, duration of treatment) unavailable in the original dataset and excluded.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Confirmed TB patients enrolled in Peru, September 2010-September 2013.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: DATADRYAD (Dryad Digital Repository) - data from the original Peru TB cohort study
Dataset_Size: 700 TB patients (213 MDR-TB, 487 DS-TB)
Geographic_Representativeness: Single-country (Peru) cohort; authors note regional variation in MDR-TB prevalence and say applicability to other regions/countries needs further multicentre verification.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Sputum (expectorated), tested by MODS drug susceptibility assay for rifampicin and isoniazid
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), defined as resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin, versus drug-susceptible TB.
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Rifampicin (rifamycin) and isoniazid
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin; isoniazid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label: MDR-TB = resistant to both rifampicin and isoniazid (via MODS DST); DS-TB = susceptible to both.
AI_Purpose: To develop a nomogram (clinical prediction tool) for identifying patients likely to have multidrug-resistant TB, based on demographic and clinical characteristics.
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression
Hyperparameter_Method: Tenfold cross-validation to select the LASSO tuning parameter (lambda), using the 1-SE criterion.
Other_Metrics: Hosmer-Lemeshow calibration test (P=0.452); decision curve analysis (DCA) showing net benefit at 70-90% threshold probability.
Internal_Validation: Bootstrap resampling (500 resamples)
Overfitting_Method: Bootstrap internal validation (500 resamples) used for optimism/overfitting correction
Clinical_Insights: Discussion of clinical/mechanistic plausibility of predictors, e.g. education level linked to economic/poverty status and TB incidence.
Generalisability_Details: Authors note regional differences in MDR-TB prevalence and state that applicability of the nomogram to other regions/countries requires further multicentre verification.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal bootstrap validation only (500 resamples), AUC 0.757 (95% CI 0.715-0.793); no external or prospective validation reported.
Integration_Point: Intended for initial clinical assessment of TB patients, particularly those who are sputum-free/smear-negative and cannot undergo phenotypic DST.
Future_Directions: Further multicentre verification of the nomogram's applicability to other regions/countries is needed.
Limitation_Categories: Regional/generalisability limitation (single-country cohort); cannot determine acquired vs. transmitted resistance; some variables (treatment regimens, duration of treatment) unavailable and excluded.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Some patient variables (treatment regimens, duration of treatment) were not available in the original dataset and were excluded from analysis.

Title: Detecting antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli using benchtop attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and machine learning
AI_Application_Type: AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation; AI Signal Processing
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Australian Research Council (ARC) Linkage project LP160100731
Population_Description: 63 ceftriaxone-resistant and 37 susceptible E. coli strains selected from a collection of clinical bloodstream isolates
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
Delivery_Platform: Instrument / device embedded; Not yet deployed
All_Models_Evaluated: svmPoly ROC 0.813, Sensitivity 0.886, Specificity 0.686; pls ROC 0.775, Sensitivity 0.960, Specificity 0.456; xgbTree ROC 0.730, Sensitivity 0.858, Specificity 0.510; RRFGlobal ROC 0.673, Sensitivity 0.835, Specificity 0.392 (independent test isolates, n=29, optimised pre-processing per model)
Best_Performing_Model: svmPoly (tuned support vector machine, polynomial kernel) — best performer by ROC value
Accuracy_Population_Set: held-back 29 independent test isolates
Sensitivity_Population_Set: held-back 29 independent test isolates
Specificity_Population_Set: held-back 29 independent test isolates
AUROC_Population_Set: held-back 29 independent test isolates
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Held-out internal train/test split evaluation on the same isolate collection; no external dataset or prospective evaluation performed
Reported_Limitations: Overnight microbial culture required as starting point; ATR sampling less sensitive/lacks spatial resolution vs IR microscopy so low-biomass or mixed isolates may not classify; proof-of-concept study with limited isolate numbers, dataset expansion needed to test analytical robustness
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Portable low-cost FTIR method could broaden access to rapid AMR diagnostics in low-resource settings
Sample_Size: 100 E. coli clinical bloodstream isolates (63 ceftriaxone-resistant blaCTX-M ESBL gene variant strains)
Conflicts_of_Interest: There are no conflicts to declare.
Inclusion_Criteria: 63 ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli strains with at least one blaCTX-M gene (WGS-confirmed) and 37 available ceftriaxone-susceptible E. coli strains from the clinical bloodstream isolate collection
Exclusion_Criteria: Susceptible isolates carrying blaCTX-M, blaSHV-2, blaSHV-102, or blaDHA-1 genes were excluded to avoid interference with the desired phenotype
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype; Genomic sequence (WGS); Other
Dataset_Size: 678 training and 278 test spectra (after removing 49 outlier spectra) from 71 training / 29 test isolates
Geographic_Representativeness: Isolates limited to a single Australian clinical bloodstream collection; availability of fully-sequenced susceptible isolates was limited
Specimen_Type_Detail: clinical blood stream isolates
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Ceftriaxone resistance in E. coli mediated by blaCTX-M ESBL gene variants, classified as a binary resistant/susceptible outcome predicted from ATR-FTIR spectra
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (primary study/classification organism); Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus (quality-control strains only, not part of the resistance classification dataset)
Drug_Classes: Third-generation cephalosporins (β-lactams); ESBL-mediated resistance
Specific_Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; ESBL
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible classification for ceftriaxone, with the resistant class defined by presence of a blaCTX-M ESBL gene detected via whole genome sequencing
AI_Purpose: To assess the potential of a simple, clinically compatible sampling procedure on a low-cost benchtop FTIR instrument for antimicrobial resistance typing
Feature_Engineering: Savitzky-Golay smoothing (polynomial order 3, window 5 or 9), first/second-order derivative transformation, normalisation to amide-I/water band maximum (1600-1700 cm-1)
Feature_Selection_Method: Comparison of different spectral wavenumber ranges (e.g. 700-900, 700-1800, 2800-3000 cm-1) extracted as model input
Class_Imbalance_Method: ROC performance metric used to optimise classifiers given 63% positive class imbalance
Hyperparameter_Method: Selected parameter combinations (degree=3, scale=0.01, C=1) for the svmPoly model across varying pre-processing conditions
Internal_Validation: Random train/test split with 10-fold repeated cross-validation during training
Train_Test_Split: 71 isolates training / 29 isolates test
Overfitting_Method: 10-fold repeated cross-validation during model training
Clinical_Insights: Important spectral intervals from RRFGlobal/pls models correlated with prior FTIR studies predicting ESBL resistance; water absorbance was not a discriminating feature
Generalisability_Details: Proof-of-concept study with limited isolate numbers; authors state dataset expansion is essential to properly test analytical robustness before broader generalisation
Maturity_Evidence: Random train/test split evaluation on the study's own isolate collection (internal validation); no external or prospective evaluation reported
Integration_Point: Clinical microbiology laboratory workflow
End_User_Described: Clinical microbiology laboratory
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Isolates cultured overnight on agar, colonies analysed next morning; microbial mass sampled directly onto the ATR crystal of a portable FTIR instrument and spectra acquired without drying
Barriers_List: High cost and technical training requirements of IR microscopy limiting broad implementation in clinical microbiology
Facilitators_List: Rapid analysis (<5 minutes including controls/cleaning); ~10% of the cost of an FTIR microscope
Future_Directions: Future work may evaluate antimicrobial resistance detection directly from biological fluids (blood/urine) rather than cultured colonies
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Variable importance from RRFGlobal (random forest) and pls models (spectral intervals); unavailable for the best-performing svmPoly model due to its polynomial kernel
Limitation_Categories: Technical/methodological limitations of ATR sampling for low-biomass or mixed isolates; sample-size/analytical-robustness limitation of a proof-of-concept study
Data_Quality_Concerns: Isolates with low microbial mass or mixed isolates may not be classifiable by ATR sampling

Title: Patient and Microbial Genomic Factors Associated with Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae Extraintestinal Colonization and Infection
Funder_Names: CDC Cooperative Agreement FOA no. CK16-004-Epicenters for the Prevention of Healthcare Associated Infections; National Institutes of Health R01 AI139240-01 and 1R01 AI148259-01; National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program (DGE 1256260)
Population_Description: Patients with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) extraintestinal colonization or infection; first clinical bloodstream, respiratory, or urinary CRKP isolate per patient (n=355), subset to ST258 isolates (n=331) for most analyses, from 21 long-term acute-care hospitals across the U.S.
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Trial / cohort dataset
Top_Predictive_Features: Patient: gastrostomy tube, central venous catheter, acute kidney injury, severe chronic kidney disease, indwelling devices, length of stay. Genomic: ICEKp10 mobile genetic element (yersiniabactin, colibactin), disruption of O-antigen biosynthetic gene kfoC, and several antibiotic resistance determinants (associated with colonization). Ranked by permutation-importance improvement to model AUROC across 100 train/test splits.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: L2 regularized logistic regression, elastic net, random forest, and support vector machine (radial basis kernel), each on 5 feature sets (patient; uncurated genomic; uncurated grouped genomic; curated genomic; patient+curated genomic). AUROC_Value: 0.62 to 0.68 (combined patient + curated genomic feature set, IQR)
AUROC_Population_Set: Combined patient + curated genomic feature set; median test AUROC IQR across 100 train/test splits
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Internal train/test split validation only (100 random 80/20 splits grouped by facility); no independent external dataset, prospective clinical evaluation, or deployment described.
Reported_Limitations: Potential misclassification of colonization vs infection via surveillance criteria for nonbloodstream isolates; only one clinical culture per patient; no rectal colonization isolates; analysis restricted to ST258 (limits generalizability to other sequence types); coarse clinical variables and no host genetic data; restriction to LTACH patients with nonrandom geographic sampling; ML method does not correct for microbial population structure.
Sample_Size: 331 isolates (ST258 subset used for the majority of analyses, out of 355 total clinical CRKP isolates)
Conflicts_of_Interest: J.H.H. was employed at the University of Pennsylvania during the study and is now an employee of, and holds shares in, the GSK group of companies; all other authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: First clinical bloodstream, respiratory, or urinary CRKP isolate per patient from 21 LTACHs; ST258 sequence-type isolates used for the majority of analyses.
Exclusion_Criteria: Non-clinical (surveillance) CRKP isolates excluded; only the first isolate per patient used.
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); Gene presence / AMR genotype; Clinical / EHR variables
Data_Source_Name: BioProject PRJNA415194 (Sequence Read Archive)
Dataset_Size: 355 clinical CRKP isolates total; 331 ST258 isolates for main analyses. Feature-set sizes: patient n=50; uncurated genomic n=2,447; uncurated grouped genomic n=3,159; curated genomic n=91; patient+curated genomic n=141.
Geographic_Representativeness: 21 LTACHs across the U.S., but with nonrandom geographic sampling (e.g., the disrupted-kfoC sublineage was concentrated in 12 LTACHs in California).
Specimen_Type_Detail: Bloodstream, respiratory, and urinary clinical isolates (extraintestinal CRKP)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Classification of CRKP extraintestinal colonization versus clinical infection (not a resistance-phenotype outcome; all isolates are already carbapenem-resistant by inclusion).
Pathogens: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP), sequence type ST258
Drug_Classes: Carbapenems; beta-lactams more broadly captured via resistance-gene features (e.g. beta-lactamase genes) in the curated genomic feature set
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary label (colonization vs. infection) defined via modified CDC/NHSN surveillance criteria: all bloodstream isolates classed as infection; modified criteria applied to classify respiratory/urinary cultures.
AI_Purpose: To determine the relative importance of patient characteristics versus CRKP genomic background in predicting which colonized patients progress to clinical infection.
Num_Models_Compared: 4 algorithms (L2 logistic regression, elastic net, random forest, SVM-radial) across 5 feature sets
Feature_Engineering: Core genome variants identified using a reference genome; accessory genes identified using Roary; curated genomic features identified using Kleborate; insertion sequences identified using panISa.
Feature_Selection_Method: Kleborate-based curation to genes/mutations linked to CRKP virulence or antibiotic resistance (curated genomic set)
Num_Features_Total: Patient 50; uncurated genomic 2,447; uncurated grouped genomic 3,159; curated genomic 91; patient+curated genomic 141
Num_Features_Selected: 91 (curated genomic features selected via Kleborate)
Hyperparameter_Method: Cross-validation on the training set, maximizing average AUROC across CV folds
Baseline_Method: Random-chance classifier (AUROC = 0.5)
Baseline_Performance: AUROC = 0.5
Internal_Validation: 100 random train/test splits with facility-level grouping (each LTACH's isolates entirely in train or test)
Train_Test_Split: ~80/20 (100 unique random splits)
Overfitting_Method: 100 random train/test splits with facility-level grouping to prevent over-/under-fitting
Clinical_Insights: Disruption of the O-antigen biosynthetic gene kfoC is associated with respiratory colonization/infection, plausibly via altered evasion of innate immunity; subsequent acquisition of the ICEKp10 element (yersiniabactin, colibactin) is associated with increased virulence/infection.
Data_Repository: GitHub (Snitkin-Lab-Umich/ml-crkp-infection-manuscript); Sequence Read Archive / BioProject PRJNA415194
Generalisability_Details: Analysis restricted to ST258 due to its disproportionate presence in the dataset; findings may not generalize to other K. pneumoniae sequence types, though the methods are presented as transferable to other lineages/pathogens.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal validation only, via 100 random 80/20 train/test splits grouped by facility; no external dataset or prospective clinical evaluation performed.

Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation importance: mean difference between test and permuted AUROC across 100 train/test data splits

Page_References: pp. 1 (abstract); pp. 3-6 (results, Figs 1-4); pp. 8-9 (discussion, limitations, methods)

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Other

Population_Description: 20,408 M. tuberculosis clinical isolates with known phenotypic drug-resistance status, curated to benchmark GenTB Predict performance

Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
Target_End_User: Clinician / prescriber; Surveillance analyst / public health
All_Models_Evaluated: GenTB-RF mean sensitivity 77.6% (95% CI 76.6-78.5%); GenTB-WDNN mean sensitivity 75.4% (95% CI 74.5-76.4%); TB-Profiler mean sensitivity 74.4% (95% CI 73.4-75.3%); Mykrobe mean sensitivity 71.9% (95% CI 70.9-72.9%), across the nine drugs shared by all four tools

Specificity_Population_Set: Rifampicin, GenTB-RF, depth-filtered benchmark dataset

AUROC_Population_Set: Rifampicin, GenTB-RF, depth-filtered benchmark dataset

Reported_Limitations: Dependence on sequencing-data quality; short-read sequencing has lower sensitivity for complex structural variants; possible erroneous ground-truth phenotypes; no prediction for newly repurposed drugs (bedaquiline, linezolid) due to limited data; unable to retest discordant isolates; benchmark performance is an average across countries
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Illumina raw sequence read datasets for which laboratory-based phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing data was available from public sources
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates excluded for failing FastQ validation (n=29), failing the M. tuberculosis taxonomy filter (n=1339), or insufficient sequencing depth (<10x across >5% of the resistance genome, n=499)
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: NCBI nucleotide database
Dataset_Size: 20,408 isolates; 19,880 after depth/QC filtering
Geographic_Representativeness: Benchmark performance represents an average across publicly available datasets that pool isolates from different countries
Specimen_Type_Detail: Raw Illumina whole-genome or targeted sequencing data (FASTQ) from M. tuberculosis clinical isolates
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Phenotypic drug resistance (binary resistant/susceptible per drug) predicted genotypically from WGS data for two multivariate models (GenTB-RF, GenTB-WDNN)
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: First-line anti-tuberculosis drugs; second-line injectables; fluoroquinolones
Specific_Antibiotics: Isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), streptomycin (STR), ethambutol (EMB), ethionamide (ETH), kanamycin (KAN), capreomycin (CAP), amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEVO), ofloxacin (OFL), para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible classification via in vitro phenotypic DST using drug-specific critical-concentration breakpoints
AI_Purpose: Open, user-friendly start-to-end web application to predict drug-resistance phenotypes to 13 drugs from M. tuberculosis WGS data
Feature_Engineering: 222 features (SNPs/small indels) plus derived variables (e.g. count of non-synonymous SNPs across resistance-conferring genes) for GenTB-WDNN
Feature_Selection_Method: Iterative backward elimination: variants selected by paring down the model and measuring loss of performance
Num_Features_Total: 992 SNPs/indels (GenTB-RF)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Class weighting (randomForest classwt parameter) tuned to maximise the sum of sensitivity and specificity
Hyperparameter_Method: Selection of randomForest mtry via smallest out-of-bag error
Hardware_Details: Harvard Medical School O2 high-performance computing environment
Baseline_Method: TB-Profiler v2.8.12 and Mykrobe v0.9.0, run with default parameters, as comparator tools
Baseline_Performance: TB-Profiler mean sensitivity 74.4% (95% CI 73.4-75.3%); Mykrobe mean sensitivity 71.9% (95% CI 70.9-72.9%), across nine shared drugs
Internal_Validation: 75%/25% train/validation split (pyrazinamide GenTB-RFv2.0 retraining)
Train_Test_Split: 75% (15,267 isolates) train / 25% (5,098 isolates) validate
External_Validation_Description: Retrained pyrazinamide GenTB-RFv2.0 benchmarked on an independent validation dataset of 5,098 isolates (25% holdout)
Clinical_Insights: Analysis of discordant predictions showed many phenotypic 'false positives' for rifampicin resistance carried canonical rpoB RRDR resistance mutations, suggesting some phenotypes may have been erroneously labelled susceptible
Data_Repository: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI); European Nucleotide Archive; GitHub (farhat-lab/gentb-site, farhat-lab/gentb-snakemake)

Feature_Interactions_Method: GenTB-WDNN multilayer perceptron modelling epistatic / gene-gene interaction effects on resistance
Limitation_Categories: Sequencing data quality/depth dependency; short-read limitations for complex structural variants; potential erroneous ground-truth phenotypes; limited data for newly repurposed drugs; geographic averaging across countries

Title: AMR-Diag: Neural network based genotype-to-phenotype prediction of resistance towards beta-lactams in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study
Funder_Names: Research Council of Norway; Indian Council of Medical Research
Population_Description: 171 bacterial isolates from human urine, blood, sputum, pus, ascitic, and cystic fluid samples, from Norway and India (90 E. coli, 76 K. pneumoniae)
Top_Predictive_Features: Beta-lactamase-associated k-mers (BLAKs) selected by NCA feature weight; predominantly from NDM, CTX-M, LAT, BIL, CMY gene families (E. coli) and TEM, OXA, SHV, CTX-M gene families (K. pneumoniae)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: 12 AMR-Diag feed-forward neural networks (one per species-antibiotic combination) evaluated for accuracy, precision and recall on WT/NWT prediction; also compared against previously published models (VAMPr/Kim et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2018) and an ensemble network
Best_Performing_Model: No single model is named best; apart from the E. coli-ampicillin network (excluded from further analysis), overall accuracy of the WT/NWT networks ranged 94-100%, with precision/recall for NWT of 100/100 in most cases (e.g. E. coli-CTX network) versus 80/80 for the excluded ampicillin network
Accuracy_Population_Set: AMR-Diag WT/NWT prediction networks, E. coli and K. pneumoniae, test subset (excluding the E. coli-ampicillin network)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: E. coli - CTX (cefotaxime) network, NWT class, test subset (Table 3)
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: E. coli - CTX (cefotaxime) network, NWT class, test subset (Table 3)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Networks were internally split (train/validation/test) and additionally cross-tested against independent, previously published external datasets (VAMPr/Kim et al.; Nguyen et al.) and external isolate collections; not evaluated prospectively in a clinical workflow or integrated into CDS
Reported_Limitations: ONT/MinION error rates may be too high for reliable prediction without error correction; single point mutations in some beta-lactamases (e.g. SHV, OXA) can completely change phenotype, so low-coverage/high-error data risks interpretation mistakes
Sample_Size: 171 bacterial isolates (90 E. coli, 76 K. pneumoniae)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships
Exclusion_Criteria: Isolates later found to be misidentified (not true E. coli / K. pneumoniae) were excluded: 2 Enterobacter spp. and 3 K. quasipneumoniae isolates (n=5 total)
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: AMR-Diag dataset (newly generated by the authors; not a pre-existing named public repository)
Dataset_Size: 171 isolates total (166 after exclusions): 90 E. coli, 76 K. pneumoniae
Geographic_Representativeness: Two countries with contrasting AMR epidemiology (Norway low-resistance, India higher-resistance) deliberately included to give a spectrum of sensitive/resistant strains and test cross-country generalizability
Specimen_Type_Detail: human urine, blood, sputum, pus, ascitic, and cystic fluid samples
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Susceptibility/resistance phenotype (wild-type/non-wild-type and susceptible/resistant) to ampicillin, 3rd generation cephalosporins and carbapenems, predicted from genomic k-mer data
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: beta-lactams (penicillins, 3rd generation cephalosporins, carbapenems)
Specific_Antibiotics: Ampicillin, ceftazidime, cefotaxime, meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Wild-type (WT) vs non-wild-type (NWT) per EUCAST epidemiological cut-off values (ECOFF)
AI_Purpose: Rapid genotype-to-phenotype prediction of antibiotic susceptibility from WGS data to speed up AST turnaround relative to traditional culture-based methods
Feature_Engineering: Genomic reads transformed into 21-bp k-mers and mapped to a curated database of unique beta-lactamase-associated k-mers (BLAKs) built from CARD and ResFinder gene entries
Feature_Selection_Method: Neighborhood Component Analysis (NCA)
Num_Features_Total: 294,636 unique BLAKs (21-bp k-mers)
Num_Features_Selected: 6 to 416 featured BLAKs, depending on species-antibiotic combination
Hyperparameter_Method: Stepwise expansion of hidden-layer neuron count (12*n increments) and NCA regularization parameter k (20 linearly spaced values, 0-0.5) via 5-fold cross-validation, selecting the network with the best prediction rate
Hardware_Details: Personal laptop, Core i7 CPU, 16 GB RAM
Baseline_Method: Previously published ML algorithms: VAMPr (Kim et al. 2020, E. coli) and an in silico MIC prediction model (Nguyen et al. 2018, K. pneumoniae)
Baseline_Performance: All models, including AMR-Diag and the comparator algorithms, showed lower accuracy on unseen/external data than on their own respective datasets
Internal_Validation: 80% train / 10% validation / 10% test split
External_Validation_Description: Cross-performance testing against previously published models/datasets: VAMPr (Kim et al. 2020) and Nguyen et al. (2018), plus additional isolates from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database
Clinical_Insights: Misclassified isolates were associated with PBP3 mutations (D350N, S357N), ompA/ompK37 porin loss, and efflux pumps - resistance mechanisms not captured by the BLAKs-based genotype model
Data_Repository: GitHub: rafiahmad-lab/AMR-Diag (code/model repository); genomic and phenotypic data available from corresponding author on request
Generalisability_Details: Genotypes are often geographically clustered, so a model trained on one country's data might not generalize to another; addressed here by using isolates from two countries with contrasting AMR profiles
Maturity_Evidence: Internal train/validation/test split plus cross-dataset testing against independently published models and datasets (VAMPr, Nguyen et al.)
End_User_Described: Doctors/clinicians who prescribe antibiotics
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Technical pipeline: k-mer counting (~3 min/file) then AMR-Diag feature extraction and prediction (~3 min/file, prediction itself a few seconds) - under 10 minutes total from sequencing data to phenotype prediction
Barriers_List: Lack of plasticity/self-updating as CARD/ResFinder databases are updated; high error rates of low-coverage/nanopore data risking interpretation mistakes; single point mutations can flip phenotype for some beta-lactamases
Facilitators_List: Ensemble of models trained on diverse datasets/resistance mechanisms improves cross-dataset accuracy
Future_Directions: Exploring self-retraining systems capable of adding new features as ARG databases (CARD/ResFinder) are updated
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Neighborhood Component Analysis (NCA) feature weight
Novel_Predictors_Details: PBP3 mutations, ompA/ompK37 porin loss and efflux pumps identified as resistance mechanisms in misclassified isolates, not represented among the BLAKs (beta-lactamase-gene) features used by the model
Limitation_Categories: Sequencing/coverage error risk; single point mutations altering phenotype; database plasticity/update lag; scarcity of diverse phenotypically-characterized genomic data; different MIC methods across sites
Data_Quality_Concerns: Low genome coverage combined with high sequencing error rate (e.g. from nanopore data) presents a high risk of interpretation mistakes, especially where single point mutations can flip phenotype
Reporting_Clarity: Detailed Methods with extensive Supplementary Tables/Figures (e.g. Tables A-T, Figs 1-7) supporting reported findings

Geographic_Representativeness: Single-centre dataset from one hospital in Madrid, Spain; no broader geographic representativeness assessed
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary target: whether a patient develops a multi-drug-resistant (MDR) infection during the first 48 hours of ICU admission (label 0 = non-MDR, 1 = MDR episode)
Pathogens: Not specified by species — generic multi-drug-resistant bacteria ('MDR germ')
Num_Pathogens: Not specified (species not identified; generic MDR bacteria)
Drug_Classes: 21 antibiotic families used as predictor variables (antibiotics administered in the first 48 h): Aminoglycosides, Amphenicols, Antifungals, Carbapenems, Cephalosporins (1st-4th generation), Glycopeptides, Lincosamides, Macrolides, Monobactams, Nitroimidazoles, Oxazolidinones, Broad-spectrum penicillins, Penicillins, Polymyxins, Quinolones, Sulfonamides, Tetracyclines, Others
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: MDR

Feature_Engineering: One-Hot-Encoding of categorical features, producing 95 binary features from the 12 original input variables

Internal_Validation: 50 repeated random 80/20 train/test partitions; hyperparameters tuned via 5-fold CV maximising AUC-Score
Train_Test_Split: 80/20% (training/test)
Overfitting_Method: Ridge (L2) regularisation in the Logistic Regression cost function, aimed at better generalisation capability

Feature_Selection_Method: an Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) prior (Neal, 2012) over
Class_Imbalance_Method: we correct it in each training fold by oversampling the minority class

Title: Identifying Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis in Chest Radiographs: Evaluation of CNN Architectures and Training Strategies

Country_Countries: Not individually named — TB Portals dataset (the primary/test dataset) drawn from hospitals in 16 countries
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study

Randomly-initialised: 6-layer CNN AUC 0.74(±.04); 10-layer CNN AUC 0.70(±.03); 12-layer CNN AUC 0.65(±.04); InceptionV3 AUC 0.76(±.03); Xception AUC 0.76(±.03). Best pretrained InceptionV3 later reached AUC 0.85 with static augmentation + additional data.
Best_Performing_Model: InceptionV3 (pretrained), AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) up to 0.85 with static augmentation and additional training data from other sources
AUROC_Value: 85% (0.85), best pretrained InceptionV3 with static augmentation + additional data
AUROC_Population_Set: TB Portals dataset (test set only); other-source images used for training only
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal 10-fold cross-validation on a single dataset (TB Portals) was performed; no external dataset, prospective cohort, or clinical deployment evidence is presented.
Reported_Limitations: The labelled DR-TB/DS-TB dataset available (TB Portals) is much smaller than what the pretrained multi-class architectures were designed for.
Sample_Size: TB Portals dataset (primary/test dataset): 1821 DR-TB + 878 DS-TB images, one image per patient
Conflicts_of_Interest: No conflict-of-interest statement is included in the paper (only a funding acknowledgment is present).
Inclusion_Criteria: Frontal (non-lateral), grayscale, pulmonary chest X-ray images from a patient's first clinical visit; one image used per patient even when multiple were acquired.
Exclusion_Criteria: Non-pulmonary images, lateral-view images, and non-grayscale images were discarded; only first-visit images were used, excluding images from later visits.
Data_Types_Used: Imaging; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: TB Portals (primary/test dataset); Montgomery County and Shenzhen chest X-ray sets and TBX11K used for additional DS-TB training images
Dataset_Size: TB Portals: 1821 DR-TB + 878 DS-TB; Montgomery County: 58 DS-TB; Shenzhen: 336 DS-TB; TBX11K: 549 DS-TB; Synthetic (GAN): 1000 DR-TB + 1000 DS-TB; Total: 2821 DR-TB + 2821 DS-TB images
Geographic_Representativeness: TB Portals dataset spans hospitals in 16 (unnamed) countries; other datasets contribute only assumed-DS-TB training images from unspecified locations.

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Other
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary DR-TB vs DS-TB label defined by drug susceptibility testing (DST) results in the TB Portals dataset; images from datasets without DST results are assumed DS-TB.
AI_Purpose: To evaluate CNN architectures and training strategies (transfer learning, data augmentation, GAN-based synthetic data) for automatically distinguishing DR-TB from DS-TB using chest X-rays.
Num_Models_Compared: 13 model configurations (8 pretrained architectures + 5 randomly-initialised/custom CNN configurations), per Table II
Feature_Engineering: CXRs cropped to the lung region via a deep-learning (U-Net) segmentation model, Gaussian-smoothed (std 0.5), resampled to 256x256, and normalised to zero mean / unit standard deviation before use.
Class_Imbalance_Method: Addition of TB images from other public sources (labelled DS-TB) and synthetic GAN-generated images to balance the DR-TB/DS-TB class distribution (final balanced total 2821/2821).

Title: Large-scale mass spectrometry data combined with demographics analysis rapidly predicts methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Laboratory Specimen Interpretation
Study_Design: Algorithm development study; Algorithm validation study; Retrospective cohort
Funder_Names: Warshel Institute for Computational Biology (The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen); Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (CMRPG3F1721, CMRPG3F1722, CMRPD3I0011)
Population_Description: Patients infected with Staphylococcus aureus at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital: a discovery population from the Linkou branch (23,099 participants, 2013-2019, 11,994 MRSA / 11,105 MSSA by cefoxitin disc diffusion) and a replication population from the Kaohsiung branch (4,962 patients, 2015-2017, 2,370 MRSA / 2,592 MSSA).
Age_Mean_Median: Discovery: 55.0 (SD 25.1) MRSA vs 54.6 (SD 22.7) MSSA; Replication: 55.1 (SD 23.8) MRSA vs 55.5 (SD 21.2) MSSA (years)
Data_Source: Hospital / clinic registry; Laboratory information system
Top_Predictive_Features: Twenty pseudo-ion mass-spectral peaks significantly different between MRSA and MSSA, ranked by Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted Q-value and log2 fold-change (e.g. pseudo-ion 230, m/z 6581-6600).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Diagnosis / species identification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: 27 L1-regularized (Lasso) logistic regression models across a grid of the penalty parameter lambda (0.13 to 0), compared by mean 5-fold cross-validation AUC; best model (lambda=0, 217 covariates) reached AUC 0.89 (discovery) and 0.85 (replication).
Best_Performing_Model: L1-regularized (Lasso) multivariable logistic regression with 217 covariates (penalty cost beta=0), selected by highest mean 5-fold cross-validation AUC.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Discovery population (Linkou cohort), optimal probability cutoff 0.5
Specificity_Population_Set: Discovery population (Linkou cohort), optimal probability cutoff 0.5
AUROC_Population_Set: Discovery population (Linkou cohort)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The discovery-trained model was locked-in and applied unchanged to an independent replication cohort (different hospital branch, different time period), i.e. external validation, achieving AUC 0.85; no prospective evaluation or clinical/CDS deployment is reported.
Reported_Limitations: The workflow cannot yet be used as a routine tool across different regions; interlaboratory SOPs and analysis pipelines vary across platforms; accuracy does not yet meet clinical standards; limited to predicting resistance to a single antibiotic; outstanding biomarker peaks require further protein-level characterization.
Sample_Size: 23,099 patients (discovery, Linkou cohort); 4,962 patients (replication, Kaohsiung cohort)
Sex_Distribution: Discovery: Male 7423 (61.9%) MRSA vs 6550 (59.0%) MSSA, Female 4571 (38.1%) MRSA vs 4555 (41.0%) MSSA; Replication: Male 1367 (57.7%) MRSA vs 1508 (58.2%) MSSA, Female 1003 (42.3%) MRSA vs 1084 (41.8%) MSSA
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients with S. aureus infection at CGMH who underwent antibiotic susceptibility testing and were categorized as MRSA or MSSA, with age and sex recorded for each participant.
Exclusion_Criteria: Unqualified mass spectra with fewer than 100 or more than 200 peaks were removed from analysis; participants with missing covariates were also excluded.
Data_Types_Used: MALDI-TOF mass spectra; Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 26,852 pre-QC / 23,099 post-QC patients (discovery, Linkou); 5,224 pre-QC / 4,962 post-QC patients (replication, Kaohsiung); 900 pseudo-ion mass-spectral features per sample
Missing_Data_Method: Complete-case exclusion — participants with missing covariates or unqualified mass spectra were excluded (3753 in discovery; 262 in replication)
Geographic_Representativeness: Two branches (Linkou, Kaohsiung) of one Taiwanese hospital foundation (Chang Gung Memorial Hospital); not described as nationally representative.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Wound (W), respiratory tract (RT), blood (B), sterile body fluid (SBF), urinary tract (UT), and others (O)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary classification of methicillin resistance (MRSA) versus methicillin susceptibility (MSSA) in S. aureus, determined by oxacillin susceptibility testing (cefoxitin disk diffusion for nonsterile specimens; broth microdilution for sterile specimens).
Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Beta-lactams (penicillins) — methicillin/oxacillin
Specific_Antibiotics: Methicillin; oxacillin (cefoxitin disk surrogate testing)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible classification by oxacillin disk diffusion (cefoxitin, nonsterile specimens, CLSI guideline) or broth microdilution (sterile specimens).
AI_Purpose: To combine longitudinal MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry spectra with patient demographics in a machine-learning (logistic regression) model to rapidly predict methicillin resistance (MRSA vs MSSA) in S. aureus infection.
Feature_Engineering: MALDI-TOF spectra binned into 900 pseudo-ions (20 Da bins across m/z 2000-20000) with per-sample intensity normalisation, combined with age, sex and specimen-type covariates.
Feature_Selection_Method: Lasso (L1-regularised) variable selection via glmnet, choosing the penalty with the highest mean 5-fold cross-validation AUC
Num_Features_Total: 900 pseudo-ions plus demographic/specimen covariates (age, sex, specimen type)
Num_Features_Selected: 217 (209 pseudo-ions, 5 specimen-type factors, 2 age factors, 1 sex factor)
Hyperparameter_Method: Grid search over the L1 penalty parameter beta (0.13 to 0), selecting the value with the highest mean 5-fold cross-validation AUC
Other_Metrics: Odds ratios (95% CI) for demographic/specimen covariates; Spearman correlation coefficients between pseudo-ion pairs; log2 fold-change and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted Q-values for differential pseudo-ion testing
Baseline_Method: Noninformative (chance-level) reference of AUC = 0.50
Baseline_Performance: AUC 0.50 (noninformative reference)
Internal_Validation: 5-fold cross-validation on the discovery (Linkou) population for hyperparameter/model selection
Train_Test_Split: Discovery population (Linkou, n=23,099) for training; replication population (Kaohsiung, n=4,962) as an independent held-out test set
External_Validation_Description: Independent replication population from the Kaohsiung branch of Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (n=4,962, 2015-2017), a different branch/time window than the discovery cohort; the locked-in discovery model was applied unchanged and reached AUC 0.85 (95% CI 0.841-0.861).
Clinical_Insights: Risk of methicillin resistance increased with respiratory-tract specimens and decreased for adult/older age groups; females had lower odds of resistance than males.
Generalisability_Details: The workflow cannot yet be used as a routine tool across different regions; robustness shown only in the independent replicate (Kaohsiung) population, while strain types, interlaboratory SOPs and analysis pipelines vary across platforms.
Maturity_Evidence: The discovery-trained (locked-in) model was applied unchanged to an independent replication cohort from a different branch/time period and maintained performance (AUC 0.85), consistent with external validation; no prospective or deployed-CDS evidence is reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians / laboratory microbiologists
Barriers_List: Cross-region and interlaboratory variability in strain types, SOPs and analysis pipelines across MALDI-TOF platforms; accuracy not yet meeting clinical standards; scope limited to a single antibiotic (methicillin).
Facilitators_List: MALDI-TOF MS is readily accessible, less expensive and easy for clinicians to operate; large-scale longitudinal data gave sufficient statistical power; independent replication confirmed robustness.
Future_Directions: Complement the approach with information on resistance to multiple antibiotics; develop more sophisticated models; further analyse outstanding biomarker peaks to identify the specific proteins involved; build robust models for local and global resistance-gene spread.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Ranking by Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted Q-value and log2 fold-change (univariate significance testing between MRSA/MSSA groups); odds ratios from the multivariable logistic regression for demographic/specimen covariates
Novel_Predictors_Details: Of the 20 significant pseudo-ions, only 5 matched peaks previously linked to MRSA/MSSA discrimination in the literature; the remaining 'outstanding biomarker peaks' were not previously characterised and the authors note they require further analysis to identify the specific proteins involved.
Limitation_Categories: Generalisability/regional transferability; cross-platform and interlaboratory variability; accuracy not yet meeting clinical standard; single-antibiotic scope; need for further biomarker/protein characterisation.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Peak-shift artefacts across mass spectra (addressed by pseudo-ion binning/normalisation); participants with missing covariates or unqualified spectra required exclusion (3753 in discovery; 262 in replication).

F1_Population_Set: Classification via regression, original (unbalanced) ICU dataset, 10-fold cross-validation, weighted average

Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug

Clinical_Insights: E.g. the association between erythromycin and oxacillin resistance weakened from 2008 (average cLift = 6) to 2015 (average cLift = 1.7), possibly reflecting clonal shifts or antimicrobial stewardship responses.
Data_Repository: Zenodo — code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3887072; data (available upon request): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3887031
Maturity_Evidence: No external or prospective validation reported; sensitivity/specificity of the technique are explicitly stated as unknown and requiring future simulation studies.
End_User_Described: Clinicians, pharmacists, antimicrobial stewardship programs
Future_Directions: Explore impact of associations on coselection and clinical antimicrobial use via clinical studies; refine association-set mining with hypothesis testing/power analysis; expand the method to Gram-negative organisms; develop interactive applications for clinicians to query/visualize a machine-learning antibiogram.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Association set mining (Apriori algorithm) with support, cross-support ratio and lift to quantify multi-way (two-plus antimicrobial) interactions among resistance traits.
Limitation_Categories: Statistical/methodological: false-negative risk from eCSR/cLift filters; unknown sensitivity/specificity of the technique; need for further hypothesis-testing and false-discovery-rate methodology; missing/inconsistent AST data across years.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Missing or inconsistent AST data is described as a common issue in this historical clinical data set, arising from changes in AST panels over the 2008-2018 study period.

Dataset_Size: 487 (model-building); 157 (prospective testing)

End_User_Described: Health staff at primary care level
