Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The paper's own held-out evaluation is a temporal (calendar-time) train/test split which the authors explicitly frame as a form of external validation; there is no prospective evaluation or clinical/CDS deployment, so the highest level the evidence supports is external validation, not the deployment level the discussion aspires to.
Reported_Limitations: Dataset lacks community-related information (community/neighbourhood/household antibiotic consumption); models are not necessarily immediately generalisable to other settings or the same setting in different time periods; under-representation of younger patients in the data.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Continuous probability outputs from antibiotic-prescription decision-support systems have been suggested to promote over-prescription of antibiotics.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Data has under-representation of younger patients, which may affect model behaviour when predicting resistance in young patients.
Ethical_Governance_Risks: Risk that continuous/probabilistic resistance outputs from a prescribing decision-support system could promote antibiotic over-prescription if output form is not designed carefully.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Hospitalized patients with positive bacterial cultures tested for ciprofloxacin susceptibility at Meir Medical Center, 2016-2019.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables
Data_Source_Name: Meir Medical Center (institutional EMR; not a named public dataset)
Dataset_Size: 10,053 susceptibility test results of 5,540 patients and 73 variables
Geographic_Representativeness: Single hospital serving ~600,000 residents in Israel; authors note ciprofloxacin resistance rates and patient covariates are comparable with other developed countries but retraining would likely be needed for other settings.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine, wound, and blood cultures (positive bacterial cultures)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary prediction of ciprofloxacin resistance (resistant vs susceptible) of a bacterial culture from a hospitalized patient.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Morganella morganii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus mirabilis, Staphylococcus aureus
Drug_Classes: Fluoroquinolone
Specific_Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible label; cultures with an intermediate susceptibility result were recoded as resistant.
AI_Purpose: To predict the probability of ciprofloxacin resistance of a bacterial culture from a hospitalized patient, to support empiric antibiotic treatment decisions.
Num_Models_Compared: 5 (four base learners plus one ensemble/super learner)
Feature_Engineering: Additional features related to previous infections with resistant bacteria, previous antibiotic usage, and previous hospitalizations were engineered from the patients' EMRs.
Num_Features_Total: 73 variables
Hyperparameter_Method: 200 random searches with five-fold, time-series cross-validation
Software_Libraries: Numpy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, XGBoost, TensorFlow, Matplotlib, SHAP
Other_Metrics: Standardized net benefit (decision curve / utility analysis), used alongside ROC-AUC and calibration.
Baseline_Method: Two naive decision-curve comparator strategies (assume all infections resistant; assume all infections susceptible); Discussion also benchmarks ROC-AUC against prior published ciprofloxacin-resistance prediction models.
Baseline_Performance: Feretzakis et al. (single internal-medicine department, Gram-stain conditioned) reached ROC-AUC 0.726; Yelin et al. (outpatients, urine only, 3 species) reached ROC-AUC 0.83.
Internal_Validation: Five-fold time-series cross-validation, used for hyperparameter tuning (200 random search iterations) rather than for final performance reporting.
Train_Test_Split: 75% training / 25% test split, based on calendar time (not random)
External_Validation_Description: Not an independent external dataset: a same-hospital test set drawn from a later calendar period than the training set, which the authors describe as 'a form of external validation'.
Clinical_Insights: SHAP-identified influential variables (previous resistance to ciprofloxacin/other antibiotics, patient origin, local resistance frequencies) are consistent with known clinical risk factors and antibiogram-based practice.
Generalisability_Details: Models are not necessarily immediately generalisable to other settings, or even the same setting in different time periods, because of variation in patients' demographics, antibiotic consumption, and the dynamic nature of AMR over space and time; site-specific retraining would likely be needed.
Maturity_Evidence: Held-out evaluation used a calendar-time (temporal) train/test split which the authors explicitly describe as a form of external validation; no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment is reported.
End_User_Described: Clinician
Barriers_List: Continuous probability outputs from an antibiotic-prescribing decision-support system have been suggested to promote over-prescription of antibiotics; output form needs careful design.
Facilitators_List: SHAP-based explainability validates model outputs against prior clinical knowledge of resistance risk factors, which can facilitate clinician trust in ML decision-support systems.
Future_Directions: Extend models with community-level antibiotic-consumption covariates; retrain on site-specific data for other settings; leverage growing EMR data to further improve AMR prediction and reduce antibiotic misuse.
Predictor_Categories_Count: 6 (demographics, functional status, previous antibiotics usage, previous hospitalization, bacterial pathogen, susceptibility results)
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Mean absolute SHAP value (Kernel SHAP, model-agnostic approximation)
Novel_Predictors_Details: Incorporating variables representing recent and local resistance patterns within the hospital, in addition to a specific patient's own EMR, is highlighted by the authors as an innovative predictor beyond prior ciprofloxacin-resistance models.
Limitation_Categories: Missing community-level predictors (community/neighbourhood/household antibiotic consumption); limited generalisability to other settings or time periods; under-representation of younger patients.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Dataset lacks community-related patient information such as antibiotic consumption in the community, neighbourhoods, and households; data has under-representation of younger patients.

Title: A modified decision tree approach to improve the prediction and mutation discovery for drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Funder_Names: Newton Institutional Links Grant (British Council); Medical Research Council UK; BBSRC
Population_Description: 32,689 (32k) M. tuberculosis whole-genome-sequenced isolates with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) data, covering lineages 1-4, including pan-susceptible, RR-TB, MDR-TB and XDR-TB phenotypes
Provider_Facing_Applications: Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra)
All_Models_Evaluated: TB-Profiler (existing curated mutation library); Treesist-TB default (multi-study); Regular Decision Tree; Single optimized Tree (Treesist-TB on a single combined study) -- compared by Sensitivity, Specificity, Accuracy and AUC for INH, RIF, EMB, PAS, CYS, ETH
Best_Performing_Model: Treesist-TB (default, multi-study decision tree)
Accuracy_Population_Set: RIF, n = 2045 isolates with complete DST (Treesist-TB default model)
Sensitivity_Population_Set: RIF, n = 2045 isolates with complete DST (Treesist-TB default model)
Specificity_Population_Set: RIF, n = 2045 isolates with complete DST (Treesist-TB default model)
AUROC_Population_Set: RIF, n = 2045 isolates with complete DST (Treesist-TB default model)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Validation used a held-out subset (~31k of 32k isolates) drawn from the same aggregated multi-study dataset, not an independent external cohort; no prospective or clinical deployment evidence is reported
Reported_Limitations: Standard machine learning approaches can overfit in subtle ways even after cross-validation, inflating performance estimates that do not translate to out-of-training-set performance; a full simulation study across ML approaches was beyond scope
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Machine learning implementations for M. tuberculosis genotypic profiling can produce over-optimistic predictive abilities and models containing mutations that are not biologically plausible or unrelated to the resistance of interest
Sample_Size: 32,689 M. tuberculosis isolates (whole genome sequencing + phenotypic DST)
Conflicts_of_Interest: There are no competing interests. WD was employed by the company Dalberg Advisors in Switzerland. The remaining authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Isolates with DST for PAS, CYS and ETH were included in the second-line analysis; DST is not available for every isolate across all drugs, as only individuals resistant to first-line treatments are typically tested for second-line resistance
Exclusion_Criteria: Excluded SNPs in hypervariable PE/PPE gene families and synonymous mutations; variants with low minor allele frequency (<1%) affected most (98.9%) of the called variants
Data_Types_Used: Genomic sequence (WGS); AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 32,689 isolates (32k)
Specimen_Type_Detail: M. tuberculosis samples/isolates (whole genome sequencing)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant/susceptible phenotype (per drug), predicted from WGS-derived genomic variants and benchmarked against phenotypic DST as the gold standard
Pathogens: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Drug_Classes: Rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH) and ethambutol (EMB) -- first-line; ethionamide (ETH), cycloserine (CYS) and para-aminosalisylic acid (PAS) -- second-line
Specific_Antibiotics: Rifampicin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), ethambutol (EMB), ethionamide (ETH), cycloserine (CYS), para-aminosalisylic acid (PAS)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR; XDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Predictive performance measured against phenotypic DST results taken as the gold standard, i.e. a binary resistant/susceptible label per drug
AI_Purpose: To predict M. tuberculosis drug resistance phenotype from whole genome sequencing data and discover new resistance-associated genomic variants, especially for poorly understood second-line drugs (CYS, PAS, ETH)
Feature_Engineering: Genomic variants (SNPs, indels) extracted per individual sub-study and combined using a consensus rule requiring a variant's gene to be detected in more than one sub-dataset
Feature_Selection_Method: Consensus rule: a gene's variants are included only if the gene is detected more than once across sub-datasets
Num_Features_Selected: 20 (RIF); 20 (INH); 10 (EMB) -- Treesist-TB identified variants, first-line drugs
Hyperparameter_Method: 5-fold cross-validation used to set the regular decision tree's depth (maximum of 15)
Baseline_Method: TB-Profiler software and mutation library (>1000 SNPs, indels or large deletions)
Baseline_Performance: RIF accuracy: 97.6% (TB-Profiler) vs. 97.5% (Treesist-TB)
Internal_Validation: Held-out residual isolates (~31k of the 32k dataset) used to check mutation frequencies across susceptible, MDR-TB and XDR-TB groups
Train_Test_Split: A subset with complete INH/RIF/EMB (or PAS/CYS/ETH) DST used for Treesist-TB benchmark analysis; residual ~31k of 32k isolates used for validation
Overfitting_Method: Customized decision tree (Treesist-TB) extracting variants across individual sub-studies, applied instead of a single optimized tree because single optimized trees include unlikely features that can arise from overfitting on DST errors/artefacts
Explainability_Methods: Intrinsically interpretable model; Decision rules / surrogate tree
Clinical_Insights: Biological plausibility of putatively causal genomic variants was assessed using Mycobrowser
Generalisability_Details: AMR models must be reliable in prediction, generalise across clinical settings and adapt to increasing data and knowledge; models must also account for pathogen idiosyncrasies, e.g. M. tuberculosis is highly clonal with no horizontal gene transfer, unlike other pathogens with plasmid-derived AMR
Maturity_Evidence: Validation performed on a held-out subset of isolates from the same aggregate dataset; no external cohort, prospective trial or clinical deployment is described
Future_Directions: Through providing software for its implementation, the utility of Treesist-TB beyond TB can be evaluated and the approach potentially refined for other AMR settings; integrated WGS/DST studies for newer anti-TB drugs (bedaquiline, clofazimine, delamanid) are needed given current low sample sizes
Novel_Predictors_Details: New/previously unreported resistance-associated variants identified for ETH (52 total; 45 absent from TB-Profiler), CYS (6 total; 4 absent) and PAS (11 total; 6 absent)
Feature_Interactions_Method: Decision tree structures maintaining double mutations and gene-gene interactions
Limitation_Categories: Overfitting risk from DST errors/mislabelling; small sample sizes for less-studied second-line and newer anti-TB drugs; possible inclusion of biologically implausible or cross-resistance markers
Data_Quality_Concerns: Most genomic variants (98.9%) have low minor allele frequencies (<1%); SNPs in hypervariable PE/PPE gene families and synonymous mutations were excluded

Title: Using machine learning techniques to predict antimicrobial resistance in stone disease patients
Population_Description: 239 patients with urolithiasis hospitalized in the urology department of a tertiary hospital (Sismanogleio General Hospital, Athens, Greece) over a 1-year period (2019), with variables collected: age, gender, Gram stain, bacterial species, sample type, antibiotics, and antimicrobial susceptibility
Data_Source: Laboratory information system; Electronic health record (EHR)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Resistance prediction (phenotype from genotype or spectra); Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Multinomial logistic regression with ridge estimator on the Gram-stain-only balanced dataset: weighted-average ROC area 0.768, F-measure 0.708. Bagging classifier on the bacterial-species balanced dataset: weighted-average ROC area 0.874, F-measure 0.783.
Best_Performing_Model: Bagging classifier (balanced dataset containing bacterial species)
Accuracy_Population_Set: Specific microorganisms (bacterial-species) balanced dataset
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Balanced dataset containing bacterial species (tenfold cross-validation), bagging classifier
Precision_PPV_Population_Set: Balanced dataset containing bacterial species (tenfold cross-validation), bagging classifier
F1_Population_Set: Balanced dataset containing bacterial species (tenfold cross-validation), bagging classifier
AUROC_Population_Set: Balanced dataset containing bacterial species (tenfold cross-validation), bagging classifier
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Only internal tenfold cross-validation was performed on a single retrospective dataset from one hospital; no external validation or prospective evaluation was reported.
Reported_Limitations: Sample size adequate for traditional statistics but small for big-data standards; retrospective design precluded investigation of all confounders (e.g. stone composition, other organisms identified at culture); single-institution data limiting generalisability.
Unresolved_Items: The paper reports two parallel model/dataset versions (Gram-stain-only vs. bacterial-species) without naming either as the 'primary' dataset; this extraction treats the higher-performing bacterial-species / bagging-classifier results as the review's unit of analysis for the *_Value fields, and records the Gram-stain results in All_Models_Evaluated.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients who did not suffer from urolithiasis or those not presenting with a positive urine culture, were excluded from analysis.
Data_Types_Used: AST phenotypic results; Demographic variables; Clinical / EHR variables
Specimen_Type_Detail: blood, urine, pus
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Prediction, from clinical/microbiological variables, of whether a positive culture in a urolithiasis patient will be resistant or sensitive to antimicrobials, to support faster empiric antibiotic selection.
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Klebsiella aerogenes, Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus
Specific_Antibiotics: amikacin, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, ampicillin/sulbactam, cefepime, cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, colistin, gentamicin, imipenem, levofloxacin, meropenem, tetracycline, tigecycline, tobramycin, trimethotrim/sulfamethoxazole, norfloxacin, aztreonam, cefoxitin, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, ertapenem, nitrofurantoin, piperacillin/tazobactam, ceftolozane/tazobactam, fosfomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, rifampin, teicoplanin, vancomycin, ceftazidime/avibactam, doripenem, ceftaroline, mupirocin, oxacillin, penicillin, pristinamycin, quinupristin/dalfopristin
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary class attribute: antimicrobial susceptibility coded as resistant or sensitive
AI_Purpose: To evaluate whether supervised ML can predict AMR patterns in stone-disease patients with positive cultures, to support clinical decision-making and faster administration of appropriate antibiotics.
Class_Imbalance_Method: WEKA's ClassBalancer technique (reweighted samples so each class had equal total weight during training)
Other_Metrics: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) 0.530 and PRC/AUC-PR area 0.886 for the bagging classifier on the bacterial-species dataset (TP rate 0.776, FP rate 0.209)
Internal_Validation: Tenfold cross-validation
Overfitting_Method: Tenfold cross-validation (k-fold CV, k=10)
Generalisability_Details: Model trained on data from a single local microbiology department, so generalisability of the results may be limited; future studies in different populations are needed.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal tenfold cross-validation only, on retrospective single-institution data from 2019; no external or prospective validation reported.
End_User_Described: Urologists prescribing empiric antibiotics
Clinical_Workflow_Details: Proposed use in the emergency-room setting: a physician inputs baseline patient information (age, gender, urolithiasis history, Gram stain or microorganism type) to obtain a resistance/susceptibility prediction and select the proper empiric antibiotic, at 77% (Gram-stain) to 87% (species) accuracy.
Facilitators_List: Relies solely on readily available clinical/microbiological data (age, gender, history, Gram stain or microorganism type); practical even in the emergency-room setting.
Future_Directions: Future studies in different populations are necessary to further validate the results.
Limitation_Categories: Sample size (small for big-data ML though adequate for traditional statistics); retrospective design (unassessed confounders); single-institution data (limited generalisability).
Data_Quality_Concerns: Sample size adequate for traditional statistical analysis but could be considered small in terms of big data; retrospective design did not allow investigation of all possible confounders such as stone composition or microorganisms identified during stone culture.

Title: Estimating the impact of health systems factors on antimicrobial resistance in priority pathogens
Country_Countries: Vietnam, Indonesia, India, Norway, Serbia, Japan, El Salvador
Population_Description: 633,820 AMR isolates spanning 2004-2017 from 70 middle- and high-income countries; majority of samples from adult (19-64y) and elderly (65-84y) age groups, with most samples collected 2009-2017.
Age_Range: 0 to 2 years; 3 to 12 years; 13 to 18 years; 19 to 64 years; 65 to 84 years; 85 and over (age-group categories reported in Table 1, not a single mean/range)
Data_Source_Other: ATLAS (Antimicrobial Testing Leadership and Surveillance) global AMR surveillance dataset, obtained via the Wellcome Trust AMR Surveillance Prize
Top_Predictive_Features: For meropenem susceptibility prediction (RF model), E. coli (pathogen species) and access to immunisation and obstetric care (of a country) were identified as the most important features via permutation-based feature importance.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: Random forest (RF) was the best-performing model; AUROC 0.94 (ceftaroline) and 0.89 (oxacillin) for S. aureus (from abstract); SVM, logistic regression, and Naive Bayes were also constructed for comparison but RF was reported as best overall (Supplementary Fig. S2).
Best_Performing_Model: Random forest (RF)
AUROC_Value: 0.94 (ceftaroline) and 0.89 (oxacillin) for S. aureus resistance (RF model; SE = 0.01 and 0.002 respectively)
AUROC_Population_Set: Staphylococcus aureus (best-performing model/dataset)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were evaluated only on an internal 80/20 train-test split; no external validation dataset or prospective clinical evaluation was reported.
Reported_Limitations: The ATLAS dataset has substantially fewer paediatric samples than adult/geriatric samples, so results cannot be generalised to the paediatric population.
Unresolved_Items: The doc_id/filename gives year 2021, but the article's own masthead and dates (received 8 March 2022; available online 6 May 2022; volume 30 (2022)) show 2022 -- confirm the intended citation year.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors have declared no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Isolates of WHO-declared critical/high-priority pathogens (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter baumannii, Enterobacter cloacae, Staphylococcus aureus) from the AMR surveillance dataset.
Exclusion_Criteria: Variables (covariates) with more than 10% missing data were discarded.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Data_Source_Name: ATLAS (Antimicrobial Testing Leadership and Surveillance)
Dataset_Size: 633,820 isolates
Missing_Data_Method: Missing phenotype/susceptibility labelled 'Not_Given'/'Not_Tested'; residual missingness imputed using a random-forest-based approach (MissForest).
Geographic_Representativeness: Covers only middle- and high-income countries (70 countries); no low-income countries included in the analysed sample.
Specimen_Type_Detail: 116 body tissue/specimen source categories (not individually named)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Multiple Antibiotic Resistance (MAR) score / non-uniform spread pattern of AMR across countries (a secondary outcome is individual-level antibiotic resistance prediction, captured under AUROC).
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter baumannii, Enterobacter cloacae, Staphylococcus aureus
Specific_Antibiotics: Cefepime; piperacillin; amikacin (additional antibiotics analysed elsewhere in the paper include ceftaroline, oxacillin, ceftriaxone, meropenem, ceftazidime, amoxicillin-clavulanate and minocycline; not all captured by this single quote)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: MAR index of a single isolate defined as a/b, where a is the number of antibiotics to which the isolate is resistant and b is the number of antibiotics tested.
AI_Purpose: To learn health-system, governance, financial, and disease-burden determinants of AMR via Bayesian causal networks and counterfactual analysis, and to predict individual-level antibiotic susceptibility using supervised machine learning.
Feature_Engineering: Continuous variables discretized into three intervals (low/medium/high) using a KNN-based algorithm.
Feature_Selection_Method: Markov blanket variable selection (from the Bayesian network)
Num_Features_Total: 334 GBD covariates (source covariate pool; not the total merged model feature count, which is not stated)
Class_Imbalance_Method: Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE)
Software_Libraries: scikit-learn (Python); wiseR, bnlearn and the Counterfactual R package were also used for the Bayesian-network/counterfactual component (see _notes)
Internal_Validation: 80/20 train-test split (single split, not k-fold)
Train_Test_Split: 80% training / 20% testing
Overfitting_Method: Two-level Bayesian network approach (principal-component-level network, then Markov-blanket variable selection) used to avoid overfitting.
Clinical_Insights: Governance quality and access to immunisation/obstetric care identified as actionable, interpretable determinants of AMR reduction.
Data_Repository: Synapse (ID syn17009517); World Bank DataBank (Worldwide Governance Indicators); IHME/GHDx (Global Burden of Disease); World Bank (Global Financial Development Database)
Generalisability_Details: Results not generalisable to the paediatric population because of its underrepresentation in the ATLAS dataset relative to adult/geriatric groups.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal train/test split evaluation (80/20) of RF/SVM/LR/NB models; no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation reported.
Integration_Point: Standalone analytics/policy web dashboard (not integrated into a clinical care workflow)
End_User_Described: Policymakers/government (implied primary audience for governance-oriented AMR determinants and the stewardship web application)
Stewardship_Details: An interactive AMR stewardship web application was created for examining global AMR patterns, but its impact on stewardship practice was not evaluated.
Facilitators_List: Access to immunisation and obstetric care; government effectiveness/governance quality
Future_Directions: Extension of this work to paediatric patients from New Delhi and other regions in India.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Permutation-based feature importance method
Novel_Predictors_Details: Access to immunisation and obstetric care identified as a surprising/important predictor of meropenem susceptibility, alongside E. coli species.
Limitation_Categories: Data representativeness (paediatric underrepresentation limiting generalisability)
Data_Quality_Concerns: ATLAS dataset has substantially fewer paediatric samples than adult/geriatric samples.

Title: Estimating the impact of antibiotic exposure on antibiotic resistance in uncomplicated UTI using machine learning causal inference
Population_Description: Outpatients with uncomplicated UTI in the Mass General Brigham health system, 2016-2021.
All_Models_Evaluated: Logistic regression, random forest, multilayer perceptron and XGBoost, compared within a TMLE causal-inference framework; no per-model numeric metric is given in the abstract beyond the statement that XGBoost significantly outperformed the others.
Best_Performing_Model: XGBoost, stated to have significantly outperformed the other model types (no numeric metric given).
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: No external validation, prospective evaluation, or deployment is described; this is a single retrospective EHR cohort from one health system with a comparison of candidate ML models, consistent with an early proof-of-concept application rather than a validated or deployed tool.
Reported_Limitations: No section is explicitly labelled 'Limitations'. The closest passage is the Conclusion's forward-looking statement that future work will need to add hospital exposures and immunosuppression to the models and extend inference to a wider range of treatments, implying these were not covered here.
Conflicts_of_Interest: Sanjat Kanjilal: GlaxoSmithKline (Advisor/Consultant), Roche Diagnostics (Honoraria). David Sontag: Adobe, ASAPP, Cureai Health, Facebook, Google, IBM, SAP, Takeda (grant/research support, advisory, or equity relationships, as listed).
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients treated with NIT, FQs or oral beta-lactams, with no baseline AMR or antibiotic exposure in the previous 12 months.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients with baseline AMR or antibiotic exposure in the previous 12 months were excluded from the final cohort.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables
Dataset_Size: 4,573 patients (2016-2021 cohort)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Risk of antimicrobial resistance to nitrofurantoin, fluoroquinolones, or amoxicillin-clavulanate at 12 months following antibiotic exposure.
Drug_Classes: Nitrofurantoin, fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin-clavulanate, oral beta-lactams
Specific_Antibiotics: Nitrofurantoin (NIT), fluoroquinolones (FQs), amoxicillin-clavulanate (AMC)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Risk (average treatment effect) of resistance to NIT, FQs, or amoxicillin-clavulanate, measured at 12 months post-exposure.
AI_Purpose: To use machine learning (logistic regression, random forest, multilayer perceptron, XGBoost) within a targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) framework to mitigate confounding by indication and model the outcome when estimating the causal effect of antibiotic choice on subsequent resistance.
Feature_Engineering: Time-windowed (temporally varying) features built from demographics, comorbidities and prior microbiology to serve as confounders.
Other_Metrics: Average treatment effect (ATE), e.g. 0.05 (0.04-0.07) for NIT resistance and 0.06 (0.05, 0.08) for FQ resistance.
Baseline_Method: Logistic regression (compared against random forest, multilayer perceptron and XGBoost)
Maturity_Evidence: Single retrospective EHR cohort (2016-2021) from one health system, with model comparison only and no external validation or prospective evaluation described.
Future_Directions: Future work will incorporate hospital exposures and immunosuppression into the models and infer impact using a wider range of treatments.
Limitation_Categories: Scope: single health system; limited to NIT/FQ/oral-beta-lactam exposures; hospital exposures and immunosuppression not yet incorporated (per the Conclusion's future-work statement).

Title: Analysis of Nucleotide Sequences Similarity and Protein Prediction of Some Resistance Genes in Escherichia coli Isolated from Iraqi Patients with Urinary Tract Infections
Journal_Source: Archives of Razi Institute, Vol. 77, No. 3 (2022)
Population_Description: Approximately 100 samples randomly collected from patients with urinary tract infections (UTIs) admitted to various hospitals between January and March 2021; E. coli identified by biochemical tests and confirmed via the 16s rRNA gene.
Data_Source_Other: Primary clinical bacterial isolates collected directly from hospital patients (not a registry, EHR or other existing dataset)
Task_Type_Other: DNA sequence alignment / SNP-mutation analysis and protein tertiary-structure homology modelling; not a trained ML classification/regression task
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Exploratory sequence and protein-structure analysis on a single set of isolates with no model validation, external testing, or clinical deployment described.
Unresolved_Items: Whether this document genuinely describes an AI/ML application, as opposed to standard Sanger sequencing and homology-based bioinformatics tools (BioEdit, RaptorX, PyMOL), is unresolved; AI-framing fields were coded conservatively and low-confidence, following the abstract's own characterisation.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients with urinary tract infections (UTIs) admitted to various hospitals, January-March 2021, with E. coli confirmed by biochemical tests and the 16s rRNA gene
Data_Types_Used: Gene presence / AMR genotype
Data_Source_Name: NCBI (reference sequence database)
Specimen_Type_Detail: bacterial isolates (from patients with urinary tract infections)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Resistance-associated nucleotide/amino-acid sequence variation (missense mutations) in the resistance genes aadA1, dfrA1, sul1 and cat1, relative to reference NCBI sequences
Pathogens: Escherichia coli (E. coli)
Drug_Classes: Aminoglycosides (streptomycin), dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors (trimethoprim), sulfonamides, phenicols (chloramphenicol)
Specific_Antibiotics: streptomycin, trimethoprim, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Not applicable
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Presence/detection of resistance-encoding genes (aadA1, dfrA1, sul1, cat1) via PCR amplification, with resistance-associated missense mutations identified by comparing sequenced amplicons to reference NCBI sequences
AI_Purpose: To investigate E. coli antibiotic resistance and protein sequences via a sequencing-based method, described by the authors as 'deep-learning methods'
Other_Metrics: Counts of nucleotide substitutions and missense amino-acid changes per gene, relative to reference NCBI sequences (not a standard ML performance metric)
Maturity_Evidence: No model validation, external testing, or prospective/clinical evaluation is reported; the study is exploratory sequence and structural analysis only.

Title: Development of a Prediction Model for Antibiotic-Resistant Urinary Tract Infections Using Integrated Electronic Health Records from Multiple Clinics in North-Central Florida
AI_Application_Type: AI Predictive and Prognostic Models; AI Clinical Decision Support Systems
Funder_Names: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH NIAID 1-R01-AI141810); University of Florida 'Creating the Healthiest Generation' Moonshot initiative (UF Office of the Provost, UF Office of Research, UF Health, UF College of Medicine, UF Clinical and Translational Science Institute)
Population_Description: 9990 patients diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) who met the study criteria; majority female (76.4%), white (67.7%), non-Hispanic (96.1%), mean age 60.7 (SD=19.8) years.
Top_Predictive_Features: Based on the best-fit pruned decision trees, the most important feature for prediction of all-cause resistant (AMR) UTI was past antibiotic use, followed by hypertension, sex, and birth control in the low antibiotic-use branch, and age and nicotine use in the high antibiotic-use branch; importance ranked by split-rank / node purity.
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Three models (decision tree, boosted logistic regression [BLR], random forest) compared via AUROC across five outcomes: BLR yielded the highest AUROC = 0.57 (AMR-UTI), 0.58 (SXT), 0.62 (NIT), 0.64 (CIP), 0.66 (MDR), outperforming DT and RF for all five outcomes (Table 2).
Best_Performing_Model: Boosted logistic regression (BLR) — highest AUROC compared to DT and RF models for all five outcomes.
Sensitivity_Population_Set: Any AMR (all-cause resistant UTI), n = 6307
Specificity_Population_Set: Any AMR (all-cause resistant UTI), n = 6307
AUROC_Value: 0.57 (SD = 0.01) for AMR-UTI (all-cause resistant UTI), BLR model
AUROC_Population_Set: AMR-UTI (all-cause resistant UTI)
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: Models were validated via bootstrap (internal) and via training on the predominant zip-code population with testing on a geographically separate population (greater-Jacksonville); no prospective evaluation, CDS integration, or routine clinical use is reported.
Reported_Limitations: Study population was relatively older with more comorbidities than may be prevalent in the general population at risk for UTI.
Equity_Fairness_Concerns: Race and ethnicity variables are proxies for societal forces rather than biological/genetic mechanisms; direct socioeconomic factors were not incorporated and are suggested for future research.
Unresolved_Items: The study reports five parallel resistance outcomes (Any AMR, SXT, NIT, CIP, MDR) with no explicit statement of which is 'primary'. This record uses Any AMR (all-cause resistant UTI, n=6307, the first-listed/largest outcome) as the primary dataset for the performance *_Value fields (Sensitivity/Specificity/AUROC).
Sample_Size: 9990 patients who met the study criteria (primary dataset)
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declare they have no competing interests.
Inclusion_Criteria: Aged 18 years or older, diagnosed with a UTI (ICD-9: 595.*-'Cystitis' or 599.0-'Urinary tract infection, site not specified') at a UF Health inpatient or outpatient center between January 1, 2011 and July 1, 2019, resided in a zip code sharing the same first three digits as the health network, and had an antibiotic susceptibility test for their infection.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results; Prescription / dispensing data
Data_Source_Name: UF Health Integrated Data Repository (IDR)
Dataset_Size: 9990 patients
Missing_Data_Method: Missing outcome status (SXT 12.3%, NIT 5.9%, CIP 6.3% missing) was handled by subsetting three new datasets restricted to non-missing outcome status, giving final populations of 9072 (SXT), 9726 (NIT), 9688 (CIP), and 10,340 (MDR and 'any' resistance).
Ethnicity_Details: Non-Hispanic (96.1%)
Geographic_Representativeness: Clinics located primarily in Gainesville and Alachua County, Florida, with additional health centers in Jacksonville, Florida — North-Central Florida only.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Urine (culture)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Antibiotic resistance, defined cumulatively as any infection with ≥1 'resistant' susceptibility finding for all antibiotics tested and by major drug (SXT, CIP, or NIT); infections resistant to all three major drug types were categorized as MDR.
Pathogens: Citrobacter species, Enterobacter species, Enterococcus faecalis, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus (plus an 'other' category)
Drug_Classes: Sulfa-trimethoprim combination (SXT); fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin, CIP)
Specific_Antibiotics: Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (SXT), nitrofurantoin (NIT), ciprofloxacin (CIP)
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug; MDR
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Cumulative binary resistance defined as ≥1 'resistant' susceptibility finding for all antibiotics tested and by major drug (SXT, CIP, NIT); resistance to all three major drug types categorized as MDR.
AI_Purpose: To develop a culture-independent diagnostic model of resistance to antimicrobial agents commonly used in the treatment of UTIs and multidrug-resistant (MDR) UTIs.
Num_Models_Compared: 3 (boosted logistic regression, random forest, decision tree)
Feature_Engineering: Past antibiotic prescriptions were recoded as 'cognate' (same drug type as the resistant infection) versus 'non-cognate' (a different drug type).
Feature_Selection_Method: None — all variables were considered for model inclusion.
Software_Libraries: mboost, randomForest, rpart, party, caret, ROCR
Other_Metrics: Predictor importance measured by odds ratios with p-values (logistic model) and by split-rank with a stratified p-value of node purity (decision trees) — importance measures, not model-performance metrics.
Baseline_Method: Comparison against prior published prediction models: Kanjilal et al. (Northeast US population) and Yelin et al. (nationally representative Israeli data).
Baseline_Performance: Kanjilal et al.: AUROC = 0.56 (NIT), 0.59 (SXT), 0.64 (CIP). Yelin et al.: AUROC > 0.70 for all resistant outcomes.
Internal_Validation: Bootstrap validation (n = 25), out-of-bag estimates
Train_Test_Split: Trained on the predominant three-digit zip-code region ('326', 78.9% of the population); tested on the geographically separate greater-Jacksonville region ('322', 21.1% of the population).
External_Validation_Description: Trained on data from the predominant zip-code region ('326') where the main UF Health hospital is located, and tested on data from the greater-Jacksonville region ('322') where a secondary UF Health hospital is located.
Clinical_Insights: Previous (especially cognate) antibiotic exposure was consistently one of the strongest predictors of future antibiotic-resistant UTIs, except for NIT-resistant UTIs, where prior cognate antibiotic use was not a significant predictor.
Data_Repository: UF Health's Integrated Data Repository at the Clinical and Translational Science Institute (available by submitting a research data request)
Generalisability_Details: Single-institution EHR data limit generalizability to other populations; external validation attempted on a geographically separate population (Jacksonville/Duval County) with similar results; application to populations outside Florida or the US will require additional studies.
Maturity_Evidence: Bootstrap (internal) validation plus external validation by training on the predominant zip-code population and testing on a geographically separate population (Jacksonville), with similar performance; no prospective or deployed-use evidence presented.
Integration_Point: Point-of-care decision-making in ambulatory and hospital settings
End_User_Described: Clinicians and persons involved with antimicrobial stewardship programs
Clinical_Workflow_Details: May help guide clinical decision-making on the ordering of urine cultures and decisions regarding empiric therapy for patients.
Future_Directions: One suggestion for future studies is to build separate models by age bracket to achieve better discrimination.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Odds ratios with p-values for the logistic (BLR) model; split-rank with a stratified p-value of node purity for the decision trees (DT).
Limitation_Categories: Single-institution / generalizability limitation; race and ethnicity used as social (not biological) proxies with no direct socioeconomic factors incorporated; ICD-9 code misclassification and measurement error.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Relying on ICD codes for comorbidity and symptom collection may have led to exposure misclassification and measurement error, which are common in studies using EHR.
Reporting_Clarity: Adheres to TRIPOD reporting; model comparison and internal/external validation are explicit (Table 2), but accuracy, PPV, F1, calibration, and confidence intervals are not reported.
Page_References: Journal pp. 1869-1882 (PDF text-layer pp. 1-14): abstract p.1; introduction pp.2-3; methods pp.3-4; results pp.4-8 (Table 1 pp.5-6); Table 2 p.10; discussion pp.8-11; conclusion/acknowledgements/disclosures p.12; references pp.12-14.

Title: Informing antimicrobial stewardship with explainable AI
Funder_Names: Health Data Research UK; UK Medical Research Council; EPSRC; Economic and Social Research Council; Department of Health and Social Care (England); Chief Scientist Office of the Scottish Government; Health and Social Care Research and Development Division (Welsh Government); Public Health Agency (Northern Ireland); British Heart Foundation; Wellcome Trust; UK Research and Innovation (JUNIPER modelling consortium, MR/V038613/1)
Population_Description: All patients from whose blood or urine cultures bacterial pathogens Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa was isolated, from 5190 hospital admission events (4507 individual patients) at Heart of England NHS Trust, Birmingham, UK (Jan 2010-Oct 2016), including a specialist cystic fibrosis unit.
Data_Source: Electronic health record (EHR); Hospital / clinic registry
Top_Predictive_Features: Past detection of a resistant or susceptible isolate on a previous admission was the strongest predictor, positively associated with resistance/susceptibility to the same drug on the current admission (e.g. I = 0.58 for co-amoxiclav).
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification; Treatment / prescribing guidance
All_Models_Evaluated: Drug-specific GBDT (XGBoost) classifiers for AUG, CIP, MEM, and TAZ resistance, ROC-AUC 0.78 (95% CI 0.76-0.81), 0.87 (95% CI 0.85-0.89), 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-0.99), and 0.79 (95% CI 0.75-0.81) respectively.
Best_Performing_Model: GBDT model predicting meropenem (MEM) resistance - ROC-AUC 0.99, the highest of the four drug-specific models.
AUROC_Value: 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-0.99) for the meropenem (MEM) model - the best-performing model in this review's unit of analysis.
AUROC_Population_Set: Admissions with laboratory testing for meropenem (MEM) susceptibility (drug-specific ROC-AUC).
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: The GBDT models were developed and evaluated only on the same single-centre retrospective cohort (a held-out test set for ROC-AUC/MSE); no external dataset or prospective evaluation is reported, and the authors state that further validation studies are necessary.
Reported_Limitations: Data on past culture susceptibility are crucial and in their absence, prediction accuracy decreases significantly; in practice these data may not always be available for all patients.
Unintended_Consequences_Harms: Discusses the general risk that a wrong AI decision could injure a patient and that AI-related mistakes could increase public mistrust, potentially scaling a single algorithm error to injuries in many patients.
Conflicts_of_Interest: The authors declared that no competing interests exist.
Inclusion_Criteria: Patients whose blood or urine cultures grew E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; Prescription / dispensing data; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 5190 admission events; 4507 patients; 125 features
Missing_Data_Method: Missing data were retained and fed directly into the GBDT (XGBoost), which natively/robustly handles missing values, rather than being imputed.
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood and urine cultures
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Binary resistant (R) vs susceptible (S) outcome of bacterial isolates to four antimicrobial agents (co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin, meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam), predicted by drug-specific GBDT models.
Pathogens: Escherichia coli; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug_Classes: Penicillin/β-lactamase inhibitor (co-amoxiclav, piperacillin/tazobactam); Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin); Carbapenem (meropenem, ertapenem); Aminoglycoside (amikacin, gentamicin); Monobactam (aztreonam); Cephalosporin (ceftazidime, cefotaxime); β-lactamase-resistant penicillin (temocillin).
Specific_Antibiotics: Co-amoxiclav (AUG), ciprofloxacin (CIP), meropenem (MEM), piperacillin/tazobactam (TAZ), amikacin (AK), aztreonam (ATM), ceftazidime (CAZ), cefotaxime (CTX), ertapenem (ETP), gentamicin (GT), temocillin (TEM).
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: Binary R/S for a single drug
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant (R) vs susceptible (S) outcome per isolate/admission event for each of four antimicrobial agents, as recorded from culture/AST test results (no MIC threshold or probability-score definition given in the text).
AI_Purpose: To predict, using an explainable AI (GBDT + SHAP) system, the probability that a bacterial isolate is resistant to specific antimicrobial agents at hospital admission, in order to inform antibiotic prescribing and improve antimicrobial stewardship.
Feature_Engineering: All categorical variables were stratified (converted) to binary variables for use in the machine learning algorithm; 125 features were included as independent variables.
Hyperparameter_Method: Bayesian optimisation
Other_Metrics: Mean squared error (MSE) and Gini impurity (as an uncertainty measure) were also used alongside ROC-AUC.
Baseline_Method: Physicians' actual (recorded) prescribing decisions - i.e. prescription-to-culture mismatch rates under true clinical practice - used as the comparator to the GBDT-assisted prescribing strategy.
Baseline_Performance: True-prescription mismatch rates: AUG 34% (32-36%), CIP 20% (16-26%), MEM 26% (22-30%), TAZ 23% (21-26%).
Internal_Validation: Held-out test set (used for ROC-AUC/MSE stratified by prediction impurity); train/test split proportions not reported.
Clinical_Insights: Prescribing AUG at any point during the admission was associated with reduced (not increased) predicted resistance to AUG itself - the only drug for which current use lowered predicted resistance to the same drug - attributed to AUG typically being prescribed only after AUG resistance had been ruled out.
Generalisability_Details: Predictions relying on past culture-susceptibility data cannot be easily extended to different cohorts or applied when such data are missing; validation studies are necessary.
Maturity_Evidence: Model evaluation relied on internal (held-out test set) ROC-AUC/MSE only; no external validation or prospective clinical evaluation performed; authors state further validation studies are necessary.
Integration_Point: At the point of hospital admission, before antibiotic-susceptibility laboratory results are available.
End_User_Described: Doctors / physicians making initial antibiotic prescribing decisions.
Clinical_Workflow_Details: At admission, before laboratory susceptibility results are available, the GBDT-predicted resistance probability would be used to order patients and withhold/switch therapy for those with the highest predicted probability of resistance.
Stewardship_Details: Using GBDT-predicted resistance probability to guide prescribing (withholding/switching therapy for high-probability-of-resistance cases) reduced mismatched-treatment percentages and total antimicrobial exposure compared with actual prescribing, for all four drugs studied.
Barriers_List: Lack of trust in AI recommendations; concerns over liability and risk of misdiagnosis; the 'black-box' opacity of AI models; difficulty inspecting/making sense of AI outputs for clinical use.
Facilitators_List: Explainable/interpretable AI (Shapley values) providing intuitive, clinically consistent explanations and uncertainty estimates, which can build clinician trust and support evaluation of AI recommendations.
Future_Directions: Future work includes modelling situations where culture information or other variables are missing, and further validation studies before broader application.
Top_Features_Importance_Method: Global gain and the Shapley absolute-sum (S) metric; the slope index (I) used as an association measure.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Prescribing AUG at any point during the admission was associated with reduced (not increased) predicted resistance to AUG itself - the only drug for which current use lowered predicted resistance to the same drug.
Feature_Interactions_Method: Visual/qualitative stratification of Shapley-value plots by cystic fibrosis (CF) status (e.g. age and length-of-stay effects examined separately for CF vs non-CF patients).
Limitation_Categories: Data availability/completeness (past culture-susceptibility data not always available); generalisability to other cohorts; need for further validation studies.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Past culture-susceptibility data, which the model relies on heavily, may not always be readily available for all patients in clinical practice.
Page_References: Methods pp. 3-6; Results pp. 7-15; Discussion pp. 15-17.

Title: A Novel Nomogram for Predicting Risk Factors and Outcomes in Bloodstream Infections Caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae
Funder_Names: Youth Program of National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 81803589)
Population_Description: Adult and older patients (>16 and <90 years) with Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection (BSI-KP, including CRKP and CSKP) at a single tertiary hospital in Eastern China, Jan 2015-May 2020; only the first BSI episode per patient counted.
Age_Range: Older than 16 years and less than 90 years (inclusion criterion)
Provider_Facing_Applications: Screening / risk stratification
All_Models_Evaluated: BSI-CRKP probability nomogram (LASSO-selected variables + multivariate logistic regression): C-index 0.816, 95% CI 0.763-0.868. 30-day mortality nomogram for BSI-KP: C-index 0.813, 95% CI 0.780-0.867.
Clinical_Maturity_Justification: An external validation subset of 81 patients was evaluated separately from the development cohort, with C-index 0.700 (95% CI 0.550-0.832); no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment of the nomogram was reported.
Reported_Limitations: Retrospective study design; small number of patients; did not identify different virulence factors between CRKP and CSKP isolates.
Conflicts_of_Interest: No conflicts of interest declared.
Inclusion_Criteria: (i) age older than 16 years and less than 90 years; (ii) blood culture positive for K. pneumoniae meeting diagnostic criteria for BSI; only the first BSI episode counted for patients with repeated episodes.
Exclusion_Criteria: Patients treated for less than 48 hours after infection were excluded (from the 30-day mortality nomogram analysis).
Data_Types_Used: Clinical / EHR variables; Demographic variables; AST phenotypic results
Dataset_Size: 237 patients (160 survivors, 77 non-survivors) in the 30-day mortality nomogram cohort
Specimen_Type_Detail: Blood (blood culture positive for K. pneumoniae; bloodstream infection)
Primary_AMR_Outcome: Carbapenem resistance in K. pneumoniae bloodstream infection (BSI-CRKP vs BSI-CSKP), defined by resistance to imipenem, meropenem or ertapenem per CLSI criteria; secondary outcome is 30-day all-cause mortality in BSI-KP patients.
Pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Drug_Classes: Polymyxins, carbapenems, beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin), tetracyclines (tigecycline), oxazolidinones (linezolid)
Specific_Antibiotics: Polymyxin, carbapenem antibiotics, beta-lactamase inhibitors, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, tigecycline (including high-dose regimen), teicoplanin, linezolid
Resistance_Phenotype_Reported: CRE / carbapenemase-producing
AMR_Outcome_Definition: Binary resistant/susceptible: isolates resistant to imipenem, meropenem or ertapenem (CLSI interpretive criteria) classified as CRKP; others as CSKP.
AI_Purpose: To predict BSI-CRKP risk and prognosis (30-day mortality) in BSI-KP patients via nomograms, to guide infection control and clinical treatment decisions.
Num_Models_Compared: 1 (single multivariate logistic regression model per outcome, built on LASSO-selected variables; no alternative algorithms compared)
Feature_Selection_Method: LASSO regression (candidate predictor screening) followed by univariate and multivariate logistic regression
Num_Features_Selected: 7 factors (BSI-CRKP nomogram, selected via LASSO)
Software_Libraries: R package (unspecified, for nomogram construction); SPSS Version 22.0
Other_Metrics: C-index (concordance index): 0.816 (95% CI 0.763-0.868) for the BSI-CRKP probability nomogram; 0.813 (95% CI 0.780-0.867) for the 30-day mortality nomogram.
Internal_Validation: Bootstrap resampling (1000 times) for calibration curve validation
External_Validation_Description: 81 patients used for external validation of the 30-day mortality nomogram; C-index 0.700 (95% CI 0.550-0.832); calibration plot indicated the external validation model was well-calibrated.
Clinical_Insights: Decreased cholinesterase identified as a novel, rarely-reported risk factor for BSI-CRKP.
Maturity_Evidence: Internal development cohort (n=252 for the CRKP model; n=237/113 for the mortality model) plus an external validation subset of 81 patients, C-index 0.700 (95% CI 0.550-0.832); no prospective evaluation or clinical deployment reported.
End_User_Described: Clinicians treating BSI-KP patients
Future_Directions: Further research needed to study optimized tigecycline dosing/use for BSI-KP.
Novel_Predictors_Details: Decreased cholinesterase identified as a novel, rarely-reported risk factor for BSI-CRKP.
Limitation_Categories: Retrospective study design; small number of patients; did not identify different virulence factors between CRKP and CSKP isolates.
Data_Quality_Concerns: Retrospective EHR-derived data source; relatively small patient sample; virulence factors not differentiated between CRKP and CSKP isolates.
